articles.text: Oakland Zoo has announced the fourth bison calf of the season, marking the 50th calf born at the Zoo since the start of its restoration partnership with the Blackfeet Nation and Indigenous LED, which began a decade ago in 2016. The adorable additions to the herd, affectionately called “red dogs” for their playful nature and bright reddish-brown coats at birth, underscore the true meaning of the Zoo’s bison restoration program. The goal is for descendants of the blended herd to prosper in the Blackfeet Territory and to be free-ranging and connected to Glacier National Park. Early in May of this year, the Zoo transported five bison – three males and two females – to Montana by trailer. After a 22-hour journey that mirrored where bison once roamed, they joined the Blackfeet herd in Browning, Montana. This multifaceted effort to promote genetic diversity aims to ensure the health and longevity of future American bison populations. The species nearly went extinct in the early 1900s, when millions were slaughtered during westward expansion to make way for grasslands used for livestock. Fifty bison calves have been born at the Oakland Zoo since 2016 when the partnership with the Blackfeet Nation in Montana began.
articles.title: 50th bison calf born at Oakland Zoo

articles.text: Fourth of July parade participants Frank and Paula Silver, owners of FMS Projects, plan to drive their 1962 Ford Falcon station wagon in the parade. The pair has participated in the parade since the late 90s before they moved to Piedmont. They used to drive their 39 Chevy in the parade before transitioning to the Falcon in the late 2000s. Frank bought the Ford Falcon as his first car in California in 1981. “I was a carpenter at the time, and I needed a vehicle to carry stuff, and so a station wagon made sense,” he said. “I saw it for sale, and it was more than I could afford. It was 19 or 20 years old, but I like old vehicles. I decided I think I’ll buy this older classic car and it’s been with us ever since.” The Falcon has remained a staple in their family and even helped the couple get together. Frank picked up Paula in the Falcon on their first date. The car was built with a manual transmission, a “three on the tree” column shift configuration, which was very popular in the late 50s, but the 60s saw a transition to automatic transmissions, which makes this Falcon one of the last manuals of its kind. The car has had minimal iterations and currently has 77,000 miles on it. “It’s got the original engine. It did get repainted not too long ago, because it needed it, and I’ve done some other maintenance over time, but for all intents and purposes it’s original,” said Frank. The Silvers have participated Frank Silver and daughter, Sydney Silver, are expected to ride in their 1962 Ford Falcon station wagon in the July 4th parade.
articles.title: 1962 Ford Falcon to be in 4th of July Parade

articles.text: Nobody knows a neighborhood like the people who live there. As a resident of the Piedmont Civic Center neighborhood for more than 41 years, I have watched many proposals come and go. Along with numerous neighbors and residents, I have spent decades advocating for the preservation of the small-town character, walkability, and safety of central Piedmont. While we have not always agreed on every issue, I believe our collective efforts have helped maintain what makes this area special. Unfortunately, I believe the Bonita Avenue parking reconfiguration is a mistake. What troubles me most is not the addition of parking spaces themselves, but the apparent lack of consideration given to the broader public safety implications. The 300 block of Bonita is not an isolated residential street. It serves as a critical corridor for Havens Elementary School, Piedmont schools including Piedmont Middle and High Schools, City Hall, the Fire Department, the Community Pool, recreation facilities, and surrounding neighborhoods. It is also an important access and evacuation route during emergencies. The City’s focus has been on creating 17 additional parking spaces. Yet many residents who live and travel this corridor daily continue to ask a simple question: At what cost? For decades, I have witnessed school drop-offs and pick-ups, community events, construction activity, emergency vehicle traffic, and the daily challenges of moving safely through this area. Experience has taught me that what appears workable on an engineering drawing does not always perform well under realworld conditions. 3756 Grand Ave., #203, Oakland, CA 94610 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Seniors
articles.title: Bonita Ave. parking reconfiguration needs a second look

articles.text: Earlier this year, Piedmont Scouting chose its new scout executive after Kate Benson left to pursue a national position with Cub Scouting. The council selected Tess English, who has more than a decade of experience working in Scouting. She’s transitioning from her role as the assistant scout executive in the Gulf Stream Council in West Palm Beach, Florida. English recently sat down with the Post to discuss her goals for Piedmont Scouting as she enters her new role. Before English applied for the scout executive role in Piedmont, she reached out to Kate Benson to discuss Piedmont and the current state of its Scouting. “I asked her about the position, about the place, about everything. We were friends before this. “She told me, ‘This is a great council. This is a great area to be in for scouting. You have lots of opportunities to make an impact. Piedmont has that small-town feel, and if that’s what you like, this is it.’ “So, I decided to throw my hat in the ring,” said English. English believes Piedmont’s Scouting is in a great spot and has Piedmont Council Scout executive Tess English the opportunity to grow exponentially over the next few years. “The current state of scouting in Piedmont is great,” said English. “We have an amazing foundation. We have some great volunteers, great youth, and great programming. We have the foundation we need to grow at this time.” She believes Scouting is one of the most relevant and impactful programs out there for young people to grow. Her goal is to change the narrative around Scouting from a relic, arguing that the program is more relevant than ever for fostering peer-to-peer connections, developing confidence in the outdoors, and strengthening youth-adult relationships. “There’s a perception that scouting is something from the past. It’s kind of like a relic, but I think what a lot of families are discovering these days is that scouting is more relevant now than ever,” English continued. “It’s an opportunity for their youth to make really strong connections with other youth. articles.text: Sol has become an incredible friend. After more than a year of painful medical challenges, this 4-year-old is now well enough to thoroughly enjoy being a cat! Sol is FIV-positive and receives a daily medication that has brought remarkable relief from his chronic stomatitis. The medication is easy to administer, and adopters should be prepared for ongoing veterinary follow-up as his recovery continues. This gentle boy has taken to copying other cats’ behavior studiously and has been great about respecting their boundaries during play, so we’d like him to have a home with at least one playful cat companion. His foster jokes that he and their own cats sound like a thundering herd of ponies when they run around! Although Sol can be cautious with new people and startles at loud noises, his friendly nature usually wins out. This Adopt Sol through Cat Town. sweet boy loves attention, enjoys sleeping between the pillows in his foster’s bed to stay close, and quickly charms everyone he meets. His trademark tongue often peeks out adorably from his toothless mouth. We think he’s a total catch for some lucky adopter — maybe you? Sol is neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and FIV-positive. articles.text: Sophia Ware, PHS Class of ’22 and recent UC Berkeley graduate, has spent her academic career chasing one question: how can she have the greatest impact on sustainability given the current global context? The methods she has used to pursue that goal have adapted with the changing times. Now she wields an unexpected tool, artificial intelligence, as a founding growth lead at a San Francisco software startup called Merivia. Her mission took shape early, growing up alarmed by the climate crisis. She started with protest, lying in the streets of San Francisco’s financial district painted in fake blood. “We called it street theater,” Ware said. “It was performative, by design and to a fault ... for the empty seats of politicians and CEOs.” Wanting more impact, she pivoted to lobbying for social and environmental policy at the municipal, state, and federal level. “I pulled up a seat at the table,” she said. But she kept colliding with bureaucratic constraints and political chokeholds. The government at this moment, she concluded, was too slow and politically burdened to move at the pace the crisis demanded. “The private sector had become the new sustainability frontier,” Ware said. Ware adapted again, fundraising for solar panels for the Piedmont High School STEAM building through an organization she built with her peers, Students for Solar. Ware’s takeaway was simple, she said. “Capital, pointed in the right direction, made a more immediate impact than protest or policy.” The question for Ware was how to do that systematically. That sent her to UC Berkeley to study environmental economics, where she discovered sustainable finance, a field that works to correct capitalism’s market failures by redirecting capital toward outcomes that account for externalities. Impact funds, philanthropies, and venture capital are among the vehicles driving this effort to value not just financial return, but social and environmental impact, Ware said. The catch is that the burden of proof falls on these actors now be accessed by every stakeholder, while staying secure and fully owned by the fund.” “We want to empower people in these funds to move away from being data search engines to get back to the heart of the work,” Ware said. “More efficiency, more impact.” She isn’t doing it alone, building Merivia alongside co-founders Conor Stayton and Ludo Federici and founding software engineer Eric Edwards. Today, Merivia works with impact investment funds and philanthropies, including the Miller Center for Social Entrepreneurship and the World Wildlife Fund, and has begun partnering on research through the Externality Investment Research Network (EIRN), equipping academics with context graphs to enable more traceable and scalable research. Ware doesn’t pretend the technology is free. Data centers draw power and water, often from communities that are already the most disadvantaged. “The question isn’t whether one should or shouldn’t work with AI because of its environmental cost,” she said. “AI is an inevitable tool. That question has been answered. Now we need more people to engage with AI and understand how we move forward to mitigate those externalities. The real question we should be asking is who ends up holding the tool.” AI isn’t going away, Ware said, and it is already making the extractive economy more efficient. If the impact economy is given the resources to adapt alongside the latest technology, it can leverage that same power to reshape our systems toward something more sustainable. “You don’t change a problem by refusing to touch it,” she said. “You change it by pulling a seat up at the table, with better tools than before.” If you’re drawn to this space, Ware said, she’d love to hear from you: investors, DAF holders, nonprofit leaders, anyone thinking about where capital and impact meet. Whether it’s trading thoughts on the future of this field or finding ways Merivia can support your work, reach out at sophiaqware@ gmail.com. More on Merivia at https://www.merivia.ai. Sophia Ware is a founding growth engineer at Merivia. themselves. To secure their funding, they must demonstrate their return on impact to investors. This, Ware said, is one bottleneck starving the impact economy. The proof depends on data scattered across countless sources and languages, locked in different people’s heads, and subject to complex regulatory scrutiny, all while the people doing the work are chronically under-resourced. The solution is twofold, Ware said. “We need to reinvent both the infrastructure we build to store our data and the tools we use to access it. That is where Merivia comes in.” Built under the Foundation Capital accelerator, Merivia develops data infrastructure for funds and foundations that moves away from tabular storage, like spreadsheets, and toward relationship-based knowledge bases. Its core technology is what Ware calls a context graph. “Think of it like a brain,” she said. “As a fund, you first input all of your data into the brain: PDFs, voice notes, transcripts, pitch decks, board updates, customer interviews, field photos, even web pages. Thousands of documents. Then you tell the brain how you think about that data: how certain LPs track their financial returns, the custom metrics certain portfolio companies use, whatever preferences or nuances there may be, any context that usually lives in the heads of your stakeholders. We graph all of it into the brain, which is then queryable by AI agents. So data that was once siloed, fragmented, outdated, or tedious to process at scale can Founding members of the AI start-up company Merivia: Eric Edwards (left), Ludo Federici, Conor Stayton, and Sophia Ware.

articles.text: If you’ve always wanted a Rottweiler, but were intimidated by the size, 35-pound Naia may be the pup for you. Naia is a 1-year-old Shepherd/Rottweiler mix with a loving personality and plenty of affection to share. This friendly young dog enjoys spending time with people and is happiest when she’s getting pets, scratches, and attention. Naia knows “sit” and enjoys treats, making training a fun way to bond and build new skills together. She is dog friendly and has participated in playgroups while living in the shelter. She was initially polite and hung back to get a sense of playgroup before relaxing and joining in the fun. In her foster home, Naia has been friendly with neighboring dogs. With her moderate energy level, Naia enjoys exploring the world and would love a home that can provide walks and ongoing training. Naia’s sweet Naia is a 1-year-old Shepherd/ Rottweiler mix nature and people-focused personality make her a wonderful candidate for a variety of homes looking for a loyal and affectionate companion. To meet Naia, submit your adoption questionnaire online at Oakland Animal Services, website and you will be contacted by her foster to arrange a meet-and-greet. For more information on fostering or adoption through Oakland Animal Services, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@gmail.com.

articles.text: During the final school board meeting of the school year on June 17, the board approved a new contract for teachers, CSEA school employees and administrators. The 3-4% raises for teachers next year, plus a $2,000 stipend, will cost the district an average of $8,072 per teacher. In the second year of the agreement, teacher salaries will increase by 3%, an average of $4,413 and another 3% in year three, costing the district an average of $4,238 per teacher. “This is a long-term goal of mine and Lindsay’s, which is to be able to have a positive impact on the lower end of the salary schedule,” said Board President Ruchi Medhekar “I’m truly delighted to have this agreement in front of us for approval.” The agreement was reached by giving teachers extra salary compensation of $700-900, following their 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th years of experience. Previously, many new teachers, without master’s degrees or other qualifications, would not see a raise until their 6th year teaching. Board Member Max Roman made the motion for approval of the teacher contracts, adding he was doing so “joyfully and celebratorily.” Teachers will now receive four weeks of fully paid parental leave for the birth or adoption of a child or the start of foster care. APT President Elise Marks called the parental leave “the piece I’m personally happiest about.” There was no paid parental leave prior to this agreement. Bereavement leave for teachers was also increased from “up to three days” to “up to five days” of paid absence on the account of the death of any member of their immediate family. The district’s contribution to health care coverage will increase by 25% over the next two years. The contract puts caps on rising healthcare costs, with coverage starting in 2028 capped at $11,413 for employee only, $22,825 for two-party coverage and $32,297 for family coverage. Teachers with advanced Master’s or Doctorate degrees will now receive stipends of $1500 instead of $1000. Although not guaranteed, the contract also says the district will “make every effort” to maintain an average class size of 26 students for 4th and 5th grade teachers. At secondary sites, the district will “make every effort” to have full-time teachers limited to 140 students registered amongst all their classes. This 140 student limit will not apply to P.E., Academy, Affinity Mentors or music. Site administrators will now meet with staff “to identify problems that may result from classes of 28 or more.” This class size number has moved down from 30 students. The contract with the teachers allots more preparation time, 20 minutes, for full-time Special teachers at the elementary level. Resource Specialist Program (RSP) teachers also gain the guarantee of being assigned only one initial assessment due within a four week period, unless they are less than 60% of the state caseload maximum. Similarly Speech Language Pathologists (SLPS) will have no more than four assessments due during any four week period. Transitional Kindergarten and Kindergarten teachers will also be paid for four hours to set up their classrooms for family classroom visits. This paid setup time occurs if teachers set up their classrooms prior to the first teacher workday. Paying for all of this will not require an additional source of revenue for the district. “The salary increases will be paid from on-going resources available to the District, not one specific source,” confirmed Chief Business Officer Ruth Alahydoian. articles.text: When people think about concussion, they often picture headaches, dizziness, or sensitivity to light. While these symptoms are common, many people are surprised to learn that concussion can also affect thinking and communication. These changes, known as cognitive-communication difficulties, can have a significant impact on everyday life, school, work, and relationships. A concussion is a mild traumatic brain injury that temporarily disrupts normal brain function. Most people recover well, but during the recovery period they may experience difficulties with attention, memory, processing speed, and executive functioning. These cognitive changes can, in turn, affect communication. For example, a person with a concussion may find it harder to concentrate during conversations, particularly in noisy environments. They may lose track of what someone is saying, miss important details, or struggle to follow lengthy discussions. Others describe feeling mentally “slower” and needing more time to process information and formulate responses. Memory difficulties are also common. Someone may forget appointments, instructions, or details from recent conversations. They may repeatedly ask the same questions or have trouble recalling names and words. This can be frustrating and may lead others to mistakenly assume they are not paying attention. Executive functioning skills— which include planning, organizing, problem-solving, and self-monitoring—can also be affected. A person may find it challenging to organize their thoughts when speaking, stay on topic, or manage complex tasks that require communication. At work or school, activities such as participating in meetings, taking notes, writing reports, or following multi-step directions may become more difficult. These challenges are often invisible. Because a person with concussion may look physically well, family members, friends, teachers, or employers may not recognize the cognitive effort required for everyday communication. This lack of understanding can sometimes lead to frustration on both sides. Speech pathologists play an important role in supporting individuals with concussion-related cognitive-communication difficulties. Assessment helps identify the specific areas affected and the impact on daily activities. Therapy may focus on strategies to improve attention and memory, techniques to manage fatigue, and practical approaches to communication in real-world settings. Simple supports can make a meaningful difference. Reducing background noise, allowing extra time to process information, breaking instructions into smaller steps, using written reminders, and taking regular rest breaks can help reduce cognitive overload. Returning to work, school, or sport should be guided by healthcare professionals and paced according to symptoms. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com.

The district will move ahead with the reinstallation but is going to wait on lockers at the Middle School and will consider smaller lockers there. Piedmont High School (PHS) Principal David Yoshihara pointed out that there are currently only one or two options online to purchase a dumb phone with the restrictive “only talk and text” features, one of which is the A6. Yoshihara anticipated the scarcity of compliant models to make identification easy by staff. PHS Math teacher Auban Willats zoomed into the board meeting on June 3, to add to the discussion on student cell phones. Board member Susy Struble expressed her distaste for a policy that allows dumb phones. “I’m very confused by the addition of permitting dumb phones. Philosophically, it just doesn’t really make sense to me. I recognize that there’s a different level of engagement perhaps with dumb phones, but it’s just this big question mark to me,” said Struble. PHS Math teacher Auban Willats called into the meeting from her classroom and expressed concern about the changes. She said she was a fan of last year’s policy with the phone hotels. Board President Ruchi Medhekar acknowledged the policy affects different constituents in different ways. She reminded everyone that the policy still gives teachers the discretion to allow students to use smartphones at times. “From a teacher’s perspective, the most important thing is engagement within a class. And Max put it really well, from our perspective we’re worried about the whole experience,” said Medhekar. Board member Max Roman was okay with the dumb phone concession for this year’s policy, and acknowledged the policy was a work in progress. “I do think that we need to try to change so that the kids aren’t constantly touching their phones, and looking at them, and moving The Easyphone Prime-A6 phone has no internet or camera, it is currently $60 and one of two “dumb phone” options for PHS students. them, and putting them in their pockets and out all day long,” said Roman. School Board VP Michael Malione injected some clarity to the discussion. “It doesn’t matter what kind of phone it is. During class, there is no device unless a teacher has approved it. So, teachers aren’t going to be looking at that phone and saying, ‘is that a dumb phone?’ If it’s out in class, it’s confiscated,” Malione said. The policy, with recent augmentations and deletions, can be viewed at Simbli.eboardsolutions. com/Meetings/Attachment.aspx- ?S=36030373&AID=1555417& MID=71054 Board member Lindsay Thomasson summed up the complexities of the new policy. “There’s a lot of nuance in the details, which we’ve heard, and I think it’s going to have to be an ongoing conversation with the policy language as written,” she said. Throughout the summer the Post prints a sampling of letters written by kids attending Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s residential camp at Lake Vera outside Nevada City in the Sierra foothills. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. “On a lake called Vera, there’s a place we know...” and it is officially back for another magical summer journey. The anticipation on Sunday morning was palpable. Old and new counselors crowded along the dusty gravel parking lot with signs in hand and excitement in their hearts. For three and a half intense weeks of staff training they had practiced, planned, and dreamed of this very moment. Then — the rumble of an engine echoes through the trees. As the bus slowly rolls into sight, the staff erupt into a vibrant symphony of song and cheer. Campers peered See Postcards from Camp on page 9 A happy camper at the throwing range. articles.text: During the May 20 school board meeting Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich led a review of the first year of the new elementary school English Language Arts (ELA) curriculum. Students at Beach, Havens and Wildwood were taught by the knowledge-based Fishtank Learning ELA curriculum, paired with “From Phonics to Reading” for K-3 or Spellography for 4th and 5th grade. “While the first year of implementation has presented some challenges and highlighted areas for growth, the curriculum shows strong potential to support students in meeting these expectations and developing as strong readers, writers, and critical thinkers,” said Havens 3rd grade teacher Michelle Kerwin. Kerwin, one of seven instructional leads for the new curriculum, addressed the board and went over the survey results from teachers. Out of 39 responses, elementary teachers ranked the “Rigor” of Fishtank Learning on the higher end, 20 rated it a 4/5 and 19 a 5/5. One teacher noted “my students are capable of writing information, opinion and narrative pieces all in one trimester, rather than splitting them up as we did in the past.” “So change can be challenging, naturally, not everyone feels comfortable with change, particularly during the early stages of implementation. So the introducPUSD adopted Fishtank Learning this year for its English Language Arts curriculum in elementary schools. tion of new curriculum is rarely a seamless transition, teachers are actively learning the curriculum alongside their students,” said Kerwin. The district has identified this year as “training and implementation.” Next year, year two, will be the “adjustment and calibration” year, and year three will be “sustainability and innovation.” This year, elementary school teachers identified three writing assessments to use throughout next year. Dolowich addressed future changes for elementary-level English Language Arts instruction. “The teachers explicitly want more concrete writing tools,” said Dolowich. “Teachers, by and large, wanted a supplement that includes concrete tools for them to access and support them in teaching writing. So we have heard them loud and clear.” “I’m thrilled with the literacy work that we have done over the last few years, and it sounds like writing is going to happen next. I really appreciate that teachers have identified that as a need,” said board member Lindsay Thomasson. articles.text: As the 2026 FIFA World Cup gets through its second of three Group Stage matches, the world’s best superstars are showing that they have come to play. The Golden Boot race is on, with Argentina’s Leo Messi putting on an absolute dazzling display and showing no signs of regression at age 39. Messi is officially the World Cup’s All-Time leading scorer with 18 goals after scoring five through two games thus far. France’s Kylian Mbappé at age 27, 12 years younger than Messi, is hot on his heels with four and 16 World Cup goals overall. Norway’s Erling Haaland also has four in his first tournament appearance. Here’s how things are going, starting with the U.S.’ Group D. Group D: United States (6 points, +5 GD), Australia (3 points, 0 GD), Paraguay (0 points, -2 GD), Turkiye (0 points, -3 GD) Who would have thought that the United States would be one of the best performing teams through the first two Group Stage matches? They stood on top after their dominant 4-1 win over Paraguay and a 2-nil win over Australia. Pending how things go in the final Group Stage match, Bosnia is the favorite to play the US in the Round of 32, and they could face the winner of Egypt and Czechia in the Round of 16. The States will be the favorite in both matches, giving them a chance to reach the Quarterfinals for the first time since 2002. The US has the option to rest players against Turkey on Thursday, June 25. Group A: Mexico (6 points, +3 GD), South Korea (3 points, 0 GD), Czechia (1 point, -1 GD), South Africa (1 point, -2 GD) Mexico has yet to concede a goal with its 1-nil win over South Korea and 2-nil win over South Africa, clinching Group A in the process. South Korea can attain second place with a win or draw against South Africa today, June 24. A win or draw for Czechia against Mexico will help them get a good third-place seeding. Group B: Canada (4 points, +6 GD), Switzerland (4 points, +3 GD), Bosnia & Herzegovina (1 point, -3 GD), Qatar (1 point, -6 GD) Canada and Switzerland play today in what will decide the group winner, while a draw will result in the Canadians winning the tiebreaker based on goal differential. Bosnia needs to avoid disaster against Qatar to get a third-place spot. Qatar’s only path to the knockout stage requires beating Bosnia. Group C: Brazil (4 points, +3 GD), Morocco (4 points, +1 GD), Scotland (3 points, 0 GD), Haiti (0 points, -4 GD) Brazil leads Morocco on goal differential after beating Haiti 3-nil, while Morocco edged by Scotland 1-nil. Brazil can win the group by beating Scotland today regardless of Morocco’s result against Haiti. Scotland can still finish first with a win over Brazil and Morocco dropping points. Group E: Germany (6 points, +7 GD), Ivory Coast (3 points, 0 GD), Ecuador (1 point, -1 GD), Curaçao (1 point, -6 GD) Germany has essentially clinched first place, but Ivory Coast remains in excellent position behind them. Ivory Coast can place second with a win or draw against Curaçao on Thursday. Ecuador can still finish second by beating Germany and having a better goal differential than Ivory Coast. Curaçao can get to the knockout stage with a win over Ivory Coast and Ecuador dropping points. Group F: Netherlands (4 points, +4 GD), Japan (4 points, +4 GD), Sweden (3 points, 0 GD), Tunisia (0 points, -8 GD) The Netherlands dominated Sweden 5-1, but the group remains wide open. A win over Tunisia can clinch first for the Dutch on Thursday, but Japan can still get first with a win and out-doing the Netherlands goal differential against Sweden. Sweden can still finish first with a win and a Netherlands loss. Group G: Egypt (4 points, +2 GD), Iran (2 points, 0 GD), Belgium (2 points, 0 GD), New Zealand (1 point, -2 GD) Egypt moved into first with its 3-1 win over New Zealand, while Belgium had been among the most disappointing teams in the tournament after tying Iran 0-0. The group is still wide open. Egypt can clinch first with a win over Iran on Friday, but Iran can win the group with a victory and Belgium can still finish first by defeating New Zealand. All four teams remain alive entering the final round. Group H: Spain (4 point, +4 GD), Uruguay (2 points, 0 GD), Cape Verde (2 points, 0 GD), Saudi Arabia (1 point, -4 GD) Spain rebounded from its surprising 0-0 tie with Cape Verde with a 4-0 victory over Saudi Arabia, but Uruguay and Cape Verde remain close behind. Spain clinches first with a win or draw against Uruguay on Friday. Uruguay can win the group with a victory over Spain. Cape Verde can still finish first if it beats Saudi Arabia and Spain drops points. Saudi Arabia must win for any chance to advance. Group I: France (6 points, +5 GD), Norway (6 points, +4 GD), Senegal (0 points, -3 GD), Iraq (0 points, -6 GD) Although it’s looking like Messi will leave the tournament as the World Cup’s all-time leading scorer, he will only be a place holder until Mbappé passes him.

articles.text: Nine Piedmont rowers raced for Oakland Strokes at the 2026 USRowing Youth National Championships at Nathan Benderson Park in Sarasota, Florida from June 11 to 14, where the club won its 26th national championship. The national title came in the Men’s U17 8+, coached by Sean Gibel, which won Sunday’s grand final with a crew that was twothirds first-year rowers. Two PHS rowers win silver medal Two Piedmont High School rowers led Oakland Strokes to silver in the Men’s Youth 4 – senior Senan Brodie at bow and junior Connor Cross in the three seat. Brodie is headed to the University of Pennsylvania in the fall to row on their lightweight crew. The boat was coached by Jovan Jovanovic. Piedmont High School sophomore Diego Branneria also rowed bow in the men’s pair that won the B final to finish 9th overall. Piedmont women Five Piedmont High School rowers anchored Oakland Strokes women’s crews. Junior Sophia Brenner and senior Geneva Johnson, who rowed stroke, were in Photos by Joel Flory Piedmont High’s Connor Cross (second from left) and Senan Brodie (second from right) took silver at the 2026 USRowing Youth National Championships with Oakland Strokes. the top eight (1V), which finished 17th overall after a 0.4-second margin in the time trial sent the boat to the C final, where it won convincingly. The boat was coached by Allison Ray. Johnson has committed to row at Boston University in the fall. Senior Claire von Metzsch of the College Preparatory School in the five seat is headed to Yale. Sophomores Paige Young (bow) and Amelia Callaway (stroke) were in the third-eight crew that finished 11th overall as the fastest third-varsity eight in the country, coached by Emma Bernou. Senior Laurel Minor rowed in the club’s second eight, which finished 15th, coached by Isaac Bier. Minor will attend the University of Virginia in the fall. “This weekend showed exactly where this program is headed,” said Allison Ray, the Oakland Strokes Director of Rowing. “We won a national title with a boat that’s two-thirds first-year rowers, and took silver in the four with three juniors returning. The future here is bright. The women’s crews showed that same depth and resilience, and proved they’re among the fastest boats in the country. Across both programs, this weekend reflected the strength of our athletes, our coaches, and the culture we keep building at Oakland Strokes,” she said. Strokes’ pathway to collegiate rowing Oakland Strokes seniors keep rowing long after high school. A total of 15 seniors from this year’s class will row in college this fall. They will be part of prestigious programs at Boston University, Columbia, Cornell, Duke, Hobart, the University of Pennsylvania, Purdue, Tufts, the University of California Berkeley, UC San Diego, the University of San Diego, UNC Chapel Hill, Wesleyan, and Yale. Piedmont High graduate Senan Brodie will row at the University of Pennsylvania in the fall and and Geneva Johnson will compete at Boston University. Looking ahead The 2027 season starts now. Oakland Strokes is opening registration for summer camps and welcoming new athletes to the club. No rowing experience is required. Middle school and high school summer camps run in one- and two-week sessions in June, July, and August. The middle school year-round program is the strongest onramp to high school rowing in the East Bay. And the high school-age team offers a free two-week trial starting August 17 for incoming and returning students considering joining. Cost should not be a barrier to the sport. Oakland Strokes offers financial aid to support athletes who need it, and the club works to keep rowing open to any young person who wants to row. Families are encouraged to ask. Information about all programs, registration links, and the free trial is available at https:// www.oaklandstrokes.org

articles.text: Audrey Lam Brown University Audrey Lam, PHS Class of 2023, was the Post’s Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year as a senior. Lam is entering her senior year on Brown University’s women’s soccer team. Last season, Brown finished 9-4-4 and fell 3-0 to Princeton in the 2025 Ivy Women’s Soccer tournament semifinals on November 6. Lam started all 17 games and was among their most active players with 1,328 total minutes, recording four assists in the process. She earned second-team All-Ivy honors. Lam also played for Oakland Soul pre-professional W League team over the last two years. In its recent season, she appeared in seven games and was among their leaders in minutes with 386. Lam helped Brown go 12-2-3 and earn the No. 3 seed in its bracket for the 2023 NCAA Tournament. They beat Quinnipiac 3-nil in the first round, but lost to No. 6 Mississippi State 2-1 in the second round. In 2023 at Piedmont High, Lam led the Highlanders to a 13-1-6 (W-T-L) record to win its first Division 4 NCS championship in 20 years. She earned the WACC’s Player of the Year in the process. He was a leader of Piedmont High’s Division 4 NCS title in 2023, when we named him the Post’s Sophomore of the Year. In 2025, Occidental went 10-4-6 (W-T-L) and won the Southern California Intercollegiate Athletic Conference championship with a 1-nil win over Redlands on November 8. articles.text: team has not only survived, it has grown. PST has expanded to approximately 190 swimmers today, while also increasing its presence at championship and national-level meets. The club has strengthened its developmental pipeline and recently added respected coaches Adrien Downey and Colby Price to lead Developmental and Age Group programming. Many within the organization credit Head Coach Stefan Bill’s unwavering leadership, along with the dedication of PST families for helping sustain the team through the pool closure years. Many PST families also played a major role in supporting Measure UU, the bond measure that helped fund the new Piedmont Community Pool project. During the early days of the Covid pandemic, parents and supporters canvassed neighborhoods, organized outreach efforts, and rallied community support to help secure the future of swimming in Piedmont. PST also made a significant financial donation in support of the project, demonstrating the organization’s long term commitment to swimming in the community. Now, with the new community pool open, PST hopes to reestablish the Piedmont pool as its home base and continue building on its momentum. Team leaders say they are especially excited about welcoming a new generation of swimmers who may discover their love for the water at the new facility. The upcoming 50th anniversary season will also serve as an opportunity to reconnect with alumni families and celebrate the program’s long history and impact on the community. As the Piedmont Swim Team prepares to start its 50th season this August, the team is hoping a return to the new Piedmont Community Pool will mark more than just a homecoming. It represents the continuation of a program that has shaped generations of swimmers, families, and community members for nearly five decades. Founded in February 1976, PST operated exclusively out of the private Piedmont Swim Club for decades before the City of Piedmont assumed pool operations in 2011. The team continued training at the Piedmont Pool until the facility closed in 2020, beginning a six-year stretch without a permanent home pool. articles.text: With only so many of our end-of-year awards to go around, some of the major contributions made throughout the year tend to get lost. In this article, we reflect on four athletes at the school who were either entering their first year as a starter or getting time in a featured role for the first time in their PHS athletic career. Four who made a huge impact in the largest role of their time at Piedmont included Sydney Latvala of the girls’ lacrosse team as a freshman, freshman Olivia Nealon of girls’ soccer, junior Rehan Mumtaz of track and football, and Ari Moskovitz of boys’ tennis as a freshman. We’ll provide more athletes in the coming weeks. Staff Photos Sydney Latvala burst onto the scene as a freshman for the girls’ lacrosse team. SYDNEY LATVALA Lacrosse As a freshman on the girls’ lacrosse team, Sydney Latvala burst onto the scene as a key starter and goal scorer. Piedmont went 6-11 last spring with Latvala earning first-team All-League honors, while the school named her its Female Newcomer of the Year at its Highlander Awards. Some of her best performances included two goals in an 6-5 win over San Rafael on April 1, while she also had two goals in a 11-10 win over Granada where she held possession for the final 32 seconds of the match to kill the game. Olivia Nealon became a starter and difference maker as a midfielder on the girls’ soccer team. OLIVIA NEALON Soccer ARI MOSKOVITZ Tennis Olivia Nealon emerged as an important player on the girls’ soccer team in head coach Matt Spencer-Harty’s debut year, helping them finish 10-2-8 (W-T-L) and earn the No. 5 seed in the D2 NCS bracket. Nealon was a routine starter as a central midfielder, earning an honorable mention for AllLeague honors. She logged two assists in Piedmont’s 3-0 win over No. 12 Acalanes in the firstround of NCS. Freshman Ari Moskovitz emerged as a key singles starter on Piedmont’s tennis team in its recent spring season. He helped the Highlanders go 16-7 overall and received the No. 12 seed in the D1 NCS Team Tournament. Moskovitz paired with Nate Welch at the WACC Individual Tournament’s doubles bracket, placing fourth overall. He primarily appeared as Piedmont’s No. 3 singles starter throughout the regular season, and is bound to take a step up the order following the graduation of Welch and Lucas Smolko. REHAN MUMTAZ Football, Track Rehan Mumtaz preceded his record-setting track season with a big campaign on the football team as a running back. He earned an honorable mention for All-League on the football team, helping them go 8-5 and reach the D7 North Coast Section Championship game as the No. 2 seed. We named Mumtaz our honorable mention for Athlete of the Month in October for his contributions on football. His biggest performance was 162 yards and two touchdowns in their 39-35 win over Washington on October 24, while he also had 98 yards and a touchdown in the Highlanders’ 27-8 win over Kennedy on October 31. In track Mumtaz broke the school 100 meter record in 11.04 seconds at the WACC Championship on May 16. He’s the school’s second-fastest all-time sprinter behind Bill Hefter’s 100-yard record of 9.84 seconds set in 1961. Rehan Mumtaz got significant playing time on the football team and put together an illustrious track season. Ari Moskovitz emerged as a key starter on the tennis team as a freshman.

articles.text: With the summer in full swing, we delve into our second of six features of trails around Lake Tahoe with the lengthy but awe-striking Rubicon Trail around Emerald Bay. The Rubicon Trail is a 5.9 mile out-and-back (11.8 round trip, 1,350 feet in elevation gain) trail that stretches around Emerald Bay with a 360 degree view of Fannette Island, bringing hikers by the historic Vikingsholm mansion, through the quaint and quiet Emerald Bay Boat Camp, with countless places to rest beside the crystal blue water on the way to the Rubicon Point Lighthouse. Starting from the parking lot in the Upper Eagle Point Campground, the Rubicon Trail goes 1.6 miles beside Lake Tahoe before reaching Vikingsholm—a 38-room mansion built in 1929 on the shores of Emerald Bay. It was the summer home of Mrs. Lora Josephine Knight. She inherited her fortune from the passing of her former husband William Henry Moore, whose law firm had controlling interest in United States Steel, Union Pacific, Rock Island Railroad and the National Biscuit Company (later named Nabisco). She was among the primary financial backers of Charles Lindbergh’s transatlantic flight in 1927. Resting on top of Fannette Island is the famous Tea House she had constructed when her mansion was finished. The trail continues beside the white sandy beach along Emerald Bay to the northern portion of the Rubicon Trail. It means you’re finally past the exhaustive foot traffic you’re bound to encounter around Vikingsholm. The northern section of the Emerald Bay gives visitors a much more private look of FanStaff Photos Take a walk along Emerald Bay on the Rubicon Trail. It provides a 360-degree view of Fannett Island and its Tea House. The view from the starting point at Upper Eagle Point Campground. The Rubicon Trail walks past the Vikingsholm mansion, created in 1929 by Lora Josephine Knight—who also arranged the construction of her personal Tea House on Fannett Island.

articles.text: Woodminster Summer Musicals’ 59th season continues July 10 with Carousel, Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein II’s classic 1945 musical about love, loss, and redemption. Carousel was adapted from Ferenc Molnár’s 1909 play Liliom, reimagining its Budapest setting as the Maine coastline. The story revolves around carousel barker Billy Bigelow, whose romance with millworker Julie Jordan costs the pair their jobs. Billy becomes unemployed just as Julie reveals her pregnancy to him, leading Billy to commit a robbery out of desperation. Woodminster Summer Musicals events are held at Woodminster Amphitheater in Joaquin Miller Park, Oakland. Woodminster is a nonprofit organization that has presented summer musicals at the amphitheater for over 50 years, traditionally featuring three to four plays or musicals over summer months and is Oakland’s longest continually running live theater. Producers Associates, Inc., the nonprofit organization that organizes the summer festival, also offers a “Kids Come Free” program designed to make live theater affordable for families. Several thousand free tickets are given to children and teens each season. Woodminster presents Carousel July 10 through 12; and again July 16 through 19. The Full Monty is presented August 7 through 9 and August 13 through 16. Rumors closes out Woodminster’s season on August 28. Visit https://www.woodminster.com/2026-season to purchase tickets. Woodminster Summer Musicals events are held at Woodminster Amphitheater in Joaquin Miller Park. Learn more

articles.text: Singakademie Graz, founded in 1854 and one of the oldest secular Austrian boarding high schools, is participating in the Golden Gate International Choral Festival in July, hosted by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. The school is attached to a singing academy and offers its pupils a comprehensive vocal education. The singing group’s signature performance at the festival is on Wednesday, July 15, at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The school’s main emphasis is on preparing its ensembles for classical choir and orchestra concerts. The singing pupils from Graz participate regularly in operas and musical productions. On international tours to Canada, China, Spain, Italy, Belgium, Finland, Latvia, Switzerland, the U.S., Germany, Hungary, France, Estonia, Luxembourg, Japan, South Africa, New Zealand, Australia, and South Korea, the young singers from Graz try to build a bridge from the rich Austrian choir tradition to international contemporary music. At national Austrian youth choir competitions, they won their category ten times and performed in many international choir competitions. In Tshwane (2018, South Africa) and in Gangneung, South Korea (2023), the young singers became “Champions of the World Choir Games” twice. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival takes place locally from July 13 to July 18. Information on the concerts and spotlight choirs can be found on their website, including which concerts are free or have paid admission for the public. https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ ggf-concerts-2026. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre has extended the world premiere musical The Lunchbox for a second and final time, with the production now scheduled to close July 12. The musical, based on filmmaker Ritesh Batra’s 2013 film of the same name, is set in Mumbai and follows an accidental lunchbox delivery that connects a young wife and a widower nearing retirement. Through notes exchanged with their meals, the two strangers form a relationship that develops into a romance. The Lunchbox is directed by Tony Award winner Rachel Chavkin, whose previous work includes Hadestown and Natasha, Pierre & The Great Comet of 1812. The production features music and co-lyrics by the Lazours, with a book and co-lyrics by Batra. The cast is led by Manu Narayan and Kuhoo Verma. Narayan’s credits include Company on Broadway, while Verma previously appeared in Berkeley Rep productions of Monsoon Wedding and Octet. The ensemble includes Hashini Amarasinghe, Savidu Geevaratne, Akshara Gunda, Shaarada Trayi Karthik, Benjamin Mathew, Vaibu Mohan, Shiv Nadkarni, Anisha Nagarajan, Nasir Panjwani, Yash Ramanujam, Sushma Saha, Kinshuk Sen, Caryna Shah, Aathaven Tharmarajah, Vishal Vaidya and Levin Valayil. The creative team also includes choreographer Reshma Gajjar, scenic designer Mimi Lien, costume designer Arjun Bhasin, lighting designer Bradley King and sound designer Justin Stasiw. Performances continue at Berkeley Rep through July 12. Tickets are available online at https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ or by calling 510-647-2949 from noon to 7 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday. articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will perform its annual Independence Day themed-program on July 4 at Shoreline Amphitheatre, an outdoor venue in Mountain View, led by conductor Ted Sperling. Maestro Sperling is a Tony award-winning music director, orchestrator and conductor and served as principal conductor of Westchester Philharmonic for six seasons. Recent conducting appearances include performances with the Chicago Symphony, Baltimore Symphony, Philadelphia Orchestra and San Diego Symphony. The theme of this year’s Independence Day performance is “Summer of 1969, The Soundtrack of a Generation,” created and commissioned by the San Diego Symphony. The concert features vocalists Morgan James, Bryonha Marie, and Noah Ricketts performing iconic songs including Proud Mary, Here Ted Sperling Comes the Sun, Blackbird, and Purple Haze. The concert begins at 7 p.m. and traditionally concludes with a grand finale of spectacular fireworks. Family-friendly activities begin at 5 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2025-26/Shoreline- 4th-of-July.

articles.text: Wynton Marsalis Wynton Marsalis returns to SFJAZZ’s Miner Auditorium next month, bringing the most recent iteration of his iconic Septet for four performances over two days. New Orleans Jazz player Marsalis, a regular performer on the Miner Auditorium stage, is a multi-Grammy award winning trumpeter, composer, and teacher whose work was the first jazz composition to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music. Marsalis comes from a lineage of jazz greats — his brothers Branford, Jason and Delfeayo are all well-known musicians in the genre. Marsalis received the SFJAZZ Lifetime Achievement Award at SFJAZZ Gala 2022 and recently announced his departure from his leadership position at Lincoln Center after nearly 40 years. Performances begin at 6 p.m. and 8:30 p.m. both days. Tickets are available online at https:// www.sfjazz.org/tickets/productions/summer-2026/wynton-marsalis-septet/.

articles.text: Exhibition leaves July 19 An exhibition showcasing the artistry of Lawrence Ferlinghetti, one of San Francisco’s most significant cultural figures, is now on view at the Legion of Honor. Ferlinghetti (1919 - 2021) was a poet, activist, publisher, and co-founder of the famous City Lights Bookstore in San Francisco, the epicenter of the Beat generation of writers. The independent bookstore is considered a literary landmark and has been a gathering space for writers since Ferlinghetti founded the store in 1955 with the now-famous Pocket Poets Series. Since then the press has gone on to publish a wide range of titles, including poetry and prose, fiction and nonfiction, international and local authors. Ferlinghetti was also an avid painter, draftsman, and printmaker, and his work across mediums often combines image and text exploring themes of isolation, violence, and human resilience. With artworks drawn entirely from the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco’s works on paper collection, this exhibition showcases Ferlinghetti’s work in printmaking, including etching, lithography, and letterpress. The exhibition is on view now through July 19. For more information, visit https://www. famsf.org/exhibitions/ferlinghetti-san-francisco. Museum exhibition preview Photo courtesy of Legion of Honor

articles.text: As part of the Singing Academy of Graz, Austria, its young boys group, “Green Guys Graz”, will be participating in the Golden Gate International Choral Festival this summer. Their spotlight performance takes place on Wednesday, July 15 alongside the Austrian chorus Singakademie Graz. The concert will take place at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The group chose the color green to represent them because this is the national color of their home province of Styria (the green heart of Austria!). A common saying in Austria means that very young people are “green” between their ears. The secret of their success is lubricating their vocal cords with a Styrian specialty – pumpkin seed oil – of course, in dark green color. Numerous first prizes at home and abroad attest to their musical quality in a wide variety of vocal styles and scenic performances. Maria Fuerntratt has been the Artistic Director of the Singing-Academy since 1995 and has taught choir pedagogy at the Music University as senior lecturer in Graz since 2007. She won the national pedagogy award (Pädagogischer Panther), Styrian folk culture award, the Antoni Martorell Premio (Vatican), long-service gold medal for Austrian choir merits. The Japanese Television NHK, Chinese CCTV, British BBC, Austrian TV all produced portraits about her and she has gained international and national concert and jury-member experiences. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival takes place from July 13 to July 18 in the East Bay, Information on the concerts and spotlight choirs can be found on their website, including which concerts are free or have paid admission for the public. https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ ggf-concerts-2026. articles.text: Two performances on Sunday were certainly thought-provoking. The first was billed as a “dream come true” and featured cellist Isaac Pastor-Chermak interpreting the two Classical Concertos by Haydn. Pastor-Chermak was ably assisted by the IPC All-Star Chamber Orchestra conducted by Jason Weinberger. The second concert was a performance of the musical Jekyll and Hyde at the Woodminster open air theater in the Oakland Hills. The memories of the first concert were enhanced by the performance of the second concert. Musical performance in general can present a perpetual conundrum. Interpretation must be aided by the performers’ intimate knowledge of musical styles in conjunction with the technical ability to realize any difficulty. Many aspects come into play. The first aspect is, shall we say, the face value? This might be considered as the benevolent presence of Dr. Jekyll. But lurking in the shadows are the darker aspects. In the case of Jekyll and Hyde this is reflected in the evil presence of Mr. Hyde. He is always ready to seize the situation. This ever-present problem lies within us. The performance of the musical was an unqualified success. Michael Parrott played the two characters to perfection. In the play, Jekyll – Hyde exposes two human characteristics. In music, however we have countless characteristics to present for interpretation. Needless to say, this ability is extremely important in the interpretation of music. I s a a c Pa s t o r- C h e r m a k explained to the audience that his concert realized a lifelong dream. It was obvious from the start that the soloist is an immensely talented performer. He exudes enthusiasm which is reflected in his delightful presence on the stage. There is no doubt that he loves playing concerts. The same Sunday’s thought-provoking concert in the Piedmont Center for the arts featured solo cellist Isaac PastorChermak accompanied by the IPC chamber orchestra, conducted by Jason Weinberger. For the occasion, the Piedmont Center for the Arts was jampacked. Listeners enjoyed the concert from beginning to end. I enjoyed the concert also, but with some reservations. It was a pleasure to hear both of Haydn’s marvelous Concertos played one after the other. The performance was enthusiastic and well intentioned. However more attention to dynamics would have made the concert even better. This is the conductor‘s responsibility. His deep knee bends and excessively generous hand gestures did not help. Another consideration are the cadenzas which are performed in a classical Concerto. It is my sincere belief that the cadenzas should be idiomatic and in the style of the composer. Some composers of the past wrote music that was so idiomatic that it passed for the music of the classical era. Two of these extraordinary talents were Fritz Kreisler (the important violinist-composer), and many members of the Casadesus family. These days, many performers reject these excellent credenzas. In a way it is like replacing the head of “winged victory of Samothrace” with a cartoon head. Nevertheless, a lifelong dream came into reality. articles.text: William Wyler film captures 7 Academy Awards Harold Russell, Dana Andrews, and Fredric March in The Best Years of Our Lives The Best Years of Our Lives is an extraordinary film, directed by William Wyler, and the winner of seven Academy Awards to include Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Actor. When the film was released in 1946, millions of veterans were returning to America from countless theaters of war across Europe and the South Pacific. Most agreed that this film, at its core, captured their experience of coming home. In fact, for a time it was called Home Again. The story opens with three soldiers who have found passage on a military flight. Each of them is eager to return to their heartland hometown of Boone and their previous lives. As the hours pass, we vaguely learn about their service backstories: Captain Fred Derry (Dana Andrews), a B47 bombardier dropping bombs over Germany; Homer Parrish, (Harold Russell), a Navy petty officer who lost both hands in a fire; and Army Sgt. Al Stephenson, who fought in the South Pacific. The three begin to bond and we learn that Fred was a pharmacy soda jerk, Al an experienced banker, and Homer a trophy-winning high school athlete. The lives that await them will slowly unfold, a montage of sorts, and it gradually becomes evident that their individual transitions are profoundly different, yet also very similar. Each struggles to cope with Open to the public. No admission fees. Closed holidays.

articles.text: It has always been fundamental to childhood entertainment to anthropomorphize animals, be it a Disney nature documentary or an animated feature such as the Lion King. Even Cinderella is helped by intelligent birds and mice. What is extraordinary about the Oscar-winning Toy Story feature films, which began in 1995, is that Pixar made familiar toys – Sheriff Woody (Tom Hanks), Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen), Bo Peep (Annie Potts) – sentient beings, meaning three-dimensional characters with emotive personalities (of course, only made manifest when no humans are present). In Toy Story 4, there is actually an ongoing discussion between Woody and Buzz regarding listening to your inner voice for guidance. In other words, their characters are interesting, likable, and nuanced, especially in Woody’s case. And they live by a code: they hope to be selected by a child who is loyal, and over time both will find meaning and purpose in their connection. Stalking Woody and crew, however, is the ever-present fear of the impending obsolescence of their play buddy, likely resulting in their being left in a closet, or sitting on a shelf where dust gathers and darkness, so to speak, is just a cardboard box away. Toy Story 4 is simply wonderful, as were its three predecessors. Imagine creating four animated features that are stand alone extraordinary in narrative and animation. Each is an engaging, witty story, heartfelt and in all respects, as best exemplified by Woody, who posseses an abiding sense of compassion, empathy and decency. In writing fiction, be it screenplays or novels, there is a distinct difference between telling and showing. Toy Story 4 “shows” its audience, from youngsters to adults, from the first frame to the last, that caring about your friends before yourself is to be valued. And as Woody points out at a critical moment in 4, “No one gets left behind.” So, as the story unfolds, Woody and crew are now part of a new world, their new child, so to speak, is Bonnie (Madeleine McGraw). Unlike Andy, now gone off to college, she leaves many of them in her closet collecting dust balls. Of course, kids are fickle (and they grow up); however, for Woody, this truth provokes familiar anxieties. His purpose, the meaning of his life, is to be in the room with Bonnie and not in the closet, peering out through the slats. He yearns to be held and played with, talked to, taken here A scene from Disney/Pixar’s Toy Story 4 Nathan Rivera and Jessie Andra Smith bring an unforgettable trilingual performance of swingin' bluesy jazzy folk. The duo has traveled all over the world, sharing their music on streets and stages with their unique sound. A fusion of jazzy folk and blues on resonator guitars and accordion, with an interesting interplay of harmonies between the two voices. Upbeat tunes rooted in the spirit of jazz, improvisation, storytelling, and humor. For advance tickets and more details, please see: https://www.ticketsignup.io/NandJessie .

Even Cinderella is helped by intelligent birds and mice. What is extraordinary about the Oscar-winning Toy Story feature films, which began in 1995, is that Pixar made familiar toys – Sheriff Woody (Tom Hanks), Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen), Bo Peep (Annie Potts) – sentient beings, meaning three-dimensional characters with emotive personalities (of course, only made manifest when no humans are present). In Toy Story 4, there is actually an ongoing discussion between Woody and Buzz regarding listening to your inner voice for guidance. In other words, their characters are interesting, likable, and nuanced, especially in Woody’s case. And they live by a code: they hope to be selected by a child who is loyal, and over time both will find meaning and purpose in their connection. Stalking Woody and crew, however, is the ever-present fear of the impending obsolescence of their play buddy, likely resulting in their being left in a closet, or sitting on a shelf where dust gathers and darkness, so to speak, is just a cardboard box away. Toy Story 4 is simply wonderful, as were its three predecessors. Imagine creating four animated features that are stand alone extraordinary in narrative and animation. Each is an engaging, witty story, heartfelt and in all respects, as best exemplified by Woody, who posseses an abiding sense of compassion, empathy and decency. In writing fiction, be it screenplays or novels, there is a distinct difference between telling and showing. Toy Story 4 “shows” its audience, from youngsters to adults, from the first frame to the last, that caring about your friends before yourself is to be valued. And as Woody points out at a critical moment in 4, “No one gets left behind.” So, as the story unfolds, Woody and crew are now part of a new world, their new child, so to speak, is Bonnie (Madeleine McGraw). Unlike Andy, now gone off to college, she leaves many of them in her closet collecting dust balls. Of course, kids are fickle (and they grow up); however, for Woody, this truth provokes familiar anxieties. His purpose, the meaning of his life, is to be in the room with Bonnie and not in the closet, peering out through the slats. He yearns to be held and played with, talked to, taken here See Toy Story 4 on page 32 Harold Russell, Dana Andrews, and Fredric March in The Best Years of Our Lives By Chris Honoré The Best Years of Our Lives is an extraordinary film, directed by William Wyler, and the winner of seven Academy Awards to include Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Actor. When the film was released in 1946, millions of veterans were returning to America from countless theaters of war across Europe and the South Pacific. Most agreed that this film, at its core, captured their experience of coming home. In fact, for a time it was called Home Again. The story opens with three soldiers who have found passage on a military flight. Each of them is eager to return to their heartland hometown of Boone and their previous lives. As the hours pass, we vaguely learn about their service backstories: Captain Fred Derry (Dana Andrews), a B47 bombardier dropping bombs over Germany; Homer Parrish, (Harold Russell), a Navy petty officer who lost both hands in a fire; and Army Sgt. Al Stephenson, who fought in the South Pacific. The three begin to bond and we learn that Fred was a pharmacy soda jerk, Al an experienced banker, and Homer a trophy-winning high school athlete. The lives that await them will slowly unfold, a montage of sorts, and it gradually becomes evident that their individual transitions are profoundly different, yet also very similar. June 20) Open to the public. No admission fees. Closed holidays. Nathan Rivera and Jessie Andra Smith bring an unforgettable trilingual performance of swingin' bluesy jazzy folk. The duo has traveled all over the world, sharing their music on streets and stages with their unique sound. A fusion of jazzy folk and blues on resonator guitars and accordion, with an interesting interplay of harmonies between the two voices. Upbeat tunes rooted in the spirit of jazz, improvisation, storytelling, and humor. For advance tickets and more details, please see: https://www.ticketsignup.io/NandJessie .

articles.text: There is a common notion that teachers are often the unsung heroes and backbones of modern society. In 2021, from the creative mind of Quinta Brunson, who serves as both creator and cast member, Abbott Elementary premiered, showcasing the trials, tribulations, and triumphs of public school teachers through the lens of a hit sitcom. The show follows a documentary camera crew granted access into an underfunded Philadelphia K-8 school, Willard R. Abbott Elementary, commonly shortened to simply “Abbott” by both its staff and devoted fanbase. The show’s pilot episode opens with Janine Teagues (Quinta Brunson), who is portrayed as an optimistic second-grade teacher whose enthusiasm often exceeds her own teaching experience. That includes teaching in her classroom with an old textbook that is missing key information that she herself had to tape in. From the get-go, money is a problem for the school – more specifically the lack of it. A narrator praises the teachers, mostly the more seasoned ones, like Barbara Howard (Sheryl Lee Ralph) a pillar of wisdom and faith to the school community, and Melissa Schementi (Lisa Ann Walter), a proud Italian-American who loves all things Philly, for what they accomplish each day in the face of many of the school’s obstacles. Janine admits to the camera that many of the young teachers don’t Abbott Elementary has had over 250 award nominations with 89 wins, including 4 Primetime Emmys and 3 Golden Globes. Abbott Elementary also boasts a 99% rating on Rotten Tomatoes and an 8.2/10 rating on IMDB; it has quickly been one of the most acclaimed sitcoms of the decade. The main characters when put together as an ensemble create a complex and entertaining group to keep viewers engaged through the season of episodes. Abbott Elementary helps remind us not to be afraid of going back to the basics. When Janine gets told by an angry parent that she’s a bad teacher, despite exhausting every option to help her student, she goes to Barbara for advice, and what Barbara tells Janine transcends the confines of the show, “People have thrown dirt on my name, others have given flowers. But it’s all a garden to me…If you come back here tomorrow, ready to do your job, having not given up on yourself or that student, well that is not failure. Sometimes that is what success looks like.” And in those three minutes of screen time, Abbott Elementary proves why it has become a hit sitcom, why it has received hundreds of nominations. Teachers don’t just teach their students, they teach the viewers themselves to continue becoming the best versions of themselves. Abbott Elementary is available to watch on Hulu and DisneyPlus. The cast of Abbott Elementary exactly have a hang on things like the veterans do. As the episode progresses we meet two more characters, Janine’s closest friend and colleague Jacob Hill (Chris Perfetti) and Principal Ava Coleman (Janelle James). Jacob is a sixth grade history teacher and self-proclaimed activist who, like Janine, is determined to give the students the best education he can. Ava on the other hand, is not well-liked by other teachers who don’t believe she’s qualified for the job of principal. Ava has no problem demonstrating this with her blase attitude throughout the episode. Towards the end of the episode, we are introduced to the final two characters, Mr. Johnson (William Stanford Davis) and Gregory Eddie (Tyler James Willams). The former is the school’s eccentric janitor, who has an abundance of life experience ranging from being a male model to an Olympic bronze medalist. The latter is a temporary substitute and past applicant for the job of principal at Abbott. Gregory’s classroom also shares a wall with Janine’s, setting up a friendship with the potential for more further down the line. As tension between the veteran teachers and the new ones becomes more apparent, we can see how Janine takes it personally, wanting nothing more than to prove herself. As of 2026 following the finale of its fifth season, with production underway for a sixth season,

articles.text: Summer Solace Tallow brings culinary mindset to skincare At Summer Solace Tallow in Oakland, skincare begins with an ingredient more commonly associated with the kitchen. Tallow, the rich, rendered fat from cattle and sheep, is the foundation of the company’s balms, soaps, face oils, lip products, mineral sunscreens and candles. For founder Megan Bre Camp, tallow is not a passing beauty trend but the product of a decade-plus of work informed by cooking, farming, herbalism and a belief that skincare ingredients should be as thoughtfully sourced as food. “We all go to the farmers markets, we are discerning about where our lettuce comes from, for example,” Megan told Piedmont Post. “We should hold that same conception when it comes to skincare, especially for our little ones.” Summer Solace Tallow, which launched in 2014, uses fresh suet, or the internal fat from pasture-raised cattle, sourced from Stemple Creek Ranch in the North Bay. Megan renders about 60 pounds of it each week, she said, working slowly to create a stable, shelf-ready tallow. “If the ingredient is fresh from the beginning,” she said, “it’s good quality from the start.” Tallow is having ‘a moment’ in skincare, and has recently appeared in drugstore skincare aisles and across social media, promoted as a simple, traditional moisturizer. Megan said the difference between her products and those on drugstore shelves lies in the source material and process. Summer Solace Tallow sources most of its ingredients within 150 miles of Oakland — her “Sea Change Tallow Soap” features mineral-rich bladderwrack seaweed harvested off the Mendocino coast by her friend Julie Druckner, while beeswax is sourced directly from her neighbor, Khaled Almaghafi, a beekeeper who runs Queen of Sheba Farms and sells at the Temescal Farmers’ Market near the brickand-mortar shop. That reciprocity fills Megan “with joy and inspiration,” she said. “My work is deeply relationship-based, I live within the community I source from and sell to at the farmers’ markets. Every ingredient I work with carries a Megan Bre Camp, owner of Summer Solace Tallow in Oakland, uses fresh, locally sourced beef suet in balms, soaps and facial products. story that I can share,” she added. For Megan, the work is rooted in a career that began in food. Raised in Alaska, she developed an early interest in native plants and sustainable cooking. After culinary school, she moved to the Bay Area and worked in vegetarian kitchens, including Cafe Gratitude in Berkeley and Greens in San Francisco. After spending time on a Maine homestead and working at Berkeley’s Three Stone Hearth, a worker-owned co-op kitchen, she began to rethink her long-held vegetarianism and explored animal fats as part of a more regional, whole-animal approach to food. Her experience at Three Stone Hearth, a community-supported kitchen focused on traditional foodways, led her to learn more about bone broth, local meats and pasture-raised ingredients. She also studied permaculture, horticulture and urban farming at Merritt College, then worked in pastry and as a chocolatier, where she learned the precision of handling fats at low temperatures. The idea for a skincare line arrived during a short break between restaurant jobs, she said. Friends with young children were dealing with eczema and skin irritation, and Megan was troubled by the petroleum-based products they were using. “I thought, I have all the skills to create something better,” she recalled. “I have a nose for scents, and I love natural perfumery and aromatherapy. I thought, I’m going to create a tallow balm.” Within weeks, she had developed the core of what became Summer Solace’s line: an unscented balm, a lavender and calendula blend, a chest and muscle rub, and products designed for hands, dry skin and everyday use. She secured permits and began approaching local shops, which placed early orders. Today, the line has grown to include soaps, candles, facial oils, body oils, scrubs and mineral sunscreens. Still, tallow remains the central ingredient. The unscented balm is among the company’s most popular products, Megan said, particularly for customers who are scent-sensitive or looking for a simple moisturizer. Its texture is dense rather than whipped, and a small amount melts into the skin when warmed between the hands. “Tallow everywhere,” she said, describing its uses on the face, hands and body. “When you make your own tallow, you really have to know this ingredient, because it behaves in a different way from [traditional] moisturizers.” The company’s Chef and Gardener balm is another practical favorite. Formulated with rosemary, myrrh and other botanical oils, it was designed for dry, hardworking hands and is used by cooks, gardeners, ceramicists and health care workers, Megan said, Summer Solace Tallow products are available in-store and online The shop is located at 5303 Claremont Avenue in Oakland
