articles.text: Richard “Dick” Hylond Rahl was born January 18, 1934 to Rolfe and Margaret Rahl. He grew up in inner city Los Angeles alongside his brothers Rolfe and Robert. He graduated from LA Polytechnical High School as valedictorian and at first, planned to attend Occidental. However, it was on a trip to Northern California to see a classmate from Poly that he decided to attend UC Berkeley instead. During registration at Cal, after being contacted by recruiters for Cal Crew due to his imposing height of 6’ 4”, Dick decided to try out for crew. This would turn out to be one of the best and most important decisions of his life; Dick embraced the grit and grind of crew, swiftly earning a spot on the varsity team. His coach, Ky Ebright, said Dick was the only rower that never missed a workout in his four years at Cal. His years with Cal Crew would see him decorated with numerous honors and awards, from receiving the Dean Witter Award, awarded annually to the crewman demonstrating the most loyalty, efficiency, and spirit, to being named most eligible athlete by The Daily Californian. Outnumbering his accolades, however, were the friendships Dick made – friendships that endured throughout his lifetime. After graduating with a degree in political science, he started his pilot training with the US Air Force, where, due to his athleticism and prominence on the crew scene, he was asked to volunteer for special service training for the US Olympic trials. He trained at the Detroit Boat Club for six months and barely missed a spot on the US Olympic team for the 1956 Melbourne Olympics, despite having rowed a world record time earlier in the trials. After the Air Force, he returned to Berkeley for law school at Boalt Hall (now Berkeley Law). There, his one-of-akind work ethic once again propelled him to the Law Review. Upon graduating, Dick took a job at Stark and Champlin in Oakland, where his law partner introduced him to Susan Emmett. The rest is history. Dick and Suzie married in 1969 and moved to Piedmont, where they lived for many years, raising their three children, Emmett, Riva, and Marisa. A dedicated family man, Dick was always there to support them. When Suzie started Piedmont Children’s Choir, he took care of incorporation, videoed performances, and chaperoned on some tours as the photographer and blogger. As the children grew up and engaged in sports, music, and theater, he never missed a game, recital, concert, pageant – you name it – Dick was always their biggest cheerleader. One day, while helping Suzie with her homework for a needlepoint class, Dick discovered he enjoyed the creativity and detail of needlepoint and began creating his own projects. He designed Christmas ornaments, pillows, chairs, and various personalized keepsakes for people for over 55 years, with his number of projects totaling in the Former Piedmont resident Dick Rahl thousands. In 1979, he decided to take a sabbatical from his probate and estate law practice to travel the world with Suzie and the three kids (ages seven, five, and three). During that year, aptly dubbed the “year of summer,” they cruised across the Pacific to Australia, spent a few months in Indonesia and time in Singapore, Hong Kong, Malaysia, and France. After several months in Spain studying Spanish, they made one last stop in the UK before cruising across the Atlantic, through the Panama Canal, and back home to California almost a year later. Over that year, Dick wrote a children’s story entitled The Way Home and would read parts of it as he wrote them to the family. When Dick’s law firm was located just off of Lake Merritt, he would walk to and from work every day, three miles each way, rain or shine! He would often detour from his route to walk the kids to school or be joined by one of them on his way home. In the case that he made the trip alone, Dick would read books while he walked and never missed a step. He practiced probate and estate law for over 35 years, becoming a named partner. During that time, he and Suzie took many family trips all around the world, continuing their love for adventure. In 2005, they sold their home in Piedmont and moved to Dallas to spend time with daughters Marisa and Riva, as well as Riva’s soon to be two sons, Evan and Reagan, to whom Dick became “Pops.” Over the last 20 years, Dick and Suzie split their time between Dallas and the Bay Area, keeping up with both family and friends. Dick was an avid supporter of Cal Crew over the years and enjoyed attending reunions and regattas over time. Dick continued his walking daily, even when his pulmonary fibrosis made it difficult. He will be remembered as a loyal friend, a loving husband, and caring father, and for his sense of humor, which he held onto right up to the end. He is survived by Suzie, his wife of 57 years, his younger brother Robert, his son Emmett, daughters Riva and Marisa, and his grandsons, Evan and Reagan Graeme. Donations in Dick’s memory should be made to: Friends of Cal Crew, and mailed to 201 Lafayette Circle, Lafayette, CA 94549 A memorial service will be held on Saturday, August 8th at 11:00AM at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, California.
articles.title: Dick Rahl dies at 92 on June 12

articles.text: Piedmont Roundup Market Observations, Insider Wisdom & The Week in Piedmont Real Estate Remember Jan from The Brady Bunch? Taxes, Taxes, Taxes… Let’s get the boring stuff out of the way first. Piedmont is putting a real estate transfer tax increase on the November ballot. The proposed change would raise the tax from 1.3% to 1.75% and is expected to generate about $1.5 million a year. The Council took the first step on June 15, and a second vote is tentatively scheduled for July 6 before the Registrar of Voters deadline on August 7. The city says the increase is needed because the budget is moving from a period of major project delivery into long-term stewardship. In plain English, Piedmont has spent heavily on capital improvements in recent years and now has to keep the new facilities running, staffed, and maintained. In The Tradition of Excellence… 43 years in Piedmont Real Estate I sat down with Anian Tunney Broker Associate and Realtor® with the kind of prepared questions any reporter brings to a profile. And then I threw most of them out. That’s because the conversation quickly turned into what it actually takes to stay in this business for 43 years – in a town where someone told her on her very first day that she’d never make it. pages.text: Wednesday, June 24, 2026 27 Features Walking on Wednesday The Forgotten Heights: Walking Piedmont’s 1907 Boom By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a good turnout of 43 walkers and six K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday on a mild, overcast morning for their last walk of spring 2026. The group had not walked the streets of the early “Grand Avenue Heights” neighborhood development for over two years. The borders of this largely forgotten piece of Piedmont history ran along Grand Avenue, Boulevard Way, and Crofton, Fairbanks, Walker, and Weldon Avenues in Piedmont and Oakland. Historical photos show how rural the area once was, and the development’s old site map reveals that today’s Wildwood Avenue was then called Highland Avenue and today’s Fairview Avenue was named Piedmont Avenue. Before setting off, the group discussed how the development fit into the history of its time. Oakland was shaken hard by the 1906 San Francisco earthquake but escaped catastrophic destruction. It suffered significant structural damage, infrastructure failures, and a massive refugee influx, but relatively few deaths and no citywide firestorm. As San Franciscans fled the burning city, ferry service across the bay became a lifeline, and Oakland’s biggest role became that of a refugee center. The most dramatic effect on Oakland was not physical damage but population growth. Within three days of the earthquake and fires, more than 150,000 refuWalkers in Front of Boulevard Way Heights Home Route picture gees crossed the bay, essentially doubling the city’s population overnight. Schools, churches, public buildings, and private homes were converted into shelters. Many refugees eventually returned to San Francisco, but thousands stayed permanently, helping accelerate Oakland’s growth in the early 20th century. In response to that growth and the demand for housing, “Grand Avenue Heights” was developed in 1907. In 1910 the Oakland Tribune wrote that the area, once called Pleasant Valley, “enjoys the finest climate in Oakland (and that means the best in the State). It is the greatest place in the world for children who can sleep out upon the sleeping porches 365 nights in the year. It is free from fog and heavy winds. It is between the two most fashionable residential districts in the county — Adams Point and Piedmont.” Advertisements also billed it as “Grand Avenue Heights (By The Parks),” and it did in fact sit between Piedmont Park and Lake Merritt. The development’s sales agent was the Frank K. Mott Company. Mott was also the mayor of Oakland from 1905 to 1915, known as “The Mayor Who Built Oakland” for presiding over the city’s disaster relief. His advertisements proclaimed the development “soon to be the center of Oakland’s most exclusive residence district ... it overlooks Piedmont Park ... part of the development is in Piedmont.” On October 21, 1908, the Oakland Tribune reported that over 3,000 people attended the opening-day sale, with $50,000 to $79,000 in lots sold that first day. The average lot went for about $2,000, with $300 down and $25 a month. This was meant to be a “high class” neighborhood, and all homes had to cost $3,500 or more to build. The group set off for the streets of Grand Avenue Heights by taking the upper trail through Piedmont Park. They emerged on Wildwood Avenue and passed Wildwood School, where happy students were enjoying outside recess. The walkers continued down to the “Five Way Stop” intersection of Wallace Road and Winsor, Warfield, and Wildwood Avenues, then went up Warfield to Boulevard Way, where they crossed the city border into Oakland. Heading up Crofton, they took a group photo at its corner with Walker — fittingly — in front of a Grand Avenue Heights home built in 1920. Up Walker, the group checked out two neighboring homes: 1025 Walker, built in 1914, and 1031, built in 1910. articles.text: Nowadays the annual ZAP Grand Tastings are on a much smaller scale. This year about 45 wineries gathered at Fort Mason in San Francisco on June 6 to pour their current releases. The atmosphere was as festive as ever and the wines exhibited their typical attractive deliciousness. There were many fine wines in the room that day and the following are the standouts – 2026’s cream of the crop. For more than a century, Zinfandel has been woven into the story of California wine. Often called America’s heritage grape, Zinfandel has survived changing tastes, shifting vineyard landscapes, and the rise of international varieties to remain one of the state’s most distinctive and celebrated wines. Although its origins were once the subject of debate, DNA research has shown that Zinfandel is closely related to grapes from Croatia and southern Italy. The variety arrived in California during the Gold Rush era of the 1850s, quickly becoming a favorite among immigrant farmers who planted it throughout the state. Many of those old vineyards, some more than 100 years old, continue to produce exceptional fruit today. Zinfandel’s appeal comes from its versatility. In the glass, it can range from bright and refreshing rosé-style wines to bold, full-bodied reds bursting with flavors of blackberry, raspberry, plum, and spice. Old-vine Zinfandels often reveal layers of complexity, with notes of dried fruit, pepper, and earthy minerality that reflect the character of their historic vineyards. Regions such as Sonoma County, Lodi, Paso Robles, and the Sierra Foothills have become closely associated with outstanding Zinfandel. Winemakers in these areas have championed the grape’s unique personality, often producing small-lot wines that showcase the character of individual vineyards. Among the leading advocates for Zinfandel are producers who have preserved historic vines and traditional winemaking methods. Organizations such as Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) have helped introduce new generations of wine drinkers to the grape through tastings and educational events. Founded in 1991, ZAP began as a group of winemakers, growers, and Zinfandel enthusiasts who wanted to celebrate a grape that was sometimes overlooked in favor of more internationally recognized varieties. At the time, many historic Zinfandel vineyards were being replaced with other grapes, and some producers feared that California’s old-vine heritage could disappear. ZAP helped bring attention to these vineyards and the unique wines they produced. One of ZAP’s most influential contributions was its annual Zinfandel tasting festival, which became one of the largest gatherings in the country devoted to a single grape variety. For many years, the event brought together hundreds of wineries and thousands of wine lovers, creating a community around Zinfandel and giving small producers a national platform. The tastings helped introduce consumers to the diversity of the grape — from elegant, restrained Zinfandels with bright acidity to powerful, fruit-rich versions from old vineyards. Once and Future is the new label of wine icon Joel Peterson. • 2024 Once and Future Zinfandel Teldeschi Vineyard The legendary Joel Peterson, founder of Ravenswood Winery, is hard at work with this new label producing wines from some of the same iconic vineyards he made at Ravenswood. articles.title: 2026 California’s Greatest Zinfandels

pages.text: 28 Wednesday, June 24, 2026 The Wine Corner 2026 California’s Greatest Zinfandels Nowadays the annual ZAP Grand Tastings are on a much smaller scale. This year about 45 wineries gathered at Fort Mason in San Francisco on June 6 to pour their current releases. The atmosphere was as festive as ever and the wines exhibited their typical attractive deliciousness. There were many fine wines in the room that day and the following are the standouts – 2026’s cream of the crop. By Pierre DuMont For more than a century, Zinfandel has been woven into the story of California wine. Often called America’s heritage grape, Zinfandel has survived changing tastes, shifting vineyard landscapes, and the rise of international varieties to remain one of the state’s most distinctive and celebrated wines. Although its origins were once the subject of debate, DNA research has shown that Zinfandel is closely related to grapes from Croatia and southern Italy. The variety arrived in California during the Gold Rush era of the 1850s, quickly becoming a favorite among immigrant farmers who planted it throughout the state. Many of those old vineyards, some more than 100 years old, continue to produce exceptional fruit today. Zinfandel’s appeal comes from its versatility. In the glass, it can range from bright and refreshing rosé-style wines to bold, full-bodied reds bursting with flavors of blackberry, raspberry, plum, and spice. Old-vine Zinfandels often reveal layers of complexity, with notes of dried fruit, pepper, and earthy minerality that reflect the character of their historic vineyards. Regions such as Sonoma County, Lodi, Paso Robles, and the Sierra Foothills have become closely associated with outstanding Zinfandel. Winemakers in these areas have championed the grape’s unique personality, often producing small-lot wines that showcase the character of individual vineyards. Among the leading advocates for Zinfandel are producers who have preserved historic vines and traditional winemaking methods. Organizations such as Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) have helped introduce new generations of wine drinkers to the grape through tastings and educational events. Founded in 1991, ZAP began as a group of winemakers, growers, and Zinfandel enthusiasts who wanted to celebrate a grape that was sometimes overlooked in favor of more internationally recognized varieties. At the time, many historic Zinfandel vineyards were being replaced with other grapes, and some producers feared that California’s old-vine heritage could disappear. ZAP helped bring attention to these vineyards and the unique wines they produced. One of ZAP’s most influential contributions was its annual Zinfandel tasting festival, which became one of the largest gatherings in the country devoted to a single grape variety. For many years, the event brought together hundreds of wineries and thousands of wine lovers, creating a community around Zinfandel and giving small producers a national platform. The tastings helped introduce consumers to the diversity of the grape — from elegant, restrained Zinfandels with bright acidity to powerful, fruit-rich versions from old vineyards. Once and Future is the new label of wine icon Joel Peterson. • 2024 Once and Future Zinfandel Teldeschi Vineyard The legendary Joel Peterson, founder of Ravenswood Winery, is hard at work with this new label producing wines from some of the same iconic vineyards he made at Ravenswood. This bottle from Dry Creek Valley’s Teldeschi Vineyard opens with aromas of cherries, chocolate, stone fruit preserves, lavender and blackberries. Medium to full-bodied, it explodes with copious juicy fruits and spicy accents, knit by soft tannins with a long savory finish. Three Wines sources Zin from ancient vineyards in Contra Costa County. • 2018 Three Wine Company Zinfandel Live Oak Vineyard Three Wine Company specializes in wines from ancient (1885) often overlooked vineyards in Contra Costa County. This wine has Petite Sirah and Carignan added to the Zinfandel for complexity. It has aromas of flowers, sweet briery fruit, raspberries, licorice and cherries that emerge from this attractive, dark ruby-colored, medium bodied The Annual Zinfandel tasting was held at Fort Mason Zinfandel. With good sweetness as well as pure fruit, this wellmade stylish effort has eight years of bottle age and is refined and ready to drink. • 2024 Terra Amata Old Vine Zinfandel This wine from the Dry Creek Valley was new to me. It bursts from the glass with a captivating bouquet in which aromas of roses, cherries and wild berries mingle with nuances of spice and forest floor. Full-bodied, satiny, and expansive on the palate, it’s multidimensional, succulent, and juicy, with amazing intensity concluding with a long, perfumed finish. • 2023 Tres Sabores Por Que No? This everything but the kitchen sink blend features Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Cabernet and Petite Verdot. It is a delicious ebullient party wine bursting with blueberry, plum, and cherry flavors. Medium bodied with great acid and tons of finesse it is refreshing and balanced with a clean finish. Fire up the BBQ and throw on the burgers. • 2022 Limerick Lane Zinfandel Banfield Vineyard From an ancient Russian River Valley vineyard planted in 1880 Limerick Lane has created a wine that boasts a dense purple color in addition to a gorgeous nose of leather, spice box, plums and blueberries. It is big and full in the mouth but exquisitely balanced. It is built to last for a decade in the cellar. • 2024 We Know Jack Zinfandel Rockpile The rather new Rockpile AVA has never disappointed me. It is showing itself to be the perfect terroir for Zinfandel. The We Know Jack wine is packed with loads of cassis and blueberry fruit along with pepper, spice, earth and leather. This is a deep, rich, full-bodied, spicy Zinfandel that is immensely satisfying. • 2024 Williams Selyem Zinfandel Papera Vineyard Williams Selyem is so famous for their world-class Pinot Noirs that their Zinfandels can get overlooked. This Russian River Zin shows a sweet nose of black fruits intermixed with smoke, dried herbs and subtle wood. Rich and explosively ripe with a multilayered texture, this exceptional wine can be drunk now or cellared for 5-6 years. • 2023 Guyomar Oblate Hailing from Paso Robles this wine is a blend of Zinfandel, Petite Sirah and Grenache. This is a big muscular gorgeous wine with a dense purple color and lovely levels of blueberry, and raspberry fruit. The wine is an opulent fleshy, classic Zinfandel. Its purity, texture and full-bodied richness are impressive. Drink it over the next five or six years. • 2022 Hendry “Block 28” Zinfandel The always reliable George Hendry crafts his Zins with a high percentage of new French oak which gives a charming exotic vanilla-tinged nose. The Block 28 is a compelling wine graced with expressive dark fruit, flowers, cocoa, and licorice. It shows gorgeous finesse, plenty of mid-palate richness and terrific overall balance. Sweet floral notes and succulent black cherries wrap around the finish. • 2023 Wilson “Snake Patch” Zinfandel The Wilson family of wineries are expert at crafting beautiful fruit-forward Zinfandels. This wine offers copious quantities of Provencal garrigue-influenced plum and blueberry fruit intermixed with earth, pepper and baking spice. This medium to full-bodied luscious heady Zinfandel is delicious and would be a great partner to BBQ’d ribs. • 2023 Robert Biale Zinfandel Pagani Ranch Biale Winery has long been a master at hand crafting powerful yet elegant Zinfandels. This wine shows a sweet nose of black fruits intermixed with smoke, dried herbs and subtle wood. Rich and explosively ripe with a multilayered texture, this exceptional wine can be drunk now or cellared for 4-5 years. • 2022 Harney Lane Zinfandel Lizzy James Vineyard Lodi is the home to this wine whose dense purple color is followed by aromas of sweet, jammy black fruits, licorice, pepper, and minerals. Deep, rich and full-bodied, this impressively extracted wine exhibits moderate tannins, adequate acidity, and an impressive finish. A great example of Lodi’s fruit-forward style of Zinfandel. • 2021 David Clinton Zinfandel Teldeschi Vineyard The David Clinton Zins are a perpetual favorite of mine at ZAP. The wine reveals ripe raspberry and cherry fruit with notions of spice and leather in its fragrant, expressive bouquet. Medium-bodied, with nicely integrated wood, and no hard edges, it will drink well for 5 to 7 years. Rockpile AVA is the source for this Dashe Zinfandel. • 2023 Dashe Zinfandel Rocky Ridge Vineyard This single vineyard Zin from the excellent Rockpile AVA has a splash of Petite Sirah and Carignan added to round out the wine. The wine gets a good dash of new French oak giving it a charming nose of blueberry, anise, black pepper, cassis, herbs de Provence and vanilla. It is a fleshy, juicy wine loaded with ripe dark red fruit, flower, mint and spices. It possesses excellent mid-palate fleshiness in an open accessible personality with great aging potential. • 2022 Perlegos Duetto Inspired by the wines of Sicily the Duetto is a 50/50 blend of Zinfandel and Nero d’Avola. Medium garnet-purple colored, the Duetto gives up very spicy notes of pepper, anise, and cloves over prunes and blackberries with hints of currant jelly and soil. It is full, soft and juicy in the mouth with a chewy frame, great acidity and peppery finish. Very different and fun. • 2021 Grgich Hills Miljenko’s Old Vine Zinfandel This is the estate’s premier Zinfandel from old vines near Calistoga. It is graced with expressive dark red fruit, flowers, mint, and licorice. It shows gorgeous finesse, plenty of mid-palate richness and terrific overall balance. Sweet floral notes and succulent black cherries round out the finish.

pages.text: Wednesday, June 24, 2026 31 Bison Calf Continued from page 1 One of the four new Oakland Zoo bison calves takes a nap by its mom’s side. Although their numbers have grown significantly, wild herds and those in private and public reserves remain genetically isolated. What nature is unable to do naturally at this point, due to decreased genetic diversity and population sizes, Oakland Zoo can provide support through a captive breeding program. “Witnessing the bison roam in their historical lands adds a profound beauty and significance that is difficult to capture without experiencing Montana firsthand. We bring these moments back to our Bay Area community, followers, and the Bay Area indigenous diaspora, truly bringing our mission to life and igniting our passion to continue advocating for this cause,” said Oakland Zoo CEO Nik Dehejia. Guests visiting the Zoo, whether from the Bay Area or around the world, can become part of the story by learning about the program that links culture, history, and animal care. Oakland is just a chapter in the ongoing story of these bison’s future, as the program reconnects them with their sacred land in Montana. “With the birth of its 50th calf, the Oakland Zoo is helping bring home far more than buffalo to the Blackfeet Nation. Together, we are restoring threads that were once severed—between people and place, culture and identity, memory and future—showing what becomes possible when restoration is rooted in relationship,” said Cristina Mormorunni, Executive Director of Indigenous LED. As bison return to Montana – more than 40 since the partnership began – the program continues to advance. Oakland Zoo Animal Care staff work daily in the 13-acre California Trail habitat to deliver gold-standard care to the herd, including enrichment, training, and herd management. The Zoo’s Veterinary Care staff provide medical services, including annual examinations, vaccinations, and hoof care. “We provide the necessary care to ensure a healthy herd of bison until their release, but the Blackfeet care for their soul. We feel privileged and proud to have participated in this journey, with four successful releases. We consider it a great honor to have the trust of our Blackfeet partners. It is an opportunity to be involved in a program that restores a part of a culture that was once taken away,” said Angela Gibson, Zoological Manager at Oakland Zoo. This ongoing effort underscores Oakland Zoo’s commitment and opens a clear path to deepen collaboration with the Indigenous LED organization. The Zoo will partner with tribes to advance conservation action, strengthen the systems that support long-term restoration, and develop the next generation of changemakers — positioning the program as a catalyst for ecosystem recovery and cultural revitalization. For more information on Indigenous LED’s conservation efforts visit: IndigenousLed.org For more information on Oakland Zoo’s Species and Habitats Campaign and the Bison Restoration Program, go to: oaklandzoo.org/habitats. The celebration continued into the weekend as more than 120 kids, parents, and siblings headed to Santa Cruz for an extended coastal adventure. articles.text: They journeyed from Rephidim, entered the wilderness of Sinai, and camped in the wilderness; Israel camped there in front of the mountain. Exodus 19:2 We live in a world of frequent goodbyes. To be human is to say goodbye to places we have come to appreciate, to say goodbye to ways of being we have grown accustomed to, to say goodbye to people we have come to love. As the people of old journey towards Sinai, they must say goodbye to Rephidim. In the biblical narrative Rephidim was a place of both human need and God’s provision. It was a place where humans questioned both God and Moses. They wondered if God knew what God was doing and they wondered if they could trust the leadership of Moses. At Rephidim God provided water to the easily distracted, easily disgruntled congregation. Rephidim was a place of both pain and provision. Inevitably, the people were called to move beyond both the memory of the pain and the security of the provision. They were to move on to new experiences, new challenges and new revelation. They were to move on carrying the lessons they are learned and the experiences they are shared. They were to say goodbye to Rephidim but never to forget it. As the people say goodbye, God, through Moses, tells them that they are being carried on eagles’ wings. As they say goodbye they are promised not protection but presence. One of the most visited exhibits at the 1893 World’s Fair in Chicago was the painting “Breaking Home Ties” by Thomas Hovenden. The poignant scene shows a young man beginning his life’s journey as he bids farewell to his family. Many wept openly before the painting because it portrayed the goodbyes they had come to know so well. We too are a people that have said many goodbyes. There are goodbyes behind us, before us and between us. Let us not take them lightly but let us not let them crush us for, as hard as they are, as real as they are, the eagles’ wings that carry us are also real, the Divine Presence that surrounds us is also real, leading us through, rather than around, our many goodbyes to places of insight, understanding, courage and hope. God bless this broken road of many goodbyes. May our goodbyes be our promise to never forget, to trust in the wings that bear us up. In the closing words of Blest Be the Ties That Bind, “When we asunder part it gives us inward pain. But we shall still be joined in heart and hope to meet again.” Pastor Jim Hopkins is Pastor Emeritus of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church at Lakeshore Avenue and Mandana Boulevard in Oakland.
articles.title: All our goodbyes

All our goodbyes By Pastor Jim Hopkins They journeyed from Rephidim, entered the wilderness of Sinai, and camped in the wilderness; Israel camped there in front of the mountain. Exodus 19:2 We live in a world of frequent goodbyes. To be human is to say goodbye to places we have come to appreciate, to say goodbye to ways of being we have grown accustomed to, to say goodbye to people we have come to love. As the people of old journey towards Sinai, they must say goodbye to Rephidim. In the biblical narrative Rephidim was a place of both human need and God’s provision. It was a place where humans questioned both God and Moses. They wondered if God knew what God was doing and they wondered if they could trust the leadership of Moses. At Rephidim God provided water to the easily distracted, easily disgruntled congregation. Rephidim was a place of both pain and provision. Inevitably, the people were called to move beyond both the memory of the pain and the security of the provision. They were to move on to new experiences, new challenges and new revelation. They were to move on carrying the lessons they are learned and the experiences they are shared. They were to say goodbye to Rephidim but never to forget it. As the people say goodbye, God, through Moses, tells them that they are being carried on eagles’ wings. As they say goodbye they are promised not protection but presence. One of the most visited exhibits at the 1893 World’s Fair in Chicago was the painting “Breaking Home Ties” by Thomas Hovenden. The poignant scene shows a young man beginning his life’s journey as he bids farewell to his family. Many wept openly before the painting because it portrayed the goodbyes they had come to know so well. We too are a people that have said many goodbyes. There are goodbyes behind us, before us and between us. Let us not take them lightly but let us not let them crush us for, as hard as they are, as real as they are, the eagles’ wings that carry us are also real, the Divine Presence that surrounds us is also real, leading us through, rather than around, our many goodbyes to places of insight, understanding, courage and hope. God bless this broken road of many goodbyes. May our goodbyes be our promise to never forget, to trust in the wings that bear us up. In the closing words of Blest Be the Ties That Bind, “When we asunder part it gives us inward pain. But we shall still be joined in heart and hope to meet again.” Pastor Jim Hopkins is Pastor Emeritus of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church at Lakeshore Avenue and Mandana Boulevard in Oakland. pages.text: Wednesday, June 17, 2026 3 Cora Wood Continued from page 1 mont could not be overlooked for the honorary role this year in Piedmont’s largest and most proud city event. “It is an honor, and it is nice to be recognized, I do appreciate that. I’m not the one that usually likes to be on the front line. I like to be in the back, like the caboose pushing the train,” she said with a smile. The parade com mit tee selected Wood to lead the parade on this historic 250th anniversary of the USA. “Over the years, Cora Wood has worked with every department and has helped just about every resident in Piedmont and beyond. Simply put, everyone knows Cora. She is the warm smile that greets you when you walk through the doors of the PRD building, the cheerful voice on the other end of the phone, and the ‘glue’ who has helped make all things PRD feel a little more magical,” said Supervisor Eva Phalen of the Recreation Department and a member of the July 4 parade committee. “I’ve worked with this committee closely for so many years. I respect what they do; they’ve given up so much time and I know that they don’t freely choose just anybody to be Grand Marshal,” said Wood. Wood grew up in Piedmont and first appeared in the parade with the Bluebirds and Campfire Girls when she was a Beach school student. The Rec Department’s rich involvement with the parade has meant that Wood has been to or been a part of around 30 Piedmont parades. Wood helped run the Fourth of July Pancake Breakfast for six years, when the Recreation Department inherited the event from the Montclair-Piedmont Rotary Club. Wood will be on the judging stand this year to vote for the parade winners and she gave some clues to float builders on how to win her favor. “I love the creative ones, and the neighborhood ones. I will vote for the floats that think outside the box,” she said. “Independence Day the Piedmont Way” is the parade theme this year, the 59th annual parade. Wood’s involvement in so many past parades will ensure that this one has that special Piedmont touch. articles.text: Work began on Monday, June 15, as the final phase of the city’s Civic Center parking reconfiguration project. The project constitutes the reconfiguration of Bonita Avenue between Vista and Oakland Avenues. This project will: • Convert the Havens Elementary side of the street from parallel parking to diagonal parking and remove the dropoff zone. • Add two new ADA parking spaces. • Convert this block of Bonita to one-way traffic, going toward Oakland Avenue. When completed, the work will create 17 new parking spaces, split between Permit A (PUSD employee) and time-limited (2-hour). The work is expected to take three to four weeks. Demolition for the new ADA ramp began on Monday. Next week, the city plans to begin grading the ADA spaces and pouring new ramps, and then the final step will be striping and signage. Previous phases of this project included a new drop-off zone on Highland Avenue across the street from Havens Elementary in January, and new time-limited parking spaces on Bonita and Magnolia in April. The city’s stated goals for the Civic Center parking reconfiguration project are to provide a better parking experience for visitors, while also reducing congestion and improving pedestrian safety. The plan was approved by the city council last summer after a series of discussions spanning several council meetings. Construction work starts on Bonita Ave. Construction workers demolish the curb to build a new ADA ramp for Havens School.
articles.title: City begins work on Civic Center parking reconfiguration project

articles.text: Handsome Jonas and Austin are looking for a calm home where they can continue growing into the affectionate companions they’re meant to be. Both one-year-olds start off shy, which makes it extra-rewarding to patiently watch their trust blossom day by day. Jonas is the more playful of the pair. He loves wand toys, treats, and lap time. Although initially quite timid, he transforms into a loving companion who enjoys being part of the action and spending time with people. Austin may hide briefly when he’s feeling nervous, but once he settles in, he’s affectionate, playful, and a truly wonderful friend. He enjoys lounging by the window and pouncing on his favorite toys. Austin also has FIV, so he will need to stay inside, but fear not: cats with FIV can live long, happy lives with routine veterinary care, and can live safely alongside cats without FIV. Adopt Jonas and Austin through Cat Town. These charming, playful boys are looking for a patient adopter and a peaceful environment where they can continue to thrive together. Give them a bit of extra time to settle in and they’ll form a deep bond you’ll cherish. Jonas and Austin are neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV negative. Learn more at www.cattownoakland.org or email adopt@ cattownoakland.org. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council voted unanimously to adopt the proposed budget for FY2026-27 after a second hearing at their regular meeting on Monday, June 15. The budget provisions city funds starting on July 1. The budget, adopted annually, serves as a major policy document and describes how Piedmont intends to finance its services and infrastructure in the coming year. Finance Director Kiran Bawa presented this year’s budget. The budget, first presented in Council Chambers on June 1, features a general fund of approximately $41 million. After a transfer of $1 million to the Facilities Maintenance Fund for deferred maintenance and sidewalk repairs in the coming year and $750,000 to the Capital Improvements Fund, the general fund will experience a Net Loss estimated at $1.0 million. This leaves the city with a projected ending general fund balance of $6.8 million. The Sewer Fund is budgeted for approximately $7.7 million in expenditures, reflecting continued investment in sewer system rehabilitation and critical underground infrastructure improvements. The Sewer Fund accounts for costs associated with the inspection, maintenance, repair, rehabilitation, and replacement of the city’s sanitary sewer system. The fund is projected to begin the year with an estimated balance of $4.6 million and end the year with $2.7 million. After completing the community pool, the budget committee introduced an aquatics fund of $2.4 million. This includes a new full-time Pool Operations Technician position. The city’s financial model projects subsidy independence by FY 2028-29. The budget reflects an increase of $572,756 toward health care benefits. The increase is primarily due to an assumed 5.0% increase in premium rates, which is the biggest driver of expenditures outside the city’s control. The Financial Planning Committee’s written report to Council endorsing the proposed plan states: “The proposed FY 2026- 27 budget reflects another year of meaningful progress toward the city’s long-term strategic priorities, while also recognizing the financial pressures and uncertainties that continue to shape the municipal landscape. Over the past year, the city has advanced several significant capital and operational initiatives that strengthen public infrastructure, improve service delivery, and support community needs.” The committee’s report encourages the city to further plan for the current state of the real estate market. Persistent inflation and elevated interest rates have weakened the housing market and may continue to affect property-related revenues. Approximately 64% of the City’s revenues are tied to property-based taxes. These trends represent a significant fiscal concern. A key priority for the proposed budget will be securing a development partner for the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Along with transitioning new facilities to sustainable long-term operations will require a focus on staffing, service models, managing costs, refining systems based on realworld use, and ensuring these major investments deliver their full potential to the community. The overall budget is meant to embrace priorities presented in a series of city council study sessions, including the completion of the Sidney and Irene Dearing Memorial Project, Sewer Enterprise Fund, street replacement at Piedmont Park, and pedestrian safety improvements.
articles.title: City Council adopts 2026-27 budget

articles.text: Sabrina is a sweet, cuddly, 4-month-old 34-pound Belgian Shepherd Malinois/Mix puppy living in a foster home awaiting adoption. Sabrina is well-mannered and enjoys spending time with her people. She loves snuggling and is happiest when she can be close to her humans. She’s an easygoing puppy with a nice medium energy level. She’s playful without being overwhelming and brings a calm, pleasant presence to the home. Sabrina gets along well with the dogs in her foster home and enjoys having canine companions around. She uses the doggie door to go outside to potty and is continuing to work on being comfortable when left alone. Sabrina can be a little klutzy at times, which only adds to her charm. She also loves sleeping on the couch and relaxing near her favorite Sabrina is a cuddly Belgian Shepherd Malinois/Mix people. To meet Sabrina, submit your adoption questionnaire online on Oakland Animal Service’s website (https:// www.oaklandanimalservices. org/) and you will be contacted by her foster to arrange a meetand-greet. For more information on temporarily fostering a dog or puppy or on adoption, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com.

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council agreed on June 15 to place a measure increasing the property transfer tax rate on Piedmont’s November ballot. The proposed ordinance would increase the transfer tax from 1.3% to 1.75%, better aligning Piedmont’s rate with neighboring cities and generating an additional $1.5 million annually. The ballot measure would require a majority vote to pass. The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee examined funding mechanisms to address the city’s deferred maintenance obligations, capital infrastructure needs, and longterm revenue sustainability. The advisory recommended that the council consider increasing the property transfer tax. If approved by voters in November, this would be the first time Piedmont’s property transfer tax has been changed in 33 years. According to the Financial Planning Committee, around 10% of the total budget is funded by the property transfer tax. The city uses the funds for capital investment and maintenance of aging facilities, buildings, and infrastructure systems. This vote was the first step in the process of placing a measure on the November ballot. A second vote is tentatively scheduled for the council’s July 6 meeting, at which time the council would have the ability to make changes to the proposed new tax rate. The deadline to submit materials to the Alameda County Registrar of Voters for the November ballot is August 7.
articles.title: City Council approves transfer tax increase for the November ballot

articles.text: The “Local Taxpayer Act” is anticipated to be on the ballot for the California statewide election this November. This act would strip charter cities of their authority to impose certain taxes on real estate. Additionally, it would require that all local special taxes obtain two-thirds voter approval, and it would invalidate certain existing taxes that were previously approved by voters. Charter cities can adopt laws concerning “municipal affairs” that differ from state statutes. As a charter city, Piedmont can impose a property transfer tax to generate funds for the city. If this authority is taken away, it would significantly affect Piedmont’s ability to finance facility maintenance and capital improvements. “For the last 15 years, we’ve used the transfer tax to fund important things the city needs to do, like replace equipment, maintain facilities, and provide for capital improvements. Without the transfer tax, the funds we’ve established for those categories would begin to be exhausted,” said budget advisory committee member Robert McBain, a former mayor and city council member. Around 10% of Piedmont’s budget is funded by the property transfer tax, or $4.2 million. Without these funds, the city would have to significantly decrease its investment into facility management, equipment replacement, and capital projects. “There’s not a lot of flexibility in the budget, and if you’re going to take out $4 million, it would significantly impact core operations,” McBain continued. “I think in a couple of years, we will begin to see a deterioration in the city’s physical infrastructure, equipment, and things like that, which will only impede core operations. To say it would be disruptive would be an understatement. It would be disruptive in the short term, and the city’s financial condition would be damaged,” said McBain. To make up for the revenue lost from the removal of the property transfer tax, Piedmont would need to go to voters for tax or fee increases. McBain believes even if the city did this, it would not replace the lost revenue from the transfer tax. The city is part of the California League of Cities, an organization that advocates for the local rights of all cities in California. Currently it is lobbying to remove the act from the November ballot. They sent a letter to the key lawmakers warning that a ballot measure sponsored by the California Business Roundtable and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association could result in local service cuts for Californians. State law allows proponents to withdraw an initiative 131 days before the November general election. Cal Cities is working to remove the initiative before the June 25 deadline.
articles.title: How a November ballot act could negatively impact Piedmont

If approved by voters in November, this would be the first time Piedmont’s property transfer tax has been changed in 33 years. According to the Financial Planning Committee, around 10% of the total budget is funded by the property transfer tax. The city uses the funds for capital investment and maintenance of aging facilities, buildings, and infrastructure systems. This vote was the first step in the process of placing a measure on the November ballot. A second vote is tentatively scheduled for the council’s July 6 meeting, at which time the council would have the ability to make changes to the proposed new tax rate. The deadline to submit materials to the Alameda County Registrar of Voters for the November ballot is August 7. How a November ballot act could negatively impact Piedmont By Jake Lannon The “Local Taxpayer Act” is anticipated to be on the ballot for the California statewide election this November. This act would strip charter cities of their authority to impose certain taxes on real estate. Additionally, it would require that all local special taxes obtain two-thirds voter approval, and it would invalidate certain existing taxes that were previously approved by voters. Charter cities can adopt laws concerning “municipal affairs” that differ from state statutes. As a charter city, Piedmont can impose a property transfer tax to generate funds for the city. If this authority is taken away, it would significantly affect Piedmont’s ability to finance facility maintenance and capital improvements. “For the last 15 years, we’ve used the transfer tax to fund important things the city needs to do, like replace equipment, maintain facilities, and provide for capital improvements. Without the transfer tax, the funds we’ve established for those categories would begin to be exhausted,” said budget advisory committee member Robert McBain, a former mayor and city council member. Around 10% of Piedmont’s budget is funded by the property transfer tax, or $4.2 million. Without these funds, the city would have to significantly decrease its investment into facility management, equipment replacement, and capital projects. “There’s not a lot of flexibility in the budget, and if you’re going to take out $4 million, it would significantly impact core operations,” McBain continued. “I think in a couple of years, we will begin to see a deterioration in the city’s physical infrastructure, equipment, and things like that, which will only impede core operations. To say it would be disruptive would be an understatement. It would be disruptive in the short term, and the city’s financial condition would be damaged,” said McBain. To make up for the revenue lost from the removal of the property transfer tax, Piedmont would need to go to voters for tax or fee increases. McBain believes even if the city did this, it would not replace the lost revenue from the transfer tax. The city is part of the California League of Cities, an organization that advocates for the local rights of all cities in California. Currently it is lobbying to remove the act from the November ballot. They sent a letter to the key lawmakers warning that a ballot measure sponsored by the California Business Roundtable and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association could result in local service cuts for Californians. State law allows proponents to withdraw an initiative 131 days before the November general election. Cal Cities is working to remove the initiative before the June 25 deadline. articles.text: Mira Sachs delivered a speech during the PHS Class of 2026’s Commencement Ceremony as the Student Speaker. Sachs was selected by the school board as a student representative to the board last year, and will attend Vanderbilt University in the fall. It feels strange to be celebrating this huge milestone here in this very spot because, since elementary school, I would celebrate the days I wouldn’t have to be on this track. I hated running the mile, and I wasn’t alone. Most of us would finish each lap begrudgingly, complaining on our way back to class about how we would have to do it again next week. But there were always the kids like Arden Sorensen-Wald and Henry DeVan who not only loved it but wanted to win. Ask them their mile time — I’m sure they still remember it. So you can imagine how I felt at freshman year orientation, sitting right here, when the speakers opened their presentation with the metaphor of running the mile: four laps and four years. And now I get it; the first lap seemed easy, lap two we had to pick up the pace, lap three barely happened but hurt the most, and on lap four all most of us thought about was the end. But now that I’m here, what I’ve discovered is that the best approach isn’t just aiming for the finish line. Even though we are at the end, I know that life will continuously offer us races: to graduate college, to get a dream job, to find a partner, to have a family. Running towards the next finish line is what keeps us sane. But the tendency to divide life into equal segments causes its meaningful moments to get lost. It’s how things inevitably go by too quickly. My mom likes to say that turning 50 is like becoming the freshman of old age — which I disagree with — but we will be freshmen, sophomores, juniors and seniors in some variation for the rest of our lives. Obviously many of us will be freshmen again next year and all the parents in the audience right now are seniors of raising children so congrats to you too, but you’re about to go through freshman orientation of supporting young adults, so don’t go thinking your race is over just yet. And Class of 2026 - neither is ours. There is a circular nature to life and it will continue to unfold as quickly as we let it. Although all of these milestones will be exciting, I do not want to just look forward to the next one. Instead, I have decided that I am going to find the right pace – and I am encouraging you all to find yours. Here are some memories from running the mile that made it more enjoyable, and if applied to life, might make it feel less like a race and more like living. slowed things down for them but it created a stronger moment to remember. So many people in Piedmont have modeled kindness for us. Mr. Hartford regularly makes days feel special with his birthday raps. Dr. Yoshihara greets us with a fist bump and addresses all 179 of us by name. And Ms. Black does exercise breaks in class when she recognizes it’s too early on a Thursday morning for Old English. I couldn’t possibly list all the kindness our mentors here have shown, but those moments stand far apart from all the random days that disappeared in our race to get here today. The next lesson I learned from the mile is that if you’re going to fake an injury, make sure it’s only you and maybe one other friend, not the whole friend group- that’s a dead giveaway. But… I’m not quite sure how that applies to life so let’s move on. My final lesson learned from the mile is to wear what makes you happy. Some people would show up in running shoes and others dared to try something new, running in colorful converse, sparkly sneakers, or if they were really bold, crocs. During our final lap I watched my classmates do exactly that. From impressive outfits, to people decked out in gear for rallies or bright smiles, this class dares to be themselves. Days can blur together if we don’t carefully consider how we show up. Whether that’s attire, attitude, or approach — what matters is being intentional. We’ve had a great run, Class of ‘26, and I’m so grateful to have done these four laps with you. How we showed up on this track said something about who we were becoming, and now, at a new place, in a new chapter, we get to decide that all over again. Running naturally separates people, and not always into usual friend groups - often just by people’s paces. My mile friends weren’t always my usual friends but they were still my speed in a different sense. Running with people outside our usual pack can open our mind to new perspectives and experiences, and takes us away from the comfortable but narrow reality of always engaging with the same few people. Kindness makes experiences more meaningful: At the track, Mr. Wiz and Mr. Best always played just the right music to push us through which also built community. I remember that for one mile someone forgot her sneakers. And the girl’s friend generously offered her one of her sneakers in exchange for the others’ flip flop. Together, they hobbled around the track in mismatched shoes…this literally

articles.text: PHS Salutatorian Niko Kalamas will attend Dartmouth College in the fall. Seniors, here we are on the last day of school. We made it through what we thought might take us forever, and look at the view that we have. Here on the field in the late afternoon, we get to look back on our home upon the hill of the past four years. I think it is unique because it is not often a graduating class gets such a perfect view of where we came from. I am grateful for it. we learned about the chaparral biome we live in and how weather affects our area. In Econ we had the Urban Plan project, bringing tangible opportunities to see how cities like San Francisco get mapped and built. Like PE hill, these challenges gradually got steeper, but we were not fazed and took advantage of the opportunities they presented. Preparation also came through our community. These hikes were only made easier together and allowed us to get to the top while realizing the value of connection. Classes at Piedmont felt more like conversations the older we got, from sharing answers to Mr. Palsa’s warm-up questions to full group discussions about Hamlet with Dr. Marks. Mr. C highlighted his wall of school pennants, showing all of the former students he connected with, and all the counselors always ran through the halls checking in with everyone. That tight-knit environment was what transformed our daunting mountains into rolling hills. This is our last day here. Which means we have more to look forward to. While I could not be more grateful for the climbs Piedmont had to offer, it is time to join our families and staff and look towards what lies next. Graduates, could you please stand up? Now, turn to face the city. Look at that view. Out there are more challenges, more new experiences, more hills. Please now be seated. Our time here has made us conditioned to conquer everything out there and I think I am not alone in feeling grateful for the obstacles ahead. We are all prepared for what lies beyond. Thank you. That hill that might be blocking our classrooms from view has been more than just a feature of the landscape. Over the past four years it has been our favorite obstacle that we learned to overcome. Whether that was on our walk to school, after running the mile during freshman PE, sports events down here at Witter or the baseball field, or going home after Day on the Green, we made this climb a routine in our lives. I am thankful we were tasked with this challenge from day one because it served as good practice for everything that followed. Whether we were aware of it or not, what did follow was preparation for our time beyond high school. In freshman English we were pushed to be curious about the world with the I-Search project. articles.text: For nearly 50 years, Jacqui Birdsong-James has been a beloved part of the Piedmont Adult School community. After nearly five decades of teaching, she is stepping away from her regular schedule, and the school hopes to find an instructor to continue the vibrant fitness community she created. Jacqui started as a physical education instructor at the Adult School in 1977, and has taught classes including body conditioning, jazz and tap dancing. For the past decade she has focused on cardio and strength training, with a devoted following for her popular Thursday morning classes. Over the years, Jacqui has seen fitness trends and technology evolve — from teaching with a 33⅓ record player and stacks of albums to today’s playlists streamed from her phone and portable speaker. But her philosophy has remained constant: helping people stay healthy, strong, and connected. Students know Jacqui not only as an instructor, but as someone who truly cares about them. She has made it a point to memorize every student’s name and take an interest in their lives. “People feel that I see them and appreciate them,” she says. “That makes a difference.” In addition to her long career at Piedmont Adult School, Jacqui served for 20 years as Director of Dance and Music for the City of Oakland, overseeing programs in more than 30 schools throughExercise instructor Jacqui Birdsong-James is retiring from teaching at Piedmont Adult School after 49 years. out Oakland. Later, she worked as General Manager of the Bob Hope Theater and Stockton Arena before retiring from that role in 2008 and expanding her teaching at Piedmont. Although Jacqui is stepping back from her long-running schedule at Piedmont Adult School, she says she is “not fully retiring” and plans to begin exploring the benefits of combining yoga with strength training. Piedmont Adult School is deeply grateful for Jacqui’s decades of dedication, energy, and care for her students. Adult School seeking new fitness instructor As Jacqui begins this next chapter, the school hopes to find an instructor who can build on the welcoming and supportive fitness community she has created. For information about teaching fitness or movement classes for adults, contact the Adult School at (510) 594-2717.

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District has reached tentative agreements extending contracts through 2029 for both the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) and California School Employees Association (CSEA). The new contracts will give teachers and staff 3-4% raises next year, a 3% raise in 2027 and another 3% raise for the 2028-29 year. Teachers voted in favor of the contracts on Friday, June 5 and the board plans to approve the updated agreements in its meeting tonight, June 17. “Nothing short of a miracle. The work required was monumental,” said APT President Elise Marks. “I want to say a profound thank you to the district management negotiating team that worked with APT.” For the 2026-2027 school year, all employees will receive a one-time bonus of $2000. The new contract also works to attract new teachers by bumping up the salary schedule for new teachers in each of their first five years. Previously, teacher salaries were stalled in their first five years. In the previous contract the minimum salary for full-time teachers was $71,576. Next year the minimum salary will increase to almost $74,000, and by 2028- 2029 it will be over $78,000. “These agreements reflect the things that this board and our labor partners have consistently stood for, which are competitive and sustainable compensation, affordable and high-quality healthcare, low class sizes, and the long-term fiscal health of the district,” said School Board President Ruchi Medhekar in the June 3 meeting. Kim Randlett led the negotiating team for the district along with Chief Business Officer Ruth Alahydoian and Stephanie Griffin. Marks thanked the district’s negotiation team for their hours at the table with APT negotiators “really listening, really wrestling with the issue, brainstorming possible solutions and compromises,” she said. “It’s my profound desire to pay teachers, who I believe are chronically underpaid throughout this country, as much as we responsibly can. And I think we’re working on that. I won’t say we’re all the way there, but we’ve made strides,” said board member Max Roman. Teachers were advocating for a return to the 2010 policy of fully-paid family healthcare coverage. The district couldn’t grant that request with rising healthcare costs, but the agreement will increase the district’s contribution to health benefits by 25% over the next two years. This agreement will grant four weeks of paid parental leave within the first year of a new child’s birth, adoption, or the start of foster care. “Most people don’t know that California teachers don’t have access to state disability and don’t get any paid parental leave, so have always had to use up their personal sick leave to stay home even briefly with a newborn,” explained Marks. The agreement does not give teachers their desired hard caps on maximum class sizes, but the parties agreed in principle to try to bring down some of the extreme class sizes. “District administration has clearly been making good faith efforts to do so, and we very much appreciate the changes so far. Students will feel the difference next year,” said Marks about class size. The agreement grants a wish from the parents clubs, and the contract now obliges teachers to make “every reasonable effort” to grade student work “within 15 school days of the due date (or from the date of submission for work accepted late).” This new agreement is projected to cost the district an additional $1,533,765 for teachers and $684,478 for CSEA employees next year. The cumulative increased cost in compensation for both groups for the next three years is projected at $4,581,671 - $1,404,298 for CSEA and $3,177,373 for teachers. articles.text: Piedmont High School seniors participated in the second annual Cap and Gown Day on May 27 by donning their purple graduation attire and heading back to their elementary schools. The students reunited with former teachers at Beach, Wildwood and Havens schools and enjoyed hanging out with elementary school students. The event was started in 2025 by Dean Olliphant and Juliana DeYoung and has quickly become a new tradition. This year the students leading the organization of the event were Luke McAuliffe, Lila Rosen, Grace Alonigreen, Sydney Olson, Zachary Dupree and Vivian Burke Class of 2026 graduates who entered the school district during middle or high school were allowed to pick a school to visit. At Havens, the cap and gown graduates walked around Becker Field as a parade, high fiving the elementary school students and hugging former teachers. At Wildwood the Class of 2026 took over the jungle gym and played games on the blacktop. At Beach, returning graduates sat in their former classrooms but this time took to the front of the room with their teachers. Cap and Gown Day, during the second to last week of school, served as a primer coalescing K-12 memories before saying goodbye to Piedmont schools. PHS graduates from the Class of 2026 returned to Beach Elementary School on May 27 for the second annual Cap and Gown Day. PHS graduates from Wildwood School returned on May 27 to where their education started. Ben Wakefield greets a former teacher at Havens School. Current Beach students face off against former Beach kids in a game of basketball. High school graduates return to play a game of gaga ball with elementary students at Havens School. PHS graduates from 2026 returned to Wildwood’s lower playground to find that the jungle gym looked a little smaller than they remembered.

articles.text: STEM programs are available at Oakland Space Academy this summer Sunday, June 21, marks the official start of astronomical summer in the Northern Hemisphere. This means that the Sun is shining directly on the Northern Hemisphere, and we experience the warm, sunny weather of summer. At Chabot, summer fun is in full swing with plenty of activities and programs. The Oakland Space Academy, the workforce development sector of Chabot, has developed several exciting STEM programs this summer to build knowledge, skills and community. Oakland Space Academy The Oakland Space Academy (the Academy) is Chabot’s STEM workforce development program. The Academy provides high school students and recent high school graduates with the knowledge, skills, and experiences needed to obtain, retain, and advance in education and employment. It helps prepare students for successful transitions into postsecondary education and careers through training, career exploration, work-based learning, support services, and employer engagement. The Academy is offering several exciting courses this summer which will provide students with the opportunity to develop scientific thinking, technical skills, and career readiness through authentic scientific investigation. The Academy’s summer of learning This summer, the Oakland Space Academy is hosting several STEM-based courses for students. Starting on June 22nd, the Academy is beginning a weeklong course called Quantitative Solar Spectroscopy: The Fate of Our Sun. In this course, students will explore ways to learn about the Sun and other stars. Through hands-on investigation, they will learn the principles of spectroscopy, collect and analyze spectral data, and compare the composition and characteristics of our Sun to other stars. Students will also gain firsthand experience using Chabot’s historical telescopes during a nighttime observation session, applying the same techniques scientists use to study objects across our galaxy. Oakland Space Academy courses strengthen foundational STEM knowledge by applying concepts from astronomy, physics, chemistry, mathematics, and data science. Join Chabot’s Summer of Fun For those who are not in the Oakland Space Academy and are within grades 8 to incoming 12th graders, Oakland Space Academy courses are available for enrollment. Visit chabotspace.org for more information about the Academy and to see all Chabot has to offer this summer! Cameron Schneider is with Chabot Space and Science Center in Oakland. articles.text: We’re still getting through the 2026 FIFA World Cup’s opening matches of the Group Stage with some surprises thus far. Perhaps one of the largest revelations happened in Group D with the United States putting a 4-1 whooping on Paraguay and Australia upsetting Turkiye 2-0. Note: Opening matches for Groups J, K, and L were not complete by Post time. Here’s how things are going, starting with the U.S. Group D. Group D: United States (3 points), Australia (3 points), Turkiye (0 points), (0 points) Paraguay How spectacular was the US’ performance against Paraguay. Their quality cannot be undervalued; leading 3-nil at halftime, plus a fourth goal that featured 26 consecutive passes before Gio Reyna’s trivela finish. Paraguay, meanwhile, isn’t bad—they beat Mexico 2-1 back in November. The United States can actually clinch the group by beating Australia this Friday, June 19 and a loss or draw by Turkey against Paraguay. As for the Aussies, we had them finishing third in the Group but could exceed those expectations after its dominant win over Turkey. If they lose to the US, the Socceroos can still get second place in the Group with Paraguay dropping points to Turkey. Group A: Mexico (3 points), South Korea (3 points), Czechia (0 points), South Africa (0 points) Mexico had a strong 2-nil opening win over South Africa, which looked like one of the worst teams in the tournament. South Korea rallied for a 2-1 win over Czechia, keeping my predictions alive. Czechia will now face South Africa, which is looking like a must-win for the European side to make it out of the group. Group B: Switzerland (1 point), Canada (1 point), Qatar (1 point), Bosnia & Herzegovina (1 point) It’s even as it gets for Group B with each of Canada vs. Bosnia, and Qatar vs. Switzerland playing to 1-1 ties. The group returns to action on June 18 with the Swiss facing Bosnia and Canada playing Qatar. I have Switzerland winning the group, Canada taking second, and Bosnia claiming a third-place, and it could certainly go in any direction at this point. Group C: Scotland (3 points), Brazil (1 point), Morocco (1 point), Haiti (0 points) Scotland seized its opportunity over low ranked Haiti with a 1-nil win, while Brazil and Morocco played to a 1-1 draw in one of the most entertaining matches of a very fun Group Stage opening game. I still think Brazil will take control of the group and will handle Haiti on June 19, while Morocco will jump in front of Scotland the same day. Group E: Germany (3 points), Ivory Coast (3 points), Ecuador (0 points), Curaçao (0 points) Germany crushed Curacao 7-1 to take command of the group, but it looks like Ivory Coast will spoil my prediction for the group by beating Ecuador 1-0. Germany faces Ivory Coast on June 20, giving Ecuador a chance to climb back in contention against Curacao. If Ivory Coast can take points against Germany, that may punch their 2E ticket. Group F: Sweden (3 points), Netherlands (1 point), Japan (1 point), Tunisia (0 points) Sweden put an impressive 5-1 stamp on Tunisia to put itself in the conversation to win the group. The Netherlands and Japan, meanwhile, played to a highly entertaining 2-2 draw. I picked Holland to take 1F, Japan in 2F, and Sweden in a third-place spot. The match to watch is the Dutch playing the Swedes on June 20, as it will have a major impact on the group’s outcome. Group G: New Zealand (1 point), Iran (1 point), Belgium (1 point), Egypt (1 point) Group favorites Belgium played to a tightly contested 1-1 tie with Egypt. Iran and New Zealand battled to a 2-2 result and lead the group by goals scored. My prediction is still alive with Belgium facing Iran on June 21, but if they fail to win, it could be all she wrote. Photo courtesy of The Fulcrum Folarin Balogun scored twice for the United States in their big opening 4-1 win over Paraguay.

articles.text: Piedmont Fencing Team is approaching the prestigious Summer National Championships in Portland, Oregon from Sunday, June 28 through Monday, July 6. The club will compete in nine events with six different athletes. Piedmont’s team includes 8th graders Maya Dvoiris and Oliver Lê, PHS freshman Spencer Tsai, Head-Royce freshman Jackson Barrow, Head-Royce 6th grader Surya Velu, and international junior from London, Nathaniel Goff. Goff headlines the group, making his third Nationals appearance and is set to compete in the Division IA Men’s Foil category. Last November Goff placed third of 65 at the AFM Super Regional in Santa Clara in the Division 1A Men’s foil event. “He had a successful first half of the season with a Top 3 finish in Santa Clara, earning his B25 rating. Nathan will be looking for a return to form at US Nationals after an early exit is Paris in February at the CEP Foil Marathon following a concussion after multiple collisions,” said coach David Sinkkonen. South Korea rallied for a 2-1 win over Czechia, keeping my predictions alive. Czechia will now face South Africa, which is looking like a must-win for the European side to make it out of the group. Group B: Switzerland (1 point), Canada (1 point), Qatar (1 point), Bosnia & Herzegovina (1 point) It’s even as it gets for Group B with each of Canada vs. Bosnia, and Qatar vs. Switzerland playing to 1-1 ties. The group returns to action on June 18 with the Swiss facing Bosnia and Canada playing Qatar. I have Switzerland winning the group, Canada taking second, and Bosnia claiming a third-place, and it could certainly go in any direction at this point. Group C: Scotland (3 points), Brazil (1 point), Morocco (1 point), Haiti (0 points) Scotland seized its opportunity over low ranked Haiti with a 1-nil win, while Brazil and Morocco played to a 1-1 draw in one of the most entertaining matches of a very fun Group Stage opening game. I still think Brazil will take control of the group and will handle Haiti on June 19, while Morocco will jump in front of Scotland the same day. Group E: Germany (3 points), Ivory Coast (3 points), Ecuador (0 points), Curaçao (0 points) Germany crushed Curacao 7-1 to take command of the group, but it looks like Ivory Coast will spoil my prediction for the group by beating Ecuador 1-0. Germany faces Ivory Coast on June 20, giving Ecuador a chance to climb back in contention against Curacao. If Ivory Coast can take points against Germany, that may punch their 2E ticket. Group F: Sweden (3 points), Netherlands (1 point), Japan (1 point), Tunisia (0 points) Sweden put an impressive 5-1 stamp on Tunisia to put itself in the conversation to win the group. The Netherlands and Japan, meanwhile, played to a highly entertaining 2-2 draw. I picked Holland to take 1F, Japan in 2F, and Sweden in a third-place spot. The match to watch is the Dutch playing the Swedes on June 20, as it will have a major impact on the group’s outcome. Group G: New Zealand (1 point), Iran (1 point), Belgium (1 point), Egypt (1 point) Group favorites Belgium played to a tightly contested 1-1 tie with Egypt. Iran and New Zealand battled to a 2-2 result and lead the group by goals scored. My prediction is still alive with Belgium facing Iran on June 21, but if they fail to win, it could be all she wrote. Boys’ Swimming 200 medley team places ninth at CIF State Piedmont High’s boys’ swimming team put together a monster 2026 spring campaign. Nik Costello proved to be a vital part of the boys’ swimming team’s record-setting year as a senior leader of the bunch. He helped lead Piedmont High’s 200 medley relay team to the CIF State Championship on May 16, coming away with the school’s firstever medal in the prestigious meet’s 12-year history, placing ninth of 18 schools with a time of 1:33.56 alongside Asher Takazawa, Connor Carnazzo, and Jeffrey Latronica. We named Costello our boys’ honorable mention for Athlete of the Year, while Carnazzo and Latronica were our Co-Freshmen of the Year. Lucas Smolko wins Div. 2 NCS singles title Tennis player Lucas Smolko won the school’s first North Coast Section Individual Tournament singles title since Barry Gilbert in 1975 by claiming the D2 crown on May 9. He shutout St. Patrick’s Oscar Swenson 6-0, 6-0 in the opening round, won 6-1, 6-4 over Armaan Mishra of Lick-Wilmerding in the quarterfinals, and beat Stuart Hall’s Edward Morfit 6-1, 6-0 in the semifinals. To get there, they defeated Naomi Lin and Caroline Sue of Alameda 6-4, 6-4 in the semifinals, won 7-6 (7-2), 6-3 over No. 4 seed Fiona Wood and Sloane Kau of Bishop O’Dowd in the quarterfinals, and opened the tournament with a heated 4-6, 6-2, 14-12 win over Berkeley’s Esra Abarbanel and Vera Ertel.
