articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School softball team’s season came to a close as the team faced off against two big rivals in back-toback games. On Tuesday, May 26, the Scots took the field one last time in the East Bay Middle School League Championship against rivals from across Hwy 13, the Montera Middle School Toros. After a rousing rendition of the National Anthem led by player representatives from each team, the game got underway. As was often the case throughout the season, pitching was once again the star of the show as 8th grade aces Madi Farboud and Bailey Gregovich would end up throwing a combined no-hitter through six nail-biting innings. The duo stifled the Toros normally potent offense allowing zero earned runs and posting nine strikeouts against a team that previously averaged 13 runs per game. The score was tied 2-2 through six innings thanks to aggressive base running from Bailey Gregovich and 6th grader Cate Penrod, who each took advantage of some sloppy throws to score on close plays at the plate. The Scots dugout was charged up as the game headed to the extra frame but alas their championship dreams would be undone by a passed ball and a fielder’s choice that allowed the winning run for Montera to score in the bottom of the seventh. Also on Monday, May 25, they played an annual exhibition game that once again pitted the players against the parents and coaches in a Memorial Day matchup at Witter field. With the all-time series knotted at 1-1, the Non-Kids looked to have a secure 8-3 lead heading into the final inning before giving up 5 runs in an error-filled 5th that ended the game in a tie. The adults still claimed a moral victory however as all were able to leave the field under their own power and injury-free. The 2026 softball season represented only the second year of the Middle School program. The Scots closed the season as the runner-up in both leagues that they played in this season, finishing 13-4, and they were the only team to win a match against the Toros (16-1). As the 8th grade leaders Abby Gregovich, Bailey Gregovich, Madi Farboud, Sarina Hill, and Simone Tornatore move on to Piedmont High School next year, the Scots look forward to continued strong contributions from players like rising 8th grader Mackenzie Ewen (.515 avg/16 RBI) and rising 7th graders, Keira Spina (.462 avg/12 RBI) and Clara Blanchard (10 RBI) next spring. Pitchers Madi Farboud (left) and Bailey Gregovich threw a combined no-hitter against Montera. Mackenzie Ewen hit .515 in her second season with the Scots. Piedmont Middle School athletes, parents, and supporters gather for a group photo at an exhibition game on Tuesday, May 26.
articles.title: PMS Softball’s stellar season comes to a close in championship game

articles.text: Yaxel Lendeborg The 2026 NBA season has officially come to an end with the New York Knicks crowned as this year’s champions. Now that the finals are behind us, the sporting world is looking toward the NBA Draft. The first round takes place on June 23, with the second round on the following day. As the Warriors reach the end of the Steph Curry era, the margin of error is shrinking, and the need to get this draft right is paramount. They missed the playoffs this past season after losing to the Phoenix Suns in the play-in tournament. The team’s needs include wing depth, a center, and a shooting guard. Below are three names the Warriors should consider at the eleventh pick to address their needs. 1. Yaxel Lendeborg Forward, Michigan Lendeborg is best known for leading Michigan to the NCAA championship this past season. He’s 6’8 and plays a mix of small forward and power forward. He averaged 15 points, seven rebounds, and three assists per game, while shooting 51% from the field. Scouts say Lendeborg is an all-around player who can defend at a very high level, and space the floor with his threepoint shot. The only downside to Lendeborg is his age. At 23 years old, many believe there isn’t much more development for him, and he’s likely close to his ceiling. Lendeborg addresses a serious need for wing talent on the Warriors roster and can play right away on a team that’s hoping to get back into the playoff hunt. 2. Aday Mara Center, Michigan Mara is a 7’3 center who was an integral part of Michigan’s title-winning season. Mara averaged 12 points, seven rebounds, two assists, and two blocks per Photo courtesy of University of Michigan game. His best trait is his ability to protect the rim. He’s expected to immediately be one of the best rim-protecting big men in the NBA. Mara’s ability to pass has impressed many scouts, who don’t often see a seven-foot big guy able to pass like a point guard. Mara’s defensive dominance and offensive upside provide the Warriors with a legit center that they haven’t had since 2016 with Andrew Bogut. Photo courtesy of University of Arizona Brayden Burries 3. Brayden Burries Shooting Guard, Arizona Burries stands out as a scoring shooting guard with the potential to be a secondary point guard. He averaged 16 points, five rebounds, and 2 assists per game while shooting 39% from threepoint range. According to many scouts, Burries’ best attribute is his shooting ability. He has a quick first step when driving towards the rim and doesn’t shy away from contact. He would fit nicely into the Warriors’ starting lineup next to Steph Curry. As the Warriors look to address numerous needs through this offseason, fans can only hope general manager Mike Dunleavy Jr. gets it right. Aday Mara Photo courtesy of University of Michigan

articles.text: Hiking with Jon has returned for the summer months, starting the summer series with a batch of hikes around the popular summer getaway for Bay Area residents at Lake Tahoe. Eagle Lake is a 0.9 mile outand-back trail near Emerald Bay and South Lake Tahoe, making just 1.8 miles of hiking to a quiet and awe-striking alpine lake. It is considered a moderately challenging route with 429 feet of elevation gain and a starting point of 6,570 feet in elevation. It’s considered a very popular trail with hundreds of visitors each day given the proximity to South Lake Tahoe just 10 miles away. Parking off of CA-89, the day starts with a jaunt past Eagle Falls, a huge cascading waterfall along Eagle Creek that feeds into Lake Tahoe. You’ll walk alongside Eagle Creek as you trek toward Eagle Lake. After a healthy winter of snow, the foliage around Lake Tahoe is lush with vegetation. Eagle Lake trail takes hikers beneath groves of pine trees, while there are portions with beautiful views of Emerald Bay beneath you for when you’d like to catch a breath. Eagle Lake requires entering the Desolation Wilderness, which you can get a permit for near the parking lot. Given the amount of foot traffic, hiking in the morning is your best bet if you want to avoid a highway of hikers. There are portions less than three-feet wide, which will require patience at times when passing others. It’s an achievable hike to see a frozen lake in the winter and spring months. Visiting in May, Eagle Lake still was covered in a thin layer of frost and ice. More adventurous minds have taken their ice skates during the winter time to skate across the hard frozen surface. Punch “Eagle Falls” or “Eagle Falls Lake” into your GPS device to find this hike. In the coming weeks, the Post will provide two more trails around South Lake Tahoe before heading to the northern side for three more trails. Return next week when we cover the Rubicon Trail around Emerald Bay. The bark of a pine tree with a slushy Eagle Lake behind. A blue jay poses for a picture by Eagle Lake. The Eagle Lake trail starts after passing Eagle Falls, a magnificent cascade down Eagle Creek into Lake Tahoe.
articles.title: HIKING WITH JON Eagle Lake, a pristine alpine lake near Lake Tahoe’s Emerald Bay

articles.text: An exhibition featuring work by Oakland-based artist Demetri Broxton, entitled Demetri Broxton: Ancestral Echoes, is on view now at the Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco. Broxton is one of four artists selected as part of MoAD’s 10th cohort of annual Emerging Artists Program (EAP) for 2026- 2027. The 2026-2027 awardees were selected from hundreds of applicants and present single artist shows at MoAD from now through early 2027. “Each of the 2026-2027 recipients have a deep reverence for ancestral legacies, Black futurity, and the interplay of personal and collective histories,” Key Jo Lee, MoAD Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs, said in a press release. “Their exhibitions at MoAD will be significant contributions to their respective mediums, and represent crucial milestones for their long-term practices.” Ancestral Echoes is an ongoing body of work that traces the Demetri Broxton artist’s family’s movement across the American South to Oakland. Broxton, who is of Louisiana Creole and Filipino heritage, uses screen-printed textiles, beadwork, cowrie shells, sequins and other materials connected to African diasporic spirituality. “I place my ancestors into new visual and spiritual contexts— ones that center dignity, protection, and possibility,” Broxton said. “Sequins and beads function as both adornment and armor, transforming each portrait into a site of reverence, where absence becomes space for reimagining.” Broxton’s exhibition is on view now through August 16. Visit https://www.moadsf.org/ exhibitions/ancestral-echoes for more information.
articles.title: Demetri Broxton: Ancestral Echoes on view now at MoAD

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Oakland Museum of California Oakland artist DJ Kream will perform at OMCA’s “Juneteenth! at the Museum,” a full-day cultural celebration, this Friday. Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) is celebrating Juneteenth this Friday, June 19, with live performances, a local artisan market, family-friendly activities and more. OMCA partners with the Black Freedom Fund, a philanthropic foundation supporting Black grassroots movements for racial justice, to present “Juneteenth! at the Museum,” a fullday cultural celebration. From 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., visitors may enjoy food and refreshments for purchase from a variety of Pan-African and Black diasporic cuisine, including Mela Bistro, Pound Bizness, Cocobreeze and more. A VIP ticket purchase includes access to OMCA’s Juneteenth Jubilee VIP, an all-inclusive Juneteenth experience featuring a catered buffet, indoor and outside lounge seating, a specialty welcome cocktail, a complimentary photo booth and more. Soul line and turf dance lessons will be offered to visitors of all ages from 12:30 p.m. to 3 p.m. in the museum’s amphitheater. Sons of the Sweet Science, a community storytelling project by filmmaker Renee Moncada that explores fatherhood and legacy, hosts an interactive activation where patrons can learn about the documentary series while engaging with community stories from Oakland. The museum’s latest exhibition, Mildred Howard: Poetics of Memory, will be on view alongside special festival programming. Visit https://museumca.org/ event/juneteenth-at-the-museum/ for a full festival lineup and to purchase tickets. Festival access begins at 11 a.m.
articles.title: Celebrate Juneteenth at OMCA this Friday

articles.text: Free performance held at Zellerbach Hall The 2026 cohort of the 24th annual Berkeley/Oakland AileyCamp performs its final showcase on July 23 at Zellerbach Hall on UC Berkeley’s campus. The full-scholarship dance camp is held over six weeks throughout the summer, offered to middle school students primarily from the Berkeley, Oakland, Richmond, and Albany unified school districts. The camp builds on Cal Performances’ nearly six-decade relationship with Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater. The dance company has regularly performed at Zellerbach Hall, appearing on UC Berkeley’s campus more than any other place in the world outside of their home base in New York City. Broxton is one of four artists selected as part of MoAD’s 10th cohort of annual Emerging Artists Program (EAP) for 2026- 2027. The 2026-2027 awardees were selected from hundreds of applicants and present single artist shows at MoAD from now through early 2027. “Each of the 2026-2027 recipients have a deep reverence for ancestral legacies, Black futurity, and the interplay of personal and collective histories,” Key Jo Lee, MoAD Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs, said in a press release. “Their exhibitions at MoAD will be significant contributions to their respective mediums, and represent crucial milestones for their long-term practices.” Ancestral Echoes is an ongoing body of work that traces the Demetri Broxton artist’s family’s movement across the American South to Oakland. Broxton, who is of Louisiana Creole and Filipino heritage, uses screen-printed textiles, beadwork, cowrie shells, sequins and other materials connected to African diasporic spirituality. “I place my ancestors into new visual and spiritual contexts— ones that center dignity, protection, and possibility,” Broxton said. “Sequins and beads function as both adornment and armor, transforming each portrait into a site of reverence, where absence becomes space for reimagining.” Broxton’s exhibition is on view now through August 16. articles.text: Henri Matisse’s Femme au chapeau is the highlight of SFMOMA’s newest exhibition. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is presenting a new exhibition focused on Henri Matisse’s Femme au chapeau, a painting widely regarded as a landmark of modern art. The exhibition, titled Matisse’s Femme au chapeau: A Modern Scandal, opened May 16 and is on view through September. The exhibition examines the history, reception and lasting influence of the 1905 portrait, which is part of SFMOMA’s permanent collection. The painting debuted at the Salon d’Automne in Paris in 1905 and became associated with Fauvism, the first French avantgarde art movement of the 20th century. The exhibition explores the work’s historical context, subject, provenance and circulation through exhibitions and publications, while also considering its impact on later generations of artists. “We are thrilled to have this opportunity to share the full story of Matisse’s Femme au chapeau—a painting that is emblematic of the artist’s radical break from convention in the early years of his career,” Janet Bishop, SFMOMA Chief Curator, said in a press release. “Arguably SFMOMA’s most art-historically significant work of art, Femme au chapeau began sending shockwaves through the art world as soon as it left Matisse’s studio and has captivated viewers ever since,” Bishop added. The exhibition also traces the painting’s ownership history. American collectors Leo and Gertrude Stein acquired the work in 1905 while living in Paris. It later entered the collection of Michael and Sarah Stein, who brought it to the Bay Area in 1935. The painting was first exhibited in the United States at the San Francisco Museum of Art, now SFMOMA, in 1936. It entered the museum’s collection in 1991 through a bequest from Elise S. Haas. “Part of our vision at SFMOMA is to encourage our visitors to see the world—and art—in new ways,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “With stunning paintings by Matisse and his peers, as well as work by some of the most exceptional artists working today, this exhibition promises to captivate SFMOMA visitors this spring.” Visit https://www.sfmoma. org/ for more information. ®

articles.text: The Orinda Starlight Village Players began their 2026 season on June 5 with the Bay Area premiere of Agatha Christie’s The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, adapted for the stage by Mark Shanahan. The play is set in an English village in 1926 where gossip is the local currency. When the widowed Mrs Ferrars is found dead by apparent suicide and shortly after he fiancé, the most prominent man in town – Roger Ackroyd, is found dead the rumors start to run rampant and the local police are stumped. However, it just so happens that the villages newest resident is world famous detective Hercule Poirot, who sets out to find the truth and find the murderer. The production is directed and designed by Matt Cardigan Smith and features local Piedmont resident Maya Rath as Gertrude Ackroyd. Other local performers include Patrick Atkinson, Wayne Goodman, Kelsey Bye, Mimi Hamilton, and Matt Hess. The play runs until July 3 at the Orinda Community Park Amphitheatre. For more information and to purchase tickets, go to www.orsvp.org. articles.text: The San Francisco Opera celebrates Pride Month on Friday, June 26 at the War Memorial Opera House, featuring a program of opera, musical theater and popular music alongside community exhibits, discussions and a post-concert dance party. The event will be hosted by drag performer, opera singer and composer Sapphira Cristal, who returns as emcee following last year’s inaugural concert. Conductor Robert Mollicone will lead the San Francisco Opera Orchestra and soloists Melody Moore, Nikola Printz and Reginald Smith Jr. The concert will feature works by composers and artists including Michael Abels, Terence Blanchard, Brandi Carlile, Umberto Giordano, Charles Gounod, k.d. lang, Jacques Offenbach, Stephen Schwartz, Michael Tilson Thomas, Luther Vandross and Stevie Wonder. The evening’s activities begin at 6:30 p.m. before the performance with a pride-themed altar created by the Marigold Project, a happy hour, educational exhibits and a pre-concert discussion featuring creators of the Rainbow Pride Flag Project. Additional displays will be presented by the GLBT Historical Society, the Hand Bookbinders of California and the National AIDS Memorial, which will exhibit panels from the AIDS Memorial Quilt. The concert begins at 8 p.m. Following the performance, attendees can participate in a dance party featuring DJ Juanita MORE!. The Pride Concert is part of a broader weekend of Pride celebrations for the company. On June 28, members of San Francisco Opera will join other arts organizations in the 56th annual San Francisco Pride Parade along Market Street. Visit https://www.sfopera. com/seasons/pride-concert-2026/ to purchase tickets. The War Memorial House hosts its second Pride concert on Friday, June 26.
articles.title: San Francisco Opera presents Pride Concert on June 26

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Michael Stehr Artist and art historian Michael Stehr’s recent lecture on Monet in Venice was brilliantly informative. The information should be factored into every musical performance. Discovering the interconnection of the arts can be a challenge. Sometimes the discovery is made obliquely. That was the case on Saturday afternoon during a lecture by the gifted artist and art lecturer Michael Stehr who grew up in Piedmont. Saturday’s lecture was about Monet in Venice. You could take it at face value, and walk away with the information that Monet was a great artist. That’s enough for lots of people. But Michael Stehr opened the world of the arts to his audience. He enlightened his audience in a marvelous way by making us understand exactly why Monet was representative of great art. We would be wise to apply Stehr’s vocabulary across the horizon of the musical arts. It would also be valuable to apply Sigmund Freud’s insights into the visual arts and in particular the musical arts. When we listen to music, we should ask ourselves: “Where is the poetry? Where is the romance? Where is imagination and inspiration? Does the performance have universality?” Perfection is important in gemstones and it increases the value of a diamond exponentially. But redundant perfection lacks humanity, which is so needed in the art of music. Saturday concert at PCA It was fun to apply this knowledge to the concert on Saturday evening in the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Clarinetist John Zorn and pianist Daniel Lockert presented a celebration of American music. Almost all of the music had a fresh quality. Leonard Bernstein’s first published work appeared early in the program. The opening was a bit stodgy musically, but it became more interesting as it progressed. During the intermission, I had a chance to look at the musical score. It is immensely difficult rhythmically. The audience would never know, because the performance was played with great ease. Next came two pieces by George Gershwin. “Promenade” which is also known as “walking the dog” is as cute as it can be. After intermission came the delightful “American Standard” by Michael Kaulkin. In general this composition is a very pleasing work. It has widely varied sections, which are completely unified. Its graceful conclusion added immeasurably. The composer was seated directly behind me and we had the opportunity to discuss many things. The audience responded warmly and took everything to heart. The two performers selected Harold Arlen’s beautiful song “Over the Rainbow” as their encore. Music performance should envision all of the colors of a Monet painting. This concert certainly did. articles.text: Finnish choir Vox Aurea Vox Aurea choir, established in 1968, is the flagship choir of the City of Jyväskylä’s education services in Finland. The choir is attending the Golden Gate International Choral Festival hosted by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. Vox Aurea’s spotlight performance is on July 17 at the Central Chinese High School Victory Hall in San Francisco. The choir will also participate in the group performances on the opening and closing nights. The choir has participated in numerous national and international competitions, receiving several awards. Vox Aurea has also released numerous recordings that showcase the diversity of choral music. The choir is made up of 50 singers aged 11 to 19. Before joining Vox Aurea, these singers usually perform in preparatory choirs that are open to children as young as three. The choir’s vocal coach is Josefiina Fagerlund. Alongside its educational work, Vox Aurea actively engages in local, national, and international collaboration, while also promoting Finnish and international choral music. Commissioning new works from contemporary composers is an established part of the choir’s activity. Their most recent recording, Pato (released in December 2020), features a collection of works commissioned by Vox Aurea during the 2010s. Sanna Salminen became the conductor of Vox Aurea in 2009. Salminen has worked for the choir since 1998 as the voice trainer and assistant conductor, collaborating intensively with Pekka Kostiainen, the previous conductor. Salminen works as a university teacher at the Department of Music, Art and Culture Studies at the University of Jyväskylä. In 2014, Salminen was awarded the Golden Medal of Merit of the Finnish Youth Choirs Association. In the anniversary year of Vox Aurea in 2018, Salminen was awarded the Heinz Hofmann Medal of the Finnish Youth Choirs Association and the Medal of Merit of the Sulasol Central Finland District. Collaboration with youth choirs from different countries is an essential part of Vox Aurea’s work. Through these exchanges, the choir has broadened its repertoire, deepened its understanding of choral traditions across cultures, and further developed its pedagogical and strategic practices. In recent years, Vox Aurea has had the privilege of working with choreographer Daniel Raaflaub from Basel, Switzerland, whose contribution has elevated the choir’s expressive performance to a new level. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival takes place from July 13 to July 18. Information on the concerts and spotlight choirs can be found on their website, including which concerts are free or have paid admission for the public. https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ggf-concerts-2026.
articles.title: Finnish choir to perform in International Choral Festival

articles.text: Curry Barker’s record-breaking indie film follows a music store employee (Michael Johnston) that makes a wish for his friend Nikki (Inde Navarette) to fall in love with him, only for it to go terribly wrong. The movie gained traction when a short clip of Inde Navarette’s acting earned thousands of views on TikTok and Instagram, translating to over 280 million dollars in the box office. The emotional outburst that made an impact on scrollers is only a glimpse into Barker’s twisted, supernatural world. If you are a fan of horror, this is a film that you will want to go watch. Just remember to be careful what you wish for… There are many choices that the filmmakers put in place to create an unsettling atmosphere. The color grading is one of those choices. While many films in the genre often use muted or cold tones, Obsession takes a different approach. The movie is colorful, and its shots are often warmly tinted, especially in yellow. It feels almost unnatural, which provides foreshadowing to the film’s events. Then there’s the use of shadow, and the use of silence, which both make the viewer uneasy before (and during) big scares. From these trends to the tiny details, it is clear that a lot of thought has gone into the film. Production, however, is just one piece of the puzzle. What really makes the movie such an Inde Navarrette and Michael Johnston in Obsession unexpected success is the stellar acting. Navarette’s strongest point is her facial expressions: under the influence of the wish, her smile (often put up around Bear, Johnston’s character) looks unnatural, and her deep frown is even creepier. Her “obsession” is apparent, but the wrongness of it all is made even more clear by the way she moves around the world. It is safe to say that she terrified everyone in the theater, and at the same time, the viewer couldn’t help but feel bad for the person under the enchantment. Put together, the response was clear. articles.text: The acclaimed post-apocalyptic film The Road is based on the Pulitzer Prize-winning novel by Cormac McCarthy (2006) whose spare prose and remarkable story telling has often been adapted for the screen by Hollywood’s directors and writers. When this film released in 2008, it received multiple nominations and awards, while some critics opined that it affirmed that film was an extraordinary medium, a nexus of sorts, able to capture and reflect upon the human condition. It was an art. Essential to that art were the actors who inhabit a character with all attendant emotions and reactions, no matter the context and range. Viggo Mortensen portrays Papa/the father, and Kodi Smit-McPhee is his young son, each are each remarkable as was the cameo appearance by Charlize Theron as the wife and mother. Viggo Mortensen and Kodi Smit-McPhee in The Road The film was was shot by cinematographer Javier Aguirresarobe, who captured its haunting, stark images with a kind of counter-intuitive depth and beauty. As the story unfolds, we realize that what has occurred is revealed only through the father and son’s journey, making their way along this post-apocalyptic road. They push a shopping cart that contains all they possess (the father does carry a hidden revolver with only two bullets in its chambers). Both are gaunt, their clothes little more than frayed rags; they are walking south, toward an ocean they can only imagine. The sky is leaden, forbidding, the forests blackened by fires, and enormous trees suddenly crash to the ground. A cold, misty rain follows them. The father is stalked by a relentless cough, his restless sleep haunted by fevered dreams of the past, his thoughts shared in a halting voice-over. Both are ever in search of food, and remain apprehensive, watching, always alert when passing through abandoned homes and broken towns. Those few who have survived can suddenly appear, some driven by panic and fear, others by an absence of all restraint and any semblance of humanity, their desperation framed by the unthinkable. And so, father and son walk on, nurturing a fragile hope. The boy, having seen more than any child can comprehend, asks his father: “Papa, we’re still the good guys, aren’t we?” His question, a need to know – do they still possess a morality that for those they encounter has long ago been discarded now ruled by a Darwinian struggle to survive. If you’re reading the above and wondering why you should seek out tis film, perhaps questioning why it would be critically praised, well, I understand. But post-apocalyptic films, some touching on sci-fi, are a solid, perhaps nihilistic filmmaking genre. Many are cautionary tales, asking the audience to consider the unintended consequences of our collective actions and behaviors and their aftermath. If the earth is our mother, are we slowly, inexplicably committing matricide? The Road. Directed by John Hillcoat. With Viggo Mortensen, Kodi Smit-McPhee, Charlize Theron. Based on a book by Cormac McCarthy. 1 hr., 59 min. Rated R. Released in 2008. Now streaming on Prime/YouTube/ Fandango/Hulu.

pages.text: Wednesday, June 17, 2026 19 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Obsession: A scare of a lifetime By Mira Sen Curry Barker’s record-breaking indie film follows a music store employee (Michael Johnston) that makes a wish for his friend Nikki (Inde Navarette) to fall in love with him, only for it to go terribly wrong. The movie gained traction when a short clip of Inde Navarette’s acting earned thousands of views on TikTok and Instagram, translating to over 280 million dollars in the box office. The emotional outburst that made an impact on scrollers is only a glimpse into Barker’s twisted, supernatural world. If you are a fan of horror, this is a film that you will want to go watch. Just remember to be careful what you wish for… There are many choices that the filmmakers put in place to create an unsettling atmosphere. The color grading is one of those choices. While many films in the genre often use muted or cold tones, Obsession takes a different approach. The movie is colorful, and its shots are often warmly tinted, especially in yellow. It feels almost unnatural, which provides foreshadowing to the film’s events. Then there’s the use of shadow, and the use of silence, which both make the viewer uneasy before (and during) big scares. From these trends to the tiny details, it is clear that a lot of thought has gone into the film. Production, however, is just one piece of the puzzle. What really makes the movie such an Welcome to the Piedmont Center for the Arts Inde Navarrette and Michael Johnston in Obsession unexpected success is the stellar acting. Navarette’s strongest point is her facial expressions: under the influence of the wish, her smile (often put up around Bear, Johnston’s character) looks unnatural, and her deep frown is even creepier. Her “obsession” is apparent, but the wrongness of it all is made even more clear by the way she moves around the world. It is safe to say that she terrified everyone in the theater, and at the same time, the viewer couldn’t help but feel bad for the person under the enchantment. Put together, the response was clear. Sitting in the theater, it was common to hear gasps, whispers, and even screams. To be fair, a lot of them were coming from me. It provided the scare of a lifetime, and while I wouldn’t bring my younger brother or my grandmother to see it (definitely NOT family friendly) I did enjoy it. Obsession is projected to stay in theaters into July, around a month longer than originally slotted. Its extended run is a testament to the fact that audiences are loving it, and it is absolutely worth watching if you enjoy being terrified, if you’re brave enough. Be sure to catch it at the Landmark Theater on Piedmont Avenue or the Grand Lake before its run ends. Obsession. Directed by Curry Barker. Starring Michael Johnston, Inde Navarrette, Cooper Tomlinson, Megan Lawless and Andy Richter. Released in 2026. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated R. articles.text: Nathan Rivera and Jessie Andra Smith bring an unforgettable trilingual performance of swingin' bluesy jazzy folk. The duo has traveled all over the world, sharing their music on streets and stages with their unique sound. A fusion of jazzy folk and blues on resonator guitars and accordion, with an interesting interplay of harmonies between the two voices. Upbeat tunes rooted in the spirit of jazz, improvisation, storytelling, and humor.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group gathered last Wednesday at the Exedra on a warm morning that was forecast to be a “Piedmont hot” day. There was a large turnout of 50 walkers and five K-9 best friends in attendance. The big turnout owed to the day’s destination: a pool party. The group hadn’t been up to the Huntleigh and Lexford loop off Hampton Road this year, and walker and realtor Stacey Isaacs had a home for sale at 11 Huntleigh Road. She wanted to show the group the house and its swimming pool. The walkers started off behind the Exedra, past the Community Hall and Tea House, and up the Highland-Guilford steps in the upper part of Piedmont Park. They emerged on Highland Avenue, crossed it, and walked the path along the long strip of grass that was once a Key System train right of way. Parked in front of the grass was one of the biggest moving vans most walkers had ever seen. The group continued up Sheridan Avenue to Wildwood Avenue, the Hall Fenway, Crocker Avenue, and Hampton Road. Along Hampton, just before Sea View Avenue, a construction project was underway. A big, deep space had been carved out of the land next to a house. The walkers guessed it might be an ADU, but a worker said no, it would be a new garage. The group went up Hampton to Hampton Park and regrouped there. Everyone said they wanted to make the climb up Hampton to Huntleigh Road and see Stacey’s listing, so off they went. They crossed LaSalle Avenue and passed through the two large white columns that marked the main entrance to the early 20th century St. James Wood real estate development. They went up the development’s signature terracotta tile inlay sidewalks to Hampton’s corner with Lexford Road, where they came to the first of two very large and beautiful southern magnolia Piedmont Heritage Trees. These trees are native to the southeastern United States, and Piedmont has many of them throughout the city. Just one block further up Hampton, at Huntleigh, the group came to the second southern magnolia. Huntleigh forms a big loop with Lexford Road, and there was some initial uncertainty about which way to go to find Stacey’s house. But Stacey was calling to the group from in front of the home, and that confirmed left was right. The walkers regrouped at the house, and Stacey told them about it. This 3,608 square foot home has four bedrooms and four and a half bathrooms, was built in 1955, and is listed for $2,995,000. However, based on what other Piedmont homes have been selling for this year, it could sell for more. It has a stone breezeway entrance with vaulted ceilings. There is a formal living room, a family room, and a gourmet kitchen. The primary suite has treetop views, and there is a patio, garden, and the pool. Stacey said that as part of the house staging, her staging company has the artwork on the walls for sale too. She invited the group inside to take a look and to enjoy some thoughtfully provided water and energy-generating donut holes. The walkers were impressed with all aspects of the inside of this lovely home, and also with the backyard pool that they circled for a group photo. They relaxed, enjoyed themselves, and had their pool party. articles.text: Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on October 13, 2021 One of the delights that comes from walking around town is discovering and actually reading the many commemorative plaques located in Piedmont. Apparently originating in the Middle Ages, historical interest groups at all levels of governments all over the world seem to have their own commemorative system of celebrating the connection of a location with a special event, person or structure. These range from a very coordinated, consistent aesthetic such as on the blue ceramic heritage plaques found throughout all of England, to the more common mixed styles found in the U.S. including Piedmont. Since the majority are quite often outside in the weather, what they all have in common is durability. Many are made of different long lasting materials such as bronze, marble, stone and zinc to name a few. Brass is however probably the most common material because of its shiny, gold-colored appearance, strength and low maintenance. Historical plaques are most often mounted to a wall, One of the most interesting “historical” plaques in town is the one marking the Piedmont Community Church’s time capsule. Buried in the main courtyard arcade, it is scheduled to be unearthed in 2035. large stone or other vertical surface. However, like many things in our age of more information and resulting reevaluation, commemorating history can now be a contentious issue. When we find out more about the dark side of celebrated historical figures, what has resulted in some cases is the removal of older plaques and statues—sometimes rightly so. This suggests that a more thorough evaluation and vetting of honorees going forward would be wise. Exclusive focus on certain genders, races or those of special status seems to be a thing of the past. It is interesting, and maybe a little sad, that studies have shown that most commemoratives (statues and monuments) generally go unnoticed after a time, probably because of simple familiarity. But I think they can be, and always will be a valuable addition to our built environment. Even though we may not be readily able to recall certain of them, I think we would certainly readily notice We have discussed the beauty, function and importance of urban design in previous columns. A city that understands these concepts should indeed honor the people who support them and make them possible. These appropriate, well-designed and well deserved plaques themselves add interest and punctuation to the urban design of the city. Piedmont’s Centennial House plaques rest on 173 homes, all built before city incorporation in 1907 and judged to have maintained the architectural style and character of the original buildings. The Wetmore house, adjacent to City Hall, is on the National Register of Historic Places. A similar sub-category of historical plaques are “donor bricks” such as this nice installation honoring the supporters of Witter Field construction. Memorial benches, found throughout the parks of Piedmont, add interesting detail as well as a welcome place to relax.

Even though we may not be readily able to recall certain of them, I think we would certainly readily notice See Walking Piedmont on page 26 We have discussed the beauty, function and importance of urban design in previous columns. A city that understands these concepts should indeed honor the people who support them and make them possible. These appropriate, well-designed and well deserved plaques themselves add interest and punctuation to the urban design of the city. Piedmont’s Centennial House plaques rest on 173 homes, all built before city incorporation in 1907 and judged to have maintained the architectural style and character of the original buildings. The Wetmore house, adjacent to City Hall, is on the National Register of Historic Places. A similar sub-category of historical plaques are “donor bricks” such as this nice installation honoring the supporters of Witter Field construction. With Joann’s arrival, the herd now includes three generations of females, forming a typical and healthy social group—an important step in promoting topnotch animal wellbeing. To help her acclimate to her new family, the giraffe team allowed her to explore her new habitat alongside her older female mentor giraffe, Maggie, the oldest female in Oakland’s herd at 14 years old. Joann then met the entire herd, the Zoo’s young bull, and two other females. With Joann’s arrival, the herd now includes three generations of females, forming a typical and healthy social group—an important step in promoting topnotch animal wellbeing. Initially taking hesitant steps, she entered the habitat and quickly gained the confidence to explore her new space alongside the rest of her herd. To help her acclimate to her new family, the giraffe team allowed her to explore her new habitat alongside her older female mentor giraffe, Maggie, the oldest female in Oakland’s herd at 14 years old. Joann spent her first few weeks in Oakland adjusting to her new home behind the scenes in the Zoo’s giraffe barns as she completed her quarantine period. During that time, she had close contact with Maggie, so she wasn’t alone. Maggie served as a role model and guide for Joann, showing her the way in this new setting, and provided muchneeded companionship during this new chapter. When it was time to introduce Joann to the rest of the giraffe herd, Maggie confidently led her onto the habitat and guided her. Joann then met the entire herd, the Zoo’s young bull, and two other females. Giraffes are typically very welcoming to new herd members, and after a brief introduction where they smelled each other, the expanded herd began browsing and foraging together. “Joann is incredibly sweet and seeks out connections with the other giraffes and her new AniPhoto Credit Oakland Zoo The Oakland Zoo added a new giraffe to the African Savanna habitat on June 5. Joann and herdmate Nuru mal Care Keepers. She is very brave, and her curiosity grows every day. We can’t wait to watch her grow here at Oakland Zoo,” said Oakland Zoo Animal Care Keeper Jessica Parke. This move follows a recommendation from the Association of Zoos and Aquariums’ (AZA) Species Survival Plan (SSP) to improve breeding success and animal welfare. Kendi, another two-year-old female giraffe at Oakland Zoo, now has a companion her age, an important part of supporting her overall wellbeing. Having a peer of the same age allows Kendi to grow up alongside another juvenile. In the wild, female giraffes often form strong social bonds, spending much of their lives together and developing friendships. They also often babysit and help raise one another’s calves. This partnership provides all the giraffes in Oakland Zoo’s herd with increased opportunities for natural behaviors such as play and more complex social relationships, mirroring those of a typical giraffe herd. It also gives females multiple “sisters” to help them raise their calves. Joann comes from a decadeslong lineage of giraffes rooted in the Bay Area, including those at Oakland Zoo. She and Maggie come from the same family tree: Tiki, a beloved Oakland Zoo giraffe who has since passed, had five offspring during her time at the Oakland Zoo, including Dadisi, Joann’s grandmother, who moved as a juvenile from Oakland to Palm Desert as part of the AZA’s Species Survival Plan. Tiki was Maggie’s grandmother and Joann’s great-grandmother. Some of Oakland’s Animal Care staff have had the great privilege of working with and learning from 5 generations of strong females in this amazing family tree. This long line of Bay Areaborn giraffes is a testament to the success of the giraffe program at Oakland Zoo and to its influence on sustainability across AZA’s giraffe population, supporting the Species Survival Program. This giraffe program has also been a leader in advancing the standard of care of this species, much of which was pioneered by Tiki and her Animal Care team. Oakland Zoo guests can now see Joann alongside the rest of the giraffe herd at the Zoo’s African Savanna habitat. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors’ latest excursion was to Livermore, and was educational, exciting, and fulfilling. The first stop was at the Lawrence Livermore Discovery Center – a true destination for inspiration! The Discovery Center offers in-person visitors an exciting glimpse into cutting-edge science and technology. The featured exhibits showcase the Laboratory’s state-of-the-art research programs, which range from high-performance computing, to bioscience and bioengineering, to advanced materials and manufacturing. They are designed to inspire the next generation of researchers by showcasing new innovations and the impactful work conducted at the Lab. Different areas of the Discovery Center feature such items as a Heritage of Innovation, Forensic Science, Biotechnology, Seismology, and there is a booth where the Seniors could test their knowledge with multiple choice questions using computers. Senior members had the opportunity to learn about energy and climate science by hopping on an energy bike to learn how much “pedal power” it takes to turn on a lightbulb, They also got a taste of Lawrence Livermore Lab’s contributions to climate science research. The Laboratory opened on September 2, 1952, initially as a branch of the University of California Radiation Laboratory. Prior to the Lab’s opening, this parcel of land was the site of the Livermore Naval Air Station, a World War II pilot training facility. Throughout its history, the Laboratory has fulfilled its national security mission, establishing itself as a hallmark of cutting-edge science and technology in service to society. After this educational visit, the Members of the Piedmont Seniors had the opportunity to step into a replica of the National Ignition Facility target chamber, which “brings star power to earth. They include (L to R): Nancy Everett, Nancy Hinsch, Sandra Ponce, Susan McCreary, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Gloria Wilmer, and Elizabeth Wierzbianska. The Piedmont Seniors visited the Lawrence Livermore Discovery Center. Pictured are (seated in front): Arlene Garfinkle; (L to R): James Ayotte, Sue Getreuer, Edith Hereso, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Gloria Wilmer, Sandra Ponce, Nancy Hinsch, and Susan McCreary; (back row): Greg Jurin, Fred Pemberton, and Nancy Everett. Seniors then turned the page as its next venture was to the Bankhead Theater in downtown Livermore to take in a Tri-Valley lighthearted production of Newsies: The Broadway Musical. The cast of this almost-three-hour musical was entirely that of teenagers, and they did an outstanding job. Their singing, dancing, and gymnastics was a pleasure to watch. Afterwards, the Seniors then ventured to Terra Mia Cucina Italiana for a cross between lunch and dinner – “linner”. This restaurant definitely was able to tickle the Seniors’ taste buds with playful culinary creations. It was an excellent way to “put the cherry on top” of a delightful, educational, and fun-filled day. If you would like to find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 a.m. to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. The Piedmont Seniors visited the Bankhead Theater to see a stage production of “Newsies: The Broadway Musical”. Pictured at the theater are (front): Greg Jurin and Nancy Hinsch; middle row (L to R): Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Gloria Wilmer, Edith Hereso, Nancy Everett, and Susan McCreary; back row (L to R): Fred Pemberton, Sandra Ponce, James Ayotte, Sue Getreuer, and Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein. The Piedmont Seniors capped off a fulfilling day with a visit to Terra Mia Cucina Italiana for a heartwarming meal. articles.text: For many older adults, later life is the first time there’s room to do something purely for themselves. When you spend a lifetime working, raising families, and caring for others, personal pursuits of happiness often have to take a backseat. Stagebridge gives adults 50 and older a place to return to the things that make you feel most alive. For some that’s acting, musical theater or singing. For others it’s storytelling, movement or clowning. For example, more than a decade ago, Stagebridge student Terry Pink Alexander attended a friend’s showcase performance and noticed a postcard for Performing Arts Summer Camp for Adults. “That summer camp is what hooked me,” she said. What began as one week of classes grew into a new era of creative exploration and lasting friendships. “This is my life. All of my very closest friends are here,” Alexander said. Next month, Stagebridge’s Encore Performing Arts Summer Camp is back, with breakfast and lunch included so people get the full camp experience. Participants might spend the morning in storytelling or improv and the afternoon singing, tapping, or drumming. The week ends with a community showcase for family and friends. For some participants, Summer Camp is a joyful week. For others, it becomes the beginning of year-round classes, performances, and friendships. And for those who can’t attend in July, Stagebridge’s fall session offers another chance to begin, with classes in acting, storytelling, improv, musical theater, singing, movement, and more. Located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland, inside the First Congregational Church of Oakland, Stagebridge is just across from Lake Merritt’s Whole Foods and steps from AC Transit Line 33. Encore Performing Arts Summer Camp for Adults runs July 13–17. Class size is limited and filling up fast. Learn more and register at www.stagebridge.org/ summer-camp-2026. Terry Pink Alexander (left) enjoys stage time each semester.

By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I am so frustrated with keeping track of my passwords. Now when I enter a password on a website like PayPal, I get a window asking if I would like to use a passkey. I don’t understand the difference between passwords and passkeys. Is this just one more thing I have to keep track of? I am already losing the battle with remembering all of my passwords and keeping them in a safe place. Felix, Oakland Dear Felix: You are not alone for sure. Passwords are one of the most important and frustrating aspects of the digital world. With all of the phishing attacks, security breaches and computer scams it seems we are constantly under threat of identity theft, credit card fraud and scams. And most of us don’t really have the skills to make a password that is not easily guessed, or accessible through data breaches. The creation of passkeys is supposed to make all of these vulnerabilities harder to crack. Passwords are strings of characters that we (or our password apps) create to use to access secure websites like our bank, PayPal, shopping sites, etc. Passkeys on the other hand, are system-generated cryptographic key pairs. Instead of typing and having to remember a password, your system creates passkeys to unlock and enable your various accounts using your device’s built-in security, such as Face ID, Touch ID, your log in password or a pin code. For this to work, iCloud Keychain must be turned on in your Mac, iPhone and iPad settings, which syncs your passkeys across all your Apple devices. To do this • Open the Apple Menu > System Settings (or System Preferences). • Click your Apple ID (or name) at the top. • Click iCloud > Passwords & Keychain and make sure it is turned If you are signing into a new website account, put in a username and submit. When you get the option to create a passkey, choose the method you would like to use to sign in, Touch ID, Face ID or “other options” such as a QR code (from a nearby device such as your iPhone) or an external security key. If you don’t want to have to remember or keep track of a key code, then Touch ID or Face ID is fine. If you want to change your password on a site to a passkey, log in as you normally do, then go to the Passwords and Security section and look for the option to, “register a passkey,” “use passkey,” or “sign in with a passkey.” The website will prompt you to save a passkey to your Mac. You will then use Touch ID or your Mac’s password to save the passkey to your Mac. The use of passkeys is replacing user generated passwords for several reasons. They are much more secure than passwords. Passwords are vulnerable to phishing and data breaches, whereas passkeys are mathematically impossible to guess and are strictly tied to the legitimate website or app, providing complete immunity to phishing. Passwords also require databases on the website’s server to authenticate, and passkeys use asymmetric cryptography: a “public key” is kept by the website, while the “private key” never leaves your device’s secure hardware. And you no longer must remember hundreds of passwords, you just have to know how to securely get into your computer account, which most of us do each day when we log in with either our computer log in password or touch ID. So when that window pops up asking if you would like to create a passkey, just enable it by clicking “continue”. You will then be prompted to use your Touch ID or enter your Mac’s login password. The passkey will then be stored in your iCloud keychain. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. articles.text: Anyone familiar with dogs will agree that canine companions are incredibly talented. From pet dogs who put a smile on their owners’ faces, to search and rescue dogs who save lives, dogs have an abundance of admirable skills. Many of those skills are grounded in their sense of smell, which is estimated to be 10,000 to 100,000 times more acute than our own. Thanks to this skill, an incredible type of service dog is becoming more common: the migraine alert dog. Migraines have cycles and the first symptoms, during the “prodrome phase,” can appear as early as a few days before any excruciating pain. Here, the enzymes in saliva start to change from their normal state; it is here that dogs begin to smell the change. At this point, a trained migraine alert dog will signal their handler, usually by pawing or booping with the nose, allowing the handler to take medication early enough to mitigate the migraine. A service dog can signal in many ways, but a pawing motion is most commonly taught because it is unusual enough to grab a handler’s attention. To teach the dog to detect the enzymatic change in saliva, the owner is asked to collect saliva samples with cotton balls when they have migraines. The samples are stored in sealed jars and labeled the date, symptoms and intensity of the migraine on a 1-10 scale. The jars are then stored in the freezer to preserve the scent. In training, a dog is shown a sample and given a verbal command to paw once they smell the sample; they are rewarded when they signal with a pawing motion. This is repeated until the dog begins to signal on their own. The nose knows: A sneak peek at migraine detection service dog training By Sierra Berrick Anyone familiar with dogs will agree that canine companions are incredibly talented. From pet dogs who put a smile on their owners’ faces, to search and rescue dogs who save lives, dogs have an abundance of admirable skills. Many of those skills are grounded in their sense of smell, which is estimated to be 10,000 to 100,000 times more acute than our own. Thanks to this skill, an incredible type of service dog is becoming more common: the migraine alert dog. Migraines have cycles and the first symptoms, during the “prodrome phase,” can appear as early as a few days before any excruciating pain. Here, the enzymes in saliva start to change from their normal state; it is here that dogs begin to smell the change. At this point, a trained migraine alert dog will signal their handler, usually by pawing or booping with the nose, allowing the handler to take medication early enough to mitigate the migraine. A service dog can signal in many ways, but a pawing motion is most commonly taught because it is unusual enough to grab a handler’s attention. To teach the dog to detect the enzymatic change in saliva, the owner is asked to collect saliva samples with cotton balls when they have migraines. The samples are stored in sealed jars and labeled the date, symptoms and intensity of the migraine on a 1-10 scale. The jars are then stored in the freezer to preserve the scent. In training, a dog is shown a sample and given a verbal command to paw once they smell the sample; they are rewarded when they signal with a pawing motion. This is repeated until the dog begins to signal on their own. In order to teach the dog that they should signal for specific scents and not the presentation of the jar, control samples (samples with no saliva) are used. Once the dog shows nearly 100% consistency, the owner transitions to breathing across the sample. This teaches the dog where to expect the source of the target scent in a daily environment. Eventually, the dog will signal their handler whenever they smell the change on the owner’s breath, despite distractions and even the presence of enticing smells like food. Migraine alert training is a life-enhancing option for people who suffer from migraines. Dogs Basil the corgi alerts his owner to an oncoming migraine. who can perform this work are superheroes within their species. Far from a common treatment option, the use of dogs to detect oncoming migraines is one that needs more research. Thanks to a dog’s incredible sense of smell, this treatment option is becoming increasingly available and could prove to be one of the most effective methods in halting migraines before they start. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.text: Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on June 17, 2020 Two large parks are located on the east and west sides of Paris and are referred to as the green lungs. These thick woods are believed to breathe in toxins and breathe out fresh air, cleansing Paris. Bois de Boulogne is in a ritzier part of town than Bois de Vincennes east of the city. Just west of the Eiffel Tower, where the Seine bends southward, the Bois de Boulogne is wholly located in the 16th arrondissement. These woods were hunting grounds for the kings of France dating back a thousand years. A maze of bridle paths crisscross through the stands of tall trees. Only a few minutes’ drive into the more southerly woods opens to the Hippodrome racecourse. Refitted in 2018 with spectacular viewing stands and adding Paris-Longchamp to its Hippodrome name, its 82 acres are designated for steeplechase with an obstacle-course of fences and moats, with grandstands for 50,000 spectators. Emperor Napoleon III ceded the woodland from the crown to the city of Paris and was present with his wife Empress Eugénie for the first Hippodrome. The races attracted a huge public and were a favorite scene for impressionists Edgar Degas and Edouard Manet. Bois de Boulogne reimagined in 1850s It was the job of the Emperor’s Minister of Public Works, Baron Haussmann (Georges-Eugène Haussmann), to reconstruct the land grant with roads, paths, and walking trails in Bois de Boulogne. Haussmann built an artificial waterfall and grotto, stocked the park with deer, planted a half a million trees, and designed an underground waterway for manmade ponds and lakes complete with their own islands. Jacqueline had left New York City and her busy social life as “debutante of the year” to study at Sorbonne in 1949 post-war Paris. Remembered as “her happiest and most carefree year,” homey comforts such as central heating and hot water were not her lot; but she had society connections and dined at the Ritz. Only 12 years later she was First Lady, enchanting the nation with her nuanced, acculturated French manners, while France was enthralled by her fluency. Enormous crowds cheered the popular 35th American president John F. Kennedy. High society flocked to the 16th, the largest of the 20 arrondissements, attracted to the woodsy, airy climate as ideal for their country homes. The city of Paris under Haussmann’s direction designed wide boulevards to bring the woodlands into reach. French 19th Century popular culture swooned over the swanky urban but still country utopia. It’s a part of Paris where renters can upgrade to more spacious living quarters with abundant space to play. The woods comprise more than half of the arrondissement’s land area. Next to the woods are handsome, understated but ornate residential apartment buildings with lots of greenery and statuary, groomed pathways, children’s attractions, and open space for pets. These residences are immediately recognizable as Haussmann buildings, and they efficiently house residents in comfort and close to nature. Today’s commute traffic loads up on these straight, broad multilane Haussmann boulevards. I see no vacant storefronts among the upscale shops and restaurants lining the streets, and sidewalk cafés are busy with patrons enjoying an outing post Covid-19 confinement. The Baron was celebrated as a national hero, although not without plenty of gripes about bulldozing old Paris. The 16th district with its pleasing visual symmetry, wide boulevards, and well-kept public areas seems to have sprung from a clean canvass, where 18th Century design leaped off the drawing table into a sparkling new district. Largely it did, although not unlike other newer sections of Paris, the new city is different from central Paris, where a mashup of historical buildings and streets is the norm. The 16th arrondissement was created during an era when the city’s population doubled to 1,600,000 literally overnight by the Emperor’s decree to annex towns that were previously independent and suburban to Paris. The Emperor could not be denied. From the Bois de Boulogne, the view looking east at the Eiffel Tower is largely unobscured. The Baron was celebrated as a national hero, although not without plenty of gripes about bulldozing old Paris. The 16th district with its pleasing visual symmetry, wide boulevards, and well-kept public areas seems to have sprung from a clean canvass, where 18th Century design leaped off the drawing table into a sparkling new district. Largely it did, although not unlike other newer sections of Paris, the new city is different from central Paris, where a mashup of historical buildings and streets is the norm. The 16th arrondissement was created during an era when the city’s population doubled to 1,600,000 literally overnight by the Emperor’s decree to annex towns that were previously independent and suburban to Paris. The Emperor could not be denied. From the Bois de Boulogne, the view looking east at the Eiffel Tower is largely unobscured. The 16th has a wealth of architecturally significant homes on Avenue Foch, which is one of the 12 avenues emanating from Arc de Triomphe de L’Etoile. Private swaths of country homes built for nobility and captains of industry were walled-in, akin to today’s gated communities. Fewer modern-day families choose to live (or can afford to) in the magnificence of 19th Century opulence. Modern times find heirs selling Boating on the Bois de Boulogne. La Grande Cascade in Bois de Boulogne has two Michelin stars and was converted from a hunting lodge of Emperor Napoleon III to a restaurant for the 1900 Paris Exposition. off the family property or wrangling a public donation. The district is awash in historical landmark buildings and museums concentrated between Place du Trocadéro and the Marmottan Monet. They include a museum of anthropology, multiple Asian art collections; modern art, architecture, Baccarat crystal, counterfeiting, fashion and beaux-arts decor; wine, dental history, and the Paris sewer network. Open to the public for admission, these are managed by the city of Paris. One might also visit the Yves Saint Lauren workshop and the former residences of prime minister Georges Clemenceau; architect Le Corbusier; and writer Honore’ de Balzac. Fondation Louis Vuitton designed by American architect Frank Gehry was completed in 2014 in Bois de Boulogne. The 16th is also a popular location for many private schools and foreign embassies, dotting many a tranquil street with a prestigious address. Bois de Boulogne has both magnetism and tranquility; and its cohesion into the 16th district demonstrates an enthusiasm for creativity and a bounty for arts, commerce, and education to share with the public. In 1929, both Bois de Boulogne and Bois de Vincennes were finally officially annexed to the city of Paris. Look for a future column about Bois de Vincennes, the eastern green lung of Paris. Patricia Forsyth and Michael Mathews moved from Piedmont to Paris last September, seemingly throwing both countries into decline, although other factors may be contributing. For comments, email pkf.empower@ gmail.com. Hippodrome Racecourse at Bois de Boulogne, by Edouard Manet, 1867 Hippodrome Paris-Longchamp reopened last year with an ultra-modern grandstand having no pillars to obstruct the 180-degree views; 500 monitors for watching the races; and betting odds posted throughout the racecourse. Event dates, due to Covid-19, are still postponed. Château Le Bois, once owned by the Renault family and the only residence in the Bois de Boulogne, was leased to the Duke and Duchess of Windsor from 1952 to 1986, upon her death. Edward VIII’s abdication from the English throne was in 1936; and he died here in 1972. The city of Paris collected a nominal rent from the couple for more than 30 years. The city of Paris followed with a 50-year lease to Mohamed Al-Fayed, owner of Harrods and the Paris Ritz, for one million francs per year. Al-Fayed’s son Dodi, and Diana, Princess of Wales visited the villa on the day before their deaths in August 1997.

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Class of 2026 celebrated with a lively graduation ceremony on Thursday, June 4, at Witter Field. Their commencement ceremony honored their accomplishments and welcomed family, friends, and teachers to witness their last gathering together before heading into the world in separate directions. This special class is heading for greener pastures. The matriculation list shows a whopping 15 students committed to Cal Berkeley, and 48 in total heading directly to a University of California site. PHS graduates will be represented at three Ivy League schools, as well as Stanford, Northwestern, Washington University in St. Louis and the University of British Columbia to name a few. These students finished the 6th grade remotely due to Covid and some were reunited with their 6th grade teacher Ted Scherman, the high school commencement speaker. He finished his speech with wise words of advice that offered perspective to the graduates: “Be kind to your parents. This moment is enormous for you. But it is everything to them,” PHS graduates assemble for one last time as a class at their graduation ceremony.

articles.text: Every year, we gather in May at the PHS amphitheater to celebrate senior athletes who go on to compete in college. They set an example for younger athletes who hope to follow in their footsteps. But the landscape is shifting so quickly that last year’s template may not work next year. We’ve seen college roster sizes shrink, eligibility rules change, and donors pour money via NIL to bolster their schools. At the pre-college level, we’re seeing an equally interesting shift: private equity firms are injecting capital into youth club teams, showcases, and facilities. KKR has influence within the soccer ecosystem including programs such as MLS NEXT and ECNL. 3STEP has acquired dozens of soccer, lacrosse, volleyball, basketball, and softball organizations nationwide. And many of the facilities these organizations use operate under agreements with companies backed by PE firms such as Unrivaled Sports. Here’s the kicker: the coaches influenced by these organizations sit at the top of the pecking order when it comes to influencing teenage athletes. They’ve convinced kids to give up other sports or risk falling behind. They’ve convinced athletes that the next pay-to-participate showcase will be the one that gets them recruited. They minimize practice—the time when athletes develop their skills—and replace it with more and more games. The result? Families spending thousands of dollars for their kids to become perpetually injured from overuse, all while doing the opposite of what college coaches want: developing skills and demonstrating adaptability by succeeding in multiple sports. More info: 94% of NCAA athletes across Divisions I, II, and III played at least two sports growing up, and 84% played two sports at the varsity level. Simply put, if your goal is to play a sport in college, you’re more likely to succeed if you play multiple sports. To summarize: if you’re exceptional at one sport, sure, you’re talented. But if you’re good at a second sport, it’s a differentiating factor. It’s your way of proving you’re self-motivated, are coachable, have a broader set of skills, and may be less susceptible to overuse injuries. The landscape of college sports will continue to evolve, and I can’t pretend to know what the future will hold. But it seems clear to me that the combination of club coaches, ChatGPT, social media algorithms, and vibes isn’t as reliable as simply asking college coaches themselves and trusting the people who genuinely care about you. Pouyan Assadi is the varsity head coach of the Piedmont High School track and field team, and the JV head coach of the PHS football team.
articles.title: A not-so-subtle shift in youth sports

articles.text: In April earlier this year Camp Augusta’s director Randy Grayson, announced that this summer would be his last in the role. Grayson spent the last 23 years at Camp Augusta building the camp into an internationally respected summer residential camp for kids. Grayson is expected to remain involved with Augusta, participating in family camps, training, and running story experiences. As a kid, summer camps helped Grayson gain self-confidence, social skills, independence, creativity, physical and leadership skills. As an adult, he spent his time trying to give that experience to future generations, spending the last three decades working on his mission. Going into his final summer, Grayson is excited that he no longer has to worry about logistics and can focus on the hands-on experience with the kids. He plans to become a grandparent who gets to do all the “fun stuff.” “I’d like to be engaged with the program in the community, and kind of flip it in the way that I have the time to spend more time with the campers and the staff, and do the clinics,” Grayson said. “I hope that this transition is a time when I can do more of what I love at camp, rather than answer 50 emails and talk about things like the food truck and budgets.” When Grayson arrived 23 years ago, the camp was $5 million in debt and required significant repairs. He was contemplating whether to stay or leave on a month-to-month basis. Ultimately, what kept him involved with the camp was the passion he observed in the people dedicated to preserving it. Randy Grayson with his family “A couple of years before I got there, they started to try and run a camp program again, where the camp actually ran for several weeks, half full, but they still were trying to make a go of it, to have it there. The camp had a candle; it wasn’t dead, it still had a flame,” said Grayson. The Camp Augusta board allowed Grayson and his staff to shape its culture. In his first year running the camp, it was 80% full and was able to run the entire summer. For the next 22 summers, the camp has been full. Having full enrollment and donors enabled the camp to rebuild its infrastructure. As Grayson steps away, he hopes he provided the kids with a sense of possibility and a belief that they can try new things. Through the camp’s playstations and evening embers, he wanted to encourage campers to try new activities and discover what they want and what they like. After collecting his final thoughts, Grayson thanked those who had attended Camp Augusta throughout his 23 years with hopes the camp continues to grow and thrive in future years. “I am delighted to leave Camp Augusta in a really strong place organizationally. We’re glad to be full every year and have a strong financial base. I hope Augusta continues to rise and grow in ways that I probably wouldn’t have imagined,” said Grayson. Grayson’s next step is to dedicate time to his nonprofit organization, A Meaning of Life. The organization’s goal is to provide resources to help people practice positive habits and improve their lives. Readers and Camp Augusta fans can find Grayson’s nonprofit at the following link: https:// ameaningoflife.org/. Randy Grayson gave a speech to the campers before the traditional oatmeal fight.
articles.title: Randy Grayson’s final summer at Camp Augusta

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department urges community members to check the trees, shrubs, and other vegetation on their property. They recommend residents trim anything growing into the roadway or hanging over the street. Keeping vegetation clear helps fire engines, ambulances, and other emergency vehicles reach homes quickly. This is especially important on narrow streets and on streets without sidewalks, where landscaping can gradually grow into the travel lane. Property owners are responsible for managing vegetation on their property, while the city maintains its city-planted street trees. The Fire Department requires property owners to maintain at least three feet of clearance from the edge of the roadway and at least 15 feet of vertical clearance above the surface of the roadway. This helps ensure Piedmont firefighters are capable of responding effectively in emergencies. Piedmont firefighters are seeing overgrown vegetation create access issues in many parts of the city. Branches and shrubs that extend into the roadway slow and impede emergency response. “In an emergency, seconds matter,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “Piedmont has many narrow streets that are tricky for large vehicles to navigate, even in the best conditions. When overgrown vegetation narrows the road, it slows our response and puts an unnecessary barrier between responders and those who need help.” The Fire Department asks all residents to trim vegetation on their property proactively, before it affects emergency access. If enforcement becomes necessary, the process begins with a courtesy notice and inspection. Property owners may be cited or fined if required clearance is not maintained, but voluntary compliance is the goal. Residents can also help emergency responders by making sure address numbers are easy to see from the street.
