articles.text: At the June 1 City Council meeting, council members agreed they want to place a measure increasing the property transfer tax rate on the November ballot. City staff is expected to prepare a draft of the ordinance to read at the council’s next meeting on June 15. At this time, the council is undecided on the exact number for the proposed increase; discussions will continue at the next meeting. The City Council requested that the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee examine funding mechanisms to address the city’s deferred maintenance obligations, capital infrastructure needs, and long-term revenue sustainability. The advisory recommended that the council consider increasing the transfer tax by either a flat or tiered rate. The recommendation was a range between 1.5% and 1.8%. According to the financial planning committee, A rate adjustment, if approved by voters, would provide a more durable source of capital funding and reduce the General Fund’s dependence on volatile annual transfer tax receipts for capital investment. The council agreed with the budget advisory committee’s recommendation to raise the property transfer tax. The increasing costs of maintenance and capital investments have prompted the city to explore ways to increase revenue. “It’s our streets, our sidewalks, our storm water drains, it’s this infrastructure that’s aging that’s getting more expensive because the cost of everything is going up, and our revenues are not matching that,” said Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen. The council could not reach a consensus on an appropriate amount to increase the transfer tax. However, they agreed to a flat-rate increase due to the volatility associated with a potential tiered system. “The transfer tax is a very volatile revenue source, and adding a tiered structure makes it even more volatile. It’s anybody’s guess as to how many large value properties are going to sell, so it becomes even harder to project revenue,” said Finance Director Kiran Bawa. In Piedmont, the transfer tax has been unchanged for the last 33 years at a rate of 1.3% or $13 per $1,000 of assessed value. The city uses the funds from the transfer tax toward capital investment and maintenance of aging facilities, buildings, and infrastructure systems. The city attempted to increase the transfer tax in 2020 with Measure TT, which would’ve increased the rate to $17.50 per $1,000 of assessed value, generating an estimated $948,462 per year for city services. The measure was defeated, with 52% voting no. Six years later, the council still believes that there is a need for an increase to help balance the city’s revenue. “The need has not gone away; the need we had in 2020 is the same. In fact, maybe we have a better understanding of the need six years later,” Mayor Andersen continued. “We were cushioned over those six years by having two bumper transaction sales years that filled up the coffers of our capital needs funds, but those were outlier years, and those are not years that we’re going to repeat anytime soon.” If the council places the transfer tax measure on the November 2026 ballot, measure materials would need to be submitted to the Alameda County Registrar of Voters no later than August 7, 2026. Discussions on the potential increase of the transfer tax will continue at the council’s next meeting on June 15. Readers who wish to attend the meeting can do so in person at City Hall or online. More information is on the City’s website: https://piedmont.ca.gov/.
articles.title: City Council may place transfer tax increase on Nov. ballot

pages.text: Wednesday, June 10, 2026 5 Clear vegetation near the street to help emergency vehicles reach your home By Jake Lannon The Piedmont Fire Department urges community members to check the trees, shrubs, and other vegetation on their property. They recommend residents trim anything growing into the roadway or hanging over the street. Keeping vegetation clear helps fire engines, ambulances, and other emergency vehicles reach homes quickly. This is especially important on narrow streets and on streets without sidewalks, where landscaping can gradually grow into the travel lane. Property owners are responsible for managing vegetation on their property, while the city maintains its city-planted street trees. The Fire Department requires property owners to maintain at least three feet of clearance from the edge of the roadway and at least 15 feet of vertical clearance above the surface of the roadway. This helps ensure Piedmont firefighters are capable of responding effectively in emergencies. Piedmont firefighters are seeing overgrown vegetation create access issues in many parts of the city. Branches and shrubs that extend into the roadway slow and impede emergency response. “In an emergency, seconds matter,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “Piedmont has many narrow streets that are tricky for large vehicles to navigate, even in the best conditions. When overgrown vegetation narrows the road, it slows our response and puts an unnecessary barrier between responders and those who need help.” The Fire Department asks all residents to trim vegetation on their property proactively, before it affects emergency access. If enforcement becomes necessary, the process begins with a courtesy notice and inspection. Property owners may be cited or fined if required clearance is not maintained, but voluntary compliance is the goal. Residents can also help emergency responders by making sure address numbers are easy to see from the street. Address numbers should be at least four inches tall, on a contrasting background, and visible from the roadway. “We need everyone to do their part and keep roads clear for emergency vehicles. It makes Piedmont safer for everyone,” said Chief Brannigan. For questions about vegetation clearance requirements, contact the Fire Department at FireInfo@ piedmont.ca.gov or (510) 420- 3030. articles.text: Graduating 8th graders were honored at Witter Field on June 3. Eighth grade students file onto Witter Field for the graduation ceremony from Piedmont Middle School on June 3. Piedmont Middle School held a commencement ceremony for graduating 8th graders on Wednesday, June 3, at Witter Field. The 188 students took their final steps as middle schoolers on the field, and afterwards ascended the stadium stairs as incoming Piedmont High School freshmen. The ceremony opened with an expression of diversity as students offered words of welcome in dozens of languages from Arabic to Yiddish. Student speeches were given by Violet Snyder and Zayna Majid, and a duet by Emmy Hong and Emma Wendel. The ceremony also served as a farewell for middle school principal Karyn Shipp and a welcome for Jamie Van Kleeck who will be the Piedmont Middle School Principal next year. Adam Saville will fill the Vice Principal position vacated by Van Kleeck, who honored the many extracurricular activities, programs and clubs participated by the students. Students stood as 8th graders and one by one walked up to receive their certificates. After hearing their name called and a handshake with outgoing principal Shipp they retook their seats as incoming high school freshmen. The PMS 8th grade band, and the 7th and 8th grade String Orchestra played Viva La Vida by Coldplay after the certificates were presented and then finished the evening with a recessional piece. Zayna Majid (left), and Annabelle Malione lead a line of classmates to receive their 8th grade graduation certificates. Anna Benson receives her 8th grade certificate from principal Karyn Shipp. Eighth graders said goodbye to the middle school building with their sights already on becoming high school students. Parents, coaches, friends and relatives were on hand to witness these teenagers take another big step into the future. Emmy Hong and Emma Wendel gave a speech to classmates. Violet Snyder addresses her classmates during their final moment together as middle schoolers. PMS incoming Principal Jamie Van Kleeck informs the Witter Field crowd of the many activities performed by middle schoolers. Ryan McMurtry walks towards his 8th grade certificate and towards high school.

The 188 students took their final steps as middle schoolers on the field, and afterwards ascended the stadium stairs as incoming Piedmont High School freshmen. The ceremony opened with an expression of diversity as students offered words of welcome in dozens of languages from Arabic to Yiddish. Student speeches were given by Violet Snyder and Zayna Majid, and a duet by Emmy Hong and Emma Wendel. The ceremony also served as a farewell for middle school principal Karyn Shipp and a welcome for Jamie Van Kleeck who will be the Piedmont Middle School Principal next year. Adam Saville will fill the Vice Principal position vacated by Van Kleeck, who honored the many extracurricular activities, programs and clubs participated by the students. Students stood as 8th graders and one by one walked up to receive their certificates. After hearing their name called and a handshake with outgoing principal Shipp they retook their seats as incoming high school freshmen. The PMS 8th grade band, and the 7th and 8th grade String Orchestra played Viva La Vida by Coldplay after the certificates were presented and then finished the evening with a recessional piece. Violet Snyder addresses her classmates during their final moment together as middle schoolers. PMS incoming Principal Jamie Van Kleeck informs the Witter Field crowd of the many activities performed by middle schoolers. Ryan McMurtry walks towards his 8th grade certificate and towards high school.

articles.text: Ted Scherman, now a retired middle school teacher, was the Commencement Speaker at Thursday’s Piedmont High School Graduation Ceremony. Class of 26, it is truly an honor to be your commencement speaker today. And in a way, I’m graduating right along with you. This is bittersweet for me, this is my swan song, and I am overwhelmed with gratitude that John Morrison - yes, of the John Morrison Gym - tracked me down 32 years ago and offered me a job. To the parents: It has been a privilege to teach your children. They are remarkable in more ways than I can count. I have taught so many kids over the years, and each one has a place in my heart. And sometimes I hear from former students, and they’re married, with children of their own. I have even taught the children of former students. What?! Graduates, I know so many of you here today. Some I had in class, some in an elective, and some through sports. And some of you, I honestly cannot believe you made it. All kidding aside, this is a distinct honor, and I thank you for asking me and for allowing me to dispense some completely unsolicited advice on this year’s graduating class. For me, the Class of 2026 will always hold a special place. Six years ago, I had the pleasure of welcoming so many of you to Piedmont Middle School, whether it was during the Welcome to 6th Grade Bootcamp, or in one of my 6th grade classes. I remember watching you adjust, find your footing, and begin to thrive. And then, just as you were hitting your stride, everything stopped. Covid shut it all down. And while we all managed somehow, I never got to say a proper goodbye to you. So here it is. Finally. Goodbye, 6th graders. Hello, graduates. I want to take a moment to congratulate you, genuinely, deeply, on making it to this point. I’m not sure everyone in this room fully appreciates what it took. Let’s go back. Elementary school. You were nervous. Will I make any friends? Will the teachers be mean? Am I going to miss my mom and dad? You rocked tetherball and were fierce on the four-square court. Ready to bring your skills to middle school. Then middle school. Even scarier. No recess? You mean we’re just supposed to stand around and look cool? What do you mean it’s not okay to wear my Winnie the Pooh t-shirt anymore? What happened to my friend, and why are they acting so weird? Then high school. The pressures shifted again. How do I stand out? Why is my friend taking five AP courses? Will any college accept me? Can I go to that party? What if I don’t want to go? It’s a lot. The pressures are real and should never be discounted. And now, look at you. Here you are. You’ve done it. Before I get to my advice, take a moment right now. Look up at the stands. Find the parents, grandparents, siblings, coaches, teachers, scout leaders, religious leaders, mentors, and every person who believed in you. Send them a silent, telepathic thank you. Because none of us goes at it alone. Everything you have achieved, and will achieve, is a combination of your own perseverance and the support of so many people. You’ve spent the last 3, 7, 10, 15 years here in this village. This hamlet. This cocoon. This nest known as Piedmont. It is a very special community, and whether you know it now or will come to know it later, you were well cared for here. Now it’s time to move on. To leave the nest. I’ve sat through a few graduations in my time, so trust me, I’ll keep this short and sweet. Three things. Just three. First: Play Play with abandon. Play until your sides hurt from laughing. At some point, kids stop playing, and I want to ask you: when did YOU stop? Games, fun, harmless pranks, playfulness with friends, a spontaneous game of tag, play is how we communicate, how we learn about one another, and how we find levity when life gets too real. It is also, frankly, a lot of fun. It’s so good for you, and for everyone around you, to be reminded not to take ourselves too seriously. Even animals in the wild maintain playfulness their whole lives – with their offspring, with their mates. When we lose that childlike quality, we lose sight of something really important. Very few jobs are life or death - unless you become a surgeon, in which case, please take that one seriously. When you move to a new town or city – and many of you will, find the rec league. Join the acting troupe. Find the outdoors club. PLAY DODGEBALL! Create the conditions for play, and the playfulness that’s been dormant inside you will push right through. Ultimately, the reason play is my number one piece of advice is simple: the joy it brings to anything you do. Play allowed me to enjoy 32 years with pre-adolescents. Imagine what it can do for you. Second: Be curious Be curious about whatever interests you. Be curious about yourself, about your loved ones, about your studies, about the world. Put the phone down. Get off YouTube and Instagram, find a trail nearby, leave the phone at home, and just go. Be curious about where your mind wanders when you let it. Most of you have no idea what you want to do when you “grow up.” Curiosity can lead you somewhere worth going. The last thing I ever imagined being was a teacher. But I got curious about it, and my dad kept saying, Teddy, you should be a teacher, and here I stand, 32 years later, giving a high school commencement speech to a community full of people I love. And one more thing about curiosity and this new chapter: you’re embarking on an adventure. The thing about adventures is that you never know what they’ll actually be like. You may have a vision. You may have heard from others what college or work or life in a new city will be like. But it won’t be that. It will be wonderful, and unpredictable, and at times, lonely and hard. Don’t be fooled by other people’s social media. While you’re sitting alone, wondering what’s wrong with you, someone else’s Instagram feed will make it look like they are surrounded by their besties and couldn’t be happier. Remember: that’s a curated moment in time. It is not reality, and comparison is the thief of joy. It takes a long time, real time, to make a true friend. Be patient with yourself. Curiosity brought me here. Let it take you somewhere wonderful. Third: Be kind to your parents This moment is enormous for you. But it is everything to them. In the blink of an eye, you went from a toddler strapped into a swing, being pushed up, up, up into the air, giggling with delight, to driving a car, which is terrifying, to sitting here today in a cap and gown. Be loving to them. Their lives exploded with love the moment you came along. You busted open their hearts in a way they never thought possible. And now, you’re leaving… I don’t think many of you remember Dutch, that was my first love. A chocolate lab. When my wife was expecting our first child, I remember thinking: how can I possibly love anything more than I love Dutch? It’s just not possible. Then Lucas came. Then Julian. Then Quincy. And my heart was forever altered, with a love that was both fiercely protective and endlessly expansive. Every parent in this room would do anything for you. Anything. So call them. Tell them thank you. Tell them you love them. Do it today, not someday, and do it regularly. Congratulations, Class of 2026. Go play. Stay curious. And call home. Thank you.

articles.text: PHS Valedictorian Nathan Tuan will be attending the University of California, Los Angeles in the fall of 2026. Good evening everyone—principals, teachers, families, friends, and most importantly, the graduating class of 2026. Graduates, we happen to be sitting in alphabetical order. Parents, you happen to be sitting in places of your own choosing. So, here’s the question: would you rather have assigned, or unassigned seating? Hold onto that thought while I tell you a story. My first memory of Piedmont High School was when I transferred here in 10th grade. On opening day, I walked into Mr. Palsa’s classroom at 8:15 a.m. After I introduced myself, he prompted me to find my seat. There was a piece of paper with a hand-drawn diagram of our seating arrangements. It was like hieroglyphics to me. I stumbled around sitting in one wrong seat after another, Mr. Palsa shaking his head each time, until I finally found the right one. A year passed. Through assigned seating charts, I built new friendships with the people I coincidentally ended up near. Our shared challenge in classes like Honors Chemistry and APUSH were incubators for meaningful relationships. When I asked you all that question, most people would probably answer unassigned. There’s comfort in deciding where to sit, who to sit with, and where you belong. But if there’s anything I learned these short, intense 3 years, it’s to keep yourself open to uncertainty. Be okay sitting with new people and trying out new things, because the freedom we have in choosing our own seats may be the very thing that restricts our horizons. Sometimes we have to sit in all the wrong seats to know when we’ve found the right one. An added bonus about leaving things to chance is that it can lead to pleasant surprises—I met Niko and Timmy in elementary school, but we separated in middle school when they transferred away. For a long time, I never had the chance to reconnect with Niko until just this year, when we happened to be in the same classes, and seated right next to each other. We picked up right where we left off. Now, he’ll be giving a speech right after mine, quite literally picking up where I leave off. So, assigned or unassigned seating? Whichever life gives you, have the courage to sit in every seat until you’ve found the right one. Class of 2026, congratulations on graduating. Thank you.

articles.text: Members of the Piedmont scouting community joined Isabelle Myers of Troop 11 and Naomi Treichler of Troop 4 to celebrate their achievement of Eagle rank on June 7. This is the highest rank in Scouts BSA, the Scouting America (formerly Boy Scouts of America) program for 11 to 17 year old youth. Lorrel Plimier, a City Councilmember representing Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, prefaced a City Proclamation with these remarks: “Our society, our world, survives because of people like Eagle scouts who are willing to serve their communities, and willing to be leaders in their communities. And this is as important now, or even more so, than it has ever been. “As young women also, you are setting an example for young girls who come behind you. And this may seem like a small thing, but I can guarantee you it’s not. It is very important. “No matter where you end up, the world needs more people like you.” Sarah King, Troop 4 Eagle Mentor, reminded fellow scouters, families, and friends, about the audacity of having women join the ranks of Eagle Scouts: “2019 was the beginning of a new era in Scouting as girls were finally welcomed into the Scouts BSA program. In Piedmont, four girls – Camille, Mollie, Lizzy, and Naomi – became members of the first female troop. If you look closely at Naomi’s uniform, you’ll notice that she wears the Founder’s Bar, which signifies that she joined Troop 4G during its inaugural year. Of those four original founders, three have now achieved the rank of Eagle Scout.” Naomi’s scouting journey started in February 2019 at Troop 406G’s (girls) open house in Sunnyvale, just days after Scouts BSA officially admitted girls. When the family decided on a move to Piedmont at the end of February, Naomi was comforted Piedmont Council Registrar Laural Fawcett (left), Troop 4 Former Scoutmaster Jeroen Grasman, and Troop 4 Eagle Scout Andrew Grasman Troop 11 Eagle Scout Isabelle Myers Troop 4 Eagle Scout Naomi Treichler Troop 4 Summer Camp Coordinator Stacy Lau (left), former Scoutmaster Walter Stokes, Assistant Scoutmaster Angela Anastasi, Eagle Mentor Sarah King, Merit Badge Counselor Kimery Leong, Tenderfoot Scout Henry Gross, and Advancement Chair Anna Kneitel Master of Ceremonies and Troop 11 Eagle Scout Theo Ferguson (left), former Troop 4 Scoutmaster Walter Stokes, former Troop 11 Scoutmaster Tom Smegal, Naomi Treichler and Isabelle Myers Piedmont Council Scouting America Scout Executive Tess English (left), Troop 11’s Martin Crawford-Jakubiak, City of Piedmont Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, and Jennifer Ferguson of Troop 11 in learning that Piedmont troops would also welcome girls in what was eventually a remaking of all Piedmont troops into co-ed units. Seven years later, Naomi submitted her Eagle application before her 18th birthday. Despite Naomi’s reserved nature, she truly enjoyed connecting with a larger community of scouts from troops outside Piedmont while at summer camp and outside the United States at the 2023 World Scout Jamboree in South Korea. Naomi joined scouting for the fun activities as soon as she could and stayed in Troop 4F (family) as its Senior Patrol Leader in 2023. “In that role” explained King, “the SPL serves as the bridge between the Scouts and the adult leadership while also running troop meetings. I think it’s fair to say this role pushed Naomi outside of her comfort zone. Imagine standing here every Monday night trying to get a room full of mostly middle-school boys to stop talking, stand quietly, and listen to the agenda. It wasn’t easy. But over time, Naomi found her voice. She learned how to rely on her composure and preparation to lead effectively. It would have been tempting to walk away, but she didn’t. In doing so, she taught the Scouts an important lesson about leadership: it isn’t always loud, but it is persistent.” In another pocket of Piedmont, Isabelle joined Troop 11 in May 2023. Isabelle’s less conventional story, started in her freshman year of high school, is an equally impressive rise through the scouting ranks on a shorter timeline and with a much busier schedule. Unlike the meandering approach to scouting of most middle school students, Isabelle had Eagle rank in her sights, and she set a very direct path to that end Scouting is all about allowing youth to set their own goals, with trusted adults providing the necessary support to guide each scout along their unique journeys. By April 2023, Isabelle had simply decided to try something new – to join in the singing, the games, and as a judge for the cooking competition at a Troop 11 campout at Dillon Beach. She was hooked. Jim Crawford-Jakubiak as Troop 11 Assistant Scoutmaster recalls a memorable comment from Isabelle from that trip: “I didn’t realize how fun scouting would be. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, June 10, 2026 Isabelle Myers, Naomi Treichler achieve rank of Eagle Scout Members of the Piedmont scouting community joined Isabelle Myers of Troop 11 and Naomi Treichler of Troop 4 to celebrate their achievement of Eagle rank on June 7. This is the highest rank in Scouts BSA, the Scouting America (formerly Boy Scouts of America) program for 11 to 17 year old youth. Lorrel Plimier, a City Councilmember representing Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, prefaced a City Proclamation with these remarks: “Our society, our world, survives because of people like Eagle scouts who are willing to serve their communities, and willing to be leaders in their communities. And this is as important now, or even more so, than it has ever been. “As young women also, you are setting an example for young girls who come behind you. And this may seem like a small thing, but I can guarantee you it’s not. It is very important. “No matter where you end up, the world needs more people like you.” Sarah King, Troop 4 Eagle Mentor, reminded fellow scouters, families, and friends, about the audacity of having women join the ranks of Eagle Scouts: “2019 was the beginning of a new era in Scouting as girls were finally welcomed into the Scouts BSA program. In Piedmont, four girls – Camille, Mollie, Lizzy, and Naomi – became members of the first female troop. If you look closely at Naomi’s uniform, you’ll notice that she wears the Founder’s Bar, which signifies that she joined Troop 4G during its inaugural year. Of those four original founders, three have now achieved the rank of Eagle Scout.” Naomi’s scouting journey started in February 2019 at Troop 406G’s (girls) open house in Sunnyvale, just days after Scouts BSA officially admitted girls. When the family decided on a move to Piedmont at the end of February, Naomi was comforted Piedmont Council Registrar Laural Fawcett (left), Troop 4 Former Scoutmaster Jeroen Grasman, and Troop 4 Eagle Scout Andrew Grasman Troop 11 Eagle Scout Isabelle Myers Troop 4 Eagle Scout Naomi Treichler Troop 4 Summer Camp Coordinator Stacy Lau (left), former Scoutmaster Walter Stokes, Assistant Scoutmaster Angela Anastasi, Eagle Mentor Sarah King, Merit Badge Counselor Kimery Leong, Tenderfoot Scout Henry Gross, and Advancement Chair Anna Kneitel Master of Ceremonies and Troop 11 Eagle Scout Theo Ferguson (left), former Troop 4 Scoutmaster Walter Stokes, former Troop 11 Scoutmaster Tom Smegal, Naomi Treichler and Isabelle Myers Piedmont Council Scouting America Scout Executive Tess English (left), Troop 11’s Martin Crawford-Jakubiak, City of Piedmont Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, and Jennifer Ferguson of Troop 11 in learning that Piedmont troops would also welcome girls in what was eventually a remaking of all Piedmont troops into co-ed units. Seven years later, Naomi submitted her Eagle application before her 18th birthday. Despite Naomi’s reserved nature, she truly enjoyed connecting with a larger community of scouts from troops outside Piedmont while at summer camp and outside the United States at the 2023 World Scout Jamboree in South Korea. Naomi joined scouting for the fun activities as soon as she could and stayed in Troop 4F (family) as its Senior Patrol Leader in 2023. “In that role” explained King, “the SPL serves as the bridge between the Scouts and the adult leadership while also running troop meetings. I think it’s fair to say this role pushed Naomi outside of her comfort zone. Imagine standing here every Monday night trying to get a room full of mostly middle-school boys to stop talking, stand quietly, and listen to the agenda. It wasn’t easy. But over time, Naomi found her voice. She learned how to rely on her composure and preparation to lead effectively. It would have been tempting to walk away, but she didn’t. In doing so, she taught the Scouts an important lesson about leadership: it isn’t always loud, but it is persistent.” In another pocket of Piedmont, Isabelle joined Troop 11 in May 2023. Isabelle’s less conventional story, started in her freshman year of high school, is an equally impressive rise through the scouting ranks on a shorter timeline and with a much busier schedule. Unlike the meandering approach to scouting of most middle school students, Isabelle had Eagle rank in her sights, and she set a very direct path to that end Scouting is all about allowing youth to set their own goals, with trusted adults providing the necessary support to guide each scout along their unique journeys. By April 2023, Isabelle had simply decided to try something new – to join in the singing, the games, and as a judge for the cooking competition at a Troop 11 campout at Dillon Beach. She was hooked. Jim Crawford-Jakubiak as Troop 11 Assistant Scoutmaster recalls a memorable comment from Isabelle from that trip: “I didn’t realize how fun scouting would be. I wish I [had] joined when I was younger.” Isabelle has definitely made up for lost time, serving in leadership roles including Patrol Leader and Troop Scribe, along her way to earning her Eagle rank. Congratulations to Isabelle Myers, Naomi Treichler, their families, and their respective parent volunteer-driven scouting communities who supported them every single step of the way.

articles.text: One of the strange things about being human is that we can travel hundreds or even thousands of miles to see something interesting, then completely ignore fascinating things that are ten minutes from our front door. When tourists come to town, they often seem to notice things that residents have stopped seeing: a beautiful view from a scenic overlook, a historic building, a quirky local business, a trail, park, or neighborhood that somehow became invisible through familiarity. The irony is that those places did not become less interesting. We simply got used to them. Psychologists call this habituation. The more often we experience something, the less attention we pay to it. It is a remarkably useful feature of the brain because it prevents us from becoming overwhelmed by information. Unfortunately, it can also make us blind to things that are genuinely wonderful. This matters because creativity begins with noticing. Before we create something new, we usually have to see something differently. That is one reason travel can feel so energizing. Everything is unfamiliar. We pay closer attention and notice details. We ask questions and find our curiosity again. But, guess what? Curiosity does not actually require a plane ticket. So here is a summer experiment: spend one afternoon acting like a tourist in your own backyard. Recently, I was taking a walk in my neighborhood and took a turn that I had never taken before. A few minutes into my walk, I passed a home with an absolutely exquisite garden, filled with flowers of all colors. It was stunning and I had never seen it before. So, this summer, visit a place you have never visited. Walk into a store you normally pass by or take a different route on your morning commute. Wander through a neighborhood you’ve never explored. And, most importantly, on your new adventures, bring a tourist’s mindset. Think about the last trip you took, you probably expected to be surprised. But, in your own neighborhood, you expect the predictable. Instead, open yourself to surprise. This experiment is not really about sightseeing –it is about interrupting the assumption that we have already seen everything worth seeing. Because creativity rarely arrives when we are looking at the world on autopilot. It tends to show up when something catches our attention and makes us look twice. This summer, before you plan your next adventure, consider spending a few hours exploring the place where you already are. You might be surprised by how much there is to discover. Nina Meehan is a keynote speaker, workshop facilitator and coach with a specialization in creativity and communication. https://ninameehan.com/

articles.text: Honorable Mentions: Andrea Martin, Nik Costello Every year provides difficult decisions for the Post’s Athlete of the Year. With so much expertise and accolades across multiple sports, we’re continuing the tradition of honoring three athletes for both girls’ and boys’ athletics. This year we’ve elected Claire Aubrecht and Lucas Smolko as our Athletes of the Year, with Andrea Martin and Nik Costello as honorable mentions. LUCAS SMOLKO Tennis Lucas Smolko finished his Piedmont High career in illustrious fashion. He won the school’s first North Coast Section Individual Tournament singles title since Barry Gilbert in 1975 by claiming the NCS Div.2 crown on May 9, and won his third consecutive Western Alameda County Conference singles title on May 1. He is the only repeat and three-time singles champion in the league tournament for boys. For the NCS title, Smolko defeated Acalanes’ Sze Ting Chen in straight sets 6-4, 6-3. To get there, he shut out St. Patrick’s Oscar Swenson 6-0, 6-0 in the opening round, won 6-1, 6-4 over Armaan Mishra of Lick-Wilmerding in the quarterfinals, and shut down Stuart Hall’s Edward Morfit 6-1, 6-0 in the semifinals. His win over Chen was a rematch of Piedmont’s February 26 match against Acalanes where Smolko lost 6-3, 7-6. Smolko’s NCS Finals appearance was the third time he reached the round in four years. He lost as a freshman to eventual Stanford player Gus Grumet of University 6-3, 6-1 and lost in a three-set 5-7, 6-1, 6-3 battle to Dylan Donovan of Head-Royce as a junior. For the WACC singles crown, he defeated Castro Valley’s Guhan Anandkumar in straight sets by scores of 6-2, 6-3 as the top seeded player. He beat Alameda’s Johnny Sanchez 6-0, 6-1 in the first round, Castro Valley’s Matthew Rodriguez 6-0, 6-2 in the quarterfinals, and Bishop O’Dowd’s Marcello Sachelari 6-1, 6-3 in the semifinals. He was our Freshman of the Year in 2024 and honorable menStaff Photos Lucas Smolko earns our Athlete of the Year award after winning this year’s D2 NCS singles title and his third straight WACC singles title. Smolko our Athlete of the Month in March and May, along with our honorable mention in April. Piedmont High named Smolko the school’s male athlete of the year in 2026. He will continue his tennis career at UC Santa Cruz. 10th of 23 runners. As the second leg on Piedmont’s 4x100 relay team at the Bayshore Meet, she and Akunna Iroh, Darcy McKee, and Nia Jackson ran a record time of 49.21 seconds to place second of 19 teams. Aubrecht was our Athlete of the Month in May and March. CLAIRE AUBRECHT Track and Field Claire Aubrecht earns our Athlete of the Year award after setting the school record in the 100 meter dash, 200 meter dash, and 4x100 relay. Co-Player of the Year, averaging 23.5 points per game and 10.5 rebounds per game. Martin won the league’s Player of the Year award, the fifth year in a row for a Piedmont player. Sophomore teammate Jenelle Solis won the 2025 honor as a freshman, Natalia Martinez won in 2024 and 2023, and Trinity Zamora won in 2022. Piedmont received the No. 3 seed in the NCS Open Division and finished third on the Section. LUCAS SMOLKO Tennis Lucas Smolko finished his Piedmont High career in illustrious fashion. He won the school’s first North Coast Section Individual Tournament singles title since Barry Gilbert in 1975 by claiming the NCS Div.2 crown on May 9, and won his third consecutive Western Alameda County Conference singles title on May 1. articles.text: FOOTBALL Football made history last fall, achieving their first berth in a North Coast Section championship since the 1976 title winning team that was elected into the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame. Piedmont finished 8-5 with the No. 2 seed in the Division 7 NCS postseason. They bashed No. 7 St. Patrick 49-7 and followed up with a 28-10 win over No. 3 Willits in the semifinals. Skylar Best, Viviane Oesterer, Cora Chun, Amalia Gray, Cora Brozowski Schrader, and Nikita Gorelik. articles.text: The Australian National Team made its headquarters at the Oakland Roots’ training facility for the 2026 World Cup. The Post was among the media members to be given an exclusive invitation to observe one of their first sessions ahead of the Socceroos’ opening group stage match against Turkiye on June 13 in Group D. Oakland and Alameda mayors Barbara Lee and Marilyn Ezzy Ashcraft were on hand to welcome the national team to the East Bay. “Australia has an incredible fan base. We are so excited to have them here, we worked so hard to qualify as a home base and to bring our Australian friends and family to Oakland, Alameda and the East Bay. People in Oakland, Alameda, and the East Bay are very loyal. When you invest in the community, they want to return that love. To be selected by the Socceroos, and to see them staying in our hotels, eating at our restaurants, and giving back to our community builds loyalty, and they are going to feel that love back,” said Roots president Lindsay Barenz. The Roots’ facility on Bay Farm Island near the Oakland Airport is the same location as the former Oakland Raiders practice site. articles.text: Performances feature famous “Spreckles Organ” Visit Legion of Honor in San Francisco any Saturday afternoon at 4 p.m. and enjoy a free organ concert in the Rodin Gallery by local classically trained organists Jonathan Dimmock, Joy-Leilani Garbutt or Christopher Keady. Dimmock is a graduate of Oberlin and Yale, and the first American to hold the prestigious position of organ scholar of Westminster Abbey. He was resident organist at St. John the Divine in New York City, St. Mark’s in Minneapolis, and Grace Cathedral in San Francisco. Dimmock is principal organist at the Legion of Honor, organist for the San Francisco Symphony, and director of music at Congregation Sherith Israel. He has recorded a Grammy-winning record with the San Francisco Symphony. Garbutt is an organist and cofounder of the Boulanger Initiative, a nonprofit organization that supports female composers. Garbutt spent a year in France researching early 20th-century organ music by female composers exclusively, and currently serves as the director of music for St. Luke’s Episcopal Church in San Francisco. Keady is the interim director of music at the famous Grace Cathedral in San Francisco, where he serves as principal accompanist for the Cathedral Choir of Men and Boys and performs on the cathedral’s Alexander Memorial Organ. Concerts begin at 4 p.m. in Gallery 10 and are free to all museum patrons. All concerts feature the museum’s historic 1924 Skinner pipe organ, called the “Spreckels Organ,” and last approximately 45 minutes to one hour. The concerts are part of the museum’s ongoing dedication to art and music, often featuring a diverse repertoire that complements the surrounding sculptures. The historic “Spreckles Organ” was commissioned by philanthropist John Spreckles and is designed to blend into the museum’s structure. Its 4,500 pipes are not outwardly visible, and the ceiling of the gallery is canvas so that the organ can be heard throughout the gallery and museum. The canvas ceiling is painted as a trompe-l’œil to resemble a marble apse. Residents of all nine Bay Area counties, including Alameda, receive free admission to Legion of Honor in San Francisco on Saturdays. Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Solano, and Sonoma residents can visit the museum during operating hours and view any of its permanent collection galleries. Visitors ages 17 and under always receive free admission to the permanent collection galleries. Visit https://www.famsf.org/ events/organ-concert to learn more and to register. The historic “Spreckles Organ” was commissioned by philanthropist John Spreckles and is designed to blend into the museum’s structure.
articles.title: Free organ concert at Legion of Honor every Saturday

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) recently unveiled its newest exhibition, Feel the Beat: Dance in Photographs, which explores the evolving dialogue between movement and photography. Feel the Beat, on view now through January 31, 2027, highlights photography’s role in shaping how dance is recorded and remembered, and how dancers have inspired photographers to view movement in a different medium. The new exhibition includes items from SFMOMA’s permanent collection,opening with a gallery devoted to Irving Penn’s images of Anna Halprin and the San Francisco Dancers’ Workshop, as well as pictures that reflect Halprin’s experimental approach to dance. The second gallery turns to Kamaitachi, the partnership between Japanese photographer Eikoh Hosoe and Butoh founder Tatsumi Hijikata. The final section of the exhibition explores ‘nightlife,’ with Malick Sidibé’s Larry Fink, Studio 54, New York City, 1977; on view now at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art photographs of dancing at parties in Mali, as well as photos by Nan Goldin, Larry Fink, Janine Gordon, Weegee, Imogen Cunningham, Barbara Morgan, Robert Rauschenberg, Richard Avedon and more. For more information, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibitions/.
articles.title: Feel the Beat: Dance in Photographs on view now at SFMOMA

articles.text: The Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture (FMCAC) in San Francisco is hosting this month’s Night Market, in partnership with Off the Grid and West Coast Craft, on June 19. The free monthly event in San Francisco runs on select Fridays from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. through December, and features live music, arts and crafts pop-up shops and hands-on workshops, as well as extended hours at nearby museums including Museo Italo Americano and FLAX Art & Design store on select dates. Fort Mason Night Market was conceptualized following the success of an inaugural night market in December that drew over 10,000 attendees. FMCAC hosts outdoor markets once a month through December that transform its iconic campus into a showcase of local artisans, cuisine, and live entertainment. Off the Grid provides more than 25 food and refreshment vendors at each event as attendees enjoy performances by local DJs, engage in hands-on creative workshops, and view public art installations from FMCAC collections. West Coast Craft, founded in San Francisco in 2013 to create a space for independent artists and designers to sell and promote their artwork, is hosted at FMCAC annually and is one of the largest arts fairs in the country. Local artisans who appear at the annual festival, which traditionally takes place in the summer, will be invited to sell their work at monthly Night Market events. “Fort Mason Center is known for being a gathering place, a space for people to exchange ideas, experience beauty, and connect with different modes of art and cultural expressions,” said Mike Buhler, FMCAC’s President and CEO. “We’re excited to collaborate with our partners to offer another way for people to come together, support local arts organizations and small businesses, and enjoy the natural beauty of the campus.” All events are free and open to the public. The next Night Market event will be held on July 24. For more information, visit https://fortmason.org/event/fortmason-night-market-2026/ Live entertainment, arts and food vending take place at the iconic Fort Mason this month.
articles.title: Fort Mason hosts Night Market on June 19

articles.text: Shotgun Players presents the Bay Area premiere of Continuity by Bess Wohl, showing at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley now through June 27. Directed by Emilie Whelan, the comedy centers on a Hollywood film production attempting to address climate change while unraveling behind the scenes. The play follows director Maria as she struggles to hold together both a chaotic movie set and the people working on it. “Continuity is zany, ambitious, and full-throated,” Whelan said in a statement. “Bess Wohl understands that the climate crisis is a human crisis and that humans standing in front of the climate crisis are actually like clowns. It is so big, and we are slack-jawed before it.” The production satirizes the entertainment industry while exploring how individuals respond to the climate crisis. According to the company, the fictional film set includes a Styrofoam ice shelf and a production relocated to New Mexico for tax incentives. Patrick Dooley, artistic director of Shotgun Players, said the play reflects the company’s 2026 season theme of “making art that Cast of Shotgun Players Continuity

articles.text: Violinist Pablo de Sarasate Truth is often stranger than fiction. Many famous people claim that they prefer to be “unrecognized“. Incognito might be their nom de plume. While some famous people love being in the spotlight and will do everything they can to gain public attention (think President Trump or boxing champion Muhammad Ali), there are others. You can take this at face value or consider the following stories. They are completely true. Way back in 1895, a friend of mine saw the immortal violinist Pablo de Sarasate sitting in the concert hall of the Milano Conservatory. Sarasate was seated toward the back of the hall on an outside seat with his two Stradivarius violins tucked between his knees. My friend told me that Sarasate had a quiet dignity. What was also interesting is that he always took his instruments with him wherever he went. When speaking of violinists, the name Jascha Heifetz comes to mind. He was a real contradiction. He appreciated being recognized and at the same time he pretended that he enjoyed being incognito. He believed that if he dressed in an “inconspicuous” way, nobody would recognize him. He donned the most outlandish clothing and pulled his hat low over his brow, thinking that he was unrecognizable. Wearing this outlandish outfit to a concert, a friend of mine recognized him and walked over to say hello. My friend asked him, “You are Jascha Heifetz aren’t you?” The man replied, “My name is Joseph.” Both were correct. The man in the outlandish outfit was, in fact Jascha Heifetz. But when the man said that his name was Joseph, this was the truth also.
articles.title: The Musical Gourmet

articles.text: His birth name was actually Joseph Heifetz. He changed the name to Jascha later on. The scene now changes to Manhattan. A music lover recognizes a famous pianist walking in a residential area. The two men began to talk. At the end of the conversation, the music lover said, “Nice to meet you, Mr. Rubenstein.” What a faux pas. The man he had been walking with was famed pianist Vladimir Horowitz – the pianistic enemy of Arthur Rubinstein. We leave the music world for a brief moment, but remain in Manhattan. An older man was going to work as greeter in Jack Dempsey’s restaurant. As he arrived at the front door in a taxi, he was accosted by two muggers. Thinking the old guy was an easy mark, they attacked him. The old guy reacted quickly. He knocked the first mugger out with a left hook, and then knocked the other guy out with a right cross. He then calmly walked into Jack Dempsey‘s restaurant to begin his work as the greeter. I forgot to tell you…the greeter in Jack Dempsey‘s restaurant was the Manassa Mauler himself… Jack Dempsey. Sometimes mistaken identity comes with a knockout punch. Returning to the world of music, we have a very beautiful story involving Paul McCartney of The Beatles. A father was walking in a park with his young daughter at his side. The little girl was an enthusiastic fan of The Beatles, and wouldn’t you know it? Paul McCartney was in that same park. The girl recognized him, and said to him that she loved all of the songs of The Beatles. Paul McCartney asked the little girl what her favorite song was and then he sang it to her. Some things speak for themselves.
articles.title: Incognito

articles.text: Dolly! A Pride Show offers audiences a festive Pride weekend experience. The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus launches Pride Month festivities with performances of Dolly! A Pride Show on June 13 at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco, bringing the music of Dolly Parton to the stage in a concert honoring queer joy, resilience and community. Described as a celebration of queer love, chosen family and self-expression, the concert features Parton’s iconic songs reimagined by the chorus. Organized in two acts with an intermission, the program moves from themes of joy and individuality to reflection, solidarity and collective strength. According to organizers, the show draws inspiration from Parton’s long-standing message of kindness, compassion and acceptance. The performance blends camp, humor and heartfelt storytelling while emphasizing the role of joy as a form of resistance and community-building. Founded in 1978, the San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus remains one of the world’s most influential LGBTQ arts organizations. The ensemble was the first openly gay chorus and helped spark a nationwide LGBTQ choral movement following its first public performance at a candlelight vigil on the steps of San Francisco City Hall after the assassinations of Harvey Milk and George Moscone. More than four decades later, the chorus continues to combine artistic excellence with advocacy and community engagement. Dolly! A Pride Show offers audiences a festive Pride weekend experience centered on music, inclusion and the enduring power of belonging. The production will be presented at 1 p.m. and 3 p.m. Tickets are available through the San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus and the Curran Theatre box office websites. Visit https://www.sfgmc.org/ dolly-a-pride-show for more information and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus presents Dolly! A Pride Show on June 13

This juried show will include more than 70 original works, all created by Signature Members using watermedia on paper, and selected by juror Michael Reardon, a well respected Oakland-based award–winning artist. Note that the CWA will be bringing its 57th Annual International Exhibition to PCA in January, 2027. Saturday, June 13, 5:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art History Lecture Join Art Historian Michael Stehr for a 50-minute illustrated lecture that celebrates the ongoing exhibition at the DeYoung Museum (running thru July 26). The DeYoung exhibition, Monet and Venice, shows many of Claude Monet’s three or four dozen originals created during a 1908 visit to Venice, where the artist found re-invigoration at a time when he badly needed it, along with examples painted by Monet’s contemporaries demonstrating the contrasts in style and perception between them. The lecture will explore both the artworks involved and their contexts, as well as the singular effects inspired by the character of Venice as background. America 250: Celebrating American Music, Old and New will include masterworks by well-known composers such as Bernstein, Gershwin, Milhaud and Price, sharing the stage with gems by Michael Kaulkin and Willson Osborne. John Zorn and Daniel Lockert will present some of the most beloved American classical music for clarinet and piano, and will provide you with hot tea and tasty treats after the music. articles.text: Veus – Cor Infantil Amics de la Unió (Catalonia) Veus – Cor Infantil Amics de la Unió, a youth choir from Catalonia in Spain will be performing this summer at the Golden Gate International Choral Festival hosted by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. It’s spotlight performance is on July 16 at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. It will also participate in the group choral performances on the opening and closing nights of the festival. The choir was founded in 1996 within the Music School created by the Societat Coral Amics de la Unió of Granollers in Barcelona. It is conducted by Josep Vila Jover, who has been with the choir since its formation. The choir stands out for the quality, eclecticism, and uniqueness of its productions. He has been the resident choir director at the Teatre Auditori de Granollers since 2017. Since 1995, Jover has served as the artistic director of the ‘Escola de Música Amics de la Unió,’ a prestigious choral school in Barcelona with over 650 students and 10 active choirs. He is regularly invited to participate in prestigious festivals throughout Europe, notably La Folle Journée (Nantes, France) and Via Aeterna (Mont Saint-Michel, France). In addition the choir has toured and participated in festivals in Japan, China, the United States, and Australia. Veus has participated in numerous international festivals and has been awarded in numerous contests and competitions. Among the most recent awards are the prize for the best interpretation of the obligatory song and the 3rd prize in the children’s category at the 7th Tokyo International Choir Competition (2024), the 3rd prize at the 53rd Toulouse Choral Competition (2022), the prize Josep Anselm Clavé for the best recording for the album Els Colors del Mar (2018), the Guido de Arezzo recognition (2017), the 1st prize at the 47th Toulouse Choral Competition (2015) and the Silver Rose Bowl at the UER Let the Peoples competition Sing! (2013). Veus performs regularly on main stages of the country, such as the Gran Teatre del Liceu (Barcelona), the Palau de la Música Catalana (Barcelona), and the Auditori de Barcelona. Internationally, Jover’s choir has performed at the Philharmonie de Paris and the Philharmonie de Luxembourg. It has shared the stage with prestigious directors such as Kazushi Ono, Jordi Savall, and Gustavo Dudamel. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival, held every three years, takes place this summer from July 13 to July 18. Information on the concerts and spotlight choirs can be found on their website https://www.piedmontchoirs. org/ggf-concerts-2026. including which concerts are free for the public.
articles.title: Barcelona choir to participate in Golden Gate Choral Festival this July

articles.text: The Family Man and It’s a Wonderful Life rely on the good will nurtured during the Christmas holidays. Yet, at the center of these two exceptional films, replete with wonderful characters and compelling plots, we see that they are not only set in different centuries and vastly different locations (Bedford Falls, N.Y. on the cusp of WWII, and in real time, Wall Street, New York City), both offer contrasting characters: Nicolas Cage as Jack Campbell, a successful Mergers and Acquisitions financier, and James Stewart portraying George Bailey, reluctant heir apparent to a small town Savings and Loan bank. Each narrative asks its audience to suspend its disbelief while managing to find its own comedic sweet spot, while pausing to remind us, in small and large ways, the timeless value of friendship, decency, love and family. Of course, each story relies on two very different angels (Clarence and Cash – portrayed by Henry Travers and Don Cheadle). Both, pushed by unexpected Donna Reed, James Stewart, and Karolyn Grimes in Frank Capra’s It’s a Wonderful Life Tea Leoni and Nicholas Cage in The Family Man events, answer that very human question: “What if?” What if George Bailey’s wish, made in a moment of financial despair, had indeed come true? In response, Clarence takes George on an unsettling tour of Bedford Falls, by way of showing him various unexpected outcomes. Jack Campbell, facing a vastly different moment, tells Cash that he has everything he could ever want. By way of backstory, we see him at the airport, preparing to board a flight bound for England, and he is shown what might have been had he listened to his long-time college girlfriend, Kate Reynolds (Téa Leoni), who asks him not to go. She clearly fears such a separation will change everything going forward. And so it does. But perhaps not. Can life ever offer an extraordinary do-over? An almost magical, transforming, “if only” opportunity in that crossroads moment. Life is about choices. What if we chose wisely, based on unexpected insights and life changing revelations regarding what is truly of value and important? And finally, if a bell rings, remember to answer. No regrets. Happy Father’s Day. The Family Man. Directed by Brett Ratner. Starring Nicolas Cage, Tea Leoni, Don Cheadle. Rated PG-13. 2hrs 5min. Streaming on Fandango/Prime/AppleTV/ YouTube It’s a Wonderful Life. Directed by Frank Capra. Starring James Stewart, Donna Reed, Lionel Barrymore. Rated PG. 2hrs 10min. Streaming on Prime/Fandango/ YouTube/AppleTV

articles.text: The Lincoln Lawyer — an episodic series (Seasons 1-5), streaming on several platforms, is a compelling courtroom-drama and legal procedural, based on the bestselling Michael Connelly novels. If you missed the series debut, and if you enjoy a deep dive into a serial character, definitely begin at the beginning and binge-watch, knowing that Seasons 3-4 are ready and good to go. Season 5 has not been released, though Netflix has announced that with the last episode the Lincoln Lawyer saga will wrap. The series has at its center Los Angeles criminal defense attorney Mickey Haller (Manuel Garcia Rulfo), referred to as The Lincoln Lawyer, a moniker derived from his preference to use the backseat of a Lincoln Town Car for his office with a driver, Izzy, an ex-client working off legal fees. His work takes him Manuel Garcia-Rulfo in The Lincoln Lawyer from courthouse hearings, trials, prisons, county jails and client appointments. His assistant, Lorna (Becki Newton), handles all incoming calls, scheduling, and endless paperwork. Each season essentially stands alone with new and carry-over plots, while the core cast returns giving the writers the opportunity to expand in complexity the returning characters. There is Mickey’s extended family and office crew: his first wife, Maggie McPhersone (Neve Campbell), who is an L.A. prosecutor; his investigator, Cisco (Angus Sampson), a rough-edged ex-biker engaged to Lorna (briefly Mickey’s second wife); and his driver, Izzy (Jazz Raycole), a past client,

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group gathered last Wednesday at its regular time at the Exedra, with a large turnout of 54 walkers and five K-9 best friends. Dave DeRoche was celebrating his birthday, and his wife, Nancy, was hosting a party for him afterward at their home. Since the group would end up in the neighborhood, Nancy also offered to lead a tour of her area above Oakland Avenue, which includes the historic Blair and Scenic Avenues. Nancy said she became interested in her neighborhood’s history after learning that noted architect Albert Farr once lived in her Oakland Avenue home. She has drawn on research by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi and historian Meghan Bennett, whose website, paintingpiedmont.com, is dedicated to the Bourgeois Bohemians of “Boho Piedmont.” The area above Oakland Avenue, Nancy explained, was a bohemian neighborhood from roughly 1890 to 1910 — a far different place from today. It was rural and sparsely populated, and writers and painters like Jack London and Xavier “Marty” Martinez lived there in unique homes, many of which they built themselves, as artists seemed to do at the time. articles.text: On Monday, June 1, there was a large turnout of 27 members of the First Mondays Reading Group in Piedmont Community Hall for their monthly book discussion. They were there to talk about their June book, Barbarian Days: A Surfing Life by William Finnegan. It won the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for Biography/Autobiography. This memoir tells the story of Finnegan’s lifelong, obsessive pursuit of surfing from his childhood in California and Hawaii to adventures chasing waves in the South Pacific, Australia, and Africa over the years. The group’s discussion of Barbarian Days reinforced the understanding that a reader’s enjoyment of a book often depends on their prior experiences and ability to connect with its subject matter. While some members found Barbarian Days fascinating and engaging, others found it difficult to relate to and tedious. The conversation underscored how differently the same book can resonate, or not, with different readers. The discussion began spontaneously with members sharing their own surfing and travel experiences, which at times seemed almost more central to the conversation than the book. For several participants, the surfing culture of the 1960s and 1970s had been an important part of their youth. The music of the Beach Boys, surfing magazines, and films such as The Endless Summer were powerful influences. For some, this was a nearly religious experience that shaped their lives. The few members of the group with surfing experience were especially able to relate to the book. They understood the obsession that, for people like Finnegan, bordered on addiction. They had experienced it themselves or witnessed it in friends and family members. Surfing provided a sense of exhilaration, like standing at the edge of a cliff. The bigger the wave, the bigger the thrill. This drive seemed to continue in Finnegan’s later life as he became a war correspondent. It was suggested he was an “adrenaline junkie.” Readers were divided not only about the book itself but also about Finnegan’s writing style. Those who admired it found his descriptions of people, places, and experiences to be vivid, elegant, and often extraordinary. Other readers thought the author’s writing was just “okay” or “good enough.” They liked parts of the book, but lost interest at other times. Readers generally agreed that the second half of the book was better than the first. Throughout the memoir, Finnegan is on both a literal and a figurative journey. His relentless search for the “perfect wave” drives his travels around the world, but surfing is more than a passion; it’s central to his life and identity. At the same time, surfing serves as a vehicle for his personal growth and self-discovery. As the memoir progresses, readers felt Finnegan mature and gain a deeper understanding of himself and his world. Because Barbarian Days is a memoir, its focus naturally remains on Finnegan. However, some readers felt Finnegan lacked self-reflection, and he did not sufficiently present the other people in the book. Several also noted the absence of humor, observing that despite its many adventures and memorable experiences, the book was rarely funny. Personal travel and living in places like Hawaii made some readers more interested in Finnegan’s story. They enjoyed his adventures, people, and the cultures he experienced, but others were looking for more about what Finnegan experienced. He seemed to be an observer but not fully engaged. Surfing always came first. There were also community aspects of Finnegan’s surfing life that readers appreciated. He and his traveling partners, along with other friends, shared a passion that bonded them. While some readers enjoyed, even loved, the book, for others it was a slow “slog.” How many ways could you describe riding Barbarian Days: A Surfing Life by William Finnegan a large wave? They didn’t care about all the surfing minutiae. One reader said her book-skimming skills were helpful to get through this book’s 464 pages. Another reader loved the repetition. It was a way to be a surfer without getting wet. Barbarian Days brought out personal experiences as well as likes and dislikes. The readers agreed they learned about surfing, which may have been more than some wanted, but they were exposed to one man’s obsession and personal growth. Readers agreed that we all have varying degrees of passions, and we hope they lead us to become better people. Future books The readers had previously selected Old Filth by English author Jane Gardam for July and The Art Thief by Michael Finkel for August. After Dick Carter presented three fiction candidates, the group chose Horse by Geraldine Brooks for their September read. With all their business done, they took a group photo outside the Community Hall. The group will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion on July 6 at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required at https://bit. ly/3R86PP4. The First Monday Reading group included Bob Hall, Sandy Threlfall, Mary Carter, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Melba Yee, Susan Southworth, Heidi Schmidt, Ken Young, Adrienne Hamlin, Darby Gragg, Tim Weishahn, Susie Backer, Phil Witte, Orrel Lanter, Bill Ahern, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Gerry Gregg, Peggy Shultz, Laura Goldman, Lois Price, Mike Henn, Nadean Guffanti, Sarah Johnson, Odette Pollar, Bella Almanzan, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus.

Edie Elmquist is one of the most active athletes in the school as the flag football team’s starting quarterback in the fall and the softball team’s starting shortstop in the spring. She recently was named the WACC Shoreline Player of the Year in softball. The softball team went 13-11 this season and reached the Div. 6 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 6 seed. They beat No. 11 California School for the Deaf 18-11 in the first round and lost to No. 3 Willits 17-7 in the quarterfinals. She led the team with a .542 batting average for 32 hits, 31 RBIs, and 54 runs scored, to go along with a team-leading 35 stolen bases. The flag fooiball team went 5-13 last season with Elmquist earning first-team All-League honors. Some of her top performances include a touchdown carry and pass in a 12-6 win over Miramonte on September 4, and a touchdown pass in their 6-0 win over Mt. Eden on September 11. articles.text: All ballots have been cast in the June 2 election, in which Piedmont residents were asked to continue to fund the schools with the passage of Measure H. As of press time the renewal, which evergreens the flat-rate per parcel tax, showed strong signs of passage based on preliminary results. At 8:17 p.m. the first drop of ballots, showed 80% in favor of the measure which needs 66.7% to pass. At this first ballot drop there were 1,649 votes for the measure and 409 votes against. Measure H would replace the current Measure G, which currently accumulates $12,000,000 for the schools annually, almost 25% of the school district’s total budget. Measure H, if passed, would not take effect until Measure G expires in 2028. Measure H promises to advance reading, writing, language, science, technology, engineering and math. The measure’s funding will also go to music and the arts, updating textbooks and other academic programs like college counseling. The passage of Measure H would evergreen the tax, keeping it intact unless voters repeal it with a separate vote. The current Measure G, has a 2% maximum annual increase, and Measure H would allow the school board to ask for up to 3% annually to keep pace with inflation.
articles.title: Measure H preliminary results

articles.text: The Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) recently hosted a party to thank donors for their contributions to the Piedmont Aquatic Center. During the event, President Patty Dunlap announced that PBF’s Spring Campaign will support the City in creating a new Nature Play Area in Piedmont Park. Karen Sullivan, PBF President during the pool campaign, recounted the foundation’s efforts to make the aquatic center a reality. PBF was an early endorser of Measure UU, and Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen credited this support as crucial to the bond measure’s passage. PBF contributed a total of $239,000 to the project, specifically earmarked for the drought-tolerant and native landscaping that now graces the Aquatics Center. For mer Mayor Valer ie Matzger and Piedmont Park and Projects Manager Nancy Kent spoke about the importance of using low-water California native plants. They led donor groups around the center to view the collection and shared plans for the upcoming Nature Play Area which will be in Piedmont’s Main Park adjacent to new swings. This project will transform an under-used section into a vibrant outdoor learning space featuring climbing logs, natural play elements and hands-on spaces where children can engage with the outdoors in meaningful ways. A PBF brochure will be arriving at every Piedmont home soon with an envelope to support the Nature Play Area or other ongoing initiatives, including the Dearing Memorial. Contributions can also be mailed to City Hall (120 Vista Ave, Piedmont, CA 94611) or made through the PBF website: www.PiedmontBeautificationFoundation.org. Valerie Matzger shows Aquatic Center native plants to PBF donors. Photo by Sharon Hom
articles.title: Beautification Foundation honors donors; announces Spring Campaign

While the fire was declared under control at 2:07 a.m., firefighters spent several more hours clearing debris and salvaging valuables for the residents who were sheltered by neighbors while other accommodations were arranged. In the aftermath of fires, smoke, heat, water damage, hidden hot spots, damage to structural components, and other factors often make buildings unsafe to occupy. The Fire Department assesses the integrity of the structure and works with property owners to recover property and restrict entry if needed.

articles.text: Did you know that Monday, June 8, is World Oceans Day? As we head into Summer, which often means spending time at the beach, I have a challenge for us. How much garbage can we prevent from ending up on our beaches, in our oceans, and in other waterways? I’m a rising senior at PHS and I have a summer challenge that is related to my Girl Scout Gold Award Project. I’m a sailor and sailing instructor, and I spend a ton of time on the water thinking about our oceans. Many of us are familiar with California Coastal Cleanup Day, which will be September 19 this year. Beach cleanups like this and other less well-known beach and waterway cleanups are incredibly important for helping clean up coastal garbage. Ocean and beach garbage is a huge problem — millions of tons of plastic and garbage enter our marine ecosystems every year. But wouldn’t it be great if we could prevent garbage from ending up there in the first place? What if we focused more attention on making sure that trash cans at beaches and waterways aren’t allowed to overflow? When trash cans overflow, lightweight plastics — bags, wrappers, cups and straws — get blown into the water and end up in the ocean and surrounding ecosystems. Preventing trash can overflow may not seem like an important solution at first, but it is one of the most immediate and impactful solutions that individual citizens can contribute to and have control over. Permanent solutions to the overflowing trash can issue is going to be slow and complicated, because it will require coordination between local governments, parks, and community organizations to increase the frequency of trash collection or expand the number, size, or design of trashcans at popular, highly used coastal areas. While I’m working on making that happen, there is a much simpler, immediate solution that each one of us can make happen. We can pledge to bring our own trash home with us from each beach outing. Each piece of plastic or garbage that is properly contained in a home trash can is a piece of garbage that doesn’t get blown into our oceans, doesn’t enter the food chain of marine life, doesn’t wash up on shore, and doesn’t break down into the microplastics that are found in our oceans. I hope you will join me for an early celebration of World Oceans Day by signing up for my Ocean Garbage Prevention Challenge, and pledge to take action - either by helping prevent garbage from ending up in our oceans, or by helping clean it up once it’s there. Please spread the word! If we can prevent more garbage from entering our oceans, we will have even less garbage to collect on California Coastal Cleanup Day on September 19. –See you at the Beach! https://forms.gle/NeG7uqSkPiTSkG
articles.title: Celebrating World Oceans Day on June 8

OPINION Beware of 580 truck access study By Wendy Silvani I’m writing to urge you not to move forward with this study. Since first becoming aware of it just weeks ago, I’ve learned much that concerns me. The premise of the study itself is questionable. Neither East nor West Oakland organizations you cite as the core reason for this study support ‘spreading the harm,’ which is the purpose of the study. This study deserves a historical response to how Caltrans prioritized alignment of its freeway network from the 1960s through the present. The scope of the study seems intentionally oversimplified and underscoped. Elements analyzed for the 880 corridor are appropriate, but the story for 580 is quite different, and the analysis is apples-to-oranges. Because of the 580’s original intent as a scenic highway (and no heavy trucks), its alignment and design are fundamentally different. Fires and landslides must be considered. Evacuations, as well as access to the many emergency services, hospitals, and schools built in proximity to 580, need to be included. Over half of Oakland’s population lives within 1,000 feet of 580. articles.text: Summer schedules at the Piedmont Community Pool begin on Monday, June 8, bringing extended weekend hours, expanded programs, and ways to enjoy both pools. A new addition for summer is afternoon “tube time” at the Competition Pool – clear inner tubes available for swimmers to relax and float. The goal is to make the larger pool more inviting for recreational use while helping ease pressure on the Activity Pool during busy periods. Swimmers must pass a swim test to use tubes in the Competition Pool. Lap swimming will continue to be available in the Competition Pool during all open hours. Starting June 6, the Activity Pool will host swim lessons on weekday Families watch swimmers in the activity pool.
articles.title: Summer hours at the Piedmont Pool start June 8

articles.text: America’s 250th anniversarypn July 4th commemorates the adoption of the Declaration of Independence in 1776, when the 13 American colonies declared their freedom from British rule. This historic milestone reflects the founding ideals of liberty, equality, and self-governance, and honors the efforts of the Founding Fathers and early Americans who fought for independence and established the United States as a republic. Governor George Pardee’s family home is a fabulous destination for a safe and enjoyable way to celebrate this important holiday.
articles.title: Spend July 4 at Pardee Home Museum

articles.text: A presentation at the June 3 Park Commission meeting will share findings from a draft report about how Piedmont can better care for its parks and open spaces so they remain healthy, well-maintained, and resilient far into the future. The meeting is tonight Wednesday, June 3, at At the meeting, project consultants will deliver a presentation sharing recommendations from a draft Sustainable Park Management Plan – a roadmap for long-term park stewardship that examines how the City maintains parks, protects natural areas, manages wear from heavy use, and makes informed decisions The Sustainable Park Management Plan is intended to serve as a tool for future decision-making, helping the City make more consistent, sustainable decisions about park maintenance and Rather than taking a one-sizefits-all approach, the document recognizes that different park areas need different strategies. A heavily used natural area may need erosion control, protected planting areas, and clearer rules for use. A highly used athletic field may need more structured rest periods, drainage improvements, or lifecycle planning. A lightly used lawn area may be a Sustainable Park Management Plan pop-up at Crocker Park. candidate for more climate-adaptive planting. • Key themes in the draft recommendations include: • Matching maintenance practices to how each park area is used. • Reducing erosion and protecting creek, ravine, and hillside areas. • Modernizing irrigation systems to improve reliability and water efficiency. • Planning for tree replacement and long-term canopy health. • Usi n g m o r e d u r a ble , drought-tolerant, and climate-adapted plants. • Protecting new and sensitive planting areas from trampling, wildlife damage, and informal access. • Planning for the full lifecycle cost of park amenities before adding or replacing them. • Using signage, education, and clearer rules to support shared stewardship. The draft plan also includes guidance for evaluating future amenities, such as play areas, picnic areas, sports courts, fenced dog parks, and off-leash dog areas. articles.text: On Wednesday, June 3, Piedmont’s school board will convene for a regularly scheduled meeting in the District Office Board Room, 760 Magnolia Avenue, at 7:00 p.m. This meeting occurs on the eve of the last day of school and will include a first reading on changes to next year’s student cell phone policy. The Mobile Communications Device policy will seek to get rid of the phone hotels in each high school classroom but it will allow high schoolers to use a non-smart phone or “dumbphone” with talk and text features only, during non-instruction times. “TK-12 students shall have their mobile devices, including phones, smartphones, smart devices, and any other personal internet-connected device turned off, or silenced, and stored during the instructional day while on campus. High school students may access a “feature” or “dumbphone” that has talk and text only (no apps or camera) during non-instr uctional/classroom times throughout the school day,” the first reading of the policy currently reads. The board will also adjust its board meeting conduct policy for public speakers, “In general, individual speakers will be allowed 2 minutes, 30 seconds to address the Board on each agenda item and 1 minute, 30 seconds to address the Board on any nonagenda item. The Board will limit the total time for public input on non-agenda items to 30 minutes and on each item to 20 minutes,” the policy reads. The board also plans to levy a 2% increase to the Measure G flat-rate per-parcel tax. This would increase the tax to $3,111 per parcel, a $61 increase. The board points to the consumer price index which is projected to increase by 3.76% in the coming year. The new proposed Measure H, if approved by voters in the June 2 election, would not replace Measure G until 2027-28. The first presentation of the evening will recognize retiring Certificated and Classified staff. The second presentation will review the current Local Control Accountability Plan (LCAP), after the completion of the second year of its three year duration. The LCAP presentation will give highlights of how the plan is meeting its four goals and offer potential changes. The meeting may be viewed on KCOM, local channel 27 and on Zoom at Zoom.us/ j/83652178370?pwd=tb0sJ5XHxRXpf9CRAa3w14tDbdx9Du.1 open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm
