articles.text: Adelaide Lee and Maya Sweeney, Havens 5th graders, were named top 10 finalists in the 2026 “Celebrate America” Creative Writing Contest. Sweeney and Lee submitted their entries as part of a writing assignment for Katy Levin’s class and were selected out of hundreds of submissions from fifth graders across Northern California. Since 1998 the contest has been sponsored by the American Immigration Council and the American Immigration Lawyers Association of Northern California. Students were asked to write an essay reflecting on the themes “Why I’m glad immigrants are part of our communities and nation” and “What does it mean to be a welcoming nation?” A Special Award Ceremony was held on May 13 at the Chinese American Citizens Alliance building in San Francisco for the top 10 finalists. Haram Naseer Ahmed, a student from Corte Madera’s The Cove School, was awarded first place in the region and will have his essay judged with winners from across the country for the national grand prize. Lee and Sweeney received trophies, medals and a cash prize for their essays, as did Ms. Levin and all the teachers of winning students. Adelaide Lee (left) and Maya Sweeney were recognized as top 10 finalists for their essays in the Celebrate America contest.
articles.title: Havens 5th graders named top finalists in writing contest

articles.text: The Piedmont Scout Council was well-represented at the Scouting America National Annual Meeting held in Dallas in mid-May. Attendees included Kate Benson, former Piedmont Scout Executive and now National Director of Cub Scouts; Glyn Burge, Piedmont Council President; Glen Tripp, Piedmont Council Commissioner; Rob James, Council Territory Leadership and Governance Lead; Rick Clark, Council Territory Finance Lead; Anne-Marie Lamarche, National Executive Board Member; and Wes Smith, National Executive Board Member. At the meeting, Scouting leaders from across the country heard an ambitious plan to double membership nationwide from 877,000 to 2,000,000 youth. Scouting America National Chair Ricky Mason emphasized the need for Scouting to help kids “learn, fail, grow, and become leaders” while spending less time on screens. “Scouting sets kids on a path of learning, achieving, and respecting and leading others. It gives them true grit, while having the most fun and adventure possible,” said Mason. Roger Krone, President and CEO, shared that youth safety and membership growth remain the organization’s top priorities and that the long-running bankruptcy case tied to sexual abuse claims has officially concluded after the Supreme Court declined to hear a final challenge earlier this year. Piedmont continues to have a strong presence in national leadership, with Anne-Marie Lamarche and Wes Smith serving on the National Executive Board. A highlight of the event came during the Silver Antelope luncheon, where Piedmont’s own Rob James received the prestigious Silver Antelope Award. Kate Benson (left), Glyn Burge, Rob James, Rick Clark, and Glen Tripp at the Scouting America National Annual Meeting in Dallas, Texas in May
articles.title: Piedmont Council attends National Scout annual meeting

pages.text: 8 8 Wednesday, June 3, 2026 In the colorful, lined sunset (far right), Leighton Mand decided to change the blue sky to an array of lined colors to better express the emotion of the piece. Piedmont art students shine in AP Art Show By Jay Russell On Monday, May 18, Advanced Placement (AP) art students from Piedmont and Millennium High displayed the best of their work in the Alan Harvey Theater foyer. Each AP student displayed at least five of their drawings, paintings or 3-D design pieces. Milana Milner’s art explored her memories through color and pattern drawings of familiar architecture. She used unnaturally bright colors to illustrate the lens of a kid growing up. “My work invokes feelings of nostalgia through painting on objects that I associate with childhood memories. In escapism through painting on objects, I take myself and the viewer away from societal pressures and societal expectations through invoking childhood memories,” said Enzo Ong. Lucas Smolko’s work accentuates landscapes using composition and color schemes. “Studying composition assisted me in creating aesthetic compositions such as leading lines, rule of thirds, and other composition Audrey Dickinson schemes,” said Smolko. These pieces will serve as cornerstones for the AP artists’ portfolio of 10 pieces presented to The College Board. “Influenced by my memories and the sensory power of music, I use candid, immersive compositions to elevate simple scenes into reflective spaces,” said Leighton Mand. The art gallery served as a powerful entry way to the theater, which concurrently hosted the Senior Awards, and as a first stop to the high school’s open house. The art of Piedmont’s most talented artists was coordinated this year by art teachers Gillian Bailey and Sarah Houchin. Enzo Ong Hadley Hayes Tobias Del Bono Lucas Smolko

articles.text: Fourteen Piedmont students won national acclaim by finishing in the Top 20 in the country on a Math Kangaroo test. An award ceremony for winners of the national competition was hosted by Advancing Learning for Piedmont Students (ALPS) on May 28. To be considered a winner, students must rank either in the top 20 nationally or top 3 in the state. This year, Superintendent Jennifer Hawn and School Board Vice President Michael Malione attended the ceremony at the Exedra to acknowledge the great results. “Seeing our students dominate the national Math Kangaroo ranks fills me with immense pride and reflects the dedication and intellectual drive of our students, teachers, and parents. This achievement is another proof point of PUSD’s exceptional mathematics teaching,” said Hawn. Malione was instrumental in bringing Math Kangaroo to Piedmont in 2020, and this year 112 Piedmont students, ranging from 1st to 10th graders, completed the optional 75-minute test on March 19. Anna Johnson worked as the Math Kangaroo Lead this year for Piedmont’s ALPS organization. A total of 60,504 students took the test nationwide, and 24,366 were from California. they are acknowledged during a May 28 ceremony called.

The evening event drew Guitar Engineering Showcase draws big crowd a large crowd of friends and family members to see the guitars built by students this year. The year-long class, created by Piedmont High science teacher Marna Chamberlain, was first offered to students in 2022, and this year marked the 5th end-of-year showcase. Students and guests enjoyed desserts while viewing this year’s custom guitars. Last fall students began drafting their designs and creating Student-made electric guitars were on display on Thursday, May 28 for the Guitar Engineering class’ Guitar Showcase. The 5th annual Guitar Engineering Showcase. Senior Sa’Mara Levi holds up the electric guitar she made this year. blueprints to build their own electric guitars. The use of hand and power tools in the Fabrication Lab was crucial to building the guitar body, contouring the neck, and building out the fret boards. Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) concepts that relate directly to guitars were used to help students make an applied learning connection. Students also created a speaker and wired their own guitars, learning the elements of soldering and circuits. The class required students to analyze guitar anatomy and costs, to compare guitar headstock design features, and to research the chemistry of paint finishes. The course, taught by Chamberlain and instructor Maureen O’Neill, utilized math and physical science aspects of the guitar such as mechanical systems, concepts of sound waves in terms of electric pickups, string tension, fretboard layout, and intonation. Around 100 guests attended the Guitar Engineering Showcase on the evening of May 28. Students were graded upon their craftsmanship, performance and ability to use tools properly. articles.text: Every summer, parents start asking some version of the same question: how can we keep the kids learning when school disappears? Sure, there are worksheets, apps, and activities focused on everything from long division to Longfellow, but what most young people need in summer isn’t more instruction—it’s permission to stay curious. And this year, space may be giving us exactly that. Between excitement around the Artemis II mission, NASA’s breathtaking new images from deep space, and a summer full of exhibitions and conversations about exploration of universes near and far, space is suddenly everywhere again. And kids are paying attention. Recently, my family listened to The New York Times Daily podcast episode where children asked Artemis II astronauts questions about going to the moon. Some were delightfully kid-specific: Do astronauts have to eat broccoli? Others were profound: Why are we spending billions of dollars looking at space when people here on Earth are struggling? What struck us most wasn’t the answers–we expect modern scientists traveling around the moon on a research mission to have profound respect for Earth, for science, and for humanity– it was the questions kids asked. Kids can move effortlessly from asking about astronaut food to wondering whether space exploration is morally worthwhile. As we listened to the kids’ questions, we found ourselves asking our own: Why the moon? Why now? What can images from distant galaxies teach us about our own planet? That spirit of curiosity is worth protecting during the slower rhythms of summer. When school pauses, curiosity doesn’t have to. Summer creates more room for the kinds of questions kids rarely have time to fully explore during the regular school year, and space naturally invites both imagination and critical thinking. At the Exploratorium this summer, we’re excited to host Life in Space, a new exhibition that goes far beyond models of rockets or artifacts behind glass. The exhibition asks a deeper question: what would it actually take for humans to survive beyond Earth? What might it be like to breathe, eat, sleep, work, and collaborate in space? It also invites bigger conversations: Should humans be doing this kind of exploration? Who benefits from it? Would you go if given the chance? These questions that pull young people from passive observation into active thinking. You don’t need to be a space expert to participate. Look at NASA’s images together. Ask your child what surprises them. Listen to a podcast and pause when questions come up. Visit a museum. Wonder out loud. Our Astronomer Emeritus, Dr. Isabel Hawkins, often speaks of looking up at the night sky in Argentina as a child and wondering about the stars. That simple act of looking up helped set her on a path to becoming a scientist who studied stars and space. Summer learning doesn’t—and in my opinion, shouldn’t—look like school to matter. Sometimes it looks like staring up at the night sky and wondering, imagining, and realizing you still have questions. Life in Space invites visitors to get real about the possibilities— and realities—of living in space. To learn more, visit exploratorium.edu/space. Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. An enthusiastic Exploratorium visitor for over four decades, Dr. Taylor champions the power of hands-on discovery: that real learning lives not in what we’re told, but in what we touch, question, and experience for ourselves—in classrooms, communities, and the curious moments of daily life. Visitors get hands-on with Exploratorium exhibits beneath a large-scale moon sculpture, created using NASA lunar imagery. articles.text: It has been a season of growth, grit, and milestone performances for the Piedmont Mountain Bike team. The season concluded with the 2026 NorCal Interscholastic Cycling League’s High School Championship on May 16-17 at Six Sigma Winery in Lower Lake, where the team camped, barbecued, and celebrated the growth of the riders, especially the seniors on the team. This year’s course was three miles with an elevation gain of 450 feet. Jasper Schuetz concludes high school career Jasper Schuetz, co-captain of the Piedmont MTB Team, concluded his high school racing career by finishing fifth of 76 riders in the Varsity Boys’ race with a time of 1:26:17.29 on the fourlap course Schuetz began his journey with the team in 8th grade. Over the past four years, he swept the Freshman category in his first season, winning every race and the Championship. As a sophomore, he led JV1 in the East Bay/ Central League and 4th in the NorCal. And during his senior year, he was the Varsity Leader for the East Bay/Central League. As an independent rider, Jasper has taken on some of the most demanding events in the sport: the Grasshopper Series Junior title, back-to-back 4th place finishes at Sea Otter Classic Under 18, U18 1st Place Winner at Lost and Found (100 miles), U18 1st Place at Heart of Gold (73 miles and 10,000 feet of climbing), winner of the Wente 2-person relay in 2025, and U18 2nd Place at the Rad Dirt Fest in Trinidad, Colorado (113 miles). He is also a brand ambassador for Pas Normal Studios in San Francisco. On May 30th, he competed in the 2026 Life Time Unbound Jasper Schuetz, a Piedmont High School senior, finished the Life Time Unbound Gravel 200-mile race in Emporia, Kansas in less than 12 hours on May 30, 2026. Gravel race in Emporia, Kansas. This 200-mile race is widely regarded as the world’s premier gravel event. This year’s edition had brutal weather making an already punishing course even more relentless. Jasper rode 11 hours and 50 minutes to place 53rd overall in a field of 1,251 riders, and also 14th in the Male 16-29 category. The 206-mile ride included heavy thunderstorms, pounding rain and wind, thick mud, muggy conditions, and 6,700 feet of elevation gain. He will return from the Unbound race to graduate from Piedmont High School. This fall, Jasper heads to Cal Poly San Luis Obispo to study Engineering and join the Mustangs Cycling Team. The Rise of the Piedmont Girls MTB Program The Piedmont Girls MTB Team had a very strong result for the season. Josephine Schuetz finished the A full Piedmont podium for the Grasshopper Adventure Series 34-mile course. Pictured are Olivia Bailey (left), Josephine Schuetz, and Mina Herrgott. Zachary Carter, a Piedmont High School sophomore, pushes through the Finish Line at the NiCA Norcal Championships at Six Sigma Winery in Lor Lake JV2 girls’ race in sixth of 47 with a time of 1:02:36.31 on the twolap course. She had a standout performance at the NICA NorCal Championships this season, having retained the leader jersey and taking 1st place for JV2 for the East Bay/Central League. Mina Herrgott and Olivia Bailey were also in the race, finishing ninth and 14th with respective times of 1:04:57.40 and 1:07:25.17. Herrgott and Bailey are NICA GRiT Ambassadors — NICA’s program dedicated to recruiting and retaining more girls in interscholastic cycling. These three sophomores continued to race the weekend after Championships at the Ukiah Mendo Gravel Epic, part of the Grasshopper Adventure Series. Josephine, Olivia, and Mina entered the Medium Course together in the Junior Women 16-18 category, and swept the podium. This ride on a 34-mile course with nearly 3,897 feet of climbing took just a little over 3 hours. Zachary Carter: Co-Captain on the Rise Zachary Carter, a sophomore and incoming Team Co-Captain, has emerged as one of the most exciting developing racers in the program. Carter finished the JV1 Boys’ Division 2 race in 16th of 78 in 1:14:42.23 over his three-lap race. This season, Zachary earned podium finishes and demonstrated the kind of consistency and drive that points to big things ahead. He has been a leader on and off the bike, and his trajectory as a racer is strong in the years to come. Other Results Kai Hsu raced the JV2 Division 2 boys’ race, placing 20th of 72 riders in 56:04.45 for his twolap race. Jack Mendelsohn placed 56th in 1:03:02.68. Emilio Roberts raced in the freshman boys’ D2 event, clocking 55:57.88 over two laps to finish 31st of 80. Chase Mellers was 38th in 58:33.63. Come Ride With Us Piedmont MTB has a high school and middle school Development Program. The team welcomes all levels of riders from first-time riders to seasoned competitors. To learn more or get involved, visit www.norcalmtb. org to find out about the NICA NorCal League and https://www. piedmontmtb.com.

He had a historic month of May, helping lead the 200 medley relay team at the CIF State Championship on May 16 to a ninth place finish of 18 schools with a time of 1:33.56 alongside Asher Takazawa, Connor Carnazzo, and Jeffrey Latronica. On the 400 freestyle team, Costello’s team placed 16th of 18 finalists in 3:07.91. It marked the first time for the school to feature two teams in the CIF State finals. At the NCS Championships on May 9, Piedmont’s 200 medley team of Takazawa, Costello, Connor Carnazzo, and Cole Carnazzo finished fourth of 16 total finalists with a time of 1:32.91.The boys’ 400 freestyle relay team of See Athletes of the Month on page 31 PHS Mountain Bike team caps strong season at NorCal High School Championships It has been a season of growth, grit, and milestone performances for the Piedmont Mountain Bike team. The season concluded with the 2026 NorCal Interscholastic Cycling League’s High School Championship on May 16-17 at Six Sigma Winery in Lower Lake, where the team camped, barbecued, and celebrated the growth of the riders, especially the seniors on the team. This year’s course was three miles with an elevation gain of 450 feet. Jasper Schuetz concludes high school career Jasper Schuetz, co-captain of the Piedmont MTB Team, concluded his high school racing career by finishing fifth of 76 riders in the Varsity Boys’ race with a time of 1:26:17.29 on the fourlap course Schuetz began his journey with the team in 8th grade. Over the past four years, he swept the Freshman category in his first season, winning every race and the Championship. As a sophomore, he led JV1 in the East Bay/ Central League and 4th in the NorCal. And during his senior year, he was the Varsity Leader for the East Bay/Central League. As an independent rider, Jasper has taken on some of the most demanding events in the sport: the Grasshopper Series Junior title, back-to-back 4th place finishes at Sea Otter Classic Under 18, U18 1st Place Winner at Lost and Found (100 miles), U18 1st Place at Heart of Gold (73 miles and 10,000 feet of climbing), winner of the Wente 2-person relay in 2025, and U18 2nd Place at the Rad Dirt Fest in Trinidad, Colorado (113 miles). He is also a brand ambassador for Pas Normal Studios in San Francisco. On May 30th, he competed in the 2026 Life Time Unbound Jasper Schuetz, a Piedmont High School senior, finished the Life Time Unbound Gravel 200-mile race in Emporia, Kansas in less than 12 hours on May 30, 2026. Gravel race in Emporia, Kansas. This 200-mile race is widely regarded as the world’s premier gravel event. This year’s edition had brutal weather making an already punishing course even more relentless. Jasper rode 11 hours and 50 minutes to place 53rd overall in a field of 1,251 riders, and also 14th in the Male 16-29 category. The 206-mile ride included heavy thunderstorms, pounding rain and wind, thick mud, muggy conditions, and 6,700 feet of elevation gain. He will return from the Unbound race to graduate from Piedmont High School. This fall, Jasper heads to Cal Poly San Luis Obispo to study Engineering and join the Mustangs Cycling Team. She had a standout performance at the NICA NorCal Championships this season, having retained the leader jersey and taking 1st place for JV2 for the East Bay/Central League. Mina Herrgott and Olivia Bailey were also in the race, finishing ninth and 14th with respective times of 1:04:57.40 and 1:07:25.17. articles.text: Fundraiser features over 40 artists Over 80 sculptures will be available for purchase this year. The 32nd annual Sculpture in the Garden at Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek will be on view June 13 through August 9, featuring over 80 sculptures from 42 artists. The event is the nonprofit’s longest-running annual art exhibit and sale that celebrates sculptural pieces with the natural, arid beauty of the garden. A range of returning local artists, as well as newcomers, are participating this year. Sculpture in the Garden also serves as a fundraiser for Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery. All artwork is available to purchase, and proceeds from this exhibit go back into the Garden to help protect the plant collection, promote education and support preservation. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, was a pioneer in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public, made possible through fundraisers like Sculpture in the Garden. The event is free with regular Garden admission. The nursery is located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek. For more information, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/event/2025-sculpture-in-thegarden/. ®

articles.text: Visit the Randall Museum in San Francisco next month and participate in a variety of kidfriendly science, engineering and art activities, ranging from free, drop-in activities to ticketed workshops. The Randall Museum is operated by the San Francisco Recreation and Parks Department and the non-profit organization Randall Museum Friends and provides a unique experience for Bay Area kids of all ages. Every Saturday morning in June, young visitors and their caretakers can join in an open discussion about resident animals with wildlife ambassadors, and get an opportunity to meet Lyra the raccoon, who was born with several health problems including deformities of the spine and jaw, or a long-tailed weasel named Scarlet who was neglected and sustained injuries while in captivity. Both have been rehabilitated by museum staff and offer a glimpse into California’s wildlife. Visitors may also join a bird-watching exhibition any Saturday morning throughout the summer, guided by Dominik Mosur, who has the unique distinction of achieving San Francisco’s record for identifying the most bird species in a one year period within San Francisco’s 49-square-mile limits. Drop-in art classes are offered every Saturday between 1 p.m. and 3:30 p.m., appropriate for children ages 4 and older. A different activity is featured each week. Visit https://randallmuseum. org to learn more. A young visitor views an exhibit at Randall Museum.

articles.text: Free admission for kids through summer Filoli Museum and historical estate debuted an exhibition, “Creating Home,” on May 30, that explores themes of home, habitat and belonging. The exhibit will be on view throughout the summer and spans the historic estate’s gardens, house, redwood groves and natural campus. It features interactive installations, storytelling experiences and educational programming designed to encourage visitors to engage with the people, animals and trees that shape the property. The centerpiece of the exhibition is a large-scale outdoor installation by California artist Jayson Fann. Constructed from naturally found wood and organic materials, the sculptural works are inspired by bird nests, tree hollows and other natural shelters found throughout the landscape. “This summer at Filoli is all about exploration, discovery, and inspiration,” Kara Newport, president and CEO of Filoli, said in a press release. “With ‘Creating Home,’ guests will uncover interactive installations inspired by the animals, trees, and stories that shape Filoli’s landscape, while ‘Kids Go Free’ makes it even easier for families to spend the day outside together. From the gardens and historic house to the redwoods and trails, there’s something around every corner waiting to spark curiosity and joy.” The exhibition opens alongside Filoli’s Kids Go Free summer promotion, aimed at encouraging family visits throughout the season. Starting May 30, children up to age 14 get in free with every full-price adult ticket. Tickets must be reserved in advance online, and the offer is valid for daytime admission only. In addition to Fann’s outdoor installations, visitors will find immersive room displays inside the historic house highlighting the stories of staff members who helped shape Filoli. Other interactive elements include projected ballroom dance lessons, listening stations featuring imagined historic conversations and opportunities for guests to share family stories. Storytelling signage, daily staff talks and family-focused educational activities will also highlight local wildlife, notable trees and the ecosystems found across the estate. “I have worked with naturally found wood since early childhood, growing up along the Platte River,” Fann said. “This lifelong practice of listening deeply to the land, shaped by flowing water, wind, lightning, thunder, and the rhythms of the landscape, continues to inform my approach to nest building. In Creating Home, these elements come together to remind us that building, belonging, and care all arise through relationships with the world around us.” For more information, visit https://filoli.org/.
articles.title: Filoli unveils “Creating Home” exhibit

Constructed from naturally found wood and organic materials, the sculptural works are inspired by bird nests, tree hollows and other natural shelters found throughout the landscape. “This summer at Filoli is all about exploration, discovery, and inspiration,” Kara Newport, president and CEO of Filoli, said in a press release. “With ‘Creating Home,’ guests will uncover interactive installations inspired by the animals, trees, and stories that shape Filoli’s landscape, while ‘Kids Go Free’ makes it even easier for families to spend the day outside together. From the gardens and historic house to the redwoods and trails, there’s someFiloli unveils “Creating Home” exhibit Free admission for kids through summer thing around every corner waiting to spark curiosity and joy.” The exhibition opens alongside Filoli’s Kids Go Free summer promotion, aimed at encouraging family visits throughout the season. Starting May 30, children up to age 14 get in free with every full-price adult ticket. Tickets must be reserved in advance online, and the offer is valid for daytime admission only. In addition to Fann’s outdoor installations, visitors will find immersive room displays inside the historic house highlighting the stories of staff members who helped shape Filoli. Other interactive elements include projected ballroom dance lessons, listening stations featuring imagined historic conversations and opportunities for guests to share family stories. Storytelling signage, daily staff talks and family-focused educational activities will also highlight local wildlife, notable trees and the ecosystems found across the estate. “I have worked with naturally found wood since early childhood, growing up along the Platte River,” Fann said. “This lifelong practice of listening deeply to the land, shaped by flowing water, wind, lightning, thunder, and the rhythms of the landscape, continues to inform my approach to nest building. In Creating Home, these elements come together to remind us that building, belonging, and care all arise through relationships with the world around us.” For more information, visit https://filoli.org/. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Berkeley Playhouse The production was extended through June 28. Berkeley Playhouse is closing its 2025-26 season with Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Tony Award-winning musical “Cats,” which continues through June 28 at the Julia Morgan Theater in Berkeley. Based on T.S. Eliot’s Old Possum’s Book of Practical Cats, the musical follows the Jellicle tribe of cats as they gather for their annual ball, where one cat is chosen for rebirth. The production is directed by Kimberly Dooley, with music direction by Michael Patrick Wiles and choreography by Kevin Gruwell. Berkeley Playhouse’s staging reimagines the musical’s traditional junkyard setting as a long-forgotten vintage theater, transforming the stage into what organizers describe as a dreamlike spectacle featuring dance styles including ballet, tap, jazz and acrobatics. “For my tenth birthday my family brought me on a day trip to San Francisco. Little did I know, it was a ruse,” Dooley said in a press release. “We were actually there to see the Broadway tour of Cats, which was not only my big birthday surprise, but also my first live musical and the beginning of my lifelong love affair with the art of theater.” “Now … decades later, what better place to set this song poem by the great T.S. Eliot and Andrew Lloyd Webber than an old theater, once forgotten but with the spark of pure magic still alive within it,” she added. The cast includes Kyle Herrera as Old Deuteronomy, Tielle Baker as Grizabella, Ted Sclavos as Munkustrap and Roeen Nooran as Rum Tum Tugger. For tickets and a complete performance schedule, visit Berkeley Playhouse or call (510) 845-8542 ext. 351. articles.text: Woodminster Summer Musicals’ 59th season opens on June 12 with Jekyll & Hyde, a retelling of Robert Louis Stevenson’s famous horror story of the same name. Woodminster Summer Musicals events are held at Woodminster Amphitheater in Joaquin Miller Park, Oakland. Woodminster is a nonprofit organization that has presented summer musicals at the amphitheater for over 50 years, traditionally featuring three to four plays or musicals over summer months and is Oakland’s longest continually running live theater. Producers Associates, Inc., the nonprofit organization that organizes the summer festival, also offers a “Kids Come Free” program designed to make live theater affordable for families. Several thousand free tickets are given to children and teens each season. Jekyll & Hyde premieres Friday, June 12. The musical based on the gothic novel follows Gabriel John Utterson, a London-based attorney who investigates a series of strange occurrences between his old friend, Dr. Henry Jekyll, and a murderous criminal named Edward Hyde. Woodminster will present four musicals this season, including Carousel (July 10-12; July 16-19); The Full Monty (August 7-9; August 13-16); and Rumors (August 28-30). Visit https://www.woodminster.com/2026-season to purchase tickets. Woodminster Summer Musicals events are held at Woodminster Amphitheater in Joaquin Miller Park.

articles.text: This summer, the Bay Area will resonate with extraordinary music as the Golden Gate International Choral Festival welcomes over 450 choristers, adjudicators, and chaperones from around the globe for a week of breathtaking performances, cultural exchange, and artistic excellence. The opening concert is on Monday, July 13, at 4 p.m. at the Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church. Taking place July 13–18, 2026, and hosted by the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, the Festival stands as one of the world’s most celebrated gatherings of young singers. Under the leadership of Artistic Director Eric Tuan, internationally recognized as one of the world’s premier youth choir conductors, the Festival promises performances of cultural significance and emotional power. “The Golden Gate Festival is a place where young people from around the world build bridges between cultures,” says Tuan. “Even in a deeply divided world, the Festival offers us the chance to connect through the universal language of music, bringing our unique cultures and voices together to create international harmony. Children who sing together cannot build walls or create conflicts. They know in a deep, visceral way that what unites us is far greater than what divides us.” The Golden Gate Festival remains the only opportunity in the United States for children’s and youth choirs to meet and compete on an international stage. This year, visiting choirs will travel from the Philippines, Georgia, Austria, Catalonia, Poland, Finland, Estonia, Czechia, and across the United States, creating a vibrant and diverse cultural exchange that defines the Festival experience and fosters lasting global friendships. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is a nationally recognized choral organization dedicated to artistic excellence, education, and community engagement. Through transformative musical experiences, PEBCC inspires young singers to achieve the highest levels of musicianship while fostering global understanding. Readers can purchase tickets on Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s website: https://www. piedmontchoirs.org/ggf-concerts-2026.

articles.text: Saturday, June 6, 11 a.m. Opening Reception, CWA Members Exhibition The California Watercolor Association introduces its Signature Member exhibition, titled The Wonder of Watercolor, with an Artists’ Reception and Awards Ceremony. This exhibit will be open to June 28, with open gallery hours every Saturday and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. This juried show will include more than 70 original works, all created by Signature Members using watermedia on paper, and selected by juror Michael Reardon, a well-respected Oakland-based award-winning artist. Note also that CWA will be bringing its 57th Annual International Exhibition to PCA in January, 2027. Saturday, June 13, 5:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art History Lecture Join Art Historian Michael Stehr for a 50-minute illustrated lecture that celebrates the ongoing exhibition at the DeYoung Museum (running thru July 26). The DeYoung exhibition, Monet and Venice, shows many of Claude Monet’s three or four dozen originals created during a 1908 visit to Venice along with examples painted by Monet’s contemporaries demonstrating the contrasts in style. The lecture will explore both the artworks and their contexts, as well as the impact of Venice as background. Doors open at 4:30 p.m. Please do arrive promptly for this event, along with cash to pay the $20 admission at the door. Saturday, June 13, 7:00 p.m. Clarinet/Piano Duo Concert In honor of America’s 250th anniversary, this will be a celebration of the rich tapestry of American classical music. America 250: Celebrating American Music, Old and New will include masterworks by well-known composers such as Bernstein, Gershwin, Milhaud and Price, sharing the stage with gems by Michael Kaulkin and Willson Osborne. John Zorn and Daniel Lockert will present some of the most beloved American classical music for clarinet and piano, The evening includes hot tea and tasty treats after the music. Please buy your advance tickets early at https://www.ticketsignup.io/america-250, as this very special instrumental combination will likely draw a crowd. Sunday, June 14, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition trio PCA’s resident Jazz & Pop Piano Trio, In the Tradition, will once again provide a peaceful afternoon of ‘40s–‘50s jazz titled Summer is Here Celebration. This month’s Sunday afternoon event celebrates the summer solstice, Fathers’ Day, and William Jackman’s 82nd birthday, with an assortment of familiar songs mostly from the early and mid-20th century, including some jazz, Latin, ballads, and blues, including Blues for Michael Morgan, written and premiered in 2021 shortly after his untimely passing. Sit back at your table, enjoy the music with complimentary snacks and soak in these wonderful sounds. Advance tickets are at https://www. ticketsignup.io/summerhere, or $30 at the door, cash/ check only. Sunday, June 21, 3:00 p.m. Complete Haydn Cello Concertos Concert Well-known local cellist Isaac Pastor-Chermak brings the IPC All-Star Chamber Orchestra, conducted by Jason Weinberger in a performance of Haydn’s two Cello concertos, written in the mid-18th century, with new cadenzas inserted by local composer Jean Ahn. This is a special performance , with VIP seats including receipt of a signed CD or other recording of the production. To be sure of a seat, purchase advance tickets at https://haydninpiedmont.eventbrite.com/. articles.text: Kajetán, the Czechia choir The Czech choir Kajetán is participating in the Golden Gate International Choral Festival. The children‘s opera choir of Josef Kajetan Tyl’s theatre was founded in 2014 in Pilsen, and it is attended by children aged 11 to 19. The choir’s spotlight performance is on July 15 at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The choir conductors are Anna-Marie Lahodová and Zuzana Kuncová, accompanist is Olga Cviková. They learn not only the basics of singing and vocal techniques, but also develop aesthetically and socially. The choir‘s repertoire includes children‘s parts of operas as well as classical choral compositions, which the choir performs at various cultural events and concerts. Currently, the children sing in productions of Hansel und Gretel, Špalíček, The Bartered Bride, The Kiss, Czech Christmas Mass, and The Nutcracker. In 2023, Kajetán achieved remarkable success in several choir competitions. Firstly, the children’s choir competition Porta musicae, where Kajetan won the Gold Medal, became the winner of the category and also became the absolute winner of the whole contest. In the Franz Schubert Choir Competition & Festival held in Vienna, Kajetán was awarded a Golden Diploma level VI. At the International Choir Competition Festival of Songs in Olomouc, Kajetán made a significant impact by clinching victory in both of its entered categories, receiving the audience award, and achieving the pinnacle of success by winning the Grand Prix, thereby becoming the absolute winner of the 50th edition of this contest. In 2024, Kajetán achieved further international recognition by winning 1st, 2nd, and 3rd places at the prestigious Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod. In 2025, Kajetán continued its success by becoming the Grand Prix winner in the children’s choir category at the European Choir Games & Grand Prix of Nations in Aarhus, Denmark, and also received three additional gold medals in other festival categories. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival takes place from July 13 to July 18. Information on the concerts and spotlight choirs can be found on their website, including which concerts are free or have paid admission for the public. https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ggf-concerts-2026.

articles.text: A scene from Captain Fantastic with Viggo Mortensen, George MacKay, Annalise Basso, Samantha Isler, Shree Crooks, Nicholas Hamilton, and Charlie Shotwell As well, they are schooled to be survivalists, to engage in extreme rock climbing, hunting, hand-to-hand combat, and they find together a harmony and web of support and concern that so often eludes families surrounded by the trappings and distractions of a consumer-driven pop culture saturated with electronics. What fractures this harmony is the death of their mother in a hospital in New Mexico where she was taken for treatment. The children, at first devastated, argue strongly, against the wishes of Ben, that they want above all else to attend their mother’s funeral. Ben fears the journey could have unintended consequences; however, he finally relents. And suddenly these children of the forest, with all of their attendant skills, are confronted with a culture steeped in all that Ben has attempted to shield them from: television, Gameboy, Walmart and a funeral, organized by their grandparents (Frank Langella and Ann Dowd), a religious ceremony that they know is against the wishes of their mother. This immersion is both humorous and revealing and for most of the children jaw-dropping. These are not feral children, but neither are they, for all of their resilience, children of this century. Painfully, gradually, Ben is faced with a truth that he has tried to avoid: while his children are supremely prepared for a good part of life, they are also woefully lacking in so many other aspects of what it means to live in a complete world. His didacticism – embedded with his values and convictions and love – has been his gift to them. But the revelation that haunts him is that Open to the public. No admission fees. Closed holidays.

pages.text: Wednesday, June 3, 2026 19 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Captain Fantastic – an Oscar-nominated film By Chris Honoré Oscar-nominated Captain Fantastic, written and directed by Matt Ross, finds a complex and revelatory sweet spot and expands on it. In so many ways this film is sublimely poetic while remaining firmly grounded as it probes the many facets of what it means to be a parent. It is also an engaging and captivating character study. At the film’s center is Ben, portrayed by Viggo Mortensen, a gifted, nuanced actor who inhabits Ben completely as he grapples with all of the subtle and overt challenges of being a single parent to six very independent children. But their collective lives are not lived in a suburban two-story home somewhere on the West Coast; rather, home is a camp of sorts, nestled in the verdant forest of the Pacific Northwest. They live in a place apart, off the grid, and their existence, that of the children, mirrors the values of their father. He strives to instill in them a fearlessness toward life, to think for themselves, to let their minds engage in the seminal questions of purpose and existence, questions that dominate their days. With the urging of Ben they fill their evenings as they search for answers in books and more books, from literature to philosophy to biology and history; his oldest son, Bodevan (George McKay), has recently decided he is a Maoist, a declaration that prompts a smile from Ben. A scene from Captain Fantastic with Viggo Mortensen, George MacKay, Annalise Basso, Samantha Isler, Shree Crooks, Nicholas Hamilton, and Charlie Shotwell As well, they are schooled to be survivalists, to engage in extreme rock climbing, hunting, hand-to-hand combat, and they find together a harmony and web of support and concern that so often eludes families surrounded by the trappings and distractions of a consumer-driven pop culture saturated with electronics. What fractures this harmony is the death of their mother in a hospital in New Mexico where she was taken for treatment. The children, at first devastated, argue strongly, against the wishes of Ben, that they want above all else to attend their mother’s funeral. Ben fears the journey could have unintended consequences; however, he finally relents. And suddenly these children of the forest, with all of their attendant skills, are confronted with a culture steeped in all that Ben has attempted to shield them from: television, Gameboy, Walmart and a funeral, organized by their grandparents (Frank Langella and Ann Dowd), a religious ceremony that they know is against the wishes of their mother. This immersion is both humorous and revealing and for most of the children jaw-dropping. These are not feral children, but neither are they, for all of their resilience, children of this century. Painfully, gradually, Ben is faced with a truth that he has tried to avoid: while his children are supremely prepared for a good part of life, they are also woefully lacking in so many other aspects of what it means to live in a complete world. His didacticism – embedded with his values and convictions and love – has been his gift to them. But the revelation that haunts him is that their lives have been unexpectedly truncated, their prism while wide and encompassing and rich has also been too narrow. Perhaps Ben has loved his children too much. Captain Fantastic is a beautifully crafted film, a story that is life-affirming and lovely, thanks in great part to exceptional writing by Ross and a fine ensemble of actors, all wonderful. Surprisingly, this story comes along at a time when so much of our lives can feel disjointed, and our values seemingly inadequate to the issues that confront us. In essence, our contemporary grid can sometimes seem frayed, at times empty and unfulfilling. And so, Thoreau’s simplicity beckons, the quiet voice that urges us to wander off the grid; it can feel so seductive, the vision/ fantasy seemingly idyllic. But there are larger truths involved than simply leaving the grid. And it is those truths that gradually begin to confront Ben and challenge his vision of the ideal. And it is those truths and their inherent cost that make up the thematic structure of this wonderful film. Captain Fantastic is currently playing at the California Theatre in Berkeley. His deep bench of award-winning animated films, each hand-drawn, using watercolor and acrylic paints, are considered so beautifully detailed (every frame stands alone) and judged to be works of art. Studio Ghibli has long resisted using computer-generated animation. Miyazaki’s thematic storytelling is compelling, often focusing on environmentalism, youthful independence, risk, and the cost of war. As well, his protagonists are often strong, young girls or resilient young women. Miyazaki co-founded the now iconic Studio Ghibli in 1985. In 2012 he was named a Person of Cultural Merit for his outstanding cultural contributions. He received an Academy Honorary Award for his profound impact on animation and cinema in 2014. His work continues to serve as an inspiration for countless animators, directors, and writers. Within a very short period, streaming has all but revolutionized what was once simply referred to as “going to the movies.” Films that were released in theaters for a limited time (hence often missed) are now available. If your youngster missed, say, Studio Ghibli’s Oscar-winning Spirited Away (2001) and The Boy and the Heron (2024), both are now streaming. All that’s required today is a television (likely wide-screen), and a subscription to, say, Prime, Netflix, Fandango, Apple tv, or Disney+. Don’t forget the popcorn. The name Studio Ghibli was chosen by Miyazaki in 1985. Surprisingly, the noun “Ghibli” references Italy’s Saharan scout plane, the Caproni Ca. 309, melded with the Arabic word for hot desert wind. pages.text: Wednesday, June 3, 2026 21 The History of Piedmont By Gail Lombardi You can thank Hugh Craig if you like living in Piedmont and not in Oakland. The San Francisco earthquake and fire in 1906 left most San Franciscans homeless. They fled to Oakland and the East Bay by ferry, and many decided to stay and build their homes here. To accommodate the earthquake refugees, Oakland began annexing as much land as possible. Oakland Mayor Mott spoke to Piedmont residents extolling the advantages of becoming part of “Greater Oakland.” He promised better sewers and roads, improved water supply, and police and fire protection. Oakland politicians thought that annexing the beauty of the Piedmont hills would be a great asset for Oakland. Taxes on the Piedmont land would swell the Oakland coffers. But a group of far-sighted Piedmont residents realized that if they did not do something, they would become part of Oakland. In a race between annexation and incorporation, Piedmont had to move quickly. To incorporate, the city had to have boundaries. With no time for a survey, Hugh Craig and others accepted the northern edge of Oakland as the southern boundary of Piedmont, and the eastern edge of Oakland as the western boundary of Piedmont. The north and east boundaries of the already existing Piedmont Sanitary District completed Piedmont’s boundaries. The ferry rides were a great opportunity for businessmen to catch up on the news and to network with one another. Hugh and Inez Craig lived in Piedmont until his death in 1919. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group has visited Piedmont’s Heritage Trees many times over the years, but last Wednesday’s walk was special. An excellent crowd of 41 walkers and three K-9 best friends gathered at the Exedra for a tour of the city’s notable Heritage Trees, led by walker and Park Commissioner Jack Fischrup and guest leader Dave Johnson, who also serves on the Park Commission. Dave was UC Berkeley’s campus landscape architect for many years. The Piedmont Heritage Tree Program was created in 2018 by the City Council on a recommendation from the Park Commission. More than 30 trees have since been designated as Piedmont’s “Heritage Trees.” The program aims to recognize noteworthy, distinctive trees in city parks and open spaces, encourage residents to visit those spaces, and promote the study of nature. After Jack’s introduction, Dave referenced his Cal predecessor, Jim Horner, and Jim’s book Trees of the Berkeley Campus, which covers every tree the group would see in Piedmont. To the walkers’ delight, Jim joined them later in the morning. Dave also noted that Piedmont has 8,000 street trees and provides trees from its corporation yard, at no cost, for the public spaces in front of residents’ homes. The first Heritage Trees were easy to find: the grove of ten surrounding the Exedra Plaza. A hybrid of two North American poplars, their Latin name is Populus nigra italica and they are commonly called “Highland Poplars.” These are relatively short-lived trees, Dave said, and will eventually have to be replaced. Behind the Exedra in upper Piedmont Park, the group admired a well-known Coast Live Oak. This native species is one of the most common in Piedmont, and this particular tree is a local icon that families have used for photos for decades. Dave pointed out that it is leaning and twisting toward sunlight, with one big branch essentially holding up the entire tree. At the Piedmont Community Hall, the walkers noted the Yulan magnolia in the front circle — a deciduous species native to central and eastern China that produces stunning white spring flowers. Just above it, in the parking lot, stands the Coast Redwood that serves as Piedmont’s Holiday Tree; the color at the top of such trees, Dave explained, indicates how healthy they are. The group passed the Tea House and climbed the Highland Guilford Steps, a grand entrance to the park’s Cherry Walk. Surrounding Heritage Trees there include Japanese maples and a grove of Prunus Akebono flowering cherries, whose beauty and seasonal importance Dave and Jack discussed. Emerging from the park, the walkers went down Highland and Guilford Avenues to a set of hidden steps leading to Hazel Lane. A highlight was a stop to view one of Piedmont’s largest Sequoia sempervirens — Coast Redwoods — which made a natural backdrop for a group photo. On Wildwood Avenue, the group examined the colorful Autumn Blaze Maples lining both sides of the street. Pointing to the grass strips in front of homes, Dave asked the walkers to imagine three feet of water atop one foot of grass — the amount needed to keep it green for a year in Piedmont. In California desert cities, it takes 15 to 20 feet. Dave and Jack also explained that California has passed a law prohibiting cities from using potable water to irrigate decorative, “non-functional” turf starting January 1, 2027 — grass that serves no recreational or community purpose, such as street medians, strips between sidewalks and streets, and areas around commercial parking lots. articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month, and offers a great movie in a comfortable setting, with a lively discussion to follow. The Flix Fest June selection is Before Sunrise, a beautifully scripted 1995 romantic drama written and directed by Richard Linklater. It is a film that is driven by conversation and chemistry between the actors, and achieved a 100% Rotten Tomatoes score through critical acclaim for its realistic dialogue, a magnetic chemistry between the leads, Ethan Hawke and Julie Delpy, and for Linklater’s naturalistic direction. It is considered by many to be one of the most romantic films ever made. The romantic dialogue begins on a train headed to Vienna, when Jesse, played by Ethan Hawke, engages Celine, played by Julie Delpy, in a cross-aisle conversation that is both playful and thought provoking. Jesse is returning to the States on a flight leaving from Vienna the next day, while Celine is returning to Paris, after a visit with her grandmother in Budapest. The early exchange is one we all might wish to have had with someone we found intriguing but were too shy to initiate. The realism and spontaneity of the conversation suggests improvisation by the actors, but actually reflects the quality of Linklater’s script. As the train pulls into the Vienna station, Jesse impulsively asks Celine to get off with him to allow them to continue getting to know each other better, albeit within the time frame of a single evening. Interestingly, the first place visited by the couple is a cemetery, where the premature passing of a 13-year-old girl was noticed during a previous visit by Celine, when she was the same age causing a poignant reflection on the effect of passing time in her life 10 years later. Visits to other locations allow for their dialogue to deepen their understanding of each other, while enjoying such varied locations as the Prater ferris wheel at sunset, and an allnight pinball machine arcade. One scene that is particularly powerful finds the couple in a vintage record shop, where they decide to listen to an unknown artist singing lyrics that have separate meanings for each of them. The tight space of the booth enhances their intimacy, which is shared in glances rather than dialogue, as the music is playing. While we are always aware of the time limit imposed on this developing relationship, the scenes are not rushed, and culminate at the train station the next morning, when Celine leaves for Paris and Jesse departs for the airport. Before Sunrise will be screened on Thursday, June 11 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 3:45 p.m., and the movie is free to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, and can bring snacks. The next movie will be American Graffiti, a 1973 coming-of-age comedy drama to be shown on July 9 at 4 p.m., rather than the normal time.
articles.title: Flix Fest movie Before Sunrise at PCA on June 11

pages.text: Wednesday, June 3, 2026 23 Don’t leave home without it: training your dog for hotels, rentals, and roadtrips By Sierra Berrick With summer vacation rapidly approaching, many dog owners are planning trips that include their furry friends. Traveling with your dog can be exciting, but stressful as well. Many dogs simply aren’t trained in the skills necessary for travel and end up causing problems for owners or negatively impacting others in public. Bad experiences with untrained dogs may even cause businesses and rentals to revoke pet access altogether. The following are a few essential behaviors every traveling dog should know to keep trips stress free and fun. In any dog training situation, safety should be the first priority. One common issue arises in doorways. Teaching your dog to “wait” at doors is essential for preventing bolting into heavy foot traffic or out of hotel rooms. The same rule applies when exiting the car to avoid dangerous situations in parking lots or unfamiliar areas. Another especially useful command is “place,” which asks your dog to go to a bed or mat and remain there calmly. This behavior is invaluable in hotel A young collie rides safely in her own seat during a roadtrip. rooms, cafés, and pet-friendly restaurants. Crate training is another must. A crate provides a safe, familiar space in new environments, helping reduce anxiety and prevent destructive behaviors. Car safety matters too! Dogs should be comfortable riding in a crate or secured in their own seat with a canine seatbelt rather than climbing on the driver or moving freely around the vehicle. Public manners are equally important when traveling with dogs. Loose leash walking in crowded areas, “leave it” or “off” for avoiding dangerous items on the ground, and a focus cue such as “watch” can make outings far more enjoyable. Keeping your dog’s attention on you helps when navigating busy sidewalks, parks, hotel lobbies, or passing other dogs. A few additional skills can make traveling significantly easier. Teaching your dog to potty on cue with a phrase like “hurry up” can help prevent accidents and keep long travel days on schedule. Dogs should also understand that excessive barking is unacceptable, especially in hotel rooms and cars. Crating your dog often helps prevent barking and anxiety in unfamiliar environments. With these skills, your dog can become a delightful travel companion. The key to successful travel with dogs is creating a safe, respectful, and enjoyable environment for everyone involved — including you, your pup, and those around you. Be sure to understand the difference between traveling with a pet versus a service dog to avoid legal confusion, and take time to ensure both you and your dog are comfortable before embarking on long trips. With consistency and practice, you and your dog can become lifelong explorers together. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.text: The Hella Chenin Wine Festival sold out for the second year. In a wine world often dominated by Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay, one Bay Area festival is making the case that Chenin Blanc deserves its moment in the spotlight. The second annual Hella Chenin Wine Fest in Berkeley drew wine lovers, sommeliers, and curious newcomers to Hammerling Wines for a lively celebration of one of the wine world’s most versatile grapes. The soldout event featured more than 70 Chenin Blanc wines from California, Oregon, South Africa, Australia, and France. Founded by Peter Andrews of Culture Wine Co., Josh Hammerling of Hammerling Wines, and Marty Winters and Alex Pitts of Maître de Chai, Hella Chenin was created with a simple mission: give Chenin Blanc “the spotlight it deserves.” The festival transformed Berkeley’s industrial West Side into a vibrant gathering place filled with tasting tables, live music, oysters, and conversations about old vines, natural winemaking, and the future of California wine. Consumers mingled directly with winemakers in a relaxed, walk-around format that felt more neighborhood block party than formal tasting. For many attendees, the appeal of Chenin Blanc lies in its remarkable range. The grape can produce crisp, mineral-driven whites, rich textured wines, sparkling bottlings, and even sweet dessert wines. At Hella Chenin, tasters sampled everything from lean, Loire-inspired styles to sun-soaked California expressions. The event also carried a charitable mission, with proceeds benefiting CHIRLA, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights. Organizers say they hope Hella Chenin becomes an annual tradition — and judging by this year’s sold-out turnout, Bay Area wine lovers are ready to keep the party going. There were many, many outstanding wines poured at the tasting. At the end of the day the following wines were the standouts – the best of the best of Chenin Blanc. • 2024 Chateau D’ Epire Savennieres The Savennieres region of the Loire Valley is the home to some of longest-lived white wines in the world. I have bottles of this very cuvee in my cellar that are 20 years old and still fresh and vibrant. The 2024 D’Epire offers a clear, fresh and aromatic bouquet of ripe pears and flint stone notes. Medium bodied and very elegant on the palate, this is a perfectly ripe and juicy Chenin with a firm and persistent structure and a very long finish. Stick this in your cellar and forget about it for a few years and you will be richly rewarded. The atmosphere was festive at the West Berkeley tasting.

I have bottles of this very cuvee in my cellar that are 20 years old and still fresh and vibrant. The 2024 D’Epire offers a clear, fresh and aromatic bouquet of ripe pears and flint stone notes. Stick this in your cellar and forget about it for a few years and you will be richly rewarded. The atmosphere was festive at the West Berkeley tasting. • 2024 Pascal Janvier Jasnieres This is the smallest and most obscure of the Loire Valley AOC’s. The wines are more opulent and fruit forward than Savennieres and Vouvray. It features white peach, melon, mint, and lime, with honey and a hint of cloves offering counterpoint to its bright fruit and glistening minerality. It has persistently mouth-watering acidity as well as a hint of sweetness. The deeply rich finish remains thirst-quenching and invigorating, with chalk, salt, and slate inflections. Enjoy this over the next 4-5 years. Wines from the Savennieres region can age well for 20 years. • 2024 Champalou Vouvray Les Fondraux Hailing from one of the iconic producers in Vouvray the 2024 Les Fondraux opens with the classical flinty fruit aromas on the still discreet but again elegant and unique nose that is crystal clear, precise, intense and aromatic, with concentrated quince and lemon aromas intermingled with chalky and even more saline notes. Crystalline, refined and elegant on the palate, this is a full-bodied, tight and complex Vouvray. The wine is still tight and very tensioned, and it will improve greatly with time in the cellar. The finish is pure, citrusy and very mineral, most of all salty and lemon fresh, with fine tannins and a firm structure. (This wine and the two listed above are imported by Kermit Lynch Wine Merchants) SOUTH AFRICA • 2023 Reyneke Chenin Blanc This hails from South Africa’s famed Stellenbosch region and is biodynamically produced. It offers up notes of green apple, lime and honeysuckle, plus slightly riper hints of peach. Luddite Winery in South Africa eschews modern technology. • 2024 Luddite Chenin Blanc A Luddite is a person who eschews technology and mechanization. That is the philosophy of this winery from the Bot River region of South Africa. The nose is broad, deep and coiled at first, highlighting stone-fruit skin, baked apple and pear aromas. The palate is rich and powerful, transitioning to a weightless, lifted finish driven by orchard fruit flavors and crushed stones. It is a wine to savor by a fire after a fine meal. This rare gem is worth searching 2024 Maitre de Chai Kierkegaard Chenin Blanc A lovely wine from the Wilson Vineyard in Clarksburg, it bursts from the glass with expressive aromas of peach, melon, lime sherbet, beeswax and custard. The medium-bodied palate is powerful and vivacious. Its concentrated, mouth-coating flavors are enhanced by flinty streaks and a crescendo of laser-like acidity, and it has a very long, expressive finish. It should be long lived in the cellar. NV Broc Cellars Sparkling Chenin Blanc Lot 24 Berkeley based Broc Cellars poured an attention-grabbing wine on the warm afternoon of the Hella Chenin tasting. The delicate, fruit-forward Lot 24 Sparkling Chenin Blanc features tart, mouthwatering notes of lime zest and crisp apples. It’s light to medium-bodied, almost completely dry and frankly delicious. 2018 T. Berkeley Chenin Blanc Norgard Farms The T. Berkeley Chenin Blanc has a crisp, almost floral bouquet with subtle touches of orange blossom and peach that emerge with aeration. The palate is medium-bodied with a light waxiness on the finish. This is well balanced with peach and mango on the entry, with well-judged acidity and a satisfying, spice box finish that lingers. With six years of bottle age this wine is still vibrant and fresh and has many years ahead of it. 2025 Teffy Chenin Blanc Jurassic Park Vineyard The Teffy Chenin Blanc has a superb nose rich in personality with ripe melon, papaya and honeysuckle that is very intense and shows stupendous clarity. The palate is crisp and very well balanced with grapefruit and crisp apple flavors, with hints of almonds towards the long finish that urges you to take another sip. This is simply excellent. The intensity of the fruit is brilliant and the length of flavor through the finish shows the quality and excitement of this wine. A rare gem worth searching for. • 2023 Failla Chenin Blanc Jurassic Park Vineyard Another offering from the famed Jurassic Park vineyard in Santa Ynez Valley. The Failla Chenin leads with a pretty bouquet of beeswax, wet wool and peach lifted by a saline twist, followed by a silky, spry palate that combines textural breadth with sleek energy through the finish. • 2022 Las Jaras Chenin Blanc Cuvee Esme Anne Sourced from a vineyard in Mendocino County the Las Jaras Chenin Blanc displays a classic, fresh and focused nose with aromas of honeydew melon, lemon blossom and green apples. Medium-bodied and with 12.5% alcohol, it delivers a fresh kiss of bitterness, accentuating a waxy mineral focus with citrus and apple skin essences. The Chenin Blanc concludes with a long, textural finish and is a solid expression of California Chenin Blanc. Bottled unfiltered. • 2025 Birichino Chenin Blanc Jurassic Park Vineyard The 2025 Birichino Chenin Blanc steadily reveals a layered bouquet of beeswax, petrol, stone-fruit pits and subtle herbal top notes. The palate fuses a soft, supple texture with a round, oily core that carries through the broad finish that lingers with mineral-driven undertones. Can’t think of a better partner to shellfish or seafood of any sort. • NV Leo Steen SOD Barrell Aged Chenin Blanc This dessert wine was one of the most fascinating finds of the Hella Chenin tasting. The wine is fortified then left to age in barrel for 12 years. It is rich and sweet yet has bracing acidity to keep it from cloying. Redolent of caramel and butterscotch, it reminds me of a fine old Madeira or 20 year old tawny port. It is a wine to savor by a fire after a fine meal. This rare gem is worth searching out. • 2024 Maitre de Chai Kierkegaard Chenin Blanc A lovely wine from the Wilson Vineyard in Clarksburg, it bursts from the glass with expressive aromas of peach, melon, lime sherbet, beeswax and custard. The medium-bodied palate is powerful and vivacious. Its concentrated, mouth-coating flavors are enhanced by flinty streaks and a crescendo of laser-like acidity, and it has a very long, expressive finish. It should be long lived in the cellar. • NV Broc Cellars Sparkling Chenin Blanc Lot 24 Berkeley based Broc Cellars poured an attention-grabbing wine on the warm afternoon of the Hella Chenin tasting. The delicate, fruit-forward Lot 24 Sparkling Chenin Blanc features tart, mouthwatering notes of lime zest and crisp apples. It’s light to medium-bodied, almost completely dry and frankly delicious. • 2018 T. Berkeley Chenin Blanc Norgard Farms The T. Berkeley Chenin Blanc has a crisp, almost floral bouquet with subtle touches of orange blossom and peach that emerge with aeration. The palate is medium-bodied with a light waxiness on the finish. This is well balanced with peach and mango on the entry, with well-judged acidity and a satisfying, spice box finish that lingers. With six years of bottle age this wine is still vibrant and fresh and has many years ahead of it. • 2025 Teffy Chenin Blanc Jurassic Park Vineyard The Teffy Chenin Blanc has a superb nose rich in personality with ripe melon, papaya and honeysuckle that is very intense and shows stupendous clarity. The palate is crisp and very well balanced with grapefruit and crisp apple flavors, with hints of almonds towards the long finish that urges you to take another sip. This is simply excellent. articles.text: Happy June! Two of the things that make Piedmont such a beautiful town are its lovely, well-tended parks and the trees that line so many of its streets. Piedmont’s Heritage Tree Program recently celebrated its eighth year. Every spring, a few of Piedmont’s most beloved trees get a little extra recognition. The City’s Heritage Tree Program invites residents to nominate trees in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces for a formal designation honoring their aesthetic, educational, or historical significance. This year, three new trees joined the growing roster: a Coast Live Oak in Upper Dracena Park, Ginkgo street trees on King Avenue, and a Redwood in lower Dracena Park. Their selection was announced at the city’s annual Arbor and Earth Day Celebration on April 23rd at Community Hall, where nominees were recognized and received a limited-edition Heritage Tree lapel pin. The program was established in 2018 by the City Council on a recommendation from the Park Commission. With this year’s additions, 37 trees or tree groups have now earned the designation. The list includes the Evergreen Dogwoods that bloom each spring in front of City Hall and the Coast Redwood that serves as Piedmont’s holiday tree. An interactive map of all designated Heritage Trees is available at piedmont.ca.gov/Heritage Trees. MORTGAGE MONEY… Our “go-to” Mortgage Money Broker, BRADY THOMAS, LA SALLE MORTGAGE, has this to share this month: One of the biggest misconceptions I see is homeowners assuming that once they retire, qualifying for a traditional mortgage becomes difficult or impossible. In many cases, the opposite is true. Over the past decade, lenders have become much more flexible in how they view investment, trust, and retirement assets. For homeowners over 59½, money held in IRAs or retirement accounts can often be used to generate qualifying income…even if they are no longer working full-time. That can open doors that many people assume are closed. I increasingly see this helping homeowners buy before selling, renovate, build ADUs, or help family members financially without relying on expensive private financing. Many retirees are far more ‘mortgage-qualified’ than they realize - they just have not been shown how the rules have evolved.

As a result, the large grass strips along Highland, Sheridan, and other City streets will not be watered after the first of next year. They will turn brown, and what to do about it is still to be determined. After passing through the Hall Fenway, where they observed its European White Birch Heritage Trees, the group made its final stop at Crocker Park, admiring the majestic Copper Beech and an Evergreen Dogwood still in bloom. The walk closed with a look at the Ginkgo trees along King Avenue, named Heritage Trees in April. Throughout the morning, Dave offered horticultural and historical detail on each species while Jack added commentary on the ecosystems they support. Particularly striking was the contrast between California natives and imported ornamentals. Native trees such as the Coast Live Oak and Coast Redwood sustain a rich biodiversity of insects, caterpillars, butterflies, pollen, and nuts that feed local birds and wildlife. The Ginkgo, often called a “living fossil” because it dates back millions of years, evolved outside California and supports comparatively few local insects. The discussion underscored the Park Commission’s growing emphasis on climate-adaptive and native species for future plantings as California grows hotter and drier. The Wednesday Walkers again showed that a simple morning stroll can become an occasion for learning, community, and a deeper appreciation of Piedmont’s urban forest. The group thanked Jack Fischrup and Dave Johnson for their excellent guidance, and expressed hope that they’ll return soon for a part two in other parts of Piedmont. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. articles.text: As of press time, Ursula Jones Dickson is leading the polls to become Alameda County’s next District Attorney. In the event of late-night drama and no candidate reaches a majority, the top two candidates advance to a runoff in the general election. In 2024, nearly 63% of Alameda County voters approved a recall of then-DA Pamela Price, who had been elected as a progressive prosecutor in 2022. The county’s Board of Supervisors then appointed Ursula Jones Dickson, a former judge with a more moderate approach, to replace Price. Jones Dickson is running to keep her role, and Price is trying to get her old job back. Gopal Krishan is an immigration, corporate, and family law attorney with no prosecutorial experience. articles.text: On the June 2 ballot Piedmont residents will have Measure H, the flat-rate per parcel tax that funds Piedmont schools. Measure H asks residents to renew the existing parcel tax, at $3,174 per parcel, which accumulates $12,000,000 for the schools annually, accounting for around a quarter of the school district’s total budget. The 2026 Measure H is not to be confused with the other Piedmont parcel tax for the schools which is dependent upon home size, at $0.25 per square foot. Measure H targets the following educational areas in Piedmont: • Advanced reading, writing, and language programs • Advanced programs in science, technology, engineering and math • Ensuring textbooks and instructional materials are up-to-date • Advanced academic programs and essential college counseling • Programs in music, visual and performing arts Measure H has been in place for 40 years. articles.text: I support Piedmont’s schools. My children received a good education here, and property values are high because Piedmont has excellent schools. The current property tax is scheduled to expire June, 2028, so it should be Nevertheless, Measure H has two fatal flaws that require rejec- 1) It is a permanent tax, unlike previous taxes that require periodic review and approval 2) It is regressive. It charges every parcel $3,174, irrespective of size or value. People with larger parcels in Piedmont receive more property value uplift from our good schools, so they should pay more in taxes to support our schools. With a rejection of Measure H now, there is time to create a better tax measure for approval in November. Vote NO now against a forever tax that eliminates periodic review. I know this is an unpopular opinion, but the truth must be said. No Forever Tax. –Bruce Joffe 3756 Grand Ave., #203, Oakland, CA 94610 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Seniors

pages.text: 2 2 Wednesday, May 27, 2026 Opinion LETTERS - MAIN 2 reasons to vote No on Measure H Editor: I support Piedmont’s schools. My children received a good education here, and property values are high because Piedmont has excellent schools. The current property tax is scheduled to expire June, 2028, so it should be renewed. Nevertheless, Measure H has two fatal flaws that require rejection: 1) It is a permanent tax, unlike previous taxes that require periodic review and approval from voters. 2) It is regressive. It charges every parcel $3,174, irrespective of size or value. People with larger parcels in Piedmont receive more property value uplift from our good schools, so they should pay more in taxes to support our schools. With a rejection of Measure H now, there is time to create a better tax measure for approval in November. Vote NO now against a forever tax that eliminates periodic review. I know this is an unpopular opinion, but the truth must be said. No Forever Tax. –Bruce Joffe Collecting photos for Where in the World For 28 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in faroff places throughout the world, and some nearby. Trusted By Jim Hopkins Divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them. Acts 2:3 The hate expressed in the murders of three people at the Islamic Cultural Center of San Diego this past Monday, May 18, is antithetical to the spirit of Pentecost, a spirit which celebrates the spiritual value of every human being. In contrast, the response of the members of the Islamic Cultural Center is the epitome of the Spirit of Pentecost. While not Christian, their words are Christ like, speaking of love, care, resilience and hope. In a tribute to her father, Amin Abdullah, the security guard at the center who was killed while trying to protect others, Hawaa Abdullah, spoke of his openness and kindness to all people. “Muslim, Christian, Jewish, those with no faith, he didn’t care, he would treat you human to human. He would smile at people he did not know. You can see his happiness, and just who he is a person, just looking at his face.” Iman Taha Hassane said, “This is not going to stop us from showing up, it’s not going to stop us from getting involved and engaged civically and politically and it’s not going to stop us from building bridges with other faith communities.” We need to claim their words as Pentecost words for the spirit of Pentecost is not about religion, ethnicity, creed, culture or class. It is about the divine touch found in simple humanity; the breath of heaven expressed in caring human words. It is about building bridges. It is not about how we worship, it is about how we express our love, where we find our hope. The prophet Joel found hope in the promise of the Spirit that would fall on all flesh. The writer of Acts found hope in the Spirit that would help people from very different backgrounds truly hear each other. John, the prophet of Revelation found hope in the promise that it was the Spirit’s ultimate work to wipe every tear from our eyes. These prophets believed that each of us, regardless of religion or race are trusted by the Holy One to sense the Spirit, see the Spirit and share the Spirit, not just at Pentecost but on all days, especially those days when hate is on the march, when hurt is abundant and hope seems far away. articles.text: Done are the toils and the wearisome marches, Done is the summons of bugle and drum. Softly and sweetly the sky overarches, Shelt’ring a land where Rebellion is dumb. Dark were the days of the country’s derangement, Sad were the hours when the conflict was on, But through the gloom of fraternal estrangement God sent his light, and we welcome the dawn. O’er the expanse of our mighty dominions, Sweeping away to the uttermost parts, Peace, the wide-flying, on untiring pinions, Bringeth her message of joy to our hearts. Ah, but this joy which our minds cannot measure, What did it cost for our fathers to gain! Bought at the price of the heart’s dearest treasure, Born out of travail and sorrow and pain; Born in the battle where fleet Death was flying, Slaying with sabre-stroke bloody and fell; Born where the heroes and martyrs were dying, Torn by the fury of bullet and shell. Ah, but the day is past; silent the rattle, And the confusion that followed the fight. Peace to the heroes who died in the battle, Martyrs to truth and the crowning of Right! Out of the blood of a conflict fraternal, Out of the dust and dimness of death, Burst into blossoms of glory eternal Flowers that sweeten the world with the breath. Flowers of charity, peace, and devotion Bloom in the hearts that are empty of strife; Love that is boundless and broad as the ocean Leaps into beauty and fullness of life. So, with the singing of paeans and chorals, And with the flag flashing high in the sun, Place on the graves of our heroes the laurels Which their unfaltering valor has won!
