articles.text: The City of Piedmont has released its proposed budget for the FY2026-2027. The City’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee met this week to review the proposed budget. The Committee will provide the City Council with its findings and recommendations in advance of budget adoption. The City Council will discuss the proposed budget at two public hearings in June: Monday, June 1, 6 p.m., and Monday, June 15, 6 p.m. The budget, adopted annually, serves as a major policy document and describes how Piedmont intends to finance its services and infrastructure in the coming year. Finance Director Kiran Bawa will present this year’s budget, her first since being appointed last year. The proposed FY2026-27 budget reflects a transition from major project delivery to longterm stewardship. Over the past several years, the City has advanced a large portfolio of housing policy work and completed an unprecedented number of capital improvements, including two of the largest, most complex projects in Piedmont’s history: the all-electric new Community Pool and the new police and fire Dispatch Center. A key priority for the proposed budget will be securing a development partner for the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Transitioning new facilities to sustainable long-term operations by a focus on staffing, service models, managing costs, refining systems based on real-world use, and ensuring these major investments deliver their full potential to the community. The proposed budget features a General Fund of $41.2 million, a 1.3% increase on the current budget. Expenditures are expected to increase by 3% over the current budget. After a transfer of $1 million to the Facilities Maintenance Fund for deferred maintenance and sidewalk repairs in the coming year and $750,000 to the Capital Improvements Fund, the General Fund will experience a Net Loss estimated at $1.0 million. The Financial Planning Committee’s written report to Council endorsing the proposed budget states, “The proposed FY 2026-27 budget reflects another year of meaningful progress toward the City’s long-term strategic priorities, while also recognizing the financial pressures and uncertainties that continue to shape the municipal landscape. Over the past year, the City has advanced several significant capital and operational initiatives that strengthen public infrastructure, improve service delivery, and support community needs.” Looking forward, the Committee is concerned about the current state of the real estate market. Persistent inf lation and elevated interest rates have weakened the housing market and may continue to affect property-related revenues. Approximately 64% of the City’s revenues are tied to property-based taxes. These trends represent a significant fiscal concern. The Committee is concerned that the statewide initiative titled the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act” would present a challenge for Piedmont. The act recently qualified for placement on the November 2026 ballot, and if it passes, it would invalidate all existing municipal real property transfer taxes in charter cities starting December 31, 2028. Loss of this revenue source, which represents roughly 10% of General Fund revenues, would have a profound impact on Piedmont. The City Council will discuss the proposed budget at two public hearings in June. Community members are welcome to attend and speak at the meetings. The City Council is anticipated to adopt the FY2026-27 budget on June 15. Readers can find more details on the budget at the following link: https://piedmont. ca.gov/news/proposed_f_y26- 27_city _budget_ published_ may_2026.
articles.title: City Council considers proposed 2026-27 budget

articles.text: Chrisi is a sweet, brindle Shepherd mix of around 2.5 years old. She has a thoughtful, observant nature and a sweet personality that shines. She responds to “sit,” politely accepts treats, and happily trots over when called. She enjoys chasing after tennis balls and engaging in light play. Once she becomes comfortable, she leans her body into your legs to enjoy pets and affection. Weighing 75 pounds, Chrisi walks nicely on leash with minimal pulling. She may do well with appropriately matched dog companions or as a solo dog with social dog friends. Come meet Chrisi at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 6:30 p.m., or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 - 3 p.m.. articles.text: Bamboo is a world-class cuddle bug, happily soaking up attention and settling in beside you for a cozy evening at home. This affectionate 14-year-old senior can make leaning against your leg feel like a full-time profession, and at night, happily climbs into bed, curls up beside you, and often rests a paw gently against you just to stay connected. This mellow gentleman would do best in a calm home with someone willing to make a few thoughtful accommodations for his comfort, like low-entry litter boxes and easy-to-access resting spots. Like many seniors, Bamboo has arthritis and kidney disease, and takes daily medication mixed easily into his wet food. Bamboo may be a lovebug, but he also enjoys playtime, such as “enthusiastically batting after wand toys from a comfortable position,” and vibing out to his catnip banana. In return for 5 minutes of toy Adopt Bamboo through Cat Town. time and extended cuddle sessions, he offers gratitude, gentleness, and yes, more cuddles. If he’s feeling overlooked, Bamboo isn’t shy about asking for attention — purring happily once he feels seen and reassured — and he may also enjoy the friendship of another calm cat companion. Bamboo is neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www.cattownoakland. org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org

After a transfer of $1 million to the Facilities Maintenance Fund for deferred maintenance and sidewalk repairs in the coming year and $750,000 to the Capital Improvements Fund, the General Fund will experience a Net Loss estimated at $1.0 million. The Financial Planning Committee’s written report to Council endorsing the proposed budget states, “The proposed FY 2026-27 budget reflects another year of meaningful progress toward the City’s long-term strategic priorities, while also recognizing the financial pressures and uncertainties that continue to shape the municipal landscape. Over the past year, the City has advanced several significant capital and operational initiatives that strengthen public infrastructure, improve service delivery, and support community needs.” Looking forward, the Committee is concerned about the current state of the real estate market. Persistent inf lation and elevated interest rates have weakened the housing market and may continue to affect property-related revenues. Approximately 64% of the City’s revenues are tied to property-based taxes. These trends represent a significant fiscal concern. The Committee is concerned that the statewide initiative titled the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act” would present a challenge for Piedmont. The act recently qualified for placement on the November 2026 ballot, and if it passes, it would invalidate all existing municipal real property transfer taxes in charter cities starting December 31, 2028. Loss of this revenue source, which represents roughly 10% of General Fund revenues, would have a profound impact on Piedmont. The City Council will discuss the proposed budget at two public hearings in June. Community members are welcome to attend and speak at the meetings. The City Council is anticipated to adopt the FY2026-27 budget on June 15. Readers can find more details on the budget at the following link: https://piedmont. ca.gov/news/proposed_f_y26- 27_city _budget_ published_ may_2026. articles.text: For Julia Banuelos, now a junior at Dartmouth College where she is majoring in psychology and economics, her leadership journey began with the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC). She credits that experience, along with National Youth Leadership Training, with shaping the leader she is today, including her recent election as sorority president. Banuelos joined PCSC as a freshman at Piedmont High School and quickly discovered it was more than a service club. “It was service with friends,” she says. That combination created a unique environment—one that encouraged participation and community service while providing many opportunities to develop leadership skills. Her defining moment came when she became president. Advisor Ken Li asked her one day, What’s your vision? What are your goals? “He helped break down something that felt daunting,” Banuelos said. “You need clarity to lead.” Banuelos is quick to emphasize that PCSC’s success is deeply tied to Li’s mentorship. Known for his dedication to student growth, Li invests hours guiding students through goal setting, decision making, and personal development. He encourages members to stretch beyond their comfort zones—whether that means leading a fundraiser, reaching out to community sponsors, or participating in programs like National Youth Leadership Training. “He truly cares about helping you become the best version of yourself,” Banuelos said. “He’s not just focused on the projects – he’s focused on the people.” PCSC’s student-led structure gave Banuelos meaningful responsibility and opportunities to learn to lead projects, and later as vice president of fundraising and then co-president. She credits coordinating a major service project involving 50-70 volunteers as really building her leadership muscle, especially when it came Julia Banuelos’ first PCSC event volunteering at Bambino Thrift Store which benefits Children’s Hospital, where she learned more about what the Crew was all about in 2019. to organizing, delegating, and managing teams. Banuelos is a big fan of PCSC. “The more you put in, the more you get out, as most things in life. PCSC is self-directed, so you can make it what you want. If you are interested in animal shelters, you can host an event and invite your friends. If you want to do build on that, you can become Julia Banuelos during a High Adventure Crew overnight trip in 2022 VP of Program and create events for the entire Crew. There are so many ways to get involved and help in the community.” Through National Youth Leadership Training, another Scouting program, Banuelos further developed her leadership abilities, progressing from participant to program leader over three summers. The experience pushed her outside her comfort zone and deepened her confidence as a leader. articles.text: Piedmonters for Inclusive Education (PIE), a volunteer-run community of parents dedicated to supporting students with disabilities, has awarded $7,530 in grants to educators across the Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD), funding critical tools, resources, and programs that promote inclusive learning environments. Through its annual grants program, PIE invites special education staff from across the district—from preschool through high school and adult transition—to apply for funding to meet the evolving needs of their students. Nearly 100% of funds raised by PIE go directly toward these teacher-driven grants, ensuring meaningful, immediate impact in classrooms. This year’s grants, awarded in partnership with Jean Fagin, Director of Special Education, funded a wide range of initiatives, including: • Specialized Literacy & Curriculum: Orton-Gillingham materials, decodable books, and adapted materials for Earth Sciences, Civics and Economics classes • Staff Resources & Technology: Subscriptions to The Informed SLP and Padlet, giving specialists access to the latest evidence-based tools • Sensory & Emotional Regulation: tactile tools, weighted supports, trampolines, and balance equipment • Community Integration & PIE Board President Betty Rojas (left), PUSD Special Education Director Jean Fagin, Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, and PIE Board Vice President and Grants Chair Meredith Lamont Life Skills: off-campus experiences and transition program supplies • Creative Expression & Inclusive Play: toys, games, and art materials to foster engagement and inclusion “These grants are a direct reflection of our community’s generosity,” said Meredith Lamont, Vice President of PIE and Chair of the Grants Committee. “Our donors trust us to put their contributions to work where they matter most. By funding the specific, on-the-ground needs identified by our district’s dedicated special education staff, we’re helping ensure that students with disabilities have the support and resources they need to truly thrive.” PIE (formerly known as PRAISE) partners with families, educators, and PUSD to ensure that students with disabilities and neurodivergences, including those with IEPs and 504 plans, receive the support and resources they need to thrive and belong. Their vision is a Piedmont community where every student feels a deep sense of belonging, inclusion, and support — academically, socially, and emotionally — and where differences are understood, respected, and celebrated. For more information about PIE or to support future grants, visit: Piedmontie.org

articles.text: Sarah Basconis passed away on April 21, 2026 with her husband Trason by her side. They were blessed to have had a 36-year marriage that was filled with love and laughter. Sarah bravely fought breast cancer with Trason constantly by her side. They were married on August 26, 1990, at the Cameron Stanford House at Lake Merritt. The Hawaiian style wedding is fondly remembered by those in attendance. Sarah grew up in Piedmont attended Wildwood Elementary School and graduated in 1985 from Piedmont High School. As a teenager in the 80s, she loved the band Journey and the lead singer Steve Perry. Her happiness was dancing to Journey when they performed at the Oakland Coliseum Day on the Green concerts. In her early twenties Sarah met Trason as they both worked at Sequoyah Country Club. Later she found such joy as an employee at Ladyfingers Bakery. She became a truly gifted baker. Lucky for us, every holiday and birthday was a celebration with her delicious cookies and cakes. For the last 20 years Sarah became a fixture at Piedmont Grocery. Many a friend and loved one insisted on Sarah’s check out register as it often included a warm hug. She was a familiar face to many and loved by all. Sarah also loved to garden and grow her own produce. She found such happiness when cooking from her own garden. Sarah Basconis, a familiar face at Piedmont Grocery for 20 years, died of cancer on April 21, 2026. We often remark that Sarah “grew up with five parents.” Sarah was born when her three siblings were teenagers. As a toddler she was often hoisted onto one of our shoulders for a walk in Piedmont Park. She was the light of our lives and enriched our hearts with her adorable heart. We are forever grateful to witness the life of this amazing woman. Sarah leaves behind her husband Trason Basconis, her brothers Steve Mikkelson and Kris Mikkelson, sister Tracy Mikkelson, sister-in-law Clara Mikkelson and cousin Pamela Perry. She has joined our parents, Milton and Monica Mikkelson in rest. She is greatly loved and will be forever missed. Please visit this website and enjoy and share in her memory. We look forward to reading your stories and seeing any photos you may have. www.forevermissed. com/sarah-ann-basconis Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
articles.title: Piedmont Grocery’s Sarah Basconis dies on April 21

The fire was declared under control by 2:07 a.m. Firefighters spent several more hours clearing debris and salvaging valuables for the residents. At 2:11 a.m., neighbors were allowed back into adjacent homes. “We are all relieved the family escaped uninjured,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “This is a great example of how fire-resistant construction saves lives. The smoke and flames were slowed by a well-sealed exterior door with tempered, double-paned glass, which gave the family extra time to get out.” The cause of the fire is under investigation. Measure H Continued from page 1 this funding basis. “Piedmont’s schools are drastically underfunded when compared with other schools in California and nationwide. A good example of this is Oakland’s current per-student funding of $23,000 compared with Piedmont’s $13,000. The parcel tax makes up most of the difference in school funding,” said Measure H Co-Chair Ted Kinch. The flat rate tax currently in place allows for a 2% increase per year for inflation. If Measure H is passed the annual adjustment of rate shall be determine, on a yearly basis, by the board, up to three percent (3%) above the rate levied in the prior year. A 3% increase next year would amount to $95, whereas a 2% increase would by $65. The passage of Measure H, which requires a 2/3 approval vote, will in effect evergreen the tax, meaning that it will stay in active unless it is repealed by voters. Both of Piedmont’s parcel tax renewals frequently win by large margins in elections, this evergreening aims to save resources by not having to campaign again when the measure expires. The current measure is set to expire in 2028, and was most recently approved in 2019. “The message I’ve heard over and over again from Piedmont residents is clear: they feel that schools are the cornerstone of Piedmont as a community. I’ve spoken to new parents who told me that Piedmont’s amazing schools, teachers, faculty and boards are the reason they joined our community,” said Kinch. Teachers and school staff in Piedmont are currently vying for more competitive pay and full health-care coverage, with this tax already in effect. “I do want to throw my strongest support behind Measure H,” said Teachers Union President Elise Marks. “If that does not pass, doom is upon us, I can’t even imagine how we would come close to sustaining even what we have now.” Measure H has the support of Piedmont’s Mayor, Betsy Smegal Andersen and Vice Mayor Conna McCart), City Council Member Lorell Plimier, the Association of Piedmont Teachers, Piedmont’s Board of Education, and all of the parents clubs from each Piedmont school. articles.text: Staff Photos Claire Aubrecht reached the NCS Meet of Champions finals in the 200 meter dash. Piedmont High’s track and field team concluded its season at the North Coast Section Meet of Champions on Friday and Saturday, May 22-23 at Dublin High. The Highlanders had 11 athletes featured, with runners Claire Aubrecht and Sebastien Swain reaching the finals of their events. In the 200 meter dash, Aubrecht fifth of seven overall with a time of 25.46, coming two spots shy of qualifying for the CIF State meet. To reach the finals, she placed eighth of 23 runners in the preliminary round, clocking a time of 25.55 seconds. “I had the big goal of going to State. This was the first time I made the finals, I’m really happy about that. I missed out on State by two places. Hopefully next year I’ll go. I really wanted to get sixth to be on the podium. I was in Lane 8, so I can’t really see people in my peripheral, but I was close enough to know whether I needed to push a little bit more. I tried to get up to a fast pace at the start, and over on the corner you just float and hold the pace, but then you push out to the corner and use the curve to your advantage—we call it slingshotting,” Aubrecht said. She also placed 10th of 23 runners in the 100 meters in 12.39, further lowering her school-record time. “Getting the school records were my goals for a while, and I really didn’t think I could get it. This year, I was focused on dropping time and the results came. I’m hoping to get to the 12.2s or 12.1s, but I’ll be happy however far I go,” Aubrecht said. Swain’s 800-meter final appearance came with a bit of adversity. After getting boxed in multiple times, he placed eighth of 10 runners in 2:01.53. He was second of 29 runners in the preliminary race with a fast time of 1:55.45—just .12 of a second behind Analy’s Owen Dawson, who won. “I was trying to win this thing,” Swain said after the finals. “The race didn’t go how I wanted, I had a bad start and there was a lot of fighting out there and boxing in and out. That made things a bit difficult, but I understand why it happened. It felt like I could never get a spot in the race, I tried to make up positions on the Staff Photos Photo by Jenni Tsoi-Best Uzoma Iroh competed in the Meet of Champions in the shot put and discus. Sebastien Swain reached the NCS Meet of Champions Finals in the 800 meter run. back stretch,” Swain described. The 2026 season took a lot of perseverance by Swain who was recovering from knee surgery he underwent last summer and rebuilding his endurance from then on. “This was the first back-toback races I’ve done since my surgery. I thought I ran pretty well yesterday, but maybe my fitness isn’t exactly where I want it to be. But I’m still doing alright. This year was a change of mentality for me and how I approach the sport. I had a great season last year, but my injury prevented me from doing endurance work. The preseason was coming to understand this season may not be everything I wanted it to be, but it was about getting back and putting in the effort, and to play the long game,” Swain said. It was also a big season for senior thrower Uzoma Iroh, who qualified for the Meet of Champions in two events. She was 13th of 23 in the shot put at 32 feet 9 inches, and was 20th in the discus at 88 feet, 4 inches. It was just her second varsity season. “For me, it was all about being consistent, getting in the gym every day, and going to the field every day. I did some offseason work, which was very important. That was a big reason why I was able to improve so much. I did a lot of research on technique, because it’s not just about strength, it’s about form and small tweaks you can make. Last year, I didn’t put as much effort as I think I could’ve. My first mark in the discus last year was around 79 feet, and I realized I had the potential to do this if I put in the work to hone in on this skill,” Iroh said. Noah Hildebrand was 20th of 22 in the triple jump at 40 feet, 4.25 inches. Saniyah Johnson was 14th in the shot put with a distance of 32 feet, 4 inches. PHS’ boys’ 4x400 team of Rehan Mumtaz, Swain, Ben Gerber, and Maddox Ma was ninth of 23 teams in 3:25.81. The girls’ 4x400 team of Aubrecht, Skylar Best, Daniela Lucaccini, and Gladwin Horsley finished 21st in 4:28.19. Best also placed 22nd in the 800 prelims in 2:26.23.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s season came to an end in the first round of the Division 4 NCS playoffs against Livermore. Piedmont High’s baseball season came to an end on Wednesday, May 20. Seeded #6 it lost 4-2 to No. 11 Livermore at Humphries Diamond in the first round of the Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs. It was a close game with both teams tied 2-2 going into the final inning, but the Cowboys tacked on their two winning runs in the top of the seventh. It was that kind of season for the Highlanders, having 14 games separated by three runs or less. Piedmont won just four of those games and tied another two. “We’ve gotten down so many times in the first inning and have found a way to claw back. We try to make it a seven-inning game, and it just went their way in the last inning. We’ve been right on that precipice of winning or losing, and it broke the wrong way more times than the right way. With freshmen and sophomores and just a couple of seniors, hopefully it breaks the right way in the future,” coach Eric Olson said. Wednesday’s loss resulted in Piedmont’s fifth defeat in a row. “It was the season in a nutshell. We got into an early deficit and fought back. Just a couple more timely hits would have been huge,” senior Diego Delventhal said. “We’ve had a lot of close games that just didn’t go our way, but the fight is fun. It’s all a part of the game,” senior Jack Meyjes mentioned. Despite the loss, it was a strong game from sophomore pitcher Massimo Mittone, throwing all seven innings. “I tried to battle to the end, it sucks to end the season this way for our seniors. I felt great out there, but there’s a few pitches I wish I had back. The first and last inning didn’t go the greatest, my changeup felt great, but my fastball wasn’t up to par,” Mittone said. Diego Delventhal went 1-for-3 with a stolen base in his final game with Piedmont High. Jack Meyjes went 1-for-2 with one RBI and one run scored in his final Piedmont appearance.
articles.title: Baseball team falls in first round of NCS

pages.text: Baseball team falls in first round of NCS Staff Photos Claire Aubrecht reached the NCS Meet of Champions finals in the 200 meter dash. Staff Photos 12 Wednesday, May 27, 2026 Sports Aubrecht, Swain reach finals at NCS Meet of Champions By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s track and field team concluded its season at the North Coast Section Meet of Champions on Friday and Saturday, May 22-23 at Dublin High. The Highlanders had 11 athletes featured, with runners Claire Aubrecht and Sebastien Swain reaching the finals of their events. In the 200 meter dash, Aubrecht fifth of seven overall with a time of 25.46, coming two spots shy of qualifying for the CIF State meet. To reach the finals, she placed eighth of 23 runners in the preliminary round, clocking a time of 25.55 seconds. “I had the big goal of going to State. This was the first time I made the finals, I’m really happy about that. I missed out on State by two places. Hopefully next year I’ll go. I really wanted to get sixth to be on the podium. I was in Lane 8, so I can’t really see people in my peripheral, but I was close enough to know whether I needed to push a little bit more. I tried to get up to a fast pace at the start, and over on the corner you just float and hold the pace, but then you push out to the corner and use the curve to your advantage—we call it slingshotting,” Aubrecht said. She also placed 10th of 23 runners in the 100 meters in 12.39, further lowering her school-record time. “Getting the school records were my goals for a while, and I really didn’t think I could get it. This year, I was focused on dropping time and the results came. I’m hoping to get to the 12.2s or 12.1s, but I’ll be happy however far I go,” Aubrecht said. Swain’s 800-meter final appearance came with a bit of adversity. After getting boxed in multiple times, he placed eighth of 10 runners in 2:01.53. He was second of 29 runners in the preliminary race with a fast time of 1:55.45—just .12 of a second behind Analy’s Owen Dawson, who won. “I was trying to win this thing,” Swain said after the finals. “The race didn’t go how I wanted, I had a bad start and there was a lot of fighting out there and boxing in and out. That made things a bit difficult, but I understand why it happened. It felt like I could never get a spot in the race, I tried to make up positions on the Staff Photos Piedmont’s season came to an end in the first round of the Division 4 NCS playoffs against Livermore. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s baseball season came to an end on Wednesday, May 20. Seeded #6 it lost 4-2 to No. 11 Livermore at Humphries Diamond in the first round of the Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs. It was a close game with both teams tied 2-2 going into the final inning, but the Cowboys tacked on their two winning runs in the top of the seventh. It was that kind of season for the Highlanders, having 14 games separated by three runs or less. Piedmont won just four of those games and tied another two. “We’ve gotten down so many times in the first inning and have found a way to claw back. We try to make it a seven-inning game, and it just went their way in the last inning. We’ve been right on that precipice of winning or losing, and it broke the wrong way more times than the right way. With freshmen and sophomores and just a couple of seniors, hopefully it breaks the right way in the future,” coach Eric Olson said. Wednesday’s loss resulted in Piedmont’s fifth defeat in a row. “It was the season in a nutshell. We got into an early deficit and fought back. Just a couple more timely hits would have been huge,” senior Diego Delventhal said. “We’ve had a lot of close games that just didn’t go our way, but the fight is fun. It’s all a part of the game,” senior Jack Meyjes mentioned. Despite the loss, it was a strong game from sophomore pitcher Massimo Mittone, throwing all seven innings. “I tried to battle to the end, it sucks to end the season this way for our seniors. I felt great out there, but there’s a few pitches I wish I had back. The first and last inning didn’t go the greatest, my changeup felt great, but my fastball wasn’t up to par,” Mittone said. See Baseball on page 29 Photo by Jenni Tsoi-Best Uzoma Iroh competed in the Meet of Champions in the shot put and discus. Sebastien Swain reached the NCS Meet of Champions Finals in the 800 meter run. back stretch,” Swain described. The 2026 season took a lot of perseverance by Swain who was recovering from knee surgery he underwent last summer and rebuilding his endurance from then on. “This was the first back-toback races I’ve done since my surgery. I thought I ran pretty well yesterday, but maybe my fitness isn’t exactly where I want it to be. But I’m still doing alright. This year was a change of mentality for me and how I approach the sport. I had a great season last year, but my injury prevented me from doing endurance work. The preseason was coming to understand this season may not be everything I wanted it to be, but it was about getting back and putting in the effort, and to play the long game,” Swain said. It was also a big season for senior thrower Uzoma Iroh, who qualified for the Meet of Champions in two events. She was 13th of 23 in the shot put at 32 feet 9 inches, and was 20th in the discus at 88 feet, 4 inches. It was just her second varsity season. “For me, it was all about being consistent, getting in the gym every day, and going to the field every day. I did some offseason work, which was very important. That was a big reason why I was able to improve so much. I did a lot of research on technique, because it’s not just about strength, it’s about form and small tweaks you can make. Last year, I didn’t put as much effort as I think I could’ve. My first mark in the discus last year was around 79 feet, and I realized I had the potential to do this if I put in the work to hone in on this skill,” Iroh said. Here’s a full rundown of Piedmont’s results at the Meet of Champions Other results In the high jump, Malia Williams was ninth of 18 athletes with a jump of five feet. Lucia Dorsey was 13th at 4 feet, 10 inches. Avedis Gourjian finished 18th of 23 athletes in the pole vault with a height of 11 feet, 10 inches. Noah Hildebrand was 20th of 22 in the triple jump at 40 feet, 4.25 inches. Saniyah Johnson was 14th in the shot put with a distance of 32 feet, 4 inches. PHS’ boys’ 4x400 team of Rehan Mumtaz, Swain, Ben Gerber, and Maddox Ma was ninth of 23 teams in 3:25.81. The girls’ 4x400 team of Aubrecht, Skylar Best, Daniela Lucaccini, and Gladwin Horsley finished 21st in 4:28.19. Best also placed 22nd in the 800 prelims in 2:26.23. Diego Delventhal went 1-for-3 with a stolen base in his final game with Piedmont High. Jack Meyjes went 1-for-2 with one RBI and one run scored in his final Piedmont appearance.

articles.text: Piedmont High named Lucas Smolko and Dahlia Osman as the school’s 2026 Outstanding Senior Athletes recipients, noting their academic success, student leadership, and prowess in their sports. LUCAS SMOLKO Tennis Tennis player Lucas Smolko won the school’s first boys’ North Coast Section Individual Tournament singles title since 1975 and became the first Western Alameda County Conference singles champion in three successive years. He was our honorable mention for 2024 Sophomore of the Year, and our 2023 Freshman of the Year. Smolko beat Acalanes’ Sze Ting Chen 6-4, 6-3 for the Division 2 NCS singles title. To reach the final, Smolko won 6-0, 6-0 over St. Patrick’s Oscar Swenson in the opening round, followed up with a 6-1, 6-4 win over Armaan Mishra of Lick-Wilmerding in the quarterfinals, and dominated Stuart Hall’s Edward Morfit 6-1, 6-0 in the semifinals. His appearance in the NCS title match marked the third of his career. He lost as a freshman to eventual Stanford Cardinal Gus Grumet of University and lost in a three-set battle to Dylan Donovan of Head-Royce as a junior. For the WACC singles crown, he defeated Castro Valley’s Guhan Anandkumar in straight sets by scores of 6-2, 6-3. Smolko entered as the top seed, beating Alameda’s Johnny Sanchez 6-0, 6-1 in the first round, CV’s Matthew Rodriguez 6-0, 6-2 in the quarterfinals, and Bishop O’Dowd’s Marcello Sachelari 6-1, 6-3 in the semifinals. DAHLIA OSMAN Flag Football, Girls’ Lacrosse Dahlia Osman concludes her athletic career at Piedmont High as a three-year starter on the flag Lucas Smolko was named the school’s Outstanding Male Senior Athlete. football team, and two-year varsity member of the girls’ lacrosse team. On the gridiron, Osman represents the school’s hallmark player from flag football’s inaugural years, finishing with 24 total interceptions in three years. She earned first-team All-League honors in 2024 and 2025, and an honorable mention in 2023. She converted from the cornerback role in 2023, to captaining the defense the next two years from the safety spot. In addition to interceptions and pass breakups, she led the team in tackles for the last two years. In lacrosse, Osman grew from a substitute role in 2025 to being a fulltime starter in 2026. The Highlanders went 6-11 this season, while she was a member of PHS’ 2025 team that reached the D2 NCS Championship game as the No. 6 seed before falling 11-10 in sudden-death overtime to No. 4 College Park. After primarily contributing as a defender in 2025, she emerged as an offensive threat as a senior. She logged a hat trick in Piedmont’s 6-5 win over San Rafael on April 1. Dahlia Osman was named Piedmont High’s girls’ Outstanding Senior Athlete. She’s pictured with flag football assistant coach Hayley Adams (left) and head coach Beth Black.

articles.text: While the club season has completed for most indoor girls volleyball players, Piedmont is seeing seven of its players continuing with post-season practices to prepare for the prestigious USA Volleyball Junior Nationals on June 19-22 in Minnesota. These seven Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School players from two Bay Area volleyball clubs– San Rafael’s Absolute and Walnut Creek’s Red Rock– have been invited to compete at the highest level of girls volleyball, playing against other top players across the country. PHS sophomore Allyson Huynh will join her team, Absolute 15 Black, in Indianapolis, where they will compete in the Liberty division at USAV Nationals. Absolute 15 Black competed in the 2026 Northern California Volleyball Association Regional Finals with a 2nd place finish on May 10 out of 136 teams in the age group. The team also competed at the Northeast Qualifier tournament in Philadelphia, PA, winning the tournament on April 5 and qualifying the team to play in the Liberty division at Nationals. This will be Huynh’s second appearance at Nationals. Huynh plays defensive specialist/libero for Absolute and is a setter and right-side hitter (opposite side or “Oppo”) for PHS. PHS freshmen Hazel Schaffer and Carina Vora from Red Rock 15 earned a bid to Nationals after a dramatic finish at NCVA Regional Finals. The team entered the final weekend ranked No. 16 following strong showings in qualifier tournaments in Las Vegas and Salt Lake City, narrowly missing earlier bid opportunities. Needing to climb into the top 15 to secure a bid, they faced immediate pressure from Huynh’s team, perennial powerhouse, Absolute 15 Black. After a hard-fought loss, the path became clear: win three straight matches to earn an invitation, or else the season ends. Behind elite setting, steady leadership and high level defensive play, team co-captain and libero Schaffer and setter Vora helped guide the team through a clutch three-match run. Their performance propelled the team to an 11th place finish on May 10, earning the team a Freedom bid to Nationals. Schaffer is a libero/defensive specialist and outside hitter for PHS, and Vora is a setter for PHS. At the 14s level: Piedmont Middle School 8th grader Campbell Miller will head to Nationals in Indianapolis with an Open bid. Her team Absolute 14 Black dominated the Northern California and Nevada competition, finishing the season No. 1 out of 143 teams in her age group in NCVA. Absolute 14 Black played in three national qualifier tournaments in the highest Open division, just narrowly missing a bid each time. In recognition of their play caliber, the team was awarded an At-Large Open bid by USAV at the close of the regular season. Miller plays middle blocker for Absolute and the PMS 8th grade team. Also from the same volleyball club, PMS 8th grader Sarina Hill will be at Nationals competing in the USA division for the third consecutive year. Her team Absolute 14 Pink earned a No. Piedmont volleyball players Allyson Huynh (top left), Campbell Miller, Sarina Hill, Sofie Bechtel, Liva Olsen; (bottom photo) Carina Vora (left), and Hazel Schaffer will feature at the USA Volleyball Junior Nationals. 6 ranking to close the 2026 season, a rare feat where two teams from the same club finish in gold. Their finish also gave the team the distinction of double-bidding for Nationals when they earned a USA division bid based on their season-close results. Earlier in the season, Absolute 14 Pink competed in the Pacific Northwest Qualifier tournament in Spokane, WA which they won commandingly. Not a single set was dropped on their road to victory at that tournament, and the team received its first bid, in the Liberty division, to Nationals on April 5. Hill is a libero/defensive specialist for Absolute, and she plays several roles, including setter and libero, for the PMS 8th grade team. At the 13s level: Sofie Bechtel, a PMS 8th grader, competes on Absolute 13 Black. The team started the season ranked No. 7 out of 105 teams in their age group from Northern California and Nevada and remained in the NCVA gold bracket throughout the season. The team capped off the season with a 5th place finish at Regional Finals on May 10, securing the team a Liberty bid to Nationals. USAV Nationals for this age group will be played in Minnesota, and this will be Bechtel’s second appearance playing at this elite level. Bechtel is a libero/ defensive specialist for Absolute and an outside hitter for the PMS 8th grade team. PMS 7th grader Liva Olsen will be seeing Bechtel in Minnesota in June. Olsen is a leftie playing oppo for Absolute 13 Pink. The team earned its bid to Nationals at the Pacific Northwest Qualifier tournament in Spokane, WA, where on the final day, Absolute 13 Pink ironically faced its local nemesis, a team from Sacramento, while both teams were 1,000 miles away from home. Absolute 13 Pink battled hard, winning the tie-break 3rd set to finish the tournament in 3rd place and earning a bid to Nationals in the Liberty division. Olsen is an oppo for Absolute and an outside hitter for the PMS 7th grade team.
articles.title: Seven from Piedmont to compete at USA Volleyball Junior Nationals in June

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School’s softball team continues its strong run through the postseason. The Piedmont Middle School Softball team took the field for two more games as they continued their dual-league playoff run. First up, the Scots faced off against backyard rivals, Montera Middle School, in the OAL championship on May 20. The Scots split the season series against the Toros and entered the game with an even mix of high expectations and high anxiety. Things started off strong as the Scots led 3-2 after two, powered by a solo “Bailey Blast” homerun from 8th grader Bailey Gregovich. The Scots kept it close thanks to a key catch by 7th grader Mackenzie Ewen on a bullet line drive to left and trailed 5-3 after five before a disastrous 6th inning put the game out of reach and ultimately led to an emotional 15-5 loss and second place medals for the team. With no time to dwell on their defeat, the Scots returned home to Witter Field the next day to take on Albany Middle School in the semi-finals of the EBMSL playoffs. The capacity crowd would not be disappointed as the matchup delivered a riveting display of high-quality play and dramatic moments in a fun-filled atmosphere. The Scots came out strong with 8th grade ace, Madi Farboud, keeping the Cobras in check from the circle and Bailey Gregovich once again jumpstarting the offense with an early HR. The Cobras would eventually find their bite, breaking through with some aggressive base runAbby Gregovich hit the game-winner to solidify a 7-6 win in the semifinals. ning and a few timely hits. By the bottom of the 6th the Scots were in a tough spot, down 4-6 with a spot in the finals on the line. Undaunted, the Piedmont dugout was belting out cheers and chants as they sent the middle of the lineup to the plate to try and spark a comeback. Leading off the inning, 6th grader Keira Spina worked her way to a full count before legging out an infield single on a sharply hit ball to third. Next up, Mackenzie Ewen fouled off multiple pitches before ripping a line drive single that easily scored Spina from third. Third to bat for the Scots and representing the winning run was veteran 8th grade catcher, Simone Tornatore. With no outs and pinch runner 6th grader Olive Dao Hoang having stolen second base, Tornatore hit a bloop single that then saw Dao Hoang opportunistically scamper home to tie the game up when the throw to third squirted away from the defense. With the home dugout now in a full-fledged frenzy and Tornatore having advanced to 3B on a passed ball, Abby Gregovich strode to the plate and calmly smacked a single through the left side. Tornatore scored easily, trotting home with arms raised, completing an epic 7-6 comeback win. Piedmont Middle School has secured a championship rematch against the Montera Toros on Tuesday, May 26. See next week’s Post for game details. Keira Spina slides into second base.
articles.title: PMS softball team advances to Championship game

articles.text: Piedmont High’s softball team made it to the quarterfinals of the Division 5 North Coast Section postseason as the No. 6 seed before losing to No. 3 Willits 17-7 on the Wolverines home field in Mendocino County on Friday, May 22. To get there, Piedmont defeated No. 11 California School for the Deaf 18-11 at Witter Field on Tuesday, May 19. They conclude their season with a 13-11 record. Their quarterfinals appearance marked the third year in a row for Piedmont to reach the round. This year, they did so with a roster that had no seniors, two juniors, four sophomores, and a whopping eight freshmen. “We have a lot of underclassmen, so this year was a learning year and have fun. A lot of these young ladies don’t have a big background in softball and are learning. Hopefully, we’ll have some good years ahead as we gain experience,” said coach Gene Denard. The Highlanders move toward 2027 with some potential building blocks o m place. Freshman Talia Perl emerged as their Day 1 starting pitcher. Sophomore Edie Elmquist appears at short stop and carried a team-high .542 batting average and 55 runs scored, and 35 stolen bases. Sophomore Hannah Joerger, meanwhile, led the team with 42 hits and 55 RBIs, to go along with a .525 batting average. Freshman Rosemary Dickinson was third on the team with 18 hits, 23 RBIs, and a .295 batting average. 17-7 loss to Willits Piedmont took a 4-1 lead following the top of the second, but Willits tied it in the bottom half and then went up 10-4 in the third inning. PHS scored three runs in the top of the fourth, but conceded four in the bottom half, and another three in the bottom of the fifth to activate the 10-run rule. Final stats: Hailey Navarro scored one run. Perl drew a walk. Joerger went 2-for-3. Dickinson went 1-for-3 with a double and one RBI. Elmquist had one run and one walk. Talati scored one run. Teah Suhr went 1-for-2 with two runs scored. Penelope Hopper went 1-for-2 with two RBIs and one walk. Samantha Schey had one run scored. Makenna Small went 1-for-3 with one run scored and one stolen base. Staff Photos Edie Elmquist had three hits, one RBI, and scored four runs against CSD, to go along with a run scored against Willits. Hannah Joerger had three RBIs on two hits against California School for the Deaf, and two hits against Willits. Talia Perl finished the year as Piedmont’s every-game starting pitcher as a freshman, giving the softball team a potential bright future

This year, they did so with a roster that had no seniors, two juniors, four sophomores, and a whopping eight freshmen. “We have a lot of underclassmen, so this year was a learning year and have fun. A lot of these young ladies don’t have a big background in softball and are learning. Hopefully, we’ll have some good years ahead as we gain experience,” said coach Gene Denard. The Highlanders move toward 2027 with some potential building blocks o m place. Freshman Talia Perl emerged as their Day 1 starting pitcher. Sophomore Edie Elmquist appears at short stop and carried a team-high .542 batting average and 55 runs scored, and 35 stolen bases. Sophomore Hannah Joerger, meanwhile, led the team with 42 hits and 55 RBIs, to go along with a .525 batting average. Freshman Rosemary Dickinson was third on the team with 18 hits, 23 RBIs, and a .295 batting average. 17-7 loss to Willits Piedmont took a 4-1 lead following the top of the second, but Willits tied it in the bottom half and then went up 10-4 in the third inning. PHS scored three runs in the top of the fourth, but conceded four in the bottom half, and another three in the bottom of the fifth to activate the 10-run rule. Final stats: Hailey Navarro scored one run. Perl drew a walk. Joerger went 2-for-3. Dickinson went 1-for-3 with a double and one RBI. Elmquist had one run and one walk. Talati scored one run. Teah Suhr went 1-for-2 with two runs scored. Penelope Hopper went 1-for-2 with two RBIs and one walk. Samantha Schey had one run scored. Makenna Small went 1-for-3 with one run scored and one stolen base. See Softball on page 29 Staff Photos Edie Elmquist had three hits, one RBI, and scored four runs against CSD, to go along with a run scored against Willits. Hannah Joerger had three RBIs on two hits against California School for the Deaf, and two hits against Willits. Talia Perl finished the year as Piedmont’s every-game starting pitcher as a freshman, giving the softball team a potential bright future

articles.text: Soprano Shannon Crowley The San Francisco Opera will conclude its 2026 Schwabacher Recital Series on June 16 with a performance featuring American bass-baritone Kyle Ketelsen and pianist Carrie-Ann Matheson alongside participants from the 2026 Merola Opera Program. The recital will include performances by soprano Shannon Crowley, soprano Charlotte Kelso, tenor Chester Seungyup Han, tenor Ryan Bryce Johnson, baritone Paul Jang and pianist Deven Shah. The program features works by Maurice Ravel, Henri Duparc, Gioachino Rossini, Giuseppe Verdi, Antonio Schira and Ottorino Respighi, as well as excerpts from Act I of Don Giovanni and Act II of Tosca. Ketelsen, who made his San Francisco Opera debut as Escamillo in Carmen in 2006, is appearing this season in the title role of Don Giovanni at the Metropolitan Opera. He will also return to San Francisco this month to perform Orest in Elektra under Music Director Eun Sun Kim. Matheson, artistic director of the San Francisco Opera Center and Merola Opera Program, has worked internationally as a pianist, conductor and vocal coach. A former assistant conductor and coach at the Metropolitan Opera, she has collaborated with singers including Joyce DiDonato and Jonas Kaufmann. The concert is held Tuesday, June 16, at 7 p.m. at Barbro Osher Recital Hall in San Francisco. The Schwabacher Recital Series presents emerging and esteemed artists from around the globe, primarily alumni or faculty of Merola Opera Program. Visit www.sfopera.com to learn more and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: SF Opera concludes 2026 Schwabacher Recital Series on June 16

articles.text: Osaka-born, Berlin-based artist Chiharu Shiota’s first solo museum exhibition in the Bay Area is now on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. Titled Two Home Countries, the exhibition spans the artist’s career across installation, sculpture, video, drawing and stage design. Shiota is best known for immersive environments constructed from densely woven strands of colored yarn, and presenting large-scale installations and other works that explore themes of identity, memory and belonging. At the center of the exhibition is Diary, a monumental installation that fills the museum’s Akiko Yamazaki and Jerry Yang Pavilion. Red threads extend across the 88-foot gallery, surrounding visitors as suspended handwritten pages from Japanese soldiers and postwar German civilians hang overhead. “Shiota is interested in what remains after a person is gone,” said Chief Curator Robert Mintz. “The installation makes history feel personal, fragmented, and profoundly present.” Other works include Two Home Countries, in which a red dress unravels into cords connecting two house-like structures, as well as sketches and videos documenting Shiota’s stage design work for KINKAKUJI (The Temple of the Golden Pavilion). “Chiharu Shiota’s work resonates because it makes emotional states visible,” Asian Art Museum Director Soyoung Lee said in a press release. “Her installations speak to the experience of living between places, histories, and identities — an experience that feels increasingly familiar to many people today.” Visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/chiharu-shiota-two-home-countries/ to learn more.
articles.title: Chiharu Shiota exhibition on view now at Asian Art Museum

articles.text: Non Stop Bhangra performs this Friday The Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) free community-gathering evening event series “Friday Nights” continues this week with live performances and weekly food concessions. OMCA hosts free community events every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout spring and summer, featuring live music, immersive arts activities and late-night museum access with the purchase of a museum ticket. Bring a blanket and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s large lawn, where live music and entertainment takes place throughout the evening. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from a stationed food truck on-site. A rotating list of vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon Streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. Non Stop Bhangra takes over the garden stage this Friday, May 29. Non Stop Bhangra crew members have performed Bhangra, traditional Punjabi folk music and dance, for Bay Area audiences for over two decades. The collective celebrated its 20-year anniversary in 2024 and recently presented the Bay Area Holi Festival of Colors in Oakland last year. Non Stop Bhangra has been featured at landmark platforms from museums, performing art centers, festivals, nightclubs, community centers and youth outreach events. Friday Night events are always free and open to the public, but late-night museum access requires a ticket purchase. Visit https://museumca.org/about-friday-nights-at-omca-with-off-thegrid/ to learn more. Non Stop Bhangra crew members have performed traditional Punjabi folk music and dance for Bay Area audiences for over two decades.
articles.title: “Friday Nights” returns to Oakland Museum of California

articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) is hosting a Spring Sing concert to honor the graduating class of 2026 and the accomplishments of all ensembles from all their choirs in this grand season finale. The event takes place on Saturday, May 30, from 3 - 5 p.m. at the Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church (1801 Lacassie Avenue). The concert includes an annual serenade of Homeward Bound to a curated program of highlights from their 2025-26 season. This includes pieces the touring choirs are taking with them on their tours for the remainder of the year. This annual culmination concert of our season provides inspiration and community for the whole family. The participating PEBCC Choirs are: T1, T2, T3, Ancora, Ecco, Ensemble, and Concert Choir. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir was established in 1982 when, at the request of community leader Susan Rahl, the twenty-two founding members of the “Piedmont Boys Choir” first gathered under the direction of founding Artistic Director Robert Geary. The Choir’s founding principles were to teach the fundamentals and art of music and perform to the highest standard in a creative and supportive environment. The Choirs have always maintained these core principles, while championing new music for youth choirs and increasingly focusing on social justice and global citizenship. Tickets are $30 for adults. Tickets for seniors, students, alumni, or children ages 6 and older are $20. Those interested in volunteering will receive a free ticket. More information on volunteering and tickets is at the following link: https://www. piedmontchoirs.org/event-calendar/spring-sing-2026. One of the participating choirs in the Spring Sing
articles.title: PEBCC’s Spring Sing concert Saturday, May 30

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony concludes its 2026 Chamber Series with a curated program highlighting contemporary voices and classical masterworks, held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on May 31. The series closes with “I, Too, Sing America,” curated by James Parrish Smith, featuring works by Brian Raphael Nabors, Anna Clyne and Antonín Dvořák. Smith currently serves as the Director of Music and Organist at the First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley. He previously served as Director of Music and Organist at the Historic Third Baptist Church of San Francisco and was the Founding Director of the Bridge to Arts and Music Program in association with the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. “This season represents an exciting new chapter for Berkeley Symphony,” said Berkeley Symphony Executive Director Marion Atherton in a press release. “We’re thrilled to welcome some of today’s most compelling conductors, each bringing their unique artistic vision to our stage.” This season “shines a light on stirring masterpieces from the classical canon alongside groundbreaking contemporary works,” Atherton added. “From Dvořák’s lyrical Eighth Symphony to Shostakovich’s spirited Ninth and Haydn’s vivid ‘Military’ SymJames Parrish Smith phony, we’re exploring rich musical territory beyond the standard repertoire while showcasing the versatility and excellence of our orchestra.” The 2025/26 season also marks the conclusion of Music Director Joseph Young’s successful sixyear tenure. Young first guest-conducted the Berkeley Symphony in 2019 as an emergency substitute conductor. Based on that concert, in April 2019, the Berkeley Symphony announced the appointment of Young as its next music director, marking his first major directorship in symphonic music. Chamber Series subscriptions are $120 and available through the symphony’s box office and website. Subscriptions can be purchased by calling the box office at (510) 841-2800 or visiting berkeleysymphony.org. Daycare Boarding Training Grooming Learn more 2101 Mandela Pkwy Oakland, CA (510) 547-3647
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony hosts chamber series concert at PCA May 31

articles.text: Festival Napa Valley will celebrate its 20th anniversary with a summer season running July 4 through 19, featuring internationally known musicians, world premieres and cultural events across Napa Valley. The 2026 season will include performances by Renée Fleming, Wynton Marsalis, Time for Three, Ray Chen and Jean-Yves Thibaudet, along with the world premiere of The Judgment of Paris by composer Jake Heggie and librettist Gene Scheer. More than 200 artists will participate in concerts, dance performances and special events throughout the valley. Programming includes admission-free daytime concerts, evening performances, family events and the annual Taste of Napa celebration. “For 20 years, Festival Napa Valley has presented some of the world’s greatest artists on stages surrounded by the incomparable beauty of Napa Valley,” Festival President and CEO Richard Walker said in a press release. “This anniversary season honors that legacy while expanding our artistic reach and community impact.” Among the season highlights is the Arts for All Gala at Nickel & Nickel Winery headlined by Marsalis. Fleming will appear in “Voice of Nature: The Anthropocene” and serve as keynote speaker for the Festival’s Music & Wellness Summit. Additional programming includes a performance of The Wizard of Oz with live orchestra accompaniment, a ballet program directed by Melanie Hamrick and a Symphonic Finale celebrating America’s 250th anniversary. “Festival Napa Valley is a beloved cultural tradition, uniting exceptional music, wine, food, and hospitality,” said Steven Stull, chairman of the Festival Napa Valley Board of Directors. “We welcome audiences from near and far to celebrate this milestone season with us.” For more information about Festival Napa Valley and to purchase tickets, visit www.festivalnapavalley.org. The music festival takes place at wineries and cultural venues across Napa Valley.
articles.title: 20th annual Festival Napa Valley held July 4 - 19

articles.text: Conductor Herbert Blomstedt When the name Bismarck is mentioned, it tends to be derogatory. For example, Bismarck herring. But the Chancellor of Germany did a few good things. Perhaps Otto Von Bismarck could have advised the noted orchestra conductor Herbert Blomstedt. This world famous conductor, now 98, has become the oldest conductor in the history of orchestral music. But at what cost? As is often said, old age is the cemetery of talent. A noted cynic described responsibility as a detachable burden which is easily shifted.

articles.text: The Girls’ Choir Canzona One of the international youth choirs participating in this year’s Golden Gate International Music Festival, hosted by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, is the Girls’ Choir Canzona from Poland. Founded in 1981, the ensemble consists of 65 singers divided into two age groups: 7 to 12 and 13 to 19. Canzona is a laureate of numerous prestigious competitions. The choir’s spotlight performance will take place on July 15 at the First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley. For more than forty years, the choir has performed extensively in Poland and abroad, including concerts in Germany, Italy, Spain, Croatia, the United Kingdom, the United States, Israel, Malta, France, Portugal, and Vietnam. The ensemble has been honored to sing for Pope John Paul II several times. Since 2008, the choir has collaborated on organizing the International Choral Festival in Murowana Goślina. The founder and long-time conductor Prof. Elżbieta Wtorkowska currently leads the women’s ensemble and provides artistic and substantive supervision to the girls’ choir and the Canzona Kameralna ensemble, led by Adrianna Wtorkowska-Kubińska and Magdalena Holec. With the Canzona choirs, she has performed in Germany, Switzerland, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Russia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Lithuania, Finland, Austria, Ukraine, England, Spain, Portugal, Bulgaria, and Greece. Its most important achievements include: a Gold Diploma at the 25th National Sea Song Competition in Wejherowo in 2022, a Gold Diploma at the International Choral Competition and Festival Cançó Mediterrània in Spain, a Gold Diploma at the National Patriotic Song Competition Musica Patriae in Poznań, and a Gold Diploma in sacred music at the International Choral Competition Chorus in Croatia in 2023. In 2024, the choir received a Gold Diploma at the National Christmas Carol Competition in Wrocław and First Prize at the European Music Festival for Young People in Belgium. In 2025, the choir won a Gold Diploma, first place in the youth choir category, and a Grand Prix nomination at the Vietnam International Choir Competition, as well as the Grand Prix and Best Conductor Award at the National Choral Competition in Lubostroń. The choir also received two Gold Diplomas at the international Chorus Inside competition in Italy. Held every three years and now in its 13th year, the Golden Gate International Choral Festival takes place this year from July 13 to July 18. Information on the concerts and spotlight choirs can be found on their website, including which concerts are free or have paid admission for the public. https://www.piedmontchoirs. org/ggf-concerts-2026.
articles.title: Golden Gate Intl. Music Festival to feature choir from Poland

This was a lesson which should be learned by every person who steps in front of an orchestra. Unfortunately, this excellent conductor has remained on the stage too long. His most recent concert with the San Francisco Symphony was a complete disaster. He had to be wheeled onto the stage in a wheelchair and then helped to the conducting podium. When he finally achieved the conductor’s position, delirium set in. A disaster ensued. I assume that the rehearsals were similar. Since the maestro does not know when to retire, the responsibility then rests with the administration of the San Francisco Symphony. Was there any mention of “mea culpa”? Performers enjoy being in the spotlight. But… It would have been far better for the San Francisco Symphony to present a concert in honor of this noted conductor. The founder and long-time conductor Prof. Elżbieta Wtorkowska currently leads the women’s ensemble and provides artistic and substantive supervision to the girls’ choir and the Canzona Kameralna ensemble, led by Adrianna Wtorkowska-Kubińska and Magdalena Holec. With the Canzona choirs, she has performed in Germany, Switzerland, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Russia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Lithuania, Finland, Austria, Ukraine, England, Spain, Portugal, Bulgaria, and Greece. articles.text: Hayao Miyazaki, writer, director, and animator is not only one of the most revered filmmakers in Japan, but his extraordinary talent is venerated worldwide. His deep bench of award-wining animated films, each hand-drawn, using watercolor and acrylic paints, are considered so beautifully detailed (every frame stands alone) and judged to be works of art. Studio Ghibli has long resisted using computer-generated animation. Miyazaki’s thematic storytelling is compelling, often focusing on environmentalism, youthful independence, risk, and the cost of war. As well, his protagonists are often strong, young girls or resilient young women. Miyazaki co-founded the now iconic Studio Ghibli in 1985. In 2012 he was named a Person of Cultural Merit for his outstanding cultural contributions. He received an Academy Honorary Award for his profound impact on animation and cinema in 2014. His work continues to serve as an inspiration for countless animators, directors, and writers. Within a very short period, streaming has all but revolutionized what was once simply referred to as “going to the movies.” Films that were released in theaters for a limited time (hence often missed) are now available. If your youngster missed, say, Studio Ghibli’s Oscar-winning Spirited Away (2001) and The Boy and the Heron (2024), both are now streaming. All that’s required today is a television (likely wide-screen), and a subscription to, say, Prime, Netflix, Fandango, Apple tv, or Disney+. Don’t forget the popcorn. The name Studio Ghibli was chosen by Miyazaki in 1985. Surprisingly, the noun “Ghibli” references Italy’s Saharan scout plane, the Caproni Ca. 309, melded with the Arabic word for hot desert wind.

articles.text: Spirited Away is an extraordinary, award-wining (Oscar, Golden Bear, Annie Award) animated feature film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. It is a compelling fairytale-adventure that will captivate its young audience. The narrative opens with Chihiro (Daveigh Chase), a young girl, 10, sitting in the backseat of the family car. Her arms are crossed, her attitude is petulant; she’s clearly not happy. The family – mother (Lauren Holly) and father (Michael Chiklis) – have decided to move to the countryside. Chihiro is already missing her friends. As it turns out they take a wrong turn, enter a tunnel, and discover they are in what appears to be an abandoned amusement park. Spotting a restaurant, they go in and her parents begin to eat. Chihiro wanders away and soon runs into a boy her own age, Haku (Jason Marsden), who takes her on a tour of the park. When she returns to the restaurant she discovers that her parents have been transformed into pigs. She learns that this shocking change was brought about by a witch named Yubaba (Suzanne Pleshette) who runs a bathhouse for tired spirits. Haku warns Chihiro to avoid the witch, but she is told she must serve the malevolent hag in order to return her parents to their original forms. articles.text: For nearly two years, the Walking on Wednesdays group had been keeping an eye on two lots on Wistaria Way, a quiet loop at the top of Wildwood Gardens. Something was being built up there, and the walkers wanted to see how it had turned out. Realtor and fellow walker Stacey Isaacs arranged a house tour, and forty-six walkers and three K-9 best friends assembled at the Exedra on a recent Wednesday morning to find out. The group headed down Highland Avenue to Wildwood Avenue and paused at the entrance to Wildwood Gardens. The neighborhood had once been part of developer Frank C. Havens’ early 20th-century “Wildwood Estate,” and two partially hidden columns still mark the original entrance for those who know to look. The walkers bypassed the lower loops and made their way up toward Wistaria. Along the way, they stopped at an active construction site. On an earlier walk, the group had assumed the project would be an ADU — but the framing now suggested a full-sized house. A worker had previously told them that 1,500 yards of soil were being removed for the foundation, with completion expected near the end of 2026. Judging by the activity, that seemed entirely possible. As the group continued up to the Wistaria loop, curiosity got the better of Lori Austin, who searched online for why the street is spelled “Wistaria” and not “Wisteria.” It turns out there’s a story. The name was coined in 1818 by botanist Thomas Nuttall to honor his friend Dr. Caspar Wistar. When Nuttall officially recorded it, however, the name was published as “wisteria” — with an “e.” Under botanical naming rules, the first published spelling generally holds, even if it contains an error. Some historians think Nuttall may have chosen the “e” intentionally, either for the sound of it or to honor a related branch of the family that spelled their name “Wister.” Many Americans in the 19th and early 20th centuries held on to the “a” spelling to better reflect Dr. Wistar’s actual name. Piedmont, it seems, was among them. The two new homes on the Wistaria loop sit on what had been a vacant lot attached to a neighboring property. After the owner died earlier this decade, the lot was donated to a local church and sold in 2022. The new owners’ initial proposals for a single large home were twice rejected by neighbors and the City over concerns about scale. They came back with a revised plan: divide the lot into two parcels and build two homes, with an ADU alongside one — a configuration now permitted under SB9, the California law that took effect in January 2022 to address the state’s housing shortage by allowing homeowners to split lots and build up to four units on a single-family parcel. The Planning and Building Department approved the project in December 2023, permits followed in July 2024, and construction began immediately. Stacey Isaacs was waiting when the walkers arrived. The two homes are a striking modern design — glass exteriors, clean lines, built into a steep hillside. The owners plan to live in the home on the right, which is nearly finished. The home on the left, 67 Wistaria, is complete and on the market: four bedrooms, four baths, two half baths, listed at $3,995,000. The lower level includes an ensuite guest room that could also serve as an ADU. The owner, Geoff Gibson, was on site and spoke with the group about what it takes to build on a hillside like this. Hillside construction can add 20 to 25 percent to costs, he explained. Forty-six piers had to be drilled 10 to 20 feet into bedrock to stabilize the structures. The homes run on solar power, with smart-home technology, multi-zone HVAC, and central air conditioning — designed to meet most of their own energy needs. Geoff had originally hoped to spend Christmas in the house. The new target is his wife’s June birthday. Construction, he noted, takes longer than you’d hope. He invited the walkers inside. The group climbed the front stairs to the main level, where a large kitchen island anchors one Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Lisa Euphrat, Brenda Ferrero, Mary Carter, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Judy Mateo, Karin Fetherston, Adrienne Hamlin, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Lori Austin, Mary Henderson, Marcia Arthurs, Claudine Bach, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Grady Knowles, Michelle Yang, Minoo Klayman, Stella Houston, Caskey Weston, Debbie Powell, Liz Dalrymple, Jim Kellogg, Lois Price, Stacey Isaacs, Irene Thompson, Mark Davis, Noemi Alvarado, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Peter Persoff, Bonnie Sherwood with K-9 best friend Zippy, Siow Fang Tan, Alicia Rivera, Sherry Jacobs, Chuck Oraftik, Sanghi Wagner, Ken Hubbert, Denny McGee, Dan Scdonis, Dave DeRoche, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to have Bernadette Shield walking with them for the first time.

Some historians think Nuttall may have chosen the “e” intentionally, either for the sound of it or to honor a related branch of the family that spelled their name “Wister.” Many Americans in the 19th and early 20th centuries held on to the “a” spelling to better reflect Dr. Wistar’s actual name. Piedmont, it seems, was among them. The two new homes on the Wistaria loop sit on what had been a vacant lot attached to a neighboring property. After the owner died earlier this decade, the lot was donated to a local church and sold in 2022. The new owners’ initial proposals for a single large home were twice rejected by neighbors and the City over concerns about scale. They came back with a revised plan: divide the lot into two parcels and build two homes, with an ADU alongside one — a configuration now permitted under SB9, the California law that took effect in January 2022 to address the state’s housing shortage by allowing homeowners to split lots and build up to four units on a single-family parcel. The Planning and Building Department approved the project in December 2023, permits followed in July 2024, and construction began immediately. Stacey Isaacs was waiting when the walkers arrived. The two homes are a striking modern design — glass exteriors, clean lines, built into a steep hillside. The owners plan to live in the home on the right, which is nearly finished. The home on the left, 67 Wistaria, is complete and on the market: four bedrooms, four baths, two half baths, listed at $3,995,000. The lower level includes an ensuite guest room that could also serve as an ADU. The owner, Geoff Gibson, was on site and spoke with the group about what it takes to build on a hillside like this. Hillside construction can add 20 to 25 percent to costs, he explained. Forty-six piers had to be drilled 10 to 20 feet into bedrock to stabilize the structures. The homes run on solar power, with smart-home technology, multi-zone HVAC, and central air conditioning — designed to meet most of their own energy needs. Geoff had originally hoped to spend Christmas in the house. The new target is his wife’s June birthday. Construction, he noted, takes longer than you’d hope. He invited the walkers inside. The group climbed the front stairs to the main level, where a large kitchen island anchors one Wildwood Gardens construction Stacey Isaacs talking with Mike Galant inside Wistaria Home end of the open floor plan and a sculptural fireplace marks the dining area. The back opens to a wide deck with views of the Golden Gate and Bay Bridges. After thanking Stacey and Geoff for the visit, the walkers continued up Wistaria to Woodland Way, then returned to the Exedra via Crocker, Wildwood, Sheridan, and Highland. A fine morning on a street that most of Piedmont has never seen. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or call (510) 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: Nestled high in the rugged hills of California’s Central Coast, Calera Wine Company has long been regarded as one of America’s most influential Pinot Noir producers. Located near the small town of Hollister in the remote Gavilan Mountains, Calera helped prove that world-class Pinot Noir could be made outside of Burgundy long before California’s Central Coast became fashionable. The winery was founded in 1975 by visionary winemaker Josh Jensen, whose fascination with Burgundy led him on an unusual journey. After studying winemaking and working harvests in France, Jensen searched California for limestone-rich soils similar to those of Burgundy’s Côte d’Or. He eventually found them in the isolated limestone deposits of San Benito County and established Calera on a mountaintop site that many at the time considered too remote and inhospitable for fine wine. That sense of isolation became one of Calera’s defining strengths. Cool nights, high elevations, and rocky limestone soils allowed the winery to produce wines with unusual finesse and structure. At a time when many California wines emphasized ripeness and power, Calera pursued elegance, balance, and age-worthiness. Jensen often spoke about allowing the vineyard to speak for itself rather than overpowering the wine through excessive oak or manipulation. Over the decades, Calera earned a near-cult reputation for elegant, age-worthy Pinot Noir wines that emphasized restraint, minerality, and site expression. articles.text: Piedmont Dental by Design welcomes partner Dr. David Ma Dr. Jill Martenson, co-founder of Piedmont Dental By Design, has announced a new partnership with Dr. David Ma, who has joined the practice after two years as an associate dentist. The partnership coincides with Dr. Martenson’s 30th anniversary at Piedmont Dental By Design, marking an important milestone and reinforcing its long-standing commitment to providing patient-centered dental care to the Dr. Ma brings clinical experience and advanced training in complex treatment planning, cosmetic dentistry, preventive care, and restorative dentistry. Known for his compassionate approach and commitment to clinical excellence, Dr. Ma shares the same values that have guided the practice for three decades: trust, comfort, and personalized care. “This partnership represents an exciting step forward for our practice,” said Dr. Martenson. “Dr. Ma has been a wonderful addition to our team, and I’m thrilled to welcome him as a partner as we continue to grow and Dr. Ma added, “It’s an honor to join Dr. Martenson as a partner. articles.text: Scooter the Great Dane runs a FastCat 100-yard dash in 8.3 seconds! Despite the convenience of a dog small enough to fit in your purse, many owners lose their hearts to giant breeds like mastiffs and great danes. These gentle giants are some of the most loving dogs out there. Although they often have shorter lifespans than smaller breeds, the years spent with these extra-large loves are full of affection and laughter. Special size comes with special needs, and many giant breeds simply aren’t built for high-impact work, preferring to cuddle on the couch. However, they still need exercise! The following activities are tailored to giant breed needs. If you’re looking for relaxing activities you can do almost anywhere, consider hiking or walking on natural terrain such as dirt trails or grass. Brisk walks in these environments provide exercise while sparing the dog’s joints from repeated impact on concrete. Swimming is another excellent option: a fun, low-impact, full-body workout. Be sure to bring a doggy life jacket. Despite their cumbersome size, giant breed dogs can excel at certain dog sports. One of these sports is Fast CAT, a timed 100- yard dash where a mechanical lure stimulates the dog’s natural prey drive. Dogs earn titles and awards for participation. Giant breeds may also enjoy dock diving, where dogs leap from a dock in pursuit of a toy. Because these sports are performed in short bursts, they can be excellent choices for dogs with lower stamina or low-impact exercise needs. For mental enrichment, consider puzzle toys that are large, durable, and food-dispensing to keep your dog motivated. Cue your dog to “find it!” and time how long it takes them to locate hidden items at varying levels of difficulty, similar to the AKC Virtual Scent Work program. And let’s not forget trick training. While giant breeds may not be suited for acrobatic tricks, they can shine with oversized props for added humor, such as giant beach balls or even pulling smaller dogs in a wagon. When engaging in these activities, remember a few important safety tips. Avoid intense exercise on concrete to protect joints. Giant breeds can also overheat quickly, so opt for early morning or evening exercise during warm weather. Regular veterinary checkups are important before beginning intense sports, and activity should always be avoided immediately after meals to prevent bloat. Although giant breed dogs may seem like perfect couch potatoes, they can also be wonderful companions in outdoor activities and sports. Because their time with us is often shorter, it’s worth making the effort to create lasting memories with your gentle giant. Whether you’re hiking a trail, splashing in the water, or teaching a silly new trick, the most important thing is spending time together and including your pup in the fun. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com.
