articles.text: Photos by Ethan Shrago and Jim Mehlinger The Scouts enjoyed a ride through the countryside at the Western Railroad Museum on a restored 1930s electric train. The train interior displays advertisements from bygone eras. Left — front to back: Steve Belcher, Ethan Shrago, Rudy Campanillo, Stephen Campanillo, Quartermaster Ryan Moon, Andrew Lavin, Quartermaster Leo Shrago, and Gabe Tucker. Right — front to back: Jim Mehlinger, Assistant Scoutmaster Jen Ferguson, David Ferguson, Julie Veit, Forrest Poole, Christian Tran, Senior Patrol Leader Ted Eisemon, Patrol Leader Jojo Shim, and Bennie Belcher. Ted Eisemon Members of Piedmont Troop 11 rode historic trains to earn the Railroad Merit Badge. The May 3 adventure was organized and led by Quartermaster Leo Shrago and Assistant Scoutmaster Jen Ferguson. Merit Badges are awarded to Scouts who have learned skills, explored hobbies, or investigated possible careers in over a hundred areas. Merit badge activities promote self-confidence, learning, life skills, and personal growth. Scouts earn the Railroad Merit Badge by studying the history, technology, safety, and career opportunities in the railroad industry. They must learn about freight and passenger operations, signals, and modern digital communications and command controls. Scouts must also complete a hands-on activity such as visiting a train museum or “rail fanning,” which includes riding trains. The Scouts enjoyed a ride through the countryside at the Western Railroad Museum in Suisun City on a restored 1930s electric train. The train interior displayed vintage advertisements from bygone eras. Outside was rolling countryside with cattle ranches, rabbits scurrying from the tracks, elk grazing in the distance, and an extensive modern windmill array. They enjoyed a guided tour of the train shed filled with a variety of trains from old steam locomotives to early BART cars. After a question and answer meeting with a train engineer, the Scouts drove to the Redwood Valley Railroad in Tilden Regional Park in Contra Costa County. The railroad builds, restores, and operates narrow-gauge steam trains for passengers. Quartermaster Leo Shrago, who volunteers at the Railway, arranged a guided tour of the train sheds and machine shop. According to his father, Ethan Shrago, Leo has been a train fanatic ever since he was an infant, when he used to fall asleep to the sounds of trains chugging along the track. He quickly moved from Brio wood trains to real model trains. Leo has been a regular visitor to the Redwood Valley Railway since he was 4, always begging to volunteer at the earliest opportunity. Since last summer, he has been working weekly at the track as a brakeman and as a worker in and around the railroad. When Leo heard that this merit badge was available, he jumped at the opportunity to help schedule a day to tackle all the requirements and was excited to share his knowledge and passion about trains with his peers. Troop 11 Scouts ended the day with a ride on the steam train through the forest. If you are interested in information about Scouting in Piedmont or joining Scouts, please visit piedmontscouting.org or email contact@piedmontbsa.org Troop 11 Quartermaster Leo Shrago reviews the written requirements of the Railroad Merit Badge during a lunch break at the Western Railroad Museum. Piedmont Scouts learn about the machine shop and train repair at the Redwood Valley Railroad in Tilden Regional Park.

articles.text: The Cancer League, Inc. hosted its annual Spring Soirée on Thursday, April 23, transforming the iconic Trader Vic’s into a tropical excursion for a cause. The event, entitled “Paradise Found,” brought together over 150 guests and successfully raised an estimated $123,000 to fund early-stage cancer research. Led by co-chairs Carrie Levy and Kelly Winniford, the evening combined a high-end boutique marketplace with the spirit of philanthropy. Guests enjoyed premier Polynesian cuisine and signature cocktails while browsing a curated treasure hunt of 15 boutiques and artisans, each generously donating 20% of their proceeds directly to the organization’s research fund. The evening’s momentum was further enhanced by a highly competitive silent auction, featuring 11 bespoke ‘Treasure Trove’ packages that drew enthusiastic bidding. “The true discovery of ‘Paradise Found’ was seeing our community come together to celebrate and support our mission,” said Levy and Winniford. “Securing $123,000 in funding directly empowers brilliant researchers at the most critical early stages of discovery. These resources are vital to Seed the Cure and spark the breakthroughs that will ultiGuests bidding and eyeing the “Treasure Trove” packages on the silent auction tables Rachelle Hebrard, Laurie Schweitzer, Deb Obendorf, and Beverly Roberts Charles Shoppers delight in the many treasures. Missy Ellis, Karen Ellis, and Amy Settlemier mately redefine the future of cancer treatment.” The funds raised at the Soirée will be added to the more than $8 million that The Cancer League has raised since 1973. Following the success of the Spring Soirée, the community is invited to save the date for the organization’s signature winter gala, The Holly Ball, on Friday, December 4, 2026. About The Cancer League The Cancer League is a San Francisco Bay Area nonprofit dedicated to funding groundbreaking cancer research at its most critical early stages. As a charitable 501(c)(3) organization, it has raised more than $4 million in the last decade alone to support innovative researchers and improve patient outcomes. articles.text: What is Measure H ? Measure H renews the core parcel tax that has provided essential local funding for Piedmont schools for nearly 40 years. This tax is expiring and must be renewed by voters to preserve the academic programs our students depend on. Measure H extends the existing tax until Piedmont voters decide this support is no What is the official ballot statement that we will be voting on? To maintain the high quality of Piedmont schools, continue funding programs in math, science, technology, engineering, English, music and arts, attract and retain qualified teachers, update instructional materials and technology, and maintain manageable class sizes, shall Piedmont Unified School District’s measure be adopted, renewing the expiring school parcel tax at the current rate ($3,051 per parcel) until ended by voters, with independent citizen oversight, annual inflation adjustments, and all funds (approximately $12 million annually) benefiting local students? What about State and Federal funding? California ranks near the bottom nationally in per-pupil education funding — and Piedmont receives even less than most California districts. Oakland Unified receives approximately $24,000 per student from state and federal sources, while Piedmont Unified receives less than $14,000. Our local parcel tax exists precisely to bridge that gap. We do not have school aged children. Why should we support Measure H? Strong schools are the foundation of a strong community. The quality of Piedmont's schools protects property values and attracts families who enrich our neighborhoods. Every dollar raised by Measure H stays right here in Piedmont — a smart investment in our community's future, whether or not you have children in the schools. When is the election? Ballots will go out first week of May. “Election Day” is June 2. All Piedmont voters will receive a mail ballot. What about State and Federal funding? California ranks near the bottom nationally in per-pupil education funding — and Piedmont receives even less than most California districts. PIEDMONT SCHOOLS Please place this sign on your window to show your support for Measure H. YESONH Not a tax increase! For almost 40 years Piedmont schools have depended on local parcel taxes to supplement limited state funding. Measure H is our primary source of locally controlled funding and must be renewed. Measure H funds: • Specialized reading, writing, and language programs • Advanced programs in science, technology, engineering and math • Ensuring textbooks and instructional materials are up-to-date • Advanced academic programs and essential college counseling • Maintaining manageable class sizes • Programs in music, visual and performing arts • Competitive salaries to recruit and keep qualified teachers here in Piedmont Measure H is not a tax increase. It merely extends the existing voter approved parcel tax with minor annual adjustments for cost of living. Piedmont USD ranks among the top school districts in California. Renewing Measure H is essential to maintain the quality of Piedmont schools. Our schools have remained exceptional because Piedmont voters have continued to support this essential local funding. Measure H will help attract and retain highly qualified teachers here in Piedmont. If Measure H is not renewed, the Board of Education would be required to cut $12M annually, resulting in teacher and staff layoffs and significant cuts to core and advanced academic programs. articles.text: The 12th annual Piedmont School Maker Faire turned the Piedmont High School campus into a Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts & Math (S.T.E.A.M.) carnival on Sunday, May 17. Around 1,000 guests attended the 2026 iteration of the event, which unleashed the creative minds of kids and adults to fabricate and build. Perennial favorites like the Nerdy Derby grabbed the attention of attendees, inspiring them to engineer vehicles to withstand the spectacular ramp spanning the height of the amphitheater. At the other end of campus budding engineers tested their ingenuity at the Maker River by modifying small vessels of cork, rubber and wood for trial runs down the handcrafted aqueduct. The event included popular hands-on exhibits like Air Rockets and LEGOS with novel attractions, including the Mini Golf Links, a rustic apple press, and workshops for crafting jewelry. Piedmont became the first school district in the nation to host an official K-12 School Maker Faire in 2014. Dave Ragones, co-founded Piedmont Makers in 2014 with Piedmonter Vince Monical. The first recorded Maker Faire took place in San Mateo in 2006. The apex of the Makers program is Team 8033, Highlander Robotics, which competes in the World Championships for a global title year after year. The 2024 robot Banshee was active on the patio in the Fabrication Laboratory, while the current 2026 robot Wisp, was on the workbench inside in the shop for inspections and a Q & A with team members. Team 8033 also offered demonstrations of the Fab Lab’s laser cutter, quickly transforming digital blueprints into wooden keepsakes. Co-Presidents of Piedmont Makers Kevin Clark and Ben Stein have been at the helm of Makers since Ragones’ transitioned to Treasurer a year ago. Vice President of the Maker Faire, Ella Grossberg, and Brian Van Osdol, VP of Elementary Education, were the Faire’s lead organizers this year. “I loved all the exhibits this year, but I was especially impressed by the projects students brought to the Faire. I saw an ionic jet engine, a smart buoy, experiments with tea, toys modified for special needs, and self designed bikes. Annual and summer pass sales for non-residents open Tuesday, May 19, at 6 p.m. through the City’s Aquatics registration portal. Pass sales to date have been significantly higher than projected in the pool’s first-year operating model. To manage capacity during the busy summer season, summer pass sales will close for both residents and non-residents on Friday, May 22, at 6 p.m. Annual passes will remain available to everyone and continue to offer the best value for community members who expect to swim regularly throughout the year. There are no plans at this time to limit annual pass sales. Summer passes for non-residents can be used beginning on Memorial Day and remain valid through the end of September. The new Community Pool has now been open for just over one month. During that time, staff have learned a great deal about how the facility is being used, when demand is highest, and how different types of swimmers and programs are sharing pool space. Staff are monitoring use patterns, exploring new approaches to balance access needs, and making operational decisions with several goals in mind: maximizing community access, balancing the needs of all user groups, and maintaining a financially sustainable operating model. Non-resident reservations for the poolside room and rooftop pavilion in May, June, and July also open on May 19 at 6 p.m. All rental reservations are made through the Aquatics registration portal at rec.us/piedmont. articles.text: Editor: I moved to Piedmont when I was seven years old. Before that, I spent my entire childhood in Montclair, where I attended Montclair Elementary for TK, kindergarten, and first grade. I had a wonderful experience at Montclair Elementary—I loved my teachers and made great memories. However, my parents were concerned about the middle school and high school options available to me. They wanted me to build friendships in elementary school that would last through high school. Since I had cousins in Piedmont who attended Beach Elementary, my parents decided it was best for us to move here and join its schools. When I began second grade at Beach Elementary, I was warmly welcomed by some of the most supportive teachers I could imagine! I quickly made a lot of new friends, and I’m still close with many of them today. Our move to Piedmont wasn’t just about finding friends and a sense of community; it was also about the exceptional education offered by the public schools. I have had amazing teachers every year, and I feel fortunate for the classes and resources available to us. I know that Piedmont schools continue to thrive thanks to the community’s commitment to funding what truly matters. That’s why I strongly urge everyone to vote YES on Measure H. Without it, we risk losing 20% of our school funding, which is vital for our resources, teachers, and community. Please make your voice heard and vote YES! –Hazel Schaeffer

articles.text: The eight Alameda County local ballot measures scheduled for the June 2, 2026 Primary Election were evaluated in April 2026 by a Ballot Watchdog group of evaluators from the non-profit and nonpartisan Alameda County Civil Grand Jurors’ Association (ACCGJA). The measures’ titles were evaluated for accuracy and fairness pursuant to the California Elections Code and the criteria established by the association for each type of ballot measure, e.g. Bond Measure, Tax Measure and Other (non-tax measure). This review by the ACCGJA is unrelated to the current sitting Civil Grand Jury; it is also unrelated to the California Civil Grand Jurors’ Association, the Alameda County Registrar of Voters, and the County of Alameda. The collective ratings represent the average score arrived at by the evaluators who are Association members and are all former grand jury members. The scoring system is comparable to the popular “Yelp” type scoring system (a score of one is worst; five is best). Like a Yelp evaluation, the ratings reflect the average of the evaluators’ educated opinions, based on the established criteria as to what should, and should not, be included in each type of ballot measure. We emphasize that the ACCGJA IS NOT evaluating the merits of the proposed measures. The evaluation is not partisan - neither liberal nor conservative. We are only concerned with the accuracy and impartiality of the 75-word ballot title being put to the voters. Those 75 words are the only thing that we know every voter sees as they vote. State law requires ballot language to be “a true and impartial synopsis of the purpose of the proposed measure and shall be in language that is neither argumentative nor likely to create prejudice for or against the measure.” Unfortunately, many jurisdictions disregard the intent of the law by exaggerating the benefits and glossing over the costs, as well as by adding extraneous verbiage designed to favor passage of the measure. No one, other than the agency promoting the measure, is required to approve the agency’s language. To counteract this, there is a growing need for citizens to actively and consistently monitor and evaluate local governments’ ballot descriptions. This current ACCGJA effort supports the findings of the 2021 Alameda County Civil Grand Jury report, The Need for Accuracy and Impartiality of Ballot Measure Questions. Additional information can be found on the Ballot Watchdog group website: https://ballotwatchdog.com/ most of the measures exhibited some degree of proponent bias, emphasizing the benefits and glossing over the costs, meaning the authors want the measure to pass. While that tilt may be understandable, it is not in compliance with the law. Results: The Ballot Watchdog review produced individual ballot measure scores ranging from 1.8 to 4.2. The average was 3.5. The most common issue that caused a reduction in the score from the maximum of 5 was a lack of clarity as to the intent and need for the measure. Another common problem for tax measures was the lack of where and how this new tax relates to the other existing taxes or bonded indebtedness of that jurisdiction. The talk will focus on universal healing precepts found in the Holy Bible, especially in Christ Jesus’ life and teachings, showing how they are available for anyone to understand and experience through the lens of Christian Science. “Fear can be overcome and even healed in our lives by discovering the strong connection and relationship we have to something bigger than ourselves—God,” says Troseth. “By learning to lean and rely on this greater, higher good, we can feel moved to love beyond ourselves—and this frees us from fear and so much more.” Troseth has been a Christian Science practitioner for many years, helping people on a daily basis through this scientific approach to prayer. She travels from her home base in Nyack, New York, to speak to audiences around the world as a member of the Christian Science Board of Lectureship. The talk is free, open to the community, and jointly sponsored by First Church of Christ, Scientist, Orinda and First Church of Christ, Scientist, Oakland.

pages.text: Wednesday, May 20, 2026 3 Perspective Local ballot measure ratings Editor: I am Michael Henn, a longtime Piedmont resident, former Piedmont Planning Commissioner, and threetime member of the Alameda County Civil Grand Jury. The nonpartisan and independent Civil Grand Jury Association, not affiliated with the sitting Grand Jury, evaluates local ballot measures’ language for fairness and accuracy. There are eight measures evaluated in the attached report including one from Piedmont. By chance, Piedmont’s Measure H achieved the highest score of the eight. As reported, local ballot measures unfairly exaggerate the measures benefits while ignoring the costs. Local ballot measure ratings for Alameda County Primary Election on June 2 Created by independent Civil Grand Jury Association The eight Alameda County local ballot measures scheduled for the June 2, 2026 Primary Election were evaluated in April 2026 by a Ballot Watchdog group of evaluators from the non-profit and nonpartisan Alameda County Civil Grand Jurors’ Association (ACCGJA). The measures’ titles were evaluated for accuracy and fairness pursuant to the California Elections Code and the criteria established by the association for each type of ballot measure, e.g. Bond Measure, Tax Measure and Other (non-tax measure). This review by the ACCGJA is unrelated to the current sitting Civil Grand Jury; it is also unrelated to the California Civil Grand Jurors’ Association, the Alameda County Registrar of Voters, and the County of Alameda. The collective ratings represent the average score arrived at by the evaluators who are Association members and are all former grand jury members. The scoring system is comparable to the popular “Yelp” type scoring system (a score of one is worst; five is best). Like a Yelp evaluation, the ratings reflect the average of the evaluators’ educated opinions, based on the established criteria as to what should, and should not, be included in each type of ballot measure. We emphasize that the ACCGJA IS NOT evaluating the merits of the proposed measures. The evaluation is not partisan - neither liberal nor conservative. We are only concerned with the accuracy and impartiality of the 75-word ballot title being put to the voters. Those 75 words are the only thing that we know every voter sees as they vote. State law requires ballot language to be “a true and impartial synopsis of the purpose of the proposed measure and shall be in language that is neither argumentative nor likely to create prejudice for or against the measure.” Unfortunately, many jurisdictions disregard the intent of the law by exaggerating the benefits and glossing over the costs, as well as by adding extraneous verbiage designed to favor passage of the measure. No one, other than the agency promoting the measure, is required to approve the agency’s language. To counteract this, there is a growing need for citizens to actively and consistently monitor and evaluate local governments’ ballot descriptions. This current ACCGJA effort supports the findings of the 2021 Alameda County Civil Grand Jury report, The Need for Accuracy and Impartiality of Ballot Measure Questions. Additional information can be found on the Ballot Watchdog group website: https://ballotwatchdog.com/ most of the measures exhibited some degree of proponent bias, emphasizing the benefits and glossing over the costs, meaning the authors want the measure to pass. While that tilt may be understandable, it is not in compliance with the law. Results: The Ballot Watchdog review produced individual ballot measure scores ranging from 1.8 to 4.2. The average was 3.5. The most common issue that caused a reduction in the score from the maximum of 5 was a lack of clarity as to the intent and need for the measure. Another common problem for tax measures was the lack of where and how this new tax relates to the other existing taxes or bonded indebtedness of that jurisdiction. For example, a proposed tax measure may fail to mention what the existing tax rate is, or whether the new tax or bond was being added to an existing similar tax or bond. Thus, voters could not learn the amount of increase or even the percentage of increase if the proposed measure were to pass. Also common was the inclusion of extraneous verbiage designed to influence a favorable vote on the measure, such as emphasizing popular or feel-good spending categories that might be improved if the measure were to pass. However, there is no guarantee that the funds would be spent on those categories, going instead to other public purposes. Intent and structure of tax (i.e. a % or rate for a sales or transfer tax, or a $ per parcel for a parcel tax) 2. Amount of the tax generated per year 3. Duration of the tax 4. Is this a Special or General tax? 5. Where is the money specifically going? (If a special tax) 6. Is there another similar tax already in place? If so that tax info should be included. 7. Will this take 2/3, vote or simple majority to pass? 8. Extraneous language unrelated to the matter which could be considered as deceptive to the voter. Before that, I spent my entire childhood in Montclair, where I attended Montclair Elementary for TK, kindergarten, and first grade. I had a wonderful experience at Montclair Elementary—I loved my teachers and made great memories. However, my parents were concerned about the middle school and high school options available to me. They wanted me to build friendships in elementary school that would last through high school. Since I had cousins in Piedmont who attended Beach Elementary, my parents decided it was best for us to move here and join its schools. When I began second grade at Beach Elementary, I was warmly welcomed by some of the most supportive teachers I could imagine! I quickly made a lot of new friends, and I’m still close with many of them today. Our move to Piedmont wasn’t just about finding friends and a sense of community; it was also about the exceptional education offered by the public schools. articles.text: On Saturday, May 16, The Orion Fund hosted a community event to provide awareness of our organization and what we do. The Orion Fund is a 20-year Piedmont all-volunteer organization that provides grants to California college students in a health crisis. The organization is known at 70+ campuses throughout the state, from community colleges to the UCs. Over the years, we have awarded 492 grants totaling $820,000. From car crashes to cancer, the organization helps students until they can recover. According to the organization, campuses have lost many resources for students in crisis. They’ve met with members of eight departments at UC Berkeley and were told about the stresses on campus due to increasing costs. With all that Cal has to offer, The Orion Fund is now their first resource for students in crisis. Helping 40 students at UC Berkeley this year. The fund’s students range from 18 to 32 years old, from first-year to graduate, and international students. These students are engaged in many academic pursuits, and come from many cultural backgrounds. They’ll go on to become parents, professors, doctors, engineers, artists, lawyers, and entrepreneurs. The organization is entirely community-funded. If you are interested, visit their website to donate: www. theorionfund.org. The Orion Fund board members, Kaylene, Emily, Pam (co-founder, president), and Florence Pam, Joyce, and Arnie Brown (Piedmont, major donors), Julie Walsh, MD, Medical Advisor for The Orion Fund

articles.text: Residents can sign up starting today for the Community Pool’s Summer Kickoff “Splash Bash,” a free and fun-filled day of activities on Saturday, May 23. The event will feature cannonball contests, a rubber ducky prize dive, an underwater treasure hunt, and other giveaways, and prizes. Registration for free 90-minute Splash Bash time slots is on the City’s Aquatics registration portal, rec.us/piedmont. Splash Bash activities will be grouped into four timed sessions to maximize participation opportunities for swimmers of all ages and abilities throughout the day and provide a predictable schedule for attending families. The pool will be open exclusively for registered Splash Bash activities on Saturday, with no open or lap swim. Regular hours and programming will resume on Sunday. Ice cream will be available for purchase at the Mr. Softee truck parked outside the pool all afternoon. For swimmers who have passed the pool swim test, activities will take place in the competition pool. Activities for all others will take place in the activity pool. Each session will feature a cannonball contest for all ages, a rubber ducky dive, and a treasure hunt – followed by open swim until the time slot ends. Non-resident registration opens Thursday, May 21, at 6 p.m. Advance registration is required for all participants. Each session is limited to 125 registered people. Registration closes when all slots are full, or at 11:59 p.m. on Friday, May 22. Swimmers can sign up for one of 4 time slots: • 11 a.m. - 12:30 p.m. • 1 - 2:30 p.m. • 3 - 4:30 p.m. • 5 - 6:30 p.m. Visit the City’s Aquatics registration portal to sign up for the event and other aquatic classes offered at the Community Pool: rec.us/piedmont. A kid jumping into the pool

articles.text: Misha is an 8-year-old Siamese mix with the soul of a cozy old friend. She’s happiest spending quiet days near her person—lounging nearby while you work, accepting head scratches, or curling up across your legs for cuddles. Although she’s shy with strangers, Misha warms up with patience and consistency and thrives in a calm, predictable home. Someone gentle and observant will quickly discover her adorable sassy side if meals are running late, as well as her love for being brushed, heating pads, and sweet petting sessions. While she does require ongoing care for arthritis, including a monthly injection at the vet, Misha still has a playful side, too! Her favorite activity is batting enthusiastically at a rainbow ribbon wand toy, sometimes scrambling in circles or trying to catch it with her toothless little mouth. Her bursts of play are short Adopt Misha through Cat Town. and senior-style, but they’re full of personality! For someone looking for a mellow, affectionate friend with a deeply comforting presence, Misha’s the kind of gal you don’t want to miss out on. She’ll make your house feel like a home. Misha is spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www.cattownoakland. org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: The Montclair Beer, Wine & Music Festival returns on Saturday, June 20, 2026, from 12:00 - 6:00 p.m., bringing together the best of local craft beverages, live entertainment, and community spirit for a lively summer celebration. Presented by the Montclair Village Association, this popular street festival will feature over 50 craft beverage tastings, including beer, wine, cider, and alcohol-free options, alongside delicious offerings from local chefs and artisan vendors. In addition to tastings, the festival offers free musical performances by local favorites – Prospect, Cardboard People, Bululú, DJ BlackWoman, and DJ2 – hosted by Candi Martinez throughout the day on the Mister Beever’s Paws & Claws Stage powered by Meet Your Core Pilates. Bring the whole family for free performances, children’ s crafts, lawn games, and other engaging activities. Get inspired at the Travel & Adventure Zone hosted by Flair Travel. Festivalgoers will also have the opportunity to explore Montclair Village’s unique boutique businesses and dining establishments, as well as browse a curated selection of local artisan vendors. “The Montclair Beer, Wine & Music Festival is a celebration of community, creativity, and local flavor,” said Daniel Swafford, Executive Director of the Montclair Village Association. “We’re excited to welcome residents and visitors alike for a day of connection, entertainment, and discovery.” The festival’s signature Unlimited Tasting Package provides attendees with access to all beverage tastings and includes a commemorative festival glass. Advance tickets are priced at $58, with day-of pricing at $68. Attendees can receive a $20 discount by joining the Montclair Cares Club, a $120 annual membership that supports community programs and events. Discounted tickets are available now at MontclairVillage. com. Proceeds support free cultural arts and community programming in the district. A scene from last year’s Montclair Beer, Wine & Music Festival Photo by Peter Marcus

articles.text: Tonight, Wednesday, May 20 at 7:00 p.m. Piedmont Unified School District’s school board will convene for a regularly scheduled meeting in the District Office’s board room at 760 Magnolia Avenue. The meeting will include a recognition of student school board members and retiring teachers and school staff. The meeting will not include a first reading on the Mobile Phone policy, that highly anticipated item is scheduled for the following meeting June 3. The meeting will include a presentation reviewing the first year of implementing the new English Language Arts curriculum, Fishtank Learning. The elementary language arts curriculum assessment and update will be presented by Ariel Dolowich, Assistant Superintendent, and Havens 3rd grade teacher Michelle Kerwin. “The presentation will focus on such elements as the process that has been established to make curriculum changes to Fishtank, highlighting what has been successful from the first year, and detail the next steps and changes that will occur for the following year,” states the board background document. articles.text: It wasn’t until 1610, when Galileo Galilei discovered four moons orbiting Jupiter, that humans learned there were moons other than our own. We know now that the Moon is just one of more than 891 moons in our entire solar system. However, our Moon is unique because it belongs to the only planet in our solar system that has life. As our closest neighbor in space, the Moon has given scientists incredible insight on both Earth and our solar system. Lunar missions conducted by NASA over the years have allowed humans to peek into our solar system’s past, long before we were ever around. In knowing more about our solar system’s past, we gain greater context of Earth’s place in our solar system. The Start Although there are varying theories about the Moon’s origin, it is widely agreed that a powerful and massive collision was the genesis event. It is theorized that approximately 4.5 billion years ago, an object about the size of Mars collided with Earth. The large and violent collision between the two objects sent molten and vaporized debris out into space. Over time, the materials from the collision formed the Moon. In the 60s and 70s, the Apollo program helped strengthen scientists’ existing theories about the Moon. The discoveries from NASA’s Apollo program helped transform existing theories about the start of the Moon. During the Apollo missions, lunar rock samples were collected and analyzed. These samples gave scientists incredible answers to long-standing questions. They could determine from the samples that during the Moon’s formation it had been molten and for millions of years it had been covered with magma. Scientists also learned that lunar rocks and Earth rocks have an incredibly similar chemical composition. The chemical composition of the two is so similar that scientists were able to conclude that the Moon had once been a part of Earth. The findings from the Apollo missions gave scientists context for future theNASA Artemis II at the pad with a full Snow Moon ories and discoveries about the Moon and our solar system. A planet full of history Every crater on the Moon tells us a story about our solar system’s past. Asteroids, meteoroids, and comets have marked the surface of the Moon for millions of years, leaving a vast history for us to explore. There is no wind or liquid water on the Moon, preserving the impact craters on the surface. Meanwhile, impact evidence on Earth has been affected by erosion, plate tectonics, and volcanic activity. By investigating the Moon’s craters, we learn more about both the Moon’s and our solar system’s past. The more scientists learn about the Moon’s craters, the better insight astronauts will have when they visit the Moon in the future. The Artemis program NASA’s Artemis program has opened the door to further investigation into the Moon and beyond. Through a series of missions, scientists will have greater insight into questions surrounding the Moon and what to expect for and from future lunar missions. In the most recent phase, Artemis II, astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen performed various tasks during their journey; analyzing and recording geologic features of the Moon. The information gained from Artemis II will help scientists develop a better geologic history of the Moon and will be crucial for future exploration of the Moon and eventually Mars. Chabot’s historic telescopes As we head into warmer weather in the Bay, there will be more opportunities to clearly view celestial objects in the night sky. Since 1883, Chabot’s inception, telescope viewings have been open and free to the public. We continue that longstanding tradition every Friday and Saturday night from 7:30PM-10:30PM (weather permitting). Our incredible telescope operators and volunteers are always eager to help answer any astronomical curiosities and questions. Visit chabotspace.org to find out more information about our 3 historic telescopes: Leah, Rachel and Nellie! Keep that #MoonJoy alive Chabot has a summer full of exploration and joy planned – and there’s something for everyone! From Sci-Fi Movie Nights in the Planetarium and Hike & Sips through the redwoods, the return of Space Week to Cosmic Camp-in sleepovers under the stars. Cameron Schneider is a staff member of Chabot Space and Science Center in the Oakland hills.

articles.text: Ted Eisemon, and Theo Ferguson The Hungteetsepoppi Lodge of the Order of the Arrow (OA) held its semi-annual Ordeal and Induction of new members on March 27-29 at Camp Augusta, near Nevada City in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada Mountains. Founded in 1915, the Order of the Arrow is the honor society of Scouting America (formerly the Boy Scouts of America), led by youths age 21 and under with adult advisors. Each Scouting council has its own lodge. Members are Scouts who exemplify the Scout Oath and Law and are elected by each troop. The Ordeal tests candidates’ character and commitment to the Scout Oath and Law. Scouts spend Friday night and Saturday reflecting on the meaning of service and labor on camp projects such as constructing benches, spreading wood chips, and laying out a labyrinth for summer camp activities. The Induction was held Saturday evening in the forest. For their exemplary service and leadership, Lodge Chief Theo Ferguson and former Lodge Vice Chief Drew Kobal were elevated to Vigil members, the highest honor in the OA. According to Lodge Chief Theo Ferguson, one thing that makes the OA unique is that it is a completely youth-driven organization. Theo is now serving his second term as Lodge Chief. The organization also provides many experiences across the nation. Theo regularly travels across California to attend planning meetings and teaches at national training events. He said that being Lodge Chief has “transformed [his] leadership and organizational abilities,” and that his favorite part has been “meeting hundreds of amazing and inspiring people from all over, creating an awesome network of peers.” Lodge Advisor Bryan Gros said that the Hungteetsepoppi Lodge has been providing service to Camp Augusta for decades. Some of the recent projects involve repairing structures that the Lodge installed years ago. Many youth spent a week or two at the camp when they were younger and really enjoyed returning to camp as Scouts. The Lodge also helps support Piedmont Scouting by assisting with the Cub program and setting up the annual Tree Lot. Adult Scout leaders may become OA members. Jen Gregovich, who is a member of the Board of Directors of Camp Augusta, as well as Troop 15 Scoutmaster, and her daughter, Abigail Gregovich, went through the Ordeal and were inducted. Council Member at Large and former Lodge Advisor Kevin Fischer and Steve Sciamanna, boyhood friends as Scouts in Troop 6, have continued their friendship and service as adult Scout leaders and OA members. Jim Mehlinger began Scouting more than seven decades ago in a troop formed by his grandfather more than a century ago. He has been an OA member for almost seven decades and participated in the induction of his grandson, Ted Eisemon. (* signifies a newly inducted member) Order of the Arrow holds induction ceremony By Michael James Mehlinger, Ted Eisemon, and Theo Ferguson The Hungteetsepoppi Lodge of the Order of the Arrow (OA) held its semi-annual Ordeal and Induction of new members on March 27-29 at Camp Augusta, near Nevada City in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada Mountains. Founded in 1915, the Order of the Arrow is the honor society of Scouting America (formerly the Boy Scouts of America), led by youths age 21 and under with adult advisors. Each Scouting council has its own lodge. Members are Scouts who exemplify the Scout Oath and Law and are elected by each troop. The Ordeal tests candidates’ character and commitment to the Scout Oath and Law. Scouts spend Friday night and Saturday reflecting on the meaning of service and labor on camp projects such as constructing benches, spreading wood chips, and laying out a labyrinth for summer camp activities. The Induction was held Saturday evening in the forest. For their exemplary service and leadership, Lodge Chief Theo Ferguson and former Lodge Vice Chief Drew Kobal were elevated to Vigil members, the highest honor in the OA. According to Lodge Chief Theo Ferguson, one thing that makes the OA unique is that it is a completely youth-driven organization. Theo is now serving his second term as Lodge Chief. The organization also provides many experiences across the nation. Theo regularly travels across California to attend planning meetings and teaches at national training events. He said that being Lodge Chief has “transformed [his] leadership and organizational abilities,” and that his favorite part has been “meeting hundreds of amazing and inspiring people from all over, creating an awesome network of peers.” Lodge Advisor Bryan Gros said that the Hungteetsepoppi Lodge has been providing service to Camp Augusta for decades. Some of the recent projects involve repairing structures that the Lodge installed years ago. Many youth spent a week or two at the camp when they were younger and really enjoyed returning to camp as Scouts. The Lodge also helps support Piedmont Scouting by assisting with the Cub program and setting up the annual Tree Lot. Adult Scout leaders may become OA members. Jen Gregovich, who is a member of the Board of Directors of Camp Augusta, as well as Troop 15 Scoutmaster, and her daughter, Abigail Gregovich, went through the Ordeal and were inducted. Council Member at Large and former Lodge Advisor Kevin Fischer and Steve Sciamanna, boyhood friends as Scouts in Troop 6, have continued their friendship and service as adult Scout leaders and OA members. Jim Mehlinger began Scouting more than seven decades ago in a troop formed by his grandfather more than a century ago. He has been an OA member for almost seven decades and participated in the induction of his grandson, Ted Eisemon. articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team continues its strong performance in the North Coast Section postseason. On Saturday, May 16 at the NCS Bayshore Area Championships, the Highlanders qualified for the prestigious Meet of Champions in 13 events by gaining a top-six finish or qualifying time. “The jump from WACC to Bayshore is one that teaches us a lot about ourselves, where we go from 12 teams up to 34 and welcome elite competition,” said coach Pouyan Assadi. “Of our 40 athletes that competed yesterday, 17 will move on either as individuals or in relays.” It was a big afternoon for junior sprinter Claire Aubrecht, who qualified to the Meet of Champions individually in the 100 meter dash and 200-meter. She was also a part of the 4x100 and 4x400 relay teams reaching the next stage. In the 100, Aubrecht clocked a time of 12.45 seconds to place seventh of 21. She met the exact time needed to qualify for the Meet of Champions. As for the 200, she finished fifth of 23 in 25.59. Both were personal best times resulting in lowering the school’s record time in each Avedis Gourjian placed third of 13 in the pole vault at the NCS Bayshore Area Championships. Malia Williams placed third in the high jump at the NCS Bayshore. Staff Photos Claire Aubrecht qualified for the NCS Meet of Champions in four events at the NCS Bayshore Area Championships. event. She was the second leg in the 4x100 relay team which posted a time of 49.21 seconds with teammates Akunna Iroh, Darcy McKee, and Nia Jackson. The team placed 2nd of 19 teams. It was another record time for the school. The 4x400 team of Aubrecht, Skylar Best, Daniela Lucaccini, and Iroh placed fifth of 11 in 4:17.39. “Claire qualified to MOC in four events, including pushing her 100m and 200m record breaking times down further, and being a part of the 4x100 that crushed last year’s all-time record breaking time by over a half second,” Assadi said. It was also a strong day for junior Sebastien Swain who reached the Meet of Champions in two events. He was second in a field of 24 runners in the 800 meters with a time of 1:56.46. He was also part of the 4x400 relay team with Rehan Mumtaz, Ben Gerber, and Maddox Ma which placed second of 18 schools with a time of 3:25.02. “Seb took second in the open 8 and was a part of the second place 4x4. Their time is the fastest since the CIF qualifying team in 2023, and was the fastest 4x4 time we’ve ever run at Bayshore,” Assadi said. Below is a full rundown of all Piedmont’s qualifiers for the Meet of Champions. Other Top-6 Results Ma qualified in the 400 with a time of 50.23, finishing fifth of 23 runners. Avedis Gourjian was third of 13 in the pole vault with a height of 11 feet, 3 inches. Noah Hildebrand placed sixth of 24 in the triple jump with a distance of 40 feet, 7 inches. Best finished her 800 meter event in 2:24.64, placing sixth of 23 runners. Uzoma Iroh placed fourth of 23 in the shot put with a distance of 33 feet, 6.5 inches, while Saniyah Johnson was sixth in 32 feet, 3 inches. Uzoma Iroh also finished third of 23 in the discus with a throw of 111 feet, 1 inch. In the high jump, Malia Williams and Lucia Dorsey both placed third of 21 athletes with a height of 4 feet, 10 inches. NEXT UP Piedmont competes in the NCS Meet of Champions at Dublin High School on Friday and Saturday, May 22-23. Friday’s preliminary races start at 12:30 p.m., while Saturday’s finals start at 11:00 a.m.

articles.text: Olive Dao-Hoang at the plate. The Piedmont Middle School softball team kept up its winning ways, notching three more victories last week as they concluded their regular season and began their playoff run. The Scots are now 12-2 for the season. On Monday, May 12, the Scots returned to the friendly confines of Witter Field, where they took care of business, besting East Bay Innovation Academy18-0 in the first-round of the East Bay Middle School Softball League playoffs. Simone Tornatore went the distance from the circle, posting a complete game shutout backed by a sparkling defense that committed no errors. The offense came early and often as the Scots set the tone with back-to-back HRs in the bottom of the first from Keira Spina (3-3, 6RBI) and Bailey Gregovich (4-4, 4RBI). On the following day, the Scots concluded their regular season in the Oakland Athletic League with a gritty 7-3 win over Elite Public Academy. Piedmont chose to showcase some of the team’s younger talent and was rewarded by key contributions from 6th graders: Clara Blanchard laced a double to right that drove in a key run, Anya Giri brought the crowd to their feet by legging out a standup triple, Mailey Small smacked a double of her own, and Cate Penrod pitched two solid innings in relief. 7th grader Mackenzie Ewen was a force on both sides of the ball, pitching 3 dominant innings striking out 5 batters while also continuing her hot streak at the plate going 2-3 with a 2B, 3B and 2RBI. articles.text: First Piedmont team to medal at State Piedmont High’s boys’ 200 medley relay team of Nik Costello, Asher Takazawa, Connor Carnazzo, and Jeffrey Latronica made school history at the 2026 CIF State Championships at Clovis West High School. It placed ninth overall out of 18 finalists and 40 total schools in California with a time of 1:33.56. They became the only relay team in PHS history to finish with a top-9 medal in the State meet’s 12-year history. It is also the first time the school had two teams as finalists after the 400 team reached its B Finals. Costello replaced usual breaststroker Cole Carnazzo on the 200 medley team, enabling Latronica to swim the last leg. Carnazzo, had an AP test and could not make it to the state meet. “This required us to switch the order so that our typical freestyler, Nik Costello, swam breaststroke. This season proved to be challenging without having a home pool to practice in, we swam at four different locations. I am excited to see what next year will bring; hopefully we will make it to states again,” coach Elizabeth Dally said. Piedmont’s 400 freestyle team featured Dimitri Secor replacing Takazawa and placing 16th in 3:07.91. It marked back-to-back appearances for Piedmont’s boys’ relay teams to reach State after last year’s 200 medley and 400 freestyle teams reached the preliminary round to finish 23rd and 21st respectively. Costello and Takazawa were both members of that group. “The whole team put in a lot of work to get faster. When we went into NCS with the No. 1 seed we knew we could get to State. We didn’t expect to get top-nine and be in the A Final. I’m really proud of our team,” Costello said. “We were going into this not expecting this at all. It was our goal to make top-three at NCS and wound up getting fourth. That podium was not expected at all. One thing we did really well this year was push the team bonding and how much trust we had in each other. There was a lot of togetherness in our team,” Takazawa said Nik Costello (left), Asher Takazawa, Connor Carnazzo, and Jeffrey Latronica made school history by finishing ninth in the 200 medley relays at the CIF State Swimming Championships. To reach the finals, the 200 team qualified by finishing ninth of 40 in 1:32.58. In the final, Takazawa clocked 23.97 seconds in the back stroke, Costello had a 26.22 breast stroke, Carnazzo had a 22.55 butterfly, while Latronica swam freestyle of 20.82. In the 400 free preliminary round, they finished 17th of 40 with a time of 3:07.23. Both Carnazzo and Latronica are freshmen. “Those two guys are fast. They are going to do many good things in the future. Jeffrey really stepped up and Connor has put on a show since WACC. It’s been great to see the young guys pop off,” Costello said of the newcomers. “I’ve known Connor and Jeffrey for so long, it’s been super cool seeing their growth. It’s amazing how they stepped up and took matters into their own hands. What they did really well was trusting the process, they depended on us to explain how the season goes, and showed up to race and perform when they needed to,” Takazawa added. Simon Lins competed in the 50 freestyle and 100 backstroke in 2022, Nina Schwab featured in the one-meter dive in 2024, while the 200 medley and 400 freestyle boys’ relay teams have now qualified in 2025 and 2026. articles.text: Staff Photos Joey Assalian helped reel in a 6-3, 6-4 win at No. 1 doubles against San Ramon Valley. Piedmont High’s boys’ tennis team’s season came to an end on Tuesday, May 12. As the No. 12 seed in the Division 1 North Coast Section Team Tournament, Piedmont fell by a score of 4-2 to No. 5 San Ramon Valley on the Wolves’ home court in Danville. The Highlanders end their season with a 16-7 overall record, while Lucas Smolko secured the school’s only boys’ NCS Individual singles title since Barry Gilbert in 1975. “We had a really good season. We finished second in the Western Alameda County Conference and had a 16-7 win-loss record. Plus, Lucas won the NCS D2 singles title, the first for the Piedmont boys in over 50 years,” said coach Jim Landes. Piedmont won the first two matches of the day to take an early 2-0 lead, but SRV roared back to win the next four matches to clinch the match. At No. 1 doubles, Ben Davis and Joey Assalian won 6-3, 6-4. After that, Carter Brookfield and Hunter Fasteau won 7-6 (7-4), 6-4 at No. 2 doubles. “Joey and Ben played really well and won in straight sets. Hunter and Carter won the first set in a tiebreak and then cruised to a victory in the second,” Landes said. After that, Nate Welch lost 6-3, 6-1 at No. 2 singles and Ari Moskovitz fell 6-0, 6-1 at the No. 3 spot. Then, Travers Kemp and Henry van den Bos lost at No. 3 doubles 7-5, 6-4 to give the Wolves a 3-2 advantage. The last two matches on the courts were Emilio Misra at No. 4 singles and Smolko in the top singles match. Smolko won the first set 7-6 (7-4) but lost 6-3 in the second. Misra won the first set 6-4, but wound up losing the final two sets by the same score, 6-4, 6-4. With San Ramon Valley clinching the match day, Smolko and his opponent agreed to end the No. 1 singles match. “It then came down to Emilio at No. 4 singles and Lucas at No. 1. Emilio won the first, lost the second and went up 4-3 in the third. I felt we had a good chance to pull the upset. Just as Lucas was splitting sets with Rishi Palle, an opponent with an even higher UTR rating than Lucas, Emilio went down 6-4 in the third. It was late and the boys were tired, so Lucas and Rishi shook hands in a draw and Ben Davis in a two-set victory at No. 1 doubles over SRV. Carter Brookfield helped win Piedmont’s No. 2 doubles match against San Ramon.

articles.text: Piedmont High announced the school’s second annual Highlander Awards at the Alan Harvey Theater. Piedmont High athletic director Tyler Small hosted the school’s second annual Highlander Awards on Thursday, May 14 at Alan Harvey Theater. The event honored the teams, coaches, and student athletes. The school honored every AllLeague honoree throughout its three seasons and each Player of the Year. Below is a rundown of each of the school’s winners. Award Recipients For Boys’ Athlete of the Year, the school named Dillon Casey of boys’ basketball. The Girls’ Athlete of the Year was awarded to Andrea Martin. The girls’ basketball team was honored as the school’s Female Team of the Year after winning the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division, reaching the North Coast Section Open Division with the No. 3 seed, and making it to the second round of the D1 CIF State postseason as the No. 3 seed. With that, Bryan Gardere was named Piedmont’s Coach of the Year. Two boys’ teams earned Team of the Year honors: boys’ basketball and the track and field team. Boys Basketball finished 19-9 and reached the D2 NCS Quarterfinals with the No. 4 seed. The boys’ track and field team won this year’s WACC title and has six athletes reaching the NCS Meet of Champions. Receiving the Highlander Legacy award was the boys’ swimming team. The boys’ 200 medley relay team and 400 freestyle relay team reached the CIF State finals in their events. Andrea Martin was awarded the school’s Female Athlete of the Year. Boys Track and Field also won Male Team of the Year. Ben Sorensen of baseball won for the boys, while girls’ winner was Sydney Latvala of lacrosse. The Iron Man and Iron Woman awards were given to athletes who competed in multiple sports. The winners included P.J. Brayer and Luke McAuliffe for the boys, and Edie Elmquist and Makenna Small for the girls. Brayer played both lacrosse and basketball, McAuliffe featured on water polo and lacrosse, Elmquist played flag football and softball, while Small played soccer and softball. articles.text: Marin Theatre Company presents the West Coast premiere of Pictures from Home, a stage adaptation of photographer Larry Sultan’s memoir about family and memory, running now through May 31 at Marin Theatre in Mill Valley. Adapted by playwright Sharr White and directed by Jonathan Moscone, the production follows Sultan as he documents and interviews his parents over more than a decade, revisiting family stories and tensions while searching for a deeper understanding of his upbringing. The play is based on Sultan’s landmark photo memoir and premiered on Broadway at Studio 54 starring Nathan Lane, Danny Burstein and Zoë Wanamaker. Bay Area actor Victor Talmadge stars as Irving Sultan alongside Daniel Cantor as Larry Sultan and Susan Koozin as Jean Sultan. Talmadge, making his Marin Theatre debut, has appeared in touring productions of “The King & I” and “The Lion King,” as well as in David Mamet’s “November” on Broadway. Cantor previously appeared at Marin Theatre in “Waste” and performed on Broadway in “Leopoldstadt.” Koozin previously played Jean Sultan in a production at Alley Theatre in Houston. Per for ma nces cont i nue through May 31 at Marin Theatre, 397 Miller Ave. Tickets are available at MarinTheatre.org or by calling 415-388-5208. articles.text: Maren Hassinger Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing, the comprehensive retrospective to date of the artist’s body of work, opens at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) June 6. The exhibition features half a century of work by Hassinger, including large-scale sculpture, site-specific installation, video, and performance, and will display more than twenty of her most notable works from the 1970s to the present. Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing will be accompanied by an extensive exhibition catalogue, featuring new scholarly essays and previously unpublished documentation of her artwork. Notable displayed works include Love (2008), a site-specific sculpture composed of pink plastic bags inflated by human breath and filled with love notes; Beach (1980), a floor installation consisting of plaster and wooden dowels; and multiple sculptures that incorporate recently harvested tree branches which BAMPFA showcases in partnership with the University of California Botanical Garden. “Maren Hassinger’s practice has been of great influence for generations of artists,” Chief Curator Margot Norton said in a press release. “We are thrilled to finally bring her artworks and their stories from across her career together through our exhibition, and to showcase Hassinger’s profound contributions to contemporary art.” “Maren Hassinger’s work invites us to reflect on the beauty and complexity of human connection, through movement, material, and shared experience,” said BAMPFA’s Executive Director, Julie Rodrigues Widholm. “Presenting this landmark retrospective at BAMPFA underscores our commitment to amplifying artists whose practices challenge conventions and inspire collective engagement across generations.” The retrospective will be on display at BAMPFA June 6 through November 29. More information about this and other public programs can be found at bampfa.org.
articles.title: Maren Hassinger Retrospective opens at BAMPFA next month

articles.text: Concert lotteries open now online Stern Grove Festival returns to San Francisco this summer with a mix of internationally recognized performers and local artists. The 2026 season is scheduled to run from June 14 through August 16 at Sigmund Stern Recreation Grove. Headliners include Al Green, Public Enemy, Patti LaBelle, and Major Lazer. Additional performers such as Japanese Breakfast, Violent Femmes, Charley Crockett, Suki Waterhouse, and Bomba Estéreo are also scheduled to perform throughout the season. The season will conclude with the annual Big Picnic Weekend on August 15 and 16. The two-day event will serve as a fundraising finale, featuring performances by Public Enemy on Saturday and Al Green on Sunday, joined by Bay Area artists including Goapele and the GLIDE Ensemble. Founded in 1938, the festival has drawn more than 5 million attendees over its history and was established with the goal of making live music freely available to the public, a mission organizers The 2026 season is scheduled to run from June 14 through August 16. say remains central today. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception, the organization has presented the free concert series “Stern Grove Festival” in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites.The festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts, including opera, theater, and music. Admission to all concerts remains free, though attendees must obtain tickets through an online lottery system in advance. For more information about this year’s lineup and how to access tickets, visit https://www.sterngrove.org/.
articles.title: Stern Grove Festival begins June 14

The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites.The festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts, including opera, theater, and music. Admission to all concerts remains free, though attendees must obtain tickets through an online lottery system in advance. For more information about this year’s lineup and how to access tickets, visit https://www.sterngrove.org/.

articles.text: An exhibition showcasing the artistry of Lawrence Ferlinghetti, one of San Francisco’s most significant cultural figures, is now on view at the Legion of Honor. Ferlinghetti (1919 - 2021) was a poet, activist, publisher, and co-founder of the famous City Lights Bookstore in San Francisco, the epicenter of the Beat generation of writers. The independent bookstore is considered a literary landmark and has been a gathering space for writers since Ferlinghetti founded the store in 1955 with the now-famous Pocket Poets Series. Since then the press has gone on to publish a wide range of titles, including poetry and prose, fiction and nonfiction, international and local authors. Ferlinghetti was also an avid painter, draftsman, and printmaker, and his work across mediums often combines image and text exploring themes of isolation, violence, and human resilience. With artworks drawn entirely from the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco’s works on paper collection, this exhibition showcases Ferlinghetti’s work in printmaking, including etching, lithography, and letterpress. The exhibition is on view now through July 19. For more information, visit https://www. famsf.org/exhibitions/ferlinghetti-san-francisco. Lawrence Ferlinghetti
articles.title: Ferlinghetti exhibition on view at Legion of Honor through July

articles.text: Installation view of Monet and Venice The de Young Museum presents Monet and Venice, the first major international loan exhibition devoted to Claude Monet’s paintings of Venice, on view now through July 26. Co-organized by the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco and the Brooklyn Museum, the exhibition features more than 100 works, including more than 20 of Monet’s 37 Venice canvases, including his iconic Water Lilies. Monet and Venice is the first exhibition dedicated to Monet’s Venetian paintings since their debut in Paris over a century ago. The exhibition centers on Monet’s only visit to Venice, Photo courtesy of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco which took place in 1908 when the artist was 68 years old. According to organizers, the trip marked Monet’s final major international journey and his last sustained focus on architectural subjects. “Although Monet visited Venice only once, his paintings of the city are among his most dazzling,” Thomas P. Campbell, director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, said in a press release. “Unlike bustling scenes painted by other artists, Monet’s Venice is hauntingly deserted, with its architecture, buildings, and canals dissolving in an atmospheric light.” Works by Monet will be lent by institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, along with private collections. The exhibition will also include works by artists associated with Venice, including Canaletto, John Singer Sargent, J. M. W. Turner and James McNeill Whistler. “His Venetian paintings are among the most luminous and poetic of his career,” added Melissa E. Buron, exhibition co-curator and director of collections and chief curator at the Victoria and Albert Museum. “His time in Venice was a critical period of creative renewal that has not previously been explored in-depth before this exhibition.” For more information, visit https://www.famsf.org/.
articles.title: Monet and Venice exhibit now on view at de Young Museum

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco’s newest exhibition, UNBOUND: Art, Blackness, and the Universe, is now on view. UNBOUND is a unique group exhibition that explores connections between Blackness and spiritual cosmologies. Organized by Key Jo Lee, MoAD Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs, the community retrospective highlights the similarities between the Black existence and “cosmic Blackness,” or Afrofuturism. UNBOUND includes paintings, glass sculptures, and installations celebrating the modern artistic genre. The exhibition features artists David Alabo, Renee Cox, Oasa DuVerney, Torkwase Dyson, Allison Janae Hamilton, Barkley L. Hendricks, Cullen B. Washington Jr., M. Carmen Lane and Sidra Bell, Michi Meko, Gustavo Nazareno, Rashaad Newsome, Chris Ofili, Mikael Owunna, Harmonia Rosales, Lorna Simpson, Didier William, and Fred Wilson. “For the past twenty years, MoAD has proudly embarked on a journey to ensure that Black creative expression is embraced, elevated, and seen by international visitors and those that call the Bay Area home,” said Monetta White, Executive Director and CEO. “The artistic depth of UNBOUND will bring intergenerational African Diasporic voices together under an innovative curatorial framework that shifts the focus through which we understand and appreciate contemporary art.” “This exhibition is a celebration of the vast conceptual capacity of Blackness, and treats Black existence with the same imaginative and intellectual openness we apply to thinking through metaphysics and the cosmos,” Lee added. “In doing so, it makes a radical claim that Blackness is not marginal, but central to how we comprehend being, time, and the universe itself.” For more information, visit https://www.moadsf.org. Allison Janae Hamilton is one of over a dozen Black artists featured in MoAD’s UNBOUND.
articles.title: UNBOUND: Art, Blackness and the Universe now on view at MoAD

articles.text: Ellerhein Girls’ Choir from Estonia Estonia’s Ellerhein Girls’ Choir will participate in the 2026 Golden Gate International Choral Festival hosted by Piedmont East Bay. Children’s Choir. The choir is one of Estonia’s most renowned choral ensembles and was founded in 1951 by Professor Heino Kaljuste. Their spotlight performance will take place on July 15 at the First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley (2407 Dana Street, Berkeley), From 1970 to 2012, the choir was led by Tiia-Ester Loitme, who also served as chief conductor of the Ellerhein choir studio from 1989. Since 2012, the choir has been conducted by Ingrid Kõrvits. The artistic team includes vocal coach Egle Veltmann, choir master and solfeggio teacher Ülle Sander, accompanist Kadri Traksmann, and manager Liina Joonas-Teder. The choir brings together girls aged 14 to 19 and performs a diverse repertoire ranging from classical choral works to contemporary music by leading Estonian and international composers. Over the years, Ellerhein has collaborated with distinguished conductors such as Eri Klas, Paavo Järvi, Tõnu Kaljuste, and Olari Elts, as well as with prominent ensembles including the Estonian National Symphony Orchestra, Estonian National Male Choir, Estonian Philharmonic Chamber Choir, and Vox Clamantis. Ellerhein Girls’ Choir has toured extensively, participating in festivals and competitions across Europe, Asia, and North America. The choir has earned numerous international awards, including four Grand Prix awards. Among its recent achievements are the Grand Prix at the Gdańsk International Choir Competition in 2019 and first place at the Lisbon Sings International Choir Competition in 2023. In 2004, they received a Grammy Award for their recording of Sibelius: Cantatas in collaboration with the Estonian National Male Choir and the Estonian National Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Paavo Järvi. Further recognition includes being named Choir of the Year by the Estonian Choral Association in 2007 and Women’s Choir of the Year in 2021. The choir has released several recordings, including Songs of Light (2017), Heavenly Songs (2023), and the CD release (2024) of the children’s opera The Lost Princess. Information about the Golden Gate International Choral Festival is on their website, including which concerts are free for the public. https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ggf-concerts-2026. ®

articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), California’s oldest youth orchestra, will present a Pops Pre-Tour Concert, the final performance of its 2025–2026 subscription season, on Sunday, June 7 at 3:00 p.m. at The Ascension Greek Orthodox Cathedral (4700 Lincoln Avenue, Oakland). The concert will feature a vibrant audience-friendly program ranging from Americana classics to Nordic masterworks, previewing the orchestra’s upcoming international tour repertoire. The program will feature Felicia Ng, one of the winners of YPSO’s Concerto Competition, performing the first movement of Sergei Golovko’s Concerto for Marimba and Orchestra. “I chose this piece because it’s energetic, blends contemporary with classical style, and has great storytelling that is especially compelling to me,” said Ng. In preparation for YPSO’s Summer tour to Finland and Sweden, the program features the final two movements of Sibelius’s Symphony No. 1 — Movement III: Allegro and Movement IV: Finale (Quasi una Fantasia). Additional program highlights include Copland’s energetic “Buckaroo Holiday” from Rodeo and popular favorites such as Leroy Anderson’s Home Stretch and Sousa’s The Stars and Stripes Forever, continuing YPSO’s Pops concert tradition. General Admission is $20; students are free (registration is required). Box Office and Concert Info: ypsomusic.org/events. As both a season finale and a moment of recognition, the concert will honor YPSO’s graduating senior musicians, celebrating their contributions to the orchestra and their next steps as they continue their musical and academic journeys. In conjunction with the concert, YPSO will launch its annual “Spring Into Music!” Silent Auction in support of YPSO programs and student tour opportunities. The auction features experiences, dining, and unique offerings from local businesses and community supporters. Proceeds help sustain YPSO’s concerts, coaching, educational activities, chamber music, and touring opportunities Felicia Ng will perform a solo at the Pops Pre-Tour Concert. for young musicians across the Bay Area. Bidding opens May 21 and closes June 7, tinyurl.com/ ypso-auction-2026. Following the concert, YPSO musicians will embark on a tour to Finland and Sweden, highlighted by three performances: • June 21 — Sibelius Hall, Lahti • June 23 — Helsinki Music Centre, Helsinki, as part of the American Celebration of Music in Finland • June 26 — Royal College of Music Concert Hall, Stockholm Young People’s Symphony Orchestra
articles.title: YPSO concludes season with Pops Concert on June 7

articles.text: The Georgian Choir of E.Mikeladze Central Music School from Tbilisi, Georgia will be participating in this year’s Golden Gate International Choral Festival. The school’s feature performance takes place on July 14, at the Oakland Asian Cultural Center. The Choir of E.Mikeladze Central Music School was founded in 2010 and teaches boys and girls aged 8 through 25. The choir performs Georgian traditional folk songs and chants. The choir’s main goal is to share Georgian culture with different parts of the world. Over the 15 years, several international projects were accomplished, including participation and awards at the Golden Gate International Choral Festival; World Peace Choral Festival, Vienna; Canti Veris Choral Festival, Prague; Tokyo International Choral Festival; and other leading events in Idaho, Rome, Norway, Latvia, Denver, Yekaterinburg, Belarus, the UK, France, and Budapest. The choir’s concert program is very unique. It lasts for 1 hour and involves virtual traveling from the western regions of The Georgian Choir of E. Mikeladze Central Music School Georgia to the east. In their concerts, the choir performs one-totwo songs from each region with appropriate verbal presentation of the meaning, history, and musical and other differences. Therefore, the international audience is always excited and attracted by the performance. Their song-study process is very traditional. Since the choir members perform Georgian through-oral traditions, they never use music sheets during rehearsals. Instead, the choir director uses the traditional oral way of teaching. Despite international challenges and objections, the choir is active in Georgia too. It usually organizes various events and participates in local choral projects. Moreover, the choir supports the cultural exchange in Georgia. They cooperate with different organizations, including the Embassies in Georgia. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival takes place from July 13 to July 18. Information on the concerts and spotlight choirs can be found on their website, including which concerts are free or have paid admission for the public. https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ggf-concerts-2026.
articles.title: Golden Gate Intl. Music Festival includes Choir from Georgia

articles.text: Weekends until May 31; 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Slavic Arts Exhibition The Center for Slavic Arts & Culture presents a vibrant spring exhibition that celebrates creativity and renewal. This unique show brings together 15 talented artists from across Slavic countries, each offering a distinct voice and perspective. Join us for this inspiring celebration of art, culture, and the spirit of spring. The gallery show will be open to the public: every Saturday and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. through May 31 with an artist on-site to explain and discuss with you. Thursday, May 21, 6:00 p.m. GIA Alumni Jewelry Presentation The California/SF Chapter of the Gemological Institute of America Alumni will present a fascinating account by Piedmont resident David Cole about the art of the machine within the realm of jewelry, spanning both historical and modern contexts. His presentation will detail the use of milling machines, lathes, ornamental turning engines, and pantographs, and will highlight examples by Fabergé, Wendy Ramshaw, Friedrich Becker, and Cartier. Cole will also discuss the craftsmanship of watch firms like Breguet. This will be a unique lecture on metalsmithing and jewelry. A Q & A and wine reception will follow the presentation. For more information, tickets and reservations, see https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/1988352672368. Saturday, May 23, 7:00 p.m. George Cole Quartet A San Francisco native and longtime guitarist for the David Grisman Quintet, George Cole recently fought and beat leukemia. Now in remission, he approaches each performance as a gift. This concert is generously sponsored by the Piedmont Post. “This music is a gift and I intend to share it for as long as I can,” said Cole. He has spent his career at the crossroads of American swing and the gypsy jazz tradition of Django Reinhardt, and Eurocana is where those two roads finally meet: music played with gypsy flair: Django died in 1953; his music is heard in concert halls, jazz clubs, and festival stages around the world, and nowhere more joyfully than in the hands of the George Cole Quartet. For six years, Cole taught guitar to two Piedmont kids who would go on to change rock and roll history – Billie Joe Armstrong and Mike Dirnt of Green Day, both Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductees. Advance tickets for this very special Eurocana experience are available now at https:// www.ticketsignup.io/colefour. Sunday, May 24, 7:00 p.m. Vitamin Em: the Band Concert Vitamin Em is a Bay Area collective of genre-defying musicians who blend jazz, fusion, funk, R&B, soul, fiddle traditions, and hints of jazzy classical music. At the heart of Vitamin Em is a deep commitment to improvisation. Featuring Grammy-nominated and award-winning artists, no two concerts are the same. The result is a concert experience that’s both sophisticated and wildly fun: an engaging fusion of sounds, textures, and personalities, delivered with enthusiasm, precision, and blazing, unforgettable improvisation. Advance tickets are strongly recommended and available at https://www.simpletix.com/e/270397. Friday, May 29, 7:00 p.m. Jason B. Sia Piano Solo Concert Acclaimed for his eloquently expressive artistry and seamless technique, concert pianist Jason Sia has captivated audiences across Europe, Latin America, Asia, and throughout the United States. In this special recital Mr. Sia will present an evening of beloved solo piano masterworks with the music of Franz Schubert, Franz Liszt, Johannes Brahms, Claude Debussy, Frédéric Chopin, Maurice Ravel, and Scott Joplin. Advance tickets are strongly recommended and available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/jasonsia. Support the programming of Piedmont Center for the Arts by donating generously to the Tip Jar at these events.
