articles.text: The Shawshank Redemption is an Oscar nominated film (7) that was adapted by director Frank Darabont from the Stephen King novella, Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption. The story can be found in a collection of King’s tales in the book titled Four Seasons. I have always believed that though this prolific and talented writer is most closely identified with stories of the surreal, drawn from that realm that exists beyond the evidence, he is far more. I would suggest that Rita Hayworth and (the) Shawshank Redemption stands apart as an example of King’s gift as a superb, imaginative storyteller and writer. Ditto the novella The Body, also made into a movie and titled Stand By Me. The Shawshank Redemption is set in a grim, rust-streaked, gothic-looking prison. Within its stark walls are housed a collection of the most hardened criminals in the state of Maine; however, if asked, they will smile and claim they are innocent. The year is 1947, and the story begins in the middle of summer night. A young, well-dressed man is sitting in his car sipping bourbon and clumsily slipping bullets into a revolver. Unsteadily, gun in hand, he walks down a path. The scene cuts to a courtroom with the man, Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), seeming cold and detached, is testifying. The next scene reveals Andy on his way to Maine’s Shawshank State Prison to serve two life sentences for killing his wife and her lover. The next scene reveals a prison bus entering the gates of Shawshank where heavily armed guards are waiting, while the inmates gather at the yard wire to watch the “fish” step off the bus and begin what will be a life beyond imagination. It’s at this point that this extraordinary film truly begins with the introduction of Red (Morgan Freeman), a man who is decades into a life sentence. He is known to be able to get contraband for a price. Andy approaches Red in the yard and asks him to get two items: a rock hammer and a poster of Rita Hayworth. I would suggest that you, the reader, watch this film more than once. It is just so good, offering memorable scenes, many standalone, each wonderfully acted and beautifully photographed. But what makes Shawshank beyond remarkable is the use of voice over. And so, between the engaging and at times humorous interactions between those who find refuge in friendship, we hear Red reflecting on his first impression of Andy, beginning with his arrival and eventual violent confrontations with the “Sisters,” inmates who are remorseless rapists. During those first years of Andy’s incarceration, we welcome Red’s soft ref lections and explanations, for his voice embodies a warmth and sincerity that transcends an environMorgan Freeman and Tim Robbins in The Shawshank Redemption Gemological Institute of America David Cole will explore the art of the machine, providing an illustrated overview that delves into the intersection of technology and aesthetic expression. He will explore the role of machine tools within the realm of jewelry spanning both historical and modern contexts to show how mechanical precision has evolved. His presentation will detail the use of milling machines, lathes, ornamental turning engines, and pantographs. He will examine significant works produced through these mechanical means, highlighting notable examples by Faberge, Wendy Ramshaw, Friedrich Becker and Cartier. This will be a unique lecture on metalsmithing and jewelry. Following the lecture, we will open it up for a Q & A. articles.text: Morgan Freeman and Jessica Tandy in Driving Miss Daisy Driving Miss Daisy, adapted from the play by Alfred Uhry, was nominated for nine Oscars and won four at the 62nd Academy Awards (1990) including the coveted Best Picture award. Perhaps it’s a stretch to say that this film is a love story; however, it is clearly a character study of two elderly people: a Jewish woman, Daisy Wertham (Jessica Tandy), 73, who lives alone in a large two-story home in Atlanta, Georgia, and has refused, adamantly, to relinquish her independence. The year is 1948. The narrative opens with Daisy sitting behind the wheel of her Packard sedan, planning to do some shopping. Intending to go forward, she puts the car in reverse and backs into a stand of trees and down a sloping bank, leaving her confused but not injured. Her son, Boolie (Dan Akroyd), after talking to the insurance company, tries to convince his mother of two facts: at her age, she is unlikely to get insurance; and without insurance, in order to to run errands or meet friends, she will need someone to drive her. Daisy is, of course, resistant, cranky, and difficult. Avoiding further discussion, Boolie hires recently retired Hoke Colburn (Morgan Freeman), a Black man, smart, easy-going, and available. And so begins a bumpy period of the two getting acquainted, Hoke ever-patient, and Daisy putting up a wall and maintaining a furrowed brow, refusing to acknowledge she needs a chauffer-driver. articles.text: A scene from Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse It’s often assumed that sequels, when compared to the original movie, will disappoint. It’s no small thing to create the magic displayed in the first release. But that’s definitely not the case with the animated Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, which was followed by the award-winning Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Actually, it could be argued that not only have the filmmakers found the energy of the first, but this latest incarnation is, in all respects, fresh, remarkable, and, well, seriously cool. Kids will be captivated by Across, and certainly not disappointed. In fact, the filmmakers are planning to follow Across with a third Spider-Verse thus completing what is proving, to be an extraordinary trilogy. Of course what carries both films are the familiar themes of tween/teen identity and friendship, the plot carried along at a frenetic pace by a deep bench of new characters. Of course, Spider-Man , aka Miles Morales (Shameik Moore) and Gwen Stacy aka Spider-Gwen (Hailee Seinfeld) are back for another adventure wherein they are catapulted across the universe, passing through countless portals, encountering a cohort of interesting and funny Spider-People. An example would be Spidey-Pavitr, from India (Karen Soni). There’s also an unexpected Spider Society, comprised of Spider-Men/Women, and other thing. Even a feline pet. But not to forget that back on Mile’s home turf, Brooklyn, he and Gwen confront the villainous Spot (Jason Schwartzman), a mad scientist who blows stuff up. Across the Spider-Verse offers a varied and compelling plot, powered by stunning animation, and great writing. It will enthrall its target audience, younger viewers, leaving them impatiently waiting for the next installment. Just a suggestion: If your young fan missed the first feature, start there. It’s outstanding and a solid introduction. Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse. Directed by Joaquin Dos Santos et al. Voiced by Shameik Moore, Hailee Seinfeld, Oscar Isaac. Released 2019. 1hr 57min. In fact, the filmmakers are planning to follow Across with a third Spider-Verse thus completing what is proving, to be an extraordinary trilogy. Of course what carries both films are the familiar themes of tween/teen identity and friendship, the plot carried along at a frenetic pace by a deep bench of new characters. Of course, Spider-Man , aka Miles Morales (Shameik Moore) and Gwen Stacy aka Spider-Gwen (Hailee Seinfeld) are back for another adventure wherein they are catapulted across the universe, passing through countless portals, encountering a cohort of interesting and funny Spider-People. An example would be Spidey-Pavitr, from India (Karen Soni). There’s also an unexpected Spider Society, comprised of Spider-Men/Women, and other thing. Even a feline pet. But not to forget that back on Mile’s home turf, Brooklyn, he and Gwen confront the villainous Spot (Jason Schwartzman), a mad scientist who blows stuff up. Across the Spider-Verse offers a varied and compelling plot, powered by stunning animation, and great writing. It will enthrall its target audience, younger viewers, leaving them impatiently waiting for the next installment. Just a suggestion: If your young fan missed the first feature, start there. It’s outstanding and a solid introduction. Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse. Directed by Joaquin Dos Santos et al. Voiced by Shameik Moore, Hailee Seinfeld, Oscar Isaac. Released 2019. 1hr 57min. articles.text: Piedmont’s Jenny Feinberg acquires Broadway Terrace Nursery In February, Piedmont resident Jenny Feinberg acquired Broadway Terrace Nursery at Broadway Terrace and Clarewood Drive. Feinberg’s love for plants and the environment drew her to the nursery, which has served the community since 1986, offering a wide selection of outdoor plants, house plants, and custom plant designs. Feinberg originally fell in love with gardening in her early 20s because of her grandparents’ green beans. “They grew a particular type of green bean, which is my favorite green bean in the world,” Feinberg continued. “One day, my grandma said ‘I’m going to stop growing them. In my grad school apartment, I started figuring out how to grow vegetables and got more into it.” After achieving her goals as the vice president of Bayer, working on environmental data and green carbon solutions, Feinberg looked toward the next challenge that would keep her engaged. It turned out to be plant nurseries. She found that Yarrow Nursery, a local plant seller in Montclair, was for sale. The owners of this location were the same people who owned Broadway Terrace Nursery, which was originally not for sale, but Feinberg saw an opportunity to reunite with the place where she grew up. “I kind of grew up going to that particular little nursery, so when they put Yarrow up for sale I thought I actually really want both. I want the nursery I know personally, and I have always gone to,” she said. After acquiring both nurseries, it was the first time Feinberg had become a small business owner. She’s enjoyed interacting with the community. Customers Broadway Terrace Nursery’s selection of plants A car crashed into Broadway Terrace Nursery in its opening week.

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, May 20, 2026 Features BUSINESS SPOTLIGHT Piedmont’s Jenny Feinberg acquires Broadway Terrace Nursery By Jake Lannon In February, Piedmont resident Jenny Feinberg acquired Broadway Terrace Nursery at Broadway Terrace and Clarewood Drive. Feinberg’s love for plants and the environment drew her to the nursery, which has served the community since 1986, offering a wide selection of outdoor plants, house plants, and custom plant designs. Feinberg originally fell in love with gardening in her early 20s because of her grandparents’ green beans. “They grew a particular type of green bean, which is my favorite green bean in the world,” Feinberg continued. “One day, my grandma said ‘I’m going to stop growing them. In my grad school apartment, I started figuring out how to grow vegetables and got more into it.” After achieving her goals as the vice president of Bayer, working on environmental data and green carbon solutions, Feinberg looked toward the next challenge that would keep her engaged. It turned out to be plant nurseries. She found that Yarrow Nursery, a local plant seller in Montclair, was for sale. The owners of this location were the same people who owned Broadway Terrace Nursery, which was originally not for sale, but Feinberg saw an opportunity to reunite with the place where she grew up. “I kind of grew up going to that particular little nursery, so when they put Yarrow up for sale I thought I actually really want both. I want the nursery I know personally, and I have always gone to,” she said. After acquiring both nurseries, it was the first time Feinberg had become a small business owner. She’s enjoyed interacting with the community. Customers Broadway Terrace Nursery’s selection of plants Jenny Feinberg in front of Broadway Terrace Nursery come in and talk to her about their gardens and what’s going on in their lives. “One of the things I really love, particularly at Broadway Terrace Nursery, it’s a lot of people’s special outing for the week,” Feinberg continued. “They look around and spend time in the nursery, and then they buy one small plant, and you just know they’ve had a great day. I’ve never had that experience in business. Because my business roles were always so remote from the customer. To have that sort of positive one-on-one experience is really fun.” But things weren’t all smooth going for her. In the opening week of the Broadway Terrace Nursery, a vehicle crashed into the storefront, running through two walls and destroying a majority of the indoor plants. What started as a celebration turned into a rebuild. “It was supposed to be this big celebration. We bought the nurseries but had to cancel our party and spent the time shoveling broken glass out of the indoor nursery,” said Feinberg They spent the next month rebuilding the indoor space and dealing with the challenges that come with an unexpected disaster. “It’s been a challenge to figure out what and how to rebuild, and how to file the insurance claims. We’re still figuring out the details but the store is rebuilt and open again to the public,” said Feinberg. Feinberg has looked toward the future with her businesses, hoping to create a place of community. At both nursery locations, she plans to launch a garden club and host classes and events for community members. Classes are expected to begin in June, with experts coming in to teach pollinator-safe gardening. Both Yarrow and Broadway Terrace nurseries source their plants from local vendors who provide native plants. “One of the big things to sort of differentiate us from the Home Depots of the world is that I’m only bringing in plants that are going to do well in Oakland, and specifically in the Oakland Hills,” said Feinberg. Broadway Terrace Nursery is located at 4340 Clarewood Drive in Oakland. Yarrow Nursery is located at 6250 Thornhill Drive in Montclair. Both locations are open from 10 a.m. - 5:30 p.m. every day. To learn more about the nurseries, readers can visit the website https://www.broadwayterracenursery.com/. A car crashed into Broadway Terrace Nursery in its opening week. articles.text: Fifty-four walkers and five K-9 best friends gathered at the Exedra on a lovely morning last week for a destination the group hadn’t visited in years. Zillow had listed a Piedmont home at 23 Valant Place for sale. The street name didn’t ring an immediate bell, but then it came back — the group had walked to Valant, a cul-desac off Trestle Glen Road, some years ago and never returned. Walker and real estate broker Stacey Isaacs agreed to meet the group there for a tour. Getting to Valant is not a short trip. The walkers went up Highland, Sheridan, and Wildwood Avenues, through the Hall Fenway to Crocker, up LaSalle to Indian Road — which crosses into Oakland and becomes Sunnyhills — then down the steep Bowles Place to a long set of wooden steps that drop down to Trestle Glen Road. Up that handsome street, lined with homes in a variety of architectural styles, is Valant Place. Along the way, the group talked about why 23 Valant Place has a Piedmont address at all. It is one of only two Piedmont homes on the street. The rest are in Oakland. The explanation starts in 1892, when the Piedmont Springs Hotel — a three-story white landmark and the city’s biggest tourist attraction — caught fire. Piedmont had no fire department, so Oakland’s was called. Oakland’s horses dragged a water tanker up Oakland Avenue for two hours. By the time the wagons arrived, there was nothing left to save. That fire is a big part of why Piedmont exists. In the late 1800s, Oakland launched what it called the “Greater Oakland Movement,” annexing neighboring towns and setting its sights on Piedmont. A vote on annexation was set for January 1907, but a paperwork error pushed it to March. During that window, a group of Piedmont residents filed to incorporate first. They liked Piedmont rural and undeveloped, and the burning hotel had made the case for a local fire department hard to argue with. Rallying support wasn’t easy. Historian Ann Swift has described the effort: “Hugh Craig and James Ballentine were having meetings every other night, practically trying to rally the troops.” The opposition pointed out that Piedmont had no experience with taxes, city services, or paved streets. “There was a sizable part of the city who thought there was no need to go through all that.” The incorporation vote passed. ation vote went forward in March and passed 63 to 43. Yet Piedmont was now its own city, so the vote was meaningless. Opponents tried again that September with a disincorporation election to merge with Oakland after all. That vote failed on a technicality: 92 in favor, 62 opposed, but a two-thirds majority, 102 votes, was required. Piedmont survived by 10 votes. In the rush of 1907, the new city drew its borders using the Piedmont Sanitary District’s sewer map, the most complete survey available. Sewer lines follow topography rather than streets, so the boundary zigged and zagged through neighborhoods in ways that still don’t make much geographic sense. On Valant Place, the city limit wraps around the end of the cul-de-sac to pull in numbers 22 and 23 while leaving the rest of the street in Oakland. Stacey was waiting for the group at the end of the cul-de-sac. She gave the walkers an update on the local market. While some Oakland neighborhoods have seen prices soften, Piedmont is going the other direction. The first home on Valant was built in 1932 with others following in the 1960s. Number 23, the newest, was built in 1993. Stacey called it the best current value in Piedmont. The empty lot at 22 Valant is listed separately, with a description that notes the steep hillside makes it “not for the faint of heart.” The trip back took a different set of hidden stairs up from Trestle Glen to the St. James Place Among those participating were Jack Fischrup and K-9 best friend Kojak, Mike Gallant, Dan Scdonis, Marcia Arthurs, Stella Houston, Mary Carter, Audrey Sung, Noemi Alvarado, Brian Hamlin, Sherry Jacobs, Sanghi Waner, Chuck Oraftik, Joan Jung, Caskey Weston, Bill Ahern, Joyce Ahern, Lori Austin, Joyce Hicks with K-9 best friend Mocha, Ken Hubbert, Eric Behrens, Stacey Issacs, Diane Jimenez, Jim Kellogg, Siow Fang Tan, Kat Lang, Lisa Euphrat, Jim Kuo, Alissa Quan, Mark Davis, Stacey Morgan, Liz Dalrymple, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Brenda Ferrero, Fleurise Montecillo, Debbie Powell, Helen Dong, Ken Moy, Quincy Dong, Claudine Bach, Dave DeRoche, Joyce Ahern, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Denny McGee, Phil Chin with K-9 best friend Rocky, Julia Chin, Bonnie Sherwood with K-9 best friend Zippy, Jasmine Cai, Irene Thompson, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Nancy Henn, Judy Sokoloff, and Dick Carter.

articles.text: LaForte & Charlotte Zhang On a cold Oregon Tuesday morning, four member of the Piedmont Community Service Crew – a youth organization affiliated with the Piedmont Scout Council – woke up to find a frog in their tent. We eventually got Neville, the frog, out of the tent, but little did we know, he would stow away into one of our bags and ride six hours home to Piedmont with us. This doesn’t include a quick pit stop at the bowling alley, nor does it include the lunch break at the trusty Subway across the street. A fellow PHS student would soon find a little creature in her backpack once she got home. You’re probably wondering, “How did this all begin?” Well, here’s how it started. In early April a group of nine PCSC members headed to Oregon to volunteer for a nonprofit education program called The Crest, based at Willow-Witt Ranch near Ashland. The crew stayed at the ranch for six nights and slept in tents Every day the crew would work from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. with an hour break at noon, doing a variety of work with the help of David Nilson, a former PCSC parent who moved to Oregon after retiring. David mentored us on how to do tasks such as sawing lumber, nailing sheets of metal, and measuring posts and beams that allowed us to create a wooden shed to protect firewood from the unpredictable Oregon weather. The crew members saw sun, rain, hail, and the most gorgeous and magnificent double rainbow all in one day. The weather changed faster than California weather. Besides construction work, the crew engaged in multiple fun activities like throwing disks on the nearby disk golf course, playing ping pong on two picnic tables shoved together, exploring the forests to visit waterfalls, getting to know the nearby farm animals, including Millie the Goat, and going to see Come From Away at the Oregon Shakespeare Festival, a moving play about a close-knit community that came together to support passengers rerouted to the small Canadian town of Gander during 9/11. Being in Oregon also allowed crew members to submerge themselves in nature, and wake up to the fresh air and beautiful landscape. “The feeling of kindness through assisting the Willow-Witt ranch was unforgettable,” said Luca LaForte. Every night crew member duos cooked dinner such as fried rice, lasagna, and hamburgers, which taught them how to work together and cook for a group of people. Overall, the crew learned essential building skills while also making remarkable memories along the way. One evening, over a homemade bowl of amazing fettuccine, brownies, and ice cream, crew members Amalia Angulo Sardi, Luca LaForte, and Charlotte Zhang interviewed Willow Witt Ranch owner and organization founder, Suzanne Willow and staff members Liz Bianco and Madi Ross of The Crest. Suzanne told the story of the ranch’s founding and their future missions and goals. The Crest, also founded by Suzanne and her late wife, Lanita Witt, is an education program for children who have a sense of curiosity, confidence, resilience, and a desire to explore the natural world. Willow-Witt Ranch helps youth participants to connect with nature and to learn how to become considerate and compassionate human beings. “You’re learning really great skills, and you’re also just learnPCSC crew members on Day 2 when the frames have been erected and rafters lifted into place:(L-R, frontback) Yiyou Fang, Toby Tsai, Luca LaForte, Noah Baldwin, Joshua Bell; Amalia Angulo Sardi, Yoko Ichikawa, Emi Donatiello, Amelie Wang, Charlotte Zhang, Dan LaForte, Jennifer Newell, Michelle Peng and (back row) Ken Li and David Nilson. ing how to be good humans by helping. And I really feel like humans are not separate from nature,” said Suzanne Willow. Piedmont Community Service Crew is a youth-led organization that empowers members to find passion and collect knowledge through service in the community. The Crew organizes volunteer events such as working at the Richmond Tiny House Village to build shelter for homeless youth and cooking for seniors at St. Mary’s Center, along with trips to assist nonprofit organizations. If you are interested in these experiences or would like to know more about PCSC, go to https://www.pcservicecrew. org/ or contact crew advisor and founder Ken Li at Ken.i.Li@sbcglobal.net Amelie Wang (left) and Charlotte Zhang learned to read construction drawings and were in charge of cutting the nine rafter timbers and cross beams to the correct length. Dan LaForte (right) cuts the first prototype siding boards. Charlotte Zhang (left), Amalia Angulo Sardi and Amelie Wang prepare corner joints between posts and beam on the front frame.

Suzanne told the story of the ranch’s founding and their future missions and goals. The Crest, also founded by Suzanne and her late wife, Lanita Witt, is an education program for children who have a sense of curiosity, confidence, resilience, and a desire to explore the natural world. Willow-Witt Ranch helps youth participants to connect with nature and to learn how to become considerate and compassionate human beings. “You’re learning really great skills, and you’re also just learnPCSC crew members on Day 2 when the frames have been erected and rafters lifted into place:(L-R, frontback) Yiyou Fang, Toby Tsai, Luca LaForte, Noah Baldwin, Joshua Bell; Amalia Angulo Sardi, Yoko Ichikawa, Emi Donatiello, Amelie Wang, Charlotte Zhang, Dan LaForte, Jennifer Newell, Michelle Peng and (back row) Ken Li and David Nilson. ing how to be good humans by helping. And I really feel like humans are not separate from nature,” said Suzanne Willow. Piedmont Community Service Crew is a youth-led organization that empowers members to find passion and collect knowledge through service in the community. The Crew organizes volunteer events such as working at the Richmond Tiny House Village to build shelter for homeless youth and cooking for seniors at St. Mary’s Center, along with trips to assist nonprofit organizations. For homeowners weighing their vote—and buyers crunching the numbers on carrying costs— it’s time to peel back the curtain on how this differs from the Measure G we already know. While the framework feels familiar, two specific tweaks in the fine print deserve a closer look. The annual growth cap. Measure G kept the tax rate hike on a leash of 2 percent per year. Measure H bumps that ceiling to 3 percent. It might not sound like much on day one, but thanks to compounding, those extra points can lead to larger bills down the road. The sunset clause. Measure G comes with an expiration date, forcing the school district to come back and ask for permission every few years. Measure H, however, is a forever tax; it has no sunset clause and stays on the books until voters actively move to repeal it. In the News: Pool Parking Pushback From very smart young journalists at The Highlander comes a well put together parking pushback. When will municipal government learn that revolutions are built on inconvenienced citizens? Piedmont’s pool parking, which is near Piedmont’s schools, is already drawing pushback from students, and the complaints are not hard to understand. The city converted 30 spaces to two-hour parking and stepped-up enforcement, which means fewer longterm spots for PHS, MHS, and PMS students and staff. The Highlander editorial argues the result will be more tardies, more tickets, and more frustration for teachers who already deal with limited parking. Students say many only learned about the changes after getting ticketed, and a student petition to reverse the decision quickly gathered hundreds of signatures. Along with a stroll through the gardens, the seniors also had the opportunity to visit the House, a stunning Georgian Revival estate built in 1917 that reflects a bygone era of luxury living, now functioning as a historic landmark. Shopping and dining are also a must when visiting Filoli, so the seniors made a day of their excursion by visiting its adorable Clock Tower gift shop, a destination for carefully curated gifts. This boutique shopping experience features Filoli grown products that can’t be found anywhere else. The stroll through the gardens, the mansion, and the gift shop, was followed by the Seniors having a delicious, fresh lunch at Filoli’s Quail Café. pages.text: 26 26 Wednesday, May 20, 2026 Seniors By Janet Epstein It was a sunny May day full of bloom when the Piedmont Seniors ventured down the Peninsula to Woodside to explore the historic Filoli Gardens. The roses had begun to unfurl and the Garden was rich in spring color. The seniors took advantage of this delightful, sunny day to enjoy the beauty of the season by roaming the magnificent 16-acre English-Renaissance style formal gardens, including its lush flowerbeds, yew-lined avenues and structured “garden rooms”. The Filoli estate boasts 654 acres of beauty nestled along the slopes of California’s coastal range. The Seniors were given a brief docent lecture regarding the history of Filoli. Originally built as a private residence in 1917, Filoli added a Pool Pavilion in 1946 for owner Bill Roth’s exercise and rehabilitation after he suffered a stroke. Today, this stunning pool is a true highlight that visitors can see when they visit the property. Filoli was opened to the public in 1975 as a nonprofit organization and site of the National Trust for Historic Preservation. The property is considered one of the finest remaining country estates of the 20th century, featuring a 54,000+ square-foot Georgian revival-style mansion, 16 acres of exquisite English Renaissance gardens, a 6.8-acre Gentleman’s Orchard, and hundreds of acres of Natural Lands with six distinct ecosystems and nature trails. articles.text: Encore performing arts summer camp for adults At a time when the world can feel full of stress and uncertainty, Stagebridge offers a much-needed burst of joy. Whether participants come for clowning, storytelling, singing around the piano, or the simple pleasure of trying something new, they will find a place alive with laughter, creativity, and connection. This July, Stagebridge will host Encore Performing Arts Summer Camp for adults, a weeklong immersion in improv, clowning, storytelling, singing, tap dancing, and more. Students spend the week learning, playing, and creating across disciplines, making Summer Camp one of Stagebridge’s most community-building events of the year. This year’s offerings include returning favorites in acting, singing, and clowning, along with new options such as drumming and Storytelling as Resistance. Participants choose one morning session and one afternoon session for the week, which culminates in a community showcase for family and friends. A sense of belonging is woven through the Stagebridge experience. Students come to learn a craft, but often leave with something deeper: a strong sense of belonging. “The stories we tell make me feel closer to my community,” said Jason Donchin, a student in Stagebridge’s storytelling program. Breakfast and lunch are included each day, giving participants time to socialize between classes in the light- and plantfilled halls of Stagebridge’s beautiful 100-year-old home. Located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland, inside the First Congregational Church of Oakland, Stagebridge is just across from Lake Merritt’s Whole Foods and a short walk from the 19th Street BART station and just steps from the bus line 33. Stagebridge is dedicated to lifelong learners ages 50 and up, with classes and events that celebrate the voices, perspectives, and experiences of older adults. Whether someone is stepping into the spotlight for the first time or returning to a long-loved creative practice, Stagebridge provides a welcoming place to grow, explore, and rediscover the joy of expression. Camp begins July 13, and class size is limited. Learn more and register at www.stagebridge. org/summer-camp-2026. Folks practice in Kim’s musical theater

articles.text: There’s a quiet truth about aging that we don’t talk about enough: more people are doing it alone than ever before. In fact, nearly 27% of Americans over 60 now live independently. But let’s reframe that right away. Solo doesn’t mean alone. Independent doesn’t mean isolated. Planning ahead isn’t about preparing for the worst. It’s about creating freedom and peace of mind so you can live fully today, travel when you want, enjoy your daily routines, and embrace life without the constant “what if” lingering in the background. If you’re navigating this chapter without nearby family, this guide is for you. These are the essential pillars I share with clients and friends to turn uncertainty into confidence. Health and Medical Directives Start with the documents that speak for you when you can’t. An Advance Health Care Directive outlines your wishes, while a Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care names someone to make decisions on your behalf. Add a HIPAA Authorization so trusted individuals can access your medical information. Your healthcare proxy doesn’t need to be family. A close friend, neighbor, or professional fiduciary can step into this role with care and clarity. Keep copies accessible, at home, with your doctor, and with your attorney. Finances Made Simple Think in four words: Automate, Authorize, Organize, Outsource. Automate bills and deposits. Authorize a trusted person as financial power of attorney. Organize your accounts in one place, whether digital or physical. And outsource when needed, a daily money manager or advisor can keep everything running smoothly. This isn’t about giving up control, it’s about protecting your independence. Daily Living and Support Technology has made independent living easier than ever. Grocery delivery, ride services, and meal programs simplify everyday tasks. Concierge services and local senior centers add both convenience and connection. Equally important is building your go-to list: a handyman, gardener, or housekeeper you trust. Having reliable support in place turns small challenges into manageable moments. Legal and Estate Planning Every solo senior should have five key documents: a Living Trust, Will, Letter of Instruction, updated beneficiary designations, and a pet care plan if needed. If family isn’t available to serve as executor or trustee, professionals can step in. This is not a compromise, it’s often a smarter, more neutral solution. Housing and Aging in Place Make your home work for you. Small upgrades, grab bars, better lighting, non-slip surfaces, can extend your independence significantly. Equally important is having a Plan B. Explore future housing options before you need them. When decisions are made from a place of strength, they feel empowering, not overwhelming.* (See my offer below.) Your Chosen Family This may be the most important pillar of all. Identify three people: one for medical decisions, one for financial matters, and one as an emergency contact. These roles can overlap, but clarity is everything. Then expand your circle. Friends, neighbors, community groups, these connections create both safety and joy. A simple daily check-in system can make all the difference. The One Thing That Matters Most If you do nothing else, create an “If Something Happens” folder. Include key contacts, insurance information, account locations, medical details, and your personal wishes. Share its

Housing and Aging in Place Make your home work for you. Small upgrades, grab bars, better lighting, non-slip surfaces, can extend your independence significantly. Equally important is having a Plan B. Explore future housing options before you need them. When decisions are made from a place of strength, they feel empowering, not overwhelming.* (See my offer below.) Your Chosen Family This may be the most important pillar of all. Identify three people: one for medical decisions, one for financial matters, and one as an emergency contact. These roles can overlap, but clarity is everything. Then expand your circle. Friends, neighbors, community groups, these connections create both safety and joy. A simple daily check-in system can make all the difference. The One Thing That Matters Most If you do nothing else, create an “If Something Happens” folder. Include key contacts, insurance information, account locations, medical details, and your personal wishes. Reader Question This week’s reader question is about disclosure, and I think this Huxley quote is applicable: “The facts are the facts, and they do not cease to exist because they are ignored.” – Aldous Huxley Question: I had a mold issue that was caused by water intrusion between the stucco and exterior siding that we didn’t know about until it had spread behind the sheetrock in our basement. The issue has been addressed — do I need to disclose it and how should I do it? Answer: Yes — if you know there was mold, water intrusion, or remediation, disclose it; you do not need to explain it away or justify it. In California, known material defects belong on the Transfer Disclosure Statement, and the safest approach is to state the facts plainly and let the buyer do their own due diligence. That is the whole point of disclosure: not to defend the condition, but to make sure the buyer is informed. Once the fact is known, the cleanest path is to write it down, be factual, and let the buyer decide what it means to them. If the issue has been remediated America is a Broker Associate and Realtor® at The Grubb Company (fixed), disclose that as well. Reader Question This week’s reader question is about disclosure, and I think this Huxley quote is applicable: “The facts are the facts, and they do not cease to exist because they are ignored.” – Aldous Huxley Question: I had a mold issue that was caused by water intrusion between the stucco and exterior siding that we didn’t know about until it had spread behind the sheetrock in our basement. The issue has been addressed — do I need to disclose it and how should I do it? Answer: Yes — if you know there was mold, water intrusion, or remediation, disclose it; you do not need to explain it away or justify it. In California, known material defects belong on the Transfer Disclosure Statement, and the safest approach is to state the facts plainly and let the buyer do their own due diligence. That is the whole point of disclosure: not to defend the condition, but to make sure the buyer is informed. Once the fact is known, the cleanest path is to write it down, be factual, and let the buyer decide what it means to them. articles.text: After considering the needs of our church and community in 2026 after five years of reorganization, new leadership, new directions, and tremendous growth, a Vision 2030 Team was formed to develop a new vision statement for our church. The statement paints a picture of what kind of church we hope to be in 2030. This is a living document and will likely change as new needs and opportunities arise. Our Vision Is To Become A Church For… Inspiring Worship Encountering God through vibrant, preaching and uplifting music, inspiring people to worship God not just on Sundays but also in their daily lives. Authentic Community Experiencing authentic community, a place to belong and grow, where deep relationships are built, faith is shared, and people of all backgrounds are welcomed, valued and supported. Compassionate Care Walking together through every season of life with love and support; offering hope, encouragement, and practical help to those facing challenges, joys, and everything in between. The Next Generation Placing high value on the growth and nurture of children and teenagers, equipping them to face today’s unique challenges with a solid faith, strength, hope and empathy. Meaningful Service Loving those in need by serving with mercy, advocating for justice and partnering with them in humility. Spiritual Growth Offering multiple opportunities for spiritual growth and transformation, meeting people wherever they may be on their spiritual journey. Empowering Leadership Developing a church culture in which volunteers have identified their giftedness and are then equipped, supported, motivated and mentored by pastors and staff in their ministry role. articles.text: Piedmont residents preparing to vote in the June 2026 primary election will decide who advances in the race to replace Gavin Newsom as governor, as well as a long list of local candidates and ballot measures. Prominent figures among the Democrats include Xavier Becerra and Tom Steyer. On the Republican side, political commentator Steve Hilton has gained visibility, especially after receiving Donald Trump’s endorsement. Under California’s electoral system, the two candidates with the most votes, regardless of party, will advance to the General Election in November. At the state level, voters will elect candidates for offices such as lieutenant governor, attorney general, treasurer, superintendent of public education, and insurance commissioner, among many others. More than half of these positions do not have an incumbent running for reelection. The position of insurance commissioner has taken center stage amid rising prices and the loss of coverage following recent wildfires in the state. At the local level, residents will vote for the U.S. Representative for District 12, State Assembly for District 14, and Alameda County District Attorney, among many others. Most of these positions have an incumbent running for re-election. Voters will decide on Measures H and A. articles.text: During the May 6 school board meeting, an empassioned discussion took place about a policy dictating the possession and use of mobile devices by students while at school. The board presented five options and has signaled that they will pursue a more restrictive policy for next year with a bell-to-bell no phones rule for all students in grades 6-12. This year, at Piedmont High, students have been allowed to have their phones at school and can use them at lunch. To enforce this, most teachers went with a “phone hotel” storage area, in which every student puts their phone into a container on the wall at the start of the period and retrieves it at the end of the period, 14 times a day. Teachers and administrators have taken the burden of policing this policy. Students caught with a phone have had them confiscated for the rest of the day. “How we’re implementing this is, by design, making students touch their phones and deal with their phones, 14 times a day. So by design, our school is literally built around phones right now at the high school level,” said board member Susy Struble. articles.text: Following the retirement last week of Planning Director Kevin Jackson, Piedmont City Council appointed Jeff Bond as the interim Planning Director. Bond will oversee the Planning Department’s ongoing projects until a permanent replacement is found. The city is working with Bob Murray & Associates to search for qualified candidates to fill the position. Bond is a professional with more than 30 years of experience. In July of 2025, he retired from the City of Albany, where he served for 20 years, the last 14 as Director of Community Development. He has a master’s degree in economics and is certified as a Chief Building Official, Residential Building Inspector, and American Institute Certified Planner. Before joining the City of Albany, Bond was a staff member at UC Berkeley involved in Interim Planning Director Jeff Bond campus planning, student housing development, and real estate initiatives. He also worked for the City of Alameda for several years as development manager, responsible for redevelopment projects, including the reuse of US Navy property. Early in his career, he worked for several land consulting firms, an economic development non-profit organization, and as a staff person in the California State Legislature. Bond has been with a variety of professional organizations, most recently as a board member of the APA California Northern Section and the Northern California Chapter of the Earthquake Engineering Research Institute. He was involved in curating the Urban Land Institute’s Urban Plan curriculum for high school students. “It is an honor to be considered for this appointment. You have a lovely community. I look forward to the chance to work with your wonderful staff and keep the momentum going,” said Bond at the council meeting on May 4. The application deadline for the position is May 24. For information about the job see https:// w w w.bobmu r rayassoc.com / search-summary?broc_id=7255.

Jim Hopkins “The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his servants what must soon take place, and he made it know by sending his angel to his servant John who testified…” (The Revelation to John 1:1–2a) In the introduction to The Revelation to John in Westminster Study Bible, New Revised Standard Version Updated Edition, Lynn R. Huber writes, “Revelation opens with the Greek word apokalypsis, which in English is translated as “apocalypse” or “revelation.” Despite its modern association with cataclysmic disaster, “apocalypse” refers to lifting a veil or making something visible. Popular misconceptions may accuse the book of being confusing or even contradictory, but Revelation is about making things knowable.” John, whomever he was, wrote to the followers of Jesus in Asia Minor towards the end of the first century C.E. in the belief that they were teachable, that in response to the instructions and visions he would share with them, they could learn, grow, change, adapt, hold on and take heart. He did not write to produce a remarkable piece of literature. He wrote to help some people he knew and loved in the belief that they would take what he wrote to heart, in the confidence that they were teachable. Although Anna Reeves Jarvis is known as the official creator of Mother’s Day, first celebrating it in memory of her mother at Andrews Methodist Episcopal Church in West Virginia in 1908, Julia Ward Howe, author of the Battle Hymn of the Republic, advocated for a Mother’s Peace Day decades before. For her the carnage and devastation of the Civil War and the Franco-Prussian Wars had been a revelation, an apocalypse, revealing that the costs of war most far almost always outweighed any supposed benefit and that the mothers of the world must come together to call for their cessation. articles.text: On Monday, May 4, Piedmont’s City Council approved a $142,236 contract for the Bonita Avenue parking and striping. It is anticipated that the work will begin in June after the last day of school. The contract documents allow for 20 working days to complete the work. The project should be completed before the first day of school on August 7. This project completes the remaining portion of the Civic Center restriping effort on Bonita Avenue from Oakland Avenue to Vista Avenue. The majority of restriping in the Civic Center area was completed as part of the 2025 Pavement Project. This segment was excluded at that time due to installation timing conflicts with the schedule for Havens Elementary School. The project includes converting Bonita Avenue to a one-way street with northbound vehicular traffic only, installing angled parking stalls along the easterly side of the roadway adjacent to Havens School, and adding two on-street angled accessible parking stalls. The city awarded the contract to D’s General Engineering of Oakland. The total budget for the project is $156,460, with funding coming from Measure BB (Local Streets and Roads), Vehicle Registration Fee (VRF), and California Senate Bill 1 (SB-1). pages.text: Wednesday, May 13, 2026 3 LETTERS - MAIN The value of investing in Piedmont schools Editor: One reason it’s imperative to renew Measure H is the importance of investing in our schools, especially to allow them to be community spaces. Measure H provides around 20% of our school district’s annual budget, roughly $12 million. When we invest in our community schools, we invest in everyone’s road to success. According to the California Youth & Families Speak initiative – a statewide alliance of community organizing and advocacy groups advancing a shared vision of racially just, relationship-centered community schools – true community schools have seen student test scores improve by what would be the equivalent of having 151 more days of learning per school year. When we invest in our schools and allow them to become true community spaces—which requires adequate funding—students in Piedmont will continue to find elevated educational opportunities and facilities. By paying a parcel tax, we make our schools stronger and with that the property values also increase. Please vote yes on Measure H. –Andson Zhou Measure H will increase property taxes in Piedmont Editor: Supporters say the funding is needed to maintain services and schools. But voters should ask a basic question: How will they measure whether the additional money produces results? Measure H does not answer that. The measure outlines spending priorities but sets no benchmarks for success. Without benchmarks, the public cannot evaluate whether additional funding improves outcomes or simply increases spending. That matters because public funding moves through layers of administration, planning, and district decisions before residents see the effects. By then, the connection between spending and results becomes difficult to verify. Measure H also creates no standard for public review. There is no measure of success or failure and no way to compare promises with actual results. At the same time, additional property taxes add to already high housing and living costs in Piedmont. If voters approve ongoing taxes, they should also have a way to evaluate whether those taxes produce results. Measure H does not provide that. – Mike Van Roy (650) 283-3989 City Council approves $142,236 contract for Bonita Avenue parking By Jake Lannon On Monday, May 4, Piedmont’s City Council approved a $142,236 contract for the Bonita Avenue parking and striping. It is anticipated that the work will begin in June after the last day of school. The contract documents allow for 20 working days to complete the work. The project should be completed before the first day of school on August 7. This project completes the remaining portion of the Civic Center restriping effort on Bonita Avenue from Oakland Avenue to Vista Avenue. The majority of restriping in the Civic Center area was completed as part of the 2025 Pavement Project. This segment was excluded at that time due to installation timing conflicts with the schedule for Havens Elementary School. The project includes converting Bonita Avenue to a one-way street with northbound vehicular traffic only, installing angled parking stalls along the easterly side of the roadway adjacent to Havens School, and adding two on-street angled accessible parking stalls. The city awarded the contract to D’s General Engineering of Oakland. The total budget for the project is $156,460, with funding coming from Measure BB (Local Streets and Roads), Vehicle Registration Fee (VRF), and California Senate Bill 1 (SB-1). articles.text: This month Caltrans is presenting two in-person meetings at St. Jarlath’s Church in Oakland, on May 16 and May 23. These meetings will be the only opportunity for the public to voice their opinions on Caltrans’ study on lifting the ban on big-rig trucks on I-580. Seating is limited, and you need to register in advance to attend. The meetings start at 10 a.m. and doors open at 9:45 a.m. People may speak for up to five minutes. In the early 1960s, during the construction of I-580 (the MacArthur Freeway), the city of Oakland enacted City Ordinance No. 6789, which prohibits trucks weighing over 4.5 tons from using I-580 between Grand Avenue and San Leandro. The ban has effectively kept large trucks from entering Highway 13 (the Warren Freeway) as well as most neighborhood streets and connecting corridors. Now, after more than 60 years, Caltrans is considering whether to repeal this ban. In early 2025, Caltrans launched a truck access study to answer how removing the truck weight restriction on I-580 would affect safety, efficiency, reliability, and traffic speed, and how this change would impact public health equity for nearby communities. Caltrans is responding to community concerns and implementing strategies recommended by the West Oakland Community Action Plan (2019) to help improve community health. Judy Cain, a representative of the group NoBigRigs580, believes the truck ban helps protect communities from pollution and traffic risks, and removing it would harm the health and safety of neighborhoods. She believes the true reason large trucks are being considered for I-580 is for improved freight efficiency. According to NoBigRigs580, the California Trucking Association has a longstanding history of lobbying Caltrans to abandon the truck ban to improve freight efficiency. The beneficiary of a repeal would be the trucking companies’ business, rather than the health and safety of civilians. Opening I-580 to big-rig trucks will increase the number of trucks traveling through Oakland to and from the Port as the trucking industry maximizes the additional roadway capacity from I-580. Repealing the ban would knowingly increase the number of people exposed to truck pollution. The group is concerned about the increased noise pollution and safety risks that come with heavy A fully loaded big rig can weigh up to 80,000 pounds. trucks. The hills around the highway would make it difficult for sound walls to be effective. This would impact schools, hospitals, parks, and neighborhoods adjacent to I-580 and Highway 13. According to the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, in 2025, California saw 10,708 crashes involving large trucks, including 232 fatal crashes and 9,753 nonfatal crashes. The increased truck traffic can lead to more accidents on the freeway and endanger pedestrians and cyclists at on- and off-ramps that intersect with city streets. The group believes the CalTrans study will not adequately address the health concerns found in the West Oakland Community Action Plan. They believe that addressing pollution from stationary sources like the port and airport will help the community more than re-routing trucks to I-580. They also support expanding and electrifying rail service and developing dedicated truck lanes on I-880 to reduce congestion and environmental impacts and improve safety by separating trucks from passenger vehicles. To learn more, visit https:// www.nobigrigs580.org/. To sign up for the listening sessions: https://www.nobigrigs580.org/ resources/#Events.
articles.title: Caltrans considers repealing I-580 big-rig truck ban

articles.text: At just one year old, Nora is a petite young tabby with the soul of a dignified grown-up— and just enough kitten energy to keep life interesting. While she enjoys lounging in sunny spots and supervising household activities, she still makes time for the occasional zoomies and enthusiastic games of fetch with her favorite mousie toy. Nora also has FIV, and with simple care, FIV-positive cats like her stay happy and healthy for years to come. The virus can’t be given to humans, and doesn’t spread easily between cats, so they can safely live with FIV-negative cats . She’s done well living with friendly cats at Cat Town! Nora likes attention and enjoys soft petting in thoughtful doses. When she’s in the mood for company, she’s happy to seek out cuddles, lap time, and conversation. Friendly and affectionate, Nora carries herAdopt Nora through Cat Town. self with an easy confidence that makes her feel right at home. She could be a lovely fit for first-time adopters or families looking for a cat who strikes a comfortable balance between playful companion and independent roommate. Nora is spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and tested negative for FeLV. Learn more at www.cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland. org.

articles.text: April in Paris brought over 100 guests to Claremont Country Club for French music, festive food, signature cocktails, lively dancing, spirited bidding, and one extraordinary result: $110,000 raised in support of cancer clinical trials at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital, Oakland. The event was honored to hear from Dr. Karen Rabin, pediatric hematologist and specialist in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and from Rachel Blanchard, whose daughter Hailey is a patient of Dr. Rabin. Both shared the real impact of clinical trials. Rachel’s story brought the room to its feet, while Dr. Rabin reminded us that 30 years ago, before trials like these, children like Hailey may not have had access to the targeted treatment she is receiving today. Dr. Karen Rabin and Rachel Blanchard Photos courtesy of Hill Branch A live band plays French music for the audience. Emcee Joe Cunningham French delicacies were served to those in attendance. Dr. Karen Rabin speaking at the April in Paris fundraiser Every $2,000 helps cover one child’s participation in a cancer clinical trial, including: • Trial coordination • Data collection • Participation support These essential costs are not covered by insurance. Every live and silent auction item sold out. The event’s evening emcee, Joe Cunningham, kept the energy high, the bidding lively, and the room ready to raise those paddles. To the event’s sponsors, donors, auction contributors, volunteers, speakers, guests, and everyone who helped bring April in Paris to life: thank you. Hill Branch looks forward to your participation next year! For those who could not attend or anyone who would like to make a gift, there is still time to support this important work. Donate now to help one child participate in a clinical trial https:// bit.ly/4uJbuJU. Members in the audience raising their paddles to bid at the auction

articles.text: Javadi is a bright, bouncy Malinois mix with a big future ahead! 5 months old and 20 pounds, she’s a smart, energetic pup who’s already showing off her potential. She may be a little shy at first, but once she warms up she’s affectionate, playful, and loves being close — especially if it means getting held like a baby!) Javadi is incredibly trainable and already knows several hand signals like sit, down, touch, and spin. She’s potty trained, sleeps through the night, and would thrive with someone excited to continue her training and channel her energy into fun activities. She could be a fantastic sport dog prospect. Like many working breed puppies, Javadi will need structure, patience, and plenty of physical and mental exercise. She’s still learning her manners and can get mouthy Javadi is a bright, bouncy Malinois mix or a bit wild when overtired, so a home without small children is best. If you’re looking for a fun, devoted, and highly trainable companion to grow with, Javadi is your girl! To meet her, submit your adoption questionnaire online at Oakland Animal Services’ website and you will be contacted by hes foster to arrange a meet-and-greet. articles.text: Researchers have found that play is not just enjoyable, it is deeply important for learning, creativity, and emotional health. Play has been linked to improved problem-solving, lower stress levels, stronger social bonds, and greater cognitive flexibility. In other words, play helps our brains stay adaptable and open to new ideas. That may be one reason why some of our best ideas seem to arrive when we are relaxed enough to stop forcing them. Somewhere along the way, though, many of us start treating play like it is extra or optional. The thing we will get to after the “important things” are finished. But, the problem is that the important things are literally never finished. There will always be another email, another responsibility, another thing to improve, solve, clean, optimize, or manage. So, play gets pushed farther and farther to the edges until it starts to feel almost irresponsible or, even worse, silly. And yet, play is often where creativity first shows up. Play that just exists for its own sake, not for productivity or strategy, but just for fun and enjoyment. Examples: Doodling silly faces in the margins of a notebook. Singing loudly in the car to your favorite song. Tossing a ball with your kid. Making up a ridiculous backstory for the person walking three dogs at once. What I find interesting is that play changes the way we pay attention. It loosens something inside of us. Play can interrupt the constant pressure to perform or produce. For a moment, we stop trying to get things right and start interacting with the world a little more freely. Children do this naturally, but adults often need to relearn it. So here is a small experiment: find one moment of play this week that has no outcome attached to it. No self-improvement angle. No side hustle potential. No hidden productivity goal. Just one small moment where enjoyment is enough. Maybe it lasts thirty seconds or twenty minutes, the length doesn’t matter. The point is to remember that creativity is not fueled only by discipline and effort. Sometimes it is fueled by lightness and curiosity. Let yourself interact with the world without immediately turning the experience into something useful. Ironically, this is often when new ideas show up anyway. You don’t have to chase new ideas, if you give them room to breathe. Nina Meehan is a keynote speaker, workshop facilitator and coach with a specialization in creativity and communication. https://ninameehan.com/
articles.title: Creativity Experiment: One Moment of Play

Play has been linked to improved problem-solving, lower stress levels, stronger social bonds, and greater cognitive flexibility. In other words, play helps our brains stay adaptable and open to new ideas. That may be one reason why some of our best ideas seem to arrive when we are relaxed enough to stop forcing them. Somewhere along the way, though, many of us start treating play like it is extra or optional. The thing we will get to after the “important things” are finished. But, the problem is that the important things are literally never finished. There will always be another email, another responsibility, another thing to improve, solve, clean, optimize, or manage. So, play gets pushed farther and farther to the edges until it starts to feel almost irresponsible or, even worse, silly. And yet, play is often where creativity first shows up. Play that just exists for its own sake, not for productivity or strategy, but just for fun and enjoyment. Examples: Doodling silly faces in the margins of a notebook. Singing loudly in the car to your favorite song. Tossing a ball with your kid. Making up a ridiculous backstory for the person walking three dogs at once. What I find interesting is that play changes the way we pay attention. It loosens something inside of us. Play can interrupt the constant pressure to perform or produce. For a moment, we stop trying to get things right and start interacting with the world a little more freely. Children do this naturally, but adults often need to relearn it. So here is a small experiment: find one moment of play this week that has no outcome attached to it. No self-improvement angle. No side hustle potential. No hidden productivity goal. Just one small moment where enjoyment is enough. Maybe it lasts thirty seconds or twenty minutes, the length doesn’t matter. The point is to remember that creativity is not fueled only by discipline and effort. Sometimes it is fueled by lightness and curiosity. Let yourself interact with the world without immediately turning the experience into something useful. Ironically, this is often when new ideas show up anyway. You don’t have to chase new ideas, if you give them room to breathe. articles.text: Piedmont’s school board awarded Chris Hart, a lifelong resident and dedicated advocate for student athletics, as the recipient of the 2026 Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award. Hart was announced as the winner in March, and was presented with the award during the May 6 school board meeting. “If there were more Chris Harts in the world, it would be a much better place,” said Cory Smegal. A member of the Piedmont High School class of 1987, Hart grew up playing many sports throughout his childhood in Piedmont. While at PHS, he played basketball for four years and competed in swimming, football, and baseball. Throughout his years of service, Chris has played a vital role in supporting Piedmont schools. He served as President of the PHS Boosters Club from 2020–2024, where he played a pivotal role in support for athletics, including developing the “Oktoberfest” fundraiser to build community and financial support, and organizing community support for the renovation of Witter Field. “There are all of these things that exist that didn’t exist before, in no small part, due to your effort. The tennis center, the refurbishment of Witter Field, the community pool, all of those things are a legacy for you forever,” said school board member Max Roman. Hart said that he was very humbled, looking at the list of past recipients. “But there was one name that jumped out to me, and that Smegal Anderson. He is also a long-standing member of the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame Committee. His volunteer work extends into civic leadership. Since 2023, he has served on the Piedmont Recreation Commission and is a member of the board of the Piedmont Scouts. Most recently, he served on the City-School Facilities Task Force, developing ideas to improve the use of limited athletic facilities across town. “In addition to the breadth of his activity, his volunteerism, it’s really how you go about it, and how you make everyone around you feel as you’re doing this. articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School and High School Music Departments invite the community to their annual Spring Concerts, featuring performances by instrumental and choral music students. All concerts will be held at the Alan Harvey Theater on the Piedmont High School campus. • Tuesday, May 19th at 7:00 p.m. The evening will kick off with the Middle School Orchestra directed by Shauna Revelli. Experience a rich and dynamic program featuring arrangements of timeless masterpieces by J.S. Bach and Ralph Vaughan Williams, alongside the electrifying energy of Coldplay’s Viva la Vida. The evening reaches a finale with the combined 6th–12th grade orchestra musicians performing Carnival of the Animals by Camille Saint-Saëns, under the direction of PHS and PMS music teachers Trevor Chaix and Revelli. • Wednesday, May 20th at 7:00 p.m. The Middle School bands, under the direction of Mary Rees, will light up the stage with the music of Michael Jackson and The Weeknd, a vibrant arrangement of Stevie Wonder’s iconic funk classic Superstition, and the evocative One Summer’s Day from the anime film Spirited Away. In addition, the PHS Jazz Band will make a cameo appearance. • Thursday, May 21st at 7:00 p.m. The final concert of the week features four PHS ensembles – Choir, String Orchestra, Symphonic Band, and Jazz Band – under the direction of Trevor Chaix. The evening concludes with the presentation of the Senior Music Awards. Travel from the big screen to the concert hall with music from Mulan, Ratatouille, How to Train Your Dragon, and La La Land. The Choir will bring the spirit of the ‘60s to life with hits from The Beach Boys, The Mamas and the Papas, and The Beatles. The Symphonic Band will have you grooving to the timeless sounds of ABBA, while the Orchestra performs the beloved Carnival of the Animals by Camille Saint-Saëns. And don’t miss the Jazz Band’s take on Love Me or Leave Me, famously performed by Ella Fitzgerald. Admission To help offset concert expenses a $5 donation is requested. Students attend for free.
articles.title: PUSD announces Spring Concerts

articles.text: “Aloha 6th Grade” celebration transformed the hall with festive balloon arch decorations, pineapple centerpieces, and a lively photo booth where students captured memories with friends throughout the evening. The dance floor stayed packed as kids danced, jumped, and sang along with friends for nonstop fun. DJ Hightop, back by popular demand, quickly settled an early question from the crowd by declaring that yes, jumping absolutely counts as dancing — a ruling that was enthusiastically embraced for the rest of the night. Students danced to current favorites like Pink Pony Club and joined in crowd classics like the Cha Cha Slide and The Macarena, which, at 30 years old, still proved surprisingly popular with the fifth grade crowd. The now-famous Sea Lion Dance was also a highlight of the night. Dinner was provided by Rico Rico Taco, followed by cotton candy and shaved ice for dessert. Havens students were all smiles during the 5th grade dance party.

articles.text: Governor Gavin Newsom’s 2024 signing into law of the California’s Phone-Free Schools Act (AB 3216), which requires all school districts, charter schools, and county offices of education to adopt a policy limiting or prohibiting smartphone use by July 1, 2026. The board plans to introduce a first reading of next year’s policy at the May 20 board meeting. The five options discussed included retaining the current lunch-only policy, using Yondr pouches to lock phones, installing lockers (regular-size or phonesize), keeping phones off and in backpacks, and using cell-phone detectors. Following discussion, the cell-phone detectors have been ruled against, as the technology is still unvetted. Pouches, like Yondr were also voted down due to recurring replacement costs for new pouches annually. Every option, aside from the detectors, includes the cost of hiring another Campus Security staff member, estimated at $75,000 annually. This staff member would not be limited to policing cell-phone use. The board policy covers cell phones, smartwatches, earbuds and headphones, and computers, aside from the school issued Chromebooks. Non-smartphones are not covered in the current policy. The current policy is preferred by students, it essentially keeps students in possession of their phone. It makes them handle it twice every period, to store it in the hotels and then to retrieve it. pages.text: Wednesday, May 13, 2026 11 No-Phone Policy Continued from page 1 Governor Gavin Newsom’s 2024 signing into law of the California’s Phone-Free Schools Act (AB 3216), which requires all school districts, charter schools, and county offices of education to adopt a policy limiting or prohibiting smartphone use by July 1, 2026. The board plans to introduce a first reading of next year’s policy at the May 20 board meeting. The five options discussed included retaining the current lunch-only policy, using Yondr pouches to lock phones, installing lockers (regular-size or phonesize), keeping phones off and in backpacks, and using cell-phone detectors. Following discussion, the cell-phone detectors have been ruled against, as the technology is still unvetted. Pouches, like Yondr were also voted down due to recurring replacement costs for new pouches annually. Every option, aside from the detectors, includes the cost of hiring another Campus Security staff member, estimated at $75,000 annually. This staff member would not be limited to policing cell-phone use. The board policy covers cell phones, smartwatches, earbuds and headphones, and computers, aside from the school issued Chromebooks. Non-smartphones are not covered in the current policy. The current policy is preferred by students, it essentially keeps students in possession of their phone. It makes them handle it twice every period, to store it in the hotels and then to retrieve it. In a student survey by The Piedmont Highlander, 93% of the 300 survey takers approved of keeping the policy the same. “The current policy already provides a reasonable balance between limiting distractions and allowing students some personal responsibility,” said PHS senior Stephanie Lee during the meeting. “Students are expected to take responsibility for their learning. If a student chooses to be distracted by their phone during class, they are ultimately choosing to take that risk with their education,” said student board member Charli Panico. “I hate the things [cell phones],” said English teacher Elise Marks. “I have felt viscerally, the difference in student attention since they appeared. However, I do want to say I think the policy as it stands, has been working really well. I almost never see a kid with their phone out in class anymore.” Many students, parents and teachers spoke eloquently for keeping the current policy, but a desire to strengthen the policy was also spoken in multitude with articulation by board members and parents. “There’s no world in which you will not know how to use the phone, or not know how to figure out responsibility about it if you don’t get the chance to practice in school. But you will absolutely not learn how to focus, how to read and think deeply, how to get A locking Yondr pouch would allow students to retain possession of phones, but replacement costs and possible subversion methods have caused them to be disfavored by the board. your brain working unless you do it when you’re a kid,” said Maxim Shusteff, the father of two PHS students. “The sense of this is inevitable and this is just how life has to be, and we have to have the technology work and be in our lives in this way - it’s just manufactured; it’s not true. This is manufactured by the companies,” said Struble. “This is not about just distraction; it is a mental health issue,” said Allison Gans, a parent, therapist and board member of Piedmont Unpluggled. “My students are struggling to focus, feeling socially overwhelmed, constantly comparing themselves, and having difficulty tolerating even short periods of discomfort without reaching for a device.” The board directed itself to get to work on a new policy for next year, with a clear preference for a bell-to-bell, no phone decision. Board members spoke positively about installing lockers, but details will not be decided until the first reading of the policy, which is scheduled for the next meeting on May 20. Five options for next year’s student mobile phone policy were discussed during the May 6 board meeting. articles.text: New PHS records set by Aubrecht, Mumtaz, Iroh Piedmont’s track and field team had a wildly successful day at the 2026 Western Alameda County Conference Championships at Burrell Field in San Leandro on Wednesday and Friday, May 6-8. With topsix finishes, the Highlanders are set to send at least 30 athletes in different events to the North Coast Section Bayshore Area meet at Hayward High on Saturday, May 16. Piedmont athletes broke several school records in the process. Ju n ior spr i nter Clai re Aubrecht finished the 100 meter dash in second of 42 athletes with a time of 12.54. Her time beat Breah Bell’s school record of 12.55 set in 2024. She also improved her school record time in the 200 meters to 25.92 and was second of 36 runners. The time eclipsed her previous best of 26.15 set on March 14 at the San Leandro Invitational. “I was super excited and didn’t believe it at first. It was really cool because I looked up to Breah for a long time. I’ve been through a learning process and need to believe in myself a bit more. I work year-round with a couple of breaks and just put in a ton of time and effort,” Aubrecht said. Teammate Uzoma Iroh also set the school’s shot put record with a distance of 34 feet, 4.5 inches to place fourth of 28. She beat Andrea Martin’s record by three inches set at last year’s WACC Championships. Iroh also set the school record in the discus with a throw of 107 feet, 2 inches, topping Alina Shahid’s 2025 mark by nearly seven inches, while finishing fourth of 27. “Claire and Uzoma are two ladies that have invested the time and energy year round.. We knew they were both going to make noise this year, so taking down these school records isn’t too much of a surprise,” coach Assadi said. On the boys’ side, junior sprinter Rehan Mumtaz broke the school 100 meter record with a time of 11.04 seconds, placing third of 42 runners. He topped Sam Shelby’s 2025 record by .01 of a second. “I was really happy, It’s been a lot of hard work. It feels great to finally have my name on the record board. Hopefully I’ll get to 10.9 soon. Since my freshman year, all I’ve been thinking about is getting my name on that board,” Mumtaz said. Mumtaz mentioned that he’s been dealing with a lingering injury, making his record time all that more special. “I was injured recently and peaked midseason. I started plateauing and stopped working out as hard after getting injured. This week, I decided to forget everything. I had a bone bruise in my heel and an issue with my tendon,” Mumtaz said. It’s worth mentioning that California high schools officially switched from yards to meters in 1980. Bill Hefter still holds the school’s all-time best mark of 9.84 seconds dating back to 1961. Converting Mumtaz’s figure to yards would put him at approximately 10.09 seconds, which would make him the school’s second-fastest sprinter of all time. To beat Hefter’s time, Mumtaz needs to run 10.76 seconds in 100 meters. He has another year to do it, and is trending in that direction. Other Top-6 Results Sebastien Swain was second of 47 half milers in the 800, clocking a time of 1:55.14. He was also second of 49 in the 1600 in 4:18.72. He will compete in the 800 meters at the NCS championships. Avedis Gourjian won the pole vault with a height of 12 feet in a field of 10. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ 200 medley team of Connor Carnazzo (left), Nik Costello, Asher Takazawa, and Cole Carnazzo qualified for State at the NCS Championships. Piedmont High’s swimming team competed at the North Coast Section Championships May 7-9 at the College of Marin in Novato. In the process, they qualified two boys’ relay teams to the CIF State Championships at Clovis West HS in Fresno on Thursday and Saturday, May 14-16. Piedmont’s 200 medley team of Asher Takazawa, Nik Costello, Connor Carnazzo, and Cole Carnazzo finished fourth of 16 teams with a time of 1:32.91. The boys’ 400 freestyle relay team of Jeffrey Latronica, Dima Secor, Costello, and Takazawa placed sixth of 16 finalists, clocking a 3:05.85 to reach State. PHS featured seven total boys’ swimmers at the NCS Championship and five girls swimmers. Below is a full rundown of Piedmont’s results. Swim Results Secor reached the 100 freestyle finals, placing seventh of 16 in 46.32. To get there, he clocked a time of 46.14 in the preliminary round to finish seventh of 38. He was also 12th of 16 in the 200 Individual Medley finals in 1:54.09. Secor was 11th of 37 in the 200 IM prelims in 1:54.16. Connor Carnazzo was eighth of 16 in the 100 butterfly finals in 50.41, qualifying by placing seventh of 40 in the prelims in 50.06. Takazawa was ninth in the 100 fly in 50.54, and was 11th of 40 in the prelims in 50.87. He also placed 11th of 16 in the 100 backstroke in 51.53, while he qualified for the finals by finishing 12th of 40 in the prelims in 52.11. Latronica was behind Takazawa in the backstroke finals in 12th, 52.03. He was 14th in the prelims in 52.50. He also tied Takazawa for ninth in the 100 fly in 50.54, and was ninth in the prelims in 50.44. Costello was 11th of 16 in the 50 free finals in 21.29. To get there, he was 10th of 40 in the prelims in 21.27. He was also 11th in the 100 free in 46.52, while he placed ninth in the prelims in 46.39. Ryan Mak was 13th of 16 in the 500 freestyle finals in 4:35.38. To get there, he was 13th of 39 in the prelims in 4:35.87. He was also 24th of 41 in the 200 free prelims in 1:43.74. Zafar Majid was 30th in the 100 backstroke prelims in 55.28. On the girls’ side, Cynthia Wu was 15th in the 100 back finals in 59.64. She had a time of 58.83 in the prelims. Sam White was 22 of 40 in the 500 free prelims in 5:22.20, and 37 of 40 in the 200 free prelims in 2:02.48. The girls’ 200 medley team of Wu, Indie Briskman, Sofia Vuori, and White were 23rd of 39 teams in the prelims in 1:55.57. The 400 free team of Charlotte Zhang, Vuori, White, and Wu were 26th of 40 in 3:50.45. NEXT UP Piedmont will send two boys’ relay teams to the CIF State Championship at West Clovis HS in Fresno on Thursday and Saturday, May 17-19.
