articles.text: Lucas Smolko (left) stands with the NCS first-place banner alongside Kingston Vora of Lick-Wilmerding, Edward Mofit of Stuart Hall, and Sze Ting Chen of Acalanes. Piedmont High senior Lucas Smolko is putting a bow on his high school career in a big way. On Saturday, May 9, Smolko won the Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament’s singles title, beating Acalanes’ Sze Ting Chen in straight sets 6-4, 6-3 at the Marin Tennis Club in San Rafael. To get there, Smolko played as clean a tournament as you could possibly ask, winning every match in straight sets. He won 6-0, 6-0 over St. Patrick’s Oscar Swenson in the opening round, followed up with a 6-1, 6-4 win over Armaan Mishra of Lick-Wilmerding in the quarterfinals, and dominated Stuart Hall’s Edward Morfit 6-1, 6-0 in the semifinals. “I was anticipating that match against Sze Ting in the final, so I wanted to make sure I did everything possible to get ready for that match. I just tried to do things in my control; getting properly prepared and trying to finish those early rounds as efficiently as possible,” Smolko said. His win over Chen was a reversal of Piedmont’s February 26 match with Acalanes when Smolko lost 6-3, 7-6. “He played really well both times I played him. The first time I played him, he was serving really great and hitting big, I wasn’t quite ready. This time, I knew what was coming. I knew I had to focus on my own service game and make sure I was holding because his serve is really hard to break,” Smolko said. During the match, Smolko started taking control after Chen won games during Smolko’s Lucas’ serve, shifting his focus to win games as the returner. “There were two turning points. He broke my serve midway through the first set on a deuce point, so I got frustrated and went to reset. I focused up and won the next three games. Seconds set was a similar story. I was up and he broke my serve, but I kept it together and won the last couple of games,” Smolko said. Smolko’s title win marked his third time reaching the finals in his high school career. As a freshman, he fell 6-3, 6-1 to Gus Grumet of University, who later played at Stanford. As a junior, he lost in a three-set battle to Dylan Donovan of Head-Royce. This time, Smolko felt his game elevated to a different point. “It was a fitting ending to my career, for sure. I learned a lot from each tournament, I don’t think I was ready to win it any of the previous years. Freshman year, my level wasn’t high enough. Last year, I wasn’t quite there physically. articles.text: No. 6 Piedmont fell 7-6 to No. 3 Miramonte in the Division 2 NCS Quarterfinals, ending its season. Staff Photos Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team’s season came to an end in the Division 2 North Coast Section Quarterfinals, narrowly falling short of upsetting No. 3 Miramonte. As the No. 6 seed, the Highlanders lost 7-6 on Thursday, May 7. The Highlanders tied the match four different times, but just couldn’t find the go-ahead goal. “It was a hard-fought game on both sides. I thought we played really well on both sides of the ball. We were missing starters on defense but guys stepped up who haven’t really played all season,” coach Andy Kittler said. “It was a close battle, we played with a lot of grit. We had a lot of guys out throughout the season, but I’m super proud of the guys who stepped up,” junior Connor Fredericks mentioned. Despite the loss, the Highlanders’ defense maintained a heavy press for all four quarters, forcing several key turnovers that led to goals. It was something they struggled to do near the end of the regular season. “It came together in the run-up to the game. We had some wakeup calls, so we really put an emphasis on playing as a team and bringing all the energy we could. They put a lot of effort and mental energy into preparing,” Kittler said. To reach the quarterfinals, Piedmont defeated No. 11 Las Lomas 12-11 in overtime on Tuesday, May 5. Piedmont finishes its season with a 7-8 overall record in Kittler’s first year at the helm. It marks a noticeable improvement from last year’s 4-11 finish. “We had an inexperienced team overall and lost some of our experienced guys, so we had to rely on people filling the gaps. We have a lot of athletes who are turning into lacrosse players, we’re convincing them that they can be great players,” Kittler said. “Something we say in the locker room is: ‘Freight Train Energy,’ we kind of lived by that all season. It’s about not stopping and always giving 100 percent,” Fredericks added. But there are some clear building blocks going toward 2027. Key players like Fredericks, Richmond, Owen Curran, Landon Heppner, Deniz Radzik and Milo Stevenson will be seniors. “The majority of our starters are juniors and underclassmen. I’m really looking forward to my senior year, we’re going to have a great team. We had people grow into their spots this year,” Fredericks said. 7-6 loss to Miramonte Piedmont trailed 3-2 through the first quarter and 5-4 by halftime. They ended the third quarter in a 6-6 tie, but the Matadors scored the only goal in the fourth quarter to win it. Miramonte scored the first two goals of the game before Landon Heppner scored after scooping a ground ball with 2:55 left. The Matadors got their third 40 seconds later, while Piedmont answered with a leaping shot by Owen Curran with 1:12 on the clock. In the second, Fredericks broke through with 7:52 remaining after receiving a pass from Timmy Kalamas. Miramonte went ahead three minutes later, but then Fredericks assisted Curran to tie it at four with 3:53 left. The Matadors scored the go-ahead as time expired to lead 5-4. Piedmont logged several shots saved in the third quarter, including a critical shot by Gianluca Richmond on the doorstep at the 6:55 mark. Fredericks later scored on a wraparound to tie it at 5-5 with 5:04 left. Miramonte scored with 3:19 left to lead 6-5, while Fredericks scored as time expired to knot it up, once again. But in the fourth, Miramonte scored the eventual game-winner with 6:20 left. In the remaining time, Kalamas had shots trail wide at the 4:07, 1:49, and 1:41 marks. Heppner had a shot go wide with 1:19 left, but that was Piedmont’s final shot attempt. Final stats: Fredericks had three goals, two assists, five ground balls, and won 12 faceoffs. Curran scored two goals Connor Fredericks scored three goals against Miramonte and five goals against Las Lomas.

On Saturday, May 9, Smolko won the Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament’s singles title, beating Acalanes’ Sze Ting Chen in straight sets 6-4, 6-3 at the Marin Tennis Club in San Rafael. To get there, Smolko played as clean a tournament as you could possibly ask, winning every match in straight sets. He won 6-0, 6-0 over St. Patrick’s Oscar Swenson in the opening round, followed up with a 6-1, 6-4 win over Armaan Mishra of Lick-Wilmerding in the quarterfinals, and dominated Stuart Hall’s Edward Morfit 6-1, 6-0 in the semifinals. “I was anticipating that match against Sze Ting in the final, so I wanted to make sure I did everything possible to get ready for that match. I just tried to do things in my control; getting properly prepared and trying to finish those early rounds as efficiently as possible,” Smolko said. His win over Chen was a reversal of Piedmont’s February 26 match with Acalanes when Smolko lost 6-3, 7-6. “He played really well both times I played him. The first time I played him, he was serving really great and hitting big, I wasn’t quite ready. This time, I knew what was coming. I knew I had to focus on my own service game and make sure I was holding because his serve is really hard to break,” Smolko said. I’ve had to learn and improve a lot throughout my whole career. I’ve really enjoyed it and just being part of a team because tennis is such an individual sport. I’m going to miss it,” Smolko said. It brings their record to 8-15-2 (W-L-T) as the team prepares for North Coast Section playoffs. It’s been an interesting league schedule for Piedmont. They split their regular season games to the Hornets on April 22 and April 24 with a 7-0 loss and 6-3 win. They similarly beat Berkeley 6-3 on April 28, but lost 12-1 two days later. “We’re playing against really good competition. We had a freshman on the mound [Ben Sorensen], and when you do that, there are a lot of unknowns. We were competitive all season against really good teams with nearly a whole squad of new players. We knew it’d be up and down,” said coach Eric Olson. One bright spot was the return of shortstop and leading hitter, senior Diego Delventhal, providing an important player for the Staff Photos The baseball team took a one-sided loss to Alameda in the first round of the WACC Tournament. postseason. “Our lineup is a little longer now. If we can get quality at bats one through nine with Diego at the top, we’ll do fine. Our offense hasn’t been the problem recently,” Olson said. Piedmont now prepares for the start of the NCS postseason, where the Highlanders have typDiego Delventhal returned from an injury in time for Piedmont’s postseason. He went 2-for-3 with a double, RBI, and stolen base against Alameda. Freshman Mason Gray went 1-for-2 with a run scored against Alameda. ically fared well. They reached last year’s Quarterfinals, were finalists in 2024, and semifinalists in 2023. Olson thinks playing in the difficult WACC league makes them more battle-tested than a typical small enrollment school. “We’ve been shaped by teams in our league, I could go down the whole list, we play a really tough schedule. articles.text: Piedmont High’s softball team suffered a first-round loss to Mt. Eden in the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division tournament, falling 18-5 at the Monarchs’ field in Hayward. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 12-10 as they approach the North Coast Section postseason. Despite the loss, it was a big game for Edie Elmquist, who hit a triple for two RBIs. Talia Perl also logged a triple, while senior Sa’Mara Levi returned to the lineup near the end of the regular season from her travel-ball team to hit a double and two RBIs. The Highlanders approach NCS as the No. 79 ranked team in the section, per Maxpreps.com. According to the NCS’ website, postseason brackets will feature up to 16 teams across six divisions, making it unclear if the top three seeds will receive firstround byes like last season. If the brackets have 16 schools each, PHS would be on track for a Division 5 berth. Their official seeding will be released on Sunday, May 17. Game Recap Mt. Eden led 11-0 following a big bottom of the first inning, and scored four more in the bottom of the second. Both teams scored once in the third inning, while Piedmont scored four times in the top of the fourth. The Monarchs scored twice in the bottom of the fourth and held PHS scoreless in the top of the fifth to activate the 10-run rule. In the third inning, Makenna Small got on base via a catcher’s interference. Edie Elmquist followed up with a bunt single. Kajsa Benson advanced both runners with a bunt of her own, while Staff Photos Freshman Talia Perl had a triple against Mt. Eden, to go along with a run scored. Sa’Mara Levi brought in Small with a groundout to second. Piedmont’s four-run top of the fourth got started with a one-out triple by Talia Perl, smacking it to the right field fence. After that, Samantha Schey hit a hard ground ball back to the pitcher, causing an error to reach first and bring in Perl from third. With two outs, Small drew a walk, and then Elmquist cracked a triple of her own on a line drive to the right field fence— scoring Small and Schey. After Benson drew a walk, Levi hit a double to left field to bring Elmquist home. Final stats: Perl went 2-for-3 with a triple and one run scored. Elmquist went 2-for-4 with a triple, two RBIs and one run scored. Levi went 1-for-2 with a double and two RBIs. Schey had one RBI and one run scored. Small scored two run. NEXT UP Piedmont (12-10) prepares for the first round of North Coast Section with the first round scheduled for Tuesday or Wednesday, May 19-20. Edie Elmquist went 2-for-4 with a triple, two RBIs and one run scored against Mt. Eden. Sa’Mara Levi hit a double and two RBIs against on Mt. Eden.

articles.text: 9 rowers qualify for Youth Nationals Ten Piedmont rowers brought home medals from the US Rowing Southwest Youth Regional Championships outside Sacramento over the weekend of May 1 to 3. Their wins helped Oakland Strokes record two historic gold medals and qualify 10 boats for the Youth Nationals. The qualifying boats, including nine of the 10 Piedmont athletes, are now headed to the US Rowing Youth National Championships in Sarasota, Florida, in June. Three Piedmont athletes rowed in the Women’s Varsity 8+, which won the gold medal, the club’s first Women’s V8+ title in 12 years: junior Sophia Brenner of Piedmont High in the two seat, senior Claire von Metzsch of College Prep in the five seat, and senior Geneva Johnson of Piedmont High at stroke. The boat is coached by Piedmont resident Allison Ray. The Men’s U17 8+, coached by Sean Gibel, also took gold, the club’s first-ever win in the event’s A Final. Piedmont rowers anchored five more Oakland Strokes boats that qualified for Nationals. Senior Laurel Minor of Piedmont High rowed bow in the Women’s 2V 8+, which took silver. Minor will attend the University of Virginia in the fall. Sophomores Paige Young (bow) and Amelia Callaway (stroke), both of Piedmont High, were in the Women’s 3V 8+ that finished fourth in the 2V A Final to qualify. Sophia Brenner also rowed in the Women’s Pair, which took silver. Claire von Metzsch (bow) and Geneva Johnson (stroke), both V8+ rowers, doubled up in the Women’s Straight Four, which finished fourth and qualified for Nationals. Senior Senan Brodie (bow) and junior Connor Cross (three Photo by Jennifer Zhang-Wheeler Oakland Strokes Varsity 8 placed first at the Southwest Regionals. Featured in the boat were Piedmont High senior Geneva Johnson (second from left), Piedmont resident and College Prep senior Claire von Metzsch (fifth from left), and Piedmont junior Sophia Brenner (second from right) Photos by Joel Flory Oakland Strokes Women’s 3V placed fourth to reach Nationals. Piedmont sophomores Paige Young (left) and Amelia Calloway (right) were members if the boat. seat) of Piedmont High were in the Men’s Four which took silver to qualify. Piedmont sophomore Diego Branneria rowed bow in the Men’s Pair (with senior Russell Arroyo of St. Mary’s at stroke), which qualified for Nationals. Senior Audrey Dickinson of Piedmont High also brought home a medal: she rowed in the four seat of an Oakland Strokes 4V crew that took silver in the Women’s Youth 3V 8+ A Final, earning a regional medal. The race is not a Nationals-qualifying event. Dickinson will attend UC Santa Barbara in the fall. The Women’s Varsity 8+ that won gold reflects the strength of the Oakland Strokes pathway to college rowing. All six seniors in the boat are headed to NCAA programs in the fall. Piedmont rowers Geneva Johnson of Piedmont High will attend Boston University, and Claire von Metzsch of College Prep is headed to Yale. Their teammates Ava Wheeler is bound for the University of Pennsylvania, Alexis Arroyo for Tufts, the coxswain Samyra Joshi for Duke, and Mako Begossi for the University of California, Berkeley. Senan Brodie of Piedmont High has committed to row for Penn lightweights in the fall. In total 15 Oakland Strokes seniors will row at college programs across the country in the fall. “What I’m most proud of is that the entire team worked for these results,” said Allison Ray, the Oakland Strokes Director of Rowing. “Sending the 1V, 2V, and 3V to Nationals together is a first for our club, and it happened because everyone felt part of the work, whether they were in those top boats or not. That speaks to the strength of Oakland.” “What I’m most proud of is the culture this squad built, working hard, being coachable, and lifting up their teammates,” said Sean Gibel, the Oakland Strokes Men’s U17/U16 Coach. “The goal was to put in the work to be a front-runner, not just a contender. Now we enter Nationals training as front-runners from the Southwest. And one of the best parts of the weekend was watching families and teammates cheering for every Oakland boat down the course. Different squads, one team.” Oakland Strokes is for athletes who want to be inspired, challenged, and compete at the highest level. The club has programs for middle schoolers and high schoolers, with no rowing experience required. Summer camps for middle and high school athletes and middle school yearround programs are open for registration now. The high school team also offers a free two-week trial in late August for athletes considering joining. articles.text: The road warrior PMS Scots softball team continued with another slate of 4 away games last week, posting a perfect 4-0 record, making this a stellar 7-1 road trip. The Scots opened the week on Monday, May 4, with a dominant 17-2 win vs Berkeley’s King Middle School Cobras. All facets were on display with Bailey Gregovich and Sarina Hill combining to defang the Cobras by allowing just 2 hits over four innings and notching 9 strikeouts while getting flawless support from the defense. The offensive effort was led by Alice Sorensen’s 4 RBIs, including legging out a homerun in the 3rd inning that set off a frenzy in the Piedmont dugout. Bailey Gregovich followed up by unleashing a bomb to right field in the 4th that looked destined to be the second HR of the afternoon but was limited to a standup triple thanks to an ill-considered stop sign by third base coach Alex Joerger. Mackenzie Ewen (3-3, 3 RBI) and Nina Stock (2 RBI) also had key contributions at the plate. On Tuesday, May 5, the Scots were back in action vs Berkeley’s Longfellow Middle School that saw the Scots come away with a 14-5 victory. Though the offense was generated largely from free passes and aggressive base running, there was some extra power on display from Simone Tornatore (2-2, 4 RBI) and Evie Joerger (2B, RBI, 3 runs scored). pages.text: Wednesday, May 13, 2026 15 Piedmont rowers power Oakland Strokes to historic weekend 9 rowers qualify for Youth Nationals Ten Piedmont rowers brought home medals from the US Rowing Southwest Youth Regional Championships outside Sacramento over the weekend of May 1 to 3. Their wins helped Oakland Strokes record two historic gold medals and qualify 10 boats for the Youth Nationals. The qualifying boats, including nine of the 10 Piedmont athletes, are now headed to the US Rowing Youth National Championships in Sarasota, Florida, in June. The boat is coached by Piedmont resident Allison Ray. The Men’s U17 8+, coached by Sean Gibel, also took gold, the club’s first-ever win in the event’s A Final. Piedmont rowers anchored five more Oakland Strokes boats that qualified for Nationals. Senior Laurel Minor of Piedmont High rowed bow in the Women’s 2V 8+, which took silver. Minor will attend the University of Virginia in the fall. Sophomores Paige Young (bow) and Amelia Callaway (stroke), both of Piedmont High, were in the Women’s 3V 8+ that finished fourth in the 2V A Final to qualify. Sophia Brenner also rowed in the Women’s Pair, which took silver. Claire von Metzsch (bow) and Geneva Johnson (stroke), both V8+ rowers, doubled up in the Women’s Straight Four, which finished fourth and qualified for Nationals. The Women’s Varsity 8+ that won gold reflects the strength of the Oakland Strokes pathway to college rowing. All six seniors in the boat are headed to NCAA programs in the fall. articles.text: Shotgun Players will present the Bay Area premiere of Continuity by Bess Wohl from May 23 through June 27 at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley. Directed by Emilie Whelan, the comedy centers on a Hollywood film production attempting to address climate change while unraveling behind the scenes. The play follows director Maria as she struggles to hold together both a chaotic movie set and the people working on it. “Continuity is zany, ambitious, and full-throated,” Whelan said in a statement. “Bess Wohl understands that the climate crisis is a human crisis and that humans standing in front of the climate crisis are actually like clowns. It is so big, and we are slack-jawed before it.” The production satirizes the entertainment industry while exploring how individuals respond to the climate crisis. According to the company, the fictional film set includes a Styrofoam ice shelf and a production relocated to New Mexico for tax incentives. Patrick Dooley, artistic director of Shotgun Players, said the play reflects the company’s 2026 season theme of “making art that meets the moment.” “This play gets at climate change, and while the world is on fire, we still have to live our lives, and do the best we can,” Dooley said. “The energy, and the humor, behind this show is the will toward life.” The cast includes Rezan Asfaw, Regina Morones, Nicholas René Rodriguez, Ije Success and Benoît Monin, along with Malcolm Rodgers, Matt Standley and Adam Mendez Jr. Purchase tickets at www.shotgunplayers.org/show/continuity/ or by calling the box office 510- 841-6500 x 303.
articles.title: Shotgun Players presents Continuity May 23

articles.text: Photo by Genesis Botello “Postcards from Dvořák” will run July 11 through 26 at venues throughout Sonoma county. The Valley of the Moon Music Festival returns for its 12th season this summer with a program celebrating the music and global influences of Czech composer Antonín Dvořák. Titled “Postcards from Dvořák,” the festival will run July 11 through 26 at venues throughout Sonoma County, combining chamber music performances on historical instruments with outdoor concerts, lectures and family programming. Led by festival co-founders and directors Tanya Tomkins and Eric Zivian, the 2026 season explores the people, places and cultural traditions that shaped Dvořák’s music during his travels across Europe and the United States. “Dvořák is a natural choice to anchor our 12th season,” Zivian said in a statement. “While deeply rooted in musical tradition, he was remarkably open to cultural influences from around the world — traveling extensively and embracing new ideas in ways that were rare for a 19th-century composer.” “His openness, heartfelt musical voice, and deep respect for other traditions continue to inspire us,” Tomkins added. “For us, he represents the power of music to bring people together across cultures and communities.” The season features seven mainstage programs at Hanna Center Auditorium, beginning July 11 with “Bohemian Homeland,” an opening-night concert inspired by Dvořák’s roots in 19th-century Prague. The festival concludes July 26 with “Final Years: Going Home,” a finale celebrating Dvořák’s return to Bohemia. Other programs include “English Impressions,” exploring connections between English and Bohemian musical traditions, and “American Roots,” highlighting the composer’s years in the United States and the influence of African American spirituals and American folk music on his work. The festival also will present music by composers including Johannes Brahms, Felix Mendelssohn, Florence Price, Harry T. Burleigh and Leoš Janáček. Organizers said the programming reflects the festival’s ongoing effort to broaden the classical canon and highlight underrepresented composers. Guest artists this season include violinists Rachell Ellen Wong, Jennifer Frautschi, Elizabeth Blumenstock and Tien-Hsin Cindy Wu. The Amizia Quartet will return as the festival’s Fellowship Quartet-in-Residence. In addition to ticketed performances, the festival will offer pay-what-you-wish outdoor concerts, a free family concert at the Sonoma Community Center and pre-concert lectures curated by Kate van Orden. Tickets and passes are available online at valleyofthemoonmusicfestival.org. articles.text: The 32nd annual Sculpture in the Garden at Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek will be on view June 13 through August 9, featuring more than 80 sculptures from 42 artists. The event is the nonprofit’s longest-running annual art exhibit and sale that celebrates sculptural pieces with the natural, arid beauty of the garden. A range of returning local artists, as well as newcomers, are participating this year. Sculpture in the Garden also serves as a fundraiser for Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery. All artwork is available to purchase, and proceeds from this exhibit go back into the Garden to help protect the plant collection, promote education and support preservation. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, was a pioneer in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public, made possible through fundraisers like Sculpture in the Garden. The event is free with regular Garden admission. The nursery is located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek. For more information, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/event/2025-sculpture-in-thegarden/. More than 80 sculptures will be available for purchase this year. articles.text: La Cumbiamba Colombiana performs this Friday Photo courtesy of Oakland Museum of California La Cumbiamba Colombiana celebrates the roots of Colombian cumbia. The Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) free community-gathering evening event series “Friday Nights” kicked off last month with live performances and weekly food concessions. OMCA hosts free community events every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout the spring and summer, featuring live music, immersive arts activities and late-night museum access with the purchase of a museum ticket. Bring a blanket and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s large lawn, where live music and entertainment takes place throughout the evening. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from a stationed food truck on-site. A rotating list of vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon Streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. La Cumbiamba Colombiana will perform a lively dance number celebrating the roots of Colombian cumbia, which weaves ancestral steps and Afro-Caribbean influences in a colorful, high-energy showcase this Friday, May 15. Combo Tezeta, whose psychedelic take on cumbia, chicha, and música tropical blends surf rock textures with hypnotic Latin rhythms, follows La Cumbiamba Colombiana’s performance. Friday Night events are always free and open to the public, but late-night museum access requires a ticket purchase. Visit https://museumca.org/about-friday-nights-at-omca-with-off-thegrid/ to learn more.
articles.title: “Friday Nights” returns to Oakland Museum of California

articles.text: The opera marks the return of Spanish director Emilio Sagi’s staging, first introduced in 2013. The San Francisco Opera opens its 2026 summer season on May 28 with Gioachino Rossini’s comic opera The Barber of Seville. The opera, featuring two international casts and conducted by Benjamin Manis, also marks the return of Spanish director Emilio Sagi’s staging, first introduced by the company in 2013 and revived in 2015. The production is a co-production with the Lithuanian National Opera and Ballet Theatre. Rossini composed The Barber of Seville in 1816 in just 13 days to meet a deadline from an impresario. Though its Rome premiere was widely considered a failure, the opera later became one of the most frequently performed works in the repertory. The opera follows Figaro, a resourceful barber, as he helps Count Almaviva win the affection of Rosina while outmaneuvering her guardian, Doctor Bartolo. The score includes well-known arias such as “Largo al factotum” and “Una voce poco fa.” American baritones Joshua Hopkins and Justin Austin will alternate in the title role. Mezzo-sopranos Maria Kataeva and Hongni Wu share the role of Rosina. Tenors Levy Sekgapane and Jack Swanson will make company debuts as Count Almaviva. Additional cast members include Renato Girolami, Patrick Carfizzi and Catherine Cook, who reprises the role of Berta after performing it in every San Francisco Opera presentation of The Barber of Seville since 1996. The third performance of The Barber of Seville on Friday, June 5 will be livestreamed. Tickets, which includes a 48-hour on-demand viewing window that begins June 7 at 10 a.m., may be purchased online at sfopera.com/ digital/livestream. All live performances take place at the War Memorial Opera House on May 28 (7:30 p.m.); June 3 (7:30 p.m.), 5 (7:30 p.m.), 6 (2 p.m.), 9 (7:30 p.m.), 12 (7:30 p.m.), 13 (7:30 p.m.), 20 (2 p.m.), 21 (2 p.m.). Visit sfopera.com to purchase tickets.
articles.title: SF Opera presents The Barber of Seville May 28 through June 21

articles.text: Cantabella Children’s Chorus is one of 11 featured choirs at this year’s Golden Gate International Choral Festival hosted by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. Founded by Director Emeritus Bee Chow in 1992, Cantabella has grown to serve children in the Tri-Valley area of Dublin, Livermore, and Pleasanton. Their spotlight performance will take place on July 15 at the First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley at 2407 Dana Street. Cantabella fosters choral artistry through the performance of music from all genres. They enhance music literacy using the Kodaly method as their pedagogical method. The choir develops healthy vocal technique for the singers through ensemble performance and group lessons. Most of all, Cantabella singers learn to cherish the joy of singing together. Cantabella has received international recognition for its performances. Cantabella was recognized with multiple awards at the Golden Gate International Children’s Festival (2006, 2009, 2015, and 2023), World Choir Games (2012), the ACDA Western Division Conference ( 2013), and the Grand Prix, World Youth Choral Festival and Competition, Jeju, South Korea (2019), Gold Medal, Sacred Music Category, World Youth Choral Festival and Competition (WYCF), Virtual Competition (2021). By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco Opera opens its 2026 summer season on May 28 with Gioachino Rossini’s comic opera The Barber of Seville. The opera, featuring two international casts and conducted by Benjamin Manis, also marks the return of Spanish director Emilio Sagi’s staging, first introduced by the company in 2013 and revived in 2015. The production is a co-production with the Lithuanian National Opera and Ballet Theatre. Rossini composed The Barber of Seville in 1816 in just 13 days to meet a deadline from an impresario. Though its Rome premiere was widely considered a failure, the opera later became one of the most frequently performed works in the repertory. The opera follows Figaro, a resourceful barber, as he helps Count Almaviva win the affection of Rosina while outmaneuvering her guardian, Doctor Bartolo. The score includes well-known arias such as “Largo al factotum” and “Una voce poco fa.” American baritones Joshua Hopkins and Justin Austin will alternate in the title role. Mezzo-sopranos Maria Kataeva and Hongni Wu share the role of Rosina. Tenors Levy Sekgapane and Jack Swanson will make company debuts as Count Almaviva. Additional cast members include Renato Girolami, Patrick Carfizzi and Catherine Cook, who reprises the role of Berta after performing it in every San Francisco Opera presentation of The Barber of Seville since 1996. The third performance of The Barber of Seville on Friday, June 5 will be livestreamed. Tickets, which includes a 48-hour on-demand viewing window that begins June 7 at 10 a.m., may be purchased online at sfopera.com/ digital/livestream. Founded by Director Emeritus Bee Chow in 1992, Cantabella has grown to serve children in the Tri-Valley area of Dublin, Livermore, and Pleasanton. Their spotlight performance will take place on July 15 at the First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley at 2407 Dana Street. Cantabella fosters choral artistry through the performance of music from all genres. They enhance music literacy using the Kodaly method as their pedagogical method. The choir develops healthy vocal technique for the singers through ensemble performance and group lessons. Most of all, Cantabella singers learn to cherish the joy of singing together. articles.text: of the years that I knew Alex, he never spoke of his compositions. May is a memorable month. It is notable for two celebrations. Nothing can be more beautiful than the celebration of Mother’s Day. This is hot on the heels of VE Day which commemorates the end of hostilities in Europe at the conclusion of World War II. That conflagration was the worst in human history. We must never forget. At the same time, we should remember some of the extraordinary things that happened. It was a miracle that music continued in the concentration camps. It is hard to imagine that the inmates performed concerts, composed music, and even created musical instruments. Many of these things are still in existence. We must remember… Shony Alex Braun was an important musician in Los Angeles for many years. Fortunately, he lived long enough that he could record some of his compositions and also speak his memories of those catastrophic years. In all They are truly memorable. In an interview which can be seen on the Internet, Alex tells a fantastic story. He was a youngster, waiting in line to be executed by the Nazis. The commanding officer noticed that Alex had a violin and asked him to play something on his violin. The performance moved the officer so much that he personally took Alex out of the execution line and saved his life. Alex is no longer with us, but his music and his memorable stories continue to inspire us. Very few of those people from that time are still with us. One of the last is Irene Perbal, who was born in 1933 in Amsterdam. She was a school mate of the famous writer Anne Frank. Despite her age, Irene retains a brilliant mind and an extraordinary ability to express herself. It would be marvelous to bring her to our area and speak in the Piedmont center for the arts as well as to instruct our young people on a better way

articles.text: Star Wars returns to theaters with a trusty duo, in theaters May 22 After seven years away from the big screen, Star Wars returns with its most reliable characters. The Mandalorian and Grogu brings Din Djarin and his Force-sensitive ward from Disney Plus to IMAX, trading streaming convenience for theatrical spectacle. The gamble appears to be paying off. Director Jon Favreau, who turned a bounty hunter and his adopted alien child into Disney Plus’s biggest phenomenon, now faces a different challenge: proving these characters deserve cinema real estate. Early screenings suggest he has cleared that hurdle, delivering action sequences designed for the biggest screens while maintaining the tone that made the series work. The plot picks up after the show’s third season. The New Republic enlists Djarin and Grogu to rescue Rotta the Hutt, son of the late Jabba, in exchange The Mandalorian and Grogu premiers in theaters May 22 for intelligence on Imperial remnants still threatening the galaxy. The mission structure gives Favreau room for what he does best: kinetic action, creature cantinas and that peculiar father-son dynamic between armored warrior and tiny green toddler. Production filmed entirely in California, a first for a Star Wars theatrical release, using a combination of practical sets and the Volume technology that revolutionized the series. The production received one of the largest allocations in California’s filming tax incentive program history, which speaks to the scale Lucasfilm wanted.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, May 13, 2026 Gemological Institute of America By Means of Tools - Metalsmithing and Machines David Cole will explore the art of the machine, providing an illustrated overview that delves into the intersection of technology and aesthetic expression. He will explore the role of machine tools within the realm of jewelry spanning both historical and modern contexts to show how mechanical precision has evolved. His presentation will detail the use of milling machines, lathes, ornamental turning engines, and pantographs. articles.text: Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on September 29, 2021. In my experience, the most difficult part of painting buildings is not finding the painting contractor, not the scraping, sanding or surface preparation, not dealing with the mess. The most difficult part is the selection of colors. Maybe this is because like most aspects of the architectural field, color selection is a curious mix of art and science, and…we all experience colors differently. Balancing the main color attributes of hue (color: red, blue, etc.), intensity (saturation or purity), and value (lightness/ darkness i.e., tints/shades) with other associated variables is simply a difficult job. In the end, from the bold, emotion-evoking colors of Mexican architects such as the famous Luis Barragan, to the restrained, subtle colors we are most familiar with in the Bay Area, exterior colors on a building reveal, perhaps more than anything else, the attitudes, ideas and personality of the owners. Building colors should first respond to the character, style, and detailing of the architecture. Schemes with multiple colors require a natural stopping/starting point for color changes such as a different material or corners and offsets in wall planes. Certain interior colors need also be coordinated, most notably curtains and shades which are seen through the windows and have to work with the exterior colors. Because all urban buildings are surrounded by neighboring buildings, as well as landscape planting, paving, and other elements, exterior color selection necessarily also involves urban design considerations; each building is part of a larger neighborhood palate. Evaluation of color requires certain steps to be successful. Most importantly, although not nearly done often enough, is to allow enough time for color selection and approval before painting starts. Once an attipainted on at least two different walls of the building with different natural light conditions. These must be allowed to dry for at least a few days before being evaluated. It is good for owners to then reflect on the samples at different times of the day for a good week before modifications are made or final approval given. This is all pretty complex, at least to me. If it’s one thing I’ve learned is that professional help (and patience) is essential in color selection. Color is mysterious, and what it does to the psyche is diverse. But the measure of success is simple in the end. It is the answer to the question: do you like it? Does it make you glad to be at that place? Does it, as Marie Kondo would ask, bring you joy? A fine example of a more “calm” color scheme that prioritizes, works with, and enhances the surrounding landscaping. Using somewhat similar colors, these two homes, after creative responses to the different architecture detailing, result in a very different feeling – both terrific! Many times, it is difficult to describe exactly why a color scheme is so attractive. But the important thing is to simply recognize it as good, and to know that you like it.

articles.text: On Monday, May 4, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had an excellent turnout of 21 participants at the Piedmont Community Hall for their monthly discussion. The weather was overcast and cool, so the group set up chairs inside the hall. They were there to talk about their May book, The God of the Woods by Liz Moore, a mystery novel. It was named a New York Times “Notable Book of the Year” and People Magazine’s #1 Book of the Year for 2024. This is the story of the disappearance of the daughter of the wealthy Van Laar family from their summer camp in 1975. It is very similar to the unsolved disappearance of her older brother years before. The setting is the camp, the Adirondack Mountains, and the Van Laar’s lavish estate. Within the plot, there are long-buried secrets of the affluent Van Laar family and the working-class community that serves them. As an inexperienced investigator unravels the mystery, a multi-threaded sequence of events with themes of class tension, family secrets, and the search for truth. The previous month, the group had read Secondhand Time: The Last of the Soviets by Belarusian Svetlana Alexievich, for which she won the Nobel Prize. This book tells the story of the demise of the USSR’s communist state through the feelings of everyday people as the country transitioned to capitalism. It may be an important book, but it is also a hard book to get through. It seemed the readers were ready for something lighter this month, and they had it with The God of the Woods. At just under 500 pages, it is not short but On hand were Marj Blackwell, Nancy Henn, Mary Carter, Lois Price, Gerry Gragg, Bill Ahern, Rob White, Adrienne Hamlin, Tim Weishahn, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Ken Young, Dale Benveniste, Lisa Euphrat, Susan Southworth, Rich Seigel, Odette Pollar, Susie Backer, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus.

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, May 13, 2026 First Monday Reading Group discusses The God of the Woods By Dick Carter On Monday, May 4, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had an excellent turnout of 21 participants at the Piedmont Community Hall for their monthly discussion. The weather was overcast and cool, so the group set up chairs inside the hall. They were there to talk about their May book, The God of the Woods by Liz Moore, a mystery novel. It was named a New York Times “Notable Book of the Year” and People Magazine’s #1 Book of the Year for 2024. This is the story of the disappearance of the daughter of the wealthy Van Laar family from their summer camp in 1975. It is very similar to the unsolved disappearance of her older brother years before. The setting is the camp, the Adirondack Mountains, and the Van Laar’s lavish estate. Within the plot, there are long-buried secrets of the affluent Van Laar family and the working-class community that serves them. As an inexperienced investigator unravels the mystery, a multi-threaded sequence of events with themes of class tension, family secrets, and the search for truth. The previous month, the group had read Secondhand Time: The Last of the Soviets by Belarusian Svetlana Alexievich, for which she won the Nobel Prize. This book tells the story of the demise of the USSR’s communist state through the feelings of everyday people as the country transitioned to capitalism. It may be an important book, but it is also a hard book to get through. It seemed the readers were ready for something lighter this month, and they had it with The God of the Woods. At just under 500 pages, it is not short but could be breezed through. It was a good not-quite-summer read. In fact, one reader listened to the audio version on a drive around Hawaii. The book brought back some readers’ childhood, summer camp memories, and experiences in the Adirondacks. The book was “a cut above most mysteries.” Many readers thought the novel was “fine,” but had issues with it. Generally, they “liked it,” but didn’t “love it” or “hate it.” It was an easy read, but “not great literature.” The readers enjoyed the relationships of the more than 40 characters, but some members of the group had to make lists to keep track of them. Readers found the dates at the start of each chapter helpful for keeping track of the narrative, but others didn’t like the author’s use of the common writer technique of short chapters and bouncing back and forth in time. Readers had issues with the characters, too. They didn’t like any of them. They were either all good or all bad people, and the rich were all bad people. That didn’t seem real. The townpeople On hand were Marj Blackwell, Nancy Henn, Mary Carter, Lois Price, Gerry Gragg, Bill Ahern, Rob White, Adrienne Hamlin, Tim Weishahn, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Ken Young, Dale Benveniste, Lisa Euphrat, Susan Southworth, Rich Seigel, Odette Pollar, Susie Backer, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. The God of the Woods written by Liz Moore were the rock on which the rich people depended. The book’s ending seemed “unbelievable,” “lame,” and even “hilarious” for one reader. Another reader found it surprising that the book was on the New York Times’ notable books list for the year. Overall, The God of the Woods was generally liked, but not loved. It was an entertaining mystery and an easy read. The stark difference from last month’s novel started a discussion about which of the two was a better or more worthwhile use of the readers’ time. This sparked reactions. “Could a book be a better read if 80% of the group didn’t want to read it?” “Aren’t there different reasons to read different types of books?” “Could a book be a medicine that might not taste good, but would make us better?” All good questions to be considered. However, the group seemed to agree that The God of the Woods was enjoyable and that was what the doctor had ordered for their May book. The readers had previously selected Barbarian Days – A Surfing Life by William Finnegan for its June book and Old Filth by English author Jane Gardam for July. Darby Gragg could not be with them this month, so Lois Price presented her three non-fiction candidates for the group’s August read, and the readers selected The Art Thief by Michael Finkel. With all their business done, they took a group photo on the patio outside the Community Hall. The group will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion on June 1 at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. Go to https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4, or call the Recreation Department at 510 420- 3070 to register. articles.text: The Wednesday before Mother’s Day meant it was time for the Piedmont Recreation Department Walking on Wednesdays group’s annual visit to the Morcom Rose Garden, up Jean Street on the other side of Grand Avenue. A good turnout of 38 walkers and six K-9 companions gathered at the Exedra on a lovely morning. As the walkers headed down Magnolia Avenue, they passed Nanci’s Musiktime near the Exedra, where young children were making music on the grass above the park’s tot lot. Also sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the program serves children ages 0 to 5 with singing, dancing, puppetry and instrument play led by instructor Nanci Schneidinger. The classes meet at the same time and place as Walking on Wednesdays. Continuing down Magnolia to Wildwood Avenue, the walkers passed homes lined with roses, California golden and yellow poppies, Mexican sage, birds-of-paradise and even a few dandelions in bloom. Near Grand Avenue, they encountered another Wednesday walking group. Children ages five and younger from Wildwood Children’s School were headed to the Dearing Park Wildwood Triangle for playtime beneath the redwoods. The children were all connected by a rope, prompting one walker to suggest something similar might better keep the Wednesday walkers together, too. The group paused briefly at Grand Avenue for an update on the long-delayed Shell Recharging Station project before crossing over and heading up Jean Street to the Morcom Rose Garden. At the entrance, framed by Sally Holmes roses in full bloom, the group gathered for a photo and a quick history lesson. The Rose Garden occupies Walkers entering Rose Garden Oakland Tribune, May 10, 1964 There were no roses in this hollow of Linda Vista Park when Oakland began its construction of a Rose Garden in 1933

articles.title: The History of Piedmont

articles.text: When addressing the history of central Piedmont, I would be remiss if I did not mention Piedmont’s Safeway store and other services. Hamby’s Market was the only grocery store in central Piedmont from 1915 to 1940. In addition to Hamby’s, Springman’s Pharmacy, and the Sweet Shop in the commercial center, Standard Oil operated a gas and service station by 1930. The expansion of Piedmont’s commercial center came after a long struggle. In 1929, the Piedmont City Council adopted an ordinance to allow businesses on Grand Avenue, on the west side from the city line to Linda Avenue, and on the east side from the city line to Fairview. Seven months later, voters turned down another zoning ordinance to extend the business district to Oakland Avenue. Today, the business district in Piedmont on Grand Avenue remains the same as it was in 1929. See more about the stores on Grand Avenue later in this article. More Stores For many years, the Piedmont City Council did “everything in its power to prevent the enlargement of the business district here,” according to news archives. Following a California Supreme Court decision in 1938, the Council reluctantly agreed to permit additional commercial development at Highland and Vista Avenues. In 1939, the Tidewater Oil Company built a gas station at the corner of Highland and Vista Avenues where Bank of America is currently located. It operated as the Flying A station into the late 1960s, when it became a Phillips 66 station. In 1940, Safeway Stores opened a new, modern supermarket at 333 Highland Avenue, occupying the space where both Citibank and Mulberry’s Market are located. Officials at Safeway wanted to meet the wishes of the residents on the architecture and invited Piedmonters to an open meeting at City Hall to review and comment on the plans for the architecture of the new store. As followers of Jesus the question we must face is “Are we teachable.” Are the congregations and communities that profess to follow Jesus teachable? Can we recognize that much of what we do in the name of Jesus is, in fact, far from Christ like? Will we change, adapt, learn? As human beings the question we must face is “Are we teachable?” Can we recognize the destruction that awaits if we continue of worship at the altar of war? Will we change, adapt, learn? Holy One, you created us to be teachable, help us to claim that identity in word and in deed. Amen. Rev. Jim Hopkins is the retired Senior Pastor of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland.

articles.text: In 1910, a group of Piedmont Church’s founding members gathered together to compose a Creed. The words reflect both the inclusive vision and the enduring mission that have guided our church for over 100 years. We favor a sane, simple and earnest piety, free alike from cant and extravagance. We assume no right to dictate to another his creed, but with charity for one another’s individual peculiarities of belief, we unite on the broad basis of the Christian religion as expressed in the following statements: God – We believe in God as the great Father of us all, who reveals Himself supremely in the person of His Son Christ Jesus our Lord, to whose life and character the Scriptures bear witness; and whose Holy Spirit continually upholds and guides all His children. Ourselves – We believe in trying to realize within ourselves lives of goodness, beauty, strength, and peace; and that the noblest career is one of mutual trust and helpfulness, after the example of Him who “went about doing good.” Others – But, besides believing that the principles of Christianity tend to the highest perfection of personal character, we hold that they make possible the greatest peace and happiness of communities, and that their hearty adoption would solve all the domestic and social problems of cities, states or nations. articles.text: Dear PUSD Families & Staff: It was wonderful to see so many elementary parents at this year’s Spring Fling. Thank you to Heather Frank, Bridget Schreiber, along with our Co-chairs Caroline, Jenny, & Zeena who did an amazing job with this year’s event. Thank you to our parents who attended and supported our efforts to fundraise for our elementary programs, including extra counseling services and field trips. As we close in on the end of the school year, I am reminded that this is the time of year we recognize our school community, our staff who do amazing work every day to make our students’ education possible. We begin the month on May 1st by honoring two essential groups: our school principals, whose vision and leadership shape our school culture, and our food services teams, the unsung heroes who “fuel” our students’ days...and yes, I am owning that awkward pun. We also celebrate National Teacher Appreciation Week (May 4-8), with National Teacher Appreciation Day on May 5 and California’s Day of the Teacher on May 13. Our gratitude extends as well to the specialists who do amazing work in support of student health and development: our school nurses, honored on National School Nurse Day (May 6), and our speech-language pathologists, recognized on National Speech Pathologist Day (May 18). If you have a moment this month, we encourage you to reach out to any of these dedicated professionals who have made a difference for your child. A simple note or kind word means more than you know. We close the month with Classified School Employee Week (May 17-23), a chance to thank the colleagues who keep our schools running: all of our staff who work behind the scenes with dedication and pride. To every member of our school community being recognized this month, thank you. articles.text: After 22 years with the City of Piedmont, Planning Director Kevin Jackson has decided to retire. pages.text: 2 2 Wednesday, May 6, 2026 Opinion By Jay Russell QUESTION: What made the Wildwood Dads Club Appreciation Day so great? Asked Tuesday, May 5, at the Chuck Corsica Golf Course in Alameda. ROHIT GIRI, Portsmouth Road The WWDC Appreciation Day gave me the opportunity to not only celebrate with fellow dads that I know but also to make new connections. RELIGION CORNER Mayo Clinic – The American Lourdes By Rev. Dr. William McNabb “Faith, hope and the healing of the spirit are the vital elements in the recovery of the whole person. Medicine treats disease, but healing embraces body, mind, and spirit. There is no substitute for the healing influence of human sympathy.” “There is no more important influence in the life of man than religion” –Dr. William Mayo My shuttle from the hotel was the Pink Line and the front of the vehicle was decorated with flamingo signs and figurines. Bess our unfailingly cheerful driver was dressed in a pink sweater, pink crocs and a headband from which sprouted two pink flamingos. The first thing you see when the shuttle drops you off at Mayo are the wheelchairs. Not just 10 or 20 but hundreds and hundreds an armada of blue wheelchairs waiting patiently for their riders to alight. Almost everyone you see is in a pair — a husband escorting a sick wife or a wife helping a sick husband. But also, a father helping the 20something son who lost a leg. Children who bore a resemblance to their wheelchair bound parent minus 30 years. In Europe people flock to shrines at Lourdes or Fatima because they are known to be places of healing. In a way the Mayo Clinis is the American Lourdes people come here from the world over to find healing. Instead of Christian faith that Lourdes runs on the Mayo Clinic runs on science — but the goal is the same. That is why I am here hoping for healing. When two young people stand at the altar to be married their vows often say “for better or for worse, for richer or poorer, in sickness and in health” they don’t linger on the meaning of those words. They are young and “health” and “sickness” seems far See Religion Corner on page 29 MIKE HAGERTY, La Salle Avenue What stood out most to me was hearing stories of other dads and their families, especially those I didn’t know well. Seeing many of them experience golf for the first time made it all the more enjoyable. SCOTT ZENGEL, Requa Place Dads from all Wildwood grades were able to join a wonderful, relaxed day of bonding after another great year of successful Dads club events to build community and raise money for the school. Highlights were the soccer golf follies, Michael Stearns hole-in-one, and an impressive cornhole finale! ALEX DANOFF, Harbord Drive, Oakland The dads brought amazing energy to the course and the cornhole boards. The vibes were immaculate. MIKE STEARNS, Grosvenor Place, Oakland The WWDC Appreciation Day was a great way to celebrate all of the success we had supporting Wildwood this year. We have a great group of dads that put in a lot of time and effort to raise funds for the school, so it’s a fun way for us to celebrate those efforts and wrap up the year. GREG WHEELER, Woodland Way What made it special was stepping off that bus in Alameda and realizing that the dads who showed up as strangers a few years ago are now genuine friends — a day like that celebrates not just the hard work, but the community we’ve built together. The world needs communitarians . . . it needs Augustans. Background Augusta had less than $20,000 in cash, and almost 5 months of unpaid bills in a pot-bellied stove amounting to more money than Augusta had to its name. There were no maps nor paper files. There was a dead computer with zero useful files on it. There are over 180,000 files now, not including media. Augusta had a one-page website. Now, it’s among the best camp websites nationally. The year before me, it ran with under 50 campers and only 2 villages for 4 weeks total. Augusta has been full for 22 summers straight, essentially without paid advertising. We have the top-tier camper return rate nationally. None of this would have been possible without the support / creation / dedication of over 800 staff and nearly 200 board members. My gratitude is immeasurable. Augusta is because they were and are. “To Reclaim and Foster the Beauty, Wonder, Awe, Potential and Innocence of Childhood” I wrote that vision statement after being at Augusta a couple of years. It’s been an honor and adventure to found and grow with this community and continually live into that vision and other community foundations. It’s been impactful in profound and diverse ways, as I hope it has been for you, too. Randall Grayson, the Camp Director of Camp Augusta Immortal? Nope. Dead? Nope, but one day and before death, my time at Augusta was destined to end, and that time is this year. I’m still here I’ll be doing the family camps, trainings, running story experiences, running peeps down in CTF, helping in tons of ways as usual, and ready to walk and talk as desired. And, after this season, I’ll be a 12-minute walk away in a house just up the road. I’ll be able to “grandparent” Augusta in the future, doing all the fun stuff as well as be available to help out here and there. Get ready for some sick SEs! :-) What’s in Randy’s future? After working for almost 35 years and 23 years at Augusta, I’ll turn my attention to a nonprofit I founded: https://ameaningoflife.org. From a scientific lens, it helps folks consider their lives more deeply and broadly, so they can live it more meaningfully and richly. From dating and friendship to purpose and ‘psychological richness,’ it’s a Swiss-army knife of practical wisdom for a life well lived. Twenty-three years ago ... with her worldly possessions stuffed into a bag, Annabelle Kerr was ready to board the bus for a two-week Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Editor: I remember when my family was moving from New York and they landed in Piedmont. There were a lot of great things about Piedmont but best of all were the schools. My dad’s work was located in Silicon Valley but we still decided to move here. I remember my mom telling me that Piedmont is not only a good school system but is strong across all three levels: elementary school, middle school, and high school. This has been evident to me through my years in all three Piedmont schools. The teachers are awesome, especially teacher Bracamonte who showed me the light in reading. But the problem is for these schools to thrive we need funding. Our schools have continued to be in the top percentage for testing throughout California because these dedicated teachers get top-notch materials to boost student learning. But this isn’t just for the kids. It’s also for all homeowners, because when we keep our schools strong, the quality of Piedmont as a whole goes up. The point is the school system is top notch, and keeping it that way makes the quality of Piedmont go up. So please vote Yes for Measure H to sustain our beautiful city and community. –Cyrus Emanuelson
articles.title: Keep Piedmont schools strong; vote Yes on Measure H

articles.text: Dear Editor, I appreciated last week’s article celebrating Mr. Ted Scherman — a true legend. My children were lucky to have him as both a teacher and camp counselor, and they agree without hesitation: that guy’s a legend. What struck me even more is how many legends my kids could name from their years in the district — more than a dozen educators each who were larger than life to them and who they’ll remember well into adulthood. They’ve also had many truly great teachers, and they can distinguish between the two. Great teachers teach the material well and support their students; legends went further. They pushed them to grow, forge real connections, and make learning stick in lasting ways. Their impact extended beyond the classroom — through lunch clubs, after-school programs, coaching, and simply being a visible, trusted presence in the community. My older kid, a Physics major, is taking a Chaucer class in college because he loved reading The Canterbury Tales his senior year with Dr. Marks. That’s legendary. Mr. Scherman is retiring alongside other such standouts. This represents a significant loss to our district and is likely the beginning of a larger wave of retirements. Piedmont has an unusually high concentration of great and legendary teachers. As a parent whose kids have spent a combined 14 years in this district, I am profoundly grateful to the adults who have taught them. This is also my final year in PUSD, as my youngest graduates. That perspective makes the moment feel especially urgent. I will be voting yes on Measure H because I care deeply that future classes will get to learn from great and legendary teachers, too. The conditions that once drew and kept these remarkable educators here are different, particularly for younger teachers. It’s up to all of us in this town to invest in the youngest residents. The adults who teach and have taught our kids are deeply invested in them. We need to do our part to ensure our schools will continue to attract and retain great and legendary teachers. –Sincerely, Liz Arney
articles.title: Vote yes on Measure H to attract and retain great and legendary teachers

My gratitude is immeasurable. Augusta is because they were and are. “To Reclaim and Foster the Beauty, Wonder, Awe, Potential and Innocence of Childhood” I wrote that vision statement after being at Augusta a couple of years. It’s been an honor and adventure to found and grow with this community and continually live into that vision and other community foundations. It’s been impactful in profound and diverse ways, as I hope it has been for you, too. Randall Grayson, the Camp Director of Camp Augusta By Randall Grayson Immortal? Nope. Dead? Nope, but one day and before death, my time at Augusta was destined to end, and that time is this year. I’m still here I’ll be doing the family camps, trainings, running story experiences, running peeps down in CTF, helping in tons of ways as usual, and ready to walk and talk as desired. And, after this season, I’ll be a 12-minute walk away in a house just up the road. I’ll be able to “grandparent” Augusta in the future, doing all the fun stuff as well as be available to help out here and there. Get ready for some sick SEs! :-) What’s in Randy’s future? After working for almost 35 years and 23 years at Augusta, I’ll turn my attention to a nonprofit I founded: https://ameaningoflife.org. From a scientific lens, it helps folks consider their lives more deeply and broadly, so they can live it more meaningfully and richly. From dating and friendship to purpose and ‘psychological richness,’ it’s a Swiss-army knife of practical wisdom for a life well lived. 23 years is a long time Tech: Google IPO (2004) / YouTube founded (2005) / Facebook started (2004) / iPhone (2007) / Instagram (2010) / Netflix streaming (2007) Politics: Obama (2008) / Same-Sex Marriage (2004) - Massachusetts / Death of Saddam Hussein (2006) / EU Expansion (2004) - 10 new nations join the EU, the largest single expansion in history. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council unanimously voted to award a $157,600 contract to EOA Inc. for the city’s Professional Clean Water Program and Municipal Regional Permit Compliance Services. Piedmont’s Clean Water Program is regulated by a Municipal Regional Permit, which is now in its third reissuance (MRP 3.0). Through MRP 3.0, the city is required to take actions that minimize pollution entering the stormwater system and the San Francisco Bay watershed. The MRP is an unfunded mandate administered by the San Francisco Regional Water Quality Control Board under the authority delegated by the Environmental Protection Agency. The city must submit an annual report to the Regional Water Board, outlining the implementation of the MRP 3.0’s 21 provisions that include, but are not limited to, the following requirements: • Maintaining stormwater management best practices at the City Corporation Yard. • Trash and debris management through street sweeping, installing and maintaining catch basin filters and public waste receptacles, and routinely monitoring litter in priority areas. • Inspecting and enforcing stormwater management best practices at construction sites and with local businesses. • Responding to spills and illicit discharges. • Developing and implementing an asset management and climate adaptation plan. • Enforcing and investing in low-impact and green infrastructure development and maintenance. “If anyone observes an oily substance, we want you to contact Public Works,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “We want to address it. We will go through the process of investigating and identifying the source with the residents. If it’s anything but rain, we don’t want it going down the drain.” If the city does not comply with the requirements of the MPR 3.0, it could face large fines. If the Regional Water Control Board enforces the federal Clean Water Act, the city could face $27,000 in penalties per day, not to exceed $342,000. If a citizen brings a complaint under federal law, it is $68,000 per day, with no cap. The proposed contract with EOA provides for a one-year term of $157,600, with the option to renew for two additional oneyear periods. The total amount is $472,800 if the contract is renewed twice. divisions from Public Works, and in 2019, he created the Planning & Building department. Jackson reflected on his time as director and was proud of the work he did to update the zoning code, building code, and the city’s design guidelines. “That was a good-sized project. It was quite enjoyable working not just to update the provisions in it, but reformat it in a modern formatting style,” Jackson continued. “We also updated the design guidelines as part of that project, as well, to finish out the 5th cycle housing element. So those were two big projects, policy-wise, that we undertook that we’re proud of.” It wasn’t just the projects that Jackson enjoyed. The hiring process was his favorite part of the job. “The thing that really pays off the most is the hiring, bringing somebody on board who shows initiative and is excited about the job is great. I give staff several hats to wear so that they stay engaged and grow professionally. And so that usually pays off in the work product as well,” Jackson explained. Jackson hopes residents remember his time with the department as “responsive to their needs as determined by the state.” In retirement, Jackson is looking forward to spending more time traveling. He has a trip to England planned in June, then visits to Switzerland, Lake Como, Italy, and Lubbock, Texas next year. He also plans to read more novels and possibly volunteer for a local non-profit.

articles.text: Payam Music opens first East Bay piano school in Piedmont Payam Music Director Dennis Ni outside the school with teachers Kiara Kramer, Gail Gallagher, and Judah Arrington. Payam Music opened its first piano school in the Easy Bay this past March at 4390 Piedmont Avenue. The school was founded in 2015 by Payam Khastkhodaei with the intention of innovating the way piano is taught to make it easier and fun for beginners. As a kid, Khastkhodaei really enjoyed playing the piano, but hated his lessons, which caused him to quit. He missed the piano so much that he eventually began playing again, rediscovering his love for it. It was in college, where he studied developmental psychology in pediatrics, that he developed a groundbreaking teaching methodology. “He was learning about language acquisition, and he thought hold on a moment. When people learn a new language they always learn to speak it first. If music is a language, then why is it taught the opposite way? He started teaching piano using what is now what we call the Payam method, which uses letters and numbers,” explained Chief Marketing Officer Deborah Kelson. The methodology uses alphanumeric notation rather than traditional sheet music to teach students to speak piano in a language they already know. Starting with letters and numbers to build confidence from day one. This has helped students understand intervals and note relationships sooner than the traditional sheet music. With the school’s in-house curriculum, every student learns based on their abilities, interests, and progress. They teach tradiTeachers personalize each lesson using Payam Music’s proprietary curriculum instead of traditional song books. tional classical music and pop or K-pop songs to bring fun into learning. “We have all of these songs that kids recognize and love, and so they’re really inspired to play, but also, because of the alphanumeric notation I mentioned, they’re able to play a song that they recognize by the end of their first lesson,” said Kelson. This innovative methodology has helped 96% of Payam Music students achieve a diploma level within four years, compared to a 2% national average for students reaching diploma level (in 12 years). Payam Music students even participate in a national arts competition. Every year, about 300,000 students participate in the National PTA Reflections Competition. In 2025, 15 of the school’s students won their district, with the majority being new to the competition, and four out of five state winners and national qualifiers came from the school. “We’re building a movement that challenges the traditional model of music education. Our methodology creates an environment where learning feels like play, and success is a natural result of students falling in love with piano,” said Khastkhodaei. Piedmont is currently the school’s fastest-growing location, and the school credits this to the community. “We really look for strong communities where education and music are valued. We want to find places where people are really excited about high-quality after-school enrichment. Those are the communities where we tend to open,” said Kelson. The company currently has eight locations open, with expansion plans for 2026. Lessons begin at age four with no upper age limit. Readers can sign up for a free orientation and a private one-on-one lesson on the company’s website, https://www.payammusic.com/.

articles.text: On Wednesday, May 6, Piedmont School Board will convene for a regularly scheduled meeting in the District office (760 Magnolia Avenue). The meeting will include the presentation of the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year award to Chris Hart. There will also be a presentation on the Elementary Reading and Math Intervention Program. The presentation aims to identify strengths, gaps and opportunities to improve equity and consistency. Intervention via pull-out intervention currently serves 6-11% of all Piedmont elementary school students. Invention cycles last around six weeks but vary per site. Also of interest to parents and students is an update on the Mobile Device policy. Superintendent Hawn will relay the findings from the year which has limited student usage of mobile devices. “While current data shows positive trends in student wellness and reduced classroom distractions, surveys reveal some friction: students report a “sneaking culture” and dissatisfaction, while teachers have grown more supportive of stricter rules steer students toward any particular pathway or to push early acceleration into honors or AP coursework. Rather, it is meant to give families the information they need to make fully informed decisions about course selection in grades 6–12 as they plan for college and career. Thank you to our counselors and administrators for their feedback and input on this document and for their remarkable support of our students and families in their pursuit of the best options for their students.

Also of interest to parents and students is an update on the Mobile Device policy. Superintendent Hawn will relay the findings from the year which has limited student usage of mobile devices. “While current data shows positive trends in student wellness and reduced classroom distractions, surveys reveal some friction: students report a “sneaking culture” and dissatisfaction, while teachers have grown more supportive of stricter rules but struggle with inconsistent enforcement and students shifting their use to Chromebooks,” the board background document states.” The meeting may be attended in person at 760 Magnolia Avenue or by logging onto Zoom.us/ j/87564012705?pwd=t3y9VbqbWiARC4omRXjG8d8UqhrPlQ.1 Piedmont Pulse Continued from page 1 and our students and families are grateful, as am I. articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School and High School Music Departments invite the community to their annual Spring Concerts, featuring performances by instrumental and choral music students. All concerts will be held at the Alan Harvey Theater on the Piedmont High School campus. • Tuesday, May 19th at 7:00 p.m. The evening will kick off with the Middle School Orchestra directed by Shauna Revelli. Experience a rich and dynamic program featuring arrangements of timeless masterpieces by J.S.Bach and Ralph Vaughan Williams, alongside the electrifying energy of Coldplay’s Viva la Vida. The evening reaches a finale with the combined 6th–12th grade orchestra musicians performing Carnival of the Animals by Camille Saint-Saëns, under the direction of PHS and PMS music teachers Trevor Chaix and Revelli. • Wednesday, May 20th at 7:00 p.m. The Middle School bands, under the direction of Mary Rees, will light up the stage with the music of Michael Jackson and The Weeknd, a vibrant arrangement of Stevie Wonder’s iconic funk classic Superstition, and the evocative One Summer’s Day from the anime film Spirited Away. In addition, the PHS Jazz Band will make a cameo appearance. • Thursday, May 21st at 7:00 p.m. The final concert of the week features four PHS ensembles – Choir, String Orchestra, Symphonic Band, and Jazz Band – under the direction of Trevor Chaix. The eveing concludes with the presentation of the Senior Music Awards. Travel from the big screen to the concert hall with music from Mulan, Ratatouille, How to Train Your Dragon, and La La Land. The Choir will bring the spirit of the ‘60s to life with hits from The Beach Boys, The Mamas and the Papas, and The Beatles. The Symphonic Band will have you grooving to the timeless sounds of ABBA, while the Orchestra performs the beloved Carnival of the Animals by Camille Saint-Saëns. And don’t miss the Jazz Band’s take on Love Me or Leave Me, famously performed by Ella Fitzgerald. Admission To help offset concert expenses a $5 donation is requested. Students attend for free. articles.text: First grade Daisy Girl Scout Troop #32605 celebrated a year of service with an end of year party at the Piedmont pool on Sunday, April 19. The troop is made up of 17 girls from Wildwood School and is led by troop leader Anne Wheeler. The pool party was a celebration of what they have done together from collecting over 600 books for a local non-profit, to participating in the annual Piedmont Derby race. The troop worked hard on their engineering skills at the Roller Coaster Design badge hosted by Wildwood’s 4th grade Girl Scout troop and, participated in the annual Girl Scout tea. The troop of 1st graders looks forward to next year when they will earn more art, entrepreneurship and life skills badges. The troop will take to the woods as well during next year’s 2nd grade campout as a Brownie Troop. Photo by Katy Bradford First grade Daisy Girl Scout Troop #32605 celebrated a year of friendship and Scouting with a pool party on April 19.
