articles.text: Photos by Xinjia Xia Honors Chinese 4 was named the winner for period 5 for their rendition of “青苹果乐园” (Green Apple Paradise). At Piedmont High School the language department Singing Competition has become one of the most anticipated student events of the year. The competition is a lively showcase where music, culture, and classroom creativity converge. This semester’s lineup delivered an especially dynamic mix of performances, with each class bringing its own personality, language focus, and artistic flair to the stage. The day started with a win for an energetic performance by Ms. Freeland’s Spanish 3 class as they kicked things off with a bold mashup of “Danza Kuduro” and “NUEVAYoL.” The group’s confidence set a high bar early in the competition. Following that, Senora Sahagon’s AP Spanish class in period 2 took a different approach, leaning into nostalgia with “Ahora Te Puedes Marchar / Noches de Verano.” Their performance balanced humor and vocal strength, weaving together storytelling and expressive acting. Ms. Guillen’s Spanish 2 class brought a modern pop vibe with “Mía” in period 3. Their polished delivery and strong group cohesion made for a smooth, engaging performance. While less theatrical than some others, their consistency and musicality earned them steady applause. One of the most talked-about acts came from the middle school, with Shannon Fierro’s Spanish 1 class who delivered a high-energy Bad Bunny mashup featuring “Tití,” “DTMF,” and “Nueva Yol.” Their enthusiasm was infectious, and despite being younger than most competitors, they commanded the stage with surprising confidence. The crowd especially responded to their playful choreography and bold song choices. The competition then shifted linguistically and stylistically with Ms. Xia’s Chinese 4 Honors class, who performed in period 5. The cultural contrast added richness to the event, reminding the audience of the diversity within the language program. Ms. Xia’s Chinese 2 students won period 6 with a medley that stood out for its emotional range, moving from lighthearted and playful to reflective and bittersweet. The transitions between songs were handled smoothly, and their expressive delivery resonated strongly with the audience. Closing the competition was Ms. Freeland’s Spanish 3 which dominated period 7, featuring an original song titled “Sueño Grande,” written by student Eli Hauser. The performance was a standout moment, not just for its originality, but for its sincerity. The lyrics, centered on ambition and identity, gave the piece a personal depth that set it apart from the covers and mashups. Overall, this year’s competition highlighted not only musical talent but also the creativity and cultural engagement fostered within Piedmont High’s language programs. From reggaeton mashups to original songwriting to Mandarin classics, each performance reflected the unique voice of its class. More than just a contest, the event served as a celebration of language learning brought to life through music. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern reporter with the Piedmont Post. Wildwood Cornholer of the Year. “This year found a better showing of appreciation for Wildwood Dads through a more inclusive approach and a broader set of activities, which meant more fun for everyone involved,”said Hagerty. The group refuels after golf.

articles.text: If the past few weeks felt full of climate conversation, you’re not alone. Between Earth Day and San Francisco Climate Week, people across the Bay Area have been surrounded by big ideas, activism, innovation, and urgency. And then, just like that, the calendar turns. The question is: what happens next? For some families, this is familiar territory. For others, it can feel overwhelming. Environmental justice work is deeply important, but it’s hard to know where to begin. What many adults underestimate is how much kids are already thinking about it. Today’s young people are far more aware of environmental change than many of us were at their age. Climate isn’t an abstract future problem; it already takes up real mental space, sometimes showing up as worry or anxiety. This must also shift the way we talk about and activate our responsibility in a more complicated time for our planet. I have vivid memories of family hikes on Earth Day or trying out non-aerosol hair products, small choices that felt somehow connected to the planet’s health. But while I grew up hearing that “kids are the future,” it didn’t feel as immediate or personal. My teenagers talk far more passionately about environmental issues in our community—like the impact flooding has on the health of our watersheds or the safety of our public transit systems—than I did when I was growing up. For many young people in the Bay Area, these changes are already immediate and local. At the Exploratorium, we have a literal front-row seat to climate change. From Piers 15 and 17, visitors encounter sea level rise not as an abstraction, but as something you can see and measure. So it’s no surprise we use this as an opportunity to turn our experiences and concerns into curiosity about what is happening, why it’s happening, and what we can do. One of the most striking ways to see this is during King Tides. A few times a year, alignment between the sun and the earth during a new or full moon raises tides one or two feet higher than normal. Along the waterfront, water will spill onto sidewalks, roadways, and even into homes and businesses. As many young people know, today’s extreme King Tides are the high tides of tomorrow. Once you’ve seen it, the questions come naturally: What happens next? Who is affected? What can be done? These shared moments matter because they make something big feel tangible. Later this year, the Exploratorium will open a free public field station on our front plaza—an outdoor space with exhibits and art focused on climate change and sea level rise, designed to bring more of these conversations into the open. But you don’t need to wait for an event or exhibit to keep the conversation going. Start at home. Notice what’s around you. Older kids and teens might track household energy use or learn about the watershed in their community. For younger children, a simple activity like Melting Ice and Rising Seas can help make those big ideas visible. Climate change is real, and it can feel overwhelming. But it’s also a space for curiosity, creativity, and shared problem-solving. So don’t let Earth Day be the only day this comes up. Keep asking. Keep noticing. Keep learning together. Because the most important part of the conversation isn’t having it once— it’s continuing it. Try the Melting Ice and Rising Seas activity at home, and explore more hands-on science at exploratorium.edu/snacks Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. An enthusiastic Exploratorium visitor for over four decades, Dr. Taylor champions the power of hands-on discovery: that real learning lives not in what we’re told, but in what we touch, question, and experience for ourselves—in classrooms, communities, and the curious moments of daily life. Families gather at an Exploratorium event to observe and learn about King Tides along the waterfront. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont High School girls’ lacrosse coach Carlton Chan officially steps down after eight years in charge. Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse coach Carlton Chan announced he is stepping down from his role following eight years at the helm. Chan was an assistant coach on the team in 2018 and was promoted to the lead role the following year. He helped lead PHS to the Division 2 North Coast Section title in 2019, and won Western Alameda County Conference titles in 2019 and 2024. He led the team to an NCS Finals appearance in 2025. Before Piedmont High, Chan coached at Skyline Lacrosse Club, which has been a feeder program for both the boys’ and girls’ sides. “I’ve been coaching for 20 years in total. When I coached U11 at Skyline the first season we went 0-11. The very last game, we finally scored a point. I thought, ‘Oh, this wasn’t a successful season,’ but then every girl came back. So, my measure of success then was just getting every girl to come back and play. That’s been my goal every single year; not necessarily to win or lose, but to make sure the girls had a great experience,” Chan said. Piedmont’s 2019 team was possibly its best team of all time. Elie Cole, Zoe Torok, Lily Keville, Widdy Tevis, and current assistant coach Sadie Tschider each went on to play at the collegiate level. His daughter Maria, eventually went on to play for the Coast Guard Academy. Tevis and Maria were juniors on that team, while Tschider was a sophomore and later became the school’s alltime leader in assists. “That same team was almost the same group of girls I coached in U11. We were good and had really strong players, and went up against great teams like Miramonte and Boo Dewitt, who was an All-American and plays at Florida. The focus of that group of girls was to get kids to play together. To get them to play as a team was in large part that they played so many years together. articles.text: Nate Welch, Ari Moskovitz place 4th in doubles Tennis star Lucas Smolko got the job done in his final Western Alameda County Conference tournament, winning the singles title for the third straight time on Saturday, May 2 at Chabot College in Hayward. He becomes the first male boys’ athlete to win three straight WACC titles and the second Piedmont High athlete to do so after Kaelli Thiel won the girls’ tournament in 2012, 2013, and 2015. Smolko faced Castro Valley’s Guhan Anandkumar in the final, winning in straight sets 6-2, 6-3. Smolko also faced Anankumar in last year’s semifinals, which featured strange mind games from the Trojans’ starter. Lucas was prepared for any antics, once again, and dispatched him handily. “It’s great to make history… Playing Guhan is tricky, I was thinking about it a lot going into today. I knew this match was inevitable and I’d end up playing Guhan in the final. I just knew to block out any mind games and if there are problems, not to be afraid to ask for line judges,” Smolko said. To get there, Smolko entered as the top seed, beating Alameda’s Johnny Sanchez 6-0, 6-1 in the first round. He followed up with a 6-0, 6-2 win over Castro Valley’s Matthew Rodriguez in the quarterfinals, and then defeated Bishop O’Dowd’s Marcello Sachelari 6-1, 6-3 in the semifinals. articles.text: Several individual victories The West Alameda County Conference championships on Friday, May 1 at Chabot College in Hayward proved to be a milestone meet for Piedmont High School, highlighted by record-breaking performances, personal bests, and a historic team victory. The meet marked a historic achievement for the program, as the Piedmont boys captured their first-ever WACC team title. As a result, they enter the North Coast Section Championships on Friday and Saturday, May 8-9 in Novato. “I am extremely proud of their hard work this season. I’m very happy they did not throw me into the pool in celebration,” coach Elizabeth Dally said with a laugh. Leading the charge was the boys’ medley relay team, which delivered a standout performance with a time of 1:31.81 in a field of 15 teams, setting a new Piedmont High School record while also breaking WACC record. The 200 medley relay lineup featured Asher Takazawa (backstroke), Cole Carnazzo (breaststroke), Connor Carnazzo (butterfly), and Nik Costello (freestyle). They topped second-place Alameda by nine seconds. All three boys relay teams qualified for the NCS Championships, including the medley, 200 freestyle, and 400 freestyle teams. On the girls’ side, the medley and 400 freestyle relay The boys’ 200 medley relay team stands with the WACC Championship banner. Pictured are Asher Takazawa (left), Nik Costello, Connor Carnazzo, and Cole Carnazzo. teams also secured spots at NCS. The 200 free team of Connor Carnazzo, Anton Secor, Zafar Majid, and Dima Secor posted a winning time of 1:28.88 in a field of 23 teams. The boys’ 400 free team of Takazawa, Cole Carnazzo, Costello, and Dima Secor won their event in 3:09.02 against 16 other schools. Individually, Dima Secor set a new school record in the 200 individual medley with a time of 1:54.40, beating 21 other swimmers. Takazawa recorded personal bests in both the 100 backstroke (51.15) and 100 butterfly (50.71). He won backstroke in a field of 25, while he was second of 26 in the flu. Costello took home two individual wins on the afternoon. He won the 50 free with a time of 21.26 in a field of 51 swimmers, while he clocked a 46.44 in the 100 free to win in a field of 46. Ryan Mak, a freshman, won two individual events as well. He won the 200 free in 1:43.02 in a field of 30 swimmers, and won the 500 free in 4:38.36 against 21 others. Connor Carnazzo (left) and Nik Costello pose with their first-place medals. Costello won four events in total at the WACC Championship. Connor Carnazo won the 100 fly in 50.66, while he also notched a personal best in the 50 freestyle with 21.81 as part of the 200 freestyle relay team. On the girls’ side, senior leader Sam White won two individual events. She won the 200 freestyle in 2:00.86 in a field of 32 swimmers, while she clocked a winning time of 5:23.08 in the 500 free against 20 other athletes. Both are NCS consideration times. Piedmont’s 200 medley relay team of Cynthia Wu, Indie Briskman, Sofia Vuori, and White automatically qualified for NCS by clocking a time of 1:52.92 to finish third of 21 teams. The 400 freestyle team of Charlotte Zhang, Vuori, White, and Wu also qualified for NCS with a time of 3:51.31 to place second of 18 teams. NEXT UP Piedmont will compete at the NCS championships, with eyes set on advancing to the state meet. The boys medley relay enters NCS as the top seed, fueling optimism for a spot at the CIF State Swimming Championships.
articles.title: Boys Swimming makes history at WACC Championship

articles.text: The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team had a historic day at Stafford Lake on Sunday, May 3, closing out a season that included two rainouts and only three completed races before the championship races coming up in two weeks. Racing in the East Bay/ Central League, Division 2, Piedmont High School earned 2nd place as a team for the day — the team’s first podium finish in memory — and finished 3rd overall for the season. The Stafford Lake course was demanding, with the high school race covering about 4 miles and 500 feet of climbing per lap, including steep climbs and technical descents. The Devo, junior development, course for middle school racers was shorter but still challenging, at about 2.4 miles and 400 feet of climbing. The biggest moment of the day came from senior and Co-Captain Jasper Schuetz, who won the Varsity Boys race by 40.5 seconds after four laps, finishing in 1:10:36.64. It was an emotional and long-awaited victory for Jasper, who has been working toward this goal for years. He was a series leader as a freshman, finished 2nd in JV1 as a sophomore, and finally reached his dream of winning a varsity race. With the win, Jasper secured the leader’s jersey for the 2026 Varsity season, as the fastest mountain biker in the East Bay/Central League. He will be competing in the Unbound Gravel, a 200-mile race in Emporia, Kansas at the end of the month. and plans to join the CalPoly SLO Cycling Team next year. The Piedmont girls also made history. Josephine Schuetz continued her first place winning streak in the JV2 Girls race. Mina Herrgott placed 5th for her first podium, and Olivia Bailey finished 6th on the day. In the season standings, Josephine finished 1st, Olivia 4th, and Mina 5th, a momentous milestone for Piedmont girls racing. Piedmont also saw breakthrough podium finishes from Zachary Carter, who placed 2nd in JV1 Boys D2, and Kai Hsu, who placed 5th in JV2 Boys D2. Piedmont High School Mountain Bike team: Olivia Bailey, Josie Schuetz, Mina Herrgott, William Carter, Kai Hsu, Jasper Schuetz, Jack Mendelsohn, Gabriel Barbosa, Zachary Carter. Not pictured, Caleb Canada, Emilio Roberts, and Chase Mellers. Jasper Schuetz won the Varsity Boys race at Stafford Lake.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team suffered an 11-6 loss to Bishop O’Dowd in the Western Alameda County Conference Tournament’s semifinals on Wednesday, April 29 at Witter Field. Piedmont beat O’Dowd 11-9 during their regular season on April 17. One year earlier PHS beat O’Dowd in the regular season before losing in the tournament. The Highlanders struggled to maintain possession in the meeting, committing turnovers at critical moments throughout the night. “Overall, if I take a step back to look at it, it was energy, focus, and just desire. O’Dowd came better prepared and wanted it more; you could just tell from the get-go. We were a little flat, especially in the first half,” said PHS coach Andy Kittler. Also dissimilar from the regular season win, Piedmont struggled to create shooting space against O’Dowd’s aggressive defense. “We’re a good second half team and didn’t come out wanting it. We didn’t prepare ourselves to start hot; we know what we need Connor Fredericks scored four goals against the Dragons. Timmy Kalamas scored twice for Piedmont. Piedmont suffered an 11-6 loss to rival Bishop O’Dowd in the WACC Tournament semifinals. Staff Photos to do, it’s just an execution problem,” Kittler said. But the season is not over. PHS opened its Division 2 North Coast Section postseason yesterday, May 5, as the No. 6 seed hosting No. 11 Las Lomas. Results were not complete by Post time. “It’s not over. To some kids, it probably feels like it’s over because this game with O’Dowd is the one that really mattered to them. But we have NCS and we can still go far, but it starts with the want-to. They have to earn it,” Kittler said. Match Recap Piedmont struck first at the 10:41 mark in the opening quarter when Connor Fredericks made a long run from behind the net to whip a shot in. Fredericks scored again on a longshot from a few yards outside the circle with 4:47 left to knot it up at two. However, O’Dowd went on a three goal run from there to end the quarter with a 5-2 lead. In the second quarter, Timmy Kalamas scored a minute and 12 seconds into the action to cut the deficit to 5-3. But after that, the Dragons scored another three consecutive to extend the gap to 8-3 with 7:24 on the clock. Fredericks turned the following faceoff into a quick goal just eight seconds late, but PHS only recorded one shot attempt in the remaining minutes. O’Dowd scored once more with 1:27 remaining, making it 9-4 at halftime. Kalamas had a shot saved 45 seconds into the third, but the Dragons scored its 10th two minutes later. After back and forth possessions, Fredericks got PHS on the board with 37 seconds left to make it 10-5. In the fourth, PHS started to pull the trigger midway through the quarter with shots on target by Kalamas and Lukas Toth. However, BOD got its final goal with 4:49 to play. Piedmont got its final goal of the game by Kalamas with 1:33 on the block. Final stats: Fredericks had four goals, gathered five ground balls, and won 16 face-offs. Kalamas scored twice. Jax Thayer had seven ground ball recoveries. Tuesday vs. Las Lomas No. 6 Piedmont hosted No. 11 Las Lomas for the first round of the D2 NCS tournament on Tuesday, May 5. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP With a win on Tuesday, Piedmont (6-7 overall) will face the winner of No. 3 Miramonte vs. No. 14 Sonoma Valley on Thursday, May 7.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team suffered a dramatic 8-7 loss to Berkeley at the Yellowjackets home field on Wednesday, April 29 to end their season, With an overall season record of 6 wins and 11 defeats, the Highlanders’ missed out on a berth in the North Coast Section playoffs. The loss came with some controversy, where Berkeley’s time keepers gave its team a huge favor at the end of the first quarter. The Highlanders committed a foul outside of the 12-meter circle with 12 seconds left on the clock. By rule, the clock should have continued rolling, but BHS stopped the clock, allowing their team to make a play in the process. Berkeley wound up scoring, which ultimately became the difference in the match. “It was a good game, but it came with some controversy. In the first quarter the clock should have run out. Instead, the Berkeley folks stopped the clock and that allowed Berkeley just enough time to make a run to the goal and score. That score mattered and Peyton Watson scored three goals in the final game of her Piedmont High career. Staff Photos Piedmont’s lacrosse season came to an end after falling 8-7 to Berkeley in the WACC Tournament semifinals. Sydney Latvala scored twice for Piedmont against Berkeley.

Berkeley wound up scoring, which ultimately became the difference in the match. “It was a good game, but it came with some controversy. In the first quarter the clock should have run out. Instead, the Berkeley folks stopped the clock and that allowed Berkeley just enough time to make a run to the goal and score. That score mattered and See Girls’ Lacrosse on page 27 Peyton Watson scored three goals in the final game of her Piedmont High career. Staff Photos Piedmont’s lacrosse season came to an end after falling 8-7 to Berkeley in the WACC Tournament semifinals. Sydney Latvala scored twice for Piedmont against Berkeley.

articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School Softball Scots coached by Steve Gregovich are currently on an extended road trip, They played four games in a week, posting a 3-1 record against various teams around the Bay Area. 13-3 win over Claremont Middle School On April 24, the Scots took down Oakland’s Claremont Middle School in a game that highlighted their strong 6th-grade class. Cate Penrod set the tone in the first two innings from the circle, holding the Claremont Knights hitless while striking out five. The offense came alive in the later stages of the game for the Scots. Key contributions from Olive Dao-Hoang, skillfully earned four walks, and Gigi Weber, who swung a big bat, going 3-for-3 with two RBIs on a sharply hit double. 4-3 loss to Montera Middle School Next came the lone loss of the week on April 27, against Oakland’s Montera Middle School. Piedmont spared nothing and brought their 8th-grade aces, getting stellar performance from Bailey Gregovich with zero earned runs, one hit, six strikeouts, over two innings. Madi Farboud pitched just as well, two earned runs, four hits, four strikeouts over three innings. In the end, the Scots fell to the rival Montera Toros due to a few miscues on defense and an inability to scratch out the key hit when they had runners in scoring position. Sixth-grader Keira Spina showed poise in the field at third and delivered one of Piedmont’s two hits. Keep an eye out for the rematch this Friday, May 8. 14-3 win over the Lazear Charter Academy The third game, played on April 29, saw the Scots leverage their experience and depth to easily handle an overmatched Oakland Lazear Charter Academy team. Mackenzie Ewen kept the opponent from pouncing early with two hitless innings and six strikeouts. The Scots patient approach at the plate yielded a few walks, and they took advantage of the few strikes they saw to generate offense against the Lazear Wildcats. Seventh-grader Evie Joerger drove in three runs, and eighth-graders Abby Gregovich and Simone Tornatore each racked in a pair of RBIs on well-struck doubles. May 1 at Edna Brewer Mille School The final contest of the week, on May 1, was a bit anticlimactic as Oakland’s Edna Brewer Middle School Panthers were short several players and had to forfeit. The teams nevertheless faced off in a congenial scrimmage that provided a low-stress way to focus on the fundamentals of defense and base running. More games to come The Scots continue their road trip this week with games on May 4 against Berkeley’s King Middle School, May 5 against Berkeley’s Longfellow Middle School, May 6 against West Oakland Middle School. The highly anticipated rematch with Montera Middle School is on May 8. ®

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Asian Art Museum The exhibition focuses on a new generation of Japanese potters. “New Japanese Clay” is on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco now through June. The exhibition brings together modern and contemporary works that reimagine a centuries-old tradition in Japanese ceramics. Infused with vivid color and sculptural ambition, the pieces range from rugged, earthbound forms that evoke stone and soil to delicate constructions that appear as light as paper or billowing fabric. Museum officials said the exhibition reflects both Japan’s rich ceramic history and the increasingly global nature of contemporary art training and practice, as well as materials used. The exhibition focuses on a new generation of Japanese potters who are expanding the expressive possibilities of clay. Robert Mintz, who organized the exhibition, said the featured artists build on the legacy of the mingei, or folk art, movement while forging distinctly experimental paths. “The artists in New Japanese Clay are challenging the conventions of functional ceramics and pivoting toward a purely sculptural experience,” Mintz said in a statement. “Their creations are meant to intrigue and delight; the vessel form is just a point of departure for spectacular experimentation.” For more information, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/new-japanese-clay/.
articles.title: “New Japanese Clay” exhibit on view through June at Asian Art Museum exhibition

articles.text: Visit the Treasure Island Museum’s free public gallery to view its growing permanent collection and learn more about the island’s three defining eras: the 1939–40 Golden Gate International Exposition, the island’s decades as a U.S. Naval station, and its ongoing redevelopment. The museum is operated by a nonprofit that preserves the island’s little-known, Pacific-themed heritage. The 1939 Exposition was held on Treasure Island in celebration of the city’s two newly-built bridges. The U.S Navy then acquired the land to use as a Naval Station from 1941 to 1997. The permanent collection includes artifacts from the exposition, such as decorative objects and cultural items, as well as photographs, postcards and ephemera that chronicle civilian and military life on the island. Artifacts range from exhibition objects like decorative Chinese dragons and a 16th-century Siamese ceramic bowl to mid-century memorabilia such as a baby contest trophy from the world’s fair. The collection also includes extensive photographs, postcards and ephemera documenting daily life on the island across generations. A mural on the museum’s back wall was designed by photo-realist Lowell Nesbitt, measuring 251 feet long and 26 feet high. The piece was commissioned for the opening of the museum, and represents scenes in the history of the Navy and Marine Corps in the Pacific since 1813. Treasure Island Museum has also developed an online collection that provides public access to digitized materials. Among the highlights is The Masthead, the naval base’s weekly newspaper, with issues from the World War II era available for viewing. Treasure Island Museum is open to the public Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and 12 p.m. to 7 p.m. on weekends. Visit https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/visit to learn more about the museum’s in-person and online offerings, and to view upcoming events and speaker series engagements. The museum is open seven days a week. Photo courtesy of SF.gov
articles.title: Treasure Island Museum offers glimpse into island’s rich past

articles.text: Showing at Toni Rembe Theater now through May 24 Photo courtesy of American Conservatory Theater The play features Kemi-Bo Jacobs as Agnes and Rory Alexander as William. American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) in San Francisco closes out its 2025-26 season with the US premiere of Hamnet, showing onstage now through May 24. Adapted by Lolita Chakrabarti, who adapted the critically-acclaimed book Life of Pi, and directed by Erica Whyman, the play explores what happens when the plague steals 11-year-old Hamnet from his loving parents, Agnes and William Shakespeare, and they must each confront their loss alone. The death of Shakespeare’s son Hamnet has been thought to have influenced his writing, specifically his great tragedy Hamlet. Hamnet made its world premiere in April 2023 at the Swan Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon, and has its West Coast premiere on the A.C.T. stage. The play features Kemi-Bo Jacobs as Agnes and Rory Alexander as William. The creative team includes set and costume designer Tom Piper, lighting designer Prema Mehta, sound designer Simon Baker, music composer Oğuz Kaplangi, and movement director Ayşe Tashkiran. “I am delighted to be revisiting this extraordinary story for U.S. audiences, and to be making this production with a stellar line-up of performers,” Director Whyman said in a press release. “Kemi-Bo Jacobs and Rory Alexander are bringing Agnes and William alive on the stage with a luminous intelligence and a profound and shocking understanding of the love and loss that shaped their lives.” Visit https://www.act-sf. org/whats-on/2025-26-season/ hamnet/performances for showtimes and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: A.C.T. closes out 2025-26 season with Hamnet

The work juxtaposes moments of lyricism and turbulence, culminating in a triumphant finale that contrasts with its darker thematic material. its technical demands and stylistic range. articles.text: This summer the Bay Area will resonate with extraordinary music as the Golden Gate International Choral Festival welcomes over 450 choristers, adjudicators, and chaperones from around the globe for a week of breathtaking performances, cultural exchange, and artistic excellence. The festival takes place July 13-18, and is organized and hosted by the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. The Festival stands as one of the world’s most celebrated gatherings of young singers. Under the visionary leadership of Artistic Director Eric Tuan, internationally recognized as one of the world’s premier youth choir conductors, the Festival promises performances of rare beauty, cultural significance, and emotional power. “The Golden Gate Festival is a place where young people from around the world build bridges between cultures,” says Tuan. “Even in a deeply divided world, the Festival offers us the chance to connect through the universal language of music, bringing our unique cultures and voices together to create international harmony. Children who sing together cannot build walls or create conflicts. They know in a deep, visceral way that what unites us is far greater than what divides us.” The Festival proudly welcomes eleven exceptional youth and children’s choirs from across the globe, including Guest Choir Young Voices of the Philippines (Philippines), as well as Cantabella Children’s Chorus (USA), E. Mikeladze Central Music School (Georgia), Ellerhein Girls’ Choir (Estonia), Girls Choir Canzona (Poland), Kajetán (Czechia), Singakademie Graz and Green Guys (Austria), Veus – Cor Infantil Amics de la Unió (Catalonia), and Vox Aurea (Finland). Guiding the festival is a distinguished panel of world-renowned adjudicators—María Guinand, Dr Maria Theresa Vizconde-Roldan, Jude B. Roldan, and Valérie Sainte-Agathe. The two-night event showcases emerging artists from the San Francisco Ballet School, founded in 1933 as part of the San Francisco Operatic and Ballet School by Gaetano Merola. By Allyson Aleksey American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) in San Francisco closes out its 2025-26 season with the US premiere of Hamnet, showing onstage now through May 24. Adapted by Lolita Chakrabarti, who adapted the critically-acclaimed book Life of Pi, and directed by Erica Whyman, the play explores what happens when the plague steals 11-year-old Hamnet from his loving parents, Agnes and William Shakespeare, and they must each confront their loss alone. The death of Shakespeare’s son Hamnet has been thought to have influenced his writing, specifically his great tragedy Hamlet. Hamnet made its world premiere in April 2023 at the Swan Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon, and has its West Coast premiere on the A.C.T. stage. The play features Kemi-Bo Jacobs as Agnes and Rory Alexander as William. The creative team includes set and costume designer Tom Piper, lighting designer Prema Mehta, sound designer Simon Baker, music composer Oğuz Kaplangi, and movement director Ayşe Tashkiran. “I am delighted to be revisiting this extraordinary story for U.S. audiences, and to be making this production with a stellar line-up of performers,” Director Whyman said in a press release. “Kemi-Bo Jacobs and Rory Alexander are bringing Agnes and William alive on the stage with a luminous intelligence and a profound and shocking understanding of the love and loss that shaped their lives.” Visit https://www.act-sf. org/whats-on/2025-26-season/ hamnet/performances for showtimes and to purchase tickets. The audience was spellbound as he performed the music of Villa-Lobos, and others.” – Piedmont Post Leo Garcia, who lives nearby, is an award-winning classical guitarist, recording artist, author, and sought-after educator. He has performed across North and South America and Europe as both a soloist and a chamber musician. Recent performances include a world premiere of Grammy-winning composer Sergio Assad’s Tres Cenas Brasileiras II for two guitars, performed with his sons. Tickets are free, but reservations are recommended, at https://www.eventbrite. com/e/1986865779030. Saturday, May 23, 7:00 p.m. George Cole Quartet A San Francisco native and longtime guitarist for the David Grisman Quintet, George Cole recently fought and beat leukemia. Now in remission, he approaches each performance as a gift – to his audience, and to himself. This concert is generously sponsored by the Piedmont Post. “Life is short,” says George simply. “This music is a gift and I intend to share it for as long as I can.” That spirit is inseparable from the music itself. Cole has spent his career at the crossroads of American swing and the gypsy jazz tradition of Django Reinhardt, and Eurocana is where those two roads finally meet: music played with gypsy flair, Django died in 1953, but his music is heard in concert halls, jazz clubs, and festival stages around the world. There’s a particularly fitting connection to Piedmont itself. For six years, Cole taught guitar to two Piedmont kids who would go on to change rock and roll history – Billie Joe Armstrong and Mike Dirnt of Green Day, both Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductees. At the heart of Vitamin Em is a deep commitment to improvisation. Featuring Grammy-nominated and award-winning artists, the group thrives on spontaneity, and no two concerts are the same. Their concerts are both sophisticated and wildly fun. Advance tickets are strongly recommended and available at https://www.simpletix. com/e/270397.

Chillingly, we are told that to successfully intercept this still unidentified ICBM is the equivalent of hitting a bullet with a bullet. Using a narrative style of rapidly changing points of view and repetition we follow the missile’s trajectory (seconds become minutes racing from single digits to double digits). And with each Anatomy of Murder is adapted from the novel of the same name, written by John D. Volker. The movie was shot in black and white, and fits nicely in the classic, broad noir-mystery genre. However, instead of featuring the hard-case, cynical private eye, made memorable by Humphrey Bogart’s Sam Spade, and later by Jack Nicholson’s J.J. Gittes, this long and engrossing courtroom procedural stars James Stewart as small town semi-retired Paul Biegler who loves the law and fly-fishing. His partner, of sorts, Parnell McCarthy (Arthur O’Connell), who drinks his scotch neat and often bunks in the office, is fully retired; however, his depth and breadth when it comes to legal precedents is extraordinary. And, of course, there’s the ever-present secretary, Maida (Eve Arden), who supervises the office. The film opens with Paul receiving an urgent phone call from Laura Manion (Lee Remick), young and very attractive, who explains, with some urgency, that her husband, Army Lt. Fredrick Manion, is accused of murder. Paul, his icebox full of trout, agrees to meet her at the sheriff’s office where the Lt. is being held. And so enters the noir femme fatale, tight clothes, a diva pooch in her arms, and the stylish large sunglasses, which, when asked, she removes, revealing a Brooks West, George C. Scott, and James Stewart in Anatomy of a Murder black eye. She smiles and says, “You should see the rest of me.” Paul soon realizes that the Lt. is edgy, volatile, and jealous of the attention Laura, flirty, provokes from men. She explains that she was raped by the barkeep, who had offered her a ride home. Slowly the defense strategy emerges: not guilty due to temporary insanity. Missing, torn, lace panties are involved, representing quite a cultural moment for all present. And so the trial begins. The visiting judge (Joseph Welch), is patient and wonderful, calling balls and strikes, and dealing with not only the D.A, but the visiting States Attorney, Claude Dancer (George C. Scott). As an aside, James Stewart is perfect as, well, Jimmy Stewart. Ditto George C. Scott. But then the entire cast represents a deep bench of outstanding actors and Anatomy of Murder is, from start to finish, excellent. Anatomy of Murder. Directed by Otto Preminger. Starring James Stewart, Ben Gazzara, Lee Remick. 2 hrs., 40 min. Released in 1959 (black & white). articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Big Hero 6 Disney’s animated Oscar nominated Big Hero 6 will appeal to an audience of kids and family. The narrative, a derivative of Marvel’s superhero characters, features 14-year-old Hiro Hamada (Ryan Potter), a nerdy, robotics obsessed kid. He lives in the futuristic Asian-like city of San Francisco where he hangs out with a cohort of extraordinary friends: GoGo Tanago (Jamie Chung), Wasabi (Damon Wayans, Jr.), and Honey Lemon (Genesis Rodriguez). Hiro spends his days submerged in techie stuff. At night, however, he engages in illegal robotic fight games. His older brother, Tadashi (Daniel Henney), worries about Hiro’s nighttime antics, so with the encouragement of both Hiro’s aunt, Cass (Maya Rudolph), and Tadashi, he agrees to visit the cutting-edge Institute of San Fransokyo. They hope to influence the young prodigy to give up his underground exploits, and come to the realization that there is a world beyond his own niche of homegrown high tech stuff. As it turns out, the visit to the university proves a success. Hiro, captivated, meets kindred spirits, sees advanced labs, and meets the distinguished Professor Callaghan (James Cromwell), head of robotics, and the inventor of a medical bot, Baymax (Scott Adsit), programed to care for his charge. It eventually becomes Hiro’s sidekick of sorts. Of course, there is a sudden turn of events, which impacts Hiro and his buds, and they soon discover that as a result, their lives have been turned upside down. What occurs? Well, they unexpectedly discover an ominous, dangerous plot that pulls the gang into a harrowing adventure that is brimming with fun, action, and imaginative science (an example being a swarm of buzzing microbots). Architect Albert Farr described the wall enclosing the courtyard as a replica of a wall in an ancient Mexican cathedral. of the courtyard (now the Guild Hall) as a Sunday School chapel with a stage, fireplace, and individual classrooms that open to the central space. The adjacent Guild Parlor, with its cozy fireplace, was designed as a meeting room for the Women’s Guild. Other rooms around the courtyard provided meeting spaces for the Piedmont Chapter of the American Red Cross, a cause quite important to Mary Alexander. During World War I, volunteers met in the Clara Barton Room and rolled bandages. The large basement was designed as a meeting place and drill hall for Albert Farr’s courtyard design in 1918 with its central fountain. The outdoor pulpit is visible just left of the main entrance. Awnings shaded the windows before the stained glass windows were installed. the Piedmont Boy Scouts, a group supported by Wallace Alexander. Farr’s design also included a kindergarten, pastor’s study, kitchen, stained glass windows, and an organ. The church was dedicated as the Piedmont Interdenominational Church on January 6, 1918, the first Sunday of the year. In 1927, the church became the Piedmont Community Church. The Christian Education building was added in 1949 and the Youth Chapel was built in the 1950s. Mowbray Hall was built in 1908 as a Sunday School but was soon used for adult interdenominational services.

articles.text: In previous columns, I have written about Wallace Alexander, Piedmont’s benefactor. In 1913, he gathered several successful Piedmont businessmen to purchase land opposite Piedmont Park, and hired Albert Farr to design the Piedmont Commercial Center, the first stores in Piedmont. Alexander also saved Piedmont Park from development in 1921 by purchasing the land (when the city had no funds) and selling it back to the city the following year. After the 1906 earthquake and fire, many San Franciscan residents fled to Oakland and the Piedmont hills and built new homes. By the 1910s, Piedmont’s population was expanding rapidly. Just as these residents needed a grocery store, they were also outgrowing Mowbray Hall, the 1908 Sunday School, and needed a church. When Wallace Alexander led a group of residents to purchase land for the commercial center, he also purchased an adjacent 1-1/2 acres and offered that land for a church. Alexander then hired Albert Farr to design it and construction began in 1916. Piedmont residents who contributed to the construction of the facility came from all faiths, and interdenominational services would be held in the new church. Albert Farr called his design “Mission” or “Spanish Colonial” and credited Junipero Serra and Jose Churriguera as his inspirations. He designed the church around a courtyard with a central fountain and an outdoor pulpit (now gone). Farr claimed the tiered fountain was an exact replica of an old Spanish fountain at the Santa Barbara Mission. The courtyard was to be planted with shrubs and was designed to be a resting place for all during the week. Farr designed the sanctuary with a domed ceiling, seating for 300, antique lamps, decorative screens to conceal the mechanisms of the organ, and elaborately carved Churrigueresque doors. articles.text: A seven-year-old watches her dog’s body language. Many new dog owners express concerns about the role children will play in a new dog’s life. It’s a true asset to have a dog who is comfortable with kids so you can feel confident the dog is reliable around them in public situations. But how do you help both your child and your new dog build a safe, respectful relationship? Here are a few tips! When you first bring home a dog, your child will likely be very excited and want to spend as much time as possible with their new companion. As the adult, it is your job to provide adequate supervision during these interactions. Young children (elementary school age and below) should never be left alone with a dog— no matter how friendly. Unfortunately, most bites occur in familiar settings due to lack of adult supervision. This also means simply being in the same room is not enough; your child and dog need your active attention. Be sure to educate your child on dog body language and canine social behavior. Kids need to understand stress signals such as a stiff body, lip licking, yawning, or turning away. Teach them to give the dog space when it walks away or hides. Most bites happen because a dog is fearful, not aggressive. Children must also learn that human signs of affection are not always interpreted
articles.title: Kids and Dogs: Building safe relationships

articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Piedmont Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month and offers a great movie in a comfortable setting, with lively discussion to follow. The Flix Fest May selection is Ramen Girl, a 2009 romantic comedy-drama directed by Robert Allan Ackerman and starring Brittany Murphy as Abby, with Toshiyuki Nishida as Maezumi, whose powerful interactions as student and teacher provide cross-cultural lessons in understanding and communication. Abby finds herself abandoned by her boyfriend in Tokyo after impulsively traveling from the States to meet him, with no knowledge of Japanese and few personal contacts. The reality of her situation causes an emotional breakdown, which places her in a neighborhood ramen shop, where the owners offer a bowl of ramen as comfort for her obvious distress. During return visits to this shop, Abby sees the happiness that ramen brings to other customers and commits to becoming a ramen chef with the shop’s owner as her teacher, or sensei. Brittany Murphy brings her comedic skills to her role as Abby, despite the frustration she experiences from communicating with her incurably grumpy teacher, who speaks no English. The movie’s plot takes us through this often painful learning process culminating in the best scene of the film, when Maezumi confronts Abby with her inability to bring soul to her broth. Frustrated by his inability to communicate this core value for making ramen to Abby, Maezumi visits his mother with Abby to get his mother’s advice. She tells Abby to put her tears in the broth to create a unique flavor for her ramen. This elicits the appropriate reaction from neighbors who are tasting her ramen for the first time. Realizing that Maezumi has found his successor, he retires after 40 years as a Master Chef, leaving Abby to sustain his legacy! Ramen Girl will be screened on Thursday, May 14, at the Piedmont Center of the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45 p.m., and the movie is free for anyone over 18. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis and can bring snacks. The next movie will be Before Sunrise, a 1995 romance film, which will be shown on June 11 at 4 p.m., rather than the normal time. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, May 6, 2026 Features PIEDMONT FLIX FEST Ramen Girl to play at upcoming Flix Fest By Gerry Gragg One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Piedmont Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month and offers a great movie in a comfortable setting, with lively discussion to follow. The Flix Fest May selection is Ramen Girl, a 2009 romantic comedy-drama directed by Robert Allan Ackerman and starring Brittany Murphy as Abby, with Toshiyuki Nishida as Maezumi, whose powerful interactions as student and teacher provide cross-cultural lessons in understanding and communication. Abby finds herself abandoned by her boyfriend in Tokyo after impulsively traveling from the States to meet him, with no knowledge of Japanese and few personal contacts. The reality of her situation causes an emotional breakdown, which places her in a neighborhood ramen shop, where the owners offer a bowl of ramen as comfort for her obvious distress. During return visits to this shop, Abby sees the happiness that ramen brings to other customers and commits to becoming a ramen chef with the shop’s owner as her teacher, or sensei. Brittany Murphy brings her comedic skills to her role as Abby, despite the frustration she experiences from communicating with her incurably grumpy teacher, who speaks no English. The movie’s plot takes us through this often painful learning process culminating in the best scene of the film, when Maezumi confronts Abby with her inability to bring soul to her broth. Frustrated by his inability to communicate this core value for making ramen to Abby, Maezumi visits his mother with Abby to get his mother’s advice. She tells Abby to put her tears in the broth to create a unique flavor for her ramen. This elicits the appropriate reaction from neighbors who are tasting her ramen for the first time. Realizing that Maezumi has found his successor, he retires after 40 years as a Master Chef, leaving Abby to sustain his legacy! Ramen Girl will be screened on Thursday, May 14, at the Piedmont Center of the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45 p.m., and the movie is free for anyone over 18. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis and can bring snacks. The next movie will be Before Sunrise, a 1995 romance film, which will be shown on June 11 at 4 p.m., rather than the normal time. Kids and Dogs: Building safe relationships A seven-year-old watches her dog’s body language. By Sierra Berrick Many new dog owners express concerns about the role children will play in a new dog’s life. It’s a true asset to have a dog who is comfortable with kids so you can feel confident the dog is reliable around them in public situations. But how do you help both your child and your new dog build a safe, respectful relationship? Here are a few tips! When you first bring home a dog, your child will likely be very excited and want to spend as much time as possible with their new companion. As the adult, it is your job to provide adequate supervision during these interactions. Young children (elementary school age and below) should never be left alone with a dog— no matter how friendly. Unfortunately, most bites occur in familiar settings due to lack of adult supervision. This also means simply being in the same room is not enough; your child and dog need your active attention. Be sure to educate your child on dog body language and canine social behavior. Kids need to understand stress signals such as a stiff body, lip licking, yawning, or turning away. Teach them to give the dog space when it walks away or hides. Most bites happen because a dog is fearful, not aggressive. Children must also learn that human signs of affection are not always interpreted the same way by dogs. This means no climbing, hugging, or pulling. Encourage your child to let the dog come to them first— and to respect the dog’s choice if they decline. It is equally important to teach both your dog and your child safe ways to interact. Encourage kids to use calm voices and to “be a tree” (stand still) if a dog becomes overly excited. Remind them to use “gentle hands” and avoid faceto-face contact. Train your dog to follow basic cues like sit, stay, leave it, and off to help them remain calm around children. Reward calm behavior and maintain clear boundaries around unsafe actions like mouthing, even if it seems gentle. You can also gradually desensitize your dog to noise and sudden movement, since children tend to be active and unpredictable. Remember, as the adult, it is your responsibility to set clear rules and boundaries. Modeling positive interactions is one of the most effective ways to teach your child how to behave around their new furry friend. Providing your dog with a safe, kid-free space when they feel overwhelmed will also help them feel secure in the home. Following these simple tips will promote a safe, predictable environment for both dogs and children. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment's Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed another beautiful walk last week, highlighted by a special "Cop on the Block" visit with officers from the Piedmont Police Department. Cop on the Block is a community-policing initiative PPD launched in 2023 to increase officer visibility, foster communication and build relationships with residents. Officers conduct scheduled, informal foot patrols in different Piedmont neighborhoods, where residents have the opportunity to voice concerns, report safety issues, ask questions and just chat with the officers. The gatherings often happen on weekdays, early mornings or evenings to accommodate different schedules. PPD releases a monthly schedule and an interactive map showing past (blue) and future (yellow) patrol locations. Capt. Chris Monahan runs the weekly activity. Earlier in April, he had officers stationed on Warfield, San Carlos, Mountain and Estates avenues. For the last Wednesday of April, he scheduled the event for 11:30 a.m. on King Avenue between Hampton Road and Lincoln Avenue so the Wednesday walkers could meet the officers. Before meeting up with the officers, the group followed a circuitous route through Highland, Sheridan and Wildwood avenues, continuing along Crocker and LaSalle. Along the way, walkers caught a peak week of spring blooms — vibrant rhododendrons, roses, dogwoods and jasmine in full color. Heading up LaSalle to King and climbing King itself, the group found no clear indication the street is named for any single prominent historical figure such as Frank C. Havens or Hugh Craig. King Avenue was part of Piedmont's early 1900s residential development, with residences documented as early as 1913. One notable historic home is 84 King Ave., the former carriage house of Wallace Alexander's early 20th-century "Brown Gables" Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo Talking to Wednesday Walkers New PPD officer S Bennett Forty walkers and five of their K-9 best friends were on hand. pages.text: Wednesday, May 6, 2026 23 Walking on Wednesday A Walk with the Cop around the Block By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment's Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed another beautiful walk last week, highlighted by a special "Cop on the Block" visit with officers from the Piedmont Police Department. Cop on the Block is a community-policing initiative PPD launched in 2023 to increase officer visibility, foster communication and build relationships with residents. Officers conduct scheduled, informal foot patrols in different Piedmont neighborhoods, where residents have the opportunity to voice concerns, report safety issues, ask questions and just chat with the officers. The gatherings often happen on weekdays, early mornings or evenings to accommodate different schedules. PPD releases a monthly schedule and an interactive map showing past (blue) and future (yellow) patrol locations. Capt. Chris Monahan runs the weekly activity. Earlier in April, he had officers stationed on Warfield, San Carlos, Mountain and Estates avenues. For the last Wednesday of April, he scheduled the event for 11:30 a.m. on King Avenue between Hampton Road and Lincoln Avenue so the Wednesday walkers could meet the officers. Before meeting up with the officers, the group followed a circuitous route through Highland, Sheridan and Wildwood avenues, continuing along Crocker and LaSalle. Along the way, walkers caught a peak week of spring blooms — vibrant rhododendrons, roses, dogwoods and jasmine in full color. Heading up LaSalle to King and climbing King itself, the group found no clear indication the street is named for any single prominent historical figure such as Frank C. Havens or Hugh Craig. King Avenue was part of Piedmont's early 1900s residential development, with residences documented as early as 1913. One notable historic home is 84 King Ave., the former carriage house of Wallace Alexander's early 20th-century "Brown Gables" estate on Sea View Avenue. The walkers climbed up and across King, and as they approached Hampton, they spotted a Piedmont Police car parked next to Crocker/Bear Park. Officer Hugo Diaz was nearby chatting with a resident. The walkers soon surrounded him, and the group moved into the park for some shade — but not before snapping a group photo with Officer Diaz and the Benny Bufano ground-granite Nursing Bear and Cubs sculpture. The piece, more than 5 feet tall and 2.5 tons, has stood in the park since 1980. It is No. 9 in a limited edition of 25, with only five believed to be in the Bay Area. Officer Diaz told the walkers he is an Oakland native. He was an art major at Cal State East Bay and did graduate work in art but ultimately decided there were greater career opportunities in police work. He joined PPD eight years ago, and his background made him a natural fit as the department's Juvenile Liaison Officer with Piedmont's schools. The walkers brought plenty of questions. Bad driving topped the list. One walker, who lives on Oakland Avenue, said he once watched a car barrel down his busy street at 58 mph. Drivers running stop signs also leave walkers uneasy. And students on electric bikes are often seen riding at high, unsafe speeds. Middle-school boys, in particular, seem to be a problem. Officer Diaz said he has been in regular communications with the schools about it, but parents need to be aware of the problem and the danger to their kids. Social media, he added, could help spread awareness. The walkers gave a nod to Piedmont's school crossing guards for their important work protecting students. Sgt. Nicole Casalnuova, who oversees PPD's Neighborhood Watch Program, joined the discussion and provided additional perspective. She noted that Piedmont officers are "police for the State of California" and can pursue vehicles outside city limits — but the endings of those chases are almost always "not pretty," so the policy is to avoid them unless violence or weapons are involved. articles.text: Your monthly go-to for real estate market trends, market stats & mortgage money matters It’s May, and as anticipated, our Spring Market in Piedmont is in full swing, showing signs of vibrant life, with several new listings selling shortly after their market debuts, some breaking records, and almost all receiving multiple offers. The demand continues to outweigh the inventory. WHAT IT TAKES TO BE A LANDLORD THESE DAYS: “Resilience, Resources & Careful Management” Thinking of moving out of your present home in Piedmont, and renting it in your absence, rather than selling it? Seems like a viable plan, allowing you to return if needed and to potentially provide an income stream in the meantime. However, there are potentially serious legal issues and challenges that might make being a landlord here far less straightforward than many assume. Strict local regulations and tenant protections can limit a landlord’s flexibility, making it more difficult to increase rent, reclaim the property, or respond promptly to problem tenants. Navigating compliance requires time, legal awareness, and sometimes, costly professional guidance. Maintenance itself is another persistent issue. Many homes in Piedmont are aging, requiring ongoing repairs both frequent and costly. Tenant expectations in an affluent community tend to be higher. Renters often expect premium amenities, rapid response times, and pristine conditions as though you are in the “Hospitality” business rather than management. Renters are often apt to file lawsuits against the homeowner should an accident occur on the property, either to themselves or guests who may visit. In addition, the social dynamic of a small, tight-knit community can add pressure. Disputes over noise, parking, or property boundaries can quickly escalate, putting you in an uncomfortable position between your tenants and your neighbors. Seeking qualified legal advice prior to signing a Rental Agreement is a must! Our “go-to” Mortgage Money Broker, BRADY THOMAS, LA SALLE MORTGAGE, has this to Many of the landlords and real estate investors I work with are reaching a quiet turning point. They’ve built wealth through real estate, but the math on staying a landlord is starting to feel different. Between fussy tenants, shifting laws, and dealing with maintenance… the headache is starting to The problem is that getting out isn’t simple. Selling an investment property can trigger a significant capital gains tax bill… sometimes enough to make people feel trapped in a property they no longer want. What I’m seeing more of is owners pairing a 1031 exchange with something called a Delaware Statutory Trust, or DST. The 1031 exchange lets them defer the tax. The DST lets them land in a large, professionally managed property where they own a share but have zero landlord responsibilities. The same tax protections, but with none of the work. It won’t be the right fit for everyone, but for the landlord who’s done with the work and not ready to hand the IRS a check… it’s worth knowing this option exists. Earlier this year, mortgage rates briefly dipped below 6% for the first time in more than three and a half years. When that happened, many buyers who had been waiting on the sidelines started shopping for homes again. Unfortunately, the improvement did not last very long. Over the past month, mortgage rates have climbed back into the mid-6% range. A major reason is the recent conflict involving the US and Iran. When global tensions rise, energy markets often react quickly. Oil prices move higher, which raises concerns about inflation. Mortgage rates are closely tied to inflation expectations in the bond market. When investors believe inflation may increase, bond yields rise, and mortgage rates usually follow, which is what we have been seeing over the past several weeks. Even with the recent rate increase, the basic housing picture has not changed much. Demand for homes remains strong in many areas, inventory is still limited, and many current homeowners today have significant equity in their homes, and very low mortgage rates. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors took a recent excursion, venturing off its usual path, to get two personal group tours, including a one-hour tour of Heath Ceramics in Sausalito. Each and every piece of the dinnerware Heath produces – start-to-finish – from being formed, glazed, trimmed and fired, is made here by a team of 40 craftspeople, almost exactly as it has been since the beginning. The tour took the group through the building’s light-filled courtyard, showroom, and sweeping semi-circle factory. Heath’s dinnerware offers strong color statements, with the intensity softened by the earthy influence of the manganese clay body. Its classic glazes are built around the natural variation and depth present in raw glaze ingredients like iron, copper, cobalt, and manganese. Their earthy quality pairs well with other natural materials like wood and stone. In its showroom, Heath even offers discounted dinnerware and one-of-a-kind prototypes that don’t quite meet its first quality standards. Heath Ceramics began as a small-scale pottery business in 1948, with Edith and Brian Heath, and has evolved into a pure and simple way of life and business that shares many forms of expression through the dinnerware it creates. Their pottery is now used by the renowned Chez Panisse of Berkeley! After the tour, the Piedmont Seniors had built up an appetite, so ventured to nearby Joinery Beer Hall + Rotisserie on the Sausalito waterfront for a laidback lunch. Here, the Seniors enjoyed hearty, seasonal fare in a warm, communal setting. Their hearty fried chicken sandwich was a fan favorite! After lunch, the Seniors went to take their second guided tour of the day, this time at the Bay Model, again in Sausalito. This is a one-of-its-kind model in the entire world! The model is a working hydraulic scale model of the San Francisco Bay and Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta System. While the Bay Model is still operational, it is no longer used for scientific research but is instead open to the public alongside educational exhibits about Bay hydrology. It provides visitors a unique opportunity to view the complete bay-delta system at a glance. The model is approximately 320 feet long in the north-south direction and about 400 feet long in the east-west direction. It is constructed out of 286 five-ton The Piedmont Seniors, at the entrance to Heath Ceramics, get ready to take their private tour. Pictured are James Ayotte, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Jan Yager, Sue Getreuer, Greg Jurin, Edith Hereso, Lois Horwitz, Nancy Hinsch, Gloria Wilmer, Shelley Stafford, and Elizabeth Wierzbianska. concrete slabs joined together like a jigsaw puzzle. Features that affect the water flow of the San Francisco Bay and Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta are reproduced, including ship channels, rivers, creeks, sloughs, the canals in the Delta, fills, major wharfs, piers, bridges, and breakwaters. Considering how they were able to navigate questionable weather so well, it was a rather delightful outing for a group of lucky Seniors! articles.text: removed. And you never know who will be the sick one or the healthy one. My wife Maureen and I have sometimes speculated about which of us will go down first. She is a bit older but eats a lot healthier. I have heart disease in my family but she has Alzheimer’s in hers. No one knows who will be called upon to do the hard work of the vows. As I watched the couples at Mayo one in the wheelchair and one pushing, it was touching to see that in a world filled with divorce, betrayal and broken promises some people really do keep their wedding vows. The love and care I witnessed — an understanding smile, an arm around the shoulder, two gnarled hands entwined brought me to tears. I began to realize I was at a holy place. I usually take lots of photos when I travel, I am obsessed with documenting my experiences but not here. It seemed too sacred a place to profane with a photo. I was like Moses at the burning bush, needing to take off my shoes because I was standing on holy ground. You must apply to the Mayo Clinic and hope you are accepted. They want to think they can help you before you schlep to the clinic. It seems that they like challenges, people that have seen other doctors but still don’t have a diagnosis. That was me, despite having excellent doctors who are part of the Stanford medical group after five years they have still not been able to figure out for sure why I am increasingly unable to walk or stand for long. My local doctors endorsed the idea of trying to get another opinion from Mayo. So, I sent off my application and was told that the Mayo Clinic closest to me in Scottsdale, Arizona was booked up but they could see me at the mother location in Rochester, Minnesota. After years of listening to Garrison Keillor talk about Minnesota on the Prairie Home Companion radio show I was excited to visit the land of 10,000 lakes. Rochester is a town of 120,000 about an hour’s drive southwest of Minneapolis. How this gleaming chrome and glass 19 story skyscraper came to rise out of this agricultural landscape is amazing. You can see it from the distance the way a traveler in France can see from a great distance Chartres cathedral rising out of the cornfields. I was here to see neurologist Dr. Brian Keegan a short, fit, balding Canadian who had traded in the white doctor’s coat for a tight blue sport jacket. He exuded both efficiency and compassion. When he spoke not a word was wasted — he got right to the point he had a lot of sick people to see, and he was not going to dawdle. And yet when you talked to him it seemed as though you had all the time in the world to share your story. It was evident his listening stills were highly tuned. I immediately felt I was in good hands. He set me up with an appointment in the physical therapy department and I was assigned to Heather Ducharme. It is hard to explain, but talking with her was being enveloped in a warm hug. Her face exuded compassion and amazing empathy. I wanted to bottle her expression and take it home with me. She brainstormed with me some ways we could deal with my increasingly feeble legs and improve my walking ability. I left with a list of home exercises for balance and strength. I also met with Dr. Jennifer Dens Higano in the physical medicine department. She was unhurried and focused and had a lovely calming sense about her. She explained the different types of neuropathies and helped me understand more about my malady. I asked her where she was from because she did not have that Minnesota accent (think movie Fargo). “I’m from northern Minnesota where we have a lot more lakes. I don’t know what the Mayo Brothers were thinking choosing to settle in the only county in MN that doesn’t have a lake!” I wish all doctors were so winsome and down to earth. I was not able to get an appointment with any of the 20 doctors in the rheumatology dept. during the week I was in MN, so I was advised to register myself as a “checker.” You register with the front desk and park yourself in the huge waiting room and wait for someone to cancel or not show up for their appointment. Being a checker, I felt a little like those sick, crippled or blind people in the Bible who would sit by the side of the road waiting for Jesus

She was able to rule out a lot of things I did not have and confirmed that I probably belonged in the neurology department. She saw on my chart that I am a retired Presbyterian minister and said at the end of the visit that she was raised in the Presbyterian church. I replied, “no wonder you’re so good.” After four days I. came away from Mayo Clinic with good news and bad news. The good news was that they settled on a diagnosis — I had peripheral neuropathy a nerve disease probably of genetic origin since my mother, brother and sister had nearly identical leg problems. The bad news is that it is a disease with no known cure. However, Heather, my physical therapist, assured me that a lot can be done to manage the disease and slow the decline through balance and strengthening exercises. I left feeling hopeful and determined to do the work I had been assigned and keep up with my exercise routine. As I walked out the door of the Mayo Clinic for the last time to board the pink flamingo shuttle I glanced over at the armada of blue wheelchairs and wondered about the lives of those who had recently ridden them. I hope they found some healing at this holy place. And my heart swelled with deep gratitude and thanks to God that as I left, I was walking, however poorly, and not riding. articles.text: Piedmont mountain climber Bill Baringer shared the chronicles of his first six climbs, to the highest peak on each continent, with the Piedmont Post. These travels were originally published in the spring of 2020 with the help of Baringer’s slideshows and travel logs. The exploits of Baringer’s climb to the top of the Australasian continent, his seventh continent, are detailed below by Baringer himself. To complete my Seven Summits journey – climbing the highest peak on each of the seven continents – I had a choice: Mt. Kosciuszko in Australia (2,228 meters, 7,310 feet – essentially the elevation of Donner Summit), or Carstensz Pyramid aka Puncak Jaya in Papua New Guinea (PNG) (4,884 meters, 16,024 feet), the highest peak in the Australasian continent. The former is achieved by taking a chairlift in the summer to the top of a ski resort, then walking an hour or two, enjoying a bag lunch, taking a couple photos, before heading home. The latter requires a helicopter flight from sea level in Timika, PNG, to a base camp at 14,000 feet – essentially the height of the tallest peaks in the contiguous United States. By Bill Baringer To complete my Seven Summits journey – climbing the highest peak on each of the seven continents – I had a choice: Mt. Kosciuszko in Australia (2,228 meters, 7,310 feet – essentially the elevation of Donner Summit), or Carstensz Pyramid aka Puncak Jaya in Papua New Guinea (PNG) (4,884 meters, 16,024 feet), the highest peak in the Australasian continent. The former is achieved by taking a chairlift in the summer to the top of a ski resort, then walking an hour or two, enjoying a bag lunch, taking a couple photos, before heading home. The latter requires a helicopter flight from sea level in Timika, PNG, to a base camp at 14,000 feet – essentially the height of the tallest peaks in the contiguous United States. articles.text: Editor: I am writing to ask the community to support Measure H. I’ve had the privilege of learning from great teachers at Piedmont’s schools since kindergarten. This year, my World Cultures teacher, Ms. Sohn, has had a strong impact on me. Learning about areas such as the Middle East and South America have helped my understanding of the world and current conflicts. I have learned about current disputes and where they stem from, and why solutions aren’t so easy. I find the “Picture of the Week” to be valuable: Ms. Sohn shares a picture each week from a news article; we need to identify the photo, what it is depicting, and why it is important. This has taught me about current events and given me an awareness of the world that I otherwise would not have had. Measure H is a critical funding source of our amazing schools. I hope that everyone in our community will support Measure H regardless of whether they have children. Measure H will ensure that Piedmont will continue to have great schools and teachers that can make an impact on the children of this community. –Henry Van Den Bos PHS Class of 2029
articles.title: Students in support of Measure H

articles.text: Editor: As a past Co-President of Beach Parents Organization, I’ve had the chance to see up close what makes our Piedmont schools so special, and how much that depends on strong community support. That’s why I’m voting yes on Measure H. This measure helps sustain the quality of education our kids experience in the classroom every day. I know many of us care deeply about our schools, and Measure H is a simple and essential way to protect what we value. I hope you’ll join me in voting yes. –Helen Shin
articles.title: Beach parent in support of Measure H

articles.text: On Earth Day Ted asked me to write a letter in support of Measure H. He didn’t ask whether I supported it, he just assumed. Like how dentists assume their friends floss. I went home and in my Voter Information Guide not a single person offered an argument against it, not even the usual cranks. So what’s Ted worried about? On the surface I suspect he’s worried because the stakes are high; the amount is about 20% of our school budget. But I think it’s deeper than that. Because on the off-chance Measure H doesn’t pass it challenges our identity. Here in Piedmont we want kids to thrive. Even for the cynics among us, thriving kids drive property values. articles.text: Romi is a gentle soul who is learning the world can be a happy place. This four-yearold 45 pound sweet pittie mix simply wins people over with her tender, soulful gaze. On a recent field trip, Romi showed just how much she enjoys getting out of the shelter. She rode calmly and quietly in the car and was easy going on leash. She passed people with curiosity, noticed other dogs without reacting. While she showed interest in small animals, she moved on easily when prompted. As she became more comfortable with the volunteer, she leaned in for pets, nudged for attention, and even gave a few kisses. Romi is hoping for a calm home with a patient person with whom she can continue to blossom at her own pace. She could thrive either as your oneand-only or alongside a confident dog friend to help show her the ropes. articles.text: Do you love a calm routine and peaceful space? Are you known for being patient, observant, and appreciating life’s little moments? We think you’ll love Thomas. Thomas is a gentle, tender-hearted tabby who’s about 2 years old, and still learning the world can be a kind place after life on the streets. He starts off shy, but for someone patient and perceptive, he offers the rare reward of watching trust take root and grow. When he feels safe, Thomas leans into soft petting and relaxes. You might even notice a curious glance, and you’ll melt the first time he chooses to sit nearby you. Win his heart and he’s a loyal, steady companion. This sweet boy feels most relaxed with confident, friendly cats nearby. He seeks them out for comfort and reassurance, helping him feel safe and continue building confiAdopt Thomas through Cat Town. dence. If you have cat experience—and understand how important it is for a shy cat to be able to go slow—then you also understand the pure joy of seeing that cat come into their own, fully confident and happy. Thomas offers a lasting bond built on trust. He’s neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www. cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org.

articles.text: The Alameda Countywide Clean Water Program is offering grant applications for up to $6,000 for community-based projects that help prevent stormwater pollution and improve the health of local watersheds, creeks, and the San Francisco Bay. Eligible projects include Litter reduction efforts, public outreach and education programs, public art projects, and production of community engagement events, wildlife habitat enhancement projects, and stormwater detention. One past recipient is the Albany Landfill Dog Owners Groups and Friends (ALDOG). A grassroots volunteer community group that encourages stewardship at the Albany waterfront. They host at least three beach cleanups a year in collaboration with the East Bay Regional Park District. Their 2017 grant helped ALDOG organize a deep cleaning of the approximately 600-footlong Albany Beach. During a “Sift the Sand” event,115 volunteers removed 2,440 pounds of tiny plastic particles and other debris from Albany Beach in just one day. Another recipient was the Friends of Sausal Creek (FOSC), a volunteer-based, nonprofit organization dedicated to the restoration and protection of Oakland’s Sausal Creek and its watershed. FOSC organized workdays, student field trips, in-the-creek litter cleanups, and public trail stewardship events, engaging a total of 1,283 participants across 15 sites. The I Heart Oakland-Alameda Estuary group was a recent recipient of the grant. In September 2024, they mobilized a group of 116 volunteers to collect trash from Jack London Aquatic Center, Estuary Park, and Clinton Basin in Oakland. They gathered up 2,460 lbs of debris. The deadline for grant submissions is May 4, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. All projects must be implemented in Alameda County. For more details and to download the application packet, visit www. cleanwaterprogram.org/grants. I Heart Oakland-Alameda Estuary’s successful Earth Day cleanup.
