articles.text: The Piedmont City Council unanimously voted to award a $368,053 contract to FJ&I Engineering, Inc. for the city’s Annual Sidewalk Repair Program. A total of 2,200 feet of sidewalk repairs will be made. In January this year, the council awarded a $147,557 contract for concrete shaving on offsets throughout the city. The program is continuing its repairs, moving towards the sidewalks slated for repairs that are damaged beyond what concrete shaving could fix. The city plans to remove and replace the damaged areas in the coming month. “Trips and falls are one of the major risks and liabilities any city has. We have a responsibility to identify these locations and do something about them,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzalez at the April 20 council meeting. The city plans to remove street trees that have outgrown their space and damaged the sidewalk. The city will first try to save the tree, work around it, or cut the roots. Occasionally, some trees The January Sidewalk Repair Program included 1,403 locations with offsets suitable for concrete shaving. are not growing healthily in the space and need to be removed. “Where a tree cannot grow healthily, we are looking to remove it and replace it, and we work with homeowners to do that,” said Gonzales. The current plan is to replace and plant new street trees that are suitable for the environment and space. They will expand the types of trees to plant and ensure they’re tailored for warmer climates and fit the required space. “We will be looking to tailor our trees for a type of climate that will be much warmer in the future. It’s about climate adaptive trees and an awareness of planting trees under powerlines,” said Parks Director Nancy Kent. The overall construction budget of the project is $404,858. Construction is expected to begin in May. Readers can find the impacted street locations on the City Council agenda or the following link: https://bit. ly/4d8H6Tg. Construction workers are conducting concrete shaving on the sidewalks.

articles.text: SAT? ACT? Should I test at all? As of today, California public schools like the UCs and Cal States are test blind, which means SAT or ACT scores are not used as part of the selection process. Some universities require SAT or ACT scores. This list has continued to grow incrementally over the past few years. The vast majority of fouryear universities within the U.S., however, continue to remain test optional. A college that is “test optional” does not require SAT or ACT scores for admission. If a student chooses to submit a score, it becomes an additional piece of information used in evaluating their application. In short, a strong SAT or ACT score could be a boon to an application! For most students, it’s worth investigating how the SAT or ACT might fit into the bigger picture. Any college that still accepts standardized test scores will take either SAT scores or ACT scores, so it’s valuable for students to get starting data points from both tests. Many schools offer the PSAT and/or PreACT to their 10th and 11th graders. Those exams are a good way to understand potential performance on the SAT and ACT. Practice tests for the SAT and the ACT are also available on their respective websites. Once a student has data from each exam, they can start thinking more broadly: How do the SAT and ACT scores compare? Are these scores on target for the schools I’m interested in or could they use some work? When should I take the test? Should I study on my own or get professional help? One of the great things about the SAT and ACT is that they are offered multiple times throughout the year, so there is flexibility around when a student can test. Students should work their SAT or ACT test date(s), and any prep they’re doing, around the things in their lives that are less flexible. For example, a student taking five AP exams in May may want to avoid taking the May SAT. For many students, the SAT and ACT are still an important part of the college admissions process but for those who plan ahead, they don’t have to be a stressful part. Emily Thompson is the Managing Director at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college consulting to Piedmont families since 1997. articles.text: Piedmont Recreation’s Play Like a Girl event returns this weekend for another actionpacked day of hands-on activities and live demonstrations with inspiring role models – all designed to get girls to consider playing sports. The event will take place Sunday, May 3, at Witter Field at Piedmont High School from 10 a.m. - 1 p.m. Aquatics sports demonstrations will take place at the Piedmont Community Pool from 10 - 11 a.m. Now in its fifth year, Play Like a Girl invites girls from 2-18 throughout the Bay Area to try their hand at sports from field hockey to flag football to roller derby. There will be 31 interactive demo stations, with guidance from skilled athletes and coaches. If a girl connects with any individual sport, there will be information available at the station about classes, leagues, and camps. Girls playing flag football at last year’s event Young girls fencing at the 2025 Play Like a Girl event Play Like a Girl will feature meet-and-greets with former WNBA player Oderah Chidom, 5-time Olympic swimming gold medalist Dana Vollmer-Grant, and other professional women athletes and Olympians. New sports this year include Badminton, Curling, Diving, Parkour, Water Polo, and Adaptive skiing. Playing sports provides lifelong benefits to girls. Participation in sports builds skills that support girls throughout their lives, teaching leadership, discipline, and teamwork. Girls who participate in sports experience lower rates of depression and higher self-esteem than their non-athlete peers. Research has shown a direct link between participation in sports and better educational opportunities, positive health outcomes, and improved career outcomes for girls: • Overall, young girls who play sports have higher grades and score higher on standardized tests than non-athletes. • Girls who participate in high school sports have higher rates of labor force participation and earn 7% higher wages than non-athlete peers. • In a 2013 study of 821 senior managers and executives, 94% of female executives reported playing organized sports after primary school. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/PlayLikeAGirl for details, to register, or to sign up to volunteer.
articles.title: Play Like a Girl event takes place May 3

articles.text: High school can be daunting, especially when you feel unprepared and anxious for what comes next. On May 2, from 5-6 p.m., Piedmont Community Service Crew is hosting a panel discussion for Piedmont Middle School eighth graders to learn more about the high school experience. The panel will be hosted in the Piedmont Middle School Multi-Purpose Room. They encourage eighth graders (and parents) to come with questions and worries about high school. A panel of six high school students, in varying grade levels, will strive to help ease 8th graders into this daunting transition. They will start with their own experiences and advice, and address burning questions that people may have. Fill out this survey (https://bit. ly/4mSbfK5) if you plan to come. Everyone is welcome, and don’t be afraid to ask questions. The Piedmont Community Service Crew is a youth-run service organization for local teens. For more information, contact Ken.i.Li@sbcglobal.net or visit their website, PCServiceCrew. org.
articles.title: Piedmont Community Service Crew hosts info event for graduating 8th graders

pages.text: Wednesday, April 29, 2026 7 Ted Scherman Continued from page 1 Piedmont Middle School and Scherman were a match made in heaven as former PMS. Principal John Morrison sensed when he hired him. He had just the right knack for reaching students in what can be a difficult age of change. “One thing I really like [about teaching 6th and 7th graders] is they’re old enough to get my sense of humor and like to have fun. I like to joke with kids, and they’re starting to understand sarcasm, right? Well, some of them,” he said with a smile. “They’re still the age where, if you want to do a skit in class, and you ask ‘who wants to be the prince?’ you’ll get as many girls’ hands going up as boys’. They are less self conscious, and just up for a good time,” he explained. Scherman got into teaching upon the recommendation of his father, a surgeon in a family of doctors. “My dad said, ‘you should become a teacher.’ And I looked at him, I laughed, and I said, ‘I’ll never be a teacher’.” Scherman took his dad’s advice to go against the family grain, and soon found his edge as a teacher in Piedmont. His first full-time assignment was in 1994. Scherman’s great attitude is deeply engrained in his character, something he learned from his first teacher, his mom. “My mom has always been a huge influence on me. She’s always been extremely hard working, but more important than her work ethic, it’s always been her attitude. She always would say ‘your attitude determines your latitude’ and essentially fake it ‘til you make it,” he said. Thirty-two years of Scherman’s students have benefited not just between the school bells, but after as well. Kera Bartlett Binns from Scherman’s 1999 class remembers him creating a rock climbing club and taking the group to Emeryville City Rock every Friday after school. Jenny An remembers a backpacking trip to the Sierras in 1999 with Sherman the summer after 6th grade. Scherman’s great attitude held firm even while leading students in freezing, polar bear plunges. Scherman’s way with his students has seemingly only improved with age; seen by more recent students, like 2014 student Audrey Edel. “Mr Sherman is one of the most amazing, kind and phenomenal teachers I’ve ever known. Everyone in the grade would look forward to dodgeball on Fridays and was eager to stop by his classroom at lunch. He touched the hearts of every student he taught and is not only a fundamental pillar of Piedmont education but of the entire community,” said Edel. Some, like colleague Ted Greenebaum, a PMS science teacher, are not convinced Scherman is really of this world. “Ted Scherman is a walking angel on this planet,” said Greenebaum. As he nears the exit door, he plans to continue to help as a volunteer with Jim Landis’ tennis teams. A former all-American tennis player in Marin County and at Cal, Scherman created championship boys’ and girls’ tennis teams at Piedmont High. A Berkeley resident, he plans to hike a section of the Pacific Coast trail and to spend more time with his wife, three sons and his mom. articles.text: Maya Sears (left), Leo Sachs, Laurel Minor, Abigail Jacoby, and Zafar Piedmont students Maximo Miller (left), Raffi Banin, Daniella Lucacini, and Amelia Oldrin finished in fourth place in the Bio Engineering Competition at UC Berkeley. and Maya Sears Piedmont High School sent 10 students to the BioEHSC Competition at the University of California on Saturday, April 4. One of the two team finished in fourth place for their project using rice cells with the aim of reducing the dependence on synthetic fertilizers. More than 80 teams competed in the competition mostly from California. Other states and international teams, including Poland, were represented. It is the largest annual bioengineering competition for high schoolers in the country and is hosted by the UC Berkeley Bioengineering Honors Society. One team from Piedmont earned a 4th place finish for their project: “Transplanting Nitroplasts Into Rice Cells to Reduce Dependence on Synthetic Fertilizers.” The team consisted of Maximo Miller, Kalyani Spieckerman, Amelia Oldrin, and Raffaello Banin, with Sophia Tsai serving as mentor, and PHS science teacher Shelley Seto-Rosen as coach. “Not only did we develop skills in academic presentation and pitching our ideas, but we also learned through structured sessions led by undergraduate and graduate students, as well as a Forbes 30 Under 30 speaker. Exploring the many real-world applications of bioengineering truly deepened my interest in the field and left me both inspired Majid and excited about its potential to shape the future,” said Lucaccini. “I loved participating in the past seven weeks, researching a niche new discovery while exploring the field of bioengineering,” said Oldrin. “The competition offered a valuable view into what bioengineering is like in the real world. Judges offered new perspectives on aspects of our design I had never considered. I’ll definitely do it again next year,” added Miller. The team of Maya Sears, Laurel Minor, Abigail Jacoby, Leo Sachs, and Zafar Majid, put together a project titled “Microneedle Patch for Osteoarthritis Prevention and Treatment.” This team included two students competing for the second year. “Doing the competition for a second time, I felt as though I knew what to expect, but it was definitely a new experience because our solution had never been done before. Navigating how to present our solution as a device that could be marketed to a large group was the most fun part in my experience,” said Minor. “Doing this competition again was fun to focus on a new aspect of biomedical engineering, and work as a group to hypothesize a new product,” said Jacoby. “The competition was a wonderful experience. I learned a lot about what it means to prepare for and present information to judges, in a professional manner. My favorite part was touring all of the Berkeley labs. I loved researching during the past seven weeks and the process of creating a solution to a very prevalent problem,” Sears stated. Microneedle project poster

articles.text: Families enjoyed a beautiful and fun day on Thursday, April 23, at Piedmont’s Annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration at Piedmont Community Hall. The event was hosted by the Piedmont Public Works Department and the Park Commission, in partnership with East Bay Children & Nature, an Emeryville-based organization dedicated to fostering stronger connections with nature in children. The event was highlighted by the announcement of this year’s Heritage Trees. The annual event, which began in 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees the Public Works Department maintains in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces, as well as the City’s commitment to environmental stewardship. The event featured information tables hosted by the Parks Commission, Sustainability Division, and SavATree. They gave younger audiences a look into what’s inside a tree. They laid out bark and a tree trunk to showcase the rings of a tree and how to tell its age. The Park Commission handed out small plants to attendees at their table, while the Sustainability Division informed families on the proper ways to dispose of their garbage. Two professional arborists were stationed outside Community Hall to answer attendees’ plant-related questions. Children enjoyed jumping into the Public Works machinery they use daily, including the Bay Area’s first fully electric closed-circuit TV sewer inspection van. Many were enthralled by East Bay Children & Nature’s signature “create-with-nature” stations that invite creativity and curiosity through play with natuA family receives plants at the Earth Day celebration. Kids playing at the create-with-nature stations. Kids dance with the band at the sing-along session. The crowd gets involved in singing Itsy Bitsy Spider. A resident receivies plant advice from plant expert, Julia Burke, as Patty Dunlap looks on. ral materials. Attendees danced to a group sing-along by a local band. The group performed two 20-minute sessions of naturethemed children’s songs. Raffle winners were called periodically throughout the event, allowing kids and adults alike opportunities to win a children’s book, toys related to Earth Day, and an array of California native and drought-tolerant plants and trees. Heritage Trees The 2026 Heritage Trees are: • Coast live oak (Quercus Argifolia) in Dracena Park • Ginkgo trees on King Avenue • A redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) in Dracena Park Nominators of selected trees were recognized at the event and received a Piedmont Heritage Tree lapel pin. Readers can find more details on these trees in the Post’s April 15 edition. pages.text: 10 10 Wednesday, April 29, 2026 Bill Baringer Continued from page 1 for a day or two before an early morning attempt up the 2,000- foot rock wall to gain access to the summit. To complete the climb, a Tyrolean traverse must be navigated: climbers walk across a single steel cable across a 150-foot gap in the rock, while holding two other cables at chest height, with hundreds of feet of exposure below. Carstensz sounded like a much more interesting expedition, so I set my sights on that peak as my seventh summit. After the training and challenges of my prior trips, I assumed this would be the simplest of all. Except it wasn’t. Over a sixyear period, I made as many bookings with expedition companies. Due to ongoing unrest in the region - including terrorists firing RPGs at helicopters and taking passengers hostage - the local authorities closed the mountain on three of those arranged trips prior to my departure from SFO. After arriving in Timika on one of the attempts, the climb was cancelled the night before we were to fly to basecamp – we were all told to catch the next flight home. Walking without a police escort in Timika was strongly discouraged. On another trip to Timika, many of us waited for nearly two weeks for weather conditions to allow helicopters to fly – not only to take climbers up, but to retrieve the climbers stranded at basecamp after summiting with no alternative method of return. During that time, five climbers were trapped on the summit ridge and exposed to heavy snow and wind. Three were rescued by expedition company guides who were only still at basecamp because of the lack of heli-taxi. The two other climbers had already died in dark irony – while attempting a memorial climb to place a plaque on the mountain where their friend had perished the previous year. In October of 2025, I returned to Timika once again. Low clouds and poor weather kept us waiting in the hotels used by expedition teams. Finally, my position in the queue secured a seat for me on the first heli flight at 7:00 a.m. the next morning. My pilot managed to thread through the constantly shifting clouds and land at basecamp. The helicopter that departed just minutes after us was forced to turn back – an expensive return-tobase flight for those passengers. Forecasts suggested a narrow window: clear skies the following day, then a return to heavy cloud cover. If I spent my first day acclimatizing, I would have a spectacular climb up dry rock the next day with great views – but risk being stranded afterward. “After an hour of discussion, I convinced him that we were going to summit that day, and for him to grab his gear.” – Bill Baringer I went to the dining tent and drank as many hot drinks as I could manage, using hydration to assist my acclimatization. I then went to the guide tent and located the Indonesian guide assigned to me by the expedition company. As I expected, he told me to go rest, wander around the valley, and to take it easy. After an hour of discussion, I convinced him that we were going to summit that day, and for him to grab his gear. We donned our climbing harnesses and helmets, threw some Photos Courtesy of Bill Baringer Papua New Guinea’s Puncak Jaya base camp at 14,000 feet. liquid and snacks and goretex climbing attire in our packs, and started up the mountain. At first I wasn’t moving quickly, having been at sea level for an extended period. But after some time I found my rhythm and worked my way up the rock walls. In many locations, ropes had been anchored to the rocks so that a climber could use an ascender (aka Jumar) and pull themselves up the wall. But I preferred to climb the actual rock with my hands and feet, and keep my ascender attached to the fixed line as a backup in case I fell. In addition, given the very threadbare sections of very old rope, I wasn’t sure how much I could trust the fixed lines. The Tyrolean traverse was good fun, though at that point the weather had deteriorated and we were subjected to sleet and snow. We finally came to the point where we could climb no higher, and found the summit plaque through the very dense clouds. I quickly consumed some snacks and donned another layer of warm clothing. I moved quickly down the rock walls mindful of loose footing and the ever-present risk of rope failure. As I approached basecamp, a Russian climber came up to meet me and offered to carry my pack. That evening, we shared dinner and hot drinks and swapped mountaineering stories in the PPD Blue dining tent until I realized I was fading and needed to crawl into my sleeping bag in my tent. Despite the elevation I fell asleep immediately and slept soundly. As predicted, the next morning was clear and bright with little wind. The helicopters came roaring into camp. There was a vivid “sun dog” in the sky – a rainbow halo around the sun – Baringer makes use of a Tyrolean traverse to span a chasm in the ridgeline by walking across a steel cable. Some frayed sections of very old rope on the fixed lines. indicating that inclement weather would be due within 24 hours. I threw my duffel into the first departing helicopter. On the flight out, we had amazing views into the depths of the world’s biggest gold mine, its scale almost as surreal as the climb itself. Carstensz Pyramid proved to be far more than a final checkmark on a list. It was a lesson in patience, persistence, and risk— where logistics, politics, and weather were as formidable as the mountain itself. In the end, the summit mattered less than the journey it demanded: years of setbacks, moments of uncertainty, and a single decisive push when the opportunity finally appeared. Completing the Seven Summits here, in one of the most remote and unpredictable corners of the world, felt not just like an achievement, but a fitting culmination of everything mountaineering had to teach me. articles.text: Saturday, April 18 marked a historic day for Piedmont High senior Layth Haddawy. At the 2026 USPA power lifting event during Spring Break, Haddawy hit a 570 pound deadlift to set a new United States record for athletes in the Age 16-17, 148 pound category. It marked Haddawy’s first official event since winning the USPA National Championship last July, when he lifted 485 pounds. His recent lift marked an 85 pound improvement. “I did one other meet but it was just to have fun competing in the weight class above me. The deadlift is as much as the strength in your body as it is about mobility. Something I emphasized was getting as flexible as possible so I get better leverage on the bar when I’m lifting it,” Haddawy said. To achieve the mark, it took some strategic planning from Layth. He opened with a 475 pound lift, increased to 518 pounds, and followed up with 540. He then loaded up 570 pounds to beat the previous highest-mark in the U.S. of 568 pounds set in 2024. “You get three attempts per lift and are allowed to take a fourth if you’re breaking a record. I had a rough meet aside from that, and bailed 550 a week prior. I wasn’t thinking 570 was super achievable. All my warm-ups felt really light, so I talked to my coach to lower my other attempts to avoid gassing myself out. I kept my first three attempts relatively lighter so that I could get a feel if I had 570 in me,” Haddawy said. In July 2024 an MRI revealed that Haddawy was dealing with a fracture in his pelvis. He suffered an avulsion fracture, which is when a fragment of bone or muscle breaks away from the main bone. Photo courtesy of Get Bent Gym Layth Haddawy, a senior at Piedmont High, celebrates after setting the national deadlifting record for ages 16-17 in the 148- pound weight class. Now Haddawy said he has learned to avoid overtraining. As it turns out, it was the change he needed to better his development. Additionally, changing his diet was another big factor. “Previously, I hadn’t given much value to resting. I went to the gym almost every day and only had one rest day, and I noticed a drastic spike in my strength when I’m taking 2-3 rest days a week. I tried to focus on recovery and eating a healthier diet… My injury was another one of the reasons I incorporated more rest days. Going 5-6 times a week, I was building up inflammation in my leg, and it was impacting my mobility. My hope is to use this extra rest to mitigate the issue as much as I can,” Haddawy said. Haddawy has been training at Get Bent in Oakland since the start of his powerlifting career. He’s watched the gym grow in size, now becoming a premier location for youth lifters. “I’ve noticed the community of people who are there has gotten a lot bigger. articles.text: PHS to host Bishop O’Dowd in WACC Semifinals tonight Photos by JC Curran Piedmont closed its regular season with a loss to Berkeley, but looks ahead to a WACC Semifinals match against Bishop O’Dowd tonight, April 29. Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team finished its regular season on Friday, April 24, falling to consecutive Western Alameda County Conference champions Connor Fredericks had one goal, one assist, 13 ground ball recoveries, and won 16 faceoffs against Berkeley. Berkeley by a score of 15-5. The Yellowjackets await the winner of Piedmont and Bishop O’Dowd in the WACC Semifinals tonight, April 29, with the championship match set for Friday, May 1 at O’Dowd in Oakland. Tonight’s game is a tantalizing rematch of WACC rivals PHS and O’Dowd. The Highlanders won their recent regular season match 11-9 in a comeback on Friday, April 17 at the Dragons’ home field. This time, Piedmont is set to host BOD at Witter Field. “Berkeley is statistically the strongest team in our league and we expected them to be quite strong. Against O’Dowd, we found a lot of looks on the back side and had good transition play. O’Dowd is always the biggest game of the season, the players and families always get up for it,” coach Andy Kittler said. The Highlanders look to avoid a similar storyline to their 2025 season, when they beat O’Dowd in the regular season but lost in the WACC Tournament. “Last year, we had a disappointing loss against O’Dowd. We showed we wanted that game more than them and we had something to prove. We know we can’t let up and slow down now, we have to keep it rolling,” junior Connor Fredericks said. Regardless of the WACC Tournament results, Piedmont is looking toward a solid ranking in the D2 North Coast Section playoffs. Maxpreps currently has them as the No. 20 seed, which puts them on pace for the No. 4 seed. O’Dowd is NCS’ No. 16 ranked school, while Berkeley is No. 7, making the next two games important for a further push up the table. 15-5 loss to Berkeley Piedmont trailed 5-2 by the end of the first quarter, and went scoreless in the second with Berkeley extended its lead to 7-2 by halftime. PHS scored once in the third, while the Yellowjackets added four of its own to lead 11-3. Piedmont landed two goals in the final going to BHS’ four. Final stats: Owen Curran scored two goals and one assist. Landon Heppner scored two goals and gathered one loose ball. Fredericks had one goal, one assist, scooped 13 ground balls, and won 16 faceoffs. Mile Stevenson had one assist and five ground balls. Timmy Kalamas had one assist. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-6 overall) hosts Bishop O’Dowd tonight, April 29, for the WACC Semifinals at 7:00 p.m. With a win, they will face Berkeley in the WACC Championship on Friday, May 1 at the same time. Owen Curran (2) had two goals and one assist against Berkeley. Milo Stevenson (13) had an assist and gathered five ground balls.

The Highlanders look to avoid a similar storyline to their 2025 season, when they beat O’Dowd in the regular season but lost in the WACC Tournament. “Last year, we had a disappointing loss against O’Dowd. PHS senior Layth Haddawy sets new national record in weightlifting By Jonathan Comeaux Saturday, April 18 marked a historic day for Piedmont High senior Layth Haddawy. At the 2026 USPA power lifting event during Spring Break, Haddawy hit a 570 pound deadlift to set a new United States record for athletes in the Age 16-17, 148 pound category. It marked Haddawy’s first official event since winning the USPA National Championship last July, when he lifted 485 pounds. His recent lift marked an 85 pound improvement. “I did one other meet but it was just to have fun competing in the weight class above me. The deadlift is as much as the strength in your body as it is about mobility. Something I emphasized was getting as flexible as possible so I get better leverage on the bar when I’m lifting it,” Haddawy said. To achieve the mark, it took some strategic planning from Layth. He opened with a 475 pound lift, increased to 518 pounds, and followed up with 540. He then loaded up 570 pounds to beat the previous highest-mark in the U.S. of 568 pounds set in 2024. “You get three attempts per lift and are allowed to take a fourth if you’re breaking a record. I had a rough meet aside from that, and bailed 550 a week prior. I wasn’t thinking 570 was super achievable. All my warm-ups felt really light, so I talked to my coach to lower my other attempts to avoid gassing myself out. I kept my first three attempts relatively lighter so that I could get a feel if I had 570 in me,” Haddawy said. In July 2024 an MRI revealed that Haddawy was dealing with a fracture in his pelvis. He suffered an avulsion fracture, which is when a fragment of bone or muscle breaks away from the main bone. Photo courtesy of Get Bent Gym Layth Haddawy, a senior at Piedmont High, celebrates after setting the national deadlifting record for ages 16-17 in the 148- pound weight class. Now Haddawy said he has learned to avoid overtraining. As it turns out, it was the change he needed to better his development. Additionally, changing his diet was another big factor. “Previously, I hadn’t given much value to resting. I went to the gym almost every day and only had one rest day, and I noticed a drastic spike in my strength when I’m taking 2-3 rest days a week. I tried to focus on recovery and eating a healthier diet… My injury was another one of the reasons I incorporated more rest days. Going 5-6 times a week, I was building up inflammation in my leg, and it was impacting my mobility. My hope is to use this extra rest to mitigate the issue as much as I can,” Haddawy said. Haddawy has been training at Get Bent in Oakland since the start of his powerlifting career. He’s watched the gym grow in size, now becoming a premier location for youth lifters. “I’ve noticed the community of people who are there has gotten a lot bigger. articles.text: Piedmont to face Berkeley in WACC semifinals today Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team split its last two games, bringing their record to 7-10 overall. PHS closed its regular season with a close 8-7 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, April 24, and then opened the Western Alameda County Conference postseason tournament with a 19-0 blowout of Washington. Both matches were played at Witter Field. Before the loss to O’Dowd, the Highlanders also suffered a narrow 10-7 defeat to Berkeley. They will get a chance for revenge on the Yellowjackets today, April 29, and will get another shot at the Dragons with a win at BHS. “O’Dowd crashed hard and worked really hard, they forced a lot of turnovers. They run a backer defense, which double-teams the ball every single time. A couple balls went the wrong way,” coach Carlton Chan said following their loss to O’Dowd. The losses to BOD and Berkeley came in similar fashion, where the Dragons got out to a 4-1 lead while the Jackets led 6-1 at one point. “I thought we played really well, it’s just little mistakes that build up. It ended up hurting us because it’s so high pressure. We just need to move as a team, move the ball around fast, and go full out in the first half,” senior Peyton Watson said. “It’s definitely rough to lose back to back, but now that we’ve played them, and know what to look for. We need to come out strong in the first quarter,” senior Dahlia Osman mentioned. Piedmont also celebrated its five seniors on the roster prior to their game against Bishop O’Dowd, including Watson, Osman, Hallie Burden, Jameson Sanford, and Naftalia Segal. “It’s scary to be ending. I’ve been playing lacrosse a long time, so it’s like a full circle moment. The loss to O’Dowd was rough, but I’m always glad to play. We’re ready for this next week,” Osman said. “It means a lot to me. When I came in as a freshman, I was so excited. I look forward to games, it’s my time to relax and enjoy myself. It’s a good separation from school, lacrosse has meant a lot to me,” Watson said. The Highlanders should still be on pace for a D2 North Coast Section berth. They are currently the No. 27 ranked school on Maxpreps, which puts them on pace for the 11th seed. Berkeley is currently No. 26 and O’Dowd is No. 23, meaning a Piedmont WACC Title could push them higher up the rankings. 19-0 over Washington Piedmont led 6-0 by the end of the first quarter and 14-0 by halftime. They added three more goals in the third quarter, and two more in the fourth. Final stats: Sanford scored five goals. Zoya Schulze scored three goals, one assist, and helped in nine draws. Watson scored three goals and one assist. Burden scored two goals and seven assists. Sydney Latvala scored two goals and won nine draws. Osman scored twice. Cory Minor and Sophie Puckett scored individual goals. 8-7 to Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont opened with a quick goal by Peyton Watson a minute into the game, but O’Dowd scored twice to end the quarter, Staff Photos Peyton Watson scored five goals against O’Dowd and three against Washington. She is a four-year varsity player. Dahlia Osman, a two-year varsity athlete, had two goals in the game with Washington.

articles.text: WACC Individual Tournament up next this weekend Piedmont No.1 singles player Lucas Smolko looks to win his third straight WACC Individual Tournament title. Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team wrapped up its regular season on Monday, April 27 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center, narrowly beating Berkeley 4-3. They recently lost 6-1 to Bishop O’Dowd at home on Thursday, April 23, lost 5-2 at Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco on Wednesday, April 22, and beat Head-Royce 4-3 in Piedmont on Friday, April 17. The squad looks ahead to the postseason playoffs, starting with the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament at Chabot College in Hayward this Friday and Saturday, May 1-2. Piedmont senior Lucas Smolko looks to win his third straight WACC Singles title, and reach his fourth straight final. According to the league’s online records, Smolko is already the only athlete in the it’s 13-year history to reach the finals three straight times and win two consecutive singles title. Smolko has a chance to further cement his legacy as the league’s most successful boys’ tennis athlete of all time as the only repeat and three-peat singles champion. “I’m trying to win it for a third time. I hope I can win it again, it would be really incredible. I love that tournament, it means a lot to win that title, represent Piedmont, and making it historic would be amazing,” Smolko said. Smolko hasn’t lost a league match this season, giving him confidence going into the tournament. “I’m feeling great. I haven’t lost a match since the start of the season. This might be my last match on these courts, so it’s a bit bittersweet. But I’m feeling great going into it,” Smolko said. 4-3 win over Berkeley Berkeley won the first two matches of the day, and all three doubles matches. Hunter Fasteau and Travers Kemp lost 6-1, 6-2 at No. 2 doubles, while Joey Assalian and Ben Davis fell 6-2, 6-2 at No. 1 doubles. articles.text: Bay Area 100, the point-topoint 100-mile trailrunning ultramarathon in the San Francisco Bay Area, is proud to announce the Dapper Don Award named for former Piedmont Middle School teacher Don James. The award is designed to honor and support unsung “first responders” of our community – the teachers. Through this program, select educators each year will receive complimentary entry into the Bay Area 100, along with other race-related support. “Don believed in the power of persistence, whether a math equation or running 100 miles. He knew how to turn hard things into a lot of fun. We can think of no better way to honor his legacy,” said race founder Adam Ray. “These exceptional people who choose to teach – they thrive when faced with challenges, so we’re happy to provide the additional challenge of running 100 miles of mountainous trails.” The program is a tribute to James, a beloved Bay Area ultrarunner and Math/Algebra teacher who spent nearly 20 years at Piedmont Middle School and a decade in the Oakland School District. Known for his signature buzz cut and a presence that intimidated students in September before revealing what a softy he was by December. Don was a fixture in both the learning and running communities. He completed the famed Western States 100 in 2002 with a sub-24-hour finish. James passed away in 2022. The Inaugural Class This year’s inaugural Bay Area 100 recognizes three teachers/runners. These individuals embody the dedication required to reach Mile 74, home to “Dapper’s Rest”—a memorial bench located near Redwood Peak and Redwood Bowl along the course—and to take it all the way to the finish on the track at Skyline High School. Military draft refusal was at an all-time high especially in the hotbed of the Bay Area, and he got cases assigned immediately to him for trial. Guy next partnered with another law graduate to open a law office, and they chose Fruitvale Avenue as a racially diverse neighborhood and cheap; they cleaned and painted the space themselves and did their own typing. Initially they took the case of every person who walked through the door, but business was slow, so Guy stayed on the panel for the public defender. Soon, his attention was turned to Employment Law, and particularly employment discrimination under the 1964 Civil Rights Act. Guy’s Plaintiff Civil Rights firm filed class action job-discrimination complaints against national insurers and giant grocers, and won case after case; and the firm grew from two employees to 165 with a trailblazer reputation for winning on behalf of women for pay equality during the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s. Westlee as a toddler with Papa Guy who was a co-owner of the Oakland A’s (Athletics) and frequently brought his grandson to home games. Guy grew up in a modest family home in North Hollywood. The nephew of Abe Saperstein, founder of the Harlem Globetrotters, he served as their ball boy when the team visited Los Angeles. After graduating in 1961 from North Hollywood High School, Guy attended UC Berkeley and then the Boalt Hall School of Law. He became an anti-war activist during his years at UC Berkeley. After university graduation, he took a two-year fellowship representing migrant farmworkers in Colorado. Guy met his wife, Jeanine, in 1967, while picketing in Los Angeles for a demonstration he organized for the Welfare Rights Organization. They lived in Berkeley from 1971 to 1995. From the Colorado fellowship, they returned to live in Berkeley. On March 2, 1972, the very Guy and his favorite all-time dog, cockapoo Wookie Guy with daughter Unmi and granddaughter Coco wearing matching safari caps on safari in Africa On safari in South Africa. Shown: Leon, Sunny, Jacobus, Guy and Westlee, Jeanine with Piedmont Post, Salix, Alison, Unmi, Coco, Roger, Tina (Guy’s sister) and husband Tom. Jeanine always carried the Piedmont Post on her travels. Guy and Jeanine celebrate Guy’s 80th birthday in Paris with 200 invited guests atop the Branly Museum’s astounding Eiffel Tower view. Actual photograph partly shows Can Can dancers live at the gala party. day his first son was born, Guy co-founded Farnsworth, Saperstein and Dennison — what became the largest private plaintiff civil rights law firm in American history, growing from two people to 165 employees. Located in Oakland, the firm, now Dardarian Ho Kan & Lee, successfully prosecuted the largest sex, race, age and disability employment discrimination class action cases in America. Guy also prosecuted False Claims Act cases against Lockheed Missiles & Space Co. regarding satellite surveillance systems, and against Raytheon, Boeing and TRW regarding the sham National Missile Defense Program. For six years, Guy was included in the National Law Journal’s list of The 100 Most Influential Attorneys in America, the only private civil rights attorney ever so honored. Guy retired at age 51 to spend more time with family, backpacking, kayaking, trekking, and international travel. He wrote three books, including Civil Warrior: Memoirs of a Civil Rights Attorney and The Getaway Guide to the John Muir Trail, his story of backpacking the 236-mile John Muir Trail with his younger son, which won an award for best guidebook from the Society of American Travel Writers. He produced a feature film, Skeleton Woman, and was given an award from Friends of the River for his work preserving American rivers. He served on Nancy Pelosi’s Democratic National Security Policy Group, and helped write the Real Security plank of the Democratic Party’s New Directions for America. He founded The New Ideas Fund think tank, co-founded Patriotic Millionaires for Fiscal Strength, and served on many environmental and other boards, including serving two years as president of the Sierra Club Foundation. Guy poured his energy into improving everything around him: his relationships, his neighborhood, his community, his country. In 2021, Guy and Jeanine moved to Paris with half their family. After surviving three strokes, open heart surgery, and three bouts of sepsis, his family nicknamed him The Comeback Kid. He recently returned to the U.S., to Seattle to be near his son Jacobus. Guy left his heart in Paris but carried his fighting spirit until he was ready for this last final journey. He is survived by Jeanine, his wife of 57 years; his son Leon, daughter-in-law Sunny (Rui Jun), and grandson Westlee; son Jacobus, daughter-in-law Alison, and grandson Salix; daughter Unmi, son-in-law Roger, and granddaughter Coco; sister Tina and her husband Tom; nieces Kelli and Deborah, and nephew Gary Jr; brothers-in-law Gary and Michael, and his best friend Geoff. Jungle Gym at Hampton sports field is a gift to the children of Piedmont from Jeanine and Guy Saperstein, with the inscription, Children embrace the ordinary with enchantment – reminding us what is important and what we were meant to be. A ceremonial plaque honors Guy Saperstein for leading the fight to preserve the basketball court. Here, Guy credits Sara Lillevand, Piedmont Recreation Director, for her devoted work to keep the court. Guy enjoyed countless hours of play on this beautiful court.

articles.text: Visit Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery on Saturday, May 2 for a chance to step beyond the garden gates and tour Ruth Bancroft’s own private iris garden. The Iris lecture and guided tour, led by members of the Mt. Diablo Iris Society, focuses on the history of Ruth’s iris collection and how to plant, care for and divide irises with demonstrations. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth when it was her private, personal garden, but is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Ruth created a garden full of dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. But long before she became known for her succulents at the Ruth Bancroft Garden, Ruth was an avid iris collector. In 1989, her garden was selected by the Garden Conservancy to be its first preservation project, and a conservation easement was established to ensure its preservation. Thanks to a generous invitation from the Bancroft family, this event gives guests and garden members a rare opportunity to view her private collection. Potted Irises will be available for sale and the Botanical illustration society will be selling their unique art, including iris paintings. The event is rain or shine. Visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/event/iris-talk-andtour/ for more information and to purchase tickets. Photo courtesy of Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery Ruth Bancroft was an avid iris collector.
articles.title: Rare Iris lecture and tour held at Ruth Bancroft Garden May 2

pages.text: Wednesday, April 29, 2026 19 The Musical Gourmet Let’s move ahead to 1964 The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet and take a music history class at USC. Mike and I usually sat next to each other and listened to our boring professor,a sure cure for insomnia. This particular class session required us to name the musical children of Johann Sebastian Bach. The students Personal recollections of came up with the usual names, such as Carl Friedrich Emmanuel Michael Tilson Thomas and Johann Christian among others. I wanted to show my erudition, and piped in with: By Joseph Gold Michael Tilson Thomas, who died on April 22, was a brilliant superstar in the world of music. In these parts, we knew him by the initials MTT. When he was a student in the public schools in Los Angeles, he was Mickey. When he and I were classmates at USC, he was Mike. Let me take you back in time. Let’s begin on Sunday, September 29, 1963. This was the date of the final concert of the Heifetz-Piatigorsky series. These two great artists played a memorable concert, assisted by an orchestra composed of the finest players in the Los Angeles area. Heifetz did not want to have a conductor, so there was no conductor on the stage. At the conclusion of the concert, Heifetz and Piatogorsky took their bows. For the final bow, Heifetz pulled out a skinny young kid to join them in the curtain calls. The audience had no idea why the skinny kid was even on the stage. And now for the first time in print, you will know that the skinny kid was Michael Tilson Thomas who had been the rehearsal conductor. “No one has mentioned PDQ Bach. How about him?” In a chastising voice, Mike reproached me saying: “hey Joe, haven’t you heard of professor Peter his final story Schikele?” I didn’t have a clue what he was talking about, but I played the part of the comedian. It was only later that I found out about PDQ Bach and his creator, Peter Schikele. Our final story is a demonstration of the heroic proportions that Michael Tilson Thomas was capable of. For a number of years he was the conductor of the Young Musicians’ Orchestra in Los Angeles. They played a concert in USC‘s largest auditorium. During the intermission I was backstage with Mike talking with him. As we were walking around, Mike had his jacket draped over his shoulders like a cape, and he was drinking something from a thermos when… all of a sudden…he fell face first down on the floor. His right arm flew out to protect himself. I helped him up, and he said: “I broke my arm.” The two of us were close to the stage and the stage manager said: “it’s time for the second half.” Thomas was scheduled to play a Mozart Piano Concerto and conduct the Orchestra from the piano. I gave Mike some words of encouragement and literally pushed him onto the stage. As I watched from the wings, Michael Tilson Thomas played one of the greatest concerts I’ve ever heard in my life. It was truly a super-human effort. The next day, when I saw him on the campus, he showed me the cast on his right arm and said: “I told you I broke my arm.” I replied something to the effect that…yes, his arm was broken, but that I was responsible for his brilliant performance. When I found out that Michael was ill a few years ago, I wrote to him reminding him of these memories. He appreciated the trip down memory lane. It is abundantly clear that Michael Tilson Thomas fulfilled all of the early expectations. He succeeded in every way and went on to a fabulous career… the likes of which have rarely seen. Ditto the plotting: it’s filled with mercenary characters who dissemble, threaten, and are typically packing heat (Mary Astor, Sydney Greenstreet and Peter Lore are wonderful). I would offer that this genre reached its zenith in Hollywood with the release of Chinatown. It was nominated for 11 Academy Awards and to the surprise of many critics won only one Oscar for Best Original Screenplay (by Robert Town). Yet this film has reached iconic noir status both for its complex plotting, cinematography, and the standout performances by Jack Nicholson and Faye Dunaway. The production, which captures the atmospherics of the 1940’s, is lushly vibrant. The opening scenes of Chinatown are simply so engaging, setting the tone for the entire Morgan Freeman, Nicolette Pierini, Madeline Carroll, and Emma Fuhrmann in The Magic of Belle Isle I immensely enjoyed The Magic of Belle Island for there is magic to be found in this story. There is also kindness, romance, and warmth, which are eventually found in the relationships that slowly blossom between what initially seem to be very different people. The story opens with western novelist, Monte (Morgan Freeman), disabled from a stroke, arriving at his summer cottage on Belle Island. He was once successful but has now lost his muse, meaning his desire to imagine and write. Instead, he has found refuge in an ever-present glass of fine scotch. Monte soon discovers that his neighbors consist of a single mom, Charlotte O’Neill (Virginia Madsen) and her young daughters Finn (Emma Fuhrman), Willow (Madeline Carroll), and Flora (Nicolette Pierini). While Monte seeks isolation, and finds solace in his cynicism and privacy, the O’Neill daughters, led by the gregarious Finn, refuse to yield to his crankiness. They make an effort to draw him out and win him over. Finn, hearing that Monte is a novelist, tells him that it is her wish to one day become a writer. She asks him to explain how imagination is so much a part of creating stories. And thus begins an engaging dialogue between Finn and Monte that is both literary and delightful and integral to the development of the story. Imagination also takes Monte into a dream wherein he dances with Charlotte in the moonlight, no longer confined to his wheel chair. The Magic of Belle Island reaches beyond what can seem today a coarseness of life. It is inherently hopeful in so many ways. And as a result, Monte becomes once again moored to life and purpose. That’s the magic, requiring no suspension of disbelief. And, I am certain, that is why Rob Reiner chose this story and its exceptional cast. The Magic of Belle Island. articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Toy Story 3 For all of the studio’s animated talents, and they’re considerable, Pixar (22 Oscars, four Golden Globes and three Grammys), the creators of the Toy Story franchise, have never forgotten that at the center of every project is a touching, compelling story. Since 1995, the adventures of Woody (Tom Hanks) and his crew – Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen), Potato Heads (Don Rickles, Estelle Harris), Hamm (John Ratzenberger), Jessie (Joan Cusack), and Rex (Wallace Shawn) – have captured the imaginations of moviegoers, both young and old. Unexpectedly, the Oscar-winning Toy Story 3 delivers not only a sweet tale, one that is wonderfully imagined, but also one that is nicely distressing. Visually, it’s a treat, a smorgasbord of crisp colors and seamless animation. Put simply, it’s brilliant moviemaking. The core story is simple yet inspired, and immediately familiar: Andy is going away to college and is cleaning out his room. He opens up his toy box and ponders what to do with Woody and company, all deeply embedded in his childhood memories. Through a series of mistakes, the gang ends up at a daycare center run by Lots-o’-Huggin’ Bear, a seemingly nice old guy who soon proves to be something else. And so begins a great adventure that is both comical and thrilling, touching on issues of loyalty, friendship, courage and seat of your pants close calls. What adults will understand is that Toy Story 3 is a coming of age story. Andy has grown up and yet still feels connected to his toys. They are, in a word, “keepers.” He can’t simply put them out by the curb. Yet he knows that he has to leave them behind in the same way he must leave his childhood (and his mother) behind. Kids will understand intuitively that much loved toys are to be treasured, the equivalent of a favored blanket. A doll or bear or a Woody are there, through thick and thin, and all those moments that comprise a childhood. These are wonderful themes and Toy Story 3 turns out to be the sweetest and best-told story thus far. Toy Story 3. Directed by Lee Unkrich. With voices of Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, Joan Cusack and Don Rickles. 1 hr., 42 min. Rated PG. Pixar Studios. articles.text: Wall-E is an Oscar-winning animated collaboration between Pixar animation studios and Disney, which debuted in theaters in 2008. It was a huge hit then as it should be now with a new generation of youngsters. Kids will be enamored with this small, irresistible tin box named WALL-E ((Ben Burtt), who has binoculars for eyes that are not only functional, but capable of a panoply of emotive expressions. We watch him scoot around the dusty, dystopian remains of an uninhabited, litter-strewn earth on tractor-like wheels. Apparently, he was left behind to collect and compact the detritus of the long-ago departed humans. The name WALL-E is actually an acronym for Waste Allocation Load Lifter-Earth Class, which captures his day-in and day-out job. The year is 2700, and the planet has long ago been abandoned by its residents, who now live on a massive cruise shiplike space station called Axiom, which is run by a big box, Buy N’ Large corporation, and managed by robots who service the denizens’ every need. The humans move about in large hover recliners, have grown fat and lazy, wanting only to consume and watch their individual screens while drinking milkshakes. pages.text: Wednesday, April 29, 2026 21 MOVIES FOR KIDS Toy Story 3 another Oscar winner by Pixar WALL-E an Oscar winner film from Pixar and Disney By Chris Honoré Wall-E is an Oscar-winning animated collaboration between Pixar animation studios and Disney, which debuted in theaters in 2008. It was a huge hit then as it should be now with a new generation of youngsters. Kids will be enamored with this small, irresistible tin box named WALL-E ((Ben Burtt), who has binoculars for eyes that are not only functional, but capable of a panoply of emotive expressions. We watch him scoot around the dusty, dystopian remains of an uninhabited, litter-strewn earth on tractor-like wheels. Apparently, he was left behind to collect and compact the detritus of the long-ago departed humans. The name WALL-E is actually an acronym for Waste Allocation Load Lifter-Earth Class, which captures his day-in and day-out job. The year is 2700, and the planet has long ago been abandoned by its residents, who now live on a massive cruise shiplike space station called Axiom, which is run by a big box, Buy N’ Large corporation, and managed by robots who service the denizens’ every need. The humans move about in large hover recliners, have grown fat and lazy, wanting only to consume and watch their individual screens while drinking milkshakes. Meanwhile, back on earth, it becomes clear that WALL-E feels deeply his isolation and loneliness, made evident by the way he peruses the memorabilia left behind. He has a place of his own where he keeps old light bulbs, hubcaps, a Zippo lighter, and one See Wall-E on page 29 A scene from Pixar’s Toy Story 3 By Chris Honoré For all of the studio’s animated talents, and they’re considerable, Pixar (22 Oscars, four Golden Globes and three Grammys), the creators of the Toy Story franchise, have never forgotten that at the center of every project is a touching, compelling story. Since 1995, the adventures of Woody (Tom Hanks) and his crew – Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen), Potato Heads (Don Rickles, Estelle Harris), Hamm (John Ratzenberger), Jessie (Joan Cusack), and Rex (Wallace Shawn) – have captured the imaginations of moviegoers, both young and old. Unexpectedly, the Oscar-winning Toy Story 3 delivers not only a sweet tale, one that is wonderfully imagined, but also one that is nicely distressing. Visually, it’s a treat, a smorgasbord of crisp colors and seamless animation. Put simply, it’s brilliant moviemaking. The core story is simple yet inspired, and immediately familiar: Andy is going away to college and is cleaning out his room. He opens up his toy box and ponders what to do with Woody and company, all deeply embedded in his childhood memories. Through a series of mistakes, the gang ends up at a daycare center run by Lots-o’-Huggin’ Bear, a seemingly nice old guy who soon proves to be something else. And so begins a great adventure that is both comical and thrilling, touching on issues of loyalty, friendship, courage and seat of your pants close calls. What adults will understand is that Toy Story 3 is a coming of age story. Andy has grown up and yet still feels connected to his toys. They are, in a word, “keepers.” He can’t simply put them out by the curb. Yet he knows that he has to leave them behind in the same way he must leave his childhood (and his mother) behind. Kids will understand intuitively that much loved toys are to be treasured, the equivalent of a favored blanket. A doll or bear or a Woody are there, through thick and thin, and all those moments that comprise a childhood. These are wonderful themes and Toy Story 3 turns out to be the sweetest and best-told story thus far. Toy Story 3. Directed by Lee Unkrich. With voices of Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, Joan Cusack and Don Rickles. 1 hr., 42 min. Rated PG. Pixar Studios. Streaming on Disney+/Fandango/Apple/ Prime. articles.text: Last Wednesday’s Walking on Wednesdays outing offered something a little different, a walk that traded steps for stories and scenery for stagecraft. Even with a bit of rain thinning the ranks, a solid group gathered at the Exedra and set off with purpose toward Piedmont High School, moving briskly to make the most of a special invitation. The destination was the Alan Harvey Theater, a place many in town know from performances and school events, but few have seen from the inside out. The walk down Magnolia Avenue had a sense of anticipation to it, less about distance and more about discovery. By the time the group reached campus, the pace had done its job, everyone arrived ready to listen, look, and learn. Inside, the visit began not with history, but with energy. In a drama classroom just off the main theater space, students were in the early stages of rehearsal. Music started, and suddenly the room came alive. The performance was informal, fast-paced, and full of spirit, offering a glimpse into the kind of work that rarely gets seen outside of show nights. The walkers, to their credit, stayed in their seats, resisting any urge to join in. After the brief performance, the students spoke about their work, describing not only what happens on stage but the collaboration behind it. There was talk of supporting one another, of learning timing and trust, and of the many small roles that make a production work. A student-run talent show, Phantasmagoria, is in the works, promising more of the same creativity and enthusiasm. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, April 29, 2026 Features Walking on Wednesday By Dick Carter Last Wednesday’s Walking on Wednesdays outing offered something a little different, a walk that traded steps for stories and scenery for stagecraft. Even with a bit of rain thinning the ranks, a solid group gathered at the Exedra and set off with purpose toward Piedmont High School, moving briskly to make the most of a special invitation. The destination was the Alan Harvey Theater, a place many in town know from performances and school events, but few have A walk behind the curtain seen from the inside out. The walk down Magnolia Avenue had a sense of anticipation to it, less about distance and more about discovery. By the time the group reached campus, the pace had done its job, everyone arrived ready to listen, look, and learn. Inside, the visit began not with history, but with energy. In a drama classroom just off the main theater space, students were in the early stages of rehearsal. Music started, and suddenly the room came alive. The performance was informal, fast-paced, and full of spirit, offering a glimpse into the kind of work that rarely gets seen outside of show nights. The walkers, to their credit, stayed in their seats, resisting any urge to join in. After the brief performance, the students spoke about their work, describing not only what happens on stage but the collaboration behind it. There was talk of supporting one another, of learning timing and trust, and of the many small roles that make a production work. A student-run talent show, Phantasmagoria, is in the works, promising more of the same creativity and enthusiasm. Rebeca Posamentier greeting walkers at Alan Harvey Theater Walkers entering the Alan Harvey Theater From there, the tour shifted into the theater itself, moving from present to past. The group climbed to the upper level of the auditorium before making their way down, pausing along the way to hear about the building’s history and the evolution of the campus around it. The story begins with the original 1921 Piedmont High School, a neoclassical structure designed by architect W.H. Weeks. Its auditorium, located at the front of the building, was once a centerpiece of school life. But like many buildings of its era, it did not meet modern earthquake safety standards and was largely demolished in the 1970s. In its place came a new set of campus buildings, more modest in style but reflective of the design thinking of the time. That version of the campus did not last forever either. By the 2010s, those structures too were deemed seismically inadequate. A new chapter began with the passage of Measure H1 in 2016, a $66 million bond approved by a strong majority of voters. The goal was clear: modernize the high school, create updated learning spaces, and build a performing arts facility that could serve both students and the broader community. Construction was not without challenges. The earlier theater was removed in 2019 to make way for a new STEAM building, and only after that was completed could work begin on the current auditorium. Pandemic disruptions and rising costs forced adjustments along the way, but the project ultimately came together, opening in 2021 as a combined academic and performing arts complex. articles.text: The puppy craze may have died down since the pandemic, but there’s still a healthy market thanks to the circle of life. When choosing a new puppy, you can comb animal shelters or reach out to breeders. While many argue that “adopt don’t shop” is the way to go, there are cases where speaking to professional breeders might be more suitable, such as when interested in specific canine sports. This article specifically addresses tips and tricks for choosing a puppy when going the breeder route. First and foremost, don’t get your heart set on the first puppy you meet. Make sure you interview many different breeders and, if possible, meet several different litters of puppies. Ensure that your breeder knows the structural standards of their breed well, in addition to possible health concerns. Buyer beware if your breeder does not perform health testing or is unwilling to show you test results! When you meet your puppy, look for some important behavioral signs such as how willingly the puppy engages with their siblings as well as people. At this young stage, puppies are building their social skills, and the ideal dog will have a fondness for interacting with others. Very shy puppies can turn out to be good dogs too, however, they may need special exposure and additional training. Look for a puppy that is very comfortable being handled. Pick them up and hold them like a baby on their back – do they wiggle and try to escape or do they look lovely into your eyes? While you’re visiting, make sure you take the time to meet one or both of the puppy’s parents. Learn about their temperaments and their quirks. Are they especially friendly? Are they show dogs and if so, are they titled? A breeder who shows their dogs actively seeks confirmation from an educated professional that their dogs’ structure is excellent enough to want to pass on to their offspring. Your best chances of obtaining a healthy dog from a breeder occur when both parents have champion titles and have both gone through extensive health testing. Make sure that you are wellversed in your breed of interest so that you can recognize a scam. Many backyard breeders will attempt to pass off their practices as professional when they know very little, particularly about health conditions. If you visit a breeder who makes you feel uncomfortable, there is no shame in walking away. The puppy shopping process is a fun and very exciting time. With these simple tips, you can go through this process worry-free and paw-sitively ecstatic to welcome your new fur baby home. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com. My husband Chris and me meeting new baby Scooter for the first time three years ago.

With roughly 460 seats, modern acoustics, improved rigging, and full accessibility, it is a far cry from its predecessors. The facility includes a green room, classroom space that doubles as a black box theater, and flexible seating arrangements that allow for different types of performances. Solar panels and other design elements help the building operate with an eye toward energy efficiency. Kim Taylor talking to walkers More importantly, the theater is busy. During the school year it hosts plays, musicals, concerts, dance performances, assemblies, and community events. It has become a hub not just for the high school, but for the city as a whole. There is even a technical theater internship program, giving students hands-on experience with lighting and sound, the unseen work that supports everything on stage. After the presentation, the group took time to explore. There were photos in the auditorium seats and on stage, a quick look backstage and in the green room, and a stop in the lobby to view student artwork from a current exhibit. It was a full morning, and by the end of it, the usual question of “how many steps?” seemed less important. The group decided to call it a day without adding extra mileage. No one had reached their typical totals, but no one seemed to mind. The walk had offered something different, a reminder that movement through a community can take many forms. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or call (510) 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: My byline promises “insider There was a very exclusive past week (No, not the Girl Scout Party) and Charlie and I managed to get added to the cater-waiter crew so we can deliver some true insider information. I am, of course, talking about Emma’s Masked Spring Garden and Tea Party; the tea was spilled. Most of the industry insiders were focused on the Compass/ Anywhere merger—Compass closed its $1.6 billion acquisition of Anywhere Real Estate on January 9, 2026, creating what amounts to a real estate empire masquerading as 14 independent brokerages. Sotheby’s, Corcoran, Coldwell Banker, Century 21— they’re all now subsidiaries of Compass International Holdings, all funneling transactions into the same vertically integrated money machine. So now you know all but a few independents are feeding the same machine—but you didn’t hear it from me because I’m not one to gossip. In the News Compass Drops Zillow Lawsuit — But Private Listing Rules Haven’t Changed Compass dropped its antitrust lawsuit against Zillow on March 18, 2026. Zillow relaxed some enforcement but made one thing crystal clear: listings marketed publicly without MLS entry within one business day still get permanently banned from the platform. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors’ latest excursion was a trip to visit the Hiller Aviation Museum in San Carlos, which preserves the legacy of flight and provides inspiration for those who visit today and for future generations. Over forty unique aircraft are on display that tell the story of aviation innovation in Northern California and beyond. Realistic flight simulators and open aircraft cockpits, including the popular Boeing 747 exhibit, ensure that every visitor gains a pilot’s eye view of the world of aviation. There are also displays about early aviation, California pioneers, air racing, women in aviation, the mechanics of flight, and urban air mobility. In every imagination there is a spark of fascination with flight. The Hiller Aviation Museum is a place where that spark is ignited, and aviation comes alive. Piedmont Seniors’ co-pilots ‘Captain’ Judy Wang, Gloria ‘Ace’ Wilmer, and ‘Wingman’ James Ayotte take their seats in the cockpit aboard the Boeing 747. The Piedmont Seniors gather near the entrance of the Hiller Aviation Museum underneath a full-scale model replica of the airplane first flown by Wilbur and Orville Wright. articles.text: ite displays during the Piedmont Seniors’ visit was the Sky Portal, an interactive exhibit that uses the real-time power of Google Earth to observe any place on the Earth, to view it from miles above the ground right down to the Earth’s surface. The Seniors could actually zoom in to see their own home using the portal. In addition to the unique thrill of finding one’s own neighborhood and house as seen from orbiting satellites and exploring exotic destinations around the world, one can investigate aviation from a sky-high perspective. Included are airports, airspace, and routes of famous flights across the country and the world, such as the flight of the Vin Fiz in 1911, the 1929 Women’s Air Derby, the final flight route of Amelia Earhart in 1937, and the recreation of her flight by Reid Dennis and Linda Finch in 1997. After the tour, the Piedmont Seniors then drove to Millbrae for lunch at La Petite Camille. Operating since the early 1990s, this family run business offers quite the menu featuring homestyle Vietnamese comfort food. The luncheon got rave reviews from each of the Piedmont Seniors, but it was then time for a little sweetness. So, the group then ventured to Burlingame for a visit to the IT’S IT factory. An ice cream legend, It’s It was created in 1928, and its creations are just as delicious today as they were on its creation day nearly 100 years ago when George Whitney placed a scoop of creamy vanilla ice cream between two freshly baked large old-fashioned oatmeal cookies and then dipped the sandwich into fine dark chocolate. The delicious combination of savory sweetness was declared by all to be “IT!” That how the IT’S-IT Ice Cream Sandwich was born and got its unforgettable name. While at the factory the Piedmont Seniors got their choice of having a vanilla, chocolate, strawberry, mint, cappuccino, pumpkin, or green tea IT’S IT, or a “Chip’s It” (vanilla ice cream between two chocolate chip cookies) or a “Super Sundae” (chocolate covered vanilla on a stick sprinkled with peanuts). Each is a delectable treat, and it was a great way to conclude the day’s outing! Allll Aboard! Piedmont Seniors get ready to step inside the Boeing 747, a marvel of aviation history. They include (L to R): Sue Getreuer, Judy Wang, Janet Epstein, Gloria Wilmer, Yorkman Lowe, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, and Jim Ayotte. Here, they experienced the luxury and grandeur of the Class cabin and got a glimpse into the iconic cockpit of the legendary “Queen of the Skies”. The Boeing 747-100 was the first production version of the iconic wide-body aircraft, entering airline service in 1970.
