By Cookie Segelstein Dear readers: This is not going to be a regular MacMama article, I have been asked by the editors to recount the experience of being with my mother as she was dying. Many of us have family members that are approaching the end of their lives, and though nothing can prepare us, it’s comforting to read positive accounts of the family members’ experiences as a loved one approaches the end of their lives. On January 15 of this year, I got a call from my 98-year-old mother’s memory care facility in San Francisco that she had had a small seizure and was on her way to the hospital. When I got there, she was still waiting to be seen by a doctor, and the paramedics were by her side. She was talkative, chatting with them, and basically in decent spirits considering where she was. After being there for nine hours, and after the x-rays and CAT scans, I eventually was able to talk to the physician in charge. She told me that my mom had severe pneumonia, and I had a couple of choices. She could stay there on IV antibiotics with a small chance that it would cure her, but a likelihood that this would cause delirium and incredible gastric distress with a kind of antibiotics they would have to use. The other choice was, they could try to give her some antibiotics in the ER on a drip, and then send us home with pills that most likely would not work because of the severity of her case. But there was a third choice. And that was basically to do nothing and to call in hospice. Because of my mother’s DNR wish, and her POLST that was filled out while she was still able to make decisions for herself, I knew this was the option that she would choose. And the idea of a dementia patient in the hospital hooked up to antibiotics with probable delirium was terrifying to me. I spoke with my sister, and she agreed that we would take Mom back to her apartment in the facility and make sure she was comfortable. The doctor wrote an order for me for hospice and thus began my experience and being with my mother while she died. My mother was 98, a holocaust survivor, and did very well in the memory care facility where she had lived for the last four years. The care was stellar, she was happy, she was active, and I felt very relieved that she was in a place where all her needs were covered. I visited her at least twice a week and sometimes more. In this new chapter of our lives together, I knew that the care staff would be very helpful to both of us in explaining how hospice was going to help my mother painlessly come to the end of her life. I made the decision to stop all my work and just be by her side for about 12 hours a day. In doing this, I was able to be involved with the wonderful hospice nurse in making decisions about her care as her system slowly shut down. The ER doctor told me that, even though it was impossible to predict, with the severity of her pneumonia and her white blood cell count, it would likely be a matter of about 10 days, but my mother had other plans. One of my violin students is a retired cardiologist from Johns Hopkins University. I asked him to look at my mother’s x-ray. He noted with surprise that she had “the bones of a 50-year-old”. And he also said to me something that really rang true eventually, and that is that holocaust survivors know how to survive; they don’t really know how to die. He told me not to be surprised if she lasted longer than I expected, as there is some research that shows that people who have been through starvation, can go without food longer than others. When we came back from the hospital, my mother’s food intake really was reduced, she found it hard to swallow, so I sat with her at meals so she could have that social time with her friends. We sang some songs and just visited with the other residents at her table. It was hard for her to drink water to take her pills, so they gave her thickened water, which seemed to help a little bit. Two weeks after she came back from the hospital she stopped eating completely. But she drank 4 to 8 ounces of this thickened water every day. The amazing thing is that even though her body and systems were failing, she still wanted to go to the morning activity, so we propped her up in her wheelchair, and brought her into the room where they had music, or exercise. And even though her voice was failing, she was still mouthing the words of the songs. I had no idea what to expect as far as when she would pass away, and I used Google’s AI, Gemini, and put in her vitals, her blood count, and the ER doctors’ summaries of her diagnostic tests to try to figure out what stage of death she was in. Every time I did that, it said she was nearing the final stage of death, and it gave me symptoms to look for that would indicate that she was actually very close, within hours or days. I was so surprised at how thorough the summaries were on this platform, and how helpful it was to me in preparing myself for her end. Eventually, I asked the care professionals at the facility to stop giving her regular meds because she couldn’t swallow them and just go to liquid morphine As she neared the last two weeks of her life, she had some unbelievably lucid moments. One of them was when my sister was able to come up from LA to visit her, which turned out to be the last time they were together. My mother woke up out of a deep nap, told us how much she loved us and said that she was very proud of us. For the first time in a long time, she asked how our children were by name, and told us to tell them she loves them. And then she said she knew we were here because of the situation that she is in, but she was not ready to go. She also started to see visions of her mother, and her late siblings. Or she would indicate that she saw a lot of children playing on the floor in her room. She also tried a few times to get out of bed, as she said she had to get ready. The week before she died, she had another lucid 15 minutes and said that she didn’t want to do this anymore, and she wanted to go with “the girls”. When I asked her who she was talking about, she just pointed to the door. I assumed she was talking about her sisters. At this point, she started sleeping almost all of the day, but for maybe 45 minutes of being awake. When she spoke, she mostly spoke Hungarian or Yiddish. On one of her wakeful hours, I removed the necklace from her neck, which was a little heart with a teeny diamond in it and told her that I was going to wear it. She put her hand on my neck and said, in Yiddish, “wear it in good health”. Her very last words to me were, “I’m going to sleep now”. At this point, it had been 3 ½ weeks with no food, and almost 4 days with no water. The day she died, was exactly five weeks after her visit to the ER. She died when I went to take a little walk. I was upset that I missed the actual moment of her death, but the hospice nurse assured me that many people die that way, as they can’t let go if there are family members in the room. At first, when I realized that I was going to stop all of my work, not only my MacMama work, but my violin teaching, I was very worried about my income. But I realized, I can make up that money, but I can’t make up the time spent with my mother. And because I was able to help manage her care, I was able to see that she had a peaceful and painless death with me by her side for all but the last moment. I learned a lot about the other residents in the memory care facility, how some of their family members are there often, how some of them don’t have any family members or at least don’t have any visitors. I got to know all of them, some of them wandered into my mother’s room occasionally, one woman in particular, another holocaust survivor, who spoke Hungarian, used to hold my mother’s hand and sing to her. I went to the activities with them, I went to arts and crafts with them, I had meals with them, I became part of their community just for those five weeks. The experience of being able to be with my mother as she left this life is something I will never forget, and I am eternally grateful that I made the choice to take the time to do that. It has made my grieving much easier, and I really learned to appreciate the caregivers that spend their days doing the work of caring for the elders in our families.

pages.text: 28 Wednesday, April 29, 2026 AMERICANS IN PARIS By Patricia K. Forsyth Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on December 15, 2021. Americans in Paris was invited to the apartment of Guy and Jeanine Saperstein, a Piedmont couple who recently moved to France with their belongings and two small dogs. The occasion was Thanksgiving with their family members who flew in for the holiday, including their son Leon and wife Sunny, Piedmont residents who are planning to move to Paris at the end of the school year. Grandson Westlee is taking French lessons twice a week to be prepared. The clan is settling on the Left Bank at the very foot of the Eiffel Tower. Jeanine is powering through unpacking boxes. At her side is Bettye, her French majordomo who knows instinctively where everything should go. Guy and Jeanine had switched apartments with niece Unmi Abkin for a better layout plus the rarities of American-style bathrooms, walk-in coat closet, and chic powder room. Thanks to her, Dylan’s first experience of school was really positive, when it could have so easily been negative. That has really set the tone for him ever since, and he is now thriving in middle school. The remarkable thing about this school district is that wonderful teachers like Mrs. Thomas are the norm, not the exception. But that doesn’t happen by chance. Piedmont attracts excellent teachers because they know that their class sizes will be smaller and their students will have access to enriching “specials” like art and drama and library. They know that their students will be supported not just academically but also socially and emotionally by school counselors. They know that their classrooms will be well-supplied with up-to-date educational materials and supplies. In short, they know that this community truly values public education – and that we are willing to step up and pay for it. No single piece of support for our school district is more important than the parcel tax, which funds more than 25% of PUSD’s budget. Passing Measure H is absolutely essential to maintaining the excellence of Piedmont’s public schools. He immediately begins to tell a seriously off-color joke, despite all efforts by his staff and secretary to stop him. He is oblivious, until he realizes a client is waiting in his inner office. Of course, it’s a classic well-dressed woman with a fox stole draped over her shoulder with a story of infidelity. She believes her husband, an important city water official, is seeing another woman. She wants the P.I. to find out. And slowly, while peeling the investigative onion, Gittes begins to realize that nothing is as it seems. The audience is asked to pay close attention; this is a challenging plot, with lots of twists, turns, secrets and characters. For most of the film I was sorting out familial relationships while concerned about J.J.’s broken nose, covered in a white tape and gauze bandages. pages.text: Wednesday, April 29, 2026 31 Food Fest Continued from page 1 and others portrayed their musical excellence to the hundreds of people coming through. People from all over the Bay Area were able to grab food originating from kitchens across the globe and then sit and enjoy an equally diverse array of entertainment. Food Fest founder Roger Tsai was once again heavily involved in the event’s production, bringing together talent and food trucks for one special day. “When I started Piedmont Food Fest back in 2022, I just hoped to have enough vendors, entertainment, and guests to make it worth everyone’s time. After that first one, I realized there was a collective excitement around celebrating the many cultures we have in the Bay Area through food, drinks, and music,” said Tsai. Tsai gave credit to the hundreds of volunteers who supported his vision to expand the festival and make it an even greater celebration. “To celebrate our fifth year milestone, we wanted to bring an even greater variety of food, drink, and entertainment to the festival,” Tsai continued. “Pulling off this vision required over 100 volunteers to plan, promote, and operate the many parts of the day, and I’m really proud of how our team showed up to deliver a memorable day for all.” The KidZone & Craft Stations were organized by Kala Hale, Abha Kothari, Sarah Eisemon, and Laura Edeen. Hundreds of kids spent their time playing at ten different carnival booths and enjoyed the favorite sno-cone station. The area was run by volunteers from the middle and high school, covering four shifts. Nine community groups and local businesses set up tables to advertise their services. These groups ranged from charity efforts to fun group activities for attendMaikaze Daiko put on a professional Japanese taiko performance. A performer of Beloved Aerial Arts dances in the sky for the passerbys to enjoy. A blindfolded Han Martial Arts master kicks roses into the crowd. The empanadas were a crowd favorite. The crowd paid close attention to the wonderful performances on the main stage. The World Harmony Chorus provides a peaceful performance for the crowd. The wine and microbrewery tasting zone ees to sign up for. In addition, a beer and wine tasting provided 13 microbreweries and wine options for older guests to enjoy. Food Fest guests had the option of many different cultural foods, including Thai, Vietnamese, and Japanese, all in front of the Exedra. Further down the hill, guests had the choice of Moroccan, Mediterranean, seafood, Spanish, Japanese desserts, soul food, and Indian food. Further options included smoothies, boba tea, poke, shaved ice, and empanadas. This reporter sampled the Nepali food truck Momolicious, and tried their Fiery Mo:mo: and Mango Lassi. At $20, the meal featured Crispy stir-fried dumplings with sweet-and-spicy sauce, onions, and bell peppers, while the drink served as a sweet reward to deal with the heat. In front of Piedmont’s vase at the Exedra, talented acrobats from the “Beloved Aerial Arts” performed while suspended in midair with three hours of graceful entertainment. Over the last five years, Food Fest has become an event that those around the Bay Area look forward to for its county fair-style entertainment and a superb selection of menus. A kid tries her hardest to knock down the clown in the KidZone. Student volunteers hand out sno-cones to the young kids in the KidZone.

articles.text: Thirty-seven Piedmonters traveled to China over spring break for a cultural exchange program which included mining, robotics, sightseeing, school visits, and delicious food all along the way. The group of five chaperones, eight parents and 24 students visited four cities- Guilin, Yangshuo, Beijing, and Tangshan- in a life changing experience highlighting the past, present and future of China and Chinese culture. This was the second iteration of the trip, masterminded by PHS and PMS Mandarin teacher Xinjia Xia. The group was three times larger than the first year. This year it included School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, PHS Principal David Yoshihara, PMS Assistant Principal Jamie Van Kleeck and 6th grade teacher Lea Lotia. “In Guilin and Yangshuo, we experienced some of the most beautiful natural landscapes in China,” said Xia. “There is a well-known saying in China: ‘Guilin’s scenery is the best under heaven.’ In Beijing, we explored China’s ancient history and culture, seeing firsthand the legacy

articles.text: Authorities have arrested a suspect in the assault and residential robbery case that occurred last month on the 400 block of Scenic Avenue. The robbery occurred on March 24 as a man returned home around 12:25 a.m. to find his front door broken open and encountered two suspects inside. The man safely fled the residence and called 911. A woman inside the home was asleep at the time of the home invasion. She reported that two suspects entered her bedroom, demanded cash, and assaulted her when she was unable to comply. The two suspects ransacked the home of valuables before police could arrive. In an update on Tuesday, March 14, the Piedmont Police Department released a statement informing the public that an arrest had been made and the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office charged the individual with robbery. Officials did not release the suspect’s identity or say whether additional arrests are expected. The investigation has involved multiple agencies, including the Oakland Police Department, the Alameda County Sheriff’s Office, and the FBI’s Oakland field office, police said. “Public safety is a shared responsibility, and this case underscores how critical interagency collaboration is, particularly our strong working relationship with the Oakland Police Department,” said Police Chief Frederick Shavies. “I am grateful to the women and men of the Piedmont Police Department for their tireless efforts and commitment to keeping our community safe.” The investigation remains ongoing. The suspects were described as two Black men in their early 20s, approximately 5’10” and 6’0” tall, wearing gray and black hoodies. Anyone with information or who may have witnessed suspicious activity around this time is urged to contact the Piedmont Police Department at (510) 420-3000. articles.text: The fifth annual Piedmont Food Fest, a homegrown multicultural event, returns to Piedmont Park this Saturday, April 25 from 11am-4pm and will showcase some of the Bay Area’s most distinctive food trucks and stalls, breweries and wineries, and live performers. Together with the kid-favorite KidZone midway, guests will be treated to a full day of memorable entertainment — including a grand finale by the Cal Band to wrap up the event in style. As an-all volunteer run event, Piedmont Food Fest is the culmination of five months of planning involving over 100 volunteers and partners from Piedmont, Oakland, and the broader Bay Area. In pursuing its mission of celebrating the diversity of the Bay Area through food and music, Piedmont Food Fest has built a unique type of community centered around collectively enjoying new experiences together. As a result, Piedmont Food Fest brings together over 2000 visitors, 30 food and drink businesses, 10 local artists and performers, as well as many local sponsors, small businesses, and community groups to mix, mingle, and get to know one another. Crowds queue up for the trucks at Piedmont Food Fest . Photo by Julie Reichle

articles.text: Chrisi is a sweet, brindle Shepherd mix of around 2.5 years old. She has a thoughtful, observant nature and a sweet personality that shines. She responds to “sit,” politely accepts treats, and happily trots over when called. She enjoys chasing after tennis balls and engaging in light play. Once she becomes comfortable, she leans her body into your legs to enjoy pets and affection. Weighing 75 pounds, Chrisi walks nicely on leash with minimal pulling. articles.text: Cameron Wolfe and Valerie Matzger The reality of climate change has led the City of Piedmont and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation to collaborate on a major shift in plantings throughout the city to drought-tolerant California native plants. This replaces the water-thirsty non-native plants that have more traditionally been grown in Piedmont. The hope is that residents will see the options available to them to make the same shift in their own gardens. Several recent projects in public spaces illustrate that plants don’t have to drink copious amounts of water to be beautiful. These plant choices can also help to reverse the loss of insect populations, which generate the life support that keeps us, and all other living things, alive. The new Piedmont Aquatic Center dramatically illustrates this shift in plant choices. Plants are a major visual centerpiece of the new pool complex. The design by SWA Landscape Architects features drought-tolerant California native plants that support biodiversity by providing sustenance for pollinators, other beneficial insects, and birds. The existing large Coast live oak has been carefully preserved and another has been planted near the pool entrance. The wonderful fragrance of Winnifred Gilman sage surrounds the entrance path and the planting areas are filled with Howard McMinn Drought-tolerant Califronia native plants are seen in the foreground of this picture of the new Piedmont Aquatic Center. manzanita and the lower-growing Pacific Mist manzanita. The hedge along the Magnolia Avenue side is another very valuable wildlife supporter, the Holly-leaved cherry. A completely donor-funded organization, PBF made an early contribution to help kickstart the campaign in the amount of $25,000 and ultimately provided a total gift of $236,000. Donations to support the work of PBF can be made by mail to City Hall, 120 Vista Ave., Piedmont, CA 94611, or by visiting its website: www.PiedmontBeautificationFoundation.org Here is a second view of the new plantings at the Piedmont Aquatic Facility. articles.text: Piedmont’s Annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration returns this Thursday, April 23, from 3:30 - 5:30 p.m., at Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. For this year’s event, the City is teaming up with East Bay Children & Nature, an Emeryvillebased organization dedicated to fostering stronger connections with nature in children. “We’re thrilled to be partnering with East Bay Children & Nature for this year’s Arbor & Earth Day celebration,” said Parks & Project Manager Nancy Kent. “The best part of this event every year is seeing the joy on children’s faces, and I think the collaboration this year is going to bring that to a whole new level. Beyond the immediate fun on the day itself, events like this help cultivate a lifelong love of nature and our planet.” The event will feature East Bay Children & Nature’s signature, “create-with-nature” stations that invite creativity and curiosity through play with natural materials. Two 20-minute sessions of nature-themed singalongs, starting at 4:15 p.m. and 5:10 p.m. Piedmont’s Public Works employees will be in attendance with the equipment they use in their daily work, including the Bay Area’s first fully electric closed-circuit TV sewer inspection van. Children will be able to climb up and sit in the cab of the Public Works trucks. There will be a raffle, and kids can enter to win a children’s book or toy related to Earth Day. The event will also feature plant giveaways. Attendees will have the opportunity to take home a California native plant for their gardens. Two professional arborists will be on hand to answer any questions about trees or plants that you may have. The annual event, which dates to 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees the Public Works Department maintains in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces – as well as the City’s commitment to environmental stewardship. The Arbor Day celebration will also include am announcement of the 2026 Piedmont Heritage Trees. Nominators of selected trees will be recognized at the event and receive a Piedmont Heritage Tree lapel pin. The Heritage Tree program, now in its eighth year, aims to raise awareness of and appreciation for Piedmont’s diverse urban forest. Heritage Trees are nominated by community members and selected by the Park Commission. articles.text: “The Taste of BYA” is an evening of community, food, drinks, and powerful stories honoring Jeffrey Church, Executive Director of Visit Berkeley, and officially introduces the community to BYA’s new leadership. The event will take place on Thursday, April 24, from 6 - 9 p.m. at the Brazilian Room of Tilden Regional Park (1500 Wildcat Canyon Rd, Berkeley). Berkeley Mayor Adena Ishii is expected to attend the event. The media will hear directly from BYA’s new Co-Executive Directors, Dr. Tiffany Lockett and Mieka Claridy, and program alumni who will share their experiences with the organization’s positive work. Local vendors attending include California Rose Catering, Rosenblum Cellars, Chris Evans Catering, The Grazing Company, Father’s Brewing, Pacific Fine Food Catering, and Hugh Groman Group. The event focuses on the impact of BYA’s critical programs for local youth and families. BYA is an organization that has served Berkeley, Oakland, and Alameda counties for over 50 years, supporting underserved children through educational, health, wellness, and career development programs. In the past year, BYA has provided services for over 500 children in need, 6,500 counseling sessions to students and their families, and donated over 40,000 pounds of food to the local community. Tickets may be purchased at BYA’s website: https://byaonline. org/events.
articles.title: Berkeley Youth Alternatives hosts Taste of BYA

articles.text: Registration for summer swim lessons for Piedmont residents at the new community pool opened on Tuesday, April 21. Residents planning to sign up should make sure their household is in the aquatics registration portal at rec. us/piedmont. For community members already verified as residents in Community Pass, resident registration options should be available immediately once you create your account. For new users, residency verification can take a couple of days, so residents who have not yet created an account should do so as soon as possible. Swim lessons begin in June and will be offered for all ages and experience levels, from “Happy Splashers” parent-and-baby water play for children as young as 6 months, to beginner, intermediate, and advanced options for teens and adults. Private swim instruction will also be available. The program mix includes adult fitness options as well, with drop-in water aerobics already underway on Tuesday mornings and morning yoga on the rooftop pavilion beginning in May. The registration por tal includes a “Fast Track” feature that works like a wish list. Residents can save programs they want to register for and complete required forms in advance, making checkout faster once registration opens. Fast Track does not reserve space in a class. Summer swim lesson registration for resident annual passholders opened on April 14. Annual passholders also receive priority registration for other aquatics programming throughout the year. The first week of the pool has brought in large crowds of people taking advantage of the drop-in pricing through April 30. The pool reached capacity this past weekend, with the busiest times of 2-4 p.m. When the pool approaches its peak capacity, annual passholders will have priority admission, and drop-in visitors may need to wait until enough swimmers leave. The city encourages families who have flexibility in their schedules to consider visiting in the morning or evening when crowds are lighter – especially if they’re bringing small children. The city encourages everyone to plan ahead for this Saturday. The Piedmont FoodFest will draw large crowds to Piedmont Park from 11 a.m. - 4 p.m. and parking will be limited. A packed crowd on Friday afternoon at the new Piedmont activity pool Staff photo
articles.title: Summer swim lesson, class registration opens April 21

articles.text: Piedmont’s Shell Station at 29 Wildwood Avenue has been in limbo ever since a city-approved plan for an EV charging hub was upended due to state laws that limit local control over EV charging station permits. Now the station’s development is in the hands of the state and the Alameda County Department of Environmental Health (ACEHD). According to ACEHD, Previous environmental investigations have identified elevated concentrations of volatile organic compounds and petroleum hydrocarbons in soil, groundwater, and soil vapor (the air between soil particles) at the site. Due to these findings, the department has required Shell to conduct both on‑site and off‑site environmental assessments at 29 Wildwood Avenue, including work under a Voluntary Remedial Action Agreement and a detailed subsurface investigation. Under this agreement, Shell voluntarily agrees to investigate and clean up environmental contamination. This work includes collecting soil, soil vapor, and groundwater samples from 29 Wildwood and two neighboring off-site residential properties. The investigations will be performed to evaluate if these contaminants have migrated beyond the site, and to verify that conditions are protective of site utility workers and adjacent residents. The latest on-site and off-site environmental investigation was conducted on March 6. Once the investigation is complete, Shell will work with ACEHD to develop and review an appropriate Remedial Action Plan. The plan will address contamination and ensure long-term protection of public health and the environment. According to a representative from Shell, the timing and feasibility of redevelopment will depend on the extent of remediation required, regulatory approvals, and other potential factors such as weather and access to adjacent properties. Because these steps are still in progress, Shell does not yet have a confirmed construction timeline for the charging station. Should residents have any questions or concerns, contact Tracy Craig at (510) 334-4866 (24/7). Project details can be found at: https://geotracker.waterboards.ca.gov and searching for the address 29 Wildwood Avenue, Piedmont. The location of the proposed EV Charging Shell Station on 29 Wildwood Ave
articles.title: 29 Wildwood Ave’s Shell Station is undergoing an environmental assessment

articles.text: Children’s Fairyland is celebrating the magic of spring with an event especially designed for the forever young at heart. Fairyland’s Mad Tea Party is the year’s first of five Happily After Hours 21+ events held at Oakland’s legendary storybook theme park. It will take place on Friday, April 24 from 6-10 p.m. The immersive adults-only Alice in Wonderland-themed party will feature Wonderland mischief and theatrical surprises, a proper tea party, local food trucks, sweet Wonderland-inspired treats, a DJ with a black light dance floor, and surprise activations throughout the park. Guests can explore the iconic park, sip on curated cocktails, mocktails, beer, wine, and other beverages. Guests can feel free to express themselves with imaginative attire, whimsical accessories, or elaborate outfits. Costumes are highly encouraged, but not required. Mad Tea Party is centered around a proper tea party at the park’s famous Jack and Jill Hill. A live DJ atop the hill will help turn the space into a whimsical world of tea, beats, and Wonderland treats. Guests can enjoy a cup of tea, themed sweets, and party favors while cabaret performers bring Alice in Wonderland to life with meandering vignettes and circus surprises. The Red Queen makes cameos throughout the evening and other performers roam the park creating wandering theatrical mischief for all to enjoy. Fairyland is a playground for the inner child of every grownup in attendance. Guests are invited to hop aboard the Jolly Trolly for delightful evening rides, play inside the Alice in Wonderland tunnel and maze, and explore other storybook sets like the Old West Junction and many more. With 10 acres of lush gardens, attractions, water features, and whimsical structures, there is something magical to discover with every corner turned. This year’s Mad Tea Party welcomes back crowd favorite DJ heyLove who blends jazz, R&B, hip-hop, house, and global rhythms into soulful, genre-defying sets. She’ll be spinning choice cuts with a black light dance floor where guests can enjoy a unique experience in the Merry Meadow under the Oakland stars in neon colored revelry. A stanchioned top of the Dragon Slide becomes an exclusive VIP lounge for a select group of people who want to enjoy an elevated experience featuring champagne, bottle service, and gorgeous photo ops. While this year’s Gilded Chrysalis Experience is completely sold out, this tier ticketing option is new and is set to become a consistent feature of the annual event. Fairyland’s Gift Shop will be open for the event where guests can find an array of adults-only merchandise rolled out for the evening and can also purchase their own copy of Fairyland’s signature piece of magical merch: the Magic Key. The newest color “All Heroes Wear Pink” was recently released and will be available on the evening of Mad Tea Party. More information and tickets are available at Fairyland.org/ mad-tea-party/. Happily After Hours: Mad Tea Party (21+) When: Friday, April 24, 2026 | 6 to 10 p.m. Where: Children’s Fairyland, 699 Bellevue Ave, Oakland, CA Cost: $28 per person | $23 for Fairyland Members Mad Tea Party is the first of five adult-only “happily after hours” events at Children’s Fairyland this year.
articles.title: Fairyland’s adults-only “Mad Tea Party” on April 24

Once the investigation is complete, Shell will work with ACEHD to develop and review an appropriate Remedial Action Plan. The plan will address contamination and ensure long-term protection of public health and the environment. According to a representative from Shell, the timing and feasibility of redevelopment will depend on the extent of remediation required, regulatory approvals, and other potential factors such as weather and access to adjacent properties. Because these steps are still in progress, Shell does not yet have a confirmed construction timeline for the charging station. Should residents have any questions or concerns, contact Tracy Craig at (510) 334-4866 (24/7). Project details can be found at: https://geotracker.waterboards.ca.gov and searching for the address 29 Wildwood Avenue, Piedmont. articles.text: Dear PUSD Families & Staff: What a remarkable spring it has been, and it’s hard to believe we are closing in on the end of the school year. Our students had the rare experience of traveling to China, Spain, and France, travels that will likely shape their understanding of the world for years to come. A heartfelt thank you to our students and families for your enthusiasm, flexibility, and trust, and to all of our dedicated teachers and administrators who initiated and chaperoned these trips. Organizing international travel for groups of students requires extensive preparation, meticulous planning, and an enormous personal commitment, and we are deeply grateful for your leadership and care. Having served as one of the chaperones on the China trip, I can say with complete sincerity that it was one of the best trips of my life. Our students experienced an incredible range of cultural, historical, and modern wonders: walking the Great Wall, taking in the breathtaking Longji Terraced Rice Fields, cruising the Lijiang River, admiring the Temple of Heaven, the Forbidden City, and Tiananmen Square in Beijing, touring factories and robotics facilities in Tangshan, and visiting two local schools where students connected with their Chinese peers. A very special thank you is owed to XinJia Xia (Xia laoshi) for her extraordinary work organizing this journey across multiple cities, hotels, schools, and cultural experiences. Her expertise, tireless effort, and joy made this trip the remarkable success it was. A video of the trip can be viewed drive.google.com/ file/d/1iZ72hcYtWFVcAp-paywqhG1sT9QavDIA/view?usp=sharing To our students: you represented your school and community with grace, curiosity, and Thirty-seven Piedmont cultural exchange participants – students, staff and parents – spent their spring break visiting China.

articles.text: During COVID in particular, what started as a shared activity became a close-knit group of families who supported one another and each other’s kids. As our kids became more involved, so did we. We’ve both served as Assistant Scoutmasters and supported the troop in different ways. Jim has served as the troop’s adult advisor for the Order of the Arrow. Martin helped pilot the Citizenship in Society merit badge nationally and has led Introduction to Outdoor Leadership Skills, the core training for adult leaders, for the past five years. Mimi and Kane have also taken on leadership roles, helping teach skills like knot-tying, fire building, and outdoor ethics to adult volunteers at those trainings. Scouting has been a really positive experience for our kids. Both earned Eagle as freshmen, so at this point the kids both outrank Jim, who never quite made it that far. Kane especially loves camping and hiking, but both of them have gained practical skills like cooking, planning, and budgeting, along with confidence, leadership, and public speaking. Just as importantly, they’ve learned to mentor younger Scouts. Since her very first campout, when older Scouts made sure she felt included, Mimi has tried to do the same for others. For us, Scouting is about more than activities or achievements. It’s about connection. It gave us the chance to spend real, uninterrupted time together doing things we all enjoy, including camping, hiking, and even launching rockets on the beach. Those are the moments that stay with you. It’s been just as meaningful to watch the other kids in the troop grow into confident, capable young adults, and to know we had a small part in that along the way. pages.text: Wednesday, April 22, 2026 7 By Martin and Jim Crawford-Jakubiak We’re longtime fans of Scouting. We were both Scouts growing up, and many of our best childhood memories are from that time. For Martin, Scouting was also a way to spend a lot of time with his dad, who was deeply involved in his troop. Some of their best memories, including Philmont, canoe trips, and countless campouts, were shared together. Martin’s dad was an Eagle Scout, and Martin earned his Eagle as well. When our kids were young, we looked for something they could do together and that we could be part of as a family. At the time, though, it didn’t seem like Scouting would be that activity. Girls were not allowed to participate, and only straight adults were allowed to serve as leaders. It was disappointing to think something that had meant so much to us might not be available to our kids or to us as a family. We were fortunate to be part of the Piedmont community, where the local council has long advocated for true inclusivity in Scouting. Over time, national policies changed, and during our kids’ childhoods, we watched Scouting become what we had hoped it could be, welcoming to all youth and all adults. When girls were allowed to join, just as our kids were reaching the age to start Scouting, we realized it could be something our whole family could be part of. Kane was excited to join Troop 11 with his friends. Mimi was more hesitant, but after her first campout in Redwood National Park, she and we were convinced it was the right fit. It quickly brought our family, and many others, closer together. Scouting has been a really positive experience for our kids. Both earned Eagle as freshmen, so at this point the kids both outrank Jim, who never quite made it that far. Kane especially loves camping and hiking, but both of them have gained practical skills like cooking, planning, and budgeting, along with confidence, leadership, and public speaking. Just as importantly, they’ve learned to mentor younger Scouts. Since her very first campout, when older Scouts made sure she felt included, Mimi has tried to do the same for others. For us, Scouting is about more than activities or achievements. It’s about connection. It gave us the chance to spend real, uninterrupted time together doing things we all enjoy, including camping, hiking, and even launching rockets on the beach. Those are the moments that stay with you. It’s been just as meaningful to watch the other kids in the troop grow into confident, capable young adults, and to know we had a small part in that along the way. articles.text: The Piedmont High School Dance Department presents its Spring Dance Concert Thursday, April 23, and Friday, April 24, at 7:00 p.m. each night in the Alan Harvey Theater. Dancing Through the Decades features a vibrant range of dance styles—including modern, jazz, contemporary, and hip hop—celebrating music and movement across a variety of eras. Featuring 42 dancers performing original choreography, the evening also highlights an original jazz piece by director Amy Moorhead, set to Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five’s iconic recording of West End Blues composed by Joe “King” Oliver. The concert is appropriate for all ages, there will be one intermission. The performance will conclude by 8:00 p.m. Tickets are available for purchase online, or at the door with cash or check made payable to PUSD. articles.text: This year's first fundraising party for Spring Fling took place on April 15 at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. The dance party, titled Nobody Puts Baby in the Corner "Dirty Dancing," brought out more than 80 Havens Elementary students and parents to dance. Parent hosts Hilary Gitter, Della Chow and Alisha Eastwood planned a party that kids and parents would enjoy in support of Piedmont’s three elementary schools. Naila Brown, the ballet and modern dance teacher at Piedmont Ballet Academy, and professional choreographer Shawl Anderson led the party in a kid and parents dance-off. “These kind efforts, to join together as a school community, are what makes Piedmont so special,” said Gitter. Hands down, the kids won the dance-off to the music of Beyonce's Crazy in Love. The party also included a warm-up to I've had the Time of My Life and a soul train line including Chaka Khan, Footloose, Sports Car, Hot to Go and of course Lush Life. The organizers said they were overjoyed to have so many families come out on a Wednesday evening with such great energy and for a great cause. A soul train line through the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse got everyone involved. A charcoal portrait by freshman Mo Wang was featured in the PHS Art Show on Thursday, April 16, in the Alan Harvey Theater’s foyer. Charcoal portrait by Akunna Iroh Charcoal portrait by Niko Kalamas Houchin, had Art 1 students use charcoal to create a larger than life self-protrait. “For my Larger Than Life self portrait, I decided to take an expressive image that reflected the facial expression made after tasting something sour. The sour facial expression can also be utilized when reacting to a painful social interaction which I think is quite relatable,” said Akunna Iroh. “The most important thing about charcoal that I learned is that there are different types of charcoal and they have their own strengths. The vine charcoal is good for shading and is easy to erase and the denser charcoal makes really dark marks,” said Nikolas Kalamas. “I created an interesting image by choosing a selfie with strong lighting and clear shadows. I made sure that there was enough contrast, because that makes it easier to use charcoal. I also picked a photo that looked like me and felt natural,” said Mo Wang This all-school art show brought all Piedmont student artists, from PHS and MHS, together to create a showcase that is greater than the sum of its parts. From freshman to senior, and from beginning to excelling artist, every artist had something to put up on the wall and be proud of. This art show celebrates art in all its forms and has become another proud Piedmont tradition.

articles.text: After three years on the Public Safety Committee, Liz Lummis O’Neil’s term has ended. She spent years emphasizing the importance of community involvement and fire safety. Liz valued the opportunity to volunteer, learn, and connect with fellow Piedmont residents, viewing it as a way to contribute positively to the community. Liz moved to Piedmont in 2016 and decided to be a part of the tight-knit community by volunteering. After attending a random City Council meeting, Liz had the opportunity to speak with the Fire Chief at the time. This led to her neighborhood having a fire safety meeting. Liz realized the idea of fire safety had been on her mind for a while, and she finally found the avenue to spread awareness. “When I came to California, way back when, in 1992, it was just after the firestorm in Upper Rockridge. So Fire Safety has always been on the top of my mind. To get to join the Piedmont Public Safety Committee meant a lot. It wasn’t sitting and hoping nothing happens, but rather being informed and taking action,” said O’Neil. After joining the Public Safety Liz O’Neil shakes hands with Piedmont Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen after receiving a volunteer award for her time with the Public Safety Committee. Committee in 2023, Liz felt her role was to act as a sounding board and keep her neighborhood informed. “I wanted to be the voice of my neighborhood. If something ever came up, I would be good at voicing our perspective and keeping our neighborhood informed,” O’Neil said. Liz reflected on her term on the Public Safety Committee, stating the importance of community involvement and informing people about wildfire safety. “One of my takeaways was that Piedmont residents like to take action and make things happen. A recent project I worked on was having Captain Callahan and some of his crew come over from the fire department to give an in-depth fire safety meeting for homes, and then did individual walk-throughs of each of the attending group’s homes,” Liz continued. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont celebrated Senior Night at the pool’s debut. Pictured are Dima Secor (left), Nik Costello, coach Elizabeth Dally, Zoe Waitkus, Sam White, Brooke Patchen, Tai March-Cunningham, and Adelina Mbise. Friday, April 17 was a momentous occasion for the Piedmont High swimming team, debuting at the Piedmont Pool against Castro Valley. It was the first time the Highlanders hosted a meet since 2019. The PHS’ boys’ team came away with a 123.5-46.5 win over the Trojans, while the girls’ fell 113-51, but concluded with some top finishes. For students at Piedmont High it’s been a long time coming. Much of the team has, e had to travel every which way to get pool time going back to their elementary school days. Over the years, they’ve traveled to almost every adjacent city you can think of to swim, including Oakland, Hayward, Moraga, Berkeley, Concord, the list goes on. Although this year’s team gets just one meet at the new Piedmont Pool, the opportunity to race in front of friends, faculty, and the community is something they relish. “It’s amazing. It’s awesome; we finally got to swim in the Piedmont Pool after being promised it 2-3 years ago. I still remember my first high school meet four years ago. We’ve swam at Laney, Berkeley, St. Mary’s, Mills College, Chabot. It’s great for future season and the classes below us. It’s led to some late nights driving home,” senior Dima Secor said. “It’s really nice to finally get the pool for at least one meet. I’m just happy it got open in the first place. Those long trips sometimes make you not want to go to practice so far away. Having practice here is so much easier,” fellow senior Samantha White said. Secor is a key figure on Piedmont’s relay teams, helping them win the 200 freestyle and 400 freestyle events against Castro Valley. Nik Costello was a member of last year’s 400 free and 200 medley teams that reached the CIF State championship. The group is shaping up to do it again. “It means a lot. We finally get to have spectators from the school to come out and watch us, that’s never really happened because we’re jumping from pool to pool. Since we’re right next to the school, we saw today people from all the other teams came over to watch after their practices were over,” Secor said. “It was great to have all my friends come and support. It was a great environment, a beautiful day, senior night, it was a fun day. I’m glad to see people support us, we got to show everyone what we can do,” Costello added. White is a senior leader of the girls’ squad, winning two individual events on Friday, the 200 and 500 freestyles. Although the girls’ team is facing a bit of a transition year, she also understands that swimming doesn’t get the notoriety it deserves after going without a pool for so long. She witnessed the height of the girls’ squad as a freshman in 2023, when their 200 medley and 400 freestyle relay teams went undefeated and won the Western Alameda County Conference title in both events. “Swimming definitely doesn’t get the recognition it deserves. A lot of people don’t realize that we have a great team; it’s hard to get people to care enough to come out and watch when you don’t have a home pool,” White said. Piedmont honored its seven seniors on Friday: Secor, Costello, White, Zoe Waitkus, Brooke Patchen, Tai March-Cunningham, and Adelina Mbise. The Highlanders now prepare for the 2026 WACC Championships at Chabot College in Hayward on May 1. Below is a list of top results from Friday, while a full photo page of the meet is featured on Page 15. Full Results Eight of Piedmont’s boys’ swimmers came away with 21 total Gold medals against Castro Valley. In fields of six swimmers, junior Asher Takazawa won the 100 backstroke in 52.95 seconds and the 100 butterfly in 51.94. Secor won the 100 freestyle in Dima Secor smiles before his dive at the debut of the Piedmont Pool.

articles.text: PHS boys’ lacrosse team beats O’Dowd 11-9, Dublin 18-5 Photos by JC Curran Connor Fredericks scored seven goals in Piedmont’s 11-9 win over rival Bishop O’Dowd. Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team concluded a highly productive week, winning its last two games to improve its record to 6-5 with one regular season match to play. In a critical rivalry match at Bishop O’Dowd they beat the Dragons 11-9, then followed up with a dominant 18-5 win over Dublin on a rainy night at Witter Field on Monday, April 20. Their win over Bishop O’Dowd was the Highlanders’ first game after returning from Spring Break. They lost the previous two matches to the Dragons, making it an important time for Piedmont High to put things together. “Ever yone gets up for O’Dowd. It’s the biggest game of the season for the guys and families, so there’s a lot of energy. I think it helped them in practice that week. There’s a lot of positive energy right now,” coach Andy Kittler said. Their win over the Dragons came in come-from-behind fashion after trailing 6-4 at halftime. Junior Connor Fredericks was key in the win, scoring seven goals. “Playing fast was the biggest factor. We didn’t let their defense get comfortable and made it clear that when we had the ball, they needed to watch out,” Fredericks said. The Highlanders beat Bishop O’Dowd in last year’s regular season meeting, but fell to the Dragons in the Western Alameda County Conference tournament. That memory remains fresh on their minds. “We look forward to that game all season, especially after having a disappointing loss to them last year. The juniors and seniors knew we had to dig deep. We all remember last year’s loss, it put a chip on our shoulder,” Fredericks said. PHS closes its regular season against two-consecutive WACC champions, Berkeley, on Friday, April 24 at the Yellowjackets’ home field. After that, the first round of the WACC Tournament is tentatively scheduled for Wednesday, April 29, with the championship round two days later on Friday, May 1 at Bishop O’Dowd. 11-9 win over O’Dowd O’Dowd struck first – 48 seconds into the action – but PHS answered just 16 seconds later when Fredericks won the faceoff and turned upfield on a long run before scoring the goal. BOD regained the lead at the 9:14 mark, but Fredericks tied things up again less than three minutes later. Owen Curran won the ensuing faceoff, leading to P.J. Brayer giving Piedmont a 3-2 lead with 6:18 left. From there, O’Dowd tied two minutes later, leading to the Dragons scoring twice in quick succession with nine seconds Landon Heppner (8) scored the go-ahead goal for Piedmont against O’Dowd in the fourth quarter. He is shown celebrating with Teddy Cordani. Timmy Kalamas (18) celebrates with Ryan Graham after a goal against O’Dowd. and two seconds left to take a 5-3 lead. The defense was tight in the second quarter with both teams scoring just once, including one by Fredericks. In the third quarter, Fredericks scored after a minute and a half, faking a shot to make the defense bite before wheeling toward the net. BOD scored with 7:54 on the clock, while Fredericks scored in similar fashion five minutes later—7-6. Curran knotted things

articles.text: Piedmont fell to O’Dowd in a pair of one-run games. Piedmont’s baseball team had a tightly contested series with rival Bishop O’Dowd losing a pair of one-run ball games. The Highlanders hosted the Dragons on Wednesday, April 15 and lost 3-2 in a heated 11-inning game. They followed up with a close 1-0 loss at O’Dowd two days later on Friday, April 17. Piedmont had to play both games without its star hitter, Diego Delventhal. “He’s a quality at bat, he’ll still be a couple of weeks, but no one is feeling sorry for us,” coach Eric Olson said. PHS held a 2-1 lead in Wednesday’s game following the bottom of the sixth, but the Dragons tied things up in the top of the seventh and scored the game-winner in the top of the 11th. In Friday’s game, Bishop O’Dowd logged the games only hit. “A lot of guys stepped up their game. We had some good pitching to prolong the game and give us a chance. The defense was solid, which is what we’re looking for. We were just one hit away from getting runs,” Olson said. The Highlanders hold a 6-10-2 (W-L-T) record with just six games left in its regular season. Coming up are two-game series with Alameda, Berkeley, and Encinal. Staff Photos 3-2 loss to O’Dowd in extra innings O’Dowd went up 1-0 in the top of the second, while Piedmont answered with two runs in the bottom of the sixth. The Dragons tied things up in the top of the seventh, and scored once more in the top of the 11th. In the bottom of the sixth, Enzo Ong led off with a walk, followed by Lucas Delventhal singling on a bunt. Jonah Cha-Foster followed up with a bunt of his own, and was ruled safe at first after colliding with the first-baseman in his way. That allowed Ong to score. Jack Meyjes then grounded out to the shortstop, allowing Delventhal to score. However, that was all Piedmont could muster. PHS had a chance to win the game in the bottom of the seventh after Aiden Bell and Max Fujimoto walked, followed by George Bishop singling on a bunt to load the bases. But after that, Massimo Mittone grounded out, a squeeze bunt by Ong failed, and Delventhal popped out. O’Dowd scored the game-winner with two outs, where Marco Cecchin stole third and then scored when Delventhal came narrowly short of throwing out Charlie Sellman to end the inning on a hard hit ground ball. Freshman Ben Sorensen had a productive outing against BOD, throwing six innings and four strikeouts in Wednesday’s no decision. George Bishop threw 4.2 innings in Wednesday’s game, striking out five.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s softball team returned from Spring Break in a big way, beating the visiting Tennyson Lancers 18-8 at the Witter Softball Field on Wednesday, April 15 in a Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline B Division game. The result improves the Highlanders’ record to 9-6 with six games left in the regular season They remain undefeated in three games against Shoreline B teams. PHS did most of its work in the bottom of the second inning when they put 12 runs on the board. They won the game with just six hits, making the most of the pitcher’s mistakes by drawing 10 walks. 12 players got on base after being hit by a pitch, and e Piedmont totaled 10 stolen bases. 18-8 over Tennyson Tennyson actually got out to a 3-0 lead in the top of the first, while Piedmont tacked on one in the bottom half. The Highlanders’ offense came alive in the bottom of the second, landing 12 runs in an overpowering half inning. Piedmont extended the lead to 16-5 after the bottom of the fourth, and then activated the 10-run rule with two more runs in the bottom of the fifth. In the bottom second, Penelope Hopper and Edie Elmquist drew one-out walks, then Elly Mak was hit by a pitch to load the bases. Hannah Joerger then was hit by a pitch to bring in Hopper, while Hanley Carling Staff Photos Edie Elmquist went 1-for-2 against Tennyson, including two RBIs, four runs scored, three walks and four stolen bases Hanley Carling went 2-for-2 with two RBIs, two runs scored and got on base twice after being hit by pitches. Then, Samantha Schey, Hailey Navarro, and Makenna Small were each hit by pitches to score Joerger, Carling, and Perl respectively. Hopper drew a walk to score Schey, Elmquist walked to score Navarro, then Mak was hit by a pitch to score Small. Joerger then cracked a double to the left field fence to bring in Hopper and Elmquist. To activate the 10-run rule, Hopper led off with a single, stole second, and took third on a wild pitch. Elmquist brought her in with a single. After Willow Thomas walked, Joerger hit another double to score Elmquist—making it 18-8. Final stats: Navarro had two RBIs, one run scored and was hit by pitches twice. articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School softball team stands proud after its 9-3 win over Albany Middle School. Pictured are (back) Anya Giri (left), Evie Joerger, Mackenzie Ewen, Bailey Gregovich, Madi Farboud, Simone Tornatore, Nina Stock, Mailey Small, (middle) Olive Dao-Hoang (left), Keira Spina, Sarina Hill, Clara Blanchard, and (front) Abby Gregovich. The Piedmont Middle School softball team returned from Spring break on Thursday April, 16 in strong fashion, beating the visiting Albany Cobras 9-3 in a four-inning game at the Witter Softball Field. The Scots once again leaned on their aces in the circle, with 8th graders Bailey Gregovich and Madi Farboud combining on a five hit, two walk, 10 strikeout effort backstopped by a tandem of Simone Tornatore and Abby Gregovich at catcher. While the offense was far from explosive, the Scots took advantage of seven free passes as well as converting two big dropped third strikes into base runners. Tornatore provided a spark at the plate with a big two RBI single with two outs in the third for her second hit of the afternoon. Bailey Gregovich also had a towering double to right center. Solid defense all afternoon kept the Cobras at bay, with two key dropped third strike outs at first on strong throws from Abby Gregovich as well as a an unassisted double play from Sarina Hill, who snared a line drive to second and then nonchalantly glided over the bag to double off the runner. The Scots will now pack their bags for an extended road trip that has them scheduled to tour eight different ballparks in the Oakland and Berkeley area before returning home for the playoffs in early May. Bailey Gregovich sends a pitch against Albany. Simone Tornatore gets a hit against Albany.

articles.text: Pianist Yuja Wang will perform at Davies Symphony Hall on April 26. World-renowned pianist Yuja Wang performs with the Mahler Chamber Orchestra at Davies Symphony Hall this Sunday, April 26. Wang, a Chinese-born classical pianist from Beijing, made her San Francisco Symphony debut in 2006 and toured Asia with the company and its former conductor Michael Tilson Thomas in November 2012. She has since become a recurring guest pianist at Davies Symphony Hall and has performed with the Berlin Philharmonic, Oslo Philharmonic, Toronto Symphony Orchestra and more. Wang is celebrated for both her stage presence and musical skills, and returns to San Francisco next month to direct a program of 20th-century favorites by Prokofiev with the Mahler Chamber Orchestra. The program included Alexander Tsfasman’s Suite for Piano and Orchestra (Jazz Suite). The Mahler Chamber Orchestra is a professional touring chamber orchestra founded by Claudio Abbado and former members of the Gustav Mahler Youth Orchestra in 1997. The orchestra consists of 45 musicians from 20 nations and performs more than 60 concerts a year worldwide. Matthew Truscott serves as concertmaster and leader for the evening concert. Performance begins at 7:30 p.m. Visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2025-26/ YUJA-WANG-MCO to purchase tickets, or call the San Francisco Symphony box office at (415) 864-6000.
articles.title: Yuja Wang & Mahler Chamber Orchestra perform at Davies this Sunday

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony concludes its 2026 Chamber Series at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on May 31 with a curated program highlighting contemporary voices and classical masterworks, held The concert, titled “I, Too, Sing America,” is curated by James Parrish Smith, featuring works by Brian Raphael Nabors, Anna Clyne and Antonín Dvořák. Smith currently serves as the Organist and Director of Music at the First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley. He previously served as Director of Music and Organist at the Historic Third Baptist Church of San Francisco and was the Founding Director of the Bridge to Arts and Music Program in association with the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. “This season represents an exciting new chapter for Berkeley Symphony,” said Berkeley Symphony Executive Director Marion Atherton. “We’re thrilled to welcome some of today’s most compelling conductors, each bringing their unique artistic vision to our stage.” This season “shines a light on stirring masterpieces from the James Parrish Smith classical canon alongside groundbreaking contemporary works,” Atherton added. “From Dvorák’s lyrical Eighth Symphony to Shostakovich’s spirited Ninth and Haydn’s vivid ‘Military’ Symphony, we’re exploring rich musical territory beyond the standard repertoire while showcasing the versatility and excellence of our orchestra.” The 2025/26 season also marks the conclusion of Music Director Joseph Young’s successful six-year tenure. Young first guest-conducted the Berkeley Symphony in 2019 as an emergency substitute conductor. Based on that concert, in April 2019, the Berkeley Symphony announced the appointment of Young as its next music director, marking his first major directorship in symphonic music. Chamber Series subscriptions are $120 and available through the symphony’s box office and website. articles.text: Visit the Randall Museum in San Francisco next month and participate in a variety of kidfriendly science, engineering and art activities, ranging from free, drop-in activities to ticketed workshops. The Randall Museum is operated by the San Francisco Recreation and Parks Department and the non-profit organization Randall Museum Friends and provides a unique experience for Bay Area kids of all ages, from pine needle basket-weaving to scrapyard robotics. Every Saturday morning in May, young visitors and their caretakers can join in an open discussion about resident animals with wildlife ambassadors, and get an opportunity to meet Lyra the raccoon, who was born with several health problems including deformities of the spine and jaw, or a long-tailed weasel named Scarlet who was neglected and sustained injuries while in captivity. Both have been rehabilitated by museum staff and offer a glimpse into California’s wildlife. Visitors may also join a bird-watching exhibition any Saturday morning throughout A young visitor meets a rabbit at Randall Museum. the summer, guided by Dominik Mosur, who has the unique distinction of achieving San Francisco’s record for identifying the most bird species in a one year period within San Francisco’s 49-square-mile limits. Other exhibitions include “Food for Thought,” which presents fun solutions to sustainability issues that children can practice at home, which help them understand new ways to reduce food waste and take part in keeping plastic out of ocean habitats. Drop-in art classes are offered every Saturday between 1 p.m. and 3:30 p.m., appropriate for children ages 4 and older. A different activity is featured each week. Visit https://randallmuseum. org to learn more. articles.text: A major retrospective of artist Maren Hassinger opens June 6 at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA), offering a wide-ranging look at her five-decade career. Titled Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing, the exhibition will be on view from June 6 through November 29. Organized as the most comprehensive survey of Hassinger’s work to date, the show will include more than twenty works spanning the 1970s to the present, alongside newly created installations and performances developed in collaboration with the artist. T he ex h ibit ion br i ngs together sculpture, installation, video, and performance, reflecting Hassinger’s interdisciplinary approach. Known for working with both industrial and impermanent materials, she has explored themes of movement, environment, and human connection throughout her career. Because many of her works are ephemeral, several pieces will be recreated specifically for this presentation. Among the featured works are Love (2008), a site-specific installation made from inflated pink plastic bags containing handwritten notes, and Beach (1980), a floor installation composed of plaster and wooden dowels. Additional sculptures incorporating freshly harvested tree branches will be produced in partnership with the University of California Botanical Garden. A central component of the exhibition will be public participation. On opening day, visitors will be invited to join Hassinger in creating a new installation titled Wrenching News by twisting and knotting newspapers in a workshop led by the artist. The piece will evolve over time through monthly workshops facilitated by Berkeley-based artist Julia Goodman. Hassinger will also return to Berkeley on September 20 to restage Pink Trash, a performance she has presented only twice since its debut in 1982. The work will involve six UC Berkeley undergraduates collaborating with the artist to scatter and transform discarded litter, which will be repainted pink. The performance will take place on the university’s Crescent Lawn. In addition to artworks, the exhibition will include archival photographs and videos, including previously unpublished images documenting early works that no longer exist. The retrospective is co-curated by Margot Norton, Chief Curator, and Anthony Graham, Senior Curator, with Curatorial Assistant Omar Jason Farah. An accompanying catalogue featuring new scholarship and interviews will be published in conjunction with the exhibition. “Maren Hassinger’s practice has been of great influence for generations of artists–from her early collaborative performances and experimental installations with Studio Z and JAM to her direct impact over decades as a teacher, and through her monumental sculptural installations in major museum collections across the United States,” said Norton. “We are thrilled to finally bring her artworks and their stories from across her career together through our exhibition, and to showcase Hassinger’s profound contributions to contemporary art.” “ For d e c a d e s , M a r e n Hassinger has created sculptures and installations that transcend disciplinary boundaries, transforming industrial and mass-produced materials into evocative abstractions,” said Graham. “This exhibition showcases how these innovative works have drawn attention to subtle movements and forms of our everyday lives, connecting us to one another and to the world around us.” “Maren Hassinger’s work invites us to reflect on the beauty and complexity of human connection—through movement, material, and shared experience. Presenting this landmark retrospective at BAMPFA underscores our commitment to amplifying artists whose practices challenge conventions and inspire collective engagement across generations,” said BAMPFA Executive Director Julie Rodrigues Widholm. More information about this and other public programs will be announced this summer at bampfa.org. Maren Hassinger
articles.title: BAMPFA unveils Maren Hassinger retrospective June 6

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), California’s oldest independent youth orchestra, presents the America 250 Festival, a celebration of American Music on Saturday, May 2 at 7:00 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. The special festival concert commemorates the 250th anniversary of the United States with an evening of chamber and orchestral works by American composers spanning more than a century of musical history. The concert also serves as YPSO’s annual Spring Concert as the third concert in its 2025–26 subscription series. As part of nationwide celebrations of America’s 250th anniversary the festival explores the musical traditions that have shaped the American orchestral landscape while highlighting the role of young musicians in carrying that legacy forward. Presented in an expanded festival format, the event features chamber music performed by YPSO musicians, followed by a full orchestral program. The festival highlights the diversity and creativity of American composers, from iconic figures such as Aaron Copland and Leonard Bernstein to influential contemporary voices including Jessie Montgomery, George Walker, and Kenji Bunch. The first half of the festival showcases chamber music performed by YPSO musicians in different ensembles, including strings, brass, winds, and percussion. These smaller ensembles offer audiences an intimate musical experience while allowing students to collaborate closely and explore a wide range of styles and traditions. “Chamber music encompasses important musical techniques of listening, blending, and playing together like no other musical genre,” said Julie Kim, YPSO’s Chamber Music Director. “At the America 250 Festival, we will feature several combinations of ensembles to showcase American composers at their best.” The second half of the program brings the full orchestra to the stage with a selection of works that highlight the breadth and evolution of American orchestral music across generations. “This America 250 Festival program represents a range of American voices in classical music, both chamber and symphonic, from the 20th and 21st centuries,” said YPSO Music Director David Ramadanoff. This project is supported in part by a grant from the National Endowment for the Arts. Tickets are $20 and students are free (registration is required). For box office and concert information, see www.ypsomusic.org/events. articles.text: April 25 – May 31 Slavic Arts Exhibition The Center for Slavic Arts & Culture presents a new art exhibit, “In Bloom,” a vibrant spring exhibition that celebrates creativity and renewal. This unique show brings together 15 talented artists from across Slavic countries, each offering a distinct voice and perspective. The collection features a rich variety of styles and techniques, from traditional to contemporary works. Join us for this inspiring celebration of art, culture, and the spirit of spring. All are welcome when the gallery show will be open to the public: every Saturday and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. from April 25 through May 31. Free to all. Sunday, May 3, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio PCA Classic Jazz Club. Join us for a relaxed afternoon with In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Marshall Perry, and Albert Brooks. – celebrating Cinco de Mayo with a tribute to Mexican composers. You’ll be able to sit for a couple of hours in a comfortable chair in the intimate clublike environment with complimentary snacks and beverages. Bring a friend and plan to meet some new ones! Tickets $30 at the door, cash or check only, or $25 in advance at https://events.com/r/tickets/1034704 Seating is limited to 50. Saturday, May 9, 6:00 p.m. Charged Particles Jazz Quartet This local quartet will present a two-hour concert called Jazz with a Spark! Charged Particles features three of the country’s virtuosos: Murray Low a keyboard wizard with dazzling Latin-jazz technique, Doug Pohorski a Bay Area bassist, recording engineer, producer, and composer, who has been performing on the upright and electric bass for over 35 years; and fiery drummer Jon Krosnick. The concert also features SF- based jazz saxophonist Tod Dickow, who performs in a wide variety of settings ranging from big bands to small combos. Tickets at https://www.ticketsignup. io/TicketEvent/JAZZWITHASPARK or at door. Sunday, May 10, 4:00 p.m. Leonardo Garcia Solo Guitar Leo Garcia is an award-winning classical guitarist, recording artist, author, and sought-after educator. Leo has performed across North and South America and Europe as both a soloist and a chamber musician. Recent performances include a world premiere of Grammy-winning composer Sergio Assad’s Tres Cenas Brasileiras II for two guitars, written for and performed with his sons. This concert will include works by Villa-Lobos, Bach, Albéniz, Granados, Barrios, and the premiere of Prelude Nº2 – Legerdemain, by Max García (his son). Advance tickets (including lowpriced student tix) are available at https://www.ticketsignup. io/garciaguitar. Saturday, May 23, 7:00 p.m. George Cole Quartet Concert A San Francisco native and longtime guitarist for the David Grisman Quintet, Cole recently fought and beat leukemia. Now in remission, he approaches each performance as a gift – to his audience, and to himself. Cole has spent his career living at the crossroads of American swing and the gypsy jazz tradition of Django Reinhardt — and Eurocana is where those two roads finally meet. There’s a particularly fitting connection to Piedmont itself. For six years, Cole taught guitar to two East Bay kids who would go on to change rock and roll history – Billie Joe Armstrong and Mike Dirnt of Green Day, both Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductees. Advance tickets for this very special Eurocana experience are available now at https://www.ticketsignup. io/colefour. articles.text: April 18 is a fateful date in American history. On that very date, the San Francisco area was shaken by immense earthquake and the city of San Francisco was destroyed by a disastrous fire. On the same date even earlier, in 1775, Paul Revere alerted American colonists that “the redcoats are coming.” That began the Revolutionary War. This year, April 18 was on a Saturday. Nothing fateful occurred. But the red coats appeared on the 19th of April in the Piedmont Center for the Arts. These red coats concluded a beautiful musical program. Here’s what happened: The University of California and Stanford are longstanding rivals in sports. That rivalry should be confined to the football field. When those same two universities collaborate musically, beautiful things happen. That’s the way it was on Sunday evening in Piedmont. Four outstanding vocal groups collaborated in a lovely musical program. Leading off came the “classical jazz” octet from Stanford. They are a completely vocal group. Somehow they were able to incorporate instrumental sounds into their singing. They are an elegant “complete package“ exuding the joy of making music. It was a delight to hear their dynamic contrasts. Second on the program was a sextet known as “Counterpoint”. We were told that this all-female group is the only one of its kind on the West Coast. Their music making was a “smooth, pop style.” Unfortunately they were not up to their usual slick style because some of the memAward-winning restaurateur Douglas Keane telling everything we need to know about the restaurant business Thrilling singing by the red-coated coral group The Mendicants.
