Advance tickets (including lowpriced student tix) are available at https://www.ticketsignup. io/garciaguitar. Saturday, May 23, 7:00 p.m. George Cole Quartet Concert A San Francisco native and longtime guitarist for the David Grisman Quintet, Cole recently fought and beat leukemia. Now in remission, he approaches each performance as a gift – to his audience, and to himself. Cole has spent his career living at the crossroads of American swing and the gypsy jazz tradition of Django Reinhardt — and Eurocana is where those two roads finally meet. There’s a particularly fitting connection to Piedmont itself. For six years, Cole taught guitar to two East Bay kids who would go on to change rock and roll history – Billie Joe Armstrong and Mike Dirnt of Green Day, both Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductees. Advance tickets for this very special Eurocana experience are available now at https://www.ticketsignup. io/colefour. COMING SOON Vitamin Em: The Band, and another Berkeley Symphony and Friends Chamber Concert More, please By Joseph Gold April 18 is a fateful date in American history. On that very date, the San Francisco area was shaken by immense earthquake and the city of San Francisco was destroyed by a disastrous fire. On the same date even earlier, in 1775, Paul Revere alerted American colonists that “the redcoats are coming.” That began the Revolutionary War. This year, April 18 was on a Saturday. Nothing fateful occurred. But the red coats appeared on the 19th of April in the Piedmont Center for the Arts. These red coats concluded a beautiful musical program. Here’s what happened: The University of California and Stanford are longstanding rivals in sports. That rivalry should be confined to the football field. When those same two universities collaborate musically, beautiful things happen. That’s the way it was on Sunday evening in Piedmont. Four outstanding vocal groups collaborated in a lovely musical program. Leading off came the “classical jazz” octet from Stanford. They are a completely vocal group. Somehow they were able to incorporate instrumental sounds into their singing. They are an elegant “complete package“ exuding the joy of making music. It was a delight to hear their dynamic contrasts. Second on the program was a sextet known as “Counterpoint”. We were told that this all-female group is the only one of its kind on the West Coast. Their music making was a “smooth, pop style.” Unfortunately they were not up to their usual slick style because some of the members were sick. The Counterpoint The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet ensemble is a female version of a barbershop quartet, featuring soloists with a vocal backup. The third group is known as the Golden Overtones. This is a larger female choir, and it was obvious that they were having lots of fun. Exuberance alternated with some really dramatic singing. Subject matter and music merged much the way that a good gospel choir would present a program. The red coats from Stanford finished the program in fine fashion. They are known as the Mendicants, and are an all-male singing ensemble. All four of the singing groups have a unity of spirit. They love making music and it shows. The philosophy of good dining Two days before the PCA concert a few of us got together to listen to the acclaimed restaurateur Douglas Keane tell us what it takes to make a restaurant successful. He opened his program with a bit of background. He grew up in Detroit where he enjoyed taking cooking classes in school. He liked cooking so much he stayed in the “cooking lane” which eventually became the fast lane to success. Along the way, he discovered that it helps to be generous. If I heard correctly, he has donated a lot of money to rescue dogs. Upon graduation from cooking school, he moved to San Francisco, where he discovered that the city had good food, but it seemed to be the same in every restaurant. That didn’t sit well with him. Being very observant he knew exactly what to do. Putting ego aside, he learned how to manage people and make people feel good about what they did. Along the way he learned how to be efficient and how to cross-train all of his co-workers. All tips are equally divided. He constantly analyzes every aspect of food service. Additionally, he is receptive to suggestions. A philosophy like this is inspirational. pages.text: Wednesday, April 22, 2026 21 Features Walking on Wednesday A favorite annual walk at Mountain View marks eight years of Walking Wednesdays By Dick Carter Last Wednesday marked the eighth anniversary of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group, and the occasion drew a strong turnout. About 52 walkers and two K-9 companions gathered at Mountain View Cemetery for a special commemorative walk. His knowledge of Mountain View Cemetery is encyclopedic, and this marked his fourth time sharing it with the walkers. During introductions, Charlene Louie and Sandra Cook, along with Dick Carter, were recognized for having participated in the group’s very first walk on April 18, 2018. These statues of ancient Greek women symbolize how well and long one has lived. Route of last week’s walk Mountain View Cemetery in 1930s Montain View Cemetery entrance Mountain View Cemetery was established in 1863 by city leaders, who commissioned Frederick Law Olmsted to design both the cemetery and a planned residential community. Olmsted, a Harvard-educated landscape architect and UC Berkeley campus designer, was managing gold mines in Bear Valley at the time. He owned 197 acres in the area, but after proposing a design fee of $1,000, the cemetery’s trustees decided it was too expensive. Stanford and Cal may have stiffed him, but the cemetery did not adopt his plans. Instead, the project went to Among those on hand were Brenda Ferrero, Stella Houston, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Helena Farber, Irene Thompson, Mary Carter, Noemi Alvarado, Kathy Rolefson, Karen Glasser, Mark Davis, Peggy Shultz, Alissa Quan, Joanne Larson, Mary Ann Barnes, Joyce Ahern, Dave DeRoche, Debbie Powell, Sanghi Wagner, Caskey Weston, Bob Wong, Cathy Laymon, Rick Eigenbrode, Marj Blackwell, Lori Austin, Audrey Sung, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Sherry Jacobs, Brian Hamilin, Adrienne Hamlin, Melba Yee, John Sumnicht, Liz Dalrymple, John Dalrymple, Sandra Cook, Claudine Bach, Bill Ahern, Lois Price, Ken Moy, Sean Brient, Charlene Louie, Arden Hall, Cynthia Kroll, Wilber Louie, Denny McGee, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Jasmine Cai, Mike Gallant, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to have Deb Kopec, Neda Thiele, and Greg Blackburn walking with them for the first time. Frederick Law Olmsted’s son, Frederick Olmsted Jr., who created the original layout. In the 1940s, his son, “Rick,” expanded the design further up the hillside, shaping the cemetery’s present form. Evanosky emphasized that Mountain View is not a park but a working cemetery with a wide variety of burial styles. Some sections feature large monuments and tombs, while others have smaller headstones or flat-tothe-ground markers, which make maintenance easier. He noted that crews mow the grounds every Tuesday and Wednesday, and that some individuals interred there belonged to larger family plots. The cemetery is non-denominational, and people of all backgrounds are buried there. However, it was not always so inclusive. If someone died before Mountain View was established in 1863, they were typically buried at the Catholic Cemetery. It was not until 1968 that the Catholic Church permitted its members to be buried at Mountain View. In 1864, the Jewish community purchased two acres from Mountain View on its northern edge, creating a dedicated burial area. Evanosky added that the name “Mountain View” is common among cemeteries nationwide, with hundreds sharing it. The walk combined history, storytelling, and a chance to reflect on the community’s past, fitting for a group that has spent eight years exploring Piedmont and its surroundings on foot. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. articles.text: The City of Piedmont’s Planning Department hosted its annual Design & Sustainability Awards on Wednesday, April 15, featuring six of Piedmont’s most ambitious home projects. The Sustainability awards honored three residents who made significant changes to live in homes with zero-waste and sustainable designs. The award added a new category honoring residents who took precautions to keep their homes wildfire safe. The event was hosted at Piedmont Community Hall. Light appetizers and refreshments were served before the awards presentation. Vice Mayor Conna McCarthey spoke at the awards and thanked the nominees. “By spotlighting these designs, we exemplify what is possible and mentor other communities to follow our lead to become safer and greener,” she said. “Thank you for proving that a structure can be both a work of art and a protective shield for the neighborhood. You have looked at the challenges of our changing environment not as an obstacle, but as an opportunity.” Sustainability Awards Following the design awards, the Sustainability Awards were presented as a separate category. Now in their third year, the awards recognized three home renovation projects that reflect the highest level of design excellence and showcase green improvements. 2026 Sustainability Award honorees: • Brandon Bercovich of Highland Avenue, • Ellen Smith & Jeff Fucigna of York Drive, • Molly Lloyd & Dan Reardon of Ramona Drive. The event ended with the introduction of a new category at the Design Awards, the Wildfire Resilience Award. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan was in attendance to introduce the award. “Wildfires are now a reality of life in California and not just in the areas we traditionally imagine them,” Chief Brannigan continued. “In the last decade, we’ve watched fires devastate communities that look a lot like Piedmont. The question isn’t whether we’ll face that risk. It’s what we do about it… The two households we’re recognizing tonight are modeling exactly that.” The winners of Piedmont’s first Wild Fire Resilience Awards were Dana Schultz and Tom & Winifred Walters. Shultz welcomed Captain Mike Carlisle for a fire department inspection of his home after creating a five-foot ember-resistant zone, Sustainability Award winner Brandon Bercovich (left) Fire Chief Dave Brannigan pictured with Tom & Winifred Walters, winners of the Wildfire Resilience Award added ember-protective mesh over vents, and moved favorite plants to safer areas rather than removing them altogether. He showcased home hardening best practices that show meaningful improvements do not have to be overwhelming projects. Tom and Winifred Walters did not originally set out to create a wildfire-resilient property – they set out to create a beautiful garden. In the review process for the awards, their home and especially their garden impressed Chief Brannigan. Their property challenges the common perception that fire-conscious landscaping must come at the expense of beauty or the enjoyment of gardening. To be eligible for the annual Design & Sustainability Awards, a project must conform to Piedmont’s design and planning guidelines and must have been completed in the previous calendar year. articles.text: High in the rugged hills of the Santa Cruz Mountains, Ridge Vineyards stands as one of California’s most respected and historically significant wineries. Known for its commitment to traditional winemaking and sitedriven wines, Ridge has built a reputation over more than six decades as a producer of some of America’s finest Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah and Zinfandel. Though the modern winery was established in 1962, Ridge’s roots stretch back much further. The Monte Bello estate, its flagship vineyard, was first planted in 1885 by Italian doctor Osea Perrone, who recognized the potential of the limestone-rich soils and high elevation. The site produced its first wine in 1892 before falling into decline after Prohibition. It was not until a group of Stanford Research Institute engineers purchased and revived the property in the late 1950s that Ridge Vineyards was reborn. From the beginning, Ridge embraced a philosophy that set it apart. The winery has long championed single-vineyard wines, believing that the finest expressions of wine come from specific sites where soil, climate, and grape variety align. This approach is exemplified in its flagship Monte Bello, a Cabernet Sauvignon-based blend that has become one of California’s most iconic wines. Ridge’s rise to international prominence came in 1976, when its 1971 Monte Bello placed fifth in the historic Judgment of Paris, a blind tasting. The result shocked the wine world by demonstrating that California wines could rival those of France. In a 30th anniversary re-tasting, Monte Bello was ranked number one, cementing its legacy as a world-class wine. Equally important to Ridge’s identity is its dedication to “pre-industrial” winemaking – a philosophy popularized by longtime winemaker Paul Draper. This approach emphasizes minimal intervention, native yeast fermentation, and transparency, including listing ingredients on labels. Long before such practices became fashionable, Ridge was quietly producing wines that reflected both authenticity and restraint. Today, Ridge operates two primary facilities: the Monte Bello estate in the Santa Cruz Mountains and Lytton Springs in Sonoma County’s Dry Creek Valley. While Monte Bello is synonymous with structured, age-worthy Cabernet blends, Lytton Springs is celebrated for its expressive Zinfandel-based wines. Together, they showcase Ridge’s mastery of both Bordeaux and California heritage varietals. Despite changes in ownership – most notably its acquisition by Japan’s Otsuka Pharmaceutical in 1986 – Ridge has remained remarkably consistent in its philosophy and style. Its wines continue to earn critical acclaim, with Monte Bello frequently cited among the greatest Cabernet Sauvignons produced in the United States. In an industry often driven by trends, Ridge Vineyards has succeeded by staying true to its principles. Its enduring focus on terroir, transparency, and tradition ensures that it remains not only a cornerstone of California wine history but also a benchmark for its future. The following wines are the Spring 2026 new releases from Ridge. The ancient Zinfandel vines at the Ridge Lytton estate in Sonoma County

articles.text: • 2023 Ridge Montebello This stunning historic Cabernet continues the legend of Montebello. Deep garnet-purple in color, it charges out of the glass with exuberant black cherry, plum and blueberry notions with touches of dark chocolate, cloves and violets. Full-bodied yet balanced, the palate is decadently fruited with black and blue berry flavors framed by firm yet plush tannins and seamless freshness, finishing with wonderfully long-lasting, baking spice nuances. This wine will develop even more complexity with time in the cellar and will last for two decades.

Known for its commitment to traditional winemaking and sitedriven wines, Ridge has built a reputation over more than six decades as a producer of some of America’s finest Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah and Zinfandel. Though the modern winery was established in 1962, Ridge’s roots stretch back much further. The Monte Bello estate, its flagship vineyard, was first planted in 1885 by Italian doctor Osea Perrone, who recognized the potential of the limestone-rich soils and high elevation. The site produced its first wine in 1892 before falling into decline after Prohibition. It was not until a group of Stanford Research Institute engineers purchased and revived the property in the late 1950s that Ridge Vineyards was reborn. From the beginning, Ridge embraced a philosophy that set it apart. The winery has long championed single-vineyard wines, believing that the finest expressions of wine come from specific sites where soil, climate, and grape variety align. This approach is exemplified in its flagship Monte Bello, a Cabernet Sauvignon-based blend that has become one of California’s most iconic wines. Ridge’s rise to international prominence came in 1976, when its 1971 Monte Bello placed fifth in the historic Judgment of Paris, a blind tasting. The result shocked the wine world by demonstrating that California wines could rival those of France. In a 30th anniversary re-tasting, Monte Bello was ranked number one, cementing its legacy as a world-class wine. Equally important to Ridge’s identity is its dedication to “pre-industrial” winemaking – a philosophy popularized by longtime winemaker Paul Draper. This approach emphasizes minimal intervention, native yeast fermentation, and transparency, including listing ingredients on labels. Long before such practices became fashionable, Ridge was quietly producing wines that reflected both authenticity and restraint. Today, Ridge operates two primary facilities: the Monte Bello estate in the Santa Cruz Mountains and Lytton Springs in Sonoma County’s Dry Creek Valley. While Monte Bello is synonymous with structured, age-worthy Cabernet blends, Lytton Springs is celebrated for its expressive Zinfandel-based wines. Together, they showcase Ridge’s mastery of both Bordeaux and California heritage varietals. Despite changes in ownership – most notably its acquisition by Japan’s Otsuka Pharmaceutical in 1986 – Ridge has remained remarkably consistent in its philosophy and style. Its wines continue to earn critical acclaim, with Monte Bello frequently cited among the greatest Cabernet Sauvignons produced in the United States. In an industry often driven by trends, Ridge Vineyards has succeeded by staying true to its principles. Its enduring focus on terroir, transparency, and tradition ensures that it remains not only a cornerstone of California wine history but also a benchmark for its future. articles.text: After a year of intentional writing, and a lifetime of learning, I am honored to introduce my newest book, Mindset In Motion™: Activate Purpose, Passion, and Peak Performance. Living and working in the Piedmont and East Bay community, I’ve had the privilege of connecting with individuals and families at every stage of life, first-time buyers, growing families, entrepreneurs, and those thoughtfully transitioning into their next chapter. These conversations, often centered around home and lifestyle, reveal something deeper: a universal desire for growth, clarity, and purpose. This book was born from those moments. It is written for individuals at every age and stage, those beginning anew, navigating change, or stepping into what’s next. While circumstances may differ, the desire to move forward with intention is something we all share. I was reminded of this while working with a client preparing to leave a longtime family home. What began as a real estate decision quickly became a reflection on identity, memories, and possibility. The challenge wasn’t just logistical, it was emotional. It required mindset, trust, and ultimately, action. That experience reinforced what I’ve seen time and again: people rarely lack opportunity. More often, they lack momentum. Mindset In Motion™ was created to address that gap. At its core, the book bridges inspiration with aligned action. It invites readers to move beyond intention and into execution, to activate purpose, sustain passion, and pursue peak performance in a meaningful and attainable way. The foundation is the Mindset In Motion Method™, a five-step framework: Goal, Believe, Internalize, Share, and Activate. Clarity of goals establishes direction. Belief fosters possibility. Internalization transforms identity. Sharing cultivates connection. And activation—consistent, intentional action—drives results. This method is designed to support anyone navigating life’s transitions, whether overcoming adversity or addiction, stepping into an empty nest, building a company or personal brand, or simply ready to conquer a longheld goal and move forward with clarity and confidence. What distinguishes Mindset In Motion™ is its practicality. Each chapter includes GOALS, ACTION, and CON NECT prompts, encouraging readers to apply the principles in real time and create forward momentum. This reflects a philosophy I’ve come to embrace: insight alone does not create change. It is the Debbi DiMaggio’s latest book Debbi DiMaggio is a Piedmont resident, real estate advisor, coach & author combination of mindset and movement that leads to meaningful progress. In a community like ours, where lifestyle, design, and quality of life are deeply valued, there is also an opportunity to pause and ask: How are we growing? Where are we going next? And what is required to get there? Because ultimately, growth is not defined by age or circumstance, but by the willingness to take the next step. As I share Mindset In Motion™ with the Piedmont and East Bay community, my hope is that it serves as both a guide and a catalyst, supporting individuals in moving forward with clarity, confidence, and purpose. Mindset In Motion™: Activate Purpose, Passion, and Peak Performance is now available on Amazon. To learn more, visit www.MindsetInMotionBook. com. — Debbi DiMaggio Piedmont Resident, Real Estate Advisor, Coach & Author GOOD THROUGH MAY 2026 GOOD THROUGH MAY 2026 GOOD THROUGH MAY 2026 GOOD THROUGH MAY 2026

articles.text: Communication Protocol - Concerns Several weeks ago, I joined a PHS Parent Club meeting where a discussion had taken place over several meetings regarding communication with teachers. Several topics emerged from parents, including how parents could provide feedback to teachers and the process for students and parents to share concerns related to a specific issue. Out of these meetings, a request emerged for the protocol for sharing concerns related to a specific issue. Linked at Docs.google.com/ document/d/1s74dDW_FC937kxLeSQSe2FtJftUkBfJNLvBf-CyPIeU/edit?tab=t.0 is a protocol to guide students and parents on communication. The protocol is TK-12; however, the request came from the high school where concerns about grades are more common. Please also note that this protocol is for the typical occurrences rather than unique circumstances that may emerge and require an alternative approach. My thanks to our PHS Parent Club parents and our teachers for their feedback on this protocol.

articles.text: Summer Adventures 2026: Camp in a Classroom Piedmont Unified School District invites you to join Summer Adventures 2026, our “camp in a classroom” experience that blends learning, creativity, and classic summer fun both indoors and outdoors. Mornings are led by PUSD teachers and feature engaging, hands-on academic enrichment including reading, writing, math, and science. In the afternoons, the program shifts into full camp mode with outdoor recreation, games, creative projects, and plenty of time to connect with friends. Designed for students entering Kindergarten through 5th grade, Summer Adventures offers a balanced, joyful day that supports learning while embracing the spirit of summer. pages.text: Wednesday, April 22, 2026 27 Mindset In Motion™: Activate Purpose, Passion, and Peak Performance By Debbi DiMaggio After a year of intentional writing, and a lifetime of learning, I am honored to introduce my newest book, Mindset In Motion™: Activate Purpose, Passion, and Peak Performance. Living and working in the Piedmont and East Bay community, I’ve had the privilege of connecting with individuals and families at every stage of life, first-time buyers, growing families, entrepreneurs, and those thoughtfully transitioning into their next chapter. These conversations, often centered around home and lifestyle, reveal something deeper: a universal desire for growth, clarity, and purpose. This book was born from those moments. It is written for individuals at every age and stage, those beginning anew, navigating change, or stepping into what’s next. While circumstances may differ, the desire to move forward with intention is something we all share. I was reminded of this while working with a client preparing to leave a longtime family home. What began as a real estate decision quickly became a reflection on identity, memories, and possibility. The challenge wasn’t just logistical, it was emotional. It required mindset, trust, and ultimately, action. That experience reinforced what I’ve seen time and again: people rarely lack opportunity. More often, they lack momentum. Mindset In Motion™ was created to address that gap. At its core, the book bridges inspiration with aligned action. It invites readers to move beyond intention and into execution, to activate purpose, sustain passion, and pursue peak performance in a meaningful and attainable way. The foundation is the Mindset In Motion Method™, a five-step framework: Goal, Believe, Internalize, Share, and Activate. Clarity of goals establishes direction. Belief fosters possibility. Internalization transforms identity. Sharing cultivates connection. And activation—consistent, intentional action—drives results. This method is designed to support anyone navigating life’s transitions, whether overcoming adversity or addiction, stepping into an empty nest, building a company or personal brand, or simply ready to conquer a longheld goal and move forward with clarity and confidence. What distinguishes Mindset In Motion™ is its practicality. Each chapter includes GOALS, ACTION, and CON NECT prompts, encouraging readers to apply the principles in real time and create forward momentum. This reflects a philosophy I’ve come to embrace: insight alone does not create change. It is the Debbi DiMaggio’s latest book Debbi DiMaggio is a Piedmont resident, real estate advisor, coach & author combination of mindset and movement that leads to meaningful progress. In a community like ours, where lifestyle, design, and quality of life are deeply valued, there is also an opportunity to pause and ask: How are we growing? Where are we going next? And what is required to get there? Because ultimately, growth is not defined by age or circumstance, but by the willingness to take the next step. As I share Mindset In Motion™ with the Piedmont and East Bay community, my hope is that it serves as both a guide and a catalyst, supporting individuals in moving forward with clarity, confidence, and purpose. Mindset In Motion™: Activate Purpose, Passion, and Peak Performance is now available on Amazon. articles.text: Marking Piedmont Scout Council’s rich history, a capacity crowd attended the 105th annual Recognition Dinner at the Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church on April 16. “Scouting is a journey we learn every step of the way. We get involved because of our kids, we stay involved because we see the power of the program,” said Piedmont Scouting President Glyn Burge. “I think sometimes we need to pause and ask ourselves, ‘Why are we doing this?’ Perhaps one answer is that scouting is more important than ever in helping our youth develop into responsible citizens and community members. I believe firmly in the scouting program and the benefits it offers all our youth.” Burge discussed Scouting America’s current turmoil with the federal government. The Pentagon threatens to cut support for the Scouts unless the organization reverts to “core values” and realigns itself with service to “God and country”. “Unfortunately, our federal government doesn’t see it that way. I hope you will join me in continuing to support the scouting programs, both in Piedmont and beyond. It’s a lot to be under attack from a government that doesn’t seem to understand what we’re trying to do,” said Burge. Paul Jahn is this year’s honoree for the Silver Beaver recognition, the highest recognition a council can give a volunteer. 2025’s Silver Beaver recipient Jim Riley presented the award to Jahn, praising him for his excelAfter the dinner, all Silver Beaver honorees gathered for a group photo. Paul Jahn was presented with the 2026 Silver Beaver award by 2025’s Silver Beaver Jim Riley. The crowd is settling in, ready for the dinner to start. NESA Outstanding Eagle Scout Award presented to Bryan Cantrill and Todd Reynolds. Kevin Fischer and Ken Li present the William Peterson Youth Leadership Award to Scouts Evan Friedman and Stephanie Lee. District Award of Merit given to Brian Kelleher and Dante Rodriguez. The crowd is cheering for President Glyn Burge’s passionate ending statement. lent work with the Scouts. Jahn has been an executive board member for the past 8 years. He is currently serving as Past President and Nominating Committee Chairman. He was a council president from 2023-2025 and has been an Assistant Scout Master for Troop 1 for the past 8 years. It is a point of pride for Jahn that a quarter of Piedmont youth have similar formative experiences in the Scouting program. Jahn notes this is possible because of “the incredible support of our community for the Scouting movement and the many wonderful, dedicated volunteers putting their heart and soul into working with our kids.” Another recognition of note was the NESA Outstanding Eagle Scout Award (NOESA), presented to two honorees, Bryan Cantrill and Todd Reynolds. The award is presented to Eagle Scouts who demonstrate remarkable achievements well beyond their Scouting endeavors by excelling in their careers/vocations at local, regional, or national levels. Cantrill has excelled in the computer science field as a software engineer. He’s a co-founder and CTO of Oxide Computer Company, and before Oxide, he spent nine years at Joyent, a software and services company. Reynolds is the Water Treatment Practice Leader at Kennedy Jenks, bringing extensive expertise in water treatment and engineering solutions, supported by a Master of Arts from the University of California, Berkeley. Before joining Kennedy Jenks, Reynolds served as a Nuclear Submarine Officer in the United States Navy. At the dinner, the council also recognized other volunteers who have made a significant difference in the community. Pack 5: Scott Zengel Pack 6: Katie Larson

It is the most affordable of the Ridge offerings and meant to be an entry level wine. While most of Ridge wines come from a single vineyard this is a blend The Geyserville blend is one of Ridge’s flagship wines • 2024 Ridge Geyserville This is mostly Zinfandel with 4 other grapes in the blend but does not meet the 75% level to be labeled Zinfandel. For many years this wine along with the Lytton Springs blend have been the flagships of Ridge Zinfandels. Widely available nationally this is a perfect ambassador for Ridge. It is graced with expressive dark red fruit, flowers, mint, and licorice. It shows gorgeous finesse, plenty of mid-palate richness and terrific overall balance. Sweet floral notes and succulent black cherries round out the finish. • 2024 Ridge East Bench Zinfandel 100% Zinfandel grapes from the Dry Creek Valley this has the classic balanced style that is typical of Dry Creek. The wine offers up notes of cinnamon, black tea, and forest floor over a core of raspberries, cassis, and blueberry jam. Medium bodied, it packs in the earthy layers on the palate with a chewy texture and a long savory finish. • 2024 Ridge Paso Robles Zinfandel The Ridge Paso Robles displays a deep garnet-purple color and delivers pronounced blueberries, and plum preserves notes with hints of baking spices, dried herbs, and potpourri. The wine reveals a medium to deep garnet color and a nose of blackberries and blueberries with hints of baking spice, garrigue and tilled earth. The full-bodied palate delivers a lot of fruit, supported by firm, chewy tannins and just enough acid, finishing with great length and balance. • 2024 Ridge Zinfandel Pagani Ranch The Zin grapes are supplemented with 9% Alicante Bouschet. Alicante is one of my favorite grapes and I believe it is responsible for adding a depth and richness to this wine. articles.text: In late 2022, Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted and Associate Pastor Don Ashburn introduced Life Groups to Piedmont Community Church. The idea of a Life Group is to create a safe place where people can connect with each other and bring honest questions about faith and life. They create a kind of “neighborhood within a community” in a time when people feel isolated and fearful and need other people whom we trust to help us and to support us and our families as we navigate new waters, life challenges and grow spiritually. The program has been a huge success. Now, in 2026, over 70 members of the congregation are participating in a Life Group. Many new members join a Life Group immediately to get acquainted and become integrated into the life of the Church. Long-time members welcome the opportunity to nurture cherished friendships and build new ones. A Life Group consists of 8-10 people who meet weekly for six weeks to discuss the Sunday sermon and the scripture on which it is based. A sermon summary and set of questions to consider is available before the meeting and fuels the discussion that is led by a group leader. Life Group sessions happen four times a year. pages.text: Piedmont Council Scouting programs are designed to help youth build character, fitness, citizenship, and leadership skills. The life lessons learned in Scouting form a foundation for youth to embrace opportunity and overcome obstacles in life. In Scouting, youth learn to do things themselves and take an active role in leading their programs. Further, Scouting programs are inclusive and collaborative. Today’s youth are our future citizens, parents, and leaders. We help youth grow into adults who make ethical choices, and who have the skills to carry those choices out. PROGRAM SUPPORT Council activities provided support to unit programs throughout the year, including: • A Camporee adventure at Camp Tamarancho that pulled Scouts BSA troops together for a skills competition in the outdoors. • The Highlander Hiker Series also included a clean up at Sausal Creek, Scouting for Food, an archery day, and a Bike Fest at Havens Elementary School. • Order of the Arrow – the honor society for Scouts BSA – provided service at Camp Augusta through two inductions in spring and fall, and supported the Cub Scout Overnighter. Top 5 merit badges earned in 2025 were: Communication Citizenship Camping in the Nation First Aid Personal Fitness TRUSTWORTHY, LOYAL, HELPFUL, FRIEND

Some examples of Eagle projects include a STEAM wall for Thornhill Elementary School, an obstacle course for Piedmont elementary schools, octagonal benches, and an online Piedmont Football historical archive. Outside of Eagle projects, Scouts BSA troops helped clean Sausal Creek, picked up 8,500 pounds of food for the Alameda County Community Food Bank, and supported camps in and out of Scouting. Estimated service to the community through these projects is more than 2,000 hours. Piedmont Community Service Crew youth spend many hours each month planning and cooking meals for the food insecure. A big project this year was planning, organizing, constructing, and funding an office for the Richmond Tiny House Village. The crew also spent 6 days building tiny houses in Oregon and took an international trip to Ethiopia. In total, the Venturers of PCSC logged 2,806 service hours. Adventure Highlight: Northern Tier High Adventure Trek Northern Tier is the premier high adventure experience for wilderness canoeing. A Council contingent of two crews ventured out from the Atikokan, Ontario base into the Quetico. This is a gorgeous and pure wilderness, with minimal traces of human travel. Each of the crews completed a 7-day canoe trek through the wilderness. “The Scouts and adults were able to experience another Crew 1 country, and this base is by far the most remote,” said Lisa Gros, one of the trip leaders. “The Quetico Provincial Park is immaculately maintained. You really get a sense of the vastness and amazing gift of being there and seeing it. As an adult, it is a gift to see the tremendous growth and resiliency in the Scouts. They truly go through a transformational process.” Trip highlights: Crew 2 • Day 2: Fern Lake was beautiful and narrow at the top, with shale-like formations. It was brutal portage on the Pickeral River. On some maps, the portage shows as two different portages, but today they form one long portage. The toughest part is not the heavy gear – it is the slippery rocks, trip hazards, mud, and the heavy and cumbersome gear, especially the canoes. • Day 6: It was a fast and efficient paddle to Beaverhouse Lake. We had one portage, which was easy and forgettable. But as we got back into the water, there was a little rapid to navigate. We all made it down the rougher water easily, though Rafi and Connor gave us a little scare with their wobble.” Crew 1 did lots of fishing (34 fish total caught!), completed portages and two merit badges, and weathered several storms. Crew 2 had more obstacles, including a guide swap part way through the trek, but rose to meet all challenges. 195 New Families Joined Council Membership Totals 183 256 Cub Scouts Scouts BSA ages 5-10 ages 11-17 23% Increase Over The Prior Year! 10 Explorers Piedmont Service Club & Piedmont Police Explorers 581 Youth 132 Venturing ages 14-20 Piedmont Community Service Crew & High Adventure Crew 294 Registered Volunteers

articles.text: On Friday, March 27, Oakland Zoo helped rescue a threeweek-old male mountain lion cub, one of the youngest the Zoo has received since joining the Bay Area Cougar Action Team (BACAT), who was orphaned in Southern California. This rescue marks the 33rd mountain lion rescue for Oakland Zoo. The mountain lion cub was brought to the Los Angeles Zoo by staff from the National Park Service (NPS) and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) on March 25. Upon arrival, the L.A. Zoo’s veterinary team conducted a thorough examination, including a physical check, blood tests, radiographs, and a CT scan. The kitten was found to be in overall good health aside from missing the toes on one foot, which had occurred in the wild. Over the next two days, the cub was bottle-fed multiple times daily, initially slowly due to several days without food, and kept in quarantine with minimal human contact. articles.text: After lengthy delays, Piedmont’s community pool opened to the public on Saturday, April 11. The journey to opening was not smooth. In 2023, inflation during the pandemic raised the construction costs for the pool to a level far exceeding what was anticipated. Piedmont Recreation Fund helped offset the shortfalls with more than 200 individual donors to raise $2.3 million for the pool. This helped the city afford the pool sizes and the multipurpose space that residents had envisioned in the planning process. Former members of the Piedmont Board of Education in support of Measure H Dear Editor: We are writing to you and the community as former members of the Piedmont Board of Education in support of Measure H, the renewal of the existing core parcel tax supporting Piedmont schools. During our time on the school board, as we reviewed budgets and made financial decisions for the district, there was one thing that was always clear: Without the core parcel tax, the Piedmont schools would not function well. The parcel tax provides critical funding for every program that makes our schools outstanding and, importantly, allows the district to recruit and keep highly qualified teachers in Piedmont. For close to 40 years, the Piedmont community has overwhelmingly supported our schools through this local parcel tax. Our schools play a critical role in sustaining the strength of our community, as well as our home values. Every resident in Piedmont benefits from strong public schools, whether or not they currently have children enrolled. We are proud to have served on the Piedmont Board of Education and are committed advocates for this funding source. We sincerely hope that you will join us in support of Measure H. articles.text: Children’s Fairyland is celebrating the magic of spring with an event especially designed for the forever young at heart. Fairyland’s Mad Tea Party is the year’s first of five Happily After Hours 21+ events held at Oakland’s legendary storybook theme park. It will take place on Friday, April 24 from 6-10 p.m. The immersive adults-only Alice in Wonderland-themed party will feature Wonderland mischief and theatrical surprises, a proper tea party, local food trucks, sweet Wonderland-inspired treats, a DJ with a black light dance floor, and surprise activations throughout the park. Guests can explore the iconic park, sip on curated cocktails, mocktails, beer, wine, and other beverages. Guests can feel free to express themselves with imaginative attire, whimsical accessories, or elaborate outfits. Costumes are highly encouraged, but not required. Mad Tea Party is centered around a proper tea party at the park’s famous Jack and Jill Hill. A live DJ atop the hill will help turn the space into a whimsical world of tea, beats, and Wonderland treats. Guests can enjoy a cup of tea, themed sweets, and party favors while cabaret performers bring Alice in Wonderland to life with meandering vignettes and circus surprises. The Red Queen makes cameos throughout the evening and other performers roam the park creating wandering theatrical mischief for all to enjoy. Fairyland is a playground for the inner child of every grownup in attendance. Guests are invited to hop aboard the Jolly Trolly for delightful evening rides, play inside the Alice in Wonderland tunnel and maze, and explore other storybook sets like the Old West Junction and many more. With 10 acres of lush gardens, attractions, water features, and whimsical structures, there is something magical to discover with every corner turned. This year’s Mad Tea Party welcomes back crowd favorite DJ heyLove who blends jazz, R&B, hip-hop, house, and global rhythms into soulful, genre-defying sets. She’ll be spinning choice cuts with a black light dance floor where guests can enjoy a unique experience in the Merry Meadow under the Oakland stars in neon colored revelry. A stanchioned top of the Dragon Slide becomes an exclusive VIP lounge for a select group of people who want to enjoy an elevated experience featuring champagne, bottle service, and gorgeous photo ops. While this year’s Gilded Chrysalis Experience is completely sold out, this tier ticketing option is new and is set to become a consistent feature of the annual event. Fairyland’s Gift Shop will be open for the event where guests can find an array of adults-only merchandise rolled out for the evening and can also purchase their own copy of Fairyland’s signature piece of magical merch: the Magic Key. The newest color “All Heroes Wear Pink” was recently released and will be available on the evening of Mad Tea Party. More information and tickets are available at Fairyland.org/ mad-tea-party/. Happily After Hours: Mad Tea Party (21+) When: Friday, April 24, 2026 | 6 to 10 p.m. Where: Children’s Fairyland, 699 Bellevue Ave, Oakland, CA Cost: $28 per person | $23 for Fairyland Members Mad Tea Party is the first of five adult-only “happily after hours” events at Children’s Fairyland this year.

articles.text: Piedmont’s Annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration is returning on Thursday, April 23, from 3:30 - 5:30 p.m., at and outside the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. For this year’s event, the city is teaming up with East Bay Children & Nature, an Emeryville-based organization dedicated to fostering stronger connections for children in nature. The annual event, which originated in 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees the Public Works Department maintains in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces – as well as the city’s commitment to environmental stewardship. The event will feature East Bay Children & Nature’s signature “create-with-nature” stations that invite creativity and curiosity through play with natural materials. There will be two 20-minute sessions of nature-themed singalongs, starting at 4:15 p.m. and 5:10 p.m. The Public Works Department will be in attendance with the equipment they use in their daily work, including the Bay Area’s first fully electric closed-circuit TV sewer inspection van. Children will be able to climb up and sit in the cab of the Public Works trucks. A raffle will be included which kids can enter to win a children’s book or toy related to Earth Day. The event will also feature plant giveaways allowing guests to take home a California native plant for their gardens. Two professional arborists will be on hand to answer questions about trees or plants. The Arbor Day celebration will include the announcement of the 2026 Piedmont Heritage Trees. Nominators of selected trees will be recognized at the event and receive a Piedmont Heritage Tree lapel pin. The Heritage Tree program, now in its eighth year, aims to raise awareness of and appreciation for Piedmont’s diverse urban forest. Heritage Trees are nominated by community members and selected by the Park Commission. A child climbs into a Public Works truck at the 2024 Earth Day celebration.
articles.title: Annual Arbor Day, Earth Day celebrations return April 23

articles.text: Polar Bear is a stunning German Shepherd Dog mix just. This well-loved, bighearted gentleman of six years has earned a special place with volunteers thanks to his calm nature and sweet personality. Despite his impressive size of 110 pounds, Polar Bear walks with amazing leash manners. When he sees the leash come out, he displays his joyful spirit by celebrating with an adorable happy-feet dance and head bob. Growing confidence: Polar Bear has gradually overcome some of his shyness and his confidence is growing. He gently nudges your hand to ask for pets and politely accepts treats. Polar Bear would do well with appropriately matched dog companions or as a solo dog with dog friends. He is eligible for Oakland Animal Services “Home Begin’s Here” program where potential adopters agree to give an eligible dog a home for a week Calling All Big Dog Lovers! on a trial basis. Come meet Polar Bear at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 6:30 pm, or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 pm. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than l must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. Annual Arbor Day, Earth Day celebrations return April 23 By Jake Lannon Piedmont’s Annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration is returning on Thursday, April 23, from 3:30 - 5:30 p.m., at and outside the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. For this year’s event, the city is teaming up with East Bay Children & Nature, an Emeryville-based organization dedicated to fostering stronger connections for children in nature. Children will be able to climb up and sit in the cab of the Public Works trucks. A raffle will be included which kids can enter to win a children’s book or toy related to Earth Day. The event will also feature plant giveaways allowing guests to take home a California native plant for their gardens. Two professional arborists will be on hand to answer questions about trees or plants. The Arbor Day celebration will include the announcement of the 2026 Piedmont Heritage Trees. Nominators of selected trees will be recognized at the event and receive a Piedmont Heritage Tree lapel pin. The Heritage Tree program, now in its eighth year, aims to raise awareness of and appreciation for Piedmont’s diverse urban forest. Heritage Trees are nominated by community members and selected by the Park Commission. articles.text: Piedmont’s Park Commission has come to a final decision to designate three trees for 2026 Heritage Tree nominations. The chosen trees are a Coast live oak in Dracena Park, the Gingko street trees on King Avenue, and a Redwood tree in lower Dracena Park. Later this year, signage will be installed near the tree locations. The Coast Live Oak (Quercus Argifolia) is located in Dracena Park in the upper section at the end of the new ADA pathway. The tree was nominated by Jack & Sharona Fischrup. The tree has a circumference of over 10 feet, measuring 24 inches from the ground. Based on those measurements, it is estimated to be 150-200 years old. “In terms of heritage, what that tree has seen is massive. It’s a very healthy and happy tree. I wanted to nominate the tree so it would catch people’s attention, so you can look up and take note,” said Park Commission member Jack Fischrup, who lives near Dracena Park. The Ginkgo trees on King Avenue, nominated by Cindy Rafton, were nominated for a second time (2020 by Tina Stott). The standout traits are the yellow leaves in the Fall that line the street of King Avenue between Lincoln and Hampton. Ginkgo trees are known as “living fossils,” having existed for over 200 million years. Its fan-shaped leaves are resistant to pests, pollution, and disease. The Redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) in Dracena Park was nominated by Richard Pryzbyla and is believed to be the largest Coastal Redwood in the park based upon its diameter. The tree stands just north of the tot swings, between the path that circles the quarry and the dog park fence. Piedmont has honored over 30 trees and plans to place signage recognizing them as Heritage Trees. The signage will be bronze plaques four inches in diameter, embedded into a large rock to be placed near the tree. Currently, four signs are expected to be installed in 2026: the Magnolia at Lexford and Hampton Triangle, the Redwood in Piedmont Park, the Dawn Redwoods in lower Dracena Park, and the Poplars at the Exedra Plaza. Photos for the Heritage Trees will be released on Earth Day, Thursday, April 24.
articles.title: Park Commission announces 3 new Heritage Trees

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District’s (PUSD) school board will convene for a regularly scheduled meeting on Wednesday, April 15, at 7:00 p.m. in the District Office’s Board Room, 760 Magnolia Avenue. The meeting will include a recommendation to appoint Adam Saville as the next Assistant Principal of Piedmont Middle School. Saville, currently the middle school’s Tech Coordinator, has 20 years of experience in public education and has experience as a school principal. Pending board approval, Saville will form a new administrative team at the middle school next year with newly promoted principal Jamie Van Kleeck. The meeting will bring more news to the middle school, as the first presentation of the evening will focus on the proposal and approval of elective courses for PMS. The presentation will outline plans to transition Health from 7th to 8th grade, introducing a 0 period P.E. to 7th/8th graders and piloting four new elective courses: Debate, Forensics, LEAD (Leadership, Empowerment, Action, Development) and Life Lab. The scope, and goals of these new courses will be described by Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich and next year’s middle school top administrators Van Kleeck and Saville. The second presentation on the evening will give an update on the Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (DEIB) programs in the district. Director of DEIB Jen Takazawa will present the report with Dolowich. “This presentation will demonstrate impact through practical application and community partnerships as well as share metrics and data used to monitor DEIB actions and inform future work,” the board background document states. The meeting may be attended in person at 760 Magnolia Avenue, the District Office’s Board Room. The meeting is also available remotely via Zoom. us/j/86109415149.
articles.title: School Board to meet in District Office tonight

articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) is rolling out the red carpet for an evening of high-stakes philanthropy. Under the theme “A Night Licensed to Give,” this year’s Spring Fling Gala invites the community to step into the world of international intrigue—not for espionage, but to fund the critical “special projects” that keep Beach, Havens, and Wildwood elementary schools at the top of their class. “We’re looking for those with a ‘License to Give’ to help us secure the assets our students need most,” said Heather Frank, PEF Executive Director. “Whether you’re a high-roller in the auction or a silent partner from home, every contribution is a move toward a more supported educational landscape.” Working with Piedmont schools, PEF has identified three key objectives for this year’s fundraising efforts: • Field Trip Transportation In the words of Lillian Round, Fourth Grade teacher at Beach, “Field trips enhance the curriculum, making it more meaningful.” By funding dedicated transportation, we ensure our young recruits can explore beyond the classroom without logistical interference. • Structured Play Structured play is the ultimate training ground. This initiative funds structured play programs that blend guided strategy with creative freedom, helping students master the art of problem-solving and empathy on the playground. • Elementary School Counseling Spring Fling continues to fund on-site counseling services to help students navigate complex emotions. As one Havens student noted, “My counselor taught me there are two sides to every story, and it is important to hear both sides,” a vital lesson for any budding diplomat. The action begins with the online auction, which is open to everyone, from Tuesday, April 14 to Tuesday, April 22. Elementary parents are invited to support these efforts by becoming a Parent Sponsor, purchasing tickets to the Gala, or attending a Parent Theme Party. Visit PiedmontSpringFling.org for all the details.
articles.title: Ed. Foundation sets Spring Fling funding goals

articles.text: Our galaxy is vast and uncharted, but our knowledge of space grows more every day through the hard efforts of scientists. With the use of powerful tools, scientists can venture into unknown territory. The Roman Telescope, named after NASA’s first chief astronomer Dr. Nancy Grace Roman, will give the closest view of the heart of our galaxy than ever before. Our Home Galaxy Galaxies are made up of stars, planets, and great clouds of dust and gas, all held together by gravity. However, not every galaxy looks the same. While most galaxies are spiral or ball-shaped, some are less structured and have irregular forms. Small galaxies have several thousand stars and reach a few hundred light-years across. On the other hand, large galaxies contain trillions of stars and stretch millions of lightyears. Oftentimes large galaxies have supermassive blackholes at their centers – like our own. Our solar system, located in a small arm of the Milky Way, orbits the center of the galaxy at over 500,000 miles per hour. At the center of the Milky Way lies a supermassive blackhole surrounded by an incredible number of stars. The closer to the center of the galaxy you get, the older the stars become. As far as we know, our solar system is the only one that possesses life. However, with powerful new instruments like the Roman Space Telescope, we will have the ability to look at planets beyond those in our solar system. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope With a view expected to be over 100 times greater than the Hubble Space Telescope, the Roman Space Telescope will provide the deepest view of the center of our galaxy than ever before. The Roman Space Telescope will give scientists unprecedented insight into dark energy, exoplanets, and infrared astrophysics. Planned to launch no later than May 2027, the Roman Telescope will conduct several surveys that will revolutionize astronomy and answer long existing questions about dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets. The final survey conducted by the telescope will study the stars and exoplanets in the area around the center of the Milky Way, known as the galactic bulge. The galactic bulge region is relatively unknown to scientists, but with a method called microlensing through the Roman Space Telescope, we can study exoplanets and planetary systems farther from Earth than ever before. The Big Picture It is still not known how common planets like Earth are, but the surveys conducted by the Roman Space Telescope will provide greater context for Earth and our solar system. The results from the surveys will help scientists distinguish commonalities in the exoplanets they discover and therefore advance their knowledge of planetary formation and habitability. It is a very exciting time in astronomy! A Galaxy Near You If you would like to explore a galaxy outside our own, Chabot Space & Science Center will be hosting a spectacular sci-fi night called A Galaxy Not So Far Away on Friday, May 1st. Guests will have the opportunity to craft their own glowing swords, get a glimpse of distant planets through our historic 8” refractor telescope known as “Leah,” and discover the mechanics of robotics alongside a familiar sassy android. Then, don’t forget to snap a pic in our Galaxy Photobooth, enjoy a themed cocktail, and discover the facts behind the fiction in your favorite intergalactic fantasy movies. Perfect for fans of all ages, this is a sci-fi inspired adventure you won’t want to miss! In more great news, Sci-Fi movie nights are back at Chabot. On Monday, May 4th, bring a friend and join us for a one-nightonly screening of Star Wars: A New Hope in our state-of-theart 70-foot Planetarium dome. Come early to enjoy light bites and themed cocktails in this fun, after-hours date night under the stars. Plus, check out our NASA Ames Visitor Center and AstroLight exhibit, open late for this event. Cameron Schneider is with Chabot Space & Science Center, 10000 Skyline Blvd. in the Oakland hills. articles.title: Exploring the center of our galaxy

Exploring the center of our galaxy By Cameron Schneider Our galaxy is vast and uncharted, but our knowledge of space grows more every day through the hard efforts of scientists. With the use of powerful tools, scientists can venture into unknown territory. The Roman Telescope, named after NASA’s first chief astronomer Dr. Nancy Grace Roman, will give the closest view of the heart of our galaxy than ever before. Our Home Galaxy Galaxies are made up of stars, planets, and great clouds of dust and gas, all held together by gravity. However, not every galaxy looks the same. While most galaxies are spiral or ball-shaped, some are less structured and have irregular forms. Small galaxies have several thousand stars and reach a few hundred light-years across. On the other hand, large galaxies contain trillions of stars and stretch millions of lightyears. Oftentimes large galaxies have supermassive blackholes at their centers – like our own. Our solar system, located in a small arm of the Milky Way, orbits the center of the galaxy at over 500,000 miles per hour. At the center of the Milky Way lies a supermassive blackhole surrounded by an incredible number of stars. The closer to the center of the galaxy you get, the older the stars become. As far as we know, our solar system is the only one that possesses life. However, with powerful new instruments like the Roman Space Telescope, we will have the ability to look at planets beyond those in our solar system. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope With a view expected to be over 100 times greater than the Hubble Space Telescope, the Roman Space Telescope will provide the deepest view of the center of our galaxy than ever before. The Roman Space Telescope will give scientists unprecedented insight into dark energy, exoplanets, and infrared astrophysics. Planned to launch no later than May 2027, the Roman Telescope will conduct several surveys that will revolutionize astronomy and answer long existing questions about dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets. The final survey conducted by the telescope will study the stars and exoplanets in the area around the center of the Milky Way, known as the galactic bulge. The galactic bulge region is relatively unknown to scientists, but with a method called microlensing through the Roman Space Telescope, we can study exoplanets and planetary systems farther from Earth than ever before. The Big Picture It is still not known how common planets like Earth are, but the surveys conducted by the Roman Space Telescope will provide greater context for Earth and our solar system. The results from the surveys will help scientists distinguish commonalities in the exoplanets they discover and therefore advance their knowledge of planetary formation and habitability. It is a very exciting time in astronomy! articles.text: An eventful month of March for PHS’s College and Career Center culminated with the “Future-Ready: Planning for your Career Right After High School” evening panel on Tuesday, March 31, in the Alan Harvey Theater. Panelists Ben Allen, Marco Casalaina, Doug Ireland and Abby Scott took the stage to help students understand the evolving job landscape. Around 80 attendees were on hand to hear the insights from the panelists, as moderated by Sara Ironside, Co-President of the Piedmont Parents Network. The event was predicated upon the turmoil in the job market by AI and a desire to look forward to what careers paths will lead to success. Casalaina, the Core AI and AI Futurist for Microsoft, highlighted the value of taking risks and experimenting in any field of interest. He informed the audience that this is just the beginning of AI reshaping the job market and these students in the audience will all be part of the change. “They reiterated the value of working in teams, finding hobbies and passions outside of school, and being curious and interesting people,” said Ironside. Panelist Abby Scott provided a key perspective for the students looking towards college and thinking about majors. She is the Executive Director of MBA Career Center at UC Berkeley. Piedmonter Ben Allen, CEO of Parnassus Investments, offered his outlook from a highly influential company. “All but one panelist majored in one thing and through different experiences found their current career by pivoting. Trying jobs and learning from them will prepare you for the next job or experience,” summarized College and Career Director Stefanie Manalo-LeClair. The evening also included a question and answer period, as Piedmont Education Foundation’s Kim Hunter fielded questions from the audience. The sentiment from the evening was to not panic because jobs are not going away. Those entering the job market will need to be adaptable. Photo by Stefanie Manalo-LeClair Moderator Sara Ironside (left) joins panels Benjamin Allen, Abby Scott, Marco Casalaina and Doug Ireland on the Alan Harvey Theater stage.
articles.title: “Future Ready” panel discusses AI impact on job market

articles.text: This spring break, Piedmont High School French teacher Bryan Smith and Piedmont Middle School Spanish teacher Shannon Fierro took five PHS students on a week-long exchange program to Marseille and Paris, France. Students Dimitri Secor, Danny King, Thomas Moision, Jo Palsa and Miles Lee made the journey, marking the second year of the exchange program led by Smith for PHS French students. French students and teachers visited Piedmont in March and it was now their turn to host the Piedmonters. The PHS students stayed with French families and attended school during the week. The group also took part in guided trips and visited neighborhoods in the Marseille area. One highlight of the 6,000 miles voyage was a beautiful boat ride to the Chateau d’If, an old prison on an island, much like Alcatraz. The island setting was the inspiration for Alexandre Dumas’ famous masterpiece novel, The Count of Monte Cristo. Another day trip started with a train ride to Aix en Provence for a tour of the city which was home to the artist Paul Cezanne. After visiting Marseille, the group went to Paris by train on Saturday, April 11. While there they took a boat ride on the Seine River and visited Notre Dame Cathedral and the Arc de Triomphe. After the week-long adventure, the group returned home on Sunday, April 12. During an exchange program to France Spanish teacher Shannon Fierro (left), stands at the Arc de Triomphe in Paris with Danny King, Dimitri Secor, Thomas Moision, Miles Lee, Jo Palsa and French teacher Bryan Smith (with the Piedmont Post). Piedmont High students Thomas Moision (left), Danny King, Miles Lee, Jo Palsa, and Dimitri Secor at the Marseille train station.
articles.title: Piedmont students visit France during spring break

articles.text: Freeing Children and Young Adults from Shame, Scales and Stigma helps parents navigate discussions of weight, body image Piedmont resident and adolescent medicine specialist Lauren Hartman’s recently published book, “Freeing Children and Young Adults from Shame, Scales and Stigma,” challenges parents to rethink how they talk to their children about weight and body image. With more than two decades of experience treating adolescents with eating disorders, Hartman draws on both research and firsthand clinical experience to help adults navigate often sensitive conversations about body image, weight and overall health. “Adolescents sometimes fall through the cracks in the healthcare system,” Hartman told the Piedmont Post. “They’re often the healthiest age group physically, but so much of what impacts them is behavioral and emotional. What they really want is to be heard.” “We’ve learned that early intervention can make a huge difference. Kids can get better,” she added. That belief in prevention is at the heart of her new book. Hartman emphasizes that eating disorders are not simply about food or weight, but are deeply intertwined with mental health and identity, especially in children. She also challenges the subtle ways “diet culture” continues to shape young people’s behavior in a world where weight-loss pills have become more widely available. “When I was growing up, diet culture was more obvious,” she said. “Now it’s much more disguised as wellness or longevity. Kids think they’re just trying to be healthy, but they’re not getting the nutrition they need.” Social media, she noted, has intensified the issue. Hospitalizations for adolescent eating disorders surged during the COVID pandemic, which she attributes to increased stress and screen time. Hartman’s book includes how triggers show up in everyday life, including in doctors’ offices. While she is careful not to place blame, she acknowledges that well-intentioned advice can sometimes do harm. Freeing Children presents a case for “weight-neutral care that respects the diversity of human bodies while promoting sustainable health.” “If [physicians] tell a young person to ‘lose weight,’ that’s not really targeting something actionable,” she said. “We need to focus on things that actually support health, like reducing stress, eating regular meals, or finding Piedmont resident and adolescent medicine specialist Lauren Hartman will speak about her new book, Freeing Children and Young Adults from Shame, Scales and Stigma, at Local Economy in Oakland on Sunday, May 3 joyful ways to move the body.” For parents, the challenge can be even more complex. Many, she says, sense when something is wrong with their children but may hesitate to speak up. “I hear from parents all the time, ‘I had a feeling, but I didn’t want to make it worse,’” Hartman said. “But early conversations, even just expressing concern, can be incredibly helpful.” She encourages families to trust their instincts and to examine the messages they model at home. From casual comments about “good” and “bad” foods to the presence of a bathroom scale, these small signals can shape how children see themselves. “We’ve inherited this legacy of body criticism,” she said. “But we have the opportunity to not pass that on.” Hartman’s new book is designed to be accessible with ready-to-use resources and strategies for repair when conversations about weight and health haven’t gone as intended. “It doesn’t have to be the same story for our kids,” she said. “We can create a different environment, one that’s more compassionate, more inclusive and actually centered on health.” Hartman will speak about her book at Local Economy in Oakland on Sunday, May 3. articles.text: On Thursday, April 9, Piedmont Garden Club hosted its Best In Show flower showcase in the community hall. The dogthemed event celebrated works of horticultural, imaginative floral designs, striking photography, and detailed canine-inspired The event was inspired by the charm and pageantry of a classic dog show. For the first half of the show, judges went around to rank the presented works in the five different divisions: Floral Design, Horticulture, Photography, Botanical Art, and Needle Art. Once the ranking was completed, attendees explored the creations by Piedmont Garden Club members. articles.text: The San Francisco Chronicle recently honored Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team with three selections to this year’s AllMetro Team. Sophomore Andrea Martin earned first-team honors, while junior Taylor White and sophomore Savannah Dennig were named to the second team. Piedmont finished last season with a 22-5 overall record and won its fourth consecutive Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division title. They also have four straight CIF State tournament berths, and three straight NCS Open Division appearances. “There have been a lot of fun postseason acknowledgments. Taylor White was an honorable mention for the Chronicle’s AllMetro team. Savannah Dennig also earned an All-Metro honorable mention selection. Staff Photos Andrea Martin earned firstteam All-Metro honors by the SF Chronicle. It shows a testament to all their hard work. To get one of these awards, you have to be one of the top teams,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Martin finished the season as the League Co-Player of the Year, averaging 23.5 points per game and 10.5 rebounds per game. It is the fifth year in a row for a Piedmont player to win Player of the Year in the Western Alameda County Conference. Sophomore teammate Jenelle Solis won the 2025 honor as a freshman, Natalia Martinez won in 2024 and 2023, and Trinity Zamora won in 2022. “Drea (Andrea Martin) is arguably a top-five player in Northern California. She may have been the 19th or 20th Player of the Year in my 23 years as coach in total. It’s a reflection of the whole program, Drea couldn’t do it alone,” Gardere said. White was a game-changer for Piedmont as well, often leading the team in rebounds each game. She averaged around 12 rebounds per game in 2025/2026, and noticeably improved as a scorer. “Taylor is one of the better defenders in the area for sure, but she’s adding to her skillsets. She led the team in rebounding and loads the stat sheets. She’s almost getting a triple-double every game,” Gardere said. Dennig is often viewed as a heart-and-soul type player on the team. She gives her all on every loose ball, plays stellar defense, is a skilled passer, and will nab rebounds despite not being the tallest girl on the floor. “Savannah came to high school with a super high motor and as a hustle player with skills to still improve. She’s one of those hard workers, and you see each year she’s getting better and better. She hit a behind the back, step back 3-pointer; and I was like, ‘Where did this come from?’ She’s put in so much work to add to her game, it’s really been impressive,” Gardere said. Piedmont lost Dennig for its final stretch in the playoffs after suffering an injury. Their season was a bit marred by injuries, notably losing Solis to a lengthy injury for much of the regular season.
articles.title: Andrea Martin, Taylor White, Savannah Dennig named to SF Chronicle’s All-Metro team

articles.text: A familiar face to Piedmont sports fans made an appearance recently in the San Francisco Chronicle. Former PHS head basketball coach, Chris Lavdiotis, was named the newspaper’s Coach of the Year after leading San Marin, the No. 2 seed, to the Division 5 CIF State Championship on March 13, upsetting No. 2 Sylmar 89-64. Lavdiotis was Piedmont High’s coach for 24 years until 2017 when former athletic director Vic Acuna controversially declined to renew his contract. The Piedmont community came out in support of “Coach Lav” in the months to follow, but the school still pivoted away. After one season as assistant coach at California Maritime Academy, Lavdiotis coached Lowell High in San Francisco in 2018, and then became Miramonte’s head coach from 2019 to 2024. He took over San Marin in Novato for its 2024-25 season, finishing 14-13 his first year. In 2025-26, the Mustangs missed out on a berth to the Marin County League’s playoff tournament, which Lavdiotis points out was a turning point for the team. Invoking former San Francisco Giants star Hunter Pence, coach Lav found the motivation tools to push his team into North Coast Section. “It started the day we found out we weren’t given a tie-breaker play-in game for the league playoffs... In our first postseason practice, I put on the board the words “legacy” and “focus.” I told our eight seniors, they need to decide right now what they want their legacy to be,” Lavdiotis said. “We started talking, and they said let’s start by winning the first game of NCS… We had a great practice and I said, ‘It’s up to you guys to bring this level of intensity every day.’ I stole Hunter Pence’s 2012 playoffs speech; the Giants were down 0-2 on an elimination game and Pence is yelling, ‘I want one more day with you guys.’ When we knew who we were playing, I told them, ‘All we’re guaranteed is three more days together, what are we going to do with it?’ We kept it loose, fun, and focused. That’s how we set the stage,” added Lavdiotis. San Marin started its post-season run as the No. 1 seed in the Div. 4 NCS bracket, San Marin opened with a 60-46 win over No. 16 Arroyo, and beat No. 8 Del Norte 64-43 in the quarterfinals to achieve a berth in the CIF State Tournament. They wound up losing to eventual-champion Chris Lavdiotis coaching his squad at the State Final. Former PHS basketball coach Chris Lavdiotis holds the Div. 5 CIF State trophy after San Marin won the state championship this year. He coached the Highlanders for 24 years. No. 4 Mission San Jose 49-45 in the semifinals, but they would get another shot at the Warriors later on in the D5 State tourney. San Marin won all but one game in the State playoffs by a margin of at least 10 points. As the No. 3 seed that year they beat No. 14 Trinity 69-55, dominated No. 6 Woodland 69-30, and then upset No. 2 Rancho Cotate 54-47. Then, they claimed revenge over No. 1 seed Mission San Jose in the Regional Finals, winning 56-46. They learned a lot from that NCS Semifinals loss, forcing the Warriors into critical mistakes after studying their offense. “By the time we got to Mission San Jose, we knew their tiny gym was going to be packed; it was loud and raucous. How we won that game was our preparation. I called one of my former assistants at Miramonte, Rich Forslund. Mission San Jose runs a box offense, and we had two days to work on this. Rich said, “I’ll come to practice tomorrow.” I told the team ‘I’m bringing the master in.’ I told Rich, this practice was his. He took them San Marin celebrates with the trophy after beating Sylmar at the Golden 1 Center in Sacramento.

articles.text: Piedmont’s track team brought four boys’ runners to the prestigious Arcadia Invitational on Friday and Saturday, April 10-11, and sent four athletes to the West Coast Relays on April 11 at Buchannan High School in Clovis. It marks the fourth time in six years for the Highlanders to send at least one athlete to Arcadia, which is considered the premier track and field event in the U.S. for high school sports. “For the fourth time in six years, we’ve had the privilege of making the trek down to Arcadia near LA to compete in the nation’s top track and field meet. For those that haven’t been, it’s truly a special meet. We watched live as around 10 different athletes hit the current #1 mark in the US this season,” coach Pouyan Assadi said. Arcadia has hosted several Olympics runners over the years. This year, 16-year-old Team USA Gold Medal winner, Quincy Wilson, ran for his Bullis School in Maryland. He came to Arcadia holding the country’s high school 400 meter record of 44.11 seconds. “We watched the most decoPhoto by Aaron Aubrecht @csevenstudio Claire Aubrecht had strong runs in the 100 and 200 meters at the West Coast Relays. Photo by Aaron Aubrecht @csevenstudio Shayna Chau competed in the pole vault at the West Coast Relays. Photo by Becky Spies Piedmont sent its relay team of Sebastien Swain (left), Maddox Ma, Marius Arno, and Rehan Mumtaz to the prestigious Arcadia Invitational. rated high school sprinter ever, Quincy Wilson, taking center stage. We also saw the fastest boys 2 mile time in the history of the United States fall, among many other spectacular moments. For our little public school to be accepted and compete is quite the honor,” Assadi said. Arcadia Invitational Piedmont sent its Sprint Medley Relay team of Rehan Mumtaz, Marius Arno, Maddox Ma, and Sebastien Swain. The SMR event goes in distances of 200 meters, another 200, 400 meters, and then closes with an 800. They finished sixth of eight teams, clocking a time of 3:37.30. “The boys were disappointed with their place but it was fun to see them battle against elite teams from different states. We’ve confirmed time and time again that we can hang with the best, and more importantly this race was a good way to get battle tested before the championship meets in a few weeks,” Assadi said. Swain also competed in the 800, but got caught up in heavy traffic around the 50-meter mark and took a tumble. Since it was ruled an honest trip instead of being shoved over by an opponent, the race was allowed to continue. Swain rounded out the field of 51 athletes, finishing with a time of 2:26.64. “Seb was in good spirits after his race. While it stinks to not get to race your event, he’ll be fine. As a former sprinter, all my events were eight athletes maximum, so it’s always crazy to me that they pack 15-plus guys into this particular race,” Assadi said.
