articles.text: Piedmont High’s swimming team is set to make its debut at the Piedmont Pool on Friday, April 17 against Castro Valley. For the first time since 2019 – seven years ago – Piedmont High School will host its first swimming event on Friday, April 17, a league meet with Castro Valley. For Piedmont High athletes and coaches, it has been no easy feat. The swimming team has split time all across the East Bay since before the pandemic, practicing at locations including Laney College, Chabot College, Concord, Hayward, Montclair, and more. With the opening of a new Piedmont pool thus week, the school’s athletic teams will finally gain some structure after more than five years of scrambling for a pool they can call their own. “Training without a home pool for so long has caused me to accept the reality of not having a consistent place to train and adapt to whatever was available,” explained swim team junior Asher Takazawa. “Over the years we’ve practiced at pools in Montclair, Emeryville, Hayward, and sometimes even farther. It hasn’t been easy, especially relying on our parents to drive us long distances to our practices before we had our driver’s licenses.” “I’m really excited about the consistency it will bring to our training and how it will help us grow stronger as a team. There’s something special about being able to train, compete, and build team culture in your own community. It also makes the sport more accessible for younger swimmers coming up, which is huge for the future of Piedmont swimming. “More than anything, it feels like an investment in us, in our team, our routines, and the pride we have representing Piedmont,” added senior Cole Carnazzo. Most of the athletes at Piedmont High weren’t even in middle school the last time their school had a public pool. And now – finally – that will change on Friday. “It means a lot to me, not just because it’s a brand new facility, but because it finally gives us a true home pool for both my club and high school team. I’ve gotten used to practicing at different pools over the years, adapting to different conditions, schedules, and commutes.“ Having everything in one place is a game changer,” Carnazzo said. “The opening of the Piedmont Pool is something really special to me,” said Takazawa. “One of my favorite memories there is when my old coach, Rob, bought me an ice cream sandwich after I lasted the longest in dropout 50s. Moments like that are what made the pool feel like more than just a place to train. Being part of the effort to support Measure UU (the bond for the new pool) and now seeing it turn into a new pool is really meaningful. It’s cool to realize that people like us played a role in making something like this happen for our community,” Piedmont enters its new home site with a boys’ team that is pushing to be one of the school’s best of all time. pages.text: Wednesday, April 15, 2026 13 Piedmont track athletes compete in Arcadia Invitational, West Coast Relays By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s track team brought four boys’ runners to the prestigious Arcadia Invitational on Friday and Saturday, April 10-11, and sent four athletes to the West Coast Relays on April 11 at Buchannan High School in Clovis. It marks the fourth time in six years for the Highlanders to send at least one athlete to Arcadia, which is considered the premier track and field event in the U.S. for high school sports. “For the fourth time in six years, we’ve had the privilege of making the trek down to Arcadia near LA to compete in the nation’s top track and field meet. For those that haven’t been, it’s truly a special meet. We watched live as around 10 different athletes hit the current #1 mark in the US this season,” coach Pouyan Assadi said. Arcadia has hosted several Olympics runners over the years. This year, 16-year-old Team USA Gold Medal winner, Quincy Wilson, ran for his Bullis School in Maryland. He came to Arcadia holding the country’s high school 400 meter record of 44.11 seconds. “We watched the most decoPhoto by Aaron Aubrecht @csevenstudio Claire Aubrecht had strong runs in the 100 and 200 meters at the West Coast Relays. Photo by Aaron Aubrecht @csevenstudio Shayna Chau competed in the pole vault at the West Coast Relays. Photo by Becky Spies Piedmont sent its relay team of Sebastien Swain (left), Maddox Ma, Marius Arno, and Rehan Mumtaz to the prestigious Arcadia Invitational. rated high school sprinter ever, Quincy Wilson, taking center stage. We also saw the fastest boys 2 mile time in the history of the United States fall, among many other spectacular moments. For our little public school to be accepted and compete is quite the honor,” Assadi said. Arcadia Invitational Piedmont sent its Sprint Medley Relay team of Rehan Mumtaz, Marius Arno, Maddox Ma, and Sebastien Swain. The SMR event goes in distances of 200 meters, another 200, 400 meters, and then closes with an 800. They finished sixth of eight teams, clocking a time of 3:37.30. “The boys were disappointed with their place but it was fun to see them battle against elite teams from different states. We’ve confirmed time and time again that we can hang with the best, and more importantly this race was a good way to get battle tested before the championship meets in a few weeks,” Assadi said. Swain also competed in the 800, but got caught up in heavy traffic around the 50-meter mark and took a tumble. Since it was ruled an honest trip instead of being shoved over by an opponent, the race was allowed to continue. Swain rounded out the field of 51 athletes, finishing with a time of 2:26.64. “Seb was in good spirits after his race. While it stinks to not get to race your event, he’ll be fine. As a former sprinter, all my events were eight athletes maximum, so it’s always crazy to me that they pack 15-plus guys into this particular race,” Assadi said. By Jonathan Comeaux For the first time since 2019 – seven years ago – Piedmont High School will host its first swimming event on Friday, April 17, a league meet with Castro Valley. For Piedmont High athletes and coaches, it has been no easy feat. The swimming team has split time all across the East Bay since before the pandemic, practicing at locations including Laney College, Chabot College, Concord, Hayward, Montclair, and more. With the opening of a new Piedmont pool thus week, the school’s athletic teams will finally gain some structure after more than five years of scrambling for a pool they can call their own. “Training without a home pool for so long has caused me to accept the reality of not having a consistent place to train and adapt to whatever was available,” explained swim team junior Asher Takazawa. “Over the years we’ve practiced at pools in Montclair, Emeryville, Hayward, and sometimes even farther. It hasn’t been easy, especially relying on our parents to drive us long distances to our practices before we had our driver’s licenses.” “I’m really excited about the consistency it will bring to our training and how it will help us grow stronger as a team. There’s something special about being able to train, compete, and build team culture in your own community. It also makes the sport more accessible for younger swimmers coming up, which is huge for the future of Piedmont swimming. “More than anything, it feels like an investment in us, in our team, our routines, and the pride we have representing Piedmont,” added senior Cole Carnazzo. Most of the athletes at Piedmont High weren’t even in middle school the last time their school had a public pool. And now – finally – that will change on Friday. “It means a lot to me, not just because it’s a brand new facility, but because it finally gives us a true home pool for both my club and high school team. I’ve gotten used to practicing at different pools over the years, adapting to different conditions, schedules, and commutes.“ Having everything in one place is a game changer,” Carnazzo said. “The opening of the Piedmont Pool is something really special to me,” said Takazawa. “One of my favorite memories there is when my old coach, Rob, bought me an ice cream sandwich after I lasted the longest in dropout 50s. articles.text: It’s springtime in the Bay Area and blooms of wildflowers are abounding throughout the entire state. Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve is the perfect – and closest – place to take in the array of colorful plants in the Oakland Hills. Sibley is most known for its stone labyrinths, but the sun has allowed vegetation to grow and keep the hills green. Throughout Sibley Regional, the sharp contrasting orange of California Poppies and purple of Silver Lupine bushes provide a sharp contrast to the orange of poppies. French Broom also is blooming in all directions. Sibley’s Round Top Loop trail is about 2.5 miles long and connects to the Quarry and Volcanic trails, where you can find the labyrinths and other geological features. The park is a popular area for dog walkers and is also child friendly. Once the loop trail connects to the Volcanic Trail, veer to the right to find the first quarry pit. It will be trail marker No. 2 on the park information pamphlet’s selfguided tour. Old quar r y operations removed massive basalt lava and exposed the interior of the Round Staff Photos California poppies are blooming at Sibley Regional Park in the Oakland hills, making it the perfect time to enjoy the springtime splendor.

articles.text: Visit Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery on Saturday, May 2 for a chance to step beyond the garden gates and tour Ruth Bancroft’s own private iris garden. The Iris lecture and guided tour, led by members of the Mt. Diablo Iris Society, focuses on the history of Ruth’s iris collection and how to plant, care for and divide irises with demonstrations. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth when it was her private, personal garden, but is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Ruth created a garden full of dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. articles.text: Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) exhibition, Good Fire: Tending Native Lands, exploring cultural and historical significance of Northern California’s native communities’ use of fire, is on view now through May 31. Good Fire presents the significance of intentional fire use by local tribes whose practices predate state and federal fire management systems. Brittani Orona, co-curator of the exhibition and Assistant Professor of Native American Studies at UC Davis, said the exhibition was developed in partnership with Native fire practitioners, artists, ecologists and cultural leaders. “From the very beginning, this exhibition has been shaped in close partnership with Native collaborators, whose guidance, stories, and practices are at the heart of Good Fire,” Orona said in a press release. “By looking to their leadership, the exhibition not only honors traditions of the past, but also points to the future of land stewardship, one rooted in sovereignty, respect, and the continuance of relationships between people, fire, and place.” Museum officials said the exhibition seeks to provide context for cultural burning amid a period of increasingly intense wildfires in the region. Cultural burning, sometimes referred to as “good fire,” has historically supported biodiversity, improved habitat conditions, and maintained access to plants essential for food, medicine, basketry and ceremonial traditions. The exhibition begins with an immersive environment designed to replicate aspects of a cultural burn through sound, imagery and interpretive material. A map of California tribal territories is featured to emphasize Native sovereignty and the place-based knowledge that shapes these practices. The first gallery section, “Working with Fire,” outlines the tools, ecological functions and cultural applications of cultural burning. It includes artworks by Harry Fonseca, a recorded fire story by Rumsen Ohlone artist Linda Yamane, and regalia by Tiśina Parker. Additional displays highlight fire-adapted plants and cultural items that rely on fire-managed landscapes. A second section, “Good Fire, Interrupted,” examines the consequences of colonial fire suppression policies that restricted or criminalized cultural burning. Archival photographs, firescarred tree samples and works by artists Brian D. Tripp and Saif Azzuz address the resulting ecological decline and the emergence of large-scale wildfires linked to decades of fuel buildup. The final section, “The Future of Fire,” focuses on current efforts to restore cultural burning and expand tribal leadership in land management. Short films and artworks by Native creators, as well as baskets from Pomo artists and the California Indian Basketweavers Association, document initiatives including prairie restoration, Land Back movements and collaborative cultural burns. “This exhibition centers Native fire practitioners and culture bearers, whose knowledge is grounded in the specific ecologies of their homelands and thousands of years of experimentation,” Ryder Diaz, OMCA Curator of Natural Sciences, said in a press release. “Good Fire invites visitors to expand their view of fire in Northern California and to respect and support the sovereignty of Native peoples, who have never ceded their right to care for their lands with fire,” he added. For more information, visit https://museumca.org/.
articles.title: OMCA exhibition Good Fire: Tending Native Lands on view through May 31

articles.text: The San Francisco Opera Guild and Neiman Marcus will host The Art of Fashion Runway Show and Luncheon on May 13 at the Neiman Marcus store in San Francisco/ The event will raise funds for music education programs across Northern California. “As a San Francisco native who spent 14 wonderful years in New York, it is especially meaningful to co-chair an event that brings together global fashion and the heart of our city,” Opera Guild co-chair Pam Preston said in a press release. “The Art of Fashion promises a beautiful afternoon, spring trend insights and a stunning runway show . . . all in support of the Opera Guild’s extraordinary education programs.” The annual benefit will feature a runway presentation highlighting spring fashion trends, along with a special appearance by Chloe King, director of fashion and lifestyle at Saks Fifth Avenue and Neiman Marcus. The event aims to support the Opera Guild’s education initiatives, which serve more than 60,000 students in the Bay Area. “The Art of Fashion is a beautiful expression of how style and the arts come together in a meaningful way,” King said in a press release. “I’m delighted to return to San Francisco to share a thoughtfully curated selection with our Bay Area clientele in mind, whose deep knowledge and sincere enjoyment of fashion conChloe King, director of fashion and lifestyle at Saks Fifth Avenue and Neiman Marcus, is a special guest at the event. tinue to inspire us. To celebrate fashion in support of the San Francisco Opera Guild’s impactful mission makes the afternoon all the more special.” Tickets range from $1,500 to $2,500, with limited availability remaining. The program begins with a champagne reception at 11 a.m. followed by the runway show at noon and a luncheon. For tickets and more information, visit sfopera.com/FashionShow or contact (415) 565-3204.

articles.text: Festival runs June 14 through August 16 Stern Grove Festival returns to San Francisco this summer with a mix of internationally recognized performers and local artists. The 2026 season is scheduled to run from June 14 through August 16 at Sigmund Stern Recreation Grove. Headliners include Al Green, Public Enemy, Patti LaBelle, and Major Lazer. Additional performers such as Japanese Breakfast, Violent Femmes, Charley Crockett, Suki Waterhouse, and Bomba Estéreo are also scheduled to perform throughout the season. The season will conclude with the annual Big Picnic Weekend on August 15 and 16. The two-day event will serve as a fundraising finale, featuring performances by Public Enemy on Saturday and Al Green on Sunday, joined by Bay Area artists including Goapele and the GLIDE Ensemble. Founded in 1938, the festival has drawn more than 5 million attendees over its history and was established with the goal of making live music freely available to the public, a mission organizers say remains central today. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception, the orgaPatti LaBelle performs at this year’s Stern Grove Festival. nization has presented the free concert series “Stern Grove Festival” in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites.The festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts, including opera, theater, and music. Admission to all concerts remains free, though attendees must obtain tickets through an online lottery system in advance. For more information about this year’s lineup and how to access tickets, visit https://www.sterngrove.org/.
articles.title: Stern Grove releases 2026 lineup

articles.text: Opera Parallèle presents the West Coast opera debut of Doubt, with music by Douglas Cuomo and a libretto by John Patrick Shanley, May 29 through 31 at Presidio Theatre in San Francisco. Based on Shanley’s Pulitzer Prize- and Tony Award-winning play, the contemporary opera features a haunting score by Douglas J. Cuomo and centers on four characters navigating suspicion, morality, and power within a Catholic school. The staging transforms the theater into a churchlike setting, placing the orchestra onstage and immersing audiences as part of the “congregation,” blurring the boundary between spectator and participant. Doubt is directed by Brian Staufenbiel and conducted by Nicole Paiement. Performances introduce a new chamber orchestra version created by the composer and an abridged libretto by Kevin Newbury. Performances are scheduled for Friday, May 29, and Saturday, May 30 at 7:30 p.m., and Sunday, May 31 at 3 p.m. at the Presidio Theatre, located at 99 Moraga Ave. The opera runs approximately 100 minutes without intermission and is sung in English with English supertitles. Tickets start at $66 and are available through the Presidio Theatre Box Office. Patrons can purchase tickets by calling (415) 960-3949 or emailing boxoffice@ presidiotheatre.org.
articles.title: Opera Parallèle performs Doubt May 29 - 31

articles.text: Osaka-born, Berlin-based artist Chiharu Shiota’s first solo museum exhibition in the Bay Area is now on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. Titled Two Home Countries, the exhibition spans the artist’s career across installation, sculpture, video, drawing and stage design. Shiota is best known for immersive environments constructed from densely woven strands of colored yarn, and presenting large-scale installations and other works that explore themes of identity, memory and belonging. At the center of the exhibition is Diary, a monumental installation that fills the museum’s Akiko Yamazaki and Jerry Yang Pavilion. Red threads extend across the 88-foot gallery, surrounding visitors as suspended handwritten pages from Japanese soldiers and postwar German civilians hang overhead. “Shiota is interested in what remains after a person is gone,” said Chief Curator Robert Mintz. “The installation makes history feel personal, fragmented, and profoundly present.” Other works include Two Home Countries, in which a red dress unravels into cords connecting two house-like structures, as well as sketches and videos documenting Shiota’s stage design work for KINKAKUJI (The Temple of the Golden Pavilion). “Chiharu Shiota’s work resonates because it makes emotional states visible,” Asian Art Museum Director Soyoung Lee said in a press release. “Her installations speak to the experience of living between places, histories, and identities — an experience that feels increasingly familiar to many people today.” Visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/chiharu-shiota-two-home-countries/ to learn more. Installation view at Asian Art Museum of San Francisco Photo by Kevin Candland
articles.title: Chiharu Shiota exhibit on view now at Asian Art Museum

The composer wanted her composition to be “under the light there is darkness.” It ended very quietly. Next came a piano trio by Fanny Mendelson, the older sister of the phenomenally gifted Felix Mendelson. From the start, you could tell that the two siblings shared many characteristics. The lightning quick piano writing and overall mood are similar. Despite what people might say, Fanny Mendelson did not have the melodic gift of her younger brother. They play in a very committed way and are able to change their tone colors as required by the music. A salient characteristic was their expressive intensity. On the negative side, the two string players engage in the all-too-common usage of portato – a palsied movement of the right hand. Sad to say, far too many modern string players abuse this technique. The music would benefit from smooth bowing. Portato is like being in a car where the driver cannot drive at a consistent speed. articles.text: On Friday last, the NASA spacecraft Artemis II emerged from the backside of the moon and began its extraordinary journey back to earth, ending the mission in the capsule named Integrity. It had been a stunning achievement thus far — high risk, high gain — and in its final moments, as it traveled through the earth’s atmosphere at the breathtaking speed of 25,000 mph (30 times the speed of sound), protected by a heat shield (withstanding temps of 3,000 degrees C), its rate of decent gradually slowed until the parachutes deploy. Globally watched by millions, the astronauts had safely returned, splashing down off the coast of San Diego. Bill Nelson, former Senator, astronaut, and NASA administrator, his voice filled with pride and even awe at what NASA had accomplished, predicted that the space agency would soon return to the moon where it would construct a platform/station to be use it as a launching pad for a manned mission to the planet Mars. In that moment, while the crew emerged from the capsule, surrounded by Navy Divers, Artemis II had demonstrated that not only did NASA possess the science, it also exhibited something perhaps best defined as metaphysical: was it imagination or a “celestial epiphany.” One filled with wonder and a sense of insignificance that begged the questions how and to what end? Matt Damon stars in The Martian And it was in that moment, listening to Senator Nelson, and thinking about the word imagination, I recalled having watched the award-winning film The Martian, released in 2015, and directed by the gifted Ridley Scott. It starred Matt Damon as astronaut Mark Watney, and became a compelling story of survival. articles.text: It is not atypical to skip through Netflix, for example, in search of a movie. The platform offers a written synopsis and a very short clip/trailer of their films. And this is how I came across the extraordinary BBC/Masterpiece period series (late 1700s) titled Poldark. It opens, for mere minutes, in Virginia at the close of the Revolutionary War and introduces red coat Capt. Ross Poldark (Aidan Turner). Cut to Cornwall, England, with Captain Poldark, recovered from a severe wound, on his way home to his father, the Poldark estate, and his intended, the lovely Elizabeth Chenoweth (Heida Reed). His arrival, however, is not as he imagined. After viewing only a few episodes of Poldark, I found the narrative to be a kaleidoscope of remarkable, multidimensional characters, as well as the promise of a rich production, complex plotting, and dramatic locations (to include the massive cliffs and turbulent ocean of Cornwall). All prove to be compelling. The portrayals are superb, the writing exceptional, sustained for five seasons, while offering action, adventure, and romance. If period films interest, Poldark is a must-see, master class in story-telling, beyond the reach of two-hour movies. Poldark. A BBC/Masterpiece Theater Series – Five Seasons. Starring Aidan Turner, Eleanor Thominson, Heidi Reed. Rated PG. Released in 2016. Streaming on Netflix/Prime/Fandango/PBS/ Apple Eleanor Tomlinson and Aidan Turner in Poldark

The Martian: an inspiring space drama By Chris Honoré On Friday last, the NASA spacecraft Artemis II emerged from the backside of the moon and began its extraordinary journey back to earth, ending the mission in the capsule named Integrity. It had been a stunning achievement thus far — high risk, high gain — and in its final moments, as it traveled through the earth’s atmosphere at the breathtaking speed of 25,000 mph (30 times the speed of sound), protected by a heat shield (withstanding temps of 3,000 degrees C), its rate of decent gradually slowed until the parachutes deploy. Globally watched by millions, the astronauts had safely returned, splashing down off the coast of San Diego. Bill Nelson, former Senator, astronaut, and NASA administrator, his voice filled with pride and even awe at what NASA had accomplished, predicted that the space agency would soon return to the moon where it would construct a platform/station to be use it as a launching pad for a manned mission to the planet Mars. In that moment, while the crew emerged from the capsule, surrounded by Navy Divers, Artemis II had demonstrated that not only did NASA possess the science, it also exhibited something perhaps best defined as metaphysical: was it imagination or a “celestial epiphany.” One filled with wonder and a sense of insignificance that begged the questions how and to what end? Matt Damon stars in The Martian And it was in that moment, listening to Senator Nelson, and thinking about the word imagination, I recalled having watched the award-winning film The Martian, released in 2015, and directed by the gifted Ridley Scott. It starred Matt Damon as astronaut Mark Watney, and became a compelling story of survival. I also found it strikingly similar, yet also vastly different from the film Cast Away where a lone Everyman (Tom Hanks as FedEx administrator Chuck Nolan) struggles to adapt, mentally and physically, to his isolation on an atoll in the vast Pacific while sustaining the will to survive. The Martian is simply just so well done with an excellent cast portraying NASA’s deep bench of engineers, astrophysicists, and administrators who initially assume that Mark did not survive. When they unexpectedly discover that he is alive, the narrative takes a dramatic turn, for the NASA astronaut (a botanist) and for those who are now committed to getting him home. The story is wonderfully riveting, a rich production, with Mark, in effect, offering the voice over (sharing his daily log). And with humor and tenacity he tries to realistically assess the challenges that confront him. This survey elicits from Mark a comment filled with resolve, confidence and hope: “I’m gonna have to science the **** out of this.” How he does that very thing is inspiring. Let the games begin. articles.text: A scene from Rango Rango, released in 2011, is pure enjoyment to watch, and kids, say, eight and above, will enjoy this Oscar-winning animated feature for its clever, comedic, western motif. Of course, at the outset, Rango (Johnny Depp) isn’t a gun slinging cliché. He’s a pet chameleon riding along in the back of the family station wagon, comfortably ensconced in a glass terrarium. The car has an accident and Rango’s container bounces out, and he finds himself stranded on the side of the highway in the Mojave Desert. It’s hot, and he’s thirsty, and after taking the advice of an armadillo named Roadkill (Alfred Molina), who caused the wreck, Rango heads out into some very forbidding territory. He eventually reaches a small western-looking town called Dirt, a place filled with talking animals such as badgers, toads, owls and possums. The mayor of Dirt is a slow moving turtle (Ned Beatty), and the most fearsome gunslinger in town is a dude named Rattlesnake Jake (Bill Nighy). He also meets an attractive desert iguana (soon to become his love interest) named Beans (Isla Fisher). When asked who he is, Rango tells the town folks that he is a tough drifter, and he embellishes his reputation by explaining that he has killed a dangerous gang called the Jenkins Brothers with just one bullet. And thus Rango reinvents himself from being a household pet into a hard case PIEDMONT HIGH SCHOOL SENIOR Sergio Leone, Clint Eastwood like hombre. Naturally, before long, Rango meets up with Bad Bill (Ray Winstone) a local, swaggering Gila monster. On the verge of a shootout, Rango is saved from slapping leather by a swooping hawk that terrifies Bad Bill. During the mayhem, Rango knocks down a water tower crushing the bird. Mayor turtle is so impressed by Rango that he appoints him town sheriff. But the denizens of Dirt still worry about the possible return of Rattlesnake Jake. articles.text: As a work of animation and imaginative story telling, Ratatouille is extraordinary. If the youngsters in your house missed it, well, it’s streaming on an expanded number of sites. At its center is Remy (Patton Oswalt), a Parisian rat who along with his large family plies the suburban garbage cans for food that he considers simply awful. And because of his reluctance to consume what they can scavenge, he is told repeatedly by his father, Django (Brian Dennehey), head of the clan, to “eat his garbage!” But when the family is forced to leave its cottage home (they live in the ceiling), Remy is separated from everyone and is swept away into a storm drain. He ends up in front of a famous restaurant named after its celebrity chef, Gusteau (Brad Garret). articles.text: On Monday, April 6, the First Mondays Reading Group had a strong turnout of 21 participants at the Piedmont Community Hall for their monthly discussion. The weather was good, and they set up chairs outside on the hall’s front patio. They were there to talk about their April book, Secondhand Time: The Last of the Soviets, a 2013 book by Belarusian Nobel laureate Svetlana Alexievich. When the Swedish Academy awarded Alexievich the Nobel Prize, it cited her for inventing “a new kind of literary genre.” It described her work as “a history of emotions –a history of the soul.” The prize committee also said she was being honored “for her polyphonic writings, a monument to suffering and courage in our time.” “Polyphony” – the use of multiple voices – has been the central device in Alexievich’s work since she published her first books 30 years ago. Secondhand Time is an oral history of the Soviet Union’s end. Alexievich chronicles the demise of the communist state through the feelings and views of its everyday, real people as the country transitioned to capitalism. These were ordinary people who rarely had the opportunity to speak, and whose experiences are often lost in official histories. The interviews are from 1991 to 2012 with Russians who still had memories of oppression, terror, famine, massacres, but also had pride in their country. These people had believed that everyone working together would bring about a utopia, and now they struggled to survive. The book provided members of the group with a new understanding of Russia’s history and its people, if they were able to get through it. It was like “walking in mud.” Some readers felt the book needed to be taken in small doses. One reader said a shot of vodka with each chapter was helpful, but unfortunately, his vodka ran out before he could finish the book. Bill Ahern also shared a set of Russian matryoshka dolls from his travels to lighten the conversation a little. For the readers who disliked the book, it was in the classic Russian writing style of epic drudgery. You had to be strong to get through it. They felt the stories of hardship were often repetitive. Bill Ahern also shared a set of Russian matryoshka dolls from his travels to lighten the conversation a little. For the readers who disliked the book, it was in the classic Russian writing style of epic drudgery. You had to be strong to get through it. They felt the stories of hardship were often repetitive. The chronology was mixed, and identities were uncertain. It was realized that this may have been desired by those in a police state. The readers recognized that these stories were first-person, original source, stream-of-consciousness reflections that comprised a tapestry of life in the communist Soviet Union and its citizens’ transition into a capitalist system. However, the change didn’t provide the rewards and freedom that many Russians expected. One member of the group felt Secondhand Time is an important book because it provides a new understanding of what was going on in the Soviet Union, but also of its people. Many were utopian dreamers, communist true believers who were willing to live in misery because there would be a better future. They were excited when capitalism and its hopes replaced their communist world, but it turned out there were some winners and many losers. There is a czarist mentality that goes way back. It accepts pain as a natural condition, and there is a need for strong, authoritarian leadership. Some of these post-Soviet storytellers yearned for the consistency of the Stalin era and also the pride of a country that was the first in space The April discussion group included Marj Blackwell, Melba Yee, Lois Price, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Laura Goldman, Mike Henn, Sandy Threlfall, Phil Witte, Heidi Schmidt, Susie Backer, Margaret Wade, Peggy Shultz, Adrienne Hamlin, Mary Carter, Bill Ahern, Orrel Lanter, Sarah Johnson, Nadean Guffanti, Bella Almanzan, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. Secondhand Time: The Last of the Soviets by Svetlana Alexievich and a world power. They were part of something bigger than themselves then, but not now. It was noted that 70% of today’s Russians support Putin, and Secondhand Time helped the readers understand why. The group’s discussion seemed to inevitably move to the situation in our country and what we are experiencing with the Trump Administration. It was asked if some of its supporters need to be part of something bigger than themselves. Readers also talked about their past personal European travel experiences, but also a more recent, domestic one in which ICE’s presence was felt. It was asked, “In today’s world, what is freedom?” The answer wasn’t clear. It was also disturbing for the group that once fringe political thinking is now mainstream and affecting our lives. It was the readers’ sincere hope that Secondhand Time would not have an American sequel. The group had previously selected The God of the Woods by Liz Moore for its May book and Barbarian Days – A Surfing Life by William Finnegan for June. After Lois Price presented three fiction candidates, the readers selected Old Filth by Jane Gardam for their July read. With all their business done, they took a group photo in the circle outside the Community Hall. The group will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion on Monday, May 4 at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. pages.text: Wednesday, April 15, 2026 23 Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers head to Linda Avenue By Dick Carter There was a strong turnout of over 40 walkers and six canine best friends last Wednesday when the Walking on Wednesdays group assembled at the Exedra for their weekly walk. The Piedmont schools were on spring break. The weather was spring-like and the Piedmont Post had reported the pathway through Linda Park’s former off-leash dog area had been reopened. There was also some early Piedmont history associated with this area that the group had never considered. This all made for a great morning to check out the park, talk some history, and walk through the Beach School campus. The walkers started off going down Magnolia Avenue, past the Community Pool to San Carlos Photo of Willam Dingee from Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website and Oakland Avenues. The group made their long decent to Grand Avenue and then the climb up and over the Oakland Avenue Bridge. Its lamp posts, lights, and guardrails make it a lovely entrance to the city, and the walkers arrived at the Linda Park’s entrance at Oakland and Sunnyside Avenues. The fencing around the park has been removed and the walkers walked a short distance up its pathway to talk about this space. During the first half of the 20th Century the Key System’s Number 11 electric streetcar ran directly from Oakland Avenue through what is now the park toward Piedmont Avenue. The park’s off-leash area was permanently closed last spring after the Regional Water Quality Control Board notified the City that it needed to take steps to eliminate erosion and runoff from the hillside. The City permanently closed and revegetated the hillside to allowed the City to address the problems and avoid Key System train on the Linda Park land Map of last Wednesday’s walk steep penalties for noncompliance. Piedmont Public Works “hydroseeded” the hillside with a spray of seeds, water, and mulch. This mixture formed a protective shell over the soil, helping to stabilize the slope while new grasses and other plants took root. The park’s hillside remains closed, as the revegetation is still in early stages. Signs asked visitors to stay on the path and for people and dogs to stay off the grass as it would be easily damaged. Other signage provided information about the revegetation project and the value of oak woodlands. A $5,000 donation from the Piedmont Garden Club’s Civic Improvement Committee will support this reforestation project. Piedmont’s parks have many mature oaks, but few areas are maintained as a natural oak woodland. Linda Park’s hillside with a naturally moist, northeast-facing slope makes an ideal location for this type of landscape. The walkers made their way through the park which had beautiful California poppies along the way and exited on Linda Avenue. The group went a few steps to Lake Avenue and climbed it to Sunnyside Avenue for some early Piedmont water history. The water for this area of Oakland and Piedmont in the late 19th Century was provided by the Linda Vista Reservoir. It used to be on the Lake Avenue side of that street at Sunnyside. The reservoir was built by the Oakland Water Company in 1892 and had a capacity of 4 million gallons. It was also part of a fierce “Oakland Water War” between private companies that lasted from 1866 to 1907. In 1866, Anthony Chabot founded the Contra Costa Water Company (CCWC), the first company to successfully pipe water into Oakland. Chabot also built major reservoirs including Lake Temescal in 1869 and Lake Chabot in 1876. William J. Dingee founded the Oakland Water Company in 1893. However, the company’s water work started earlier after the CCWC refused to provide water to Dingee’s properties in the Montclair and Piedmont hills. Oakland Water became a direct competitor to Chabot’s CCWC. The competition became literal warfare. Newspapers reported both companies worked to disrupt each other’s supply, engaged in rate wars, sabotaged equipment, and publicly claimed the other’s water was “unfit for human consumption”. The war ended in 1898 when Oakland Water and CCWC merged. The new company was known as the CCWC, but Dingee was in control. However, the new CCWC lasted only until 1906. The Peoples Water Company, whose president was Frank C. Havens, was created and it took control of CCWC and other local water companies 1907. Dingee’s fortunes collapsed in about 1908. One report said he was swindled by a business partner. Following the collapse of his financial empire and subsequent bankruptcy, Dingee lived out his years in obscurity in Sacramento and died in 1941 at the age of 87. articles.text: Tucked between the rugged Pacific coastline and the bustling tech corridors of Northern California, the Santa Cruz Mountains American Viticultural Area (AVA) stands as one of the state’s most distinctive wine regions. Officially established in 1981, the Santa Cruz Mountains AVA was among the first American appellations to be defined by its mountainous terrain rather than political boundaries – a reflection of the dramatic landscape that shapes its wines. Stretching across three counties – San Mateo County, Santa Clara County, and Santa Cruz County – the AVA rises from near sea level to elevations exceeding 2,600 feet. This variation creates a tapestry of microclimates, where cool ocean fog from the Pacific meets warm inland air. The result is a long growing season that allows grapes to ripen slowly, developing complexity while retaining natural acidity. The region’s history dates back to the 19th century, when pioneering winemakers first recognized its potential. Today, a mix of historic estates and small, family-run vineyards defines the area. Wineries such as Ridge Vineyards and Mount Eden Vineyards have helped cement the Santa Cruz world-class wines, particularly Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, and Chardonnay. Unlike the expansive valley floors of Napa or Sonoma, vineyards here are often carved into steep, forested slopes. This rugged topography limits large-scale production but rewards careful, hands-on viticulture. Many growers emphasize sustainable and organic farming practices, working in harmony with the natural environment. The wines themselves reflect this balance between power and restraint. Cabernet Sauvignons from the mountains tend to be structured and age-worthy, with notes of dark fruit, graphite, and mountain herbs. Pinot Noirs, influenced by the cooling maritime air, often display bright red fruit flavors, earthy undertones, and vibrant acidity. Chardonnays range from crisp and mineral-driven to richly textured, depending on site and winemaking style. Despite its proximity to San Francisco and San Jose, the Santa Cruz Mountains AVA remains somewhat under the radar, offering a quieter, more intimate wine country experience. Narrow, winding roads lead visitors through redwood groves and scenic vistas, with tasting rooms that prioritize authenticity over grandeur. As interest grows in terroir-driven wines and sustainable practices, the Santa Cruz Mountains continues to attract attention from wine enthusiasts and critics alike. For those willing to venture off the beaten path, this storied AVA offers a compelling glimpse into California winemaking at its most nuanced and expressive. On March 29 the Santa Cruz Mountains Wine Growers Association put on a tasting at Mountain Winery in Saratoga. Over 50 wineries poured their current releases. It was a wonderful showcase for what the region can produce. There were many outstanding wines, but the following wines were the standouts – truly the cream of the crop. Jeff Emery from Santa Cruz Mountain Vineyards has made a sparkling version that jumps out of the glass. The nose is packed with cranberry fruit and warm baking spices. In the mouth it crackles with fizzy energy and ends up with a super clean totally dry finish. Totally unique this wine is truly a party in your mouth. Did You Know (Tax Edition) • How Piedmont Funded Itself Before Prop 13 In 1907, Piedmont voters narrowly rejected Oakland annexation by 10 votes, creating an independent city that needed its own revenue system. Early Piedmont taxes were revolutionary for their simplicity: levies based on land size rather than market value. A hillside parcel’s acreage mattered more than its price tag—a practical approach when property values were uniform. For seven decades, this system worked. Wealthy residents who could afford Piedmont’s estates paid proportional taxes; modest cottages paid less. The flat assessment approach meant predictability. Schools and services were funded through straightforward land-based levies without the political drama of modern parcel tax elections. articles.text: A different kind of dental experience in the East Bay In an era where health care often feels rushed and impersonal, one Piedmont High School alumnus has built a dental practice around a guiding principle often attributed to William J. Mayo of the Mayo Clinic: “The best interest of the patient is the only interest to be considered.” Dr. Josh Bernstein, a 1975 graduate of Piedmont High, operates a boutique dental office in nearby Oakland serving patients throughout Piedmont, Berkeley, and the greater San Francisco Bay Area. His practice is widely known for natural-looking smile makeovers using porcelain veneers and advanced cosmetic dentistry—helping patients achieve confident, healthy smiles that still look entirely like themselves. “When done right, dentistry shouldn’t look like dentistry,” says Dr. Bernstein. “It should just look like you—on your best day.” Dr. Bernstein is a Clinical Instructor in Cosmetic Dentistry, and while Cosmetic Dentistry is a cornerstone of the practice, much of Dr. Bernstein’s work centers on patients who are anxious, fearful, medically compromised, or who have avoided the dentist for years. He is also a Clinical Instructor in I.V. Sedation and the author of The Book on Painless Dentistry, and he has built a reputation for making dental care accessible— even for those who once thought it was impossible. “If someone has been afraid of the dentist for 10 or 20 years, and we can help them finally feel comfortable—that’s incredibly rewarding,” he says. The practice also provides specialized care for elderly patients, individuals with dementia, and those with developmental disabilities, working alongside an anesthesiologist group to deliver hospital-level sedation in an outpatient setting. Unlike many offices, Dr. Bernstein’s practice is out-of-network with insurance providers, allowing for a more individualized personal service and a focus on the highest quality care. At the same time, his team helps patients maximize their insurance benefits by preparing and submitting their claims. Services such as porcelain veneers, Invisalign, and comprehensive restorative dentistry are tailored to each individual, with an emphasis on subtle, natural, durable results. “We’re not creating a ‘perfect’ smile,” Dr. Bernstein explains. “We’re creating your smile—just at its best.” The office itself is intentionally small, with just two operatories and a close-knit team. That scale supports a level of personal service that Dr. Bernstein Spectacular views of Piedmont and the Oakland Hills Dr. Bernstein and his entire staff are passionate about safety. believes should be standard—but rarely is. “We have a goal that is unusual these days: to run 100% on time, every day,” he says. “And every patient gets my personal cell phone number. That level of access shouldn’t be unusual—but today, it is.” Though his practice serves patients from across the Bay Area, Dr. Bernstein’s connection to Piedmont remains strong. He recalls his high school years fondly—including a second-place finish in the Piedmont High’s Leonard J. Waxdeck Birdcalling Contest, where he shaved his head to portray the bald eagle. That same clean-shaven look also coincided with his participation in the North Coast Section swimming championships, reflecting an early blend of discipline, performance, and a willingness to stand out. Today, those same qualities continue to shape his approach to dentistry. “Technology will keep evolving,” he says. “But at the end of the day, it’s all about how you treat people—that’s what counts” For more information about Dr. Bernstein’s Oakland-based cosmetic and sedation dental practice, visit www.allnewsmiles. com. The office has an understated, elegant feeling, like a spa.

articles.text: Reader Question (Tax Edition) “The hardest thing in the world to understand is income taxes.” – Albert Einstein to his accountant Leo Mattersdorf from Time Magazine Feb 1963 Question: I am confused about closing costs. What’s the difference between non-recurring and recurring closing costs and why is the buyer for my house asking me to help cover them? Answer: The second part of your question is easier: closing costs are expensive, and most buyers are cash strapped. The first part is the important one. Non-recurring closing costs are one-time expenses tied to the transaction itself: lender fees, appraisal, title insurance, escrow fees, recording charges, and similar items. Recurring closing costs are ongoing costs that get prepaid at closing, usually things like property taxes, homeowners’ insurance, mortgage interest, and sometimes HOA dues. Those are not “buying the house” fees so much as “starting the clock” expenses. Seller-paid closing costs can help the seller by keeping the deal alive without having to drop the purchase price, which may protect the appraisal and the neighborhood comps; in a cash-tight market, a buyer who needs help with closing costs may still be fully qualified to buy, so a seller credit can be the practical difference between closing and starting over. Real Estate Roundup for March 2026 March brought 22 property transactions. Median sale price held $2.95M, with closed deals ranging $1.61M–$4.39M. Three new listings priced $1.8M–$2.8M suggest sellers believe the window is open. Average DOM for closed deals: 11 days. One property lingered at 60 DOM—a reminder that even Piedmont has ceiling prices. Active inventory climbing modestly. Off-market activity perAmerica is a Broker Associate and Realtor® at The Grubb Company sists—pending deals show minimal MLS time, confirming private networks still funnel transactions away from public view. Piedmont issued 151 permits in March across multiple categories. Permit activity tells you what owners are doing after they buy and before they sell. Get ready for another year filled with pickup trucks and hoping for a parking spot at Mulberry’s during the weekday. There were 99 residential permits in March across remodels, systems, and site work. Sewer permits were the busiest named category with 18 issued, followed by 13 mechanical permits and 12 solar permits. Eleven renovation and addition permits carried the biggest declared values. There were also 9 electrical permits, 7 roof permits, 5 plumbing permits, 5 window and door permits, 4 seismic upgrades, 3 ADU permits, and 2 EV charger permits. articles.text: Crimson at three-weeks-old, on March 27 cub and transported it to Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital. After Crimson’s intake examination, the kitten was found to be healthy. Zoo Veterinary and Animal Care staff will continue to monitor his foot closely as he grows to ensure he uses the leg properly and it doesn’t cause any complications. “I’ve had the privilege of witnessing countless rescues. There is something so deeply moving about watching our team pour themselves so completely into a single life. Their skill, their sleepless nights, and their quiet determination motivate me. I can only hope that Crimson’s story and the work at Oakland Zoo impact all of you as it does me,” says Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. The Zoo is optimistic that Crimson will have a good life regardless of his history. He has been handling his bottle feedings very well, and the team is feeding him around the clock due to his very young age and needs. Although his health appears good at this time, he is at a delicate stage, and the Zoo will monitor him closely as he grows. Crimson is currently being bottle-fed every three hours by Animal Care and Veterinary staff and will continue this routine for the next few weeks. Zoo staff have the challenging task of providing the care Crimson’s mother would have offered in the wild, while also managing routine feedings and socialization, and allowing him space to exhibit wild behaviors and act as much like a wild mountain lion as possible. In the wild, mountain lion cubs need about 12-18 months with their mother to learn essential survival skills. Because Crimson is so young, he lacks the skills necessary to be released back into the wild. After he successfully rehabilitates at Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital, the Zoo hopes to introduce Crimson to Clover, the female cub rescued earlier in March who is also receiving care at Oakland Zoo. Mountain lion kittens tend to thrive with a companion, a strategy the Zoo has successfully used with other rescues, including Briar, who has become a resident at Oakland Zoo and now lives with Silverado and Coloma at the Zoo’s California Trail mountain lion habitat. While Oakland Zoo and CDFW prefer these kittens to remain in the wild, the pairing of Clover with Crimson will help improve their overall wellbeing and secure a brighter future for both cubs. CDFW follows a thorough process before starting rescue and rehabilitation efforts for wild mountain lions. In this case, Crimson was found alone and vocalizing frequently, which is unusual for a solitary mountain lion kitten to do for long periods. The National Park Service made multiple den visits, monitored GPS collar and camera data, and continued observing the kitten. NPS biologists observed that Crimson’s mother had likely moved dens, and she was not returning to care for him. After two days, he appeared noticeably weaker, having lost 10% of his body weight, prompting NPS, in close consultation with CDFW, to retrieve and relocate him for rehabilitation. articles.text: It’s not a topic most people like to consider; our dogs are the center of our lives for many years, providing joy, companionship, and laughter. One day the time will come for you to say goodbye. Perhaps they have been diagnosed with an untreatable condition, or maybe they’re just getting older. Taking the time to learn about how to care for a dog in hospice will ensure their physical needs, as well as your emotional ones, are met. At this stage, it is important to prioritize comfort, pain management, and quality of life. Pain management is essential for dogs reaching the end of their life. Work closely with a vet to manage any pain, nausea, and stress. This may involve simple prescription medication, or the use of non-FDA approved supplements (a growing number of which have been found to support aging dogs in many ways). Be sure all family members know what medications are needed and when to avoid accidentally missing a dose. To support a dog’s mobility and comfort, consider investing in equipment such as orthopedic bedding to prevent pressure sores, particularly for dogs with limited movement. You may also need some mobility aids like rugs on slippery floors, ramps for loading into the car, or harnesses/slings to assist with walking. For dogs who tend to slip, purchase non slip pads which are stuck to the dog’s paws with gentle adhesive. Hygiene and nutrition are essential to track. For a dog losing control of bowels or bladder, check regularly for wetness or soiling to keep skin clean and dry. Offer your beloved pet enticing food or use appetite stimulants to keep them at a safe weight. And finally, ensure fresh water is always accessible. Now is your moment to spend as much time as possible with your furry friend. After Crimson’s intake examination, the kitten was found to be healthy. Zoo Veterinary and Animal Care staff will continue to monitor his foot closely as he grows to ensure he uses the leg properly and it doesn’t cause any complications. “I’ve had the privilege of witnessing countless rescues. There is something so deeply moving about watching our team pour themselves so completely into a single life. Their skill, their sleepless nights, and their quiet determination motivate me. I can only hope that Crimson’s story and the work at Oakland Zoo impact all of you as it does me,” says Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. The Zoo is optimistic that Crimson will have a good life regardless of his history. He has been handling his bottle feedings very well, and the team is feeding him around the clock due to his very young age and needs. Although his health appears good at this time, he is at a delicate stage, and the Zoo will monitor him closely as he grows. Crimson is currently being bottle-fed every three hours by Animal Care and Veterinary staff and will continue this routine for the next few weeks. Zoo staff have the challenging task of providing the care Crimson’s mother would have offered in the wild, while also managing routine feedings and socialization, and allowing him space to exhibit wild behaviors and act as much like a wild mountain lion as possible. In the wild, mountain lion cubs need about 12-18 months with their mother to learn essential survival skills. Because Crimson is so young, he lacks the skills necessary to be released back into the wild. After he successfully rehabilitates at Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital, the Zoo hopes to introduce Crimson to Clover, the female cub rescued earlier in March who is also receiving care at Oakland Zoo. Mountain lion kittens tend to thrive with a companion, a strategy the Zoo has successfully used with other rescues, including Briar, who has become a resident at Oakland Zoo and now lives with Silverado and Coloma at the Zoo’s California Trail mountain lion habitat. While Oakland Zoo and CDFW prefer these kittens to remain in the wild, the pairing of Clover with Crimson will help improve their overall wellbeing and secure a brighter future for both cubs. CDFW follows a thorough process before starting rescue and rehabilitation efforts for wild mountain lions. In this case, Crimson was found alone and vocalizing frequently, which is unusual for a solitary mountain lion kitten to do for long periods. The National Park Service made multiple den visits, monitored GPS collar and camera data, and continued observing the kitten. NPS biologists observed that Crimson’s mother had likely moved dens, and she was not returning to care for him. After two days, he appeared noticeably weaker, having lost 10% of his body weight, prompting NPS, in close consultation with CDFW, to retrieve and relocate him for rehabilitation. Oakland Zoo will continue to update the public on Crimson’s recovery and future introduction to Clover on social media. For more information, please review the FAQ below… What happened to Crimson’s mom, and what could have possibly led to him being abandoned? Is this rare? Mountain lions rarely abandon their offspring, and it is also uncommon for a mountain lion to have only one kitten in a den. While CDFW cannot officially confirm why the mother abandoned the kitten, she may have done so because of the kitten’s abnormal hind limb, specifically the missing toes, which could have triggered an instinct in the mother to relocate her other potential kittens and conserve resources by establishing a new den site. What are the next steps before Crimson is introduced to Clover? Before Crimson can be introduced to Clover, he is going to need to be larger and more robust. Currently, he is much smaller than Clover, and for his safety, the team needs to wait for him to grow so they can play appropriately. Oakland Zoo Veterinary and Animal Care staff may start “fenceline howdies” between Clover and Crimson when he is ready, so they can get used to each other’s presence before introducing them physically in the same space. How is Clover doing? The female mountain lion who was rescued in early March. Clover has been recovering well, is currently stable, and is getting close to her ideal body weight for her age. She is getting used to the Zoo and hospital environment and is beginning training with Animal Care staff. Why did the kitten have an ear tag upon arrival? How do researchers track mountain lions? Mountain lion researchers use ear tags so that animals can be identified in the future, if they are captured, or found to have died, or seen in a photo. The National Park Service has been studying the small, isolated mountain lion population in the Santa Monica Mountains for more than 20 years to better understand their behavior and ecology and how to conserve them. Understanding how often females reproduce, how many kittens they have, and the fate of those kittens is a critical part of that work. In general, researchers track mountain lions using GPS and VHF radio-collars. Comfort and Compassion: A Guide to End of Life Care for Dogs By Sierra Berrick It’s not a topic most people like to consider; our dogs are the center of our lives for many years, providing joy, companionship, and laughter. One day the time will come for you to say goodbye. Perhaps they have been diagnosed with an untreatable condition, or maybe they’re just getting older. Taking the time to learn about how to care for a dog in hospice will ensure their physical needs, as well as your emotional ones, are met. At this stage, it is important to prioritize comfort, pain management, and quality of life. Pain management is essential for dogs reaching the end of their life. Work closely with a vet to manage any pain, nausea, and stress. This may involve simple prescription medication, or the use of non-FDA approved supplements (a growing number of which have been found to support aging dogs in many ways). Be sure all family members know what medications are needed and when to avoid accidentally missing a dose. To support a dog’s mobility and comfort, consider investing in equipment such as orthopedic bedding to prevent pressure sores, particularly for dogs with limited movement. You may also need some mobility aids like rugs on slippery floors, ramps for loading into the car, or harnesses/slings to assist with walking. For dogs who tend to slip, purchase non slip pads which are stuck to the dog’s paws with gentle adhesive. Hygiene and nutrition are essential to track. For a dog losing control of bowels or bladder, check regularly for wetness or soiling to keep skin clean and dry. Offer your beloved pet enticing food or use appetite stimulants to keep them at a safe weight. And finally, ensure fresh water is always accessible. They put smoke, air filtration, air scrubber machines, and dehumidifiers in the building to prevent smoke damage. The fire comes just one month after announcing the house’s plans to reopen its museum after an 18-month closure due to a lease dispute with the city. The museum and events space will be closed until further notice. The Camron-Stanford House was built in 1876 and was home to five influential families during its time as a residence before becoming the first museum in Oakland. It is the last Victorian house on Lake Merritt, developed by Samuel Merritt himself. According to Akin, the house is in a rough financial situation. Because of their lengthy closure, they had to let go of their staff in January due to funding constraints. The museum is continuing its fundraising efforts and is looking for volunteers to help. “We are desperate for funds. Were desperate for volunteers. We just want to save this place, and it seems a little overwhelming, but we have a lot of support from the community, so just trying to rally and organize,” said Akin. To find updates on the status of the house, you can go to cshouse. org. If you’d like to donate to their GoFundMe, it can be found at the following link: www.gofundme. com/f/save-the-camronstanford-house. Those interested in volunteering at the Camron-Stanford house can sign up at their website. The house offers docent training to volunteers and is starting its training on April 25. articles.text: Piedmont Church is incredibly fortunate to have Dr. Stephen Main as our Minister of Music. We consider him a treasure. He is an extraordinarily talented and award-winning musician, conductor, composer and teacher. He leads one of the most excellent and eclectic church music program in the Bay Area. The musical offerings at our church range from Greek Orthodox chants to Shaker folk music to spiritual/gospel to jazz to contemporary pieces to traditional/classical literature. While music each Sunday is typically performed by Stephen at the 3,000-pipe organ and the 35-voice choir with soloists, there often is a small to medium group of other instrumentalists accompanying the choir. Larger ensembles perform at Easter and on Choir Sunday in June. The annual Christmas concerts, which began in 2010, feature an entire symphony orchestra and 45-voice choir. Each year, there is also an Americana Sunday program and a program featuring historical French horns with no valves. In addition to directing our Chancel Choir, Stephen also conducts a handbell choir that performs five times a year. Every week is a musical surprise. Stephen is a multdimensional musician, playing not only the organ and piano, but also the violin, bass, lute COME FOR THE MUSIC AND STAY FOR COFFEE TO MEET NEW FRIENDS!

articles.text: Piedmont’s urban forest is facing serious challenges with rising temperatures globally due to climate change. Nancy Kent, Piedmont’s Parks & Projects manager, spoke with the Post to discuss why Piedmont’s trees are dying and what the city plans to do. As summer heat continues to increase, trees planted 40 to 50 years ago are not well-equipped to deal with this changing climate. Piedmont’s Dracena Park has lost more than 50 trees due to increasing temperatures and less rainfall. “A lot of the conifers are the ones that we’ve seen die out,” said Kent. “These were all trees that were planted 50 years ago, and their natural range was probably colder than Piedmont. They can no longer survive in the current landscape they’re in because it’s just hotter and drier, and the rain is coming at different times or infrequently.” The tree most heavily impacted is the California coast live oak (Quercus agrifolia). It’s Piedmont’s third most abundant tree in the canopy and arborists believe that this oak may struggle as the climate continues to warm. In response, the city is actively planting trees that are more adaptive to the changing climate. According to Kent, this is new territory for the city, which has the challenge of projecting 50 years down the line that the trees they plant now will still be healthy. Dead trees marked for removal in Dracena Park
articles.title: Piedmont’s urban forest changing due to climate change

articles.text: On Thursday, April 2, at around 1:45 a.m., a magnitude 4.6 earthquake shook Bay Area residents out of their sleep. The earthquake originated near Boulder Creek, an unincorporated area in the Santa Cruz Mountains. Over 27,000 people in the region reported feeling the temblor, including in areas far from the epicenter like Sacramento and Santa Rosa, according to the USGS. The Bay Area remains at high risk of a damaging earthquake, according to the USGS, which estimates a 72% chance of a 6.7 magnitude or higher. An earthquake this large would cause a lot of damage to very populated areas. The best way to protect yourself and others in case of an emergency is to prepare for the worst and hope for the best. Piedmont’s Fire Department has shared tips on what residents should prepare in case of a large, damaging earthquake. Step one is to create a household emergency communication plan. In this plan, the department recommends that residents identify an out-of-area contact who lives outside the Bay Area to act as a central information source. articles.text: Building beloved community through storytelling On the evening of March 31st, energy filled the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse as the Piedmont community gathered for an evening with New York Times bestselling author Kate Schatz. Hosted by the Piedmont Affinity Mentors in partnership with the TriSchool Parent DEIB Committee, the event brought together students, families, and educators for a powerful conversation on storytelling, identity, and collective responsibility. Schatz, an author, activist, and public speaker, is widely known for co-authoring Do the Work: An Antiracist Activity Book with W. Kamau Bell and for the Rad Women series, created with illustrator Miriam Klein Stahl. Her most recent book, Where the Girls Were, continues her work highlighting stories that challenge narratives and expand how we understand history and belonging. The evening opened with remarks from Piedmont’s Director of Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging, Jean Takazawa. She grounded the event in Martin Luther King Jr.’s vision of the “Beloved Community.” She emphasized that this vision is built through everyday acts of care and listening, not just single moments. “This is the work we are doing Photo by Jean Takazawa The Affinity Mentor panelists and author Kate Schatz in the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on March 31. articles.text: A week later his disciples were again in the house, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were shut, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.” — John 20:26 The Vanderbilt Divinity Library Revised Common Lectionary website suggests this prayer for the week after Easter. I trust that it speaks to you as it does to me. O God, your Son remained with his disciples after his resurrection, teaching them to love all people as neighbors. As his disciples in this age, we offer our prayers on behalf of the universe in which we are privileged to live and our neighbors with whom we share it. The current NASA Artemis II moon flight reminds that we are part of local communities as well as part of a universe that stretches to infinity. As such, Jesus’ words to his disciples as they hid behind closed doors in the days after that first Easter, “Peace be with you,” urge us to open our eyes and our hearts and see that while we are tempted to concern ourselves only with our own survival, we are responsible to care for the seas, the skies and stars. Our call is to seek the well-being of strangers, sojourners, seers and seekers in all times and all places. Jesus’ invitation to his disciples then and now, is to think large rather than to live small. I can’t help but believe that the Jesus who emerged from the tomb to say “Peace be with you,” would be well pleased with the words of astronaut Christina Koch, after the crew of Artemis II got back in touch with mission control after traveling past the dark side of the moon. Speaking to the people of Earth, Ms. Koch described a future when people will regularly go to the moon: “We will explore. We will build. We will build ships. We will visit again. We will construct science outposts. We will drive rovers. We will do radio astronomy. We will found companies. We will bolster industry.” But she ended by saying “We will inspire but ultimately, we will always choose Earth. We will always choose each other.” Peace be with you. Choose Earth. Choose each other. Pray for the well-being of the universe. Friends, join with me in believing that Easter has implications of cosmic proportion. Jim Hopkins is Pastor Emeritus of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland and currently Interim Pastor at Shell Ridge Community Church in Walnut Creek.
articles.title: After Easter

I hope we will have the chance to share future performances with you. –Ayaka Isono Pianist, Ensemble Humanité Measure H will help support schools Editor: Every morning, our three kids — a fifth grader, a third grader, and a kindergartner — head off to Havens Elementary, walking with us or with friends from the neighborhood. At Havens, parents volunteer for lunch duty, step in as substitute teachers, and rally around every classroom. This is a community that shows up. But above all, the teachers and staff are exceptional — dedicated professionals who know our kids by name and push them to grow. Jill attended Piedmont schools herself and had the same experience. She’s still in touch with some of her elementary and middle school teachers decades later. That kind of lasting impact doesn’t happen by accident. But it does require investment. Measure H renews the existing parcel tax that funds over $12 million — more than 20% of the PUSD budget. This is not a tax increase. It’s a continuation of nearly 40 years of community commitment. If Measure H fails, the district would be forced to cut $12 million annually, leading to devastating teacher layoffs and gutted programs. Whether or not you have children in our schools, Measure H protects what makes Piedmont, Piedmont. Please vote yes. –Jill & Dan Saper Havens Elementary parents seasonal festivals, engaged citizens, and devoted public servants all make up the fabric of life here. Each of these things matters. But none of them were the reason we chose to move to Piedmont. We moved here because of the value this community places on its schools. And in that, we are hardly unique. On June 2nd, Piedmonters have another opportunity to stand behind what we value. Measure H represents a commitment this community has made to education for the past 40 years — to the teachers who shape our children into thoughtful, capable citizens; to the classrooms stocked with challenging and current materials; to the athletics programs, math competitions, engineering courses, and everything else that adds up to a great education. That is what the parcel tax makes possible. Not just programs and materials, though it funds those too. It makes possible a culture — a signal sent to every teacher, every student, and every family new to this city — that education is not a background consideration here. It is the foundation. Vote yes on Measure H. –Ted Kinch Yes on Measure H Co-Chair Vote Yes on Measure H Editor: Every community makes choices that define it. The 2026 Sustainable Living Award honorees show that there is no single path to more sustainable living. Their stories reflect different starting points, different motivations, and different routes to electrifying their homes. Hear their stories and celebrate them at next week’s Design and Sustainability Awards Gala Design & Sustainability Awards Gala on Wednesday, April 15, 6:00 p.m., hosted at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. The Sustainable Living Awards, now in their third year, add a new dimension to the Planning Commission’s longstanding Design Awards program, which recognizes home renovation projects that reflect the highest level of design excellence. The addition of award categories showcasing green improvements is part of the City’s ongoing commitment to helping community members incorporate more sustainable choices into their homes and daily lives. Winners if the 2026 Sustainability Awards honorees are: Brandon Bercovich, Ellen Smith and Jeff Fucigna, and Molly Lloyd and Dan Reardon. Brandon’s electrification journey began with a heat pump and grew into a full home transformation. articles.text: Piedmont City Council has selected 19 residents to serve in appointed volunteer positions, following interviews with applicants on March 23. For most Committees and Commissions the appointees officially began their term of service on April 1. Individuals were selected from a pool of 23 applicants, include 6 members and Committee members and 13 returning volunteers. Commissioners serve threeyear terms, with a maximum of two consecutive terms. The City will hold a public Volunteer Appreciation reception in the City Hall courtyard at 4:45 p.m. on Monday, April 20. The reception will recognize outgoing Commissioners, Betty C. Howard Award winners, the return of the former Volunteer of the Year Award, and the new Young Volunteer of the Year award. The City is still seeking a volunteer to fill a vacancy for a Parking Hearing Officer. This position serves as an Administrative Hearing Officer for appeals of parking tickets issued by Piedmont Police, and is a good fit for someone with a legal background. Applications can be completed at piedmont. ca.gov/Commissioner and will remain open until the position is filled. A schedule of all upcoming meetings is available on the City’s events calendar at piedmont.ca.gov/events. Planning Commission, Recreation Commission, and Park Commission meetings are broadcast on the City’s cable channel, KCOM-TV (Comcast channel 27). These meetings are also livestreamed online and available for later viewing at piedmont.ca.gov/ MeetingVideos.
articles.title: City Council makes 19 appointments to Commissions and Committees

articles.text: Piedmont Gas & Auto Repair, located at 340 Highland Ave, reopened after a lengthy closure to satisfy new California laws. The station took down its fences late last week and is actively serving gas to drivers. The station was closed under a state mandate that took effect on January 1. A California law effective September 25, 2014, changed the underground storage tank (UST) program regarding design and construction. The law states that a single-walled storage tank must have secondary containment and a continuous leak detection system If not stations were to be closed by December 31, 2025. Single-walled storage tanks increase the risk of leaking due to rust and corrosion. The law is intended to prevent hazardous substances from polluting soil, groundwater, streams, and other sources of drinking water. If the station had not complied it would have faced serious fines of $500 to $5,000 per day per underground storage tank according to the State Resources Control Board. The station could also have been be red-tagged by the Unified Program Agency, which could prevent fuel deliveries and dispensing. Piedmont Gas & Auto Repair has spent the last three months removing its single-walled underground storage tank and replacing it with an underground tank that complies with the secondary containment and leak detection system requirements. Drivers pumping gas at the reopened Piedmont Gas & Auto Repair.
articles.title: Piedmont Gas & Auto Repair reopens for business
