articles.text: Hamlet is an AI-powered civic technology platform that makes local government meetings searchable and accessible. Sunil Rajaraman, the CEO and founder of Hamlet, became passionate about local government when he decided to run for the Orinda, CA City Council. He wanted to get more involved in the community, and by attending local council meetings, he noticed a significant barrier to entry for those interested in local government. “As an average resident, it’s impossible to understand what’s happening unless you attend regularly or read the transcripts. It’s a huge time commitment,” said Rajaraman. He identified that the barrier to entry for local government was so time-consuming. Most people are unable to focus on their local government’s decisions, which impact our day-to-day lives the most. “I think that the problem is that you know most people are focused on federal-level politics,” he stated. “The stuff that affects our day-to-day lives that flies under the radar is local politics. And while it’s great, we have a lot of people engaged at the federal and state level, but council chambers are empty.” Rajaraman would use AI to simplify council meetings and get up to speed on hot topic issues. Through his use of AI, he was inspired to create a platform that could help local communities easily digest their local governments’ meetings. “Everybody should have access to as much of that raw information as possible,” he continued. “I think that’ll make American communities better if people actually understand what’s happening in their city councils and planning commissions.” Through this, Rajarman founded Hamlet, his AI company designed to make local meets more accessible. Hamlet indexes thousands of government meeting transcripts from city councils, planning commissions, zoning boards, and other public bodies across the United States. They then make this information searchable by using a combination of official transcripts, video recordings, and AI-powered transcription. “I want people to be engaged so we can put better people into office in certain cities and make sure people are informed about how the decision-making and democratic process works at the local level,” said Rajaraman. Rajaraman’s company uses Hamlet to create city deep dives on their platform, The District. The District is a data-driven deep dive into local cities, highlighting the biggest topics and data about who has spoken the most at council meetings or the most repeated topics. To avoid potential biases, the company writes about cities Sunil Rajaraman, CEO & founder of Hamlet AI with no financial ties to the company. Readers can follow this link to read about Piedmont’s deep dive: https://district.myhamlet. com/articles/piedmonts-deliberation. The next steps for Hamlet are to continue expanding and improving their coverage of local government. “We’re adding more and more cities to our database, and we want to build the most important company focused on local government,” Rajaraman said. “We should understand how local government makes decisions. And within that, residents should understand it transparently.” To learn more about Hamlet and look at Piedmont’s council meetings broken down, you can find them at the following link: https://www.myhamlet.com/
articles.title: Hamlet AI revolutionizes nationwide local government public meeting coverage

articles.text: When people talk about “finding your people,” the advice is usually some version of: join something. Join a book club. Take a class in something you are interested in. Find a group to volunteer with on a topic that you are passionate about. And that is not actually bad advice, but it is incomplete. Because finding your people is not only about where you go a few times. It’s about what happens next. There’s a study from the University of Kansas that looks at how long it takes to form friendships. The numbers are surprisingly high. It takes about 40 to 60 hours to become a casual friend, 80 to 100 hours to become a friend, and around 200 hours to become a close friend. Which means most friendships don’t fail because we chose the wrong activity group. They stall out somewhere around hour two. Does this sound familiar to you? You have a good first conversation and discover you both like the same podcast, or the same kind of music, or the same way of spending a Saturday morning. And then… nothing really happens after that. The connection stays theoretical. So I’ve been thinking about that first step differently. Yes, shared interests matter. They make it easier to start. A book group, a ski club, a random conversation about something you both enjoy. That’s often where it begins. But that’s not where friendship is built. At some point, someone has to do the slightly uncomfortable thing of continuing it. Asking, “Do you want to grab a coffee sometime?” or suggesting a walk or a hike. You’ve got to follow up instead of assuming it will happen naturally because it won’t! And then doing it again… and again. Those first 39 hours will likely feel awkward and a little uneven because you are still figuring each other out. The conversation won’t always flow and you might feel like you are oversharing or not sharing enough. It can seem easier to retreat back to surface-level interactions or to keep things contained within the original context, but this is the part that actually builds towards something. Finding common ground is not just about discovering one thing you both like. It is about slowly learning each other’s lives. The parts that overlap and the parts that don’t. What matters to the other person. What they are carrying. What they are excited about. That kind of connection does not happen quickly. It takes time, and it takes some willingness to stay in the awkward middle where nothing is fully formed yet. So here is a small experiment. The next time you have a conversation with someone where there is even a hint of shared interest, do one more thing. Make one specific invitation. Not “we should do this sometime,” but something real with a time, a place and a simple plan. And then follow through. You do not need to join whole new group and you do not need a perfect alignment of interests. You just need one interaction, and then another, and then enough time for something real to start to take shape. Nina Meehan is a keynote speaker, workshop facilitator and coach with a specialization in creativity and communication. https://ninameehan.com/
articles.title: Connection Experiment: Finding your people

articles.text: instruction, including a desire to review and adjust our current math pathways, curriculum needs, best practices in instructional practices, and a need for additional assessment data. This work will be done in close collaboration with our teachers, whose classroom expertise is essential to building a system that serves our students. Our goal is to move beyond the limitations of the current program to better support the needs of every learner. Whether a student requires additional support to master foundational fluency, is seeking a rigorous path toward advanced STEM coursework, or falls into the “solid middle” where consistent challenge is key, our redesign will focus on creating clear, high-achieving endpoints for every math pathway we offer. A central priority of this discussion is the development of a more comprehensive assessment system. We recognize the need for more information about achievement, in addition to classroom grades, to understand each student’s mathematical progress and potential readiness for acceleration. By implementing a system of regular benchmark assessments, we aim to provide both teachers and parents with shared information about achievement. This transparency will ensure that placement decisions are grounded in evidence, reducing the stress of transitions and ensuring students are placed in the environment where they will be most successful. Over the coming months, we will be evaluating our course pathways, curriculum, assessments, and instructional practices to ensure our students build durable skills from elementary school through graduation and beyond. We are committed to a “multiple entry point” design, allowing students to access advanced coursework at different stages of their development. Meaningful engagement with our teachers and parents is foundational to this process, and we look forward to providing opportunities for our community to share feedback and learn more about our data-driven insights. Together, we are building a more flexible, rigorous, and transparent math experience for all PUSD students. resources on the state of AI, as well as links to online AI Literacy activities and mini-courses for our high school students. • AI at Home Newsletter #1 – Smore.com/n/d4sh3 • AI at Home Newsletter #2 – Smore.com/n/a84we • Secondary Student Newsletter #1 – Smore.com/n/f9mgz • Secondary Student Newsletter #2 – Smore.com/n/9ynjak Additionally, at the high school, students were offered a challenge, to design an 11”x17” poster that uncovers the “hidden” AI in a technology that we use, often every day. articles.text: On the weekend of March 14, the Highlander Robotics team traveled to San Francisco with their new robot “Wisp” for the FIRST Robotics Competition’s San Francisco District Event at St. Ignatius High School. There they won the FIRST Impact Award and qualified for the NorCal District Championship in April. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game each January, played by two alliances of three robots in an arena roughly the size of a basketball court. Roughly 3500 teams of 9th to 12th graders construct an entirely new robot each season and competitions begin eight weeks after kickoff. In this year’s game called Rebuilt, robots shoot 6-inch foam balls into an 8-foot high funnel while crossing field obstacles and climbing rungs of a ladder before time runs out. At their first competition of the season, the Highlanders finished qualification rounds ranked 5th of 38 teams with an 8-4 record. During alliance selection they were chosen as the second pick of the draft by Alliance 2, captained by the Aragon Robotics Team from San Mateo. In the opening round of the double-elimination playoffs they defeated Alliance 7, Deus Ex Machina, the SOTA Cyberdragons, and Bay Robotics. In the second round they fell to the third-seeded OtterBots alliance and dropped to the lower bracket, where they were eliminated in Round 4 by the 4th seed Pit member Sattvik Sapuram works to maintain Wisp between rounds. The team has 62 students from 12 local high schools. Drive team members Sam Charlson (left), Mason Kim, Cassie Colby, and Max Seiden prepare strategy before their match. Alliance and finished 4th overall. In the awards ceremony the Highlanders were awarded FIRST’s most prestigious award, the Impact Award, which honors the team that best represents a model for other teams to emulate and embodies the mission of FIRST. Judges cited the opening of a multi-level robotics practice space partnership with Piedmont Makers, the adoption of the scouting software that the Highlanders publish each year by over 800 teams, and the team’s open source software training curriculum as reasons they were deserving of the award. The Highlanders competed next in Glendale, Arizona on March 27–29 before heading to the NorCal District Championship at the Cow Palace in San Francisco April 9-12, where the top 60 teams in the region will vie for berths at the World Championship in Houston. The robot Wisp was operated by driver Max Seiden and operator Mason Kim, and supported by drive coach Cassie Colby and human player Sam Charlson. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert and is composed of 62 students from 12 high schools around the area. They work out of the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab at Piedmont High School. For more information visit the team on the web at frc8033.com. The Highlanders robot “Wisp” (8033) shoots a barrage of balls at the Hub alongside alliance partner 4973. articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team wrapped up a busy week, competing in three events in just four days. The Highlanders sent six athletes to the prestigious Stanford Invitational in Palo Alto on Friday and Saturday, April 3-4, and sent two to the Dave Shimansky Pole Vault Invitational on April 4 at San Ramon Valley HS in Danville. Both the boys and girls teams won a Western Alameda County Conference meet with Alameda on Wednesday, April 1 at Burrell Field in San Leandro. At the Stanford Invitational, Piedmont notably qualified its 4x400 relay team and Sebastien Swain in the 800 to the famous Arcadia Invitational on Friday and Saturday, April 10-11. It is considered the marquee event throughout the year for track and field. Swain will also run alongside Rehan Mumtaz, Marius Arno, and Maddox Ma in the 4 x 400 relay. “The Arcadia Invitational is the #1 high school track and field event in the world. Over 200 athletes that competed at Arcadia went on to compete in the Olympics, like Noah Lyles who holds the boys all-time 100 meter record, Marion Jones who holds the girls all-time 200m record, and Sydney McLaughlin who holds the girls all-time 300 hurdles record. This year the fun name is Quincy Wilson, who as a 16 year old received a gold medal as a member of the Team USA 4x400m team. Somehow our little public school has sent at least one athlete to Arcadia every year since 2021,” coach Pouyan Assadi said. Swain finished 12th of 18 in the 800 at the Stanford Invitational, in a fast time of 1:56.21. It marked just his sixth event since returning from knee surgery. “We’re trying to not get too excited but it sure seems like Seb’s just a few steps away from being fully back. For me, it’s less about his time and more about how he ran those two races. He was confident and aggressive,” Assadi said. In the 4x400, Mumtaz, Swain, Arno, and Ma finished 13th of 23 teams with a time of 3:27.21. They were the second fastest team from the North Coast Section behind Windsor, which placed ninth. “I’m pumped about how the boys ran that 4x4,” said Assadi. “Seb was the key as he moved us from fifth to second. Maddox took us home and showed us why he was a no brainer decision to anchor,” Mumtaz and Ma also ran in the 4x100, while Diego Hurwitz and Jason Shum replaced Swain and Arno. They finished 22nd in 43.79. Dave Shimansky Pole Vault Invitational results Avedis Gourjian finished the boys’ event sixth of 24 athletes with a height of 11 feet, 6 inches. On the girls’ side, Shayna Chau Photos by Steve Zirkelbach Sebastien Swain finished 12th in the 800 meters at the Stanford Invitational, qualifying for the prestigious Arcadia Invitational in the process. PHS’ 4x400 relay team of Rehan Mumtaz (left), Marius Arno, Maddox Ma, and Sebastien Swain placed 13th at the Stanford Invitational and qualified for the Arcadia Invitational.
articles.title: Track & Field athletes compete in Stanford Invitational

articles.text: Piedmont High’s baseball team split its last pair of games on the road, beating Oakland Tech 6-4 on Thursday, April 2, but lost 4-2 against San Leandro on Tuesday, March 31. The pair of games brings the Highlanders’ record to 5-5-2 (W-L-T) entering the midway mark of the season with 12 games left. “The kids are going to be really different than they are right now. We have a lot of sophomores and want that upward trajectory. We played some really tough teams at the start of the season, and that’s going to make us better in the long run,” said coach Eric Olson. Piedmont’s win over the Bulldogs came in extra innings, scoring the eventual game-winner in the top of the eighth. Diego Delventhal, their usual shortstop, was the winning pitcher after entering in the bottom of the seventh. The Highlanders now travel south to for the Central Coast Classic, a four-game tournament in the San Luis Obispo area from Tuesday, April 7 through Friday, April 10. 6-4 nail biter over Oakland Tech Piedmont went up 3-0 in the top of the second and extended the gap to 5-1 in the top of the fifth. The Bulldogs tied the game with a pair of runs in the both the bottom of the sixth and seventh. PHS’ eventual game-winner came in uncharacteristic fashion, where Oakland Tech’s pitcher committed a costly balk with two outs, allowing Max Fujimoto to score. The Highlanders’ threerun second inning started with a single by Jack Meyjes, who advanced to second on a wild pitch. Aiden Bell hit a one-out single to move Meyjes to third, while Fujimoto brought him in with a single. Bell scored after Massimo Mittone hit a ground ball to cause an error, while Enzo Ong scored Fujimoto with a sacrifice bunt. Their two-run fifth inning started with walks by Diego and Lucas Delventhal, while Meyjes cracked a one-out double to score Staff Photos Diego Delventhal was the winning pitcher against Oakland Tech after entering in relief in the seventh inning. Jack Meyjes had RBIs against Oakland Tech and San Leandro. Max Fujimoto scored the eventual game-winner against Tech. Lucas. Ben Sorensen loaded the bases with a walk, leading to Bell drawing a walk to score Diego. Oakland Tech tied with two runs in the bottom of the sixth and seventh. In the top of the eighth, Fujimoto reached first on an error, then stole second with one out. Lucas Delventhal hit a two-out single to move Fujimoto to third. With Diego Delventhal at the plate, Tech’s pitcher committed a balk before his first pitch, allowing Fujimoto to score. In the bottom of the eighth, Tech started with a single and a walk. After that, Diego Delventhal forced a fielder’s choice, where shortstop Lucas Delventhal threw out Tech’s runner at home. Diego then struck out the next batter. After an intentional walk to load the bases, Diego threw a four-pitch strikeout to put down the Bulldogs final batter looking. Final stats: Diego Delventhal scored a run and walked twice. Meyjes went 2-for-4 with a double, run scored and an RBI. Mittone had an RBI. Lucas Delventhal went 1-for-3 with a run scored and two walks. Fujimoto went 1-for-4 with two runs scored, an RBI and a stolen base. Bell went 2-for-3 with a run scored, an RBI and a walk. Ong had an RBI. Diego was the winning pitcher with 1.2 innings of work, striking out three, allowing no runs and one hit. 4-2 loss to San Leandro San Leandro went up 4-0 by the bottom of the fourth inning, while Piedmont scored its two runs in the top of the sixth and seventh. Final stats: Diego Delventhal had an RBI. Meyjes went 1-for-2 with an RBI and a walk. Mittone went 1-for-1 with a run scored and a walk. Jonah Cha-Foster scored a run, a walk and a stolen base. Sorensen went 1-for-3 with a double. Ong went 1-for-3. Tuesday vs. Arroyo Grande Piedmont played Arroyo Grande at Atascadero HS on Tuesday, April 7. See next week’s Post for game details. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, April 8, 2026 Sports Baseball team tops Oakland Tech in extra inning By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s baseball team split its last pair of games on the road, beating Oakland Tech 6-4 on Thursday, April 2, but lost 4-2 against San Leandro on Tuesday, March 31. The pair of games brings the Highlanders’ record to 5-5-2 (W-L-T) entering the midway mark of the season with 12 games left. “The kids are going to be really different than they are right now. We have a lot of sophomores and want that upward trajectory. We played some really tough teams at the start of the season, and that’s going to make us better in the long run,” said coach Eric Olson. Piedmont’s win over the Bulldogs came in extra innings, scoring the eventual game-winner in the top of the eighth. Diego Delventhal, their usual shortstop, was the winning pitcher after entering in the bottom of the seventh. The Highlanders now travel south to for the Central Coast Classic, a four-game tournament in the San Luis Obispo area from Tuesday, April 7 through Friday, April 10. 6-4 nail biter over Oakland Tech Piedmont went up 3-0 in the top of the second and extended the gap to 5-1 in the top of the fifth. The Bulldogs tied the game with a pair of runs in the both the bottom of the sixth and seventh. PHS’ eventual game-winner came in uncharacteristic fashion, where Oakland Tech’s pitcher committed a costly balk with two outs, allowing Max Fujimoto to score. The Highlanders’ threerun second inning started with a single by Jack Meyjes, who advanced to second on a wild pitch. Aiden Bell hit a one-out single to move Meyjes to third, while Fujimoto brought him in with a single. Bell scored after Massimo Mittone hit a ground ball to cause an error, while Enzo Ong scored Fujimoto with a sacrifice bunt. Their two-run fifth inning started with walks by Diego and Lucas Delventhal, while Meyjes cracked a one-out double to score Staff Photos Diego Delventhal was the winning pitcher against Oakland Tech after entering in relief in the seventh inning. Jack Meyjes had RBIs against Oakland Tech and San Leandro. Track & Field athletes compete in Stanford Invitational By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s track and field team wrapped up a busy week, competing in three events in just four days. The Highlanders sent six athletes to the prestigious Stanford Invitational in Palo Alto on Friday and Saturday, April 3-4, and sent two to the Dave Shimansky Pole Vault Invitational on April 4 at San Ramon Valley HS in Danville. Both the boys and girls teams won a Western Alameda County Conference meet with Alameda on Wednesday, April 1 at Burrell Field in San Leandro. At the Stanford Invitational, Piedmont notably qualified its 4x400 relay team and Sebastien Swain in the 800 to the famous Arcadia Invitational on Friday and Saturday, April 10-11. It is considered the marquee event throughout the year for track and field. Swain will also run alongside Rehan Mumtaz, Marius Arno, and Maddox Ma in the 4 x 400 relay. “The Arcadia Invitational is the #1 high school track and field event in the world. Over 200 athletes that competed at Arcadia went on to compete in the Olympics, like Noah Lyles who holds the boys all-time 100 meter record, Marion Jones who holds the girls all-time 200m record, and Sydney McLaughlin who holds the girls all-time 300 hurdles record. This year the fun name is Quincy Wilson, who as a 16 year old received a gold medal as a member of the Team USA 4x400m team. Somehow our little public school has sent at least one athlete to Arcadia every year since 2021,” coach Pouyan Assadi said. Swain finished 12th of 18 in the 800 at the Stanford Invitational, in a fast time of 1:56.21. It marked just his sixth event since returning from knee surgery. “We’re trying to not get too excited but it sure seems like Seb’s just a few steps away from being fully back. For me, it’s less about his time and more about how he ran those two races. He was confident and aggressive,” Assadi said. In the 4x400, Mumtaz, Swain, Arno, and Ma finished 13th of 23 teams with a time of 3:27.21. They were the second fastest team from the North Coast Section behind Windsor, which placed ninth. “I’m pumped about how the boys ran that 4x4,” said Assadi. “Seb was the key as he moved us from fifth to second. Maddox took us home and showed us why he was a no brainer decision to anchor,” Mumtaz and Ma also ran in the 4x100, while Diego Hurwitz and Jason Shum replaced Swain and Arno. They finished 22nd in 43.79. Dave Shimansky Pole Vault Invitational results Avedis Gourjian finished the boys’ event sixth of 24 athletes with a height of 11 feet, 6 inches. On the girls’ side, Shayna Chau See Track and Field on page 29 Max Fujimoto scored the eventual game-winner against Tech. Lucas. Ben Sorensen loaded the bases with a walk, leading to Bell drawing a walk to score Diego. Oakland Tech tied with two runs in the bottom of the sixth and seventh. In the top of the eighth, Fujimoto reached first on an error, then stole second with one out. Lucas Delventhal hit a two-out single to move Fujimoto to third. With Diego Delventhal at the plate, Tech’s pitcher committed a balk before his first pitch, allowing Fujimoto to score. In the bottom of the eighth, Tech started with a single and a walk. After that, Diego Delventhal forced a fielder’s choice, where shortstop Lucas Delventhal threw out Tech’s runner at home. Diego then struck out the next batter. After an intentional walk to load the bases, Diego threw a four-pitch strikeout to put down the Bulldogs final batter looking. Final stats: Diego Delventhal scored a run and walked twice. Meyjes went 2-for-4 with a double, run scored and an RBI. Mittone had an RBI. Lucas Delventhal went 1-for-3 with a run scored and two walks. Fujimoto went 1-for-4 with two runs scored, an RBI and a stolen base. Bell went 2-for-3 with a run scored, an RBI and a walk. Ong had an RBI. Diego was the winning pitcher with 1.2 innings of work, striking out three, allowing no runs and one hit. 4-2 loss to San Leandro San Leandro went up 4-0 by the bottom of the fourth inning, while Piedmont scored its two runs in the top of the sixth and seventh. Final stats: Diego Delventhal had an RBI. Meyjes went 1-for-2 with an RBI and a walk. Mittone went 1-for-1 with a run scored and a walk. Jonah Cha-Foster scored a run, a walk and a stolen base. Sorensen went 1-for-3 with a double. Ong went 1-for-3. Tuesday vs. Arroyo Grande Piedmont played Arroyo Grande at Atascadero HS on Tuesday, April 7. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-5-2 overall, 2-0 league) faces three more teams in the Central Coast Classic. They play Lompoc at Righetti HS in Santa Maria today, April 8, at 3:00 p.m., play at Paso Robles on Thursday, April 9 at 7:00 p.m., and visit Nipomo on Friday, April 10 at 3:00 p.m. Photos by Steve Zirkelbach Sebastien Swain finished 12th in the 800 meters at the Stanford Invitational, qualifying for the prestigious Arcadia Invitational in the process. PHS’ 4x400 relay team of Rehan Mumtaz (left), Marius Arno, Maddox Ma, and Sebastien Swain placed 13th at the Stanford Invitational and qualified for the Arcadia Invitational.

articles.text: Staff Photos Dahlia Osman scored three goals against San Rafael, the first hat trick of her lacrosse career. Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team won a 6-5 battle against San Rafael on Thursday, April 1 at Witter Field. They have four matches left in the regular season. It’s been a matter of persevering through injuries for Piedmont this season. “I feel like we are the (Golden State) Warriors. It’s like every game we are without someone. I’ve never had a team where we were without so many bodies. But they are figuring it out, they are getting better every day. That’s all we care about,” said coach Carlton Chan. Piedmont has a young squad, including freshman Sydney Latvala as a key player. She scored twice and had an assist against San Rafael. The Highlanders currently the No. 25 ranked school in North Coast Section by MaxPreps.com, which will put them on pace for a No. 9 seed in the Division 2 bracket. “It’s all about effort. Everyone is trying hard and putting 100 percent into everything. The ground balls really matter and we’re focusing on improving on that. I feel like we’re making stronger connections on attack and stay calm,” Latvala said. 6-5 win over San Rafael Both teams were tied 2-2 through the first quarter. The the Highlanders’ defense holding the Bulldogs without a goal in the second quarter, while scoring one of their own to take a 3-2 lead into halftime. Piedmont scored once in the third quarter while conceding two, making it 4-4 going into the final going. San Rafael scored the first goal in the fourth quarter, but PHS roared back with the final two goals of the game. In the first quarter, San Rafael struck first at the 7:39 mark. Piedmont won the ensuing faceoff, scoring just 33 seconds later when Elliott Hondorp sent in a shot. The Bulldogs went back ahead a minute later, while Dahlia Osman scored with 1:09 remaining to tie it up. Sydney Latvala, a freshman, scored the go-ahead for Piedmont at the 8:34 mark of the second quarter to make it 3-2. In the third, San Rafael took the lead with back-to-back goals at 4:37 and three-minute marks, giving the Bulldogs a 4-3 advantage. After that, Osman scored again with 1:35 remaining to Sydney Latvala had two goals and an assist against San Rafael. knot things at 4-4. San Rafael scored nearly four minutes into the fourth quarter to give itself a 5-4 advantage, but that was the last time the Bulldogs got on the scoreboard. Latvala tied the score with 6:41 left in the game to make it 5-5. Then, with 4:38 left, Osman launched in her third goal, giving the senior her first career hat trick. From there, the Highlanders held on defensively to kill the remaining time without conceding again. Final stats: Hondorp had one goal, won one draw, and scooped one ground ball. Osman scored three goals. Latvala had two goals, one assist, won two draws, and gathered one ground ball. Hallie Burden had one assist, won five draws, and gathered one ground ball. Goalie Allie King had two saves. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-7 overall) returns from Spring Break on Tuesday, April 14, and will host Northgate at 7:00 p.m. The girls’ lacrosse team returns from Spring Break on April 14.

articles.text: Your eyesight is correct, Piedmont readers. The Highlanders’ softball team recently put up scores more akin to a football game in a pair of recent wins, beating Urban in San Francisco 22-11 on Friday, April 3 and winning 35-30 the previous day at San Lorenzo. It marks the school’s most runs in a single game since scoring 22 runs in 2022 also against San Lorenzo. Their 35 runs are Piedmont’s most ever since online records began on MaxPreps.com in 2005. In the pair of slugfests, the Highlanders totaled 26 hits, 30 steals, and remained patient at the plate with 51 total walks, including 28 on SLZ and 23 on Urban. “In high school softball, if you stay patient, stay disciplined at the plate and on the base paths, and capitalize on pitchers’ mistakes, good things are going to happen,” said coach Gene Denard. “We’re getting better at seeing the ball and hitting the ball.” The pair of wins brings Piedmont’s record to 8-6, while they are now 2-0 against Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline B Division teams. 35-30 over San Lorenzo Piedmont trailed 4-3 after the bottom of the second, and then San Lorenzo piled on 13 runs in the bottom of the third to put the Highlanders at risk of the mercy rule with a 17-3 lead. That’s when PHS answered with 12 runs of its own, cutting the deficit to 17-15. With the Grizzlies leading 21-16 after the bottom of the fifth, the Highlanders exploded for 16 runs in the top of the sixth to go up 32-21. SLZ scored five in the bottom half, 32-26, while the Highlanders scored three more in the top of the seventh. The Grizzlies fell short of a comeback with four runs in the final inning. In their 16-run top of the sixth, Hannah Joerger hit an RBI single to score Kajsa Benson, while Teah Suhr followed with an RBI single to score Rosemary Dickinson, Talia Perl had an RBI single to score Joerger, and then Elly Mak singled in Hailey Navarro to tie it at 21-21. Edie Elmquist drew a walk to score Perl, Benson was hit by a pitch with the bases loaded to score Mak, Samantha Schey scored on a passed ball, and then Elmquist scored on another passed ball. Joerger had another RBI single to score Benson, while Dickinson scored on a groundout by Suhr. Penelope Hopper singled in Joerger, Mak singled in Navarro, Perl scored on a passed ball, and Benson closed with an RBI single to score Elmquist. Final stats: Navarro had one walk and four stolen bases. Perl went 3-for-3 with two RBIs, seven runs scored, four walks and three stolen bases. Joerger went 3-for-5 with four RBIs, three runs scored, two walks and one stolen base. Dickinson scored four runs, four walks and one stolen base. Elmquist went 1-for-3 with three RBIs, four runs scored, five walks and three stolen bases. Suhr went 2-for-6 with a double, four RBIs, three runs scored and four stolen bases. Hopper went 1-for-3 with one RBI, one run scored, four Staff Photos Hannah Joerger totaled 10 RBIs in Piedmont’s wins over San Lorenzo and Urban. Edie Elmquist totaled nine runs scored and six stolen bases in Piedmont’s wins over San Lorenzo and Urban. Elly Mak had five hits in Piedmont’s wins over SLZ and Urban, including five RBIs and seven runs. walks and two stolen bases. Benson went 2-for-6 with four RBIs and two runs scored. Mak went 2-for-3 with four RBIs, four runs scored and one stolen base. Schey went 2-for-3 with three RBIs, three runs scored, two walks and one stolen base. Willow Thomas had one walk and one stolen base. 22-11 over Urban Piedmont scored three in the top of the first and two in the second inning to lead 5-1. Holding an 8-2 lead after the top of the fourth, Urban tied it up with six runs in the bottom half, and then went ahead 11-10 after the fifth inning. But that was it for the Blues, with Piedmont landing 12 runs in the top of the sixth and held Urban scoreless in the bottom half to activate the 10-run rule. Final stats: Perl went 1-for-4 with one RBI, one run scored, two walks and two stolen bases. Joerger went 1-for-4 with a triple, six RBIs, two runs scored and two walks. Dickinson had two RBIs, two runs scored, five walks and one stolen base. Elmquist went 2-for-2 with a double, two RBIs, five runs scored, four walks and three stolen bases. Kailee Talati went 1-for-2 with three RBIs, three runs scored, three walks and two stolen bases. Benson went 1-for-1 with a double, two RBIs, four runs scored, five walks and one stolen base. Mak went 3-for-4 with one RBI, three runs scored and two walks. Schey went 1-for-3 with two RBIs, one run scored, three walks. Thomas had one RBI, one run scored and two walks. articles.text: Piedmont High’s swimming team split its dual meet against Alameda on Friday, April 3 while competing at Encinal. The boys’ team won 89-81 over the Hornets, improving their Western Alameda County Conference record to 3-0, while the girls lost 106-56. The Highlanders look ahead to a monumental meet against Castro Valley on Friday, April 17, where they will host their first meet at the newly renovated Piedmont Pool. It marks the first time the school has hosted an athletic event since before the COVID-19 pandemic in 2019. League Meet vs. Alameda results It was a strong showing for junior Asher Takazawa and senior Dima Secor, leading the way with two wins in individual events. Takazawa won the 100 meter freestyle with a time of 49.97 in a field of six swimmers. Nik Costello was behind him in 50.75. Takazawa also was victorious in the 100 backstroke, clocking a winning time of 55.62 against five others. Sophomore Zafar Majid was behind him in second in 1:00.03. Secor won the 100 butterfly with a time of 56.82 in a field of six, while freshman Connor Carnazzo followed closely in second, 57.47. Secor also won the 200 individual medley in 1:57.50 in a field of five. Costello was victorious in the 50 freestyle, winning with a time of 22.44. The boys’ relay teams were also successful with three different wins. The 200 medley team of Jeffrey Latronica, Takazawa, Carnazzo, and Costello won against three Alameda teams in 1:37.25. Piedmont’s 200 freestyle team of Anton Secor, Carnazzo, Latronica, and Costello won in 1:30.81 in a field of four teams. Their 400 free relay team of Dima Secor, Anton Secor, Majid, and Latronica won in 3:18.88 against two Alameda teams and Piedmont’s B team. As for Piedmont’s girls’ team, sophomore Cynthia Wu won two individual events, while senior Sam White won one. Wu won the 50 free with a time of 25.66 in a field of six athletes. Fellow sophomore Charlotte Zhang finished in second, clocking a 27.75. Wu also won the 200 free with a time of 2:05.34 against four others. Freshman Sofia Vuori followed her in second, finishing in 2:12.65. White won the 100 butterfly in 1:10.22 against two other Alameda swimmers. Piedmont also took second in three relay events. Vivian Sohn, Brooke Patchen, Zhang, and Vuori was second of three in the 200 free relay in 1:59. In the 400 free, Wu, Vuori, Zhang, and White were second of four in 4:12. As for the 200 medley relay, Patchen, Indie Briskman, Vuori, and Zhang was second of four in 2:06.63. NEXT UP Piedmont will host Castro Valley for a league meet on Friday, April 17 at the Piedmont Pool at 3:30 p.m. Photos by George White Asher Takazawa (diving) won two individual events against Alameda, along with one relay event. Dima Secor won three races against Alameda.

articles.text: Piedmont’s Competition Pool After a lengthy construction process and significant delays, Piedmont’s community pool is opening this weekend on Saturday, April 11. Many residents are excited to jump into the new pool, but none moreso than Piedmont High School boys water polo coach, Rik Krumins. Krumins has coached at PHS for the past 10 years alongside John Savage in both an assistant and head coaching role. This past year, Krumins and Savage led the team to a 16-9 record and an 8-1 record in the West Alameda County League. In the wait for a new pool, both the girls’ and boys’ water polo teams have struggled to find a continuous place to practice. As construction for the pool began, the team trained in North Berkeley (King Pool), then over the course of time, they’ve been training and competing at Berkeley High School, Mills College, Laney College, Chabot College (Hayward), and Campolindo HS in Moraga. “This has been the biggest challenge for both the girls and boys teams in retaining athletes for the program over the course of the construction,” said Krumins. “I have been lucky enough that the water polo athletes have amazing parents and support groups who have been willing to commute to these facilities over the past 5-6 years, but we have taken a hit.” Now that the pool is open, the ease of access for student athletes and teams to practice will help the program tremendously. “This is a game-changer for the student-athletes as well. The ability to walk across campus to compete in front of their own student body will bring immense joy to these athletes. Something our water polo and aquatics programs have missed since the pool closed,” Krumins said. Krumins has had the opportunity to walk through the facility and has peered over the fence “thousands of times.” The competition pool will be where the sports teams will stake their presence, and Krumins is satisfied with its dimensions and adaptability. “Piedmont HS students will be training and competing in a proper ‘world aquatic’ (Olympic, Collegiate, High School) sized facility,” Krumins continued about the opportunity for youth programs. “The flexibility with nets and pool design allows the Piedmont Recreation Department, in partnership with me, to run youth water polo clinics and junior programs. Here is an opportunity to offer this for our youth, and I plan on doing this.” The coaching staff submitted the 2026 training and competition schedule last week for the desired pool times. The team has not yet been provided the schedule, but they’re anticipating it will be published soon. Its season starts in the fall. articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School girls softball team notched its first win of the season in dominant fashion on Monday, March 30, at Witter Field, beating El Cerrito’s Korematsu Middle School 10-0 in four innings. The Scots are led by a talented core of 8th graders who set the tone on both offense and defense. Bailey Gregovich and Madi Farboud both pitched nearly flawlessly in the shutout, striking out 6 while yielding only 4 hits and not walking a batter. Catcher Simone Tornatore went the distance behind, not allowing a single passed ball and making a key tag at the plate to stop a run. Defensive gems also came from 6th grader Keira Spina, who made a sensational catch at shortstop with the bases loaded in the first inning that deflated Korematsu’s early surge, and from 7th grader Mackenzie Ewen who snared a sharp liner to left in the third inning. The Scots offense was spurred by Farboud with three RBIs, Ewen with two RBIs, as well as a host of other contributors up and down the lineup. Spina, Clara Blanchard, Olive Dao-Hoang, Cate Penrod and Evie Joerger all drove in runs. Middle school softball is a relatively new sport to Piedmont since last year with many players having played in recreational softball and baseball through Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation. The team made it to the middle school championship last year where it lost to Berkeley’s Willard Middle School. This season, Piedmont Middle School is scheduled to play Albany, Berkeley’s King, Longfellow, and Willard, as well as schools in the Oakland Athletic League. Next up, the Scots will face off against Albany Middle School after Spring Break on Thursday, April 16, at 6 pm at Witter Softball Field. articles.text: Now Showing Through April Women in Focus by Denise Deleray is showing through April at Studios 11 at 560 Second Street in Oakland. The show is a compelling portrait exhibition exploring both the diversity and shared humanity of women across cultures. Featuring over a dozen works, the show presents faces from around the world— each portrait offering a unique story, while collectively revealing striking similarities in expression, presence, and identity. The exhibit also features an interactive portion of mixable miniature portraits. Denise Deleray, a San Francisco native, has been painting at Studios 11 for nearly a decade. She is especially drawn to portraying women as a way to raise awareness of important or under-recognized figures throughout history. The charming Studios 11 gallery sits just behind The Grand Gallery at the same address. While The Grand Gallery features over 30 local artists and has been operating for about two years, Studios 11 has a much longer history—serving as an independent creative space for over 15 years, evolving alongside a variety of neighboring front-facing galleries. • Gallery Hours: Saturday and Sunday 12 - 5 p.m. • Opening Reception: Saturday April 11, 2026, 1 - 4 p.m. For more information contact via email: Denisedeleray@mac. com.
articles.title: Women in Focus

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is hosting Art Bash, the museum’s signature annual fundraiser, on Wednesday, April 29. Art Bash raises more than $2.5 annually to benefit the museum’s education and family programs, as well as community engagement events that benefit over 150,000 people every year. The event transforms the museum’s entire campus into a multi-layered experience of art, performances and social activities. This year’s celebration also marks the 10th anniversary of SFMOMA’s building expansion. Art Bash 2026 begins with a ticketed dinner featuring a live auction of works by contemporary artists led by Phyllis Kao of Sotheby’s and a multisensory installation created by Jeffrey Gibson. After the dinner phase, the event broadens to a museum-wide party with immersive art installations by Bay Area artists Rose D’Amato and Rupy C. Tut. alongside “Zenni: The Art of Seeing,” an immersive photo experience for attendees. This year’s musical lineup, presented in partnership with Stern Grove Festival, features Shannon & The Clams, Ruby Ibarra and Wonway Posibul during the main party, while premium lounge performances will include Cruise Control and DJ heyLove. Tickets may be purchased at sfmoma.org/artbash. SFMOMA’s Art Bash returns this spring.
articles.title: SFMOMA annual Art Bash returns April 29

articles.text: The international photography exhibition Ocean Photographer of the Year will make its U.S. debut April 24 inside a historic World War II aircraft hangar at Alameda Point. The exhibition, presented by Oceanographic Magazine and Blancpain, will run for one month and feature a selection of winning and finalist images from the global Ocean Photographer of the Year competition. The show is hosted locally by West End Arts District in partnership with Bay Photo Lab. Now in its fifth year, the competition received more than 15,000 submissions from photographers worldwide. The exhibition includes images from categories such as wildlife, fine art, adventure, conservation, human connection, and young photographer of the year, along with the Female Fifty Fathoms Award recognizing women in ocean photography. “We’re thrilled to bring Ocean Photographer of the Year to Alameda Point and to invite the community to experience this powerful ode to the ocean in such a unique setting,” said Tara Pilbrow, Executive Director of West End Arts District. “By breathing new life into Alameda Point’s military history, we’re also expressing our commitment to the kind of future we want to see – one rooted in creativity, environmental awareness, and shared cultural experiences.” Alongside the international exhibition, visitors can explore “Bay Perspectives,” a gallery featuring ocean photography focused on the San Francisco Bay and the California coast. The space will also include interactive marine science exhibits presented by the Sailing Science Center. “The stories behind these photographs are as compelling as the visuals themselves – they challenge us to see the ocean not just as a place of wonder, but as a world in need of our care,” said Daryl Karp, director and chief executive officer of the Australian National Maritime Museum. Public hours are Saturdays and Sundays from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with additional programs scheduled on Thursdays and Fridays. An opening gala hosted by Bay Photo Lab will mark the company’s 50th anniversary. “Our mission is to share the ocean with non-ocean goers and photography is the most awesome conduit to do that,” said Will Harrison of Oceanographic Magazine. “Underwater photography is one of the most powerful allies in our fight to preserve and protect the ocean,” added Gaël Nicolle of Blancpain. For more information and to purchase tickets to the exhibition and events, visit www.westendartsdistrict.org.
articles.title: Ocean Photographer of the Year exhibit at Alameda Point April 24

articles.text: Production runs through April 16 at War Memorial Opera House The San Francisco Ballet performs August Bournonville’s La Sylphide at the War Memorial Opera House this Friday, April 10 to Thursday, April 16. La Sylphide follows James, a young Scotsman who becomes enchanted by a mysterious sylph on the day he is set to marry Effie. Drawn away from his wedding, James follows the sylph into the forest, leaving behind his fiancée and his former life. There, the witch Madge gives him a magical scarf, promising it will allow him to hold the sylph forever. Instead, when James places the scarf around her shoulders, the spell destroys her wings and causes her death. As James mourns, Effie marries Gurn, a rival who remained at her side. First staged in 1836, the ballet remains one of the defining works of the Romantic era, known for its light footwork and technique. Guests may enjoy live bagpipe music on the front steps of the Opera House from master bagpiper Fred Payne before each performance of La Sylphide. For showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet. org/productions/la-sylphide/. San Francisco Ballet’s past production of La Sylphide

articles.text: Shotgun Players’ 34th season opened with The Goat or, Who is Sylvia? by Edward Albee, playing at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley now through April 19. The Tony Award-winning play centers on Martin Gray, a successful architect whose personal life unravels after he tells his wife and son that he is in love with a goat named Sylvia. The disclosure leads to conflict within his family and raises questions about morality, loyalty and acceptance. The production is directed by Shotgun Players company member Kevin Clarke. In a statement, Clarke said the play “tests the limits of permissiveness” and asks audiences to consider the characters’ perspectives. William Giammona plays Martin Gray; Erin Mei Ling Stuart portrays his wife, Stevie Gray; Kevin Singer appears as Ross, a longtime family friend; and Joel Ochoa plays the couple’s son, Billy. The play premiered on Broadway in 2002 and won the Tony Award for best play. It was also named a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for drama in 2003. Perfor mances r un now through April 19. Showtimes are 7 p.m. Wednesdays and Thursdays, 8 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays and 2 p.m. on Sundays. A haptic tour and live audio-described performance will be offered April 12, with the tour at 1 p.m. and the performance at 2 p.m. Post-show discussions will follow Thursday and Sunday performances. The Ashby Stage is located at 1901 Ashby Ave. Tickets are available at shotgunplayers.org or by calling 510-841-6500 ext. 303. Cast members in Shotgun Players’ The Goat or, Who is Sylvia? articles.text: The Chicago-based ballet company returns to UC Berkeley this month. Cal Performances welcomes The Joffrey Ballet back to Zellerbach Hall for three performances of Midsummer Night’s Dream, marking the West Coast premiere of the work by Swedish choreographer Alexander Ekman. The Joffrey Ballet is based in Chicago and is known for blending classical ballet with contemporary work. The company has been the resident dance company at Lyric Opera House since the 2021–22 season and continues an eight-year residency partnership with Cal Performances that began in 2024. Ekman’s Midsummer Night’s Dream takes inspiration from Scandinavian midsummer traditions rather than William Shakespeare’s play of the same name. pages.text: Wednesday, April 8, 2026 17 SF Ballet’s La Sylphide opens this Friday Production runs through April 16 at War Memorial Opera House By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco Ballet performs August Bournonville’s La Sylphide at the War Memorial Opera House this Friday, April 10 to Thursday, April 16. La Sylphide follows James, a young Scotsman who becomes enchanted by a mysterious sylph on the day he is set to marry Effie. Drawn away from his wedding, James follows the sylph into the forest, leaving behind his fiancée and his former life. There, the witch Madge gives him a magical scarf, promising it will allow him to hold the sylph forever. Instead, when James places the scarf around her shoulders, the spell destroys her wings and causes her death. As James mourns, Effie marries Gurn, a rival who remained at her side. First staged in 1836, the ballet remains one of the defining works of the Romantic era, known for its light footwork and technique. Guests may enjoy live bagpipe music on the front steps of the Opera House from master bagpiper Fred Payne before each performance of La Sylphide. For showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet. org/productions/la-sylphide/. articles.text: The Quiet Girl has been referred to as a whisper of a film, and it is that and so much more. Based on the 2010 novella Foster by noted Irish author Claire Keegan, and the 2023 winner of the Oscar in the Best International Feature Film category. It is an unassuming, beautifully written coming-of-age drama about a nine-year-old girl named Cait (Catherine Clinch) whose silence has become her refuge. The film opens with Cait lying in a lush tall-grass farm field, hidden, looking up at a blue sky. A voice in the distance is calling her name. We soon discover that she lives with an impoverished farm family. To her shame, on occasion, Cait wets her bed, and is harshly ignored by both her parents (Kate Nic Chonaonaigh and Michael Patric) and many siblings. School is a struggle, some classmates cruel, and something to be endured, a place where she is often ignored or ridiculed. Cait’s father, Da, is shiftless, preferring to spend time in a local pub drinking his pint than preparing for the seasonal harvest. Finding it difficult to feed all the children (Cait’s mother, Mam, is once again pregnant), the parents decide to send Cait to spend the summer with a distant cousin, Eibhlin (Carey Crowley), and her husband Sean (Andrew Bennett), who are rural dairy farmers. Da drives her to the distant farm, saying little, and is so disengaged that when he leaves Cait with the the trunk of the car. And it’s with this couple (it takes Sean a bit longer than Eibhlin to warm up to the girl) she experiences a kindness and generosity of attention and concern that she has never known before. Cait comes to realize, slowly, tentatively, that there is a world, and a way of being in that world, which is far different from the one she has known growing up. Expecting indifference or cruelty she discovers the opposite, an unexpected loving embrace, and so her silence, her reflexive response to life, is slowly lifted Catherine Clinch and Carrie Crowley in The Quiet Girl couple, absent even a goodbye, he drives off with her suitcase still in and Cait, in effect, comes out of hiding and begins to blossom. The Quiet Girl is a beautiful film, gentle and moving, subtle yet deeply emotive. It is a narrative about the power of kindness that is all too often underrated if not absent; yet, when encountered, it can heal, even delight, and be transformative. As it does with Cait. The Quiet Girl. Written and directed by Colm Bairead. Starring Catherine Clinch, Carrie Crowley, Andrew Bennett. 1 hr., 34 min. PG-13. Released in 2022. Now streaming on Disney+/ Prime/HULU/Fandango/Apple tv.

articles.text: The Incredibles is an award winning, critically acclaimed animated action feature from Pixar – Walt Disney Studios to include a 77th Academy Awards Oscar (2005) and a Hugo Award, which was the first in the category of animated feature. It stars a family of under-theradar superheroes. The patriarch of the family is Mr. Incredible (Craig T. Nelson), a popular superhero, beloved for his dramatic rescues, foiled bank robberies, and super-powered interventions. But despite his passion for what he does, the public grows weary of the collateral damage that occurs with each rescue. As a result he and his new wife, Elastic Girl (Holly Hunter), are forced into what is called the Superhero Relocation Program, and required by the government to live normal lives, using the names Bob and Helen Parr. Now flash forward 15 years. Bob is an insurance salesman, and he and Helen have three children – Dash (Spencer Fox), Violet (Sarah Vowell), and baby Jack Jack. As it turns out, Bob is growing increasingly dissatisfied with his mundane life. He yearns for the good old days when he was Mr. Incredible, and reminisces each day on the way to work (stuck in traffic) with Lucius Best, Mr. Frozone (Samuel L. Jackson), while they listen to a police scanner, tempting both of them to help out. They know that they’ve got the right stuff. One day, a mysterious woman named Mirage (Elizabeth Pena) appears and makes them a job offer, and Bob seizes the opportunity to return to his role of Mr. Incredible. He is convinced that like those days of yesteryear, he can make a difference. He soon runs into an archenemy called Syndrome (Jason Lee), and it doesn’t take long before Mr. Incredible’s whole family is involved in running battles and action-oriented chases with this nemesis. The Incredibles is one of Pixar’s best, a wonderful example of high tech animation, lushly created backgrounds, slap-dash humor and jokes, with superhero costumes and signature masks. The kids will love it, as will the adults. The Incredibles. Directed and co-written by Brad Bird. Voiced by Craig T. Nelson, Holly Hunter, Samuel L. Jackson. From Pixar and Walt Disney Studios. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated PG. Released in 2004 in theaters. Streaming on Prime/ Disney+/apple tv/Fandango. A scene from The Incredibles

articles.text: The Madison is a solid Paramount+ neo-western series set in Southwestern Montana along the Madison River. The first episode opens with two brothers, Preston Clyburn (Kurt Russell) and Paul Clyburn (Matthew Fox), fly-fishing on a wide, slow-moving river. Friendly banter passes between them as they trade suggestions about which fly is most likely to snag a good-size trout. Paul has long ago left his successful career for a life doing exactly what the two men are doing in that moment. In contrast, Preston and family – wife Stacy (Michelle Pfeiffer) and daughters plus children) live in New York City, all accustomed to an urban life style only affluence can offer. The Madison was was written by the talented and prolific Taylor Sheridan, whose western sagas debuted with the popular series Yellowstone and continued with the prequels 1883, and 1923. All three are exceptionally well-done productions and perfectly cast. Unexpectedly, the Clyburn family is swept up in a tragedy that rocks their world and asks them to examine what it means to confront an unexpected loss Michelle Pfeiffer and Kurt Russell in The Madison for which they feel completely unprepared. The Madison is just so good, and for those who enjoy this episodic tale, Paramount+ has announced that there will be a second season. A final note: I sat with my wife and watched The Madison for a second time. It was then, as the credits rolled, we noticed the following: “In Loving Memory of Robert Redford.” It was in the second episode that the family gathered together in an Idaho hotel suite and decided to watch A River Runs Through It. The meaning of this heartfelt tribute to Redford, an extraordinary filmmaker and storyteller, is soon revealed. The Madison. Directed by Christina Alexander Woods. Starring Kurt Russell, Michelle Pfeiffer, Beau Garret, Elle Chapman. Written by Taylor Sheridan. Season 1 of 6 episodes. Released in 2026. Streaming on Paramount+/Prime/Roku.

articles.text: Hearing the news that Robert Redford, at the age of 89, had died caused me to pause and I felt a sense of disbelief. I suddenly realized that though I had seen recent photos of the actor, and watched The Old Man and the Gun (2018), purported to be his last film, I knew that decades had passed, evident in the deep lines in his face, in the almost casual and polite demeanor implicit in the narrative, the gun a mere prop. Was the film a metaphor, this smiling portrayal of an elderly bank robber who loves what he does – though on occasion he is caught and spends time in jail, he returns, not for the money but for the doing. Or is The Old Man and the Gun his very fond, even gentle way of saying farewell? I have since been struck by his timeless presence on the screen, something I had taken for granted, realizing now that he seemed to defy the gravity of aging. He would always be the all-American Hubbell Gardiner in the film The Way We Were (1973), or Sundance in the hugely popular Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969). His filmography is stunning, the variety and number of leading roles extensive. In recognition of his contribution to the film arts, the Academy presented him with an honorary award for his work as actor, director, narrator (voice over) and producer as well as the creation of the Sundance Festival in 1981, which annually has nurtured, screened and honrod the work of independent filmmakers. There isn’t space to list the many films in which he portrayed a leading character. His legacy, to include his efforts as an environmentalist, will ever be with us, and in the aggregate will remain an enduring tribute to his love of this larger than life art form and the power of film to tell a story. articles.text: A River Runs Through It, released in 1992, is a gently told period drama, beautifully photographed by Oscar-winning Philipe. Rousselot. It is set in Missoula, Montana, during a time that stretches from the end of WWI to the beginning of the Great Depression. The narrative, with voiceover by director Robert Redford, is based on the 1976 autobiography by Norman Maclean. The film follows the Maclean brothers, Norman (Craig Scheffer) and Paul (Brad Pitt), who as youngsters thrived in the bucolic surrounds of rural Missoula. They were taught the discipline, if not the art, of fly fishing on the nearby Blackfoot River by their Presbyterian minister father (Tom Skerritt) who gently merged religion with the early mornings the three spent standing in the rippling river, casting their lines out onto the eddying, rippling surface. Their time together, often spent sitting among the Ponderosa pines on the river banks, or finding a metronomic rhythm as they fished, moments when the morning light shimmered off the wet rocks, all of it a metaphor for their union, captured in the lyrical words of Maclean and spoken by Robert Redford. “In the slanting sun of the late afternoon the shadows of great branches reached from across the river, and the trees took the river in their arms. The shadows continued up the bank until they included us.” Regrettably, Norman Maclean passed away before the film was completed; however, his words frame a final, touching moment as Maclean, now nearing the end of his life, stands at the edge of the river, and with trembling hands slowly ties a fly to his line, and seemingly lost in the moment gazes off into the distance. “Eventually, all things merge into one, and the river runs through it. The river was cut by the world’s great flood and runs over rocks from the basement of time. On some of the rocks are timeless raindrops. Under the rocks are the words, and some of the words are theirs. I am haunted by waters.” A River Runs Through It. Directed by Robert Redford. Starring Brad Pitt, Craig Shaffer, Tom Skerritt. Voiceover by Robert Redford. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated PG. Released in 2011. Now streaming on Prime/Apple/Fandango/MGM+/Roku. Tom Skerritt, Craig Sheffer and Brad Pitt in A River Runs Through It

articles.text: April 11-12, 11:00 a.m. – 2 p.m. Karen LeGault Fine Art Show “Art of the Garden: Portals to the Unseen,” local artist Karen LeGault’s showing of watercolor paintings on mulberry and other papers is not to be missed! Her collection provides a poetic, understated elegance that is both dramatic and powerful with its striking choice of colors while exhibiting a calming, healing sense of tranquil peace that is breathtaking to behold. Karen’s work is a fascinating exploration of movement, energy and the cycles-of-life, depicted in rich, nuanced nature-filled compositions that include flowers, table poems, ponds and landscapes. Gallery hours are 11 am to 2 pm Saturday, followed by a closing reception on Sunday from a 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Saturday, April 11, 7:00 p.m. Benicia Chamber Players Concert Benicia Chamber Players present three sweeping and rarely heard Romantic piano trios: English composer Alice Verne-Bredt’s Phantasie Trio, French virtuoso Cécile Chaminade’s first piano trio, where fiery strings meet a glittering, driving piano part, showcasing the virtuosity of each performer and Fanny Mendelssohn’s Piano Trio in D minor. Performed by musicians Nigel Armstrong, Brady Anderson, and Jon Lee, this program presents the piano trio at full Romantic scale. Advance tickets available at https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/1984634337729. Sunday, April 12, 4:00 p.m. Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Concert The Music of Muses is a poignant program that explores the many forms of inspiration that move artists to create. Spanning solo works to chamber ensembles, the concert features the music of Reena Esmail, Beethoven, Jennifer Higdon, Bedřich Smetana, Anton Webern, and Juan Pablo Contreras. Together, these works offer a deeply human meditation on creativity, memory, and the transformative power of artistic devotion. Please buy advance tickets early, as these chamber concerts typically sell out! Go to https:// purchase.berkeleysymphony.org/ChooseSeats/1601. Thursday–Saturday, April 16–18, 7:00 p.m. PHS Advanced Acting Student Play PHS senior Ben Wakefield’s stage play, Mouthwashing, is his adaptation of the story written by Johanna Kasurinen for Wrong Organ’s video game of the same name. The story follows the crew of a cargo spaceship after a mysterious crash leaves them stranded in space. Directed by Wakefield, the show features Colin Cameron, Sadie Shoop, Matias Seelenberger, Noah Sarlin, and Declan Murphy. Advance tickets are available at https://mouthwashingplay.ludus.com/. Saturday, April 18, 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Opening Reception Slavic Arts Exhibition The Center for Slavic Arts & Culture presents a new art exhibit, comprising works by multiple artists from the 13 Slavic countries. The public is welcome at an opening reception on Sunday, April 18. The art will be shown every Saturday and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. through May 31 with an artist on-site. Free admission. Sunday, April 19, 6:00 p.m. Cal v. Stanford Head-to Head a cappella The Stanford Mendicants and Counterpoint, two separate groups of a cappella singers, will perform assorted songs alongside members of the Cal Jazz Choir and the UC Berkeley Golden Overtones. Alums from both schools are welcome. Advance tickets are available at https://events. com/r/tickets/1036479. Seating is limited to 80 so that the singers may sit down while not singing. articles.text: April is a month of anniversaries. The Spanish explorer Ponce de Leon landed in Florida in April 1513 saying he was searching for the fountain of youth. In reality, he was probably looking for riches and land for the Spanish government. But that is not the intent of our story. There are many ways to educate our senses. Always keep in mind that it is advantageous to live the good life. While searching for the fountain of youth we can find success in many ways. Perhaps you might enjoy the mythical liquid elixir. To this, we should add the enjoyment of good food and good music. On Park Boulevard just a short distance from Piedmont is the BlackBerry Bistro. I ate there many years ago and decided to try it again. The format and atmosphere now are completely different. Our friendly waitress told us that the Blackberry Bistro is now owned by Eritreans. The decor is elegant and beautiful and is matched by elegant and beautiful cuisine which is gracefully served. The menu is extensive and features the usual items and also some Eritrean cuisine. We chose smoked salmon Benedict accompanied by creamy grits. The food was excellent and my wife and I had lots of fun. Prices are reasonable. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, April 8, 2026 The Musical Gourmet Some words of advice By Joseph Gold April is a month of anniversaries. The Spanish explorer Ponce de Leon landed in Florida in April 1513 saying he was searching for the fountain of youth. In reality, he was probably looking for riches and land for the Spanish government. But that is not the intent of our story. There are many ways to educate our senses. Always keep in mind that it is advantageous to live the good life. While searching for the fountain of youth we can find success in many ways. Perhaps you might enjoy the mythical liquid elixir. To this, we should add the enjoyment of good food and good music. On Park Boulevard just a short distance from Piedmont is the BlackBerry Bistro. I ate there many years ago and decided to try it again. The format and atmosphere now are completely different. Our friendly waitress told us that the Blackberry Bistro is now owned by Eritreans. The decor is elegant and beautiful and is matched by elegant and beautiful cuisine which is gracefully served. The menu is extensive and features the usual items and also some Eritrean cuisine. We chose smoked salmon Benedict accompanied by creamy grits. The food was excellent and my wife and I had lots of fun. Prices are reasonable. Last week’s music Easter Sunday is not necessarily the best day to present a concert. Nevertheless, the Cathedral of Saint Mary in San Francisco features concerts on almost every Sunday. I received a personal invitation from the outstanding pianist and teacher Jeanette Tietze to attend a piano concert on Easter Sunday. It was scheduled to begin at 4 p.m. At precisely 4 p.m., the young and slightly built Xie Sackett seated himself at the piano. It was instantly apparent that he is a “no muss no fuss” pianist of immense talent. The program was a classic The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet because music from almost every era was on the program. A prelude and fugue by Bach started the program. Sackett has a beautiful tone, which is crystal clear, round and mellow. His interpretation seemed to be improvised. Listeners could imagine themselves listening to Bach himself seated at the organ engrossed in his thoughts and improvising as only he could. Other pieces on the program were a Sonata by Mozart, an impromptu by Schubert and representative pieces by the ragtime composer William Balcom, the Hungarian post-Romantic Erno Dohnanyi and two pieces by Chopin. As the concert progressed, I began to think that the only ingredient missing was a lack of dynamic contrast. The problem was actually with the piano, which was a bit recalcitrant in the tonal department. In reality, Xei has all of the spice needed. Despite his youth, he has a mature approach to music. Make sure to keep an eye on him. Time for dinner After the concert I was in the mood for some southern Italian food. The area near Davies Symphony Hall is loaded with restaurants and southern Italian cuisine was offered in the restaurant Doppio Zero. Its owners are from Naples and Puglia and the cuisine is representative of southern Italy. Doppio Zero is a very lively restaurant replicating the cuisine of Naples. While it is famous for pizza, I was in the mood for lasagna which was like a homemade lasagna. The atmosphere made us feel like we were eating in a fine home. Enthusiasm was everywhere. A very colorful beet salad was the perfect side dish to the lasagna. Those things should have been enough. But when you have a special dinner, you need a special dessert. A lemon sorbetto concluded the week on a very high note. Mythical elixirs are usually evasive. Always keep in mind that the good life is within reach. Education (and enthusiasm) can stave off dotage. Southern Italian food at its finest. Doppio Zero restaurant in San Francisco. Welcome to the Piedmont Center for the Arts April 11-12, 11:00 a.m. – 2 p.m. Karen LeGault Fine Art Show “Art of the Garden: Portals to the Unseen,” local artist Karen LeGault’s showing of watercolor paintings on mulberry and other papers is not to be missed! Her collection provides a poetic, understated elegance that is both dramatic and powerful with its striking choice of colors while exhibiting a calming, healing sense of tranquil peace that is breathtaking to behold. Karen’s work is a fascinating exploration of movement, energy and the cycles-of-life, depicted in rich, nuanced nature-filled compositions that include flowers, table poems, ponds and landscapes. Gallery hours are 11 am to 2 pm Saturday, followed by a closing reception on Sunday from a 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Saturday, April 11, 7:00 p.m. Benicia Chamber Players Concert Benicia Chamber Players present three sweeping and rarely heard Romantic piano trios: English composer Alice Verne-Bredt’s Phantasie Trio, French virtuoso Cécile Chaminade’s first piano trio, where fiery strings meet a glittering, driving piano part, showcasing the virtuosity of each performer and Fanny Mendelssohn’s Piano Trio in D minor. Performed by musicians Nigel Armstrong, Brady Anderson, and Jon Lee, this program presents the piano trio at full Romantic scale. Advance tickets available at https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/1984634337729. Sunday, April 12, 4:00 p.m. Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Concert The Music of Muses is a poignant program that explores the many forms of inspiration that move artists to create. Spanning solo works to chamber ensembles, the concert features the music of Reena Esmail, Beethoven, Jennifer Higdon, Bedřich Smetana, Anton Webern, and Juan Pablo Contreras. Together, these works offer a deeply human meditation on creativity, memory, and the transformative power of artistic devotion. Please buy advance tickets early, as these chamber concerts typically sell out! Go to https:// purchase.berkeleysymphony.org/ChooseSeats/1601. Thursday–Saturday, April 16–18, 7:00 p.m. PHS Advanced Acting Student Play PHS senior Ben Wakefield’s stage play, Mouthwashing, is his adaptation of the story written by Johanna Kasurinen for Wrong Organ’s video game of the same name. The story follows the crew of a cargo spaceship after a mysterious crash leaves them stranded in space. Directed by Wakefield, the show features Colin Cameron, Sadie Shoop, Matias Seelenberger, Noah Sarlin, and Declan Murphy. Advance tickets are available at https://mouthwashingplay.ludus.com/. Saturday, April 18, 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Opening Reception Slavic Arts Exhibition The Center for Slavic Arts & Culture presents a new art exhibit, comprising works by multiple artists from the 13 Slavic countries. The public is welcome at an opening reception on Sunday, April 18. The art will be shown every Saturday and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. through May 31 with an artist on-site. Free admission. Sunday, April 19, 6:00 p.m. Cal v. Stanford Head-to Head a cappella The Stanford Mendicants and Counterpoint, two separate groups of a cappella singers, will perform assorted songs alongside members of the Cal Jazz Choir and the UC Berkeley Golden Overtones. Alums from both schools are welcome. Advance tickets are available at https://events. com/r/tickets/1036479. Seating is limited to 80 so that the singers may sit down while not singing. articles.text: Last Wednesday was April Fool’s Day, and the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group may have thought the weather gods and activity leader Dick Carter were trying to fool them when they assembled at the Exedra. The walkers say it never rains on Wednesday mornings in Piedmont, but the forecast called for showers around 11 a.m. It was also the first Wednesday in April — the American Heart Association’s National Walking Day — and Dick had planned a long walk to visit homes from the mostly forgotten 1907 “Grand Avenue Heights” development on the city’s southwest side. Getting there meant going through Piedmont Park, and those trails get slippery when wet. Better to be safe. There was plenty of other fun sightseeing to do, so the plan changed. Last spring, Piedmont came down with eagle mania. A pair of bald eagles nested in a eucalyptus tree at the edge of Mountain View Cemetery, and their eaglets hatched in May — the first bald eagle chicks in the Oakland/ Piedmont area in recent history. Wednesday walkers made the pilgrimage, along with just about everyone else. The eagles returned last month, which made the corner of Moraga and Monte Avenues — where the nest is visible — the group’s new destination. There was plenty to see along the way. The first surprise came crossing Highland Avenue, where the construction fence around the Valero gas station was finally gone. Months of work, apparently complete. Just across Highland Way stood Piedmont Community Church. Last August the walkers had discovered a memorial meditation garden at the back of the church and wanted to see it again. The garden includes a labyrinth and fountain dedicated to church member Judy Wright’s late husband Bob, who died in 2024. It was created as a Girl Scout Gold Award Project by church member Sonja ten Grotenhuis, then a Piedmont High senior and now at Boston University, with help from Suzie Skugstad, Church Council President Paul Schroeder, and other volunteers. Walker Mike Gallant noted a new magnolia alba — white champaca — at the garden’s entrance, a tree whose fragrant flowers can be used to make perfume. From Highland the group went up Oakland Avenue to the one-block Hardwick Avenue and down to the Landon Court culde-sac, with its view of San Francisco. Two absent group members happen to live there. In the spirit of the day, a walker rang the doorbell. No answer — the missing walkers were presumably off having their own fun. The front of the house served nicely as the backdrop for the group photo. Down Blair and Highland Avenues, up Park Way and Monte to the corner of Moraga. No birdwatchers were around, but a friendly neighbor came out with an update. The eagles weren’t visible just then, but they were back — taking turns sitting on their eggs, which need to be regularly rotated. He thought the eaglets would hatch a couple of weeks earlier this year. When asked if he’d like to be named in the Wednesday Walkers’ column, he declined. The birders who monitor the eagles, he explained, are pretty strident about all things eagle, and it’s better for novices like himself to stay anonymous. A few facts from last year’s visit bear repeating. Bald eagles typically live 20 to 30 years in the wild. Young birds are dark all over and don’t develop that distinctive white head and tail until around age four or five. Nests are built with large sticks — usually 4 to 6 feet across and 3 feet A good turnout of 31 water-resistant walkers and two K-9 best friends at the Exedra were ready for any April 1st challenge and the fun. On hand were Denny McGee, Claudine Bach, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Jim Kuo, Dan Scdonis, Peggy Shultz, Lori Austin, Cathy Laymon, Sherry Jacobs, Mary Carter, Rick Eigenbrode, Alissa Quan, Bill Ahern, Sanghi Wagner, Liz Dalrymple, Ken Moy, Mike Gallant, Gloria DaSilva, Marcia Arthurs, Chuck Oraftik, Dave DeRoche, Jasmine Cai, Phil Witte, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Lois Price, Melba Yee, Charlene Louie, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Caskey Weston brought her visiting-from-Los Angeles daughter Ariel Hirsch to walk with them.
