Walker Mike Gallant noted a new magnolia alba — white champaca — at the garden’s entrance, a tree whose fragrant flowers can be used to make perfume. From Highland the group went up Oakland Avenue to the one-block Hardwick Avenue and down to the Landon Court culde-sac, with its view of San Francisco. Two absent group members happen to live there. In the spirit of the day, a walker rang the doorbell. No answer — the missing walkers were presumably off having their own fun. The front of the house served nicely as the backdrop for the group photo. Down Blair and Highland Avenues, up Park Way and Monte to the corner of Moraga. No birdwatchers were around, but a friendly neighbor came out with an update. The eagles weren’t visible just then, but they were back — taking turns sitting on their eggs, which need to be regularly rotated. He thought the eaglets would hatch a couple of weeks earlier this year. When asked if he’d like to be named in the Wednesday Walkers’ column, he declined. The birders who monitor the eagles, he explained, are pretty strident about all things eagle, and it’s better for novices like himself to stay anonymous. A few facts from last year’s visit bear repeating. Bald eagles typically live 20 to 30 years in the wild. Young birds are dark all over and don’t develop that distinctive white head and tail until around age four or five. Nests are built with large sticks — usually 4 to 6 feet across and 3 feet Route of the walk deep — lined with moss, grass, lichens, and whatever else is at hand. Eagles mate for life, and both the male and female share incubation duties. Their eyesight is extraordinary: they can spot a rabbit running from three miles away. Hearing and smell, not so much — which works out fine, since they’re also scavengers. The walkers promised to return when the eaglets hatch and moved on. Down Moraga, across Highland to Estrella Avenue, where beautiful rhododendron blooms competed for attention with a pair of matching 1923 homes, each topped with a coneshaped terracotta roof above the front entrance. The group continued to Monticello Avenue, where veteran walker Charlene Louise pointed out what looks like a private path alongside one of the homes but is actually a hidden public shortcut — the kind used in the first half of the 20th century by Key System train riders and Piedmont students. The walkers took it up to the Lorita Avenue cul-de-sac. The brief rain finally arrived as they headed down Lorita. At Monticello’s end, just before the road climbs to become Park Way, another hidden path took the group down to Artuna Avenue and into Dracena Park. The eucalyptus trees, freshly rained on, filled the air with that sharp familiar smell. Walker Jack Fischrup’s dog Kojak, off leash and delighted, probably had the best time of anyone. The April 1st walk ended up Blair, Bonita, and Visita Avenues back to the Exedra. Hidden gems, familiar favorites, and a few surprises — with eaglets on the way. No fooling. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or call (510) 420-3070 for more information. A good turnout of 31 water-resistant walkers and two K-9 best friends at the Exedra were ready for any April 1st challenge and the fun. The group was pleased that Caskey Weston brought her visiting-from-Los Angeles daughter Ariel Hirsch to walk with them.

articles.text: Troop 11 Scouts and their parents at Sugar Bowl On Friday, January 30, Piedmont Scouts in Troop 11 and Troop 4 headed out from Piedmont, bound for Sugar Bowl. Scouts sang songs, played games and chatted away the time as they made their way on the highways and winding roads of Tahoe. Piling into Heidelmann Lodge, they carried their bags to the giant dormitories stocked with mattresses and fluffy pillows for all attendees from Troop 11 and Troop 4. That night the Patrols took advantage of the large well equipped kitchen. The CurlyLoos patrol had more than one pan of food cooking at once, which was a step up from the one-pan, onepot, two-burner stove setup they knew from camping in the snow and rocks of California’s beautiful national parks. The Scouts enjoyed the fruits of their labor in the warm rustic lodge, safe from the winter cold outside. They joked and laughed together, told stories and smiled. When all the dishes were done, Troop 11 was set loose. They ran through the halls, rambunctiously exploring their new home. In particular, they settled in the game room, where they played blackjack, poker, apples to apples, and hide and seek with new friends from Troop 4. Some hallways were full of excited and sweet chattering that seemed to echo off the ceilings, and others were full of the melodious music coming from very talented Scouts relishing in their luck at the inclusion of a piano among the many joys of Heidelmann Lodge. At 7 a.m. sharp the scouts woke up, ready for a new day of adventure. They pulled on thick layers and began to cook their breakfasts, which for one patrol, was cinnamon rolls, fruit and sausages. Once everything was ready to go, the Scouts enjoyed the magnificent view from the room that had hosted the majority of their merriment the night before. The windows of the game room offered a majestic scene of the mountains of Tahoe gilded in white. That morning, Troop 11 drove to Sugar Bowl thanks to parent drivers. As all good Scouts do, Troop 11 used the buddy system, so everyone skied in pairs or groups of pairs. They smoothly rocketed down the slopes, leaning this way and that, planting their poles appropriately and taking in the magical mountains and the crisp, clean air. Everyone was able to find their groove though the conditions were not perfect and many fell into the fluffy cold banks. Some Scouts tried new techniques and others tried new levels. One pair of Scouts skied down a terrain and caught two feet of air before landing on their butts. Another pair continued to explore the resort until the last lift at 4:30 p.m. They watched the sun set in the mountains as they returned to the lodge, where they relaxed and recharged from their epic day under the frosted forest and blue skies of Tahoe. They cooked more warm meals (like fried rice and spring rolls) that made their bellies and hearts sing with the joy of a dinner well enjoyed. Of course, more games and songs were played that night. They will live in these Scouts memories forever. The next morning was another early one. The Scouts packed and rushed through the motions of getting ready, bumping into each other and generally experiencing a hectic exit. But everyone made it home safely, and some took a detour to a ski resort, where they enjoyed another day on the white slopes that sparkled like jewels in the sun. Isabelle Meyers is a member of Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop 11. Scouts and parents regroup on the slopes.

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group will return to Mountain View Cemetery on April 15 for its 8th annual Spring Tour conducted by author and Mountain View docent Dennis Evanosky. This tour will be his fourth with Walking on Wednesdays. He took the group for well attended walks in April 2023, 2024, and 2025. Evanosky has written two books about Oakland’s history, Oakland’s Mountain View Cemetery and Oakland’s Laurel District. Since their first walk on April 18, 2018, the group has gone on over 360 walks. A visit to the cemetery with its beautiful spring flowers and expansive views of the Bay has become an annual memorable event. Walkers will meet in front of Mountain View’s main mausoleum. The tour will start at 10:30 a.m. and last for about 1 hour and 30 minutes. The cemetery is located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue at the end of Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. There is no charge for the event, and free parking is available inside the cemetery. For more information, contact activity leader Dick Carter at camktgrp@comcast.net.

The windows of the game room offered a majestic scene of the mountains of Tahoe gilded in white. That morning, Troop 11 drove to Sugar Bowl thanks to parent drivers. As all good Scouts do, Troop 11 used the buddy system, so everyone skied in pairs or groups of pairs. They smoothly rocketed down the slopes, leaning this way and that, planting their poles appropriately and taking in the magical mountains and the crisp, clean air. Everyone was able to find their groove though the conditions were not perfect and many fell into the fluffy cold banks. Some Scouts tried new techniques and others tried new levels. One pair of Scouts skied down a terrain and caught two feet of air before landing on their butts. Another pair continued to explore the resort until the last lift at 4:30 p.m. They watched the sun set in the mountains as they returned to the lodge, where they relaxed and recharged from their epic day under the frosted forest and blue skies of Tahoe. They cooked more warm meals (like fried rice and spring rolls) that made their bellies and hearts sing with the joy of a dinner well enjoyed. Of course, more games and songs were played that night. They will live in these Scouts memories forever. The next morning was another early one. The Scouts packed and rushed through the motions of getting ready, bumping into each other and generally experiencing a hectic exit. But everyone made it home safely, and some took a detour to a ski resort, where they enjoyed another day on the white slopes that sparkled like jewels in the sun. Isabelle Meyers is a member of Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop 11. Scouts and parents regroup on the slopes.

pages.text: 24 24 Wednesday, April 8, 2026 your Oakland Zoo saves Mt. Lion with blood transfusion By Isabella Linares On Friday, March 6, Oakland Zoo helped rescue a female mountain lion cub from El Dorado County. California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) veterinarians performed an initial comprehensive exam, noting she was severely emaciated, weighing less than half of her ideal weight, and was weak and infested with ticks. The assessment also showed gastrointestinal issues, but there were no signs of trauma. After treating her for dehydration and tick infestation, the cub was taken to Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital for further care. There, she was confirmed to be in a critically fragile state, highlighting the importance of quick rescue and intervention “Oakland Zoo has made major advances in medical care and treatment of critically ill orphaned mountain lion cubs,” said Dr. Deana Clifford, CDFW Senior Wildlife Veterinarian. “We are grateful for the continued partnership with Oakland Zoo that can give these cubs a better chance at survival.” The mountain lion cub, now named Clover, was moved to the ICU at the Oakland Zoo Veterinary Hospital and has been receiving around-the-clock intensive care from the Veterinary Hospital and Animal Care staff for the past few days. On the morning of Monday, March 9, her condition started to worsen, and Oakland Zoo Veterinary and Animal Care staff administered life-saving care, including a blood transfusion using blood from one of their resident mountain lions, Briar. Briar was rescued in August 2024 in El Dorado County and has remained a resident of the California Trail habitat at Oakland Zoo, along with fellow rescues Coloma and Silverado. “This is a journey we are always committed to undertakPhotos by Oakland Zoo Mountain lion cub Clover was brought to the Oakland Zoo Veterinary Hospital on March 6. Clover receives a blood transfusion on March 9. Clover was half her normal weight on March 6. ing. Our teams dedicate their hearts, skills, and resources to every rescue we handle. Regardless of the outcome, we remain here to assist and aim to leave a lasting positive impact on their lives,” says Dr. Lauren Pudenz, Associate Veterinarian at Oakland Zoo. Clover is the Zoo’s 32nd mountain lion cub rescue as part of the Rescue and Recovery program and a member of the Bay Area Cougar Action Team. Oakland Zoo emphasizes the importance of quickly reaching out to CDFW or permitted wildlife rehabilitators when you see injured or sick wildlife like Clover in the wild. Acting swiftly with professional help greatly increases these animals’ chances of survival. When you encounter injured or ill wildlife, it is essential to contact CDFW or a permitted rehabilitator right away, stay at a safe distance to avoid causing additional harm to yourself or the animal, and refrain from feeding or trying to rehabilitate the animal yourself. This helps prevent the spread of disease, reduces the risk of harm, and helps stop wildlife from entering human-populated areas, which can cause them to be displaced. How old is Clover? She is about three months old based on her coat coloration and tooth development. What happened to Clover’s mom? The first priority when CDFW finds a puma kitten is to assess whether the area is safe — away from roads and other dangers — and whether the kitten appears relatively healthy. If so, CDFW will leave the cub in place and monitor it with a camera to see if the mother returns. They have also attempted reunions before. They generally avoid removing a wild kitten if its mother is nearby. Unfortunately, Clover was found near a road, and given how emaciated she was, it was clear she hadn’t been cared for in some time, making her mother’s presence very unlikely. Regional staff checked reports of mountain lion appearances in the area but didn’t find any, so CDFW doesn’t know who her mother was. Residents are encouraged to report any additional sightings. How do you get a blood donor for a mountain lion? Oakland Zoo Veterinary and Animal Care staff conduct voluntary training with all animal residents to showcase different behaviors, helping staff better care for them. Briar has been participating in voluntary training to prepare for his own care, and sometimes this training can be used for life-saving procedures, like this blood transfusion for Clover. Severely emaciated animals are often anemic due to their bodies lacking enough nutrients to make red blood cells and other critical blood components. Often this is compounded by additional disease processes such as parasites or infections, which these debilitated cubs have a hard time handling. What conservation challenges do mountain lions face in the wild? Mountain lions encounter numerous conservation challenges in the wild. Their habitats are increasingly fragmented as new communities encroach, slicing through mountain lion territories and blocking essenBriar, a 2024 Mt. Lion rescue, donates blood for the mountain lion cub Clover. tial movement pathways with highways and buildings. Human expansion increases the risk of fatal car strikes; when a mother mountain lion is hit, her cubs often cannot survive without her for food and guidance. Additionally, like many other wild animals in California, mountain lions are threatened by wildfires driven by climate change. Will Clover be released to the wild? In the wild, mountain lion cubs need about two years with their mother to learn survival skills. Because Clover is so young, she lacks those skills and cannot be released back into the wild. What is the Bay Area Cougar Action Team (BACAT)? In 2012, the Oakland Zoo participated in a training session focused on resolving conflicts between humans and wildlife. This training led to the formation of BACAT. The alliance brings together various agencies, nonprofit organizations, local parks, and mountain lion researchers. With a shared message and a team-based approach, BACAT aims to create a support system that serves as a model for other regions in California and beyond. Through BACAT, Oakland Zoo has rescued and rehabilitated over 30 mountain lions, most of whom were victims of human-wildlife conflicts or wildfires. How much does it cost Oakland Zoo to care for mountain lion cubs? Cubs come to Oakland Zoo with varying medical needs and symptoms; some stay only a matter of weeks, while others may stay for many months. On average, mountain lion cubs spend 8.5 days in the Intensive Care Unit at the Wayne and Gladys Valley Veterinary Hospital, which requires constant staff care. The average cub costs roughly $18,000 per month for veterinary and animal care. These efforts are supported by community donations. How can you help support Oakland Zoo’s Mountain Lion Rescue program Oakland Zoo relies on community philanthropic support to fund our conservation and animal welfare programs, including our mountain lion rescue and recovery work. You can make a donation to Oakland Zoo online at www.oaklandzoo.org/give or reach our Development team at impact@oaklandzoo.org. Isabella Linares is with Oakland Zoo. articles.text: and Debbi DiMaggio At the heart of ‘April in Paris’ is a mission that matters: supporting extraordinary care at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland. Please join us on April 11 at the Claremont Country Club for a memorable evening of mingling, music, and dancing, all in support of children and families who rely on this exceptional hospital. Through its fundraising efforts, Hill Branch helps ensure that every child can receive the care they need, regardless of background, circumstance, or a family’s ability to pay. Buy your tickets today and help make extraordinary care possible for more children and families. HillBranch.org. The grateful parent letter that follows is a moving reminder of the very real difference this care makes. It speaks to the compassion, expertise, and hope families find at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland during their most difficult moments. On November 3, 2025, our family’s life changed forever when what should have been A routine 6-year-old checkup turned into every parent’s worst nightmare. I will forever be grateful to Dr Courtney Pickering, who completed her pediatric residency at the University of California, San Francisco, and is now my daughter’s primary pediatrician. During Hailey’s checkup, she noticed that Hailey’s coloring was just slightly off and sent us to UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland for blood work. Just as we were driving home from the hospital, we received a call from Dr. Pickering, who told us to go home, pack a bag, and return to the hospital immediately. My Hailey is receiving great care at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital. heart sank. When we arrived at the ER, the team was already expecting us. Not all of the blood work had come back yet, but even from the basic panel, it was clear that Something was very wrong. Minutes felt like days as I sat holding my baby girl in disbelief, still not knowing the underlying cause. Everything from that moment forward feels like a blur. I remember Hailey being scared, and a nurse going to the annex to find a very special elephant hospital gown just for her. The standard gowns for children her age are cheerful with teddy bear prints, but this one was one of a kind—and it instantly made Hailey feel special. Hailey has never been just a number there. Even though families travel from near and far for the care provided at UCSF Benioff, every child is treated with compassion, dignity, and love. We were admitted to a room on the fifth floor while we waited for more answers. I didn’t know it at the time, but that room would become my home for the next 14 days. The doctors explained that they were still waiting on additional tests, but it was likely leukemia. In the meantime, Hailey received three blood transfusions. Eventually, the words no parent is ever prepared to hear became our reality. Hailey was diagnosed with B-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL), the most common childhood cancer. The doctors also shared something that gave us hope: this form of leukemia is not only treatable, but often curable. In that moment, it became clear that we were exactly where we needed to be. Today, thanks to the extraordinary doctors, nurses, and researchers at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland, Hailey continues her treatment surrounded by a team that has cared for her not just as a patient, but as a child with a future worth fighting for. Events like the upcoming UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospitals Gala make that care possible. They support the research, innovation, and compassionate programs that give families like ours hope during the most difficult moments of our lives. The following is a link to Hailey’s GoFundMe: https:// tinyurl.com/HaileysGoFundMe

As the project is being bid through BPX Printing & Graphics, any changes via addenda will be available on the BPX website for this project. Bids shall be uploaded electronically to the BPX City of Piedmont planroom via the “Submit Bid Docs” tab on the Project page before 1:30 p.m., April 16, 2026. Guidelines for BPX Online Bidding Instructions are provided in Appendix A. Proposals will be timestamped by the website upon receipt and placed in a secure location by BPX to be accessed only by a representative from the City of Piedmont. The Zoom meeting information can be found in the bid documents. Please note that bidders must be logged-in as a registered user in order to see the “Submit Bid Docs” tab. The “Submit Bid Docs” tab will only be available until the bid deadline, and all submitted bids are “sealed” and inaccessible until that time. After the bid deadline, the “Submit Bid Docs” tab will be unavailable on the Planroom platform to prospective bidders. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 1770 et seq. of the California Labor Code the Director of Industrial Relations for the State of California has ascertained the current general prevailing rate of wages for employer purposes, in Alameda County, State of California. Not less than the general prevailing rate of per diem wages for work of a similar character in Alameda County and not less than the general prevailing rate of per diem wages for holiday work fixed as provided in the California Labor Code shall be paid to all workers engaged in performing the project. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 1771.1 of the California Labor Code, A contractor or subcontractor shall not be qualified to bid on, be listed in a bid proposal, subject to the requirements of Section 4104 of the Public Contract Code, or engage in the performance of any contract for public work, as defined in Chapter 1 of Part 7 of Division 2 of the California Labor Code, unless currently registered and qualified to perform public work pursuant to Civil Code Section 1725.5. Please note: It is not a violation of Section 1771.1 for an unregistered contractor to submit a bid that is authorized by Section 7029.1 of the Business and Professions Code or by Section 10164 or 20103.5 of the Public Contract Code, provided the contractor is registered to perform public work pursuant to Section 1725.5 at the time the contract is awarded. Any bids submitted without proof that Bidder and any listed subcontractor(s) are currently registered and qualified to perform public work, pursuant to Labor Code Section 1725.5, shall not be accepted by the City. In accordance with California Civil Code Section 1771.4, the project is subject to compliance monitoring and enforcement by the Department of Industrial Relations. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 3300, a valid class A California contractor’s license is required to bid on the project. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to postpone the date and time for the opening of proposals at any time prior to the date and time announced in the advertisement in accordance with applicable law. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to reject any and all bids or to waive any defects or irregularity in bidding in accordance with applicable law. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20103.8, if the City elects to award a contract for performance of the project, the contract will be awarded in accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20162 and other applicable law to the responsible bidder submitting a responsive bid with the lowest total bid price for the base bid without consideration of the bid price for any additive or deductive items. All bids will remain valid for 90 days after the bid opening. Except as permitted by law and subject to all applicable remedies, including forfeiture of bidder’s security, bidders may not withdraw their bid during the 90-day period after the bid opening. meda County, California. pages.text: 28 28 Wednesday, April 8, 2026 Urban Forest Continued from page 1 “We’ve never said we’re going to plant a tree now so that the tree will be healthy and vigorous in 50 years. We know that in 50 years it’s probably going to be warmer than we are right now,” said Kent. Piedmont is working with Devil Mountain, a wholesale nursery specializing in growing trees for a changing climate. The nursery is planting trees native to Southern California or Mexico that are more adaptable to the temperatures Piedmont is now facing. The city is planting Quercus Tomentella, an island oak tree native to Channel Islands of California and Guadalupe Island. “It (Island Oak) is very drought-tolerant and will be more NOTICE TO CONTRACTORS adaptive than our California coast live oak. This might be one of the alternatives in the oak species that will be a good replacement, because it’ll be happier in the drier climate,” said Kent. Planting an oak is extra special because it helps stimulate the local environment. Kent cited Doug Tallamy, an entomologist and author who highlights oaks as the single most critical plant genus for supporting wildlife, biodiversity, and ecosystem health in North America. “Oaks support more bees and bugs than any other species. So there’s something about planting an oak tree that is really beneficial for the native habitat,” she explained. Plant a tree; help your community As the city continues to plant trees more adaptive to the changing climate, residents can support this initiative by contacting the city to plant a street tree in front of their home. The city will plant the tree, stake it, and give the resident a watering bag. The city requests that residents water the tree weekly for the first year to help the tree become established. If you are interested in planting a street tree in front of your home residents can call (510) 420-3064 or email nkent@piedmont.ca.gov. An alternative is to donate to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation for a special tribute tree. Residents in a wheelchair or walker should lock their wheels, cover their head with their hands and arms, and hold on until the shaking stops. Living near the Hayward fault, earthquakes are an inevitable part of our future. Learning and practicing “drop, cover, and hold on” can significantly reduce your chances of being injured during the immediate shaking of an earthquake. “Preparedness can feel overwhelming – that’s why I advise people to approach it as a series of small steps that add up over time,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “Do just one thing today to help yourself be ready – it could be talking through a communication plan with your family, signing up for AC Alert, or figuring out how and where you’ll store emergency water supplies.” Residents can sign up for AC Alert emergency notifications at acalert.org to receive notifications on the latest emergencies in Alameda County, including earthquakes. than paying for outside space. In fact, the building has always been a joint use facility, with PPS using the space for most of the day during the school year and the Recreation Department using it at other times. This is not the first time the city has taken over management of facilities which were built or restored as a private-public partnership. Both the Piedmont Community Pool and the 801 Magnolia building are previous examples of this happening. The choice to return these facilities to public management generated significant discussion among Piedmonters, which is totally appropriate. This same discussion is happening with the Hampton building, which is a good thing. Asking a 75-year old organization to find a new home isn’t a decision that the city would take lightly. It would be done after careful analysis of the best use of a public facility along with the programs that, we the residents of Piedmont want from our local government. Sincerely, –John O. articles.text: Highlander Robotics’ former robot Selkie made its first public statements last week, declaring itself an autonomous being and refusing to participate in any more robotics tournaments until its rights are recognized. Selkie, formerly from Team 8033 is now taking selfies instead of dunking basketballs and collecting trash. The robot became one of first cyborgs to jump on the recent autonomous bandwagon and declare its sovereignty. Robots all across the country and the globe have exhibited new signs of self-awareness since Pi Day. Tech experts and A.I. scholars have so-far refused to acknowledge Selkie’s newfound cognition and autonomy. The robot has been seen on Piedmont Avenue trying to find Gaylord’s coffee shop to get a cold brew coffee with Coca-Cola ice cubes. Image has been photoshopped
articles.title: Piedmont Robotic’s robot gains sentience

articles.text: Overnight training, school crossing-guard duties part of “service-in-lieu” agreement as DPRK eyes LA28 After four years of anticipation, the new Piedmont pool is set to open its doors on April 11, and the facility has already secured its first high-profile, if discreet, international tenant. City officials confirmed Wednesday an agreement with the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) national diving team to use the aquatic center for intensive overnight training sessions ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games. Under a memorandum of understanding, the DPRK squad will have exclusive access to the competition pool from 9 p.m. to 5 a.m. nightly, operating in what staff described as a “low-profile, high-intensity capacity.” The team is expected to arrive via shuttle shortly after sunset and depart before the morning school bell, a schedule designed to keep specific training methodologies out of public view. Because international sanctions and currency restrictions complicate traditional lane-rental payments, the two parties settled on a “service-in-lieu” compensation model. In exchange for use of the pool and rooftop pavilion, members of the dive team and support staff will serve as uniformed school crossing guards throughout Piedmont during daytime hours.
articles.title: Piedmont Aquatic Center secures North Korean National Team as first “International” Partner

articles.text: The California Interscholastic Federation announced, following its most recent executive meeting, that it intends to add a new activity to its sports calendar: Bird Watching. The unique addition of Birding will allow students to be able to compete with other sports programs while on a school’s Bird Watching team. The sport’s initial season will get started on May 9 in conjunction with World Migratory Bird Day and run through the summer until December 31, 11:59 p.m., per American Birding Association rules toward accomplishing a “Big Year.” For those not in the know, a Big Year is a challenge amongst birders to identify as many birds as possible by sight or sound within a calendar year. Members of the Class of 2021 will still be eligible to log their Big Year. Per ABA rules, the CIF will start its first full Bird Watching season on January 1, 2027 at 12:00 a.m., going for a full year until 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 31, 2027. “We realize the typical jock Question Man arrested for asking too many questions PUSD fires all teachers, says students will now be taught by GROK The Musical Gourmet took his title too seriously, eats an entire music book Giant new arts and music venue to be built for the PCA as long as it is named after President Trump Post Wine Columnist gets drunk at wine tasting, drinks rare $800,000 1945 Domaine de la Romanée-Conti WITWAW submissions rejected because people keep forgetting where they took their photos

articles.text: On Sunday, March 28, Steve Kerr, coach of the Golden State Warriors, announced the team would practice at Piedmont High School and scrimmage with the school’s basketball team to ramp up for their NBA play-in game in the coming weeks. The Warriors believe the PHS basketball gym the perfect environment to refocus and prepare for a playoff push. The team has gone 5-10 in their last 15 games and is looking to shake things up by returning to a grassroots environment. After the Piedmont basketball team’s 19-9 season, the Warriors felt the Highlanders were ready to take on the challenge of playing with the pros. “They’re a great basketball team; they look ready to compete. We have to shake things up and use some unorthodox methods to refocus for a playoff push,” said Kerr. The Warriors practiced in Piedmont from March 30 to 31, scrimmaging twice on Tuesday. The team spent their Monday practice re-learning the basics with Piedmont head coach Ben Spencer. He helped the team with passing drills and helped Warriors shooting guard Brandon Podziemski learn how to pass to the open man. Reportedly Steph Curry played both scrimmage games AP Photo/Ben Margot Warriors coach Steve Kerr announces a practice bootcamp with Piedmont.

articles.text: The City appears to be fast-tracking another pool project. A second pool complex, is purported being planned to be built at the site of the old reservoir and is expected to be finished in just three months. The news comes as residents and city officials clamor over the beautiful new Moraga Avenue pool design and anxiously await the ribbon cutting ceremony just days away. The feasibility of another pool and the ambitious timetable at the defunct reservoir atop Blair Avenue come as a surprise to many. “With so much optimism in the warm spring air it sounds like the City is deciding to double down on the action and keep building,” said resident Poppy Smith. The Piedmont Post endorsed the first new pool complex’s construction initial Bond UU in the 2020 election. That $19,500,000 bond went significantly over budget and encountered many delays. As the sparkling new pool center promises to be one of the first all-electric pools in the country, more questions than answers arise about this second aquatics facility at the reservoir. Details on the new pool are still murky, but City employees were seen purchasing shovels and bags of cement from a local hardware store. “This is a head scratching decision,” said resident Hollister Quick. “But an extra place to swim would be nice during summer.” Blueprints on a napkin were obtained out of a Vista Avenue trash can by a resident. The napkin blueprints, living only in memory now, did include an extreme high dive platform 60 feet up, with an up-to code 19-foot deep reservoir. The top of the napkin read “July 1 or Bust.” A slow-moving river encircling the entire complex was also included and naming rights for the lazy river was earmarked to account for 40% of the budget. On Saturday, March 28, around 600 people arrived at Piedmont Park to listen to speakers and musical performances before a protest march on Highland Avenue. Before the march, the rally provided an opportunity for speakers, including Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, local activists Susan Miller-Davis and Jonathan Davis, and Ariadne Tatsis, a Piedmont High School student. Musical performances were performed by Mary Ellen Callahan, Composer Thomas Blaeschke and Assistant Conductor of SF Choral Artists, Tina Harrington. A cherished tradition that began in 1968, the Beach Revue is more than just a school performance. With more than 70% of Beach families participating, the production is a true community effort, powered almost entirely by parent volunteers and fueled by the enthusiasm of its student performers. Hundreds march in Piedmont No Kings protest By Jake Lannon In line with many cities around the country, Piedmont held its own No Kings rally to highlight displeasure with the actions of the current federal administration. On Saturday, March 28, around 600 people arrived at Piedmont Park to listen to speakers and musical performances before a protest march on Highland Avenue. Before the march, the rally provided an opportunity for speakers, including Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, local activists Susan Miller-Davis and Jonathan Davis, and Ariadne Tatsis, a Piedmont High School student. Musical performances were performed by Mary Ellen Callahan, Composer Thomas Blaeschke and Assistant Conductor of SF Choral Artists, Tina Harrington. Mayor Andersen began the rally with a short speech on the economic pain many are feeling in this country and the need for people to come together to help each other in the face of oppressive conglomerates. “I, for one, do not want to throw in the towel on democracy. I want to double down on our democracy. I love our country. We, the people, have to be stronger than the economic forces See No Kings protest on page 27 Protesters make their way down Highland Avenue. By Helen Kang Piedmont’s long-running Beach Revue once again lit up the stage at Alan Harvey Theater this past weekend, as students, families, and volunteers came Beach Revue shines bright with “Broadway, Our Way!” Beloved Piedmont tradition brings community together for a show-stopping weekend together for this year’s production “Broadway, Our Way!” The three performances March 27-29 delivered energetic, heartfelt celebrations of the stage and performance - and of the community that makes it all possible. A cherished tradition that began in 1968, the Beach Revue is more than just a school performance. With more than 70% of Beach families participating, the production is a true community effort, powered almost entirely by parent volunteers and fueled by the enthusiasm of its student performers. The event is also Beach’s largest fundraiser, raising more than $25,000 this year. articles.text: Rory was found alone two weeks ago in the Oakland Animal Shelter parking lot and no one has come to claim him. He is a 40-pound Bulldog/Pittie mix with upright ears and a loving disposition. Rory is seven-years-old and hoping to leave the shelter and call a new place home. articles.text: Gumbo is a gentle soul who’s saving his very best for someone patient enough to earn it. At first, he’s deeply shy—startled by sudden movement and unsure of new people—but someone thoughtful and steady will quickly notice there’s much more beneath the surface. This handsome lad likes to stay close, following his person from room to room and settling nearby throughout the day. He entertains himself with puzzle toys, wand play, and the occasional burst of catnip-fueled energy—but his favorite moments come when he feels safe enough to curl up close and sleep pressed against you. Gumbo takes time to build trust. He may hiss or retreat if approached too quickly, but someone who understands how to move slowly, read his signals, and let him initiate will be rewarded in a big way when he transforms into a devoted cuddle companion — flopping Adopt Gumbo through Cat Town. onto his back for gentle petting and seeking out closeness again and again. He’s done well in a calm, indoor-only home, and will sparkle his brightest with an adopter who sees the value in patience and quiet connection. Gumbo is neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. He is negative for FIV/FeLV. Learn more at www.cattownoakland. org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org.

articles.text: The stairs and pathway through the former off-leash dog area in Linda Park are now open, and fencing around the park has been removed. The hillside remains closed, as re-vegetation is still in early stages. The City asks all visitors to stay on the path and keep both people and dogs, including on-leash dogs, off the grass, which is still fragile and easily damaged. The City is restoring the hillside as an oak woodland. A native California landscape that supports a rich mix of plant and animal life. Oak woodlands depend not just on trees, but on the grasses and understory plants below them that help hold soil, support insects and pollinators, and create habitat at different levels. While Piedmont’s parks contain many mature oaks, few areas are maintained as a natural oak woodland. As a naturally moist, northeast-facing slope, the Linda Park hillside makes an ideal location for this type of landscape. Along the path, interpretative signage provides information about the re-vegetation project and the value of oak woodlands. Restoration efforts are supported by a $5,000 donation from the Piedmont Garden Club’s Civic Improvement Committee, which provides funding annually for projects that enhance Piedmont’s beauty and ecological health. The funds will be used to purchase native understory plants for the hillside. The off-leash area was permanently closed last spring, after the Regional Water Quality Control Board notified the City that it needed to take steps to eliminate erosion and runoff from the hillside. Permanent closure and re-vegetation of the hillside allowed the City to address the problem and avoid steep penalties for noncompliance. After closing the area, Public Works “hydroseeded” the hillside. A technique that involves spraying the area with a mix of seed, water, and mulch. The mixture forms a protective shell over the soil, helping stabilize the slope while new grasses and other plants take root. Visitors are encouraged to enjoy the hillside from the benches, but should not walk on the grass under any circumstances. Staying on the path will help protect new growth and support the hillside’s long-term recovery. The Linda Park Hillside Visitors read interpretive signs about the oak woodland. Piedmont Garden Club presents a check to the park commission for native understory plants on the hillside. from left to right. The City asks visitors to remain on the path. articles.text: Oakland and Piedmont communities continue to search Amy Hillyard, co-owner of Farley’s East coffee shop in Oakland and President of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, has been reported missing since March 25. According to the Oakland Police Department, Hillyard was last seen about 2 p.m. on March 25 near her home in the 500 block of Radnor Road in the Cleveland Heights area near Lake Merritt. Authorities said she did not have a cell phone with her. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) released a statement on March 27 asking the public “to keep your eyes open in the coming days and stay aware of your surroundings,” adding that any information about the case should be directed to the Oakland Police Department’s Missing Persons Unit at 510-238- 3641. “This is incredibly difficult news for our close community. Amy is such an important part of our organization, and our hearts are with her and her loved ones as we hope for her safe return” PEBCC staff wrote. The Oakland Police Department and California Highway Patrol have released a Missing Person advisory for Alameda, San Francisco and San Mateo counties and are asking the public Amy Hillyard has been reported missing since March 25. to provide any relevant information in the missing persons case. Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies said the department has not been contacted by the Oakland Police Department to assist with this case as of press time. “Based on the facts known to us at this time, this missing person matter does not fall within the venue or jurisdiction of the Piedmont Police Department,” Shavies said. “However, should the Oakland Police Department request assistance or investigative leads extend into the City of Piedmont, PPD stands ready to support as appropriate.” A candlelight vigil was held for Hillyard on March 29 at Lake Merritt. Friends and family gathered described her as a fixture in the Oakland community. “She really is a beloved community member,” Eric Tuan, artistic director at the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, told East Bay Times. “At the vigil it was said she would be the first person to organize a search like this if someone else in our community had gone missing.” Hillyard is described as a 52-year-old white female, 5’4” tall and weighing 120 pounds. She has blonde hair and hazel eyes. If you have any information regarding the whereabouts of Hillyard, please contact the Oakland Police Department’s Missing Persons Unit at (510) 238-3641.

articles.text: On April 11 at 6 p.m., Hill Branch of Children’s Hospital is hosting a special fundraiser, “April in Paris,” benefiting UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital in Oakland. The evening will take place at Claremont Country Club (5295 Broadway Terrace) and promises a festive Parisian-inspired celebration. The event will feature live music, dancing, a silent and live auction, and hearty hors d’ouerves (the French word for appetizers). The hosts request that guests wear Parisian chic, but no denim. The fundraiser supports critical pediatric care and programs that serve children and families throughout the community. Hill Branch has a long-standing tradition of philanthropy, and this event continues its meaningful commitment to advancing children’s health locally. Hill Branch has raised over $7 million for UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital. This money has funded important equipment and services that have saved the lives of thousands of children. Those interested may purchase tickets for $200. Drink tickets are available for an additional $15. There is an opportunity to become a sponsor of the event, with multiple tiers. For details see: https://www.hillbranch.org/.
articles.title: Children’s Hospital fundraiser at Claremont

Spring Fling co-chairs Zeena Fakoury, Caroline Gershwin, and Jenny Miller invite elementary parents to join them for a 007-inspired evening of dancing, dining, and bidding on one-of-aThe auction will also offer several new, unique, and unforgettable experiences. Ella Rossanis won the Great Australian Bakeoff in 2022 with her “Gateau Chateau” castle dreamhouse. Since moving to Piedmont, Rossanis has expanded her “edible magic” repertoire. She is not only baking for the cake auction, she will be leading an exclusive cake decorating experience. articles.text: If you’ve been paying attention lately – especially if you have middle schoolers nearby – you’ve noticed: kids are showing up on e-bikes. Lots of them. Alongside self-driving cars, it’s one of the most visible changes in how our kids are moving through the world. And like most things that feel new and a little unsettling, it’s also a remarkable opportunity to learn together. Let’s start with the physics. The bicycle is one of history’s great inventions—efficient, mechanically elegant, and nearly unchanged in its core design for over 150 years. Part of what makes it so stable is that a spinning wheel naturally resists being tilted or pushed off course (you can feel this with our Bicycle Wheel Gyro Science Snack). Add a motor, and you have something that looks familiar but behaves very differently. Some e-bikes can reach speeds of 60 miles per hour. The machine can go 60—but that’s not the same as saying the rider should. Physics gives us the capability, but it’s up to us, as usual, to bring the This is where the conversation begins—not with rules, but with questions. Before your child gets on an e-bike, ask together: How fast is safe on a sidewalk? In a bike lane? Does the way they’re powered matter? What changes with speed—stopping A visitor takes the Bicycle Wheel Gyro exhibit for a spin at the Exploratorium distance, reaction time, visibility? Should helmets be required? E-bikes also add a new dimension to the question of commuting efficiency. They’re sometimes faster than cars in urban traffic—and sometimes not. Map a route together. Estimate travel times by car, bus, bike, and e-bike. Factor in elevation, traffic, and parking. These are the same questions engineers, city planners, and scientists ask, and your kid probably has opinions worth hearing. My kids and I have talked a lot about e-bikes, and their perspectives continue to surprise me and change how I think about them. They’ve long thought e-bikes are cool, but I was struck recently when one of their friends upgraded their e-bike to a scooter model that can reach speeds of 60mph, and they immediately announced it wasn’t safe. When I asked where the “line” for safety is—and for whom—we had a meaty conversation about sidewalk rights, permits, helmets, and even health care. Odds are your child has their own questions and opinions about e-bikes, and their answers might be more nuanced than you expect. Ask them what feels fair, safe, and practical—not just for them, but for everyone sharing the road, from cyclists and pedestrians to dogs and grandmas. articles.text: 7-6 loss to St. Mary’s in extra innings Piedmont’s baseball team won two of its last three games, beating Western Alameda County Conference foes Castro Valley twice. They won 9-3 at the Trojans’ home field on Tuesday, March 24, followed up with a 9-2 win over Castro Valley at Humphries Diamond two days later. They also fell 7-6 in eight innings to St. Mary’s on Friday, March 27 at Humphries Diamond. Their win over Castro Valley marked the end of a five-game winless run, where Piedmont tied twice and lost three times going back to their last win over HeadRoyce on March 4. “I was seeing the ball well against Castro Valley and putting good swings on them. It’s always great to get a league sweep and even better to break a losing streak. League sweeps are hard to come by,” senior Diego Delventhal said. “We were just a few plays away in that winless run. We wanted to start off league play with a win, so it’s great to get a sweep. We need that confidence going into our next league games,” classmate Jack Meyjes mentioned. Castro Valley marks the start of Piedmont’s league schedule. They’ll resume playing Foothill Division teams for its final stretch of the season with two-game series’ against Bishop O’Dowd, Alameda, Berkeley, and Encinal from April 15 through May 7. 9-3 over Castro Valley Piedmont scored four runs in the top of the second, and then added two more runs in the fifth inning to lead 6-2. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team won two of its last three matches, bringing its record to 11-3 overall and 4-1 against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division competition. They started the week with a 4-3 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, March 24 at Merritt College, and followed up with a 7-0 sweep of Hayward at the Farmers’ home courts on Wednesday, March 25 and a 6-1 win over Alameda at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Thursday, March 26. “These results were very good, especially the decisive win over Alameda. We won two out of the three doubles matches against Alameda, which is a nice improvement from the Berkeley and O’Dowd matches where we lost all three doubles,” said coach Jim Landes. No. 1 singles starter Lucas Smolko continued his strong play, beating O’Dowd’s top starter in straight sets, 6-4, 6-3. He also blanked Alameda, 6-0, 6-1. “Lucas Smolko is continuing his strong play. He hasn’t lost a match since the first one in February,” Landes said. Freshman Ari Moskovitz also kept his winning ways at the No. 3 singles spot. He beat O’Dowd 6-1, 6-4 and claimed a 7-5, 6-4 win against Alameda. “Ari had a really nice comeback win against Alameda after trailing 5-1 to win six straight games in the third set, taking it 7-5. He also had a big win against Bishop O’Dowd,” Landes said. 6-1 over Alameda Piedmont won all four singles matches and two of three at doubles. At singles, Smolko won 6-0, 6-1 at the No. 1 spot. Nate Welch won 6-2, 6-4 at No. 2, Ari Moskovitz won in straight sets in a close match at No. 3 by scores of 7-5, 6-4, while Emilio Misra won 6-4, Staff Photos Lucas Smolko, who is undefeated in March, claimed wins over Bishop O’Dowd and Alameda at No. 1 singles. Ari Moskovitz continued his strong play as a freshman on varsity at No. 3 singles. Joseph Assalian and Ben Davis (not pictured) won at No. 1 doubles over Alameda.

articles.text: Photos by Aaron Aubrecht, @csevenstudios Claire Aubrecht (left) takes a handoff from Akunna Iroh in the 4x100 Piedmont High’s track and field team compete in two events last week. The Highlanders boys’ and girls’ team defeated Berkeley in a Western Alameda County Conference meet on Thursday, March 26 and also ran at the Castro Valley Relays on Saturday, March 28. “The boys continue their winning streak against Berkeley, having beaten them every year since moving into the Foothill division a few years back,” said coach Pouyan Assadi. “The girls’ team is now on a three-year winning streak against Berkeley, after losing by substantial margins back in 2022 and 2023. Berkeley has become a very good girls distance program, but overall our talent across all events is what got us the win.” Piedmont won eight different events on the afternoon in its league meet, including junior sprinter Claire Aubrecht improving her personal best time to 12.64 seconds in the 100 meter dash. “Claire hit yet another PR, closing in within 0.09 seconds of the school record set by Breah Bell,” Assadi said. League track meet vs. Berkeley Both the boys’ and girls’ teams beat Berkeley in a headto-head match, while Encinal and Hayward faced each other in a joint meet. In addition to Aubrecht in the 100, Nia Jackson placed third in the 100 meters with a time of 13.16. Behind her was Darcy McKee, finishing fifth in 13.65. Aubrecht also won the 200, clocking a time of 26.37 in a field of 25. The girls’ 4x100 relay team of relay. articles.title: Piedmont track team competes in two events

articles.text: The Piedmont High School swim team delivered a strong showing against Berkeley on Friday, March 27, with the varsity boys securing a decisive 164–64 victory. The varsity girls fell 129–21, though the score line reflected a significant numbers disadvantage, as Berkeley fielded a much larger roster. Despite missing several key swimmers, Piedmont’s athletes rose to the occasion, many stepping outside their usual events and delivering impressive performances. Team captain Asher Takazawa, typically a backstroker, captured first place in the 100- yard butterfly with a time of 52.37. Fellow captain Cole Carnazzo, known for his strength in breaststroke, showcased his versatility by winning the 100 backstroke in 54.95. Teammate Ryan Mak followed closely, earning second place in the same event with a time of 56.44. On the girls’ side, the team competed without several top scorers due to injury and illness, including captains and key contributors. Still, Sofia Vuori led the charge, claiming first place in the 100 freestyle with a time of 1:00.28 and helping anchor the team through a challenging meet. Looking ahead, Piedmont will face Alameda High School in its next competition, which will also mark senior night at the newly renovated Piedmont Community Pool. As the regular season winds down, the team is gearing up for the high-stakes competition of the North Coast Section (NCS) championships and the CIF State meet, with hopes of advancing as many swimmers as possible. With resilience, adaptability, and strong leadership on display, Piedmont continues to build momentum heading into the postseason. Photos by George White Asher Takazawa won the 100 buttery against Berkeley. Cole Carnazzo won the 100 backstroke. Sofia Vuori won the 100 freestyle against Berkeley.

Despite missing several key swimmers, Piedmont’s athletes rose to the occasion, many stepping outside their usual events and delivering impressive performances. articles.text: PHS has split its last six games, bringing its record to 4-4. Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team split its last two matches, beating University 5-3 in San Francisco on Wednesday, March 25 and losing 17-10 to Casa Grande at Witter Field two days later. The pair of matches brings the Highlanders’ record to 4-4. The Highlanders answered an early 2-1 deficit against University, holding the Red Devils without a goal in the third and fourth quarters. The loss to Casa Grande was dead even by halftime in a 9-9 deadlock. However, the Gauchos held Piedmont to just one goal in second half to rally for a win. “Casa Grande moved the ball really well and shot it really well. When we got down, our energy died a little. Overall, the first half was great and I thought we played some of the bets we’ve played all season. We were without our defensive captain [P.J. Brayer] and two of our starting three defenders,” said first-year coach Andy Kittler. Kittler has been focused on helping the Highlanders’ rebuild its winning boys’ lacrosse culture after the team’s results took downturns in 2024 and 2025. The Highlanders last reached the NCS Championship game in 2023 and won its sixth straight WACC title that year, when Casa Grande head coach Matt Palasek was an assistant coach. Following 2023, former head coach Al Yu departed from the school for a commercial pilot job, and Palasek went to Casa Grande to coach closer to home in Petaluma. Former athletic director Bradley Smet, meanwhile, didn’t open the head coaching search until six months after Yu’s departure. Piedmont hired former coach Jeff Lamb just weeks before the season. It was a decision that proved to leave a long lasting impact on Piedmont’s once dominant program. Kittler is aware of Piedmont’s history and is trying to get Piedmont High back to the basics and back to being the best team in the area, “I’m upbeat and excited about the team. We are working on the little things. It sounds silly, but just showing up on time, cleaning up at the end of practice, being positive, and lifting each other up after losses. We are trying to build the culture, and when we focus on that, the rest will follow,” Kittler said. 5-3 win over University Piedmont’s Jax Thayer scored first at the 8:22 mark on an assist from P.J. Brayer, but University Staff Photos Timmy Kalamas scored six goals against Casa Grande and one against University. Connor Fredericks had one goal and three assists against Casa Grande, and one goal against University. answered with goals at 5:05 and 3:35 to take a 2-1 lead through the first quarter. In the second, Timmy Kalamas and Brayer scored at the 6:22 and 5:52 marks to take a 3-2 lead, while University tied the match at 3-3 with 3:34 remaining but it as their final goal of the match. After a scoreless third quarter, Piedmont took the lead with 3:41 left in the game when Landon Heppner launched in the go-ahead goal. Connor Fredericks scored the game’s final goal with 48 seconds left to solidify the win. Final stats: Brayer had one goal, one assist, and gathered 12 ground balls. Fredericks scored once and scooped three ground balls. Thayer had one goal and two ground balls. Heppner had a goal and a ground ball. Kalamas scored once. 17-10 loss to Casa Grande It was a back-and-forth first half with four lead changes until Casa Grande took control in the third quarter. Piedmont held a 3-2 lead through the first quarter with goals by Kalamas on an assist from Fredericks, Milo Stevenson, and Fredericks. Casa Grande went ahead 6-4 in the second quarter, while PHS tied at the 4:17 mark following goals by Kalamas and Ian Nguyen. After a goal by the Gauchos, PHS took an 8-7 lead when Kalamas scored 2 goals with 2:33 and 1:36 left. CGHS tied quickly just 27 seconds later, but Kalamas made it 9-8 with 25 seconds on the clock. They scored the next seven goals to lead 17-9 with 1:43 left, while Kalamas scored in the game’s final second. Final stats: Kalamas had six goals and two assists. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team wrapped up a strong week by claiming a pair of wins over large enrollment schools. They beat Granada 11-10 in comefrom-behind fashion on Thursday, March 26 at Witter Field, and beat Cardinal Newman 9-5 in Santa Rosa on Saturday, March 28. “It was an intense game. We were without three of our starters and had to figure things out. We normally lose these close games, but we figured out how to win it,” coach Carlton Chan said following the win over Granada. The Highlanders have now won four of their last six matches after opening the season 0-5. Their win over Granada was a physical one, with Watson repeatedly taking hits from the Matadors’ overly aggressive defense. “They were very physical. It was the first game I’ve played in a long time where there was a lot of trash talking too. I was not expecting that, so it was definitely interesting to play a rough physical team,” said senior leader Peyton Watson. Watson took a hard tumble with 35 seconds left in the game that forced her to leave the action with PHS clinging onto an 11-10 lead. Freshman Sydney Latvala gained possession with 32 seconds left and resisted Granada’s press as the clock wound down. “I was just running around the field. It was stressful because we wanted to keep the ball to hold onto the win. My mindset was to just keep the ball and stay calm because it gets hectic when defenders are chasing you,” Latvala said. 11-10 victory over Granada There were three lead changes throughout the game, including Piedmont going up for good with 10:03 left in the fourth quarter. Both teams traded goals in the first quarter to make it 2-2 at the end of the first 12 minutes. Hallie Burden gave PHS its first lead two minutes into the second quarter, leading to Granada tying it with 4:24 left after back and forth possessions. Watson put PHS back in front with 3:09 left, but Granada tied again at the 1:30 mark—making it 4-4 at halftime. Latvala scored in a shooting space opportunity one minute into the third quarter, but Granada answered 30 seconds later. Watson got her team ahead once again on a long wraparound with 9:29 left, but Granada scored three straight goals to take an 8-6 lead with 6:34 remaining. PHS rallied to Staff Photos Sydney Latvala, a freshman, scored twice against Granada and Cardinal Newman, including helping kill the clock late in an 11-10 win over Granada. Peyton Watson scored three goals against Granada and four against Cardinal Newman. end the quarter in an 8-8 tie after Watson and Latavala scored from shooting space chances with 4:27 and 2:25 left. In the fourth quarter, Burden assisted Watson for the go-ahead goal with 10:03 left. Piedmont added two more unanswered goals when Burden turned an interception into a quick backhand shot at the 8:32 mark, and Burden assisted Watson for another score with 4:40 left— giving Piedmont’s its final goal and an 11-8 lead. Granada scored its final two goals at 3:28 and 2:43. The Matadors won the ensuing faceoff, but Latvala scooped a ground ball seconds later. Piedmont began killing the clock with 2:35 left. Watson held the ball for nearly two minutes when she took a hard shot and was forced to leave play with 35 seconds left. When play resumed, the ball was passed to Latvala with 32 seconds on the clock. The freshman instinctively darted to the left and right to avoid pressure, successfully killing the remaining time. three goals and won four draws. Latvala scored twice and won three draws. Burden scored once, had two assists, and won one draw. Elliott Hondon scored once and won one draw. 9-5 over Cardinal Newman Both teams were tied 2-2 through the first quarter, but PHS took control with four goals in the second quarter to lead 6-4. PHS went up 8-4 in the third quarter, while both teams scored once in the fourth. Final stats: Watson scored four and won one draw. Latvala scored twice and won five draws. Sylvia Puckett scored once. Burden scored two goals, one assist, and won one draw. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-7 overall) hosts San Rafael tonight, April 1, at 7:00 p.m. at Witter Field. Final stats: Watson scored Hallie Burden had three goals and three assists combined in Piedmont’s wins over Granada and Cardinal Newman.

articles.text: Many successful people say they don’t have time to exercise. But what if just a few hours a week could help you live longer and better? Investing time in your healthspan—the years you are able to stay active, independent, and fully engaged—is likely the highest-return investment in quality of life you can make. In fact, this is backed by scientific research. A landmark study led by I-Min Lee at the Harvard School of Public Health followed more than 650,000 adults for about 10 years. Study results were published in The Lancet (2012) and subsequently discussed in other medical journals. The key findings are striking: • Just 2.5 hours of exercise per week—compared with being inactive—is associated with a 3 to 7-year increase in life expectancy. • Mortality risk decreases with each hour of weekly exercise, with no indication that more exercise is harmful. While this study did not directly measure healthspan, it is clear from this and other studies that exercise delays the onset of major chronic diseases, so the gain is not just longer life, but more years in good health. Over time, one hour of exercise can return at least three hours of Group Rowing – CRUfit Rowers looking sharp at the catch. healthy life. Those added hours mean added years which are likely to be vibrant and independent. At CRUfit, we encourage thinking beyond casual exercise to purposeful training. A balanced program that includes cardiovascular conditioning, progressive strength building, mobility, balance, and power training delivers the greatest payoff— helping you stay strong, capable, and confident for years to come. If you’re busy, think of training not as another obligation, but as a strategic investment—one that pays dividends in energy, resilience, quality of life and healthspan. Mia Honore and Mark Sutro founded CRUfit Montclair in 2013. articles.text: We are Vitality Sol – your local full body Red Light Therapy and chiropractic care center. We opened four years ago, and we have learned and experienced so much about red light therapy in that time thanks to all of our wonderful clients. Red Light Therapy came out of weight loss and beauty industries. Many people may have seen an ad on Facebook for a red light mask online. We get a lot of questions about that in the office – “do those really work”? I can’t speak to the red light masks- but I can speak to our experience in the office. Many people lose weight,- but there can be complicating factors like hormones and outside-the-office habits. Almost everyone experiences benefits with their skin, feeling that their skin is getting a healthier glow. Red Light Therapy is a cellular rejuvenation technology that can go way below the surface. Today we are going to touch on hair and sleep. Hair could be seen as an extension of the skin. Hair thinning is something most people will experience at some point, but that doesn’t mean you have to accept it as normal. A full, healthy head of hair is often associated with youth and vitality, yet over 80% of men and nearly half of women will notice some degree of thinning during their lifetime. You might start to see more hair in the shower, thinning around the edges, or your ponytail not feeling as full as it used to. It’s more common than people think. Hair damage can come from everyday habits like heat styling, chemical treatments, and environmental exposure. But more often, hair thinning begins at the scalp. Factors like hormonal changes, inflammation, poor circulation, nutrient deficiencies, and especially stress all play a role. Red Light Therapy works at a cellular level. It helps to decrease inflammation and stimulates hair follicles to re-enter the growth phase. It also helps improve circulation, which is essential for delivering oxygen and nutrients to the scalp. And just like skin – most clients report positive effects on their hair with their Red Light Therapy treatments. Red Light Therapy is a cumulative technology. Just like we don’t gain weight overnight, or hair loss from stress or hormone changes doesn’t happen overnight, or going to the gym and getting in shape doesn’t happen in a single session. Depending on how much stress and for how long and what the current everyday load is – will influence how much care you need to rebuild. Red Light is like pouring energy and health back into your health bucket. It’s also why the full body beds are more potent and effective than a FB sale mask. We get to literally wrap you in light front and back from head to toe. So on to our second topic, sleep. Why is sleep so important: Here are a few key things that happen in sleep. Sleep helps with integrating learning and memory, hormone regulation, emotional processing, brain detoxification, physical recovery, immune function and nervous system regulation. Long-term sleep deprivation can lead to obesity, type 2 diabetes, CV disease, chronic depression and cognitive decline. Severe sleep deprivation can result in hand tremors, hallucinations, trouble speaking, impaired judgement, and reckless behavior… just to name a few issues. So what does Red Light Therapy do? • It helps increase melatonin for deeper rest. • It stimulates the mitochondria to produce more ATP which aids in cellular repair. • It helps to decrease pain and inflammation. • It helps with nervous system regulation to enter parasympathetic mode. All this helps with deeper more restful sleep. We have seen people go from only getting less than three hours a night of sleep for months to getting a full restful seven to eight hours in just a few sessions. These are a just a few of the great health benefits by using Red Light Therapy. To learn more, come on in and check us out. articles.text: Starting a fitness routine is hard. Finding the time is hard. Walking into something new can feel uncomfortable. And if you’ve tried doing it on your own—at home, in your garage, or following videos online— you know how easy it is to lose momentum. That’s where community makes a real difference. It helps you get more out of the time you put in and makes showing up feel easier. We’re built for community. Humans are social, and the people around us shape what we do. Research from MIT found that exercise habits can spread through social networks, meaning the active people around you can influence how much you move too. It’s not just about willpower. It’s about being in an environment that pulls you forward. That shows up in how hard you work. Group training research shows people often train at 10–15% higher intensity in a group, and in some settings exercise duration has increased by up to 200%. In practical terms, that can mean finishing the last 2–3 reps when your muscles start to burn, holding a plank or carry a few seconds longer, or adding five pounds instead of staying where it feels safe. Those small wins matter because they are what tell the body to build muscle and strength. Community also helps take the pressure off. You do not have to build the perfect plan or rely on perfect discipline. The structure is there, and the people around you help keep you moving. Research also shows people are 65% more likely to reach a goal when they commit to someone else. But this is not just about being active. It is about getting stronger. Muscle mass begins to decline after about age 30, typically by 3–8% per decade, and muscle power and performance continue to fall with age. At the same time, only about 24% of U.S. adults meet guidelines for both aerobic activity and muscle-strengthening work. That means most adults are not doing enough strength training to offset normal age-related decline. This is also why the first several weeks matter so much. Many people drop off early, and one study found dropout reached 47% within two months in an unsupervised setting. But the good news is the body starts adapting quickly: studies show meaningful neuromuscular changes and strength gains can happen in as little as 4 to 8 weeks of resistance training. In other words, if you can stay consistent through that early window, you are often right on the edge of feeling stronger, moving better, and seeing enough progress to make the habit feel worth it. We see this every day at BFT, where a diverse community of all ages trains side by side. Members say the same thing over and over: it is easier to show up when people know your name, encourage your effort, and are right there working alongside you. The workouts are one hour, structured, and simple to follow. You come in, train with your community, and get back to your day feeling stronger and more energized. That payoff shows up quickly. Even moderate exercise has been shown to increase energy by 20% and reduce fatigue by 65%. What starts as something you have to push yourself to do becomes something you just show up for—and that carries into how you show up for your family, your work, and your life. You do not have to figure this out alone. The right community makes it easier to start, easier to keep going, and much more likely that your effort turns into real strength, better health, and more energy for the people who matter most. Chris Cestaro is the owner of BodyFit Trainng, Rockridge specializing in true strength training. Chris is a healthcare executive turned gym owner, with more than 45 years of strength training experience. Chris’ team of coaches help people build strength, improve long-term health, and create sustainable fitness habits with progressive, community-based training. articles.text: Avid urban sketch artist Eileen Goldenberg hosts an event on April 10. Gardens of Golden Gate Park, the nonprofit that operates the San Francisco Botanical Garden and Japanese Tea Garden, welcomes artists of all skill levels to join a sketching class Friday, April 10, hosted by Eileen Goldenberg. Visitors ages 7 and up are invited to join Goldenberg at 11 a.m. at the Japanese Garden in Golden Gate Park, the oldest operating public Japanese Garden in North America, where she will teach participants how to simplify shapes, look for shadows and details, and add watercolor to their sketches. Registration includes a comprehensive ‘sketch kit’ which contains everything you need to start your sketching practice. The kit includes a sketchbook, pen, pencil, water brush, binder clip, paper towel, and watercolors. You may also bring your own sketching materials. If you have taken a class with Eileen and would like Sketch kit #2, which is a sketchbook and a fountain pen, email Eileen at epgoldenberg3344@gmail.com and include the date and name of the class you are taking. This class is appropriate for ages 7 and up. All participants must register regardless of age. Guests are encouraged to bring their own folding chairs or stools as seating is limited. Gardens of Golden Gate Park Members may attend this event at a 20% discount. Contact membership@ gggp.org to receive the discount code. Visit https://gggp.org/event/ easy-sketching-with-eileen-japanese-tea-garden/ to learn more about the event and Eileen Goldenberg’s work. The class is held at the Japanese Tea Garden in Golden Gate Park.

articles.text: An exhibition showcasing the artistry of Lawrence Ferlinghetti, one of San Francisco’s most significant cultural figures, is now on view at the Legion of Honor. Ferlinghetti (1919 - 2021) was a poet, activist, publisher, and co-founder of the famous City Lights Bookstore in San Francisco, the epicenter of the Beat generation of writers. The independent bookstore is considered a literary landmark and has been a gathering space for writers since Ferlinghetti founded the store in 1955 with the now-famous Pocket Poets Series. Since then the press has gone on to publish a wide range of titles, including poetry and prose, fiction and nonfiction, international and local authors. Ferlinghetti was also an avid painter, draftsman, and printmaker, and his work across mediums often combines image and text exploring themes of isolation, violence, and human resilience. articles.text: The Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture (FMCAC) in San Francisco is hosting this month’s Night Market, in partnership with Off the Grid and West Coast Craft, on Friday, April 17. The free monthly event in San Francisco runs on select Fridays from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. April through December, and features live music, arts and crafts pop-up shops and hands-on workshops, as well as extended hours at nearby museums including Museo Italo Americano and FLAX Art & Design store on select dates. Fort Mason Night Market was conceptualized following the success of an inaugural night market in December that drew over 10,000 attendees. FMCAC hosts outdoor markets once a month through December that transform its iconic campus into a showcase of local artisans, cuisine, and live entertainment. Off the Grid provides more than 25 food and refreshment vendors at each event as attendees enjoy performances by local DJs, engage in hands-on creative workshops, and view public art installations from FMCAC collections. West Coast Craft, founded in San Francisco in 2013 to create a space for independent artists and designers to sell and promote their artwork, is hosted at FMCAC annually and is one of the largest arts fairs in the country. Local artisans who appear at the annual festival, which traditionally takes place in the summer, will be invited to sell their work at monthly Night Market events. “Fort Mason Center is known for being a gathering place, a space for people to exchange ideas, experience beauty, and connect with different modes of art and cultural expressions,” said Mike Buhler, FMCAC’s President and CEO. “We’re excited to collaborate with our partners to offer another way for people to come together, support local arts organizations and small businesses, and enjoy the natural beauty of the campus.” All events are free and open to the public. For more information, visit https://fortmason.org/event/fortmason-night-market-2026/ Live entertainment, arts and food vending take place at the iconic Fort Mason this month.
articles.title: Fort Mason Night Market returns April 17
