articles.text: Left Coast Chamber Ensemble is a consortium of 17 Bay Area musicians. The Left Coast Chamber Ensemble (LCCE) will hold its annual gala at 3 p.m. Sunday, April 12, at the Women’s Faculty Club on UC Berkeley’s campus. The 2026 gala marks the organization’s 33rd season and raises support for its artistic and educational programs. The afternoon event will feature Maurice Ravel’s Piano Trio by Anna Presler, Tanya Tomkins, and Eric Zivian. Hors d’oeuvres, wine and dessert will be served. Guests may participate in live and silent auctions featuring arts experiences, wine selections and concert tickets. Auction items include a one-year membership to the Doug Adams Gallery, Center for the Arts & Religion at the Graduate Theological Union, two tickets to a show at the West Edge Opera 2026 Festival, and more. Founded in 1992, Left Coast Chamber Ensemble is a consortium of 17 Bay Area musicians known for presenting thematic chamber music programs that pair contemporary compositions with traditional repertoire. The ensemble performs a wide range of classical music, including chamber, vocal, orchestral and multimedia works, with an emphasis on connecting music of the present with influences from the past. In addition to its concert series, the organization commissions new works, sponsors an annual composition contest and maintains education programs designed to broaden access to contemporary classical music for diverse audiences. To learn more about the 2026 gala, and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.leftcoastensemble. org/2026-gala.
articles.title: Left Coast Chamber Ensemble hosts annual gala April 12

articles.text: Opera San Jose closes its 2025/26 season with Verdi’s classic opera La Traviata, premiering Sunday, April 19. La Traviata is an opera in three acts by Giuseppe Verdi, based on the novel La Dame aux Camélias by Alexandre Dumas fils. Opera San Jose’s production includes Mikayla Sager, most recently seen cast as the company’s Mimìs in La Bohème, as Violetta and former Opera San Jose Artist-in-Residence WooYoung Yoon as her young lover. Opera San Jose’s Former Conductor in Residence Johannes Löhner returns to make his principal conducting debut with inaugural Director-in-Residence Tara Branham returning to direct La Traviata. Set in 19th-century Paris, it tells the tragic love story of the courtesan Violetta Valéry and the young nobleman Alfredo Germont. After meeting at a party, Alfredo confesses he has long loved Violetta. Though ill with tuberculosis and accustomed to a life of luxury and independence, she eventually falls in love with him. The two leave Paris to live together in the countryside. Their happiness is disrupted when Alfredo’s father, Giorgio Germont, asks Violetta to leave Alfredo. He argues that their scandalous relationship threatens his family’s reputation and his daughter’s marriage prospects. Mikayla Sager, most recently seen cast as the company’s Mimìs in La Bohème, is cast as Violetta in Opera San Jose’s production of La Traviata. Sacrificing her own happiness, Violetta secretly agrees and returns to her former life without explaining why. The opera will be performed onstage April 19 through May 3. Doors open 90 minutes before the performance, 12:30 p.m. for matinees and 6:00 p.m. for evening performances May 1and 3 performances will be conducted by Conductor-in-Residence Noah Lindquist. A preshow discussion is held at 1:00 p.m. for matinees and 6:30 p.m. for evening performances. The organ player will be performing 30 minutes before curtain. Visit https://www.operasj.org/ productions/la-traviata to purchase tickets. ®
articles.title: Opera San Jose closes season with La Traviata

articles.text: Free shows in Oakland, SF, Emeryville San Francisco Opera’s popular Bohème Out of the Box returns to the Bay Area this month, with free outdoor performances of an abridged version of Giacomo Puccini’s La Bohème at select locations in San Francisco, Emeryville, Oakland, Woodside and Concord. Launched during San Francisco Opera’s centennial season in 2023, Bohème Out of the Box is designed to bring opera beyond traditional venues and into neighborhoods throughout the region. Since its debut, the production has toured the cities of Alameda, Albany, Hayward and Los Gatos, as well as corporate and community sites across Silicon Valley. The one-hour production, performed on a converted shipping-container stage with piano accompaniment, opens April 11 and 12 at Crane Cove Park in San Francisco. Presented in Italian with live English translations available on mobile devices, the cast includes current and former Adler Fellows Alexa Frankian as Mimì and Edward Graves as Rodolfo, joined by Eugene Brancoveanu, Sofia Gotch, Gabriel Natal-Báez, James McCarthy, and Olivier Zerouali. The production will then travel to Christie Park in Emeryville on April 18, Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts in Oakland on April 19, Filoli Historic House & Garden in Woodside on April 22 and Todos Santos Plaza in Concord on April 25 and 26. Families are invited to attend free workshops 30 minutes before each performance, offering children an introduction to opera through movement and storytelling centered on Puccini’s music. Admission is free and seating is first come, first served. Registration is encouraged for most venues and required for the Woodside performance. Visit https://www.sfopera. com/seasons/opera-out-of-thebox/ for more information and to register. Admission is free and seating is first-come, first-served.

articles.text: What constitutes the main event? While you are pondering this question, let’s consider it. The concert on Saturday in the Piedmont Center for the Arts was a benefit concert for the East Bay Center for the Blind. Judging by the size of the crowd, the concert was an overwhelming success. It was a “Schubertiade” because it featured the music of Franz Schubert. Concerts are something like boxing matches. There are the preliminaries and then comes the main event. The preliminary event on Saturday was a youthful work by Schubert, the “Sonatensatz.” Even though Franz Schubert was one of the greatest child geniuses of all time, this particular work was inconsequential. We were told that the composer wrote this piece when he was very young. There are many better works from the pen of the youthful Schubert. The performance featured pianist Ayaka Isono, violinist Maki Ishii and cellist Thalia Moore. I must say it was a rather lackluster warm-up, even though it was well played by the musicians. Then the floodgates opened and we were treated to one of the greatest compositions of all time - Schubert’s monumental Quintet for Strings. The featured players were violinists Maki Ishii and Michael Long, violist Paul Ehrlich, and cellists Victoria Ehrlich and Thalia Moore. Even though Beethoven had been dead about one year, he still towered over all of the musicians in Vienna. Schubert was in his shadow. In Italy, Paganini was creating a sensation on his violin. Schubert admired Paganini above all composers and that’s why he chose to make his first concert outside of Italy in Vienna. It was his idea to visit Beethoven and ask him to write a “Storm” for him. The concert was arranged but Paganini was very disappointed that Beethoven had died the previous year. Needless to say, Paganini’s concert in Vienna was sensaSaturday’s concert in the Piedmont Center for the arts was a Schubertiade devoted to the music of Schubert. The musicians are Victoria Ehrlich (left), Paul Ehrlich, Michael Long, Thalia Moore, Mahi Ishii and Ayaka Isono.

English composer Alice Verne-Bredt’s Phantasie Trio unfolds in shadowy textures and dramatic surges. French virtuoso Cécile Chaminade brings brilliance and turbulence in her first piano trio, showcasing the virtuosity of each performer. In her Piano Trio in D minor, Fanny Mendelssohn balances stormy urgency with luminous lyricism. The music will be performed by musicians Nigel Armstrong, Brady Anderson, and Jon Lee. Each piece is guided by a distinct muse: the Hindu concept of darshan, a secret love, misty Appalachian landscapes, a child lost too soon, and three iconic Mexican women whose lives shaped a nation. articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Piedmont Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month, offering a great movie in a comfortable setting, followed by a lively discussion. The Flix Fest April selection is an Academy Award-winning book-tofilm adaptation of the 1922 novel by Elizabeth von Arnim titled Enchanted April. The movie will be screened on Thursday, April 9, at the Piedmont Center of the Arts on 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 3:45 p.m., and the movie is free for anyone 18 years or older. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis and can bring snacks. The movie’s opening scene takes us to post-WWI London on a dreary, rainy day, when Lottie Wilkins (Josie Lawrence) spots a newspaper ad advertising a castle in Italy with ‘sunshine and wisteria’ available to rent for the month of April. Seeking an escape from her loveless marriage and mundane life, Lottie invites her friend, Rose (Miranda Richardson), to join her in renting the Castello San Salvatore above the town of Portofino. To share the castle’s expense, Lottie and Rose invite a socialite, Lady Caroline Hester (Polly Walker), and aging dowager Mrs. Fisher (Joan Plowright), to join them in this ladiesonly adventure! The castle’s stunning scenery and the beauty of its lush flora enchant the women and help them begin a process of rediscovery. Lottie and Rose invite their husbands to join them, and each enjoys a renewal of their marriage that had atrophied in London. Lady Caroline escapes the obsessive male attention of her privileged social life and finds true romance from her surprising connection to the castle’s owner. Lastly, Mrs. Fisher finds wonderful friendships with each of the other women, helping shed her preoccupation with her Victorina past. In the movie’s last scene, she gives an emphatic symbol for this change when she drives her walking stick into the muddy path, leaving it and her past behind. The next movie will be Ramen Girl, a 2008 comedy to be shown on May 14 at the normal time of 1 p.m. Polly Walker in Enchanted April.

The next movie will be Ramen Girl, a 2008 comedy to be shown on May 14 at the normal time of 1 p.m. Why commands fail— and how to fix them By Sierra Berrick Many pet owners experience the frustration of investing time and effort to teach their dogs a series of commands, only to find they do not achieve the desired response. Perhaps your companion wags politely and stares at you without complying. Or perhaps they offer a different behavior in hopes of earning praise. Several common training errors account for this, and with modest adjustments, you can restore reliable responses. The most frequent cause of disobedience of known command is excessive repetition by the owner. For example, if a dog fails to sit on command, the owner may repeat, “sit, sit, sit,” which renders the cue meaningless over time. Do not issue a command you are not prepared to follow through on. State the cue once. If the dog does not comply, give a clear verbal negative marker to communicate the refusal is incorrect. If the dog continues to ignore the command, insist on completion: guide the collar up under the chin to lift the nose and lower the rear to the floor, thereby shaping the sit. Again, avoid repeating the word. A second common pitfall occurs when frustration takes over. Consider a dog who does not come when called. The instinct may be to scold once they arrive. Do not. However long it takes, when the dog complies, mark the behavior with verbal praise or a reward. Positive reinforcement at the moment of success is essential for repeating the behavior on cue later. Finally, ensure expectations are reasonable. Practice makes perfect! If a command is not rehearsed regularly, irritation is unwarranted. Introduce new cues with patience in short, focused sessions. Infrequently used commands require the same approach; a dog may need a moment to recall a cue that has not been practiced. In short, the handler’s approach determines the dog’s response. Patience during instruction, accountability for known cues, and consistent reinforcement will maintain a healthy bond and clear behavioral expectations. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com. articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group had a record 73 walkers and four K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday for its weekly walk. The reason for the big turnout was the opportunity to have a tour of the new Piedmont Pool, which opens to the public on Saturday, April 11. The pool starts a new chapter in the history of places where Piedmonters have swam. Some walkers thought this history starts in 1964 when the former community pool was built. However, it actually goes much further back and was not always as nice as the new pool. The story starts shortly after the first European settler, Walter Blair, came to the area in 1852. He created a quarry in what is now Dracena Park to extract stone that was used to pave Oakland and Piedmont’s early streets and railways. In 1873, his crew struck water from a subterranean creek, and it turned the bottom of the quarry into a lake about 60 feet deep. Attempts to pump the water out failed and the lake became an occasional swimming hole for Piedmont boys. Sadly, there were multiple drownings in it. One was in 1888 and another in 1895. The quarry was finally fenced and locked. For more than 40 years “Blair’s Pond” existed with ducks. The City finally drained it and turned it into a recreational grass field in 1997. A second early Piedmont swimming spot was Tyson Lake. In 1914 James Tyson, a successful lumber and shipping businessman, bought 30 acres of Piedmont land to build his mansion at the top of the Glen Alpine Road/Sotelo Avenue loop. Tyson had three sons and dammed a small creek that ran through his property to create a reservoir that became a swimming hole for his sons and neighborhood boys. Tyson was a supporter of the new Piedmont Boy Scouts Council and made the lake available for scouts to earn their swimming merit badges. In the 1930s Tyson transferred the title of his lake to a homeowners association and the lake later became an attraction for local teenage boys. In 1949 four of them were caught swimming nude in it and each fined $25. Tragically, a 17-year old boy drowned there in 1951 and a 19 year-old did too in 1952. From the 1940s through the 1960s Piedmont residents swam at local natural springs, pools at Oakland clubs like the Athens Athletic Club and the Claremont Country Club, as well as at regional swim clubs and recreational parks. Some Piedmont youth learned to swim in backyard pools that were being built during this period. Under a later lease in effect from 1993 to 2008, the club paid $38,500 in annual rent to the city. Throughout this entire period, the club was responsible for all pool expenses including the original construction, capital improvements, and routine maintenance. From 2008 to 2011 the City granted a three-year lease extension that waived the annual rent to help the club remain financially viable. However, maintenance expenses became increasingly difficult for the club, and the City took over operations in 2011 following disagreements with the club over the lease renewal. In November 2020, Piedmont voters passed a $19.5 million Measure UU bond to build a new facility. The old pool was drained and demolished in September 2021 to make space for it. Since 2021 the City has planned and built the new, all-electric aquatics center that meets its sustainability goals. The total cost of the new complex is now approximately $35 million and is the largest capital project in the City of Piedmont’s history. This final amount is significantly more than the original project budget of $28.9 million that was approved before construction began in early 2023. The project was primarily funded by Measure UU, which ultimately provided approximately $25.2 million because of favorable interest rates and credit ratings. The nearly $6 million budget gap between the initial construction estimate and the final cost was driven by several unexpected issues. Two old buried fuel tanks and soil contaminated with naturally occurring arsenic were discovered and the site had to be remediated. The City decided to use electricity to power the facility, and additional costs were incurred to create what is the second all-electric municipal pool complex in California. There were also significant delays caused by severe winter weather and utility coordination with PG&E. Finally, there was a 32% spike in the California construction cost index between the initial 2020 estimate and the start of construction in 2023. To cover the additional costs, the City utilized a total of nine different funding sources. Over $2.1 million in private donations was raised by the Piedmont Recreation Facilities Organization and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. Funds also came from the City’s Facilities Capital Fund and State clean energy grants and a zero-interest loan from AVA Community Energy was obtained. A shallower activity pool has three 25-yard lap lanes and will be for kids and swim lessons. Its temperature will be 83 to 85 degrees. The larger, 27-meter competition pool has 12 lanes that start at seven feet of depth and are 12.5 feet at the diving well. Its temperature will be 79 to 80 degrees. articles.text: James Suckling’s tasting featured over 200 wineries from around the world. San Francisco’s wine scene took center stage on March 8, 2026, as internationally renowned critic James Suckling brought his “Great Wines of the World” tasting tour to the city’s scenic Fort Mason Center. The event, part of a three-city U.S. series, served as a vibrant finale and drew wine professionals, collectors, and enthusiasts from across the country. Held at the Gateway Pavilion overlooking San Francisco Bay, the tasting offered a sweeping snapshot of the global wine landscape. More than 200 producers poured over 400 wines from 35 regions, spanning Bordeaux, Burgundy, Tuscany, and Piedmont, alongside top estates from California, Oregon, and Washington, as well as emerging producers from South America. The event’s format encouraged both discovery and dialogue. Attendees moved through a lively walk-around tasting, sampling wines that had all received 92 points or higher, including numerous bottles rated close to perfection. The opportunity to speak directly with winemakers and estate owners added depth to the experience, transforming it from a simple tasting into a forum for exchange about vintages, vineyard practices, and global market trends. With approximately 2,500 attendees at the San Francisco stop, the event highlighted the Bay Area’s importance as both a cultural hub and a key market for fine wine. Beyond the numbers, however, the tasting reflected broader industry conversations – how to engage new consumers, sustain interest in premium wines, and navigate a changing global marketplace. Ultimately, the March 8 tasting was more than a showcase of exceptional bottles. It was a celebration of wine as a global language – one that connects regions, traditions, and people. Under Suckling’s curatorial eye, San Francisco once again proved itself a vital crossroads for the world of wine. This was a tasting of wines that had already shown they were winners, but at any large tasting like this, some wines that stand out at the end of the day – wines you do not forget. The wines reviewed below are those unforgettable wines. They are the Cream of the Cream of the crop. The tasting filled the Grand Pavilion at Fort Mason in San Francisco.
articles.title: James Suckling’s Great Wines of the World tasting

articles.text: • 2023 Willamette Valley Vineyards Pinot Noir Founder’s Reserve One of the finest Oregon Pinots I have tasted, the Willamette Valley Vineyards Founder’s Reserve, has enticing aromas of cherries, raspberries, pomegranates, fresh herbs, sweet oak and forest floor that sashay out of the glass. The mid-palate is silky and direct, quickly gaining momentum, power and delineation. Equal parts fresh and tenacious, this has immediate appeal while displaying all the hallmarks of a long life in the cellar. Stellar juice! • 2021 Stanton Petite Sirah Napa Valley (Great Value) I recently had a 15-year-old bottle of this wine that was stunning - a baby with years ahead of it. Petite Sirah used to be widely planted in Napa Valley but has mostly been budded over to Cabernet Sauvignon. Kudos to Stanton for preserving these wonderful old vines. Aromas of smoke, cedar, black pepper, leather and blackberry inform the nose of a smooth, textured, dense, full-flavored offering that conceals enough structure to evolve for another two decades. This impeccably balanced, lengthy Petite Sirah is a stunning example of how well this varietal does in California. • 2021 Bonterra Cabernet Sauvignon “The McNab” This enchanting Cabernet hails from The McNab Ranch in Mendocino County, one of the first organic vineyards planted in the United States. It is located in a beautiful box canyon near Ukiah with flowing streams and grazing sheep. It shows fresh notes of cassis, cherries and chocolate on the nose. It’s medium-bodied and supple with great finesse and layers of zingy blueberry fruit. Refreshing and light on the palate it makes you want to pour another glass. The quintessential food wine it would pair well with meats, cheese or pasta.

Full-bodied, round, lush and juicy on the palate, with great finesse and stimulating salinity on the elegant finish, this is a dense, sensual Chardonnay that should drink well over the next 5 years. • 2023 Firetree Fidem Chardonnay This Chardonnay from the Carneros AVA has inviting aroOregon’s Willamette Valley Vineyards Pinot Noir was outstanding. mas of peach, beeswax, flint and well-integrated oak spice. The medium-bodied palate has a silky texture and concentrated, layered flavors. It’s balanced by bright, energetic acidity and has a long, succulent finish. • 2023 Pahlmeyer Chardonnay Napa Valley The Pahlmeyer Chardonnay has expressive scents of melon, hazelnut, lemon, nectarine and flint. The full-bodied palate has an elegant texture and is bursting with spicy fruit. It is beautifully balanced and has a long fragrant finish. Perfect partner to roast chicken. Red Wines • 2023 Willamette Valley Vineyards Pinot Noir Founder’s Reserve One of the finest Oregon Pinots I have tasted, the Willamette Valley Vineyards Founder’s Reserve, has enticing aromas of cherries, raspberries, pomegranates, fresh herbs, sweet oak and forest floor that sashay out of the glass. The mid-palate is silky and direct, quickly gaining momentum, power and delineation. Equal parts fresh and tenacious, this has immediate appeal while displaying all the hallmarks of a long life in the cellar. Stellar juice! • 2021 Stanton Petite Sirah Napa Valley (Great Value) I recently had a 15-year-old bottle of this wine that was stunning - a baby with years ahead of it. Petite Sirah used to be widely planted in Napa Valley but has mostly been budded over to Cabernet Sauvignon. Kudos to Stanton for preserving these wonderful old vines. Aromas of smoke, cedar, black pepper, leather and blackberry inform the nose of a smooth, textured, dense, full-flavored offering that conceals enough structure to evolve for another two decades. This impeccably balanced, lengthy Petite Sirah is a stunning example of how well this varietal does in California. • 2021 Bonterra Cabernet Sauvignon “The McNab” This enchanting Cabernet hails from The McNab Ranch in Mendocino County, one of the first organic vineyards planted in the United States. It is located in a beautiful box canyon near Ukiah with flowing streams and grazing sheep. It shows fresh notes of cassis, cherries and chocolate on the nose. It’s medium-bodied and supple with great finesse and layers of zingy blueberry fruit. Refreshing and light on the palate it makes you want to pour another glass. The quintessential food wine it would pair well with meats, cheese or pasta. Bonterra’s “The McNab” Cabernet Sauvignon was one of the finest wines of the tasting. • 2023 Denner “Dirt Worshipper” This Paso Robles wine is mostly Syrah with a splash of Petite Verdot. The Dirt Worshipper is dark and concentrated, with a plush velvety texture and a sweeter fleshed-out nose. Black pepper, blueberry fruit and charred aromas mingle with notes of rye bread, giving the wine a Syrah identity that feels confident and complete. This wine just cries out for a grilled rib eye steak. • 2022 Gamble Estates Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve Napa Valley A beautifully proportioned Cabernet Sauvignon that boasts of seductive aromas of vanilla, cinnamon and clove allied to waves of dark cherries and blackberries. It’s full-bodied and concentrated but also delivers a wonderfully silky mouthfeel and tremendous length, supported by plentiful ripe tannins. • 2021 Ramos Pinto Quinta de Ervamoira This blend of native Portuguese varieties from the Douro Valley is tightly wound, powerful and yet gloriously fruity, both delicious and impressive. The lush blueberry fruit is mixed with hints of earth and leather with a lovely round mouthfeel. There are ample tannins on the long, savory finish. • 2023 Pine Ridge Cabernet Sauvignon Napa Valley Deep garnet-purple colored, the nose opens with profound notions of blueberry preserves, chocolate cake and black olives with hints of eucalyptus and fragrant earth. Full-bodied rich, ripe and concentrated, it has a solid structure of grainy tannins and a lively line of freshness finishing long and perfumed. • 2022 St. Michael-Eppian Sanct Valentin Pinot Noir Riserva Produced by the St. MichaelEppian Cantina in the Alto Adige See Wine Corner on page 25

articles.text: It was a warm, sunny March afternoon when Cub Scout Den 7, Pack 3 and parents set out into Henry W. Coe State Park on the thin dirt trail leading to our campsite. Our hefty backpacks held all our supplies for the next few days – tents, sleeping bags, food and water, first aid kits, pots, and camp stoves. It was hard, hiking with the heavy backpacks and it was easy to slip on some loose pebbles and lose our balance. Nevertheless, the hike was beautiful, with spectacular sights at every turn, like the bench overlooking a vast, majestic valley. Other times we were surrounded by towering trees. I felt so connected to nature. It was just us on the trail – nobody but ourselves and the trees. We had planned to stay at the Manzanita Point Group Camp, but once we got there we decided to keep hiking. Even with the filters that we brought along with us, the water in the nearby pond was too dirty to use. To get to the clearing where we would spend the night, we had to hike another mile and a half, cross a stream, and push through a few bushes. Some of us stumbled back down the thin poison oak-covered trail to the creek near our campsite to filter the water that we would use to cook dinner. After we had boiled the water, we poured it into bags of dehydrated food and waited. When we opened the dry food, it didn’t look very good. It was wrinkled and covered in powder, but with the water, suddenly it looked normal. The food wasn’t necessarily the best, but it was warm, and it filled us up. Because our food would be eaten by hungry animals if we left it out, one of the parents put it in a bag and hung it from a tree branch. Because they needed to be small and light enough to carry, our tents were a little cramped. Also, because we were so far away from our busy modern world, the animals were louder than I’d heard before. The next morning, after waking up and Piedmont Pack 3, Den 7 fifth graders and parents, at the end of their weekend backpacking trip in Henry W. Coe State Park. having breakfast, our group set out to China Hole to go swimming. The water was cold, but we got used to it quickly. One of us even found some small animal bones in the water. We noticed that there were some good skipping rocks, and so most of the time we were there we were skipping the rocks. We also found a piece of driftwood that worked better than most of the rocks. After getting out of the water we ate a meal of mainly snack food. We hiked back to our campsite and started stuffing our supplies into our bags to get ready to move. We had enough water to last the rest of our trip, and we wanted to make the final hike back a little bit easier, so we hiked up the hill to Manzanita Point campground, where we had originally planned to stay. One of the scouts brought a hammock which we tied between two trees and took turns swinging each other fast. After a relaxing night of stargazing, some of us brought out our lanterns to play card games at the picnic table. We retreated to our tents for the night. When we woke up, we had to pack again. We made our final hike back to our cars on a road instead of a trail and at one point, we were all tired of walking. When we got back to our cars, we took a picture with all our gear on, signaling the end of our backpacking trip. Even if there was some pain along the way, it was an amazing first backpacking experience. It was also our last trip as Cub Scouts, after all these years together we were splitting up and going our separate ways. I’m glad that we went out with a bang. articles.text: Hi all, It’s April, and as anticipated, our Spring Market in Piedmont is in full swing, showing signs of vibrant life, with several new listings selling shortly after their market debuts, some breaking records! MORTGAGE MONEY… Our “go-to” Mortgage Money Broker, BRADY THOMAS, LA SALLE MORTGAGE, has this to share this month: Earlier this year, mortgage rates briefly dipped below 6% for the first time in more than three and one half years. When that happened, many buyers who had been waiting on the sidelines, started shopping for homes again. Unfortunately the improvement did not last very long. Over the past month, mortgage rates have climbed back into the mid-6% range. A major reason is the recent conflict involving the US and Iran. When global tensions rise, energy markets often react quickly. Oil prices move higher, which raises concerns about inflation. Mortgage rates are closely tied to inflation expectations in the bond market. When investors believe inflation may increase, bond yields rise and mortgage rates usually follow, which is what we have been seeing over the past several weeks. Even with the recent rate increase, the basic housing picture has not changed much. Demand for homes remains strong in many areas, inventory is still limited, and many current homeowners today have significant equity in their homes, and very low mortgage rates. For now, the housing market continues to adjust to a “higher-rate” environment while buyers watch closely for signs that inflation and rate may stabilize again. articles.text: A veteran from USS Hornet, he served on ship as volunteer docent Joseph Leather, a long time Piedmont resident, passed away on March 14, 2026 in his home with his family by his side. Joe was born in Ecorse, Michigan on August 4, 1932. He enlisted in the Navy following graduation from high school and was stationed on the USS Philippine Sea and USS Hornet during the Korean War. While in the Navy he met his future wife on a blind date. They married on February 9, 1957, and shared 69 years together. Following his discharge from the Navy in 1956, Joe began working for United Airlines at the San Francisco Maintenance base. He began as a mechanic and went on to become an inspector and later supervisor in the engine shop. He enjoyed his work at United and dedicated 39 years to the company. Wilma and Joe visited England multiple times and traveled all around Europe and Japan as they visited their daughter and son-in-law who lived in multiple locations. When the USS Hornet was brought to Alameda to be restored, he immediately volunteered. He worked with the Duct crew repairing areas throughout the ship. As the ship opened to the public, he became a docent. He enjoyed giving tours and meeting people from different locations. Having served on the USS Hornet, the ship became his second home for 25 years. Working with other volunteers, he took great pride in bringing the ship back to life. He served on the Docent Board and contributed many hours to special events. He loved his ship and was proud of the role he played in preserving an important part of our history. Joe loved the outdoors and in the last few years he became an avid bird watcher. He enjoyed watching the birds build a nest in his bird house, and was quite excited about the eagles nesting nearby in the cemetery. He belonged to the Oakland Casting Club, Veterans of Foreign Wars, and United Retiree group. He Joe Leather, a veteran of the Korean War, died on March 14 at age 94. loved fishing and tying flies. A military graveside service was held on March 20, 2026, in Mountain View Cemetery. Joe is survived by his wife, Wilma, and daughters Carol Stellman and husband Robert; and Linda Collett and husband David. He is also survived by five grandchildren, Marie Stellman, Diana Stellman, Bradford Collett, Nathaniel Collett, Brenton Collett, and four wonderful great grandchildren, Charlie Collett, Oliver Collett, Henry Collett and Liam Collett. In lieu of flowers, he preferred memorial gifts to the USS Hornet Museum, P.O. Box 460; Alameda, CA 94501.

articles.text: As the April 11 opening of the new Community Pool nears, the City is adding more time-limited parking and increasing parking enforcement in the Civic Center. The goal is to keep short-term parking available for people visiting the pool and other Civic Center destinations, including City Hall, Veterans Hall, school sites, the Alan Harvey Theater, Piedmont Center for the Arts, and local businesses. Starting the week of April 6, parking on Bonita Avenue between Magnolia and Vista Avenues that currently is unrestricted will become time-limited, primarily 2-hour spaces. Some employee parking spaces on Magnolia Avenue are being converted to 2-hour visitor parking. Three new ADA parking spaces will be marked. Two in front of the pool entrance, and one in front of the Corey Riech Tennis Center. Cumulatively, these changes will more than double short-term parking along Magnolia, Bonita, and Vista Avenues with a total of 30 new time-limited spaces. The City will begin updating parking signage next Friday, April 3. Increased parking enforcement will begin the week of April 6. These parking updates are the first phase of a broad plan to improve the parking experience for Civic Center visitors. A second phase, planned for the summer, would convert Bonita Avenue between Vista Avenue and Oakland Avenue to one-way traffic (northbound toward Oakland Avenue). This would eliminate the school dropoff zone on Bonita and add additional ADA, time-limited, and employee parking spaces on the street. The City Council approved the parking changes for the Civic Center in May 2025 after several months of discussion. A community survey was completed by more than 500 residents. All the green curbed spaces on Bonita (diagonal and parallel) will become time limited parking - mostly 2 hours.
articles.title: More short-term parking in Civic Center ahead of pool opening

Cumulatively, these changes will more than double short-term parking along Magnolia, Bonita, and Vista Avenues with a total of 30 new time-limited spaces. The City will begin updating parking signage next Friday, April 3. Increased parking enforcement will begin the week of April 6. These parking updates are the first phase of a broad plan to improve the parking experience for Civic Center visitors. A second phase, planned for the summer, would convert Bonita Avenue between Vista Avenue and Oakland Avenue to one-way traffic (northbound toward Oakland Avenue). This would eliminate the school dropoff zone on Bonita and add additional ADA, time-limited, and employee parking spaces on the street. The City Council approved the parking changes for the Civic Center in May 2025 after several months of discussion. A community survey was completed by more than 500 residents. All the green curbed spaces on Bonita (diagonal and parallel) will become time limited parking - mostly 2 hours.

articles.text: Agape is a Greek word which means unconditional, sacrificial and selfless love. The meal will conclude with Communion. The cost is $20 for adults, $10 for children. Scan the QR code in the photo to register no later than Wednesday, April 1, 5pm. Good Friday, April 3, is observed with a traditional service of Tenebrae, the Latin word for “darkness”. The service begins at 7:30pm in the Sanctuary. This is a dramatic and moving ritual. As the story of Jesus’ path to death on a cross is read out loud, candles and lights are gradually extinguished, until the entire Sanctuary is in darkness, except for one candle. At the conclusion of the service, everyone departs in silence. Easter Sunday services, celebrating the joyous resurrection of Jesus three days after his crucifixion, will be held Sunday, April 5 at 8:30 and 10am. The services are identical and include liturgy, a sermon by Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted and special music provided by Dr. Stephen Main and the Chancel Choir. They will perform the spiritual Great Day arranged by Warren Martin a cappella and O Clap Your Hands by Dr. Main and written for choir, organ, brass and percussion with ancient text from Psalm 47. The 10am service will also be live streamed on our website at PiedmontChurch.org. You are most welcome to participate in any or all of these events. Maundy Thursday worship takes place at 6pm in Guild Hall during a family-friendly dinner called an Agape Meal. Communion is served by clergy, staff and lay leaders. Holy Week is the most important week in Christianity. It began on Palm Sunday, March 29 and will conclude on Easter Sunday, April 5.Midweek observances in preparation for Easter include Maundy Thursday and Good Friday. Maundy Thursday, April 2, remembers Jesus’ Last Supper with his disciples, when he called on them to “love one another” and instituted the sacrament of Communion. Unlike most services at Piedmont Church, Maundy Thursday worship takes place at 6pm in Guild Hall during a family-friendly dinner called an Agape Meal (pronounced uh-gah-pay).
